After not playing this game for a while- this is genuinely the most frustrating, disappointing game I have ever played. Don't get me wrong, the execution is done well in many aspects, I just don't think that it is a good  or fun video game.

You basically fight in a single lane, there is one, maybe two flank routes (if you're lucky). If you come across a character that hard counters you, you die, if you run into someone with their ult, you die, if you are not glued to the ass of a healer, you die. You are taking damage for literally most of the game, and a good portion of the attacks are either completely unavoidable (why are there so many fucking hitscanners???), stun-lock you or do some other wacky particle effect AOE explosion bullshit fuckery, or just plain insta-kill you. The game literally just boils down to a numbers game- which team has the highest dps and the best healing, any actual mechanical skill comes secondary. Every game is a battle of attrition and momentum and there are almost no interesting 1v1 matchups or skirmishes. The fighting is 90% concentrated in one area.

Mindbogglingly, there are also no true pick (assassin) classes in the game, so if the other team is stomping and is constantly overhealed, there is literally nothing you can do. Compare this to TF2, where a single player can have massive impact if they are good enough, in Overwatch it feels like there's just nothing you can do if the other team has the upper hand. 

You move very slowly in this game, and most characters have extremely limited to no movement tech, so 1v1 match ups (which seldom occur), usually just boil down to which character counters which, so again, there are many instances where there's just nothing you can do even if you have perfect aim / movement.

Don't get me started on the particle effects. Somehow this game has a good art style but horrible visual clarity due to the amount of fucking particle effect attacks and visual noise on screen. Another thing that I have seen no one mention, is that most tanks in this game are MASSIVE, so if a friendly tank gets in front of you (which they will), you are effectively blind. In a game that mostly takes place around narrow choke points instead of wide open arenas, you can see how this can be problematic. I don't know what it is with modern games wanting to be as visually over-stimulating as possible over having actually good visual design.

The biggest mistake they made though, was balancing this game entirely around competitive instead of casual gaming. It just doesn't work. 

I wanted to like this game but I just can't, it's fundamentally incompatible with how I view a fun, balanced game.

⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ Overwatch – A Love-Hate Relationship

Overwatch is an amazing game. Beautiful heroes, satisfying abilities, incredible teamwork, and the unique experience of losing a match so badly that you start questioning your life decisions.

One minute you're feeling like an esports champion, the next you're respawning every 5 seconds wondering if your teammates are playing with their monitors turned off. 😂

Despite all the chaos, it's still one of the most fun competitive shooters out there. The gameplay is addictive, the heroes are unique, and landing a perfect ultimate combo feels better than winning the lottery.

What Blizzard Should Improve:

Matchmaking: Please stop putting five beginners against a coordinated team of professional aim trainers. Not every match needs to feel like the Overwatch World Cup.

Ranked System: Make ranks reflect actual individual performance and consistency. Winning or losing shouldn't feel like a coin toss.

Match Balance: One-sided matches aren't fun. Give us more competitive games instead of 10 minutes of emotional damage.

Servers & Ping: Improve regional matchmaking and server availability. Players outside Europe and North America deserve some love too.

Smurfing & Toxicity: Do something about smurfs, throwers, and people who think typing insults is a competitive ability.

More Communication: Give players better tools to coordinate without needing to become professional Discord administrators.

Final Thoughts

Overwatch is a masterpiece buried under a mountain of questionable matchmaking decisions.

I complain about it, I rage at it, I blame my teammates, and somehow I still launch it again the next day.

10/10 gameplay. 3/10 matchmaking. 100/10 emotional damage.

Wait a minute

To give Blizzard credit, the game has come a long way in the past year or so. They've added a ton of heroes, committed to frequent balance updates (something I desperately wish other games would do, *cough GW2 PvP cough*), and generally seem much more interested in keeping the game alive and evolving.

But tragically, they still can't get this freaking game right. At least not in ranked, if you're playing without a premade team.

To get teams that click repeatedly you need the stars to align. 

Blizzard wants to have its cake and eat it too. They want a game where individual agency is comparatively limited and teamwork is king, where players depend heavily on their teammates to capitalize on opportunities, cover weaknesses, coordinate engagements, and generally function as a cohesive unit.

It's like some sort of lovely Leninist utopia of video games where everyone works together for the greater good, everyone knows their role, and the collective triumphs over individual selfishness.

Except that's not how humans work.

People log into shooty bang bang games because they want to kill fools, do cool shit, and feel badass. Yes, some people absolutely love playing as a team, but expecting five random strangers to consistently function as an organized unit is a pretty enormous design assumption.

And yet Overwatch is built around that assumption.

If you're going to make a game this dependent on team coordination, then you need a matchmaking system sophisticated enough to accommodate this team dependence. You can't just assemble two teams of roughly equivalent skill ratings and assume they're going to function as coherent units.

Something has to give. Either matchmaking needs to do a much better job accounting for how players function together, or the game itself needs to give individuals more opportunities to make consequential plays without requiring their teammates to read their minds. Or both. 

What's worse than Blizzard's ranked experience is the community who conditions itself to take it like some sort of self flagellating nun. 

Overwatch players sometimes talk about ranked like it's some sort of Dark Souls endurance trial. Every miserable match is a lesson, every frustration is a personal failing, and the answer to everything is some variation of "skill issue bro, just improve your own gameplay."

Obviously individual skill matters. Obviously you can climb if you're consistently better than your rank.
But the ability to climb over hundreds of matches and the ability to meaningfully influence the match you're currently playing are two completely different things.


A player can deserve a higher rank, climb successfully over time, and still spend an absurd number of individual matches feeling like they're fighting their own team's inability to function rather than the opposing team.

A matchmaker can theoretically produce reasonably balanced win probabilities while still producing games that feel absolutely miserable to play.

And simply telling people to "get good" doesn't address that. It explains how to overcome the problem statistically over time. It doesn't explain why the problem should be so prevalent in the first place.

I don't need to win every match. I don't need perfect teammates. I don't even need every game to be particularly close.

What I want is to feel like my decisions, my mechanical execution, my positioning, and my ability to recognize opportunities have a meaningful impact on the outcome, even when my teammates aren't cooperating particularly well.

Ingredients for Beef Wellington:
a good beef fillet
(preferably Aberdeen Angus) of around 1kg/2lb 4oz
3 tbsp olive oil
250g/9oz chestnut mushroom
include some wild ones if you like
50g/2oz butter
1 large sprig fresh thyme
100ml/3.5 fl oz dry white wine
12 slices prosciutto
500g/1lb 2oz pack puff pastry
thawed if frozen
a little flour
for dusting
2 egg yolks
beaten with 1 tsp water

Step 1

Heat oven to 220C/fan 200C/gas 7.

Step 2

Sit the 1kg beef fillet on a roasting tray, brush with 1 tbsp olive oil and season with pepper, then roast for 15 mins for medium-rare or 20 mins for medium. When the beef is cooked to your liking, remove from the oven to cool, then chill in the fridge for about 20 mins.

Step 3

While the beef is cooling, chop 250g chestnut (and wild, if you like) mushrooms as finely as possible so they have the texture of coarse breadcrumbs. You can use a food processor to do this, but make sure you pulse-chop the mushrooms so they don’t become a slurry.

Step 4

Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil and 50g butter in a large pan and fry the mushrooms on a medium heat, with 1 large sprig fresh thyme, for about 10 mins stirring often, until you have a softened mixture.

Step 5

Season the mushroom mixture, pour over 100ml dry white wine and cook for about 10 mins until all the wine has been absorbed. The mixture should hold its shape when stirred.

Step 6

Remove the mushroom duxelle from the pan to cool and discard the thyme.

Step 7

Overlap two pieces of cling film over a large chopping board. Lay 12 slices prosciutto on the cling film, slightly overlapping, in a double row.

Step 8

Spread half the duxelles over the prosciutto, then sit the fillet on it and spread the remaining duxelles over.

Step 9

Use the cling film’s edges to draw the prosciutto around the fillet, then roll it into a sausage shape, twisting the ends of cling film to tighten it as you go.

Step 10

Chill the fillet while you roll out the pastry.

Step 11

Dust your work surface with a little flour. Roll out a third of the 500g pack of puff pastry to a 18 x 30cm strip and place on a non-stick baking sheet.

Step 12

Roll out the remainder of the 500g pack of puff pastry to about 28 x 36cm.

Step 13

Unravel the fillet from the cling film and sit it in the centre of the smaller strip of pastry.

Step 14

Beat the 2 egg yolks with 1 tsp water and brush the pastry’s edges, and the top and sides of the wrapped fillet.

Step 15

Using a rolling pin, carefully lift and drape the larger piece of pastry over the fillet, pressing well into the sides.

Step 16

Trim the joins to about a 4cm rim. Seal the rim with the edge of a fork or spoon handle.

Step 17

Glaze all over with more egg yolk and, using the back of a knife, mark the beef Wellington with long diagonal lines taking care not to cut into the pastry.

Step 18

Chill for at least 30 mins and up to 24 hrs. Heat oven to 200C/fan 180C/gas 6.

Step 19

Brush the Wellington with a little more egg yolk and cook until golden and crisp – 20-25 mins for medium-rare beef, 30 mins for medium. Allow to stand for 10 mins before serving in thick slices.

Played Hundreds of hours on and off since the 2016 beta (originally on PS4)
I’ve been around since the very beginning. Back during the 2016 beta, my internet was absolute garbage as i lagged constantly and avoided PvP games like the plague, but early Overwatch still managed to hook me. I loved the game around 2017, and I was even that unironic space nerd who genuinely loved Horizon Lunar Colony.

By late 2020, playing Tank completely broke me. 6v6 tanking felt like a second job, and seeing how 5v5 turned out, it’s just as miserable. The role is exhausting either way, so I walked away.

Recently, I decided to give it another shot. I figured the problem was how I was engaging with it, so I stripped away everything that caused friction:
 * Swapped to DPS exclusively; never touched Tank again.
 * Strictly Quick Play; zero Competitive.
 * Looked past the fact that the game somehow looks, sounds, and feels aesthetically worse than OW1.

I even committed to the whole "wholesome mental" approach. If someone was flaming, I’d tell myself, "They’re probably just having a rough day, keep the vibes positive." I tried to bring genuine casual empathy back into the lobby. I remember spotting an enemy player in Quick Play who was clearly brand new and hopelessly outmatched. After killing him twice, I purposely played poorly and let him kill me six times just so he could feel good, get a win, and not quit the game in frustration. We lost that match, but I walked away feeling good because another person actually got to have fun.

Then one day, reality hit me mid-match.
Why am I doing mental gymnastics and playing unpaid therapist just to tolerate a video game?

It’s Quick Play. It is supposed to be the casual mode, but every lobby is overrun by people sweating their lives away, refusing to hold back on clearly outmatched players, spamming "diff," and throwing tantrums before the first team fight even finishes. Modern PvP has turned into a miserable tabletop campaign: you sit down for a casual game of D&D, and some guy with an optimized min-max build sucks the life out of the room, ruins everyone's night, and calls you a loser for not tryharding.
Forcing yourself to babysit the emotional state of a lobby just to keep from tilting isn't gaming anymore, it’s emotional labor.

Mid-game, I just exited to desktop, opened the launcher, and clicked uninstall.

The relief was instant. No more babysitting miserable lobbies, no more sweating in casual modes, and no more pretending this game is still fun. Co-op and PvE games are just better; everyone gets to play, everyone gets to have fun, and nobody is optimizing the soul out of your evening.

If you find yourself constantly fighting your own brain just to survive a couple of matches, save your sanity and just delete it.

I've played PUBG since before its full release. I have over 4,000 hours on both accounts.

That number means something. It means I didn't just try PUBG and move on. I stuck with it. I came back to it. I played it through bad patches, bad performance, cheaters, bugs, questionable decisions, and years of frustration. A lot of those hours were with friends, especially over the last three years after taking a long break.

And honestly? That is the part that hurts.

Was PUBG good when it first came out? Not really. It looked rough, ran badly, and often felt like it was barely holding itself together. But it was fun. It had something special.

Did it get better when it went free-to-play? A little, maybe. But not enough. The bugs stayed. The cheaters multiplied. The game kept finding new ways to disappoint you. And still, I kept playing, because despite everything, I was having fun with my friends.

Over the years, I watched PUBG slowly turn more and more into a cash grab. Season passes, collaborations, skin boxes, endless cosmetics, monetization everywhere. The soul of the game started to feel buried under all of it.

But I still played.

Not because the game deserved endless forgiveness, but because the moments with friends were worth it.

Every few matches, you run into someone who is very obviously cheating. Not “maybe they’re just good” cheating. I mean the kind where everyone in the squad goes quiet because we all know exactly what just happened. Did that make me quit? No. We complained, we sighed, we queued again.

And the worst part? That anti-cheat still doesn't seem to stop the most blatant cheaters. But somehow the people ruining matches every day are still there.

I tolerated a lot.

Cheaters? Fine, queue again.

Bugs? Annoying, but whatever.

Bad performance? Been there before.

Greedy monetization? Disappointing, but not surprising anymore.

I kept making excuses for this game because I wanted to enjoy it with my friends.

But now I can't even reliably open it.

That is where it finally breaks me.

Sometimes I get lucky and reach the lobby. We queue, we play a match, maybe we win, maybe we lose. And then the real game begins trying to get PUBG to work again. My friends sit there waiting while I restart, relaunch, crash, fail to load, get stuck, or hope that this attempt will be the one that actually lets me back in.

Thirty minutes can disappear just trying to enter the lobby of a game that is almost ten years old.

And what makes it even worse is that this does not seem to be some brand-new, isolated issue. You can find people talking about this on Reddit, Steam, and other platforms for months now. Around three months of players reporting the same kind of problem, and still there has been no real acknowledgement.

Not a fix. Not a workaround. Not even a simple message saying, “Hey, we know something is wrong and we’re looking into it.”

Just silence.

That silence is what really kills any remaining goodwill. Bugs happen. Technical problems happen. But when a game has been around this long, and when players are clearly struggling just to launch and play it, pretending the problem does not exist feels insulting.

I play PUBG with my friend to relax my mind after a long day.

And somehow this game has managed to turn “relaxing with a friend” into a full-time anger management course.

Nothing is more peaceful than dropping into a city, spending 15 minutes looting, finding absolutely everything except the one gun you need, and then getting sent back to the lobby by a guy sitting in a bathroom since 2014.

The aiming system deserves a special award.
The aim does not aim.

You move your mouse 2mm and your crosshair decides to explore the entire map. Trying to control the aim feels less like playing a shooter and more like negotiating with a wild animal.

Enemy: standing completely still.
Me: 640 hours of experience.
My crosshair: “Interesting. I think I’ll look at the sky.”

And recoil? Absolutely beautiful. I shoot at someone and my gun immediately applies for a NASA internship.

The best part is when you finally get good loot, good positioning, full health, perfect attachments and enough confidence to believe you're actually good at the game...

BOOM.

Dead.

From somewhere approximately 17 kilometers away by a player whose entire strategy was apparently “sit down and wait for someone to have fun.”

Teammates are another amazing feature. My friend and I queue together for some peaceful gaming, only to spend the next 30 minutes arguing over who stole whose ammo, who drove us into a tree, and why neither of us has a first-aid kit despite looting an entire hospital.

Then comes the circle.

Because apparently walking peacefully toward the safe zone would be too enjoyable. Instead, the game watches you carefully calculate your route and says:

“No.”

Now you're sprinting across an open field while 14 people are shooting at you, your teammate is 800 meters away looting a frying pan, and your character has decided that climbing a tiny rock is apparently impossible.

Cheaters? No no, they're just incredibly talented professional athletes.

Getting one-tapped? Skill issue.

Bullets not registering? Internet issue.

Aim going everywhere except the enemy? Feature, not a bug.

Dying after 25 minutes? Free meditation session.

And somehow, after all of this, I still launch another game.

That's the real achievement of PUBG: making me hate the game while simultaneously making me press “Play Again.”

I don't play PUBG because it's relaxing.

I play PUBG because apparently my brain believes getting shot by a 14-year-old hiding behind a bush is cheaper than therapy.

Playing with my friend is the only reason this game survives on my PC. Without him, I'd probably uninstall it.

With him, I uninstall it, restart Steam, stare at the desktop for 30 seconds, and reinstall it.

10/10. Terrible game. Fantastic memories. Would suffer again.

# **PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS**

## 🎮 **My Experience**

PUBG is honestly one of the games I keep coming back to. The idea is simple: land, loot, survive, and be the last one standing. But somehow, every match turns into a completely different experience.

Sometimes you land in a busy place and immediately start fighting. Other times, you spend 10 minutes just looking for a decent gun, only to get shot by someone hiding in a random building. 😂

## 🔫 **The Gunplay**

I really like the gunplay in PUBG. The guns feel different, and you actually have to practice if you want to get better. You can't just run around shooting everything and expect to win.

There are times when you hit a really nice shot and feel like a pro, then the next game you can't hit anything. **That's just PUBG.**

## 👥 **Playing With Friends**

PUBG is way more fun with friends. Playing squads, talking on voice chat, making stupid decisions together, and somehow surviving makes the game really enjoyable.

The best moments are when your whole team is almost dead, you have barely any supplies left, and somehow you still manage to win the fight.

Of course, sometimes your friends are also the reason you lose. 😂

*"Don't worry, I got you!"*

**Dies 5 seconds later.**

## 🗺️ **The Maps**

I like that there are different maps to play, so the game doesn't always feel the same. You can choose to land somewhere crowded if you want action or go somewhere quieter and take your time.

The map also plays a big part in the game. Sometimes you have a great position, and sometimes the safe zone decides to spawn on the complete opposite side of the map. 😭

## 😭 **The Bad Part**

PUBG can definitely be frustrating.

You can spend a lot of time looting, get good weapons and equipment, survive several fights, and then suddenly get eliminated by someone you didn't even see.

And when you finally reach the top 10, your heart starts beating like you're playing for a million dollars.

Then you get killed.

Back to the lobby.

**"One more game."**

## 🏆 **Final Thoughts**

Overall, PUBG is a really fun battle royale, especially when playing with friends. It can be frustrating sometimes, but that's also part of what makes the good moments feel so much better.

Getting a Chicken Dinner after a long and difficult match is still one of the best feelings in the game.

**Would recommend.**

2300 hours, and I’m done.

I’ve played this game for over 2,300 hours, and it genuinely hurts to see what it has become.

Ranked has become increasingly difficult to take seriously because of the amount of blatant cheating. This isn’t just “closet cheating” anymore. You regularly encounter players using Aimbot, ESP/Wallhack, aim-lock, no-recoil scripts, and other obvious cheats.

I’ve seen players tracking enemies through terrain, snapping onto targets with Aimbot, landing completely unnatural long-range spray transfers, and even using Aimbot while driving at full speed.

You can spend 10 minutes rotating, positioning, and making smart decisions, only to have the entire squad instantly deleted by someone who isn't actually playing the same game.

And the punishment system makes the situation even more frustrating.

You get a notification saying a cheater was banned, but what does that actually accomplish when they can simply purchase another cheap recycled account and return to ranked almost immediately?

The legitimate players lose their RP, time, and motivation, while the cheater loses an account that costs almost nothing to replace.

That isn't an effective deterrent.

Meanwhile, KRAFTON continues releasing expensive skins and progressive gachas while the core competitive experience is being damaged by cheating.

I don't expect a perfect anti-cheat system. I understand that cheat developers will always try to stay ahead.

What I expect is a serious effort to protect the legitimate player base.

Detect cheaters faster. Make repeat offenders harder to return. Improve the ban system. And most importantly, stop making legitimate players pay the price for matches ruined by confirmed cheaters.

After 2,300 hours, this isn't a review from someone who simply hates the game.

It's a review from someone who wanted this game to succeed.

But right now, ranked feels less and less like a competitive shooter and more like a battle between legitimate players and whoever has the better cheat.

KRAFTON, fix the anti-cheat. Before you lose the players who actually kept this game alive.

[h1]A game that never reached it's true potential.[/h1]

This is easily one of the best games made in the past 10 years, with that said... 

Through poor management, cheating issues, poor optimization, scope creep, it failed in making a lasting impact in the gaming community. Yes, there is still an active community but there was a time where if this game had the attention it deserved it could have had the same legacy that counter-strike had with FPS competitive shooters, that's how good the concept was.

Somewhere in 2019-2020 there seemed to be a shift to prioritize micro transactions and the skin market, which basically turned the game into a cheap version of itself that felt more like an arcade shooter. Bunny ears and all. 

Then they launched the mobile version which sucked the soul out the game. More skins, micro transactions, simplistic gaming mechanics. The PC version started to feel more like the mobile version eventually.

New maps, game modes, weapons, etc... were delayed for way too long. Performance still felt sluggish even with multiple rounds of updates, it just never got that polished AAA feel until 3-4 years into release. 

There was a massive exodus of players who felt like the project had been abandoned and the game started feeling stale and dated. The competitive scene in this game was very fun to participate in, but in classic PUBG/KRAFTON fashion, they decided to prioritize third-person competitive play over FPS which alienated everyone except Asia regions.

PUBG was a fantastic game that has been plagued by poor decisions since launch. 

For those people that had been there since beta, it's a total heart break of what this game once was and what could have been.

**Counter-Strike 2 – A Complete Disappointment**

CS2 is honestly one of the biggest disappointments in the history of competitive gaming.

What happened to Counter-Strike? We went from having CS:GO, a game with personality, competitive integrity, and an incredible community, to this unfinished, frustrating mess called CS2.

Let's talk about the anti-cheat. VAC is an absolute joke. Cheaters are everywhere, blatant hackers can ruin entire matches, and legitimate players are left wasting their time. You can spend thousands of hours improving your aim, movement, and game sense, just to get destroyed by someone using cheats. The competitive experience is pathetic when you can't even trust the integrity of your matches.

Valve seems completely disconnected from its player base. We keep getting skins, cases, and cosmetic content, while one of the most important aspects of the game remains neglected: ACTUALLY STOPPING CHEATERS.

CS:GO had problems, but at least it felt like Counter-Strike. It had character, atmosphere, and an identity. CS2 feels like a soulless replacement that nobody asked to experience in this state. Source 2 was supposed to be an upgrade, but what did we really gain? Better graphics? For what, if the actual gameplay experience is constantly ruined?

The game that once represented competitive excellence now feels like an endless cycle of frustration:
- Useless anti-cheat against blatant cheaters.
- Unfair and frustrating matchmaking.
- A community losing patience.
- Updates that don't address the biggest problems.
- Valve prioritizing monetization while fundamental issues remain.

The most insulting part is that Counter-Strike has an enormous budget, a massive player base, and one of the most successful competitive gaming communities in history. Yet players still have to beg for basic competitive integrity.

**CS2 isn't the evolution of CS:GO. It feels like a downgrade wearing a new coat of paint.**

I don't care about another case, another skin collection, or another meaningless cosmetic update. FIX THE ANTI-CHEAT. FIX THE GAME.

Counter-Strike used to be a legend. Now it's a frustrating reminder of what happens when developers take their loyal community for granted.

**Valve, you didn't just replace a game. You replaced an experience that people spent years loving, and somehow made it worse.**

Some may disagree but I just don't feel the same way about CS2 as I did about GO and I don't think that it is the nostalgia of GO that blurs my views on CS2. Truly, I understand where valve is in development and wanting to keep growing the game we all love. However, what I don't yet understand is why they did not leave GO as a standalone. Today when I play CS I feel the remnants of GO but in my opinion the game has changed drastically. At this point I am indifferent on CS2 as I still enjoy the game from time to time however, I just wanted to write this review for the new generation of CS players who will now grow up playing this game just like me. To them I say, when I started playing CSGO I saw 1.6 and source available for me to play but chose to play valves newest edition of counterstrike and I am in pity for you that you will likely not have the chance to play the game that was CSGO. Coming from the good old days of CS 1.6, seeing how far Counter-Strike has evolved with CS2 is honestly exciting. The game still captures that same competitive spirit, skill-based gameplay, and adrenaline that made me fall in love with Counter-Strike in the first place. The graphics, animations, sound design, and overall feel bring a fresh experience while keeping the core of what makes CS so special. There's nothing quite like landing a perfect headshot, clutching a round, or outsmarting the enemy team. CS2 has huge potential and is a great step forward for the franchise. However, one major issue that needs serious attention is the RED TRUST FACTOR system. It can be extremely frustrating when legitimate players get caught in low-trust lobbies or experience poor matchmaking without a clear explanation. Valve really needs to improve transparency and make sure loyal players aren't unfairly punished by a system they can't properly understand or control. Despite that frustration, I still love the game and believe CS2 can become something truly special. Here's hoping Valve continues listening to the community and gives us the Counter-Strike experience we've loved since 1.6!

I have spent considerable hours observing this curious battlefield called Dota 2, where five men gather against five others, each convinced that victory is a matter of skill, yet most defeated by their own impatience.

It is a remarkable game, not because it teaches men how to conquer, but because it reveals how poorly they govern themselves.

I have witnessed a man lose his composure because his support failed to purchase a ward, another abandon reason because his carry missed a last hit, and a third surrender his dignity entirely by typing insults to strangers whose names he shall forget by morning.

How fragile is the human mind, that a fictional tower can command such genuine anger?

The game itself is not the enemy. It is our attachment to its outcomes.

You cannot control whether your teammate feeds. You cannot command the enemy to miss his ultimate. You cannot guarantee that your carry understands the meaning of farming efficiently. These things lie beyond your authority.

What remains yours is your decision: whether to play with discipline or surrender yourself to frustration.

I have also noticed that men celebrate MMR as though it were a measure of their worth. They climb from Herald to Immortal, yet remain slaves to the next victory. They win a match and immediately desire another. They lose one and demand revenge.

Tell me, then, who is truly imprisoned? The man in Herald who enjoys his game, or the Immortal player who cannot sleep because he has lost twenty-five points?

On Teammates

Do not expect wisdom from every player you encounter. Some are learning, some are careless, and others appear to have mistaken the minimap for an ornamental decoration.

Accept this as part of the game.

A wise player does not waste his entire match mourning the mistakes of another. He corrects what he can and endures what he cannot.

On Losing

A defeat is not necessarily a misfortune. It is an opportunity to discover the weakness in your judgment.

Perhaps you engaged without vision. Perhaps you pursued an enemy too far. Perhaps you purchased an item not because it was useful, but because you wished to imitate a professional player.

Examine your mistakes without hatred. There is little virtue in repeating them.

𝗢𝗻 𝗪𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴

Victory is pleasant, but do not become intoxicated by it. The same player who praises himself after winning may curse the heavens after losing.

Neither outcome should determine your character.

𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭

8/10

A remarkable exercise in human psychology disguised as a strategy game.

Dota 2 teaches patience, discipline, cooperation, humility, and the difficult art of accepting what cannot be controlled.

However, its greatest enemy is not Roshan, the enemy carry, or even a particularly troublesome Pudge.

It is the player's own ego.

I would recommend this game to those who wish to understand human nature. But I would advise them to mute the chat, for philosophy has its limits.

I played Dota way back when it was a core part of the Warcraft 3 custom games library. At the time I liked it but didn't put a whole lot of time into it. Fast forward a few years to when it was released on steam and I got an invite from a friend to play. I sank my fair share of time into the game with him, racking up over 1,000 hours in my first year of play.

As time went by I left the game and came back multiple times, making sure to let my enjoyment build for the game between those stints of absence. Between starting my first game of Dota 2 and now, I have managed to accrue more than 5,400 hours in the game. So you might be wondering why I am not recommending the game.

When I first started play, so much of it felt fresh and interesting but most importantly of all, it felt loved. Not just because of the developers but by the people like me who picked up and played the game for hours every day. This meant when those regular updates were dropped to keep the game fresh it felt like the developers cared about the experience they were delivering. However, a sense of stagnation for the game as set in. What's worse is that within the past few months Deadlock has received so much love and care that it has left a sour taste with regards to Valve as a development team, with October producing 6 new characters to the game.

All it feels like now is that Dota has become a 'Cash Cow' for the business and Deadlock is the 'Star', which feels as if the fans are getting taken for granted.

INGREDIENTS
-3 cups (600 grams) of cooked day-old rice

-2 eggs

-3 tbsp of cooking oil

-40 grams of bamboo shoot, diced

-40 grams of carrot, diced

-40 grams of pea

-3 rehydrated shitake mushrooms, diced

-3-5 pieces of rehydrated dried scallop

-40 grams of Jin Hua ham, diced

-40 grams of chicken thigh, diced (you can also use chicken breast)

-1.5 tbsp of Chinese cooking wine

-40 grams of shrimp, diced

-40 grams of rehydrated sea cucumber, diced

-20 grams of scallions, diced

-1+1/4 tsp of salt

-3 tbsp of cooking oil


Let's go through a few important ingredients before we get to the cooking instructions.

Rice (剩米饭): The leftover rice from takeout or day-old rice will be the best option. If you don’t have any, you can cook some one day ahead. The fluffiness of the grains determines the final result of this dish. 

Sea cucumber (海参): This is the luxury part of this recipe. Depending on the quality and varieties, the price can be between 400 to thousands of dollars per pound. Don’t worry, you can replace it with fresh sea scallop (I have tried it, it is equally delicious). It is not about the price, most of you may not have access to buy it because I got it shipped from China. Even if you do, you may not have the time and attention to prepare it. Rehydrating dried sea cucumber is an extremely time-consuming process, which includes 48 hours of soaking, 1-3 hours of simmering, then another 48 hours of soaking. That is why only time-honored local restaurants will do this.

Jinhua ham (金华火腿): it is a special cured meat from Jin Hua, Zhe Jiang province. It was listed as a tribute from Song Dynasty to Qing Dynasty. If you don’t have access, a thick cut of Italian prosciutto will do just as good.

Bamboo shoot (笋): It provides a crunchy texture. You can replace it with any hard vegetables that you like. Such as celery, asparagus, green beans...


INSTRUCTIONS
-Soaked the dried shitake mushrooms and dried scallops 2 hours ahead. Squeeze the mushroom to remove the water and dice finely. Put the scallop in a small blender to blend for 10 seconds or until it becomes nice and fluffy. Set them aside.

-Put the Jinhua ham and chicken breast into a bowl along with a drizzle of Chinese cooking wine. Steam for 20 minutes. Save the steaming liquid for later use. Dice the ham and chicken finely.

-Dice the rehydrated sea cucumber (or fresh sea scallop) and fresh shrimp. set it aside

-Blanched the bamboo shoot, carrot, peas in boiling water for about 40 seconds. Set it aside.

-Crack 2 eggs and whisk them until you don’t see any obvious egg white.

-Heat your wok until smoking hot. Add a few tbsp of oil. Toss in the egg. Stir with a pair of chopsticks as fast as you can or until all the egg is crumbled into small little bits. Remove the egg from the wok and set it aside.

-You should have some oil left in the wok. If not, you can add a little more. Turn the heat back on high. Toss in the Jin hua ham, shredded scallop, diced shitake mushroom, sea cucumber (or fresh scallop), shrimp, and chicken thigh. Sauté for a couple of minutes.

-Add the cooked day-old rice; keep stirring on high heat for a few minutes or until you can see some grains dancing and jumping at the bottom of the wok.

-Add the blanched vegetables and the crumbled egg. Drizzle in the steaming liquid. Keep stirring until everything is well mixed.

-Add some salt to taste. Give it a final toss. Before serving, sprinkle some diced scallion and your fried rice is done.



If you are wondering, where is the MSG? Actually, We do not use MSG for the authentic Yang Zhou fried rice, I will explain why:

In this recipe, sea cucumber, shrimp, chicken, egg, scallop, and mushroom have a high content of flavorful amino acids, such as glycine, alanine, and glutamic acid. If we season them with salt, they become the sodium salt of amino acids.

Ham is a piece of protein that is cured by salt. Over time, the fermenting process produces even more sodium salt of the amino acids.

The full name of MSG is monosodium glutamate; it is an artificial and pure single type of amino acid salt. If you add it to a dish that is already well balanced with all kinds of flavor amino acid salts, it is not going to do anything - that’s why we don’t add MSG.

Dota 2 is a great MOBA that's being held back by nothing more than its player base and mediocre management.

Before you're allowed to play ranked, you're forced to endure 100 hours of unranked matchmaking. Doesn't sound too bad in theory, until you realize that unranked is essentially a free-for-all with absolutely no standards.

You'll be matched with players who can barely manage to breathe without choking on their own saliva, as well as players with over 7,000 games under their belts. You'll encounter smurfs and players who don't care about winning. Not necessarily because they don't want to win, but because they refuse to learn, hiding behind the classic excuse: "It's unranked, bro."

While unranked isn't something you're supposed to take particularly seriously, when you're still grinding through those 100 hours, you don't really have a choice. You're effectively being held hostage by people who have absolutely no respect for your time.

Furthermore, there isn't a single good region to play in, as each one comes with its own unique brand of toxicity.

Play on EU East, and you'll be greeted by four egotistical morons suffering from main character syndrome, who refuse to play support and wouldn't buy a ward to save their lives.

Play on EU West, and you'll be met with four misfits who refuse to communicate in English.

Play on NA, whether East or West, and there's a 50% chance your match will contain bots. And no, I'm not talking about Valve's bots. I'm talking about mediocre, third-rate scripts that run down lanes and die repeatedly.

"Are you sure they're not just new, bad players?"

Yes, I am. Every single one of these bots follows the same naming conventions and behavioral patterns: "AdjectiveName####", usually accompanied by a QR code or a picture of a girl as their profile picture. They also constantly spam chat wheel emotes, making them about as subtle as a brick through a window.

And the saddest part of all this is that the game itself is genuinely fantastic.

When you find yourself in a match with nine other like-minded individuals who have even a shred of competitive spirit and genuinely want to win, there's no other game that comes close to the satisfaction of winning an intense, hour-long match of Dota.

The hero design is amazing, the mechanics are smooth and satisfying, and the items are meaningful, often fundamentally changing how you approach and play the game. There's an incredible amount of depth here, and very few games can deliver the same experience.

People often say that Valve doesn't care. Personally, I think Valve is ashamed of its own creation and, more importantly, the community it has cultivated.

I would pay every cent I have, and every cent I will ever earn, just to gather the entire player base into one gigantic trebuchet and launch them into shark-infested waters.

Welcome to the Never-Ending Game.

Dota 2 is a strange place.

You enter looking for entertainment, spend hundreds of hours trying to understand it, thousands more trying to master it, and eventually realize that you might never truly understand it.

It's a game where five strangers are expected to work together like a perfectly coordinated team, where one tiny mistake can destroy a 60-minute match, and where the difference between an absolute genius and a complete fool is sometimes just one decision.

Every hero has a story. Every item has a purpose. Every match has its own chaos.

You can experience the most incredible comeback of your life, followed immediately by a defeat so ridiculous that you start questioning your existence.

There are beautiful moments hidden between all the madness. A perfectly executed team fight, a game-winning Black Hole, an unexpected Rampage, or that one teammate who actually knows what they're doing.

And then there is the other side of Dota 2...

The toxicity, the endless arguments, the questionable decisions, the matchmaking, and the occasional feeling that the entire universe is personally against you.

Yet, somehow, you keep coming back.

Maybe it's the complexity. Maybe it's the competition. Maybe it's the satisfaction of finally pulling off something you've been practicing for weeks.

Or maybe we've all just lost our minds.

Dota 2 isn't a game you simply finish. It's a journey with no final destination, where even after thousands of hours, there is still something new waiting to surprise you.

You don't always win. You don't always improve. Sometimes you don't even enjoy playing.

But when everything comes together, there is nothing quite like it.

**A beautiful disaster. An endless obsession. A game unlike any other.**

Would recommend. 10/10.

Dota 2(도타 2)는 밸브 코퍼레이션(Valve Corporation)이 개발하고 유통하는 PC용 AOS(MOBA) 장르의 멀티플레이어 온라인 전략 게임이다. 워크래프트 III: 레인 오브 카오스와 그 확장팩 더 프로즌 쓰론의 유저 제작 지도(유즈맵)인 'DotA(Defense of the Ancients)'를 정식 후속작으로 계승하여 제작되었다.

게임플레이

각 매치는 5명으로 구성된 두 팀이 맞붙는 방식으로 진행된다. 플레이어는 각각 고유한 능력과 능력치, 플레이 스타일을 가진 120여 명의 '영웅(Hero)' 중 하나를 선택해 제어한다. 한 팀은 빛의 진영인 '레디언트(Radiant)', 다른 한 팀은 어둠의 진영인 '다이어(Dire)'가 되어 경기하며, 게임의 최종 목표는 자신의 기지를 방어하면서 상대 진영의 본진 중심 건물인 '고대 요새(Ancient, 한국 내 유저 호칭: 본진/네서스)'를 먼저 파괴하는 것이다.
플레이어는 경기 내에서 미니언 역할의 컴퓨터 캐릭터(크립)나 적 구조물, 적 영웅을 처치하여 경험치와 골드를 획득하고 영웅을 성장시켜야 한다. 획득한 골드로 영웅의 스탯을 올리거나 특수 능력을 부여하는 아이템을 구매할 수 있다. 도타 2는 완전한 무료 공개(Free-to-Play) 모델을 채택하고 있어 모든 영웅을 처음부터 무료로 플레이할 수 있으며, 유료 결제 요소는 게임의 밸런스에 영향을 주지 않는 캐릭터 외형 꾸미기 아이템이나 패스 상품 등으로만 제한된다

Dota 2 is one of the best games ever made — and also one of the hardest to recommend without a warning label. It has a massive, thriving player base with millions of concurrent users, a thriving esports scene, and a level of depth that few games can match. But it is also brutally complex, unforgiving to newcomers, and demanding in a way that can feel overwhelming.

The Good: A Game That Rewards Dedication

The core of Dota 2 is sublime. Every match is a chess game played at real-time speed, where decisions matter, teamwork is essential, and the skill ceiling is essentially infinite. The game is free-to-play with no pay-to-win mechanics, which is remarkable given its scale. The hero pool is enormous — over 100 characters, each with unique abilities, roles, and playstyles — and the item system, map dynamics, and meta shifts keep the game fresh even after thousands of hours. When everything clicks, Dota 2 delivers a sense of satisfaction that few other games can match. The million-plus online count is proof that this formula works.

The Bad: A Mountain of Complexity

Here is the catch: Dota 2 is incredibly hard to learn. The mechanics are deep and layered — last-hitting, denying, creep aggro, stacking, pulling, ward placement, timings, power spikes, and dozens of other systems that are never explained properly in-game. Then there is the hero problem: with 100+ characters, each having multiple abilities, remembering what every single one does is a massive undertaking. You need to know not just your own hero, but every enemy hero's abilities, cooldowns, and counters. That knowledge gap is brutal for new players.

The learning curve is less a curve and more a cliff. The game does have a tutorial, but it barely scratches the surface. Most players learn through trial, error, and a lot of frustration — often while being flamed by teammates. It is not a game you can casually pick up and enjoy immediately. It demands time, patience, and a willingness to lose repeatedly while you figure things out.

Verdict!

Dota 2 is a masterpiece of game design, but it is not for everyone. If you are willing to invest the time to learn its complex mechanics and memorize the abilities of over 100 heroes, you will find one of the deepest and most rewarding competitive games in existence. If you want something you can learn in a weekend, look elsewhere. It is brilliant, it is massive, and it is merciless — and that is exactly why its community loves it!

[h1]A One of a Kind Experience[/h1]

Destiny 2 delivers an experience that is completely different from anything I played before. It [u]had its highs and lows,[/u] and horrible decisions were made by Bungie along the way, which led to Destiny’s near death. But it’s [u]currently in possibly the best state it has ever been.[/u]

The so called “last” update [u]reworked nearly all the content to make it relevant again[/u] and so much more. And after the news of the continuation of Destiny 2, the long-standing executives have left the studio. [u]Bungie’s leadership team has been completely overhauled[/u] and is now, hopefully, in the hands of people who care as much about the franchise as their fans do.

Great promises were made, such as bringing [u]all the past content,[/u] like campaigns and more, [u]back into the game[/u] that was previously removed.

[hr]

[h1]Gameplay — 10/10[/h1]

[u]The fluid cycle between jump and run, gunplay, and powerful abilities,[/u] combined with actually smart and interactive enemy AI that reacts in meaningful ways, like starting to push you when you are low on health, seeking cover to avoid getting shot, and leaping away when near a grenade, [u]makes the many factions so fun to engage with.[/u]

[h1]Story — 6/10[/h1]

Hit or miss. [u]You can get a story that is easily forgettable, and the next can be a fantastic 10/10 story that makes you feel connected to the universe of Destiny immediately,[/u] like The Red War, Forsaken, The Witch Queen, or The Final Shape.

[h1]Difficulty — 10/10[/h1]

Perfect difficulty, from really easy patrols to really hard raids. [u]There is an activity that matches your skill perfectly for everyone,[/u] whether you are a casual player or someone looking for a challenge.

[h1]Accessibility — 2/10[/h1]

My one big complaint is that with the removal of The Red War campaign, the [u]New Light experience is horribly confusing[/u] for new players. Most don’t get past the Cosmodrome or don’t know where to go from there once they reach the Tower, which makes getting friends hooked on the game near impossible.

I hope that with the return of The Red War campaign, this issue will be resolved.

[hr]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

A really fun and unique game, especially with friends, with a rather unforgiving start that  [u] feels very rewarding once you get past that first confusion[/u] and see what Destiny has to offer.

Leaving a negative review for this game pains me so much considering what a mastery of artistry and pure sauce this game is, and what it used to be. Every environment is intriguing, every enemy faction is special in their own way, and genuinely every weapon i've used has felt nothing short of incredible to handle--looking past that, as hard as it is for me to do that considering my history with the game and love for its craft, there are a myriad of issues that stack up and make a lot of the experience sour (i like sour things but like... the gross kind of sour, like sour milk). 

Writing down my issues with this game in a way that makes sense has proven to be pretty difficult, as they are a swirling pool of what, why, and what ifs, but to put it into a single phrase: most design and story angles are fragmented and really difficult to understand. The past few weeks i've played this game on have had me pretty much always wondering if there's something i'm missing, which is a stark contrast from when i played this game many years ago. The story has been left practically aimless, with over 2/3 of it being either vaulted or straight up gone because they remove the previous season's story quests whenever there's a new season to take the stage. Even after watching a recap video do i still have question marks above my head because a lot of the more recent story points are playground logic? The "nuh uh i'm actually using my secret powers right now" kind of stuff.

Build-crafting also has me constantly feeling like i'm missing something. There are lots of perks and special weapon abilities that have jumped to the spotlight because of their raw ability, but even more that have been reduced to fluff and fodder due to power creep over the years. That much is simple enough to understand, but what makes a build effective or "good" is often times also esoteric. Hidden/unintended/unexplained interactions between gear are load bearing in many cases, which has lead me to literal spreadsheets just to find a basic explanation for stuff.

This last point is more of a personal issue than something inherently wrong with the game, but i find it very unfortunate that many if not most of this game's most interesting and unique confrontations are found within raids. I do not have 5 other friends who play this game, and i really don't want to take my chances with looking for a group considering the horror stories i have seen from playing with raid groups. If i were to find a group that is not somehow bigoted/sweaty and instead comfortable enough for me to exist in, experiencing and exploring a raid for the first time is a pipe dream considering that people will most likely be teaching me from their own experience, or expecting me to look up guides before even starting one. This makes me yearn for the dungeons this game has to offer, which are also pretty interesting, except they are all locked behind individual dungeon keys that cost 20 slices of cheddar each. This is especially rich considering that most of the dlc is now considered "legacy" and no longer relevant. Again, these are personal issues.

As a brand new player, this game is a chaotic, unintuitive mess. After you finish the brief tutorial in the starting area and arrive at the main hub, the game completely abandons you. Because bungie deleted the original base campaign years ago, there is zero natural narrative momentum, no chronological story path, and no clear direction on where to go next.

Instead, the map floods your screen with an ambiguous web of planetary icons, out of order expansion intros, locked activities, and arbitrary prerequisites. The game does virtually nothing to explain the lore, the chronological order of surviving campaigns, or how to properly work your way up to endgame content like Dungeons and Raids.

If a game requires you to close the application and spend hours studying youtube guides and wikis just to figure out what to play next, its onboarding design is fundamentally broken. The graphics are good and gunplay is fantastic, but for a newcomer, the user interface and new player experience are completely disrespectful of your time.

Sure, you can run around like a headless chicken clearing random planet quests with zero context, but for some, including me, that is a waste of time. Defenders will claim this confusion is inevitable for a long running mmo, but mmos like ff14, wow, swtor etc prove otherwise, they preserve a clear, linear path from day one to the endgame, no matter how late you start or how many expansions they added. Destiny 2 doesn't.

Avoid this if you want a coherent story experience that actually respects your time.

Love the game—the myriad weapons, the setting, the multitude of activities, and so on. No complaints there. However, coming back to the game and finding that it now uses BattlEye has meant nothing but headaches for me. I tried every fix the Internet could suggest, but BEDaisy (confirmed culprit) delivers one BSOD crash after another—on launch, in the middle of fights, browsing the in-game store. Until that changes, Destiny 2 is a great game I won't be playing.

UPDATE: After much experimentation, I noticed a pattern: the crashes occur always after my PC goes into deep sleep. After a manual restart, the game runs and launches normally. It's a workaround, not a solution, but at least I can play—without the BSODs. And judging D2 on its own merits, I'm having tons of fun, so I'm changing my review to a thumbs-up.

Destiny 2 is one of those games I really want to love without having to explain myself afterwards.

Because when it's good, it's REALLY good.

The shooting feels fantastic. Few games make simply firing a weapon this satisfying, and the combination of abilities, exotic weapons, and ridiculous space magic is hard to beat. There's something incredibly satisfying about clearing a room full of enemies and immediately looking for another room.

But bloody hell, Bungie knows how to complicate a good thing.

The story can be genuinely interesting, assuming you can figure out what happened, what's still playable, and why half the characters are talking about events you apparently needed a time machine to experience.

Then there's the DLC situation. You install a free game, start enjoying yourself, and eventually discover that understanding what you actually own requires more research than buying a used car.

And the menus. Good lord, the menus.

It's frustrating because the actual gameplay deserves so much better than the confusion surrounding it. I don't mind grinding for something worthwhile, but I do mind feeling like I need a YouTube tutorial just to understand what I'm supposed to be doing next.

Still, I can't bring myself to give it a negative review. There's too much good here, especially if you enjoy looter shooters and have friends to play with.

I have played this game for 1776 hours, and here is what I can tell from having been on this journey since the launch of Destiny in 2014.  Bungie has over the past 12 years forgotten and remembered why gamers love Destiny so many times that I get whiplash trying to count.  

I have played Destiny 2 for approximately half of the games service life, and you might be thinking 'wow only 1776 hours in 5 years of playing'.  Yes, I happen to have a family, other hobbies, and other games that I enjoy playing.  This is, amongst others, the reason why I spent half of the service life not playing the game.  For a significant duration of the game's service life; the time commitment required to keep pace with the release of new content was similar to that of a full time job.  I did not and currently do not, nor do I want to, have that amount of free time to dedicate to playing a singular game.  

For reference there are 2080 professional working hours in a year (52 weeks * 40 hours/week = 2080 hours).  I have on average played this game approximately 6.8 hours per week during the years that I have played it (1776 / 5 = 355 hours/year => 355 / 52 = 6.8 hours/week).  There were many 'seasons' where I could not commit the time to finishing the content that I had paid for.  This eventually resulted in the permanent vaulting of content in which I never got to play.  

Another reason why I stopped playing this game, several times, revolves around the content being released.  As you might imagine with content being released at the speed and scale at which it was the content quality declined.  For the entirety of the game's service life the quality of story writing ping ponged back and forth season to season, DLC to DLC.  As well the gameplay suffered across the board with rampant and sometimes weekly game balance changes. This continuously flipped the 'meta' upside down.  This left filthy casuals, such as myself, to frequently scramble and grind to obtain the 'meta' gear for taking part in the high level content.  Time to grind that I, and many others, did not and do not have.  I find that this most personified in the frequent description of several famous youtubers that have stated regarding this game;  "We are so back" immediately followed by "It's all over".

For all of the flaws that Destiny has had over the years, it still remains one of the best gameplay and story telling masterpieces of all time.  If one were to look at the good in the game, they would see spurts of the most elegant and powerful story writing present in the industry.  Gameplay that is engaging and fun like no other in the market.  World building and artwork that put most AAA development houses to absolute shame.  By no small margin does Bungie provide this.  This is truly a masterpiece, and will forever be one of my favorite games to play.  

If you have made it this far, thank you for reading.

Bungie, 

Thank you for the wonderful entertainment that you have provided your fans for the past two decades. This journey has been incredible. See you starside.

Best Regards,
Saint Mater

- My final rating is heavily impacted by the history of poor decisions made by Bungie throughout the game's lifespan:

- Removed Paid Content (Vaulting): It is unacceptable that Bungie removed entire story campaigns that players originally paid for, such as the Red War, Curse of Osiris, Warmind, and Forsaken.

- Misleading Free-to-Play Model: If you download the game for free, there is barely anything meaningful to do besides basic patrol zones. Almost all core endgame content, raids, and story arcs are paywalled behind DLCs.

- Microtransactions & Silver: While it leaned close to Pay-to-Win mechanics in the past, you can at least earn decent cosmetic items through Bright Dust nowadays without spending real money on Silver.

-Massive File Size: It is simply not worth downloading over 100 GB for a game where free-to-play users barely get a fraction of playable content.

Final Verdict
- Final Score: 6.5 / 10 (Weighted down by years of controversial publisher decisions).

Recommendation: DO NOT download it if you only intend to play free-to-play. Only consider it if you find the Expansion Collection heavily discounted and want a polished sci-fi shooter experience with friends.

It’s hard to clearly judge Destiny 2. The beautifully designed world clashes with the character models, whose faces look like they belong in The Sims. It seems to be a standard in modern gaming that every character has to look like a Ken or Barbie doll. The game is quite well optimized and has some interesting combat ideas, like battles during meditation that create a mirrored version of the real map in their dreamlike form. The vehicles are incredibly agile and fast, making travel over long distances a real pleasure (the shortcut tab+E after 4 hours of gameplay has carved itself into my mind as an instant dopamine trigger). Unfortunately, all these advantages are ruthlessly destroyed by the itemization system. I understand that nowadays games need to cater to mindless mobile gamers, but if you have to shove item power everywhere, at least let it mean something. In the first 4 hours of playing, I found about 250 items - almost all legendary (I don’t know how humanity could lose this war if under every rock there’s a legendary plasma rifle). All weapons had item power between 300 and 305... So what? Does that mean a legendary soup spoon deals as much damage as a quantum black hole launcher because both have item power 302? The game supposedly has something called damage potential, but its noticeable impact on damage dealt is minimal and you have to dig deep into weapon stats to find it. To sum up: another game trying to be Fortnite with a mobile vibe, and it turned out too well, but nobody needed it... I just feel sorry for the artists because they really made a beautiful world. Time to go back to ArcRiders.

1,716 hours on Steam. Thousands more memories that no playtime counter could ever measure.

Destiny 2 is more than a game to me. It is a universe I have lived in, a community I have grown alongside, and a place that has given me memories I will carry for the rest of my life.

I've experienced the highs and lows. The excitement of discovering something new, the frustration of wiping endlessly during a raid, the adrenaline of finally defeating an impossible boss, and the absolute chaos of six Guardians shouting because somebody forgot a mechanic for the fifteenth time.

And somehow, those are the moments I treasure most.

Because somewhere along the way, Destiny stopped being about the loot, weapons, armour or next expansion.

It became about the people.

The random Guardians who stopped to help. The strangers who became fireteam members. The fireteam members who became friends. The people who patiently explained mechanics, revived you when things went wrong, and stayed for one more attempt when everyone was exhausted.

Some of us may never meet in person. Some have stopped playing years ago. Some usernames on my friends list might never light up again.

But I remember those moments.

There's something beautiful about gaming that people outside these communities don't always understand. You can spend hours fighting imaginary enemies in an imaginary universe and somehow create friendships and memories that are completely real.

And if there's one thing I will be eternally grateful to Destiny for, it is this: Destiny gave me a friend for life.

Out of millions of players, countless fireteams, random encounters, raids and adventures, this game brought someone into my life who became so much more than another Guardian on my friends list.

Someone I can genuinely call a lifelong friend.

Two people who might never have crossed paths in the real world found each other in a fictional universe and built a friendship that exists far beyond it.

Weapons get sunset. Seasons end. Expansions come and go. Servers won't run forever.

But that friendship? That is something no Content Vault can ever take away from me.

Even if I never launched Destiny again, I would still be grateful for every hour spent playing, because those hours led me to someone I hope will remain part of my life forever.

I came to Destiny for the game. I stayed for the memories. And somewhere along the way, I found a friend for life.

No exotic weapon, god roll, raid title or flawless achievement could ever mean more to me than that.

Of course, Destiny hasn't always been perfect.

I've been disappointed with Bungie's decisions, frustrated by the game's direction, monetisation, seasonal repetition, and especially the Destiny Content Vault.

Watching entire destinations, campaigns, missions and experiences disappear from a universe I loved was genuinely heartbreaking.

Not simply because we lost content, but because we lost pieces of our shared history.

The Red War. The destinations we first explored. The missions that introduced us to this universe. The experiences that newer Guardians never got to discover.

These weren't simply missions or destinations. They were places where memories were made, where friendships began, and where strangers became fireteams that would remain together for years.

For so long, I wished that Destiny could become whole again.

And now, seeing content finally being unvaulted, I cannot express how happy that makes me.

Thank you. Genuinely.

I know restoring older content isn't as simple as flipping a switch. I don't expect everything to return overnight. But seeing these steps towards restoring our universe gives me something I haven't felt this strongly in a long time.

Hope.

Hope that new Guardians will experience the journey that brought us here. Hope that veterans can revisit the places where their adventures began. Hope that Destiny's incredible history will be preserved instead of slowly disappearing.

Destiny deserves to be experienced as a living, connected universe, not merely remembered through YouTube videos and stories told by veterans.

I want the next generation of Guardians to understand why we fell in love with this game.

And despite every criticism I have, I want Bungie to know something.

I still believe in Destiny.

I wouldn't have spent 1,716 hours here if I didn't.

I criticise this game because I care. Because I know how extraordinary it can be. Because I've experienced those moments when the music, storytelling, atmosphere, gameplay and community come together to create something very few games can replicate.

There is something magical about standing beneath an alien sky, hearing that incredible soundtrack, and realising how much imagination and love went into creating this universe.

Destiny has given me wonder, challenges, laughter, frustration, excitement and companionship.

Most importantly, it reminded me that even in a universe built around endless conflict, the greatest thing we have is each other.

To the developers, artists, composers, writers and everyone who poured their hearts into Destiny, thank you. Your work has meant more to some of us than you might ever realise.

You didn't simply create a video game. You created a place where people from different countries, backgrounds and walks of life could find something in common.

A universe where strangers became teammates, teammates became friends, and sometimes, those friends became family.

To the Guardians who taught me, helped me, carried me, laughed with me, wiped with me and stood beside me, thank you for being part of my journey.

To the new Lights, I hope you experience the same wonder that made so many of us fall in love with Destiny.

And to the Guardians who have put down their weapons, moved on with life, or never returned...

Your Light was here. Your stories mattered. And somewhere out there, someone still remembers running alongside you.

I don't know what the future holds for Destiny or how many adventures await us.

Perhaps one day I'll log in for the last time without even realising it. No grand farewell. No final raid. Just an ordinary evening when I close the game, expecting to return tomorrow, only for life to take me somewhere else.

But when that day comes, I won't think about the hours I wasted.

I'll remember the laughter. The late-night raids. The impossible victories. The people who stood beside me.

And above all, the friend for life this wonderful, frustrating, beautiful game gave me.

Because I didn't just spend 1,716 hours playing Destiny. I spent 1,716 hours making memories.

And if the Tower needs defending again, if another impossible raid boss stands between us and victory, or if a new Guardian needs help through their first dungeon...

I'll be there.

Not because Destiny is perfect. Not because I agree with every decision.

But because, after everything, this universe still feels like home.

And a home isn't made special by the walls surrounding it.

It's made special by the people you share it with.

Eyes up, Guardian.

Per audacia ad astra.

Through boldness, to the stars.

Thank you, Bungie. Thank you, Destiny. And thank you to every Guardian who made this journey worth taking.

See you starside. ❤️

From one Guardian who still believes.

Let me just start off by saying that I've played this game since the beginning. 

I pre ordered Destiny 2 and once it came out, I never really looked back. At one point, probably sometime before Forsaken, I had my Hunter, Titan, and Warlock all maxed out with pretty much every armor and weapon exotic unlocked. I have probably put over 1,200 hours into the game on PlayStation alone.

Destiny 2 was a huge part of my gaming life for a long time. The PvP was always a lot of fun and honestly still is. I remember putting together fireteams with friends on the weekends for Trials of the Nine, grinding Competitive Crucible, and just messing around in PvP for hours. Even when you were losing, there was always that feeling of wanting to play just one more game.

The raids are another thing that really stuck with me. I still remember how excited I was when my friends and I finally completed Prestige Leviathan, Eater of Worlds, and Spire of Stars. At the time, those completions felt like genuine accomplishments. You could spend hours wiping on the same encounter, getting frustrated, laughing at stupid mistakes, and then finally having everything come together. There was nothing quite like seeing that final boss go down after struggling with it for hours.

I think one of the biggest things Destiny gave me, though, was the people I met along the way. I've met some genuinely great people through this game, whether it was through Fireteam Finder, PlayStation Communities back when that was still around, raids, or just randomly joining up with other players. Some of those people I never would have met otherwise. That's something I don't think gets talked about enough when it comes to Destiny. You can log on expecting to play for an hour and somehow end up spending the entire night playing with a group of people you had never even met before.

Coming back after being away for three years or more has definitely been a little overwhelming. I logged in and immediately had what felt like 50 quests thrown at me. I'm still not entirely sure which campaign I'm supposed to start with or what order I'm supposed to be doing things in. I think Bungie could do a much better job of giving returning players some kind of direction because there is a lot to take in when you've been gone for that long.

At the same time, I do appreciate the freedom. Destiny has always been a game where you can kind of make your own path. You can chase a weapon, run strikes, play Crucible, work through a campaign, join a raid, or just wander around and see what you end up doing. I wouldn't want the game to completely take that freedom away just because it can sometimes be confusing for returning players.

The biggest disappointment coming back has probably been seeing how much content has been vaulted. There are locations, campaigns, and activities that I remember spending countless hours playing that just aren't there anymore. Makes it disappointing to come back to a game you loved and realize that parts of it are simply gone.

With Bungie talking about bringing those DLCs and locations back, though, I think that's a step in the right direction. I'm genuinely happy to hear that they're looking at bringing that content back because I think new and returning players should be able to experience it.

That said, I still don't think it should have been vaulted in the first place.

Despite all of that, coming back after so many years has made me realize just how much I missed Destiny. The gunplay still feels great. The worlds still have that same atmosphere. The music still hits in the same way. Even just walking around the Tower again brought back memories of spending countless nights playing this game with friends.

It's kind of like coming back to a place you haven't been to in years. A lot has changed, some things are gone, and there are plenty of things you don't recognize anymore, but there's still something familiar about it.

After more than three years away, I'm glad to be stepping back into the boots of a Guardian. I don't know how long I'll stick around this time, and I don't know what Bungie has planned for the future of Destiny, but I'm genuinely hopeful.

For all of its problems, there is still something about Destiny that keeps pulling me back.

Eyes up, Guardian.

2,522.9 hours. 100% completed. I have made some questionable life choices.

I don't even know how you're supposed to review Destiny 2 after putting over 2,500 hours into it.

At this point, I've spent enough time in this game that I should probably be paying rent in the Tower.

I've played through expansions, seasons, events, campaigns, dungeons, raids, Nightfalls, PvP, exotic quests, countless activities and an absolutely unreasonable number of hours doing things that I swore I wasn't going to grind again.

And somehow...

I keep coming back.

That's the weird thing about Destiny 2. It's a game that can simultaneously be one of the best games I've ever played and one of the most frustrating things I've ever played.

When Destiny is at its best, very few games come close.

The gunplay is incredible. The abilities feel amazing. The movement is satisfying. The raids and dungeons can be some of the best co-op experiences in gaming. And when you put together a build that completely clicks, there's something incredibly satisfying about watching everything on screen disappear.

Then there are the moments where you spend three hours farming for one weapon roll, get absolutely nothing useful, question every decision you've made in your life...

...and then log back in tomorrow and do it again.

The community is another huge part of the experience. Some of my best gaming experiences have come from playing Destiny with other people. Whether it's finally clearing a difficult raid encounter after hours of wiping, helping someone get an exotic, or just messing around with friends, those are the moments that make the grind worth it.

I've also watched this game change constantly over the years. Some changes have been fantastic. Some have made me wonder what Bungie was thinking. There have been incredible expansions, disappointing seasons, amazing weapons, terrible metas, content I never wanted to leave and content I was perfectly happy to see disappear.

But after 2,522.9 hours, the fact that I'm still here probably tells you everything you need to know.

Destiny 2 isn't perfect.

It can be grindy. It can be frustrating. It can waste your time. It can make you hate whatever activity you're currently playing.

And then you'll get the perfect drop, clear a raid you've been struggling with, discover a ridiculous build, or have one of those completely chaotic moments with your friends...

...and suddenly you remember why you play.

2,522.9 hours. 100%.

At this point, I'm not sure whether I play Destiny 2 or Destiny 2 plays me.

8/10. Would probably complain about it while continuing to play for another 500 hours.

I had this game on the blizzard launcher before they switched over so my hours aren't exactly accurate. Back then I played the game with my dad and we both had a blast. The gunplay, spontaneous group content, movement, abilities, all fun as hell. I never transferred my account in time so I lost everything. I started playing again years later with a group of friends and again we had fun with the anniversary content and running through the dungeons, but all the nerfs, content removal and system changes put a hamper on things. The last expansion I played was Lightfall which added strand which is a ton of fun to use. The world content for Lightfall is decent but felt like a bit of a slog and was very repetitive while I was playing. The story had cool fight scenes and gameplay, but didn't have much substance to the narrative.

The story though. I don't even know where to start. Literally. Class stories and campaigns have been removed. They have removed key story content including the Red War, Curse of Osiris, Warmind, and Forsaken. Removed story missions are now only playable in random order in weekly/daily content that everyone speed runs. Exotic narrative quests like the old one for Drang and Sturm are just gone and remove any attachment you have to getting and using the unique weapons you have outside of how cool they look, the grind it took to get them, or how viable they actually are. I used to care about some of the characters, but they either wrote most of them to be completely incompetent or killed them off. New players have to go on you tube or forums to watch lore content or old gameplay videos just to get an understanding of how things started and why things are the way they are now. All of that should be provided in-game through normal gameplay or even optional missions that bring you back, but it just isn't. I'm all for intricacies and secrets being put in text and hidden throughout the world, but baseline understanding and world building should be established naturally through gameplay.

PvP has a clear meta that changes as things get nerfed/buffed for each mode, but if you're okay with that then you'll have fun.

I can't speak on the newer content as I haven't had a desire to come back to the game.

TLDR; If you want a game where you can just shoot shit, grind, and get stronger either solo or with friends it's fun, but content removal and bad decisions have removed the charm that once made this game and its world feel unique and special for me.
