STORY: So far? It started slow and mildly interesting. Then it picks up the pace. Then a BIG reveal, literally. 100% not helpful to push the story but a reveal nonetheless. Then a cliffhanger. Then a new story that is still, in a Sentinel connection way still connected to you but very less about you. Then finally the cliffhanger continuation (tiny portion) and THEN another completely new story. Rinse and repeat.....For now. Don't get me wrong, the story is actually good. Just a very messy direction. So if you are into a focused story telling you might get bored of it because it's mostly 10% about you, 10% about who you were, 10% of searching an answer and 70% of being a giga chad helper.

COMBAT: The combat is actually fun until it gets frustrating when you hit the endgame where you will mostly get one shot and thank every known gods you mysteriously survived a hit that killed you in too many to count resets. This is not about getting good, that part is mildly frustrating until you memorize patterns and you can comfortably dodge and i-frame. What I'm talking about here is getting competitive in the form of completion time and the only way to do that is by NOT dodging as much and wasting you're buffs or having a fully whale team that cares less if you miss a buff. If you finally decide to get sweaty, there is a combat style known as quick swap. Fun, until fingers starts complaining.

POWERCREEPING: Yes, there is. Not a Huge leap that makes older characters practically unusable. But as you have a growing roster you will definitely notice it.

TEAM MANAGEMENT: It started as okay, this works into okay...... I skipped this character and now the main damage dealing character I like is losing a considerable damage loss without the one i skipped.

EVENTS: Are pretty generous with rewards. Most of it are fun.

GACHA: Yes, the part where probably the biggest debate is. I need to be clear here that I'm talking mainly of the gacha system here.
SO, having a guaranteed gacha in the form of weapon banners, we can safely say, "It is better than nothing." Which is true to all gacha games. Not the guaranteed part but the "It is better than nothing" part. From here, many people would start to compare to their hearts content. THIS gacha is better because WE have THIS, THIS gacha is better because THEY don't have THIS and so on and so forth. Honestly? I do comparison to justify my spending. Maybe most of us do because most comparison stems from how generous the game is in relative to actually getting what you want. You will hear a lot of people complain about losing the 50/50, most of them are complete f2p and dolphins. Most whales are just prepared to lose and thank the gods every win. As for my personal opinion, the game is generous enough to at least get you a couple of limited and their weapons, maybe more limited if you skip their weapons. Gacha is the source of income so I wouldn't be an idiot to say remove it. But I think they could have done a better job about it.

That said, thank you for reading. I can have more stuffs to talk about but would like to put in what I think would make it better.

1. Change the limited resonator ceiling. If they would keep the 50/50 then maybe half the ceiling which would drop to 40 and remove soft pity. Both f2p and spenders would appreciate this because f2p would be having more resources if they decided that if they lose the 50/50 they will keep the hard pity on the next limited. For spenders this means you basically get to secure the character without feeling robbed. Whales would feel more happy spending and would justify less of their actions, which says a lot. The other option is just remove the 50/50. In my opinion, a game that is positively accepted would not lose profit from removing 50/50, heck maybe it would even encourage more spenders because there is the fact that they want the character and KNOWS that they will get it without any risk.

2. Remove team synergy. Not in the sense of remove buffs but in the sense of not having a specific support ruins the damage table completely. I'm talking about who benefits who rather than mechanics. Mechanics are fine, that is only natural as the game ages that it wants to make it interesting and not go stale. For example I love Jinhsi, old character that somehow got forgotten to still not have a real buffer. Mechanics like tune break from 3.0 is fine because what i said earlier, makes the game not go stale so new characters that benefit from it is more acceptable rather than a topic of debate. By removing who benefits who opens up a more fun way to play as you can team up characters without the risk of significant damage drop. Instead of putting it on their outro skill (how this game applies buff) just put it in sonata extra effect (set bonus of echoes which is the game's version of gears).

Developed by Kuro Games, the title translates the fast-paced, high-APM philosophy of Punishing: Gray Raven into an expansive sci-fi post-apocalyptic world, outpacing Genshin and room-based titles like Zenless Zone Zero with fluid traversal mechanisms like wall-running and grapplehooks alongside a player-friendly guaranteed weapon banner. While it struggles with an exposition-heavy narrative opening, optimization hurdles on lower-end devices, and a tedious sub-stat tuning system for its captured Echo gears, its exhilarating boss encounters and high skill ceiling firmly establish it as a premier alternative for combat-focused gacha enthusiasts.

Performance is usually good in most places and battle, except the city of Lahai-Roi, which runs like absolute shit. Unreal really is a crap engine for performance and my PC ain't a potato!

QoL fixes and additions are a common aspect of each patch. By the time something is brought up as a problem, Kuro is already pushing out a solution or working on one. I usaully have very little to complain about in terms of something being tedious and somehow they're annoucing a new feature that makes those little chores even more efficient which weren't even on my radar.

The wuthering waves ebb and flow.

Flow
+ Excellent combat system. Switching between 3 resonators. Intro/Outro attacks, special skills, ultimates. Very flashy and satisfying.
+ Visuals. Not everyones style but I think it looks really good. There is an abundance of beautiful scenery in this game.
+ Character models. No elaboration neccessary.
+ Great introduction of Scar.
+ Story. Good characters. (Jinhsi, Scar, Changli, Phrolova, Mya, Hyuki etc.) Really good world building. Interesting history. I overall like the story, only some bits were not for me like the Black Shore arc or the story bits around Chisa and Lynae which were a bit too slow paced. At some points the story gets a bit too confusing but overall the cutscenes throughout the story are (especially later in the game) well done.
+ Pretty good voice acting as far as I can tell.
+ Some fun side activities. There are a few activities in the open-world that I didn't like but overall exploration in this game is very good.
+ Beautiful open world.
+ A gazillion of echoes to collect.
+ Impressive cutscenes.
+ This game sometimes turning into a sidescroller is pretty cool.
+ Some really epic OST (Rinascita!)
+ Some enemies (echoes) have a story about why they exist which is pretty cool. They are described as lingering frequencies, like the Fisalia girls, for example, that didn't pass the trials.
+ Hyuki!


Ebb

- Parrying doesnt feel good cause it's the same button as your light attack
- Mute Protagonist. She does talk at some points but mostly just nods which is odd.
- Not every content is being shown on the map and there is no way (ingame) to find all chests, challenges and so on. There is the lootmapper but why not just show it then.
- V-Synch and some other graphic options simply do not work.
- Some boring, unfun challenges. Very frustrating, bad designed ones.
- You spend a bit too much time doing menial tasks, especially in 1.0.
- Dialoges in Quest. They are often artificially long and a bit boring. Also they repeat many things and there are quite a lot of grammar mistakes. Some side quests are especially tedious like almost all of the quests in Jingzhu or some of the companion stories. There could also be a little more actual gameplay during main story quests.
- Running up walls and climbing often sucks, cause you often end up being stuck on some protrusion.
- A lot of the companion quests are quite slow and boring even later when they are part of the main quest.
- Gacha-system. If you spend a lot of real money in this game you get significantly stronger. Upgrading your Resonators or pulling for new ones is very expensive. You can however play through the story without the need of a perfect meta team. If you are smart about your pulls, you can actually clear most of the end game content but it still takes a lot of time. That time invested can be swiped away and the game encourages you to do just that. Also you will never get the max amount of wavebands (to make the character the strongest) or level up your weapons with duplicates without spending real money. You have to be ok with the fact that if you decide to not spend an insane amount of money, your favorite team will never be as strong as it could be.
- Depending on your team, exploration can get very annoying. I, for example, had no one in my main team that could use free aim and I had to switch teams on many occasions in the open world. This is just annoying and bad. I see no reason why everyone shouldn't be allowed to use free aim for the completion of open world activities.
- Annoying weeklies.
- The echo menus are horrible.
- Movement could be more fluent.
- Bad translation. Lots of grammar mistakes and odd writing in the beginning of the game but it gets significantly better the further you get in the game.

Gacha system aside, this game is good. Combat and exploration are well done, story is good aswell but this being a live service game, the story never ends until the game ends so its kinda hard to rate properly. Now that I have rated this game, I will delete my screenshot folder and move on for now.

I'm a casual player and when it goes to playing games, I mainly focus on what kind of story/narrative such games could offer. So, this review will only cover my experience following the story of wuwa (main story, side story, exploration story) and how it handles the worldbuilding/lore within said game.

Please note that currently I'm still in Huanglong and soon to be in Rinascita. This is my initial experience playing the first chapter of the game. Think of it as an opening to the world of wuwa, like a prologue maybe, and whether this "opening" deliver or not, whether it works well to make me fall in love with the lore tidbits or not (I wont talk about character writing because it's not my main focus).

1. I must say that Huanglong starts ... pretty rough. The conflict starts simple (which is good as starter, just like how it should be in any games), with a basic and straightforward premise, but what makes it rough is the driving plot in which your MC does to finish each checkpoint. I dont wanna put it into detail here bcz Im afraid it would be a spoiler. But what I wanna say is that your MC really walks a lot, getting into one place into another, yet the driving plot around these exact checkpoints feels too basic. It lacks narrative that makes me pop like "wow!" or "ooh so that's it!" because everything appears so basic, with a plot that is easy to guess, no crazy revelations, no deep talking bcz most conversations run casually just like everyday conversation (with most of them being repetitive such as when npcs asking rover's opinion, or asking rover's condition and what he/she is planning to do, basically they put too much "care" on rover's wellbeing, and all of these happen even during near-climax when "war is incoming and jinzhou is in grave danger". It kinda feels repetitive, so much information/topic being discussed again and again, even tho it's already clear from the very beginning.

2. Lore dump everywhere bruh. It really breaks the immersion of the convesation that is running at that time; because as an open-world game, they should know how to distribute lore in the main quest and side quest, or even in npcs talking or some archives you can find scattered in some areas, not everything (literally everything) needs to be loaded in the main quest. The characters casually mentioning strange terms, and rover's always asking to elaborate, which ended up the characters giving explanation that sometimes feel so much to grasp. Not to mention that some terms being explained more than once, feels like lecturing instead of the conversation runs smoothly.

3. The plot itself feels long (starting from solving puzzle, fighting overseer, meeting blackshores, go to war with threnodian, handling crisis with the sentinel, then fight the sentinel, etc etc) but it also feels jumpy to move between overaching conflicts. I can feel that the dev just put those conflicts and groups intro (fractsidus, blackshores, midnight ranger, court of savantae, etc) to extend the story, like cram it into one big narrative, yet what I get is just basic conversations followed by lore dump, with no surprise, no reveal. As a nation raging in endless war with threnodian, and crisis with the sentinel vs fractsidus scheme, there is no dialogue full of strategy on how to handle such conflicts. As I said earlier, the conversation in huanglong's arc feel way too casual, and mostly too linear, while lore/info dump sometimes being put out of place (like intentionally being thrown away just to prolong the dialogue, instead of making the narrative feels like a complete puzzle it ended up look jumpy and messy, especially with the constant repetition).

4. Side quest and exploration quest mostly borrows the same formula of the main quest. Maybe slightly worse because they repeat the same explanation about certain lore, the lore doesnt appear as expanding but instead being repeated again and again (different sentences, but same context). I still remember how in the main quest they explain more than once about certain terms like threnodian, retroact rain, taced discord, tacet field, waveworn phenoomena, sentinel Jue's ability of altering time, etc etc and it feels highly redundant. Meanwhile, certain npcs in the side/exploration quest would sometimes repeat that same info/lore as if they really try hard to make rover understand. I know that rover is amnesiac, but I dont think he/she is dumb enough to be constantly in need of such reminder again and again.

Well, that's only Huanglong (jinzhou). I will update my review soon after I finish rinascita, Im gonna review everytime I complete a nation's main quest (apart from some of their exploration quest and side quest) and see how the story/worlbuilding in this game expand more. 

6/10 rating for how they handle the worldbuilding/lore and integrate them into the main quest (as of now) -- lore dump, which also falls repetitive.
6/10 rating for how the conversation among characters run in the main quest (as of now) -- way too casual, too basic and simple.
5/10 rating for how they make the conflict appears engaging in the main quest (as of now) -- not much room for the conflict to expand narratively, how the chars handle/discuss the conflict narratively, and how the conflict ends in a plot twist format (turns out no plot twist, even there is no big reveal in the aftermath).

P.S. I play the game on medium spec PC. It runs well but with minimum settings, but still the visual looks decent and yeah no crash or laggy so far.

For the sake of playing and reviewing the game's story at least until lahai roi arc, and bcz I'm still in Huanglong, I will regard this game as RECOMMENDED bcz I dont have much to complaint apart from the story/lore/worldbuilding (as of now).

300+ hours played. Negative review.

A lot of my playtime was sunk cost. WuWa has just enough good stuff that I kept thinking the rest would catch up. Combat is pretty good, quickswapping is fun, Hiyuki’s iai attacks scratch the monkey-brain SHING itch, exploration can be enjoyable, and the elementary-school-level puzzles can be relaxing.

1.X WAS FUCKING AWFUL

The opening throws Frequencies, Resonators, Tacet Discords, the Lament and pseudo-science at you before giving you much reason to care.

WuWa too often mistakes information density for depth.

Then 1.0 tries an “Avengers Assemble” moment around the Ovathrax/Threnodian of War climax. The cast rolls up like I’m supposed to scream “HOLY SHIT, EVERYONE’S HERE!” when many barely had enough development to matter. It wanted an ensemble payoff it hadn’t earned.

WUWA HAS LORE. THAT DOESN’T MEAN IT HAS GOOD WORLDBUILDING.

A major concept should roughly go:

1. Introduce it.
2. Develop it until the audience understands how it affects the world.
3. Use, break, exploit, or subvert it.

WuWa constantly goes:

STEP 1 → FUCK STEP 2 → STEP 3.

Tethys. Mount Firmament. Fabrictorium of the Deep. Fortune-telling. Chaos. Journeying Paradise.

These are huge ideas, yet Kuro often introduces them in the same arc where Rover is already exploiting their rules. The lore exists, but rarely gets enough time to become part of the world.

Compare that to Morrowind’s Morag Tong. They are not just “cool legal assassins.” The Great Houses are powerful and full of grievances, so sanctioned assassination acts as a pressure valve for disputes that might otherwise become open war. One faction touches law, religion, House politics, culture and the balance of power.

That is worldbuilding. WuWa too often gives me the PowerPoint instead.

If a phenomenon is supposedly world-changing, show me what it does to normal life: industries, laws, superstitions, religion, politics. WuWa often rushes past that connective tissue to reach the next revelation.

IUNO IS THE BEST EXAMPLE

Put a gun to my head and ask me to explain exactly how we saved Iuno in plain English.

We went into the sea, collected memories, grew a tree, did metaphysical shit, cut it down, and now she’s back.

I guess???

Yes, there is lore explaining it. That is not the point.

The story introduces the metaphysical rules, explains the exception, and uses that exception to solve the climax almost simultaneously. I have barely internalized what “Chaos” means or what the causal rules are before Rover is already navigating around them.

Fantasy can be completely insane and still feel coherent. The audience just needs time to understand the rules before those rules become the solution. WuWa often introduces the knife five minutes before Rover needs to stab God with it.

That is why supposedly enormous revelations can land as “apparently that’s a thing now” instead of “holy shit, that changes everything.”

ROVER IS THE CENTER OF THE FUCKING UNIVERSE

Fractsidus? Rover.
Sentinels? Rover.
Ancient systems? Rover.
Historical figures? Probably knew Rover.
Regional crisis? Rover is uniquely qualified to fix it.

At this point I don’t wonder about a new region’s history. I wonder what Past Rover did there.

Everyone also glazes Rover. Jiyan is THE GENERAL, yet the story bends over backwards to involve the newly awakened amnesiac in military strategy. Important people trust, admire, or attach themselves to Rover absurdly quickly.

I’d kill for someone to ask: “Who the fuck are you and why should I care?”

ROVER IS ALSO BORING AS HELL

The most important person in history has the personality of drywall.

Calm. Nice. Helpful. Mildly amused. Mildly concerned.

The voice and attitude are so neutral that gigantic revelations land like being told the grocery store closes early.

WuWa is extremely linear, so this is not a blank-slate RPG excuse. I’m not meaningfully defining Rover’s morality or major decisions. The game already decided who Rover is, so why not give them a stronger personality?

I hope Rover gets their memories back someday because maybe their personality is stored in there too.

THE AMNESIA IS A BOTTOMLESS MYSTERY BOX

Planescape: Torment handles amnesia vastly better. The Nameless One’s past creates enemies, victims, relationships and consequences Current Him must deal with. His missing past is the problem, not just a source of cool reveals.

Rover’s amnesia too often feels like an infinite writing coupon.

New ancient connection? Past Rover knew them.
New organization? Past Rover was involved.
Another revelation? Past Rover researched it.
Why doesn’t Rover remember? Amnesia.

Past Rover also discarded the context behind countless failures and decisions. Memory is not just trivia; it is reasoning. Erase your mistakes and you erase what you learned from making them.

Brilliant. We kept the notebook and deleted the scientist.

CHARACTERS FEEL LIKE BANNER ADVERTISEMENTS

Too many characters feel written around their banner cycle instead of integrated into an ongoing cast.

A new character gets major relevance, cinematics, trauma and lore while being sold, then often fades away once the marketing cycle moves on.

Chisa is the perfect example. She effectively loses around twenty years of everyone else’s lives. Her family thought she was dead. Her friends aged without her. She returns to a world that moved on.

That should produce grief, alienation and the horror of lost time. Instead, the reunion and aftermath get nowhere near the weight the setup deserves.

Temporary story content makes it worse. Xiangli Yao’s original introduction was heavily tied to an old event, while Somnoire has recurring lore and characters but event-limited context. New players can hit material that assumes Rover knows people or concepts they never got to meet.

Canon story should not evaporate.

THE MAIN QUEST SOMETIMES BARELY WANTS YOU TO PLAY IT

Some story fights are so protected that failure barely feels possible, and missed QTEs can continue for you. If the cinematic finishes the action anyway, why ask me to press the button? If a fight refuses to let me lose, the boss threatening me becomes theater.

SIDE QUESTS ARE OFTEN BORING AS FUCK

Side quests should be where the worldbuilding breathes: local culture, beliefs, politics, jobs, families and how ordinary people live around all this insane technology and metaphysics.

Instead, too many amount to: talk to NPC, walk 200m, press F, kill three enemies, return.

Some companion quests are alright. Most side content is forgettable.

THE GACHA STILL SUCKS

“But it’s better than Genshin!”

I know. I don’t care.

If one guy shoots me in the head and another shoots me in the foot, the second guy treated me better.

I HAVE STILL BEEN FUCKING SHOT.

Older limited characters can disappear for stupid lengths of time while the roster keeps expanding. In a character collection game, that is ridiculous.

Pulling a character and finding their materials, bosses, Echoes or region story-gated is also annoying. Congratulations on your new character; please finish your homework before using them properly.

THE GOOD STUFF IS WHY THIS IS SO FRUSTRATING

Combat is good. Quickswapping is fun. Hiyuki goes SHING and brain goes :D. Exploration can be pretty good. The puzzles are easy as hell, but sometimes square peg → square hole → chest is enough.

That is why I kept playing.

Kuro needs patience. Let concepts breathe. Let characters remain part of the world after their banners. Let people distrust Rover. Let someone else be the expert. Give Rover an actual personality. Stop using amnesia as an infinite generator of retroactive importance.

You have a world.

USE THE FUCKING WORLD.

After 300+ hours, I’m negative not because WuWa has nothing good in it, but because it constantly reminds me how much better it could be.

If Steam ever starts refunding human lifespan, Kuro owes me about twelve and a half days.

Overall, Wuthering Waves is a fun open-world action RPG with excellent combat and great visuals. The story and progression can be hit-or-miss, but the gameplay is good enough to keep me coming back.

TLDR; S-tier gacha, B+ tier F2P game

Probably have around 700 hours and 18 lost 50/50s on the game; I only added it to Steam not too long ago. Furthermore, I have quite a bit of time on other gachas: ~30 hrs in Genshin, ~100 hrs in ZZZ, and ~100 hrs in Endfield. I'll be drawing comparisons to them here and there, for better or for worse. For further context, I play exclusively on PC with a controller, in English and am a light spender (battlepass and daily login).

[b]Positives:[/b]

* BEAUTIFUL game. The environmental design is breathtaking on good graphics settings, to the point where I could cry seeing people playing on mobile. Few games have turned me into such a tourist, constantly taking pictures. Other than the environment, I think the UI, character models, VFX, and music are also really good. The music especially is really good at times, with some notable ones getting into my playlist alongside the Lichdragon Fortissax boss fight music.
* The combat is super responsive, fun, deep, and visually amazing. No other gacha game (that I've played) even comes close.
* The mobility is very good. Wanting to replay Genshin is an impossibility if I can't sprint up walls; I've had enough rock climbing simulators. As much as I wish I could simply use the wings instead of the motorcycle for flying around, since the wings feel just that AMAZING to use, the motorcycle is good enough.
* The rendered animations are hype, but that's not really anything new, just worth mentioning.
* Performance has rarely been a problem on near-maxed graphics settings (though I've only recently started getting crashes, not sure why).
* I think the story is pretty good and interesting (at least after Jinzhou), even if I'm averse to amnesia plots. Playing as a dude recovering his memories and going around the world saving anime girls from interstellar gods and trauma does not get old too quickly. (However, there is a big caveat as to the main story experience, which I'll get into below.)
* I think there's a good diversity of characters without having to go in weird directions. Call me a tourist, but I appreciate that. Use-wise, there's quite a lot of team variety, though there are distinct metas, ofc.
* Guaranteed weapon on hard pity (looking at you, ZZZ) is appreciated (gacha anchoring at its finest).
* The events are really good; I've especially really loved the rhythm and roguelike events.
* The native, in-built guidebook is a really good addition for people to use without having to open a wiki for many things, though needing the guidebook in the first place is a bit questionable.

[b]Negatives:[/b]

* The main story experience is HORRIBLE. Mind you, I don't skip dialogue in the main story, and my perspective will come from that. (Note: if skipping everything is the solution, then that just proves that it's bad.) The entire experience after every update is:

  5 minutes of dialogue with inconsequential responses in between → walk 20 meters → more dialogue → walk another 50 meters → fight 3 enemies with the most boring and weak characters in the game → more dialogue → travel somewhere → dialogue → cinematic (hype) → 10-minute boss fight with the boring characters → cinematic (hype) → dialogue → repeat next update

  What doesn't help is that the dialogue is often very boring. The voice acting can often be dull, and the animation and character interactions are uninspired at best. Zenless clears in this regard. (However, roughly since Denia was added, I've noticed slightly more expressive interactions, which is a good thing to see.)
  This bad experience, especially when the story isn't particularly interesting at the start of the game, makes it very hard to introduce new people to the game. (Alongside resource management and whatnot.)
* Though I'm generally positive about the combat, wanting to make the best use of your newly gained limited Resonator will require a PhD to understand the 3–10 paragraph skill descriptions that introduce you to like 10–15 new terms that are further referenced by 5 other new terms. Most people, myself included, just throw their hands up in the air and search for rotation guides because the complexity creep is ridiculous, and it was already pushing it with Cartethyia from a year ago.
* Echo management is horrible. Even if the cap of 3000 may sound like a lot, I've had to manage it one too many times. Wish they'd either increase the cap or make the tool less confusing to use. (The tool itself is fine, but the way it works is hit or miss.)
* There is an issue with audio mixing that has plagued the game for the entirety of my time playing it, where the moment you move any other slider aside from the master volume, all audio mixing goes out of whack. Furthermore, the music is often too loud during dialogue and may completely ruin the atmosphere.
* Game size is...[b]too big.[/b]

[b]Extra thoughts:[/b]

* Let me use the wings in all new areas, I beg. The motorcycle feels super clunky and unwieldy in comparison.
* Gacha game design aside, I think they could increase the reserved energy.
* Having to patch the game and then restart it almost every other day is really annoying
* Be able to change the main stats of echoes in a batch.
* Have the equipped weapon show on the character (still upset about Zani *cries in sig*).
* Not sure if I'm simply dense or something, but the newish Tune Strain/Tune Rapture/Mistune/Off-Tune/... mechanics do not make much sense to me, but oh well.

[b]F2P Friendly?[/b] About as much as any other gacha game, to be honest. While 1 or 2 (mainly Verina) standard banner characters are pretty decent, alongside some 4-stars (Mortefi and Sanhua), they are undoubtedly outclassed by the limited banner characters. The standard banner 5-star weapons, on the other hand, are amazing in terms of versatility, very often landing in the top 3 best weapons for any given Resonator. Even some 4-stars are surprisingly amazing, like Variation on Shorekeeper.

That all being said, you can comfortably complete the game's main content (excluding endgame activities like ToA, WiWa, TH, and EM) without spending anything, as long as you manage your resources and build a decent enough team. Whether or not you'll enjoy that is up in the air.

[b]Update:[/b]
* Fingers still crossed that they add for companion quests for the newer resonators (especially Augusta, Lucilla, Hiyuki, Hsin, Qingxiao (unbiased))
* Still praying that I get to use wings in the new regions instead of the fuckass motorcycle and swordflight (at least lemme take pictures while flying cmon)
* Echo management has been massively improved
* Allegedly with the introduction of the launcher, that they'll be rolling out, you'll be able to adjust the download size as well as make it adaptive (huge if true). If they make it so new players only install the starting region, I think that will make it a lot easier to get new people into the game (also making Shorekeeper more than a rental, tearing holo wifey away from you is brutal. As someone who played way before that was a benefit, I do still wish for her to be permanent character all new players can unlock in some way).
* I've come up with a bit of a conspiracy theory that they are purposely making the kits complex and convoluted so people look up guides, so they see what is "optimal", and what happens to be optimal is often characters and weapons that you do not have. So I believe the kit complexity indirectly leads to FOMO which leads to higher likely hood to pull. (if true, genius.)

[h1]GREAT GAME. AWFUL MONETIZATION. F2P PLAYERS DESERVE BETTER.[/h1]

Wuthering Waves is a genuinely good game buried under a monetization system I simply cannot support.

And instead of just saying [i]“gacha bad”[/i], let's look at the actual numbers.

[h1]THE F2P REALITY[/h1]

A normal F2P player receives only [b]60 Astrite per day[/b] from Daily Activity.

One pull costs [b]160 Astrite[/b].

That means an entire day of dailies gives you only:

[b]0.375 pulls.[/b]

[list]
[*][b]1 pull[/b] = about [b]2.7 DAYS[/b] of dailies
[*][b]10 pulls[/b] = about [b]27 DAYS[/b] of dailies
[*][b]80 pulls[/b] = about [b]213 DAYS[/b] of dailies
[/list]

And here's the important part:

[b]80 pulls does NOT even guarantee the limited character you actually want.[/b]

The Featured Resonator banner has an [b]80-pull hard pity[/b], but your first 5-star has only a [b]50% chance[/b] of being the featured character.

Lose the 50/50?

You may need another 80 pulls.

[h1]160 PULLS = 25,600 ASTRITE[/h1]

At 60 Astrite per day, that represents roughly:

[h1]426 DAYS OF DAILY ASTRITE[/h1]

[i]For ONE guaranteed limited character.[/i]


[h1]WANT THEIR SIGNATURE WEAPON TOO?[/h1]

The limited weapon banner can require another:

[b]80 pulls = 12,800 Astrite[/b]

So in the worst case:

[b]Character:[/b] 160 pulls  
[b]Weapon:[/b] 80 pulls  

[h1]240 PULLS = 38,400 ASTRITE[/h1]

That's the equivalent of:

[b]640 DAYS OF DAILY ASTRITE.[/b]

Yes.

[b]640 days.[/b]


[h1]"BUT THE GAME GIVES YOU MORE ASTRITE!"[/h1]

Yes, it does.

You also receive Astrite from:

[list]
[*]Events
[*]Story
[*]Exploration
[*]Chests
[*]Achievements
[*]Endgame activities
[*]Patch rewards
[/list]

But there is one massive difference:

[b]Most exploration, story, chest and achievement rewards are ONE-TIME rewards.[/b]

Once you have completed them, they are gone.

You cannot endlessly farm Astrite just because you are willing to play more.

Your normal repeatable daily income still remains extremely limited.

For Version 3.6, F2P calculations put the total rewards at roughly:

[b]11,800 Astrite + 12 limited character pulls[/b]

if you complete essentially everything available during the patch.

That's roughly:

[h1]85 LIMITED CHARACTER PULLS[/h1]

during an entire six-week patch.

Now remember:

[b]Worst-case guarantee for ONE featured character = 160 pulls.[/b]

So even completing practically an entire patch worth of F2P content does not necessarily guarantee the limited character being advertised to you.


[h1]AND IT GETS WORSE FOR NEW PLAYERS[/h1]

Some of those Astrite rewards come from difficult endgame activities.

Version 3.6 has roughly [b]2,800 Astrite tied to endgame content.[/b]

Meaning a newer F2P player may not even be capable of earning the full theoretical F2P amount.

So when people say:

[i]"You get around X amount of pulls every patch!"[/i]

remember that those calculations often assume you:

[list]
[*]Log in consistently
[*]Complete the events
[*]Complete the new content
[*]Explore
[*]Do the endgame
[*]Claim all temporary rewards
[/list]

Miss content?

[b]Those pulls are gone.[/b]


[h1]NOW LET'S TALK ABOUT DUPLICATES[/h1]

Characters don't simply end after obtaining them once.

Each character has [b]six additional Sequence Nodes[/b].

To fully max out a limited character, you generally need to obtain that character:

[h1]SEVEN TIMES.[/h1]

One original copy + six additional copies.

And then, of course, there is still their separate signature weapon.

So the monetization doesn't stop at:

[i]"Congratulations! You got the character."[/i]

There are additional character copies and weapons waiting behind even more banners.


[h1]THIS IS THE PART I REFUSE TO SUPPORT[/h1]

I have absolutely nothing against developers making money.

Wuthering Waves is free.

Servers cost money.

Developers deserve salaries.

Artists, programmers, animators, composers and voice actors deserve to be paid.

[b]That is not the problem.[/b]

Sell me:

[list]
[*]Skins
[*]Cosmetics
[*]Mounts
[*]Battle passes
[*]Expansions
[*]A subscription
[*]A complete character for a reasonable fixed price
[/list]

I will happily pay for a game I enjoy.

What I do NOT want to support is a system built around:

[list]
[*]Premium currency
[*]Limited-time banners
[*]50/50 mechanics
[*]Pity systems
[*]Character duplicates
[*]Signature weapons
[*]Fear of missing out
[*]Constantly rotating characters
[/list]

All conveniently designed around making spending money extremely easy.


[quote]
[b]A game being free does not automatically make every monetization system reasonable.[/b]
[/quote]


[h1]60 ASTRITE VS. 160 ASTRITE[/h1]

This single comparison tells you a lot.

[b]Daily reward: 60 Astrite[/b]

[b]One pull: 160 Astrite[/b]

You don't even receive enough premium currency from an entire day's standard daily activity to make:

[b]ONE pull.[/b]

Not ten pulls.

Not a guaranteed character.

[b]One pull.[/b]

And one pull doesn't guarantee anything meaningful.


[h1]"BUT WUWA IS MORE GENEROUS THAN OTHER GACHAS!"[/h1]

Maybe.

But this argument completely misses the point.

[quote]
[b]“Better than another gacha” does NOT automatically mean consumer-friendly.[/b]
[/quote]

If one game charges you $1,000 for something and another charges you $700, the second system does not magically become good simply because something worse exists.

The comparison should not be:

[i]"Is this gacha nicer than another gacha?"[/i]

The comparison should be:

[b]"Does this game respect my time and my money?"[/b]


[h1]THE SAD PART? THE GAME ITSELF IS REALLY GOOD.[/h1]

The combat is excellent.

The animations are beautiful.

The world looks fantastic.

The characters clearly have a lot of work put into them.

There are obviously incredibly talented developers behind this game.

[b]And that's exactly why the monetization disappoints me so much.[/b]

A genuinely great game should not need psychological monetization systems designed around limited availability, random outcomes and repeated copies of characters.


[h1]I DON'T HATE WUTHERING WAVES.[/h1]

I actually WANT games like this to succeed.

But I don't want this monetization model to become something we simply accept as normal.

There is a massive difference between:

[b]"I want to support a game I love."[/b]

and

[b]"I feel pressured to spend because the character I want disappears soon and I might lose a 50/50."[/b]


[h1]PLEASE THINK BEFORE YOU SPEND.[/h1]

If you enjoy Wuthering Waves completely F2P:

[b]Good. Enjoy it.[/b]

If you buy a small monthly pass because you enjoy the game:

[b]That's your choice.[/b]

If you spend money on characters because you understand the system and can comfortably afford it:

[b]That's also your choice.[/b]

But please understand what these systems are built around before spending hundreds or even thousands.

Don't let FOMO decide how much your entertainment is worth.


[quote]
[h1]GOOD GAMES DESERVE SUPPORT.

PREDATORY MONETIZATION DOES NOT.[/h1]
[/quote]

[b]Your money is your vote.[/b]

[b]And this is one monetization model I personally refuse to vote for.[/b]

This is the first gacha game that I've played besides the Battle Cats, so I can't personally compare it against other gachas, but my god is this game fun. I've spent a lot of time playing factory games like Satisfactory, and I've fully 100%ed both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, which have similar combat and exploration experiences, so this game was right up my alley. 
The main reason I started playing this game in the first place after finding it in the Steam store was the integration of Satisfactory-esq factory building into an RPG gacha game, and after experiencing the factory gameplay in it's entirety, I can say that it absolutely lived up to my interest. It's not nearly as in-depth or as technically challenging as dedicated factory games can be, but it's still plenty of fun, and as of the most recent game update, has a pretty substantial amount of depth. 
As far as the semi-open world exploration and story goes, Endfield also holds up really well. It's a bit slow to start in the beginning, and the whole first region feels a bit lackluster, but the more recent content releases in the second region have really stepped up the storytelling, and I've been super engaged with them. (To the point where I'm now starting the original Arknights to get more story context for Endfield!) The character designs are fantastic, and I love how characters from different backgrounds have distinct accents depending on the region they're from in the English dub. The map is super dense with detailed environments and side quests, and there's tons of collectibles to be found everywhere, with cosmetic rewards for finding all of them.
The combat in this game is another highlight. As someone who's never touched an open world gacha before, it took me a while to really understand the combat system, but it takes a decently long time for the content to become even remotely challenging, so it was never really an issue for me. Once you flesh out your roster of operators and start to build teams that properly synergize with each other, damage rotations become really satisfying to pull off. As far as I can tell, Endfield is very accessible to free to play players, as I've been able to clear pretty much every single piece of content in the game with a fully free to play team. The only content I'm still struggling with are a couple of boss time trials, and some of the timed DPS check stages in endgame content, though the only reward from these stages are flashy medals to display on your profile, so I don't see an issue there!
My only complaint with Endfield is that it doesn't have the best performance on my first-gen Steam Deck, and it stutters quite a bit even on the lowest settings. I've heard that Hypergryph are working on dedicated game optimizations for Steam Deck users, so I hope that this will get better in the future. I've had no issues on my main PC running Linux, and can run the game at a stable 120fps in 1440p with max settings. (If you play on Linux, I would recommend running DW-Proton, as I believe there are still some issues with standard proton versions and the game's anti-cheat.)
The game seems to only be getting better and better with each new patch, and I will definitely be sticking with it as it continues to grow! I highly recommend trying this game out, you won't regret it :)

TL;DR:
• Pros: Generous gacha rates overall, responsive devs (Hypergryph), no need to rush or chase meta teams, and fully clearable with F2P units.
• Cons: Repetitive endgame gear grind and stubborn RNG specifically when farming weapon etchings.
• Verdict: Worth playing whether you want a relaxed pace or a brutal challenge.

----------------------------------------------REVIEW-----------------------------------------------

     I've been playing Arknights and Arknights: Endfield for a good while before Endfield was brought onto Steam, and it is a great game. If you are just starting out, there is plenty to do, so do not feel like you have to rush the story plot. Don't get FOMO—play casual or play hardcore, the choice is yours.

     The RNG is not as bad as other games in the gacha space, and the dev team, Hypergryph, really does listen to the community. If there was ever a gacha game I would endorse or back—and I have played plenty—it would be Endfield hands down.

     The endgame loop can be repetitive, as upgrading simply requires putting time into your team by artificing their gear and etching your weapons. While I stated earlier that the RNG is generous, in my experience, it is generous everywhere except etchings. I have run the same location for a while now trying to get the exact etching I want and it still hasn't dropped. Even so, I am not mad because I have gotten everything else I ever wanted in the game.
If you do want to spend, the battle pass is worth the price as it significantly boosts your account with materials. The $5 monthly top-up is also worth it if you want plenty of currency to summon on every banner. On the note of summoning, do not feel like you have to get every single character. Some of us do, and that is okay; some don't care, and that is okay too. Every team comp you see online is just meant to show good synergy if you happen to have those units. Those videos showing fast, single-team clear times should be used as a reference, not the standard—you can easily play through the whole game with the F2P team.

     With all that stated, you should definitely give the game a chance. It is easily approachable with a solid learning curve for developing your gaming skills. It can be fun and relaxing, or you can turn it up to brutal and unforgiving. 

     Give it a shot—I believe that this game truly deserves it.

Ultimately, I think that it is fine that Endfield exists, and that there is no problem if you are a fan of it, whether you're new to the series or not. However, as a very dedicated OG Arknights fan, this is THE most disappointing release that I have ever experienced when it comes to an IP that I love. I will be using this review system to vent my frustrations, as there is no such system elsewhere, at least not officially in English, and I have been holding on to these thoughts for close to a year now. My time played on Steam is very low, I know. I have put, I would estimate, around 200 hours into the launcher version, so take the Steam hours with a grain of salt. 

Everything about Endfield feels antithetical to what Arknights stands for in my mind. The entire gameplay loop is that very homogenized, standard, typical, "safe", whatever you wanna call it, 3D gacha gameplay. Like any Mihoyo game, there is an "open world" to "explore", which is just a handful of kinda-sorta large sorta-kinda "open" maps to walk around in, which can be further boiled down to "levels" that just have some extra running room in any direction, with minor collectibles and landmarks scattered throughout. There is no environmental design space here that hasn't already been tread by other developers years ago. Despite this, you are STILL limited in what exactly you can "explore", based on story progress which makes sense, but also arbitrary factory progress, which is much less rewarding than the developers had maybe intended. The map design in general feels very shallow and uninteresting as a result. Original Arknights is entirely level-based, and it leans into this by developing brand new tower defense challenges to overcome with your units every content update. Load-bearing "new" there, as Endfield's design feels downright unoriginal in too many places, which is my key point here.

Speaking of units, Endfield also suffers from having very uninteresting team building and general combat design, at least to me. Looking online, you'll see a 50/50 split, but it is undeniable that, yet again, there is nothing new to the design space here. Primary attack, special button, ult button. You control a team of characters that you can freely switch between, each of which having abilities that interact with each other and the enemies a little bit differently. There's, essentially, DPS characters, and DPS-enabling characters. These characters can equip "gear" with passive set-based effects, made to further improve performance after their base skills have been fully invested into. Sound familiar? It is, again, *exactly* like every other 3D gacha out there. There is a little bit of nuance in terms of how you more literally approach fights in this game versus the others, but frankly, the same can be said for all those other gachas, too, so that's not exactly a positive mark for Endfield. Arknights OG remains to be the most open-ended and diverse gacha in terms of individual character strength, their roles, and usability in a variety of maps, almost 7 years after release. Saying otherwise would be sort of disingenuous, and for this point being one of the main reasons that I love the original game, I could not be more disappointed with Endfield. 

I'm going to ignore saying anything substantial about the factory gameplay here, as it is honestly a little interesting to me, but it is just unrewarding to invest into. As it stands, you're required to invest into certain corners of it to progress in the maps and story, but otherwise, it is only used for the previously mentioned gearing system. But it also seems like the developers are still figuring out how exactly they want the day-to-day player to interact with the factory in general, so in order to avoid saying anything about it that will age poorly, I will end my thoughts on it here.

The last thing I will touch on is the story. I like the original Arknights' worldbuilding and general narrative quite a lot. Individual character threads can be very gratifying to follow through with reading as well. While the writing on a dialogue level is not my favorite, the other aspects of what is given to you makes up for that, and keeps the world of Terra feeling fresh and alive. I cannot say anything nearly as nice about Talos-II, the Endfield planet. Yes, I know, the game is still very early in development, especially for a gacha. But this is a gacha with a legacy; it is the soft sequel to Arknights itself. It's a little unfair to assume that fans of the original will NOT have expectations for said sequel, and frankly, I am not interested in anything that is happening on Talos-II, at all. Nothing feels like it has weight or consequences, not for the characters nor for the factions involved. I sincerely do not understand what exactly I am supposed to feel invested in when it comes to the narrative. All I want to know more about is how Talos-II is connected to Terra and Rhodes Island, which has a lot more to do with being invested in Arknights OG than it does being interested in Endfield. It is not absolutely horrendous, it is just a disappointment.

Again, the game in a vacuum is fine. If you like this type of 3D "exploration" gacha with the pseudo third-person action gameplay, then there's probably a lot for you to dig into here. It might be overwhelming, but a lot of gacha fans should consider that a good thing. My main point is that I am simply disappointed as an Arknights fan, and that I was expecting much more thoughtful gameplay and writing alike. I am just thankful that the original game never went away or lost steam in terms of its content updates. If you like Arknights for the same reasons that you dislike most other gachas, then please, do not set your expectations high for Endfield. Hopefully, that way, you will appreciate it more than I have.

Sadly, in the end, I do not recommend this game.

Basically, this game feels like the embodiment of "jack of all trades, but master of none"

At its core, the game is a third person open world gacha game, like Genshin, and all the other games like Genshin, but it is also a factory game, and a tower defense game, and a "parkour" game, all wrapped into one, and all these parts never really seem to mix together properly, at least for me. If you are a fan of any one of those genres, you're better of finding a game that specializes in that genre alone.

Aside from all the different parts of the game not really meshing well together, the game also bombards you with a ton of both limited time and permanent game modes and challenges, making the gameplay feel even more tedious and diluted.

This game is supposed to be a gacha game, and the main goal in every gacha game is grinding materials for pulls, but because of the sheer amount of stuff to do, the material rewards are spread really thin, so you either have to do ton of "dailies" everyday, or spend money. Of course this is also true for other gacha games, but I feel like the ratio is especially bad for this game. For someone like me who plays other games, even other gacha games, it feels like trying to squeeze blood out of a rock.

These are main reasons why I can't really recommend this game. The graphics, the music, even the character designs, are all amazing, but ultimately this is a game that doesn't respect your time, it demands a lot, while giving comparatively little, even when compared to other gacha games, and that's saying a lot

They tried to inject factory building mechanics into a gacha game and completely failed miserably. You will spend most of your time not actually fighting, or even doing quests. Instead you will creating production lines for better gear and items to sell to access better gear to make more production lines. That is if you can even get production lines to stay producing, which then you will need to figure out the flow rate of items so you can adjust and hopefully not run out of resources. This is important because the same resources that help you create better factories and gear also are used to power your factories. That's right, you have a power grid that you have to set up to even have factories that run. However, you need to remember this is a gacha fighting game so you will get timed events that will determine your rewards based on well your team fights.

You will have a few weeks to fight in these events but you most likely will not be able to because you either do not have the right team or gear to continue and/or you have not progressed far enough in the main quest line to reach these events. Either way you will be losing out on many things in events that would make your progress easier through quests because you were not able to progress through quests to get to play events. They put way too many mechanics in this game and still expect you to pay to get better characters/improve characters.

Overall this is still a gacha game, so don't play this expecting any different. The factory mechanics in this game would have been a good idea had the gacha mechanics not been involved. I know the game is free because of the gacha mechanics but it doesn't make sense when coupled with the factory mechanics.

With some tweaking of the factory mechanics and removal of gacha events it may have been a great game, but ultimately it became overbloated garbage. It will feel fun at first because it is not too much like other gacha games, though you will eventually become annoyed and disappointed when it is just another time sink. You have been warned.

For context, I'm an OG Arknights player who played through Chapter 13 and eventually dropped the game. I'm also a Day 1 Endfield player, so I came into this game already familiar with the Arknights universe and genuinely interested in seeing what they would do with it.

Unfortunately, Arknights: Endfield has been pretty underwhelming for me. It has a lot of potential, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.

1. Great world-building and character designs, but lackluster storytelling.

I'll give credit where it's due. The world-building is great, and the character designs are genuinely good. The setting itself has a lot of potential.

But the way they actually use these characters and the world in the story? Pretty disappointing.

The dialogue and storytelling feel painfully mid. Having an interesting world and well-designed characters doesn't mean much when the story fails to make me care about what's happening.

And this isn't something I expected to be perfect. I already had my issues with the original Arknights' storytelling, particularly Chapters 10–13, which eventually made me drop it. I was hoping Endfield would improve on that, but unfortunately, it hasn't really convinced me either.

2. Combat looks good, but gets boring pretty quickly.

Visually, the combat is impressive. The graphics, animations, and effects are well done, and I have no complaints about the presentation.

But the actual gameplay? Most of the time, it just holding left-click.

There's nothing particularly exciting about the combat itself. It looks flashy, sure, but looking good and being fun to play are two different things.

I expected something more engaging, especially from a game carrying the Arknights name.

3. The gacha system is fine if you only want one copy, but terrible if you want duplicates.

I can see this system working for people who only care about obtaining a single copy of a character.

But if you're someone who wants duplicates? Good luck.

Unless you're lucky, the system feels pretty unforgiving. In the worst-case scenario, you could end up pulling multiple 5-stars and still only walk away with a single copy of the featured banner character.

I understand that it's a gacha game, but that doesn't automatically make the system any less frustrating.

4. Where did the dark atmosphere of the original Arknights go?

This is probably one of my biggest disappointments.

As someone who played the original Arknights up until Chapter 13, one of the things that kept me interested was its dark and serious atmosphere.

The original wasn't afraid to explore depressing themes, morally questionable decisions, and the uglier sides of its world. That atmosphere was a huge part of what made Arknights stand out to me.

Endfield, on the other hand, feels like it has lost a lot of that identity.

I understand that Endfield is supposed to be its own game, and I'm not expecting it to be a carbon copy of the original. But considering that it's part of the same franchise, I was hoping it would retain at least some of that darker atmosphere.

For me, it just doesn't hit the same.

5. Event rewards feel lackluster.

The event rewards are honestly pretty disappointing.

I think events should feel rewarding enough to make players want to participate. But here, the rewards just don't feel like enough.

I'm not expecting the developers to hand out everything for free, but there should at least be a decent balance between the effort you put in and what you get out of it.

Right now, that balance doesn't feel great.

Overall:

I've been playing Endfield since Day 1, and as someone who spent a considerable amount of time with the original Arknights, I really wanted to like this game.

And to be fair, it's not all bad. The graphics are great, the character designs are good, and the world-building has a lot of potential.

But that's exactly what makes it frustrating.

The foundation is there, yet the game doesn't do enough with it. The story is mediocre, the combat gets repetitive, the gacha system is frustrating for anyone aiming for duplicates, and the event rewards don't feel particularly worthwhile.

Most importantly, it doesn't have the same dark atmosphere that originally got me interested in Arknights.

I already lost interest in the original Arknights around Chapters 10–13 because I wasn't enjoying the direction of the story anymore. I was hoping Endfield would give me a reason to get invested in this universe again.

Unfortunately, it hasn't.

I'm not saying Endfield is a bad game. It's just I expected a lot more than what I'm getting.

Maybe it'll improve over time, but as it stands, I can't recommend it.

It has it's issues though: the most effective strategy seems to be to bring an overbuilt healer or shielder, or alternatively run into the range of the enemies attacks, just so that you can I-Frame, because otherwise your teammates get themselves killed...; in general, it's either trivial, or you get stomped, nothing in between, and actually building a team is pain. 

Then onto the next part I can't stand: the factory, which is also responsible for most of the awful tutorial dumps. It is almost essential to progression, despite the marketing having claimed it weren't necessary for progression, or playing the game. It actually, for the most part, and as long as you don't care for exploring the entire map, it really isn't, but it absolutely is, if you do. You see, this game has great art, and environmental storytelling, and good-enough to actually good music. For me, most of it's value, besides in hoping, and nowadays even trusting the devs to deliver better story, lore, and connection to the mainline Arknights story, lies in visual tourism, exploration, and just admiring the game's beauty. The game just made me actually detest the factory though, by forcing it onto me when I first started playing at launch, instead of letting me approach it at my own pace. Maybe that's better now, maybe some other players have higher tolerance for this sort of stuff, but I didn't come for Factorio, I came for Arknights+Action Combat+3d., so the game burned me out of this part of the game almost immediately. Another issue I have with the game is the rampant oversexualization of some characters in the opening of the game. There is just no reason for it, and coming from Arknights mainline, it actually made me loose quite a bit of trust in the developer, if they're willing to sell their characters like this. They toned it down since.

So all in all, I give a cautious recommendation, if you have a high tolerance for awful tutorials, awful onboarding, and an awful story and characters' characterization at the beginning, you get rewarded with some bits of good story that were released later, characters that aren't sold primarily through fan service and forcing uncomforatble implied romance with a character I couldn't care less about (in part because it was forced onto the player), and absolutely gorgeous visuals.

In other words, this game became more of Arknights, and I like it, and am hopefull for the future.

[h1]Steam Review: Arknights: Endfield[/h1]
[i]Playtime Note: Played since launch on the original launcher before migrating to Steam. Praise Gaben![/i]

[h2]TLDR; Verdict: 8 / 10 — A Solid, Sci-Fi Factory ARPG[/h2]
[h3]The Good[/h3]
+Anime Aesthetic: Sharp, high-quality 3D anime visuals that stand out from the typical Genshin-style rendering.

+Active Squad Combat: Real-time combat keeps all 4 characters active on the field simultaneously rather than swapping one by one.

+Automation Mechanics: Deep factory-building system—the factory must grow!

+Atmospheric World: Beautiful environmental design across the map (minus the goo clearing).

+Deep Lore: Serves as a narrative continuation for long-time Arknights fans (though fully accessible to newcomers).

[h3]The Bad & The Clunky[/h3]
-Tedious Loops: Both general gameplay tasks and late-game factory maintenance can become quite tedious over time.

-Gacha Model: Gacha systems inherent to the genre (no 50/50 pity system helps, but core gacha mechanics remain a downside).

-Performance Issues: Notable crashing issues earlier in the game's lifespan (especially in Wuling during v1.0–v1.1 on Windows). Performance on Linux was aweful, and returning to Windows in later patches shows fewer crashes, though some micro-stutters persist.

[b]tl;dr:[/b] The perfect example of the "potential meme" in a game form. Maybe one day it will be great, but I'm reviewing its current state, not what it could be.

As someone who was super into OG Arknights (before stopping around the Ho'olheyak banner), I thought this would be a great way to jump back into Arknights. Oh boy, was I wrong. At least it worked as an ad for the original game, as I found myself wanting to play that instead.

First off, the game has amazing graphics and runs great - though you've probably heard that many times before. The audio design is also fantastic; the sound effects and crunchy, bass-heavy feedback are really well done. And... that's about where the good things end.

[h2]Factory - aka Factorio at home[/h2]
It's not terrible, but because of how it's set up, there is really only one optimal way to build. Experimenting on your own only makes sense if you either genuinely love the logistics of it or you can somehow beat the solved meta layouts. Personally, I stopped caring about the factory after having to rebuild it from scratch every single patch.

[h2]Gacha[/h2]
This whole game suffers from a "X is great, but Y ruins it" design philosophy, starting with the most important part of the genre: the gacha.
[table equalcells=1]
    [tr]
        [th]The good[/th]
        [th]Countered by the bad[/th]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]120-pull guarantee instead of the usual 180[/td]
        [td]Pity does NOT carry over between banners - stop midway and you lose all progress[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]You get free pulls after doing 30 pulls[/td]
        [td]They don't count toward the 120 guarantee[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]No 75/25 chance weapon banner split[/td]
        [td]Weapons require their own scarce, separate gacha currency[/td]
    [/tr]
[/table]

On top of that, the devs are already showing their greedy side. Instead of the standard 10 tickets for banners, you get 5 banner-limited tickets, that expire when the banner ends, making long-term saving impossible. Plus, the pull-currency shop resets per patch instead of monthly like most gachas (including OG Arknights). 

Worse, they designed a system where pulling a character early actually feels like losing. Since character pulls generate the tokens needed to roll for weapons, getting a character early means you won't have enough tokens for their weapon - unless you use a credit card-sized solution or keep rolling on a banner after obtaining the character.
Initially, game was also super stingy when handling standard banner pulls. Something that is baseline in other games had to be fought for here. But hey, at least each survey asks why you didn't pull 6 copies of the character. That's important.

[h2]It gets worse: The Story[/h2]
The story is pure garbage - no sugarcoating it. It's yet another generic amnesiac-protagonist slop fest, where every single character exists solely to glaze the Endministrator for merely breathing. In OG Arknights side stories explored the world and its characters, even different concepts. Endfield side stories just exist to remind you how amazing your main character is. 

The main story is painfully bland. I quit the game after 1.3 because nothing ever happens, and characters speak so vaguely they manage to say nothing at all. You can  literally google `vagueposting king` (term without a single word related to the game) and find characters/screenshots from Endfield - it's that bad. "Let them cook" doesn't apply here. If they still need time to set up the story, they don't need more of it, they need new cooks. The 1.4 boss was an exception, not the new norm. In it's current form the story lacks any stakes/risks anything to bother investing time in it. It feels afraid to be anything but generic. Also I do not believe the take that early gacha stories have to be bad and Endfield is just part of the victims. They can be good, for example HSR had a great initial story with Belobog that culminated in a very nice boss fight.

Nothing in its current story feels earned, and there are zero stakes or risks worth investing time into. It feels terrified of being anything other than generic. 

[h2]Combat - aka I wish I was playing anything else[/h2]
This part is slightly subjective, as I'm not a fan of the game this combat system borrows from. Initially combat was supposed to be tactical, using slowed/stopped time, to plan out fights with manually placing AoE skills But because the devs so proudly proclaimed on stream that they hadn't compromised their original vision of the game - they completely changed it. 

What we have now is an awkward mashup of action and tactics that fails at both. Damage relies heavily on skills, which cost 1SP each with a max cap of 3 SP. Once you use all your skills, you're left holding auto-attack, hitting enemies with what feels like wet pillows while waiting for SP to regenerate - with a generous dodge button thrown in just to keep you awake.

[h2]Music - how did we fail here too[/h2]
Original Arknights made Hypergryph famous for being a music company disguised as a video game developer. What happened between games to turn the soundtrack into such a snoozefest? Not every OG track was a certified banger, sure, but in Endfield I can barely name a memorable track outside of the login screen and the 1.4 boss theme. The Contigency Contract event had a decent track, I guess, but if we have to compare CC themes then OG also beats Endfield like it's not even a contest.

[h2]Stop comparing it to OG Arknights![/h2]
This is my biggest gripe Nothing here warrants having "Arknights" in the title. Yes, returning faces show up with paper-thin explanation for why they're in the sqeuel, and  major lore points of the original are brought up only to be immediately brushed aside. One of the earliest themes of OG Arknights, the infected and persecution - is basically summarized as "yeah, there were some issues back then, don't worry about it". It feels like "Endfield featuring an Arknights collab" rather than a true sequel.

[h2]So much to do - yet nothing to see[/h2]
The community loves saying this game "respects your time" - and I agree, to the point where there's barely any reason to play it. 

[table equalcells=1]
[tr]
    [th]Game system[/th]
    [th]How it "respects your time"[/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
    [td]Tower defense (it IS an Arknights game, after all)[/td]
    [td]Relegated to a tiny resource gain that doesn't matter in the long run, and automatic material farming[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
    [td]Death Stranding-style courier deliveries[/td]
    [td]Completely pointless to engage with since passive/idle methods make way more money[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
    [td]"You don't have to pull every character"[/td]
    [td]True, until you DO pull someone and realize their kit is heavily nerfed without a specific team to enable their skills.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

Furthermore, it feels like the devs are actively walking back their own mechanics without knowing how to remove them. Previously, you had to use the factory to craft character gear; now, the devs just hand ouyt maxed gear sets so you can skip the factory entirely. There's also a feature to spend double stamina for double drops that requires special tickets - except the devs hand out so many tickets that the requirement has zero reason to exist now.

[h2]Longer tl;dr[/h2]
Maybe it'll be great one day, but right now I don't see how it recovers without a soft relaunch. The story remain its biggest anchor: even if 2.x somehow turns out amazing, new players will still have to slog through the absolute garbage fire that is 1.x to get there.

I spent hours venting and pouring my frustration into this review that I hit the character limit for a Steam review. I'll try to make it shorter but also comprehensible.

I have a love hate relationship with Arknights Endfield. On one hand, this is like one of the best action character swapping gacha game in the market with a unique hook of having automation/factory building mechanic for overall progression. But on the other hand, I'll always lament on how that factory building system is either underbaked or have too much annoyance that I wouldn't recommend this game if you're coming to this in hope for an alternative to the big factory building games like Factorio or Satisfactory. 

For clearance first, if you came into this game as someone who wants to experience the character swapping action combat, or if you are a fan of the original Arknights game, I can safely say you will come out satisfied. However, being a game that was advertised also as a factory building game, I have to criticize that aspect. My Steam game time was only like a few minutes, but I played Endfield the first time when I got into one of the closed beta BY CHANCE, played through it since 1.0, already at account level 60, and played up until Zhuang Fangyi's banner where I fell out of love for this game, and I stopped. But there are some days that I would go back to it, although not much substance are gained from those sessions.

In short, my main grievance with Endfield is the factory building system because it has some mechanics that I think is clashing with the whole philosophy of a factory building game either deliberately or not. My main criticism is that Conveyor Belts only have 1 speed, which bottlenecks every other factory systems in general, including but not limited to:

- Multiple belt placement for higher number ratios (ex: when there is like a 30 mat A and 60 mat B requirement for a process, you put out 3 line of belts, 1 for mat A and 2 for mat B).
- Space concerns due to limited land space, limited logistic ports, and multiple belt placements.
- No elevation/conveyor tunnel system leads to more space wasted for belts.

Other than that, the update cycles locking some improvements like the addition to raw material to properly supply a production feels really bad for the time before the update when you don't have the supply to 100% effectively produce a product. After I quit there's apparently gases system that improves the productivity of machines, so I thought I was so left out and felt my factories that I made before are such a waste because there's a better way to do things now is such a bad feeling. I love the gameplay loop of going back to the drawing board but doing it every update because they trickle in those improvements felt insulting and lack of freedom of expression in making the factory, which I think IS the main philosophy of a factory game.

As of when I played the game, the factory building system felt very restrictive and lack of freedom, where the main philosophy of a factory building game is that I have the freedom to create however I want, experiment the system that I designed, and seeing it work as intended, and if it's not working as intended, I get to troubleshoot and redo everything until it's working as the player's intended rather than the developer's intension. Due to the nature of Endfield being a gacha game, I don't think it will come to that point anytime sooner.

A few unordered points:

**Story: [u]Good[/u]**

Game has a marginally better story than ZZZ, but not even close to WuWa. I appreciate that the MSQ and the "Important" quests in the game are voiced, but you (the protag) are still mostly unvoiced. I don't know if this gets better after Valley 4.

**The Game and How It Feels: [u]Bad[/u]**

AKE as a game is overwhelmingly held back by the total lack of any sort of rewarding feeling after doing anything, EVEN after the game rewards you with a spoonful of Oroberyl (the pull currency). I guess if you are trying to do a dopamine detox, then it might work for you.

This game is the EXACT description of "Maintaining an account" rather than enjoying the game. You log in, have to do a ton of things, from stock trading and daily 100 to completing your weekly routine, collecting passively generated resources across all the maps/zones, selling goods to your outposts, and then making sure your energy is spent and checking that you have nothing that will expire.

And then finally, you can quit/log off.

**Combat: [u]Bad[/u]**

The combat of this game... half of it happens before active combat (team synergy is half the building process), and the other half is spamming [E].

The flow of combat does not encourage dodging enemy attacks at all because there is barely any reward for doing so over simply tanking enemy hits. There is JUST punishment for not dodging some of the tougher hits.

When you do dailies and aren't engaging in boss fights (where no thought is required), the game's combat boils down to "hold left click".

**Pulls: [u]Disaster[/u]**

You can lose 50/50s multiple times before you get the operator you want. I don't care that you still make progress toward hard pity; the whole f***ing point is that the utterly f***ing s*** feeling hits you multiple times.

YOU CAN LOSE 50/50 ON WEAPON BANNERS.

I literally lost 50/50 on my weapon banner on 7 of 8 10-pulls, and I have no idea if I will get enough Arsenal Tickets in time.

YOU ARE FORCED TO PULL on operators you don't want or don't want copies of JUST to get more weapon pulls.

A weapon 10-pull costs 1980 Arsenal Tickets (AT). The game only gives you 100 AT PER WEEK via weeklies, with the OCCASIONAL less-than-100 AT tickets in the credit store.

**Characters: [u]Good[/u]**

AKE has some of the best in-theme-looking characters. I genuinely feel the operator designs in this game look so good and fit so well in the universe.

AKE also has some REALLY F***ING COOL voice actors and accents.

I guess the only gripe I have is that you occasionally hear a different accent when Ulting (I don't mind the different language, but the ACCENT change is JARRING).

**Factory/Automation: [u]Not great[/u]**

A good AIC system that is obstructed by a horrible user interface and user experience.

It does not respond as rapidly to clicks as other games. It feels like your mouse cursor is made of jelly sometimes.

You can only make 1 tier of transport belts, which makes things really awkward when a building requires multiple units of the same item per second and belts operate at half an item per second.

**Endmin's Mask: [u]Cataclysmically bad[/u]**

Utterly f***ing ruins immersion. Don't care "bUt It'S LoRE". It totally spoils all story immersion, and I have since modded it out.

**Overall**

I'm about to ditch this game. I'm pondering whether I should just skip the story forward to experience Si's story, which looks like it is really good.

Edit. Final note. I was respecful during my in-game survey submissions even though it doesn't feel like I will be personally respected by Hypergryph.
