Mentioned it above, played quite a few gacha games, some even for years and Endfield feels the most fair so far.
You have Gacha for Operators and weapons. For both you have a guarantee after X Pulls to get either a specific item or a guarantee to get a 6* / 5* Item.
I have not spent a single euro in the game and have most operators unlocked and equipped with the recommended rare to legendary weapons. And I didnt even min/max my pulls (waiting for 120 Pulls to get a guaranteed pull for example)
    [*] The Art
Now this is an overall point. The Music, The Animations, Artworks, Character Designs - I like all of them. Sure some can use refinement but lets be fair, in the gacha the primary thing is to collect beautiful operators and I think they especially nailed that.
[/list]
[h3]The Ok parts:[/h3]
[list]
    [*] Combat
Its nothing astounding. You control one operator, the other 3 fight along you. If you get certain conditions you can trigger a Combo move, which varies per Operator. If you stagger and enemie or debuff them enough you can trigger a Finisher essentially. And if the combat goes on long enough or you saved it up, you can trigger skills and Ultimates.

Basic attacks have a 4-6 Pattern, where the final attack recharges some SP and deals more damage. Perfect doges also recharge some SP.
The Ultimates look cool but the combat overall is rather basic
    [*] DJING & Multiplayer/Social Aspect
DJing is your "Home" essentially. Talk to operators, increase their trust, assign the to tasks to get more progression materials. Its a nice to have - if you have friends they can also travel to your ship, inspect your "Arsenal" help out with the tasks and trade in your ship (usually way more profitable than just trading in singleplayer). Otherwise you can share Blueprints, Import and export them for factories and across the world you will find Structures constructed by other players. Be it turrets, Ziplines or stashes - All nice to have but its still a single player in the essence.
    [*] Operator Progression
You need to level up with items (combat gives 0 XP), every 20 Levels you need to promote and you need the gacha to "progress" the operators. All which boost the Skills (normal attacks, active skills, combo skills, UItimates), give passive boni (+5% Speed crafting on DJING for example) and boost normal stats (like Intelligence or Strength).
The annoying part can be the gaccha progression since that is based on luck if you pull the Operator again.
Otherwise there is Armor sets and Weapons that all have their own stats so you can mix and match based on the operator. All very basic and nothing special.
[/list]

[h3]What I dislike[/h3]
[list]
    [*] The AOC/Factory building
I do love Factory building games - I do love the aspect of building them, organizing them, expanding them. But in Endfield you can really feel that it is a side product. The initial recipes essentially have a 1:1 ratio. Mid/Late factories take up massive space, a lot of the products you can only make in the factories you don't really need at all. Nothing can be upgraded and my biggest gripe about it all, are the belts. They feel to slow, I feel the bridges/splitters cause a delay and are just overall unsatisfactory.
    [*] The Performance
I attached my specs to the Review and I really often get stutters. I mostly play on 4K but even reducing it to 1440p didn't help. While my FPS tracker says 60FPS, thats not what I'm seeing. It can happen coming out of a menu, cutscene just walking around or mid combat. It crashed on me several times now as well but the most annoying part is the random Bluescreens. The last one could be a causation vs correlation situation but I have had like 20 Blue screens since I started playing the game.
    [*] The UI/Menu structure
It feels very bloated with all the information all the time. Def. not the worst. The most annoying part for me is the menu navigation. I cannot remember all the hotkeys for example the recipe chain stuff. So its a lot of clicking through menus, scrolling and hoping you are in the correct one. After a while you know where to find that, but its not easy to navigate.

Yes you need a Gryphline account and you have to link it to steam. But once its linked and you start the game, it automatically logs you in via Steam. Cannot abort it, cannot use another account, cannot "wait" in the login screen.

[h3]Two Weeks on Talos-II[/h3]

After two weeks with Arknights: Endfield, I can say one thing: [b]this probably isn't a game for everyone.[/b] It's not quite your usual gacha RPG, and that's part of what makes it interesting. It brings together familiar elements while adding enough of its own ideas to feel different.

I've never played the original Arknights, but that hasn't stopped me from enjoying Endfield. There are probably references and familiar characters I'm missing, yet the story feels accessible enough on its own. It has its moments, although, like many gacha games, it takes its time getting somewhere.

[h3]A Party That Actually Feels Like a Party[/h3]

One of the first things I appreciated was the combat system. Your operators don't simply disappear when you switch characters. They're actually there, fighting alongside you, and you can freely rotate between them.

It sounds like a small detail, but it makes the party feel like an actual team. There are plenty of possible combos and reactions between operators, which makes experimenting with different compositions rather enjoyable.

Most operator designs also fit the game's aesthetic quite well, giving the world a consistent visual identity.

[h3]Somehow, I Became a Factory Manager[/h3]

[b]The factory system is probably one of Endfield's strongest features.[/b]

Imagine something along the lines of Factorio, but presented in a 3D world reminiscent of Satisfactory. It's not quite either of them, but it's an interesting combination.

You can build production lines, develop settlements, trade manufactured materials for Stock Bills, and even defend your outposts with automated turrets.

Some processes take time, but the game usually gives you something else to do while everything is running. Better yet, your factory keeps producing even when you're offline. There's something strangely satisfying about logging back in and finding that your little industrial operation has been working without you.

I also appreciate how character progression connects to these systems. Improving operators, abilities, and equipment requires materials from both the world and your production facilities, making the factory feel like an important part of progression rather than an isolated minigame.

Then there's Sanity, a rather appropriate name for the energy used to claim rewards from Index activities.

And, of course, there's the delivery system. Transporting packages between locations can earn a surprising amount of Stock Bills.

Apparently, running an industrial empire also involves becoming a delivery boy. Someone has to keep the economy moving.

[h3]A Few Things That Could Be Better[/h3]

The tutorials can be rather restrictive. Whether you're learning operator mechanics or setting up factory systems, the game sometimes insists that you follow every instruction exactly, even when you've already understood what it wants you to do.

I understand why. For someone unfamiliar with factory games, that guidance can be genuinely useful. Still, I would have appreciated a little more freedom to experiment.

Then there's the gacha system.

During the beginner banner's 40 pulls, I somehow managed to get the exact same operator the game had already given me for free.

[i]It's reassuring to know my luck remains consistent, regardless of which game I'm playing.[/i]

The rewards toward limited-banner pulls also feel somewhat scarce, and the banner rules themselves are more confusing than I'd like. I'm still getting familiar with how everything works, especially the way previous limited operators can appear in later banners.

As for multiplayer features, you can add friends, but I haven't explored much beyond helping accelerate production aboard other players' Dijiang. I'm still unsure how much direct cooperative gameplay is available, particularly for bosses or Index activities, so that's something I have yet to discover.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]

There's still plenty I haven't explored, and two weeks aren't enough to judge every system in a game like this.

But so far, I've genuinely enjoyed my time with Arknights: Endfield.

It has interesting combat, a distinctive factory system, and enough interconnected activities to keep me occupied. It also has its rough edges, especially when it comes to overly guided tutorials and a gacha system that could be easier to understand.

[b]Would I recommend it? Yes, but not to everyone.[/b]

If you're looking for a straightforward action RPG, the amount of resource management and production might not be your thing.

But if the idea of exploring an unfamiliar world, fighting alongside your operators, and occasionally spending far too much time optimizing conveyor belts sounds appealing, there's a good chance you'll enjoy it.

[i]It's a rather unusual combination, but for the right kind of player, I think it works surprisingly well.[/i]

I have actually probably put at least 150 hours to 200 hours now into Endfield upon writing this and I will be speaking as someone who once was a avid Gacha Player (Fgo, Azur Lane) but never played the OG Arknights.

I didn't have much want to play Endfield at first back in 1.3 (back in like April 2026), as I had already missed a couple of content updates, and didn't know anything about OG Arknight's story, but let me tell you I am so glad I chose to get this game and catch up. I can say this with my full chest, this game is great. It is a fr ethical gacha you can play completely free to play and still get a lot of enjoyment out of it. I personally after playing so much have sunken maybe about 80$ into the game, I don't really whale, its just that I like to support companies that have passion in their game and make great updates that make me wanting to play more. You can absolutely play this game free to play, paying like I have isn't needed at all.

Lets talk about the story first because as a non-OG Arknight's player this was my biggest worry. Firstly, this game is pretty far removed from the OG game, with it making still making references to the source material that if you are an OG player, will make you happy. Some characters return from the first game, though as "Reconvener's" with new names and usually updated lore as they are usually treated as a new character. Plot points and worldbuilding like Originium comes from the first game and it does a good enough job explaining everything that you will eventually understand stuff, even if you dont at first. As of writing this there is two hub areas minus your ship, which is Valley IV and Wuling. Valley IV is good, its basically a prologue to the story that sets up who you are, the main conflict, and some side characters (almost all rollable). I found myself liking this part of the story, but its like a solid 6.5/10 to a 7/10. Its good, but its a bit tedious doing some side missions (the Quarry particularly), and it took me generously about 2 weeks to beat Valley IV, which was when I was un-invested in the story, and was kinda doing like a couple side quests a day. The 2nd and 3rd Boss here are really cool, 1st Boss is kinda eh, but generally I would say once you get to the 2nd Boss that's when the game starts to pick up and I started to really enjoy it. Wuling however is a completely different beast and the story is just incredible. I would like to say its a 10/10, though it only loses some points from it setting up a lot of stuff that hasn't had payoff at the time of writing. That being said though, every boss in Wuling is magnificent, the plot is really interesting, and all the characters we meet here (again all rollable) are really good. I particularly really liked Tangtangs storyline, as well as Arcane's.

Gameplay wise, the game is pretty action focused. The combat at first may seem pretty shallow, though it has surprising depth when you start to team build and make combos with other characters. I would say there's not really a bad character in the game. Even some 4 stars are still usable in the right circumstance, though I think a couple are a bit weak, and may get "buffed" when they gain synergy with another character. Every 6 star in the game is good, I wouldn't say any are outright bad, with the more you get the more synergy you have. The challenges in the game also provide unique roadblocks; Umbral Monuments and Echoes of War; two challenge events that commonly come up, are less about "Oh I will beat this enemy with 200% in every stat" and more "oh they added looney tunes bullshit to this fight, and if these enemies touch each other, they explode and kill me instantly"; which makes challenges fun and challenging at the same time, and stir up the gameplay loop.|

Music in this game might genuinely be some of the best Soundtrack I have heard in a while; I would genuinely nominate this game for GotY when it comes to soundtrack. There are some Boss themes, and parts in quests that have some incredibly scores; and Contingency Contract; another event, has its own theme that is some incredibly hype rock music every time so far.

The factory stuff is good, I personally didn't play the game to play the "Factory Glorp" but found myself on nights redoing parts of my factory to refine it, or watching YT videos about tricks to improving factory design. If its not your thing though you can easily get blueprints from friends, or watch guides.

Comparing this though to other Gacha, I played FGO for a long time, though long before they added a lot of the Lost Belts so while I cant comment on those, I think this games story as of right now completely destroys Fgos story, like up there with Babylon and Camelot consistantly; and Azur Lane, well I will not comment on that because its a bad gacha.

I would definitely recommend the game! I think the story alone is worth it; its fully voice acted so its interesting to watch play out. Characters even after their quests as well will still make cameos in the story, or show up on your ship so you will consistantly run into your favorites; and I believe there is plans to add more story's for them later like OG Arknights.

Also the game runs pretty well, I personally have a pretty shitty graphics card (4gb) and it can run the game, and it doesnt look bad at all.

Overall, I would definitely recommend at least giving this game a shot. Fair warning though, it is one of those games which starts off with a LOT of tutorials and a fairly slow-start story - but if you stick through it and enjoy the vision of the what the game is building up to be, you'll probably like it. 

Some pros
- The factory building is casual, but fun. So far it hasn't gotten too complex, and the game has many optional walkthrough tutorials for those who don't know how it works but want to get involved. And if you're truly too lazy to do it, you can copy other people's bases with blueprints. 
- The combat is really good. Casual at face value, and has a lot of depth for people who wanna look for it. The obvious team comps are good, however there is a TON of flexibility in combat, and many unconventional ways to minmax an encounter varying based on the mechanics. Whether you're a casual or tryhard, you'll probably find some satisfaction in it. 
- As long as you have enough restraint to save some pulls, the gacha is very fair. TLDR: Save 120 pulls, and you can guarantee your character. Don't waste pulls or weapon pulls if you can't guarantee, and you will find yourself with a really comfortable flow of currency. Going by these rules, you should expect to get 1 in every 2/3 characters f2p, with 1 in every 2 of their signature weapons. If you lose a 50/50, you can even randomly get characters from the last two banners, which is nice. 
- Weapon banner currency is a residual of character pulls. Yes, that means you don't have to save up separate pulls for weapons in this game. Every character and dupe earns you Arsenal Tickets, which you can use to buy max rarity generic weapons or pull for character signature weapons. 
- Good weapon options. The free track of the battlepass ensures that you ALWAYS have a good weapon for your character, and the generic high rarity weapons are also very good. These are ordinarily 85-95% as good as a signature weapon. You're never at a dead end if you get unlucky. 
- Good rate of progression. The game gives plenty of resources, and progressing through the game you'll never feel as though you hit a wall. 
- Interesting story (so far). I won't get into any specifics, and yes this is an amnesiac MC plot, however this story actually does have quite an interesting world and setting. The Endministrator in recent patches has started to become much more of their own character, and I've quite enjoyed the existing story content. I only ask that HG make an optional challenge mode, as it is much too easy. 
- The soundtrack is immaculate, and the game is visually great. Very good art style, and probably the single cleanest translation of anime characters to a 3d environment. 

Some cons
- Lack of a real endgame. As of now, we have some challenge stages through Echoes of War and Umbral Monument. Echoes is your basic time attack mode, and Umbral is your mechanical complexity based mode. Both are fun, but they're one-time completions, meaning you're done when you're done. Past that it's just the daily loop - though HG has announced they're working on a repeatable endgame mode called Shattered Protocol, likely to arrive in the next 2 versions. 
- Some pain points in the gacha. I like the system overall and understand it's statistically very good amongst gachas, but it doesn't feel very satisfying to pull. If you win your first 50/50, the guarantee at 120 pulls vanishes, and you earn less weapon banner currency for the same amount of pulls. On the flipside, going to 120 pulls does not guarantee you the weapon - it only gets you a decent ways over halfway to guaranteeing it. This is a system that heavily punishes greed, but gives you JUST short of clearing everything with the bare minimum. My advice, **always save for guarantees, don't gamble carelessly**.
- Some flaws with overall storytelling. The game has gotten MUCH better about this in recent updates, however the Valley IV arc of the game suffers heavy from amnesiac MC tropes, glazing the MC for being this amazing hero of the past, and shying away from digging into worldbuilding topics too closely. I suspect a lot of this was growing pains for learning how to write a story in a 3d setting, however that doesn't mean it doesn't exist as a problem. 

TLDR: It's a really solid game with a few points that need improvement. Worth trying.

I played Endfield back in early September on my Google Account ever since Discord promoted Endfield for Orbs and just before they fully released it on Steam. I recently finished the main storyline as a F2P player, so I have some things to talk about.

The Gacha System (Headhunting) & Progression

The gacha system is transparent, displaying x amount of attempts until pity. There are different kinds of tickets that are only used in specific banners, such as the Chartered Exclusive tickets. THESE do have an expiry date and CANNOT be carried over and only used in one specific banner. 

There are also banners for weapons through Arsenal Issue, which also display x amount of pulls until pity. Weapons have a thing called Potential where you get duplicates of said weapon to fully unlock it's potential. It's similar as using tokens for Operators but with weapons.

Gacha system aside, it is free to play friendly. It is possible to progress through the main storyline, you do not need to pay for the best gear, operators and weapons. You just need to be strategic in which operators to invest in the most. My first team was the Endmin, Perlica, Chen and Snowshine in that order. 

It wasn't until I fought Lady Si that I had to switch, upgrade and fit better gear for my operators and I had to look up a guide to create a Mono-Physical team. While team-building in this game is versatile, you do need to make an informed decision whenever or not your team is worth investing in long-term. I found it difficult to fully put resources into two planned teams and only had enough to make for only one team in the end.

AIC Factory & User Interface (UI)

I'm not a big fan, but I can recognize the appeal of why people like this part of the game. It is very essential to progression in quests and storylines, especially when you reach Wuling City. I personally find the system confusing and overwhelming at first, but there are Simulations to complete in order to fetch pre-made blueprints. There are community blueprints too, just make sure to click IMPORT BLUEPRINT and not type in the SEARCH BLUEPRINT section. Also make sure that the blueprint sharing code you are copying is from your specific region, like NA/EU and Asia.

The UI can be overwhelming sometimes, I kind of wish there was a Simple Mode where there could be less stuff displayed on screen. It is a double edged sword because at the beginning the game was pretty helpful with guiding through the mechanics. When I reached Wuling though, it got really complicated with their AIC system. It took an entire 2nd playthrough for me on Steam on a brand new account to completely understand what was going on.

Credit Shop

If you are a F2P like me, this shop will be your best bet to gain pulls for banners for operators and weapons. You can gain credits by visiting other friends in Dijang and assist them with Clue Gathering and speeding up Production, 5 times each per day. Some days you can purchase Arsenal tokens or Oroberyl at a discount, sometimes with none. This is one of multiple ways you could gradually build your way pull a character or a weapon you want in a banner.

Story & Characters

Cutscenes are very cinematic and beautiful, especially in moments such as introductions to characters, boss fights, and new areas to explore. Storywise however, I don't find myself too overly attached to other characters and operators. TL;DR, it's pretty mid.

The closest operator that I found the most intriguing was Laevatain and their Story Quest, due to their common struggles with the Endmin with losing their memories and the main theme of forging your own identity. This Story Quest in particular gives the Endmin more depth in their character, putting on a strong brave face while acting as someone that they don't remember being. 

I wish there were more moments and story beats similar to Laevatain's Story Quest, especially in a world where the Endmin is constantly put on a pedestal by a lot of people around them.

I also feel like majority of the operators and characters sound like a bunch of yes-men to me, which is not a bad thing as there are solid lore reasons for this, as they are all loyal to the Endmin because of the Zeroth Directive, but character-wise it is pretty bland to observe long-term.

[UPDATE] I think it's because the way the story always focuses around the Endmin and you RARELY see two operators interact with one another without the Endmin's presence ONSCREEN and that's probably why it gave that impression that the Endmin is a Mary/Gary Sue.

I would like to see more variety of story/character explorations that involve different perspectives of what others see in the Endministrator, but in a negative/grey area. I'm pretty sure there are at least some people in this universe who envy or fear our MC. Any emotion other than constant praise would be such a breath of fresh air.

A suggestion I would love to give is the ability to playback cutscenes in the Archives area. There is so much to do that there are times where I wanted to go back and recall pieces of information or lore, only to be locked out of it once a quest/storyline has been completed.

Overall, I think it's an alright game. I had no performance issues on Steam and on the Launcher itself. There are some areas that do need polishing, but that should not take away from the overall experience. I would recommend this to anyone who likes any games related to Factorio, worldbuilding and exploration.

As someone who played Endfield with the Gryphlink launcher until recently (therefore, I have quite a few more hundreds of hours than shown on steam), I can say that there's no additional performance gain, it's purely just to keep track of playtime.

For the uninitiated, Arknights: Endfield is a sequal to the Arknights mobile game. It's a gacha game combining great combat mechanics with a story that is all over the place in the best way possible, and we threw a factory-building mechanic in there as well because yes.

If you're a fellow whose time is precious and should be spent doing other things, this game may be a little on the tedious side given the factory (which is immediately negated by the blueprint system, allowing you  to copy mega factories that people post online), but the rest of the game is nowhere near as time consuming. However, the factory *is* essential to gameplay, both for combat and for the story, so don't think you can skip it.

The visuals are, despite the fact that we're actively ruining it all with are factory, absolutely stunning, especially in Wuling.

You of course don't need the highest settings, but as someone who has played on both his desktop PC (specs provided along with my comment) and on his laptop (ryzen 7 5600u with integrated graphics and 16GB of RAM), it's night and day between the highest and lowest settings. The game also runs on mobile for quick dailies. The point I'm trying to make is that the required specs aren't all that high, but you'd definitely need something more powerful if you want to enjoy the beauty this game has to offer.

Music is yet another slamdunk; the first CC (Contingency Contract) for Endfield made sure that the CC brand built by Arknights was *not* tarnished, and even outside of CC the music in general perfectly fits the vibes that the visuals evoke within the brain.

If you're a fellow who has a bunch of time to burn (like me during the summer), then this is a game you could spend 10 hours a day on depending on how immersed you get.

For the fellow Arknights players who are thinking of trying out Endfield; it's a completely different game, but there are a few familliar faces, so don't fret. The story is, admittedly, much more lighthearted than the original arknights lore... but I'm sure that that's a temporary thing for now.

I would really like to like this game, however I find there to just be a few issues that make it rather difficult to enjoy. 

My main gripe with this game is the sheer amount of ui and menu screens and buttons all shoved in your face all at once. Operating the pause menu feels like a genuine challenge and the amount of moving elements make it feel really disjointed, especially for a person like me.

The character design is another thing I am rather iffy on. I get it is a gacha game and blah blah blah personal preference but, what if I just really want to play the game for the fun combat, but my favorite operator to play as essentially has her heirlooms hanging out for the world to see, and I, personally find it really uncomfortable? Some characters look sick, I love the endmin, chen and perlica, but pretty much every female operator after that has some sort of heavily revealing clothing, especially the rarer ones, which are usually the operators you want to play as.

I mostly downloaded this game for the factory gameplay, coming from Satisfactory with ~700 hours, but I find that actual factory management and, hell, even gameplay is really slow and clunky, especially early game. The tutorials basically hold your hand the entire time, barely give you any space to explore and learn at your own pace, and feel really strict and rigid. I get that I am basically comparing apples to oranges here, but I feel like a lot more games handle the tutorials a lot better. For me personally, it was a genuine effort to muster the want to actually continue playing the game once I finally reached the AIC, because I was just so bored and burnt out from the game itself.

Overall, combat, fun as hell, I love it.
Art direction is amazing, I love the world design and character art, however some character designs genuinely piss me off.
Factory gameplay is underwhelming, slow and pretty clunky.
Story is genuinely forgettable to the point where I would rather just play the game without one.

If maybe the UI and some other elements were improved on, and the game was much more entincing to play, I will change my review to positive, but for now it is a negative review.

Arknights: Endfield is far more than a spin off, it's a fully realized 3D action RPG that stands on its own. and a "little" bit of Capitalism.

The Operators are one of the highlights. Hypergryph really nailed the character design, over 20+ Operators to choose from, each with distinct personalities, roles, and combat styles, from frontline Guards and Defenders to Supporters and ranged specialists.

What I like is that they all feel viable and have real synergy together in the 4 person squad. You're constantly switching between them (optional) to pull off combo skills and ultimates. The designs are also fantastic, faithful to classic Arknights.

What truly sets it apart is the integration of exploration and industry. Exploring Talos-II is a joy thanks to excellent art direction, atmosphere, and soundtrack, but the base building and factory automation system is what elevates the experience. Building and optimizing production lines for Endfield Industries adds a deep, rewarding gameplay loop that keeps you constantly engaged. (The Factory Must Grow)

The gacha system (Headhunting) is surprisingly player friendly. It has a standard pity system, guaranteed 6-star within 80 pulls, with a 50/50 for the featured operator. If you lose the 50/50, the next featured is guaranteed within just 40 more pulls. Soft pity starts kicking in around 65 pulls too.

Weapon banners are also separate and generous, and you get a lot of the currency just from playing, daily logins, weekly quests and progressing through the story and the factory system. It feels designed to let active free to play players still get the operators they want without having to spend heavily.

Performance and polish on PC are outstanding for a free to play gatcha. The worldbuilding is strong, the characters are well written, and the game is welcoming to newcomers while still rewarding for long time Arknights fans.

An incredibly polished, content rich, and addictive RPG. May Capitalism be whit you.

My Mostly Spoiler-Free Arknights: Endfield Review 

TL;DR: If you're interested in the gameplay, give it a try. The factory-building and combat are satisfying, the worldbuilding is excellent, and the story has improved tremendously in the later patches. There's still room for improvement in the endgame and performance, but I think the game has a lot of potential.

I've tried most of the gacha games on the market, and almost all of them feel like mobile games first and PC games second. Arknights: Endfield, however, feels like a proper PC title. The factory-building mechanics and action combat activate my neurons in all the right ways.

I initially tried this game simply because I make an effort to try as many free-to-play games as possible. However, the gameplay quickly hooked me. Learning how to pilot a team, optimize character builds, and squeeze the most out of your characters is incredibly satisfying.

I was initially hesitant to commit to another gacha game because some of them offer very few pulls and pressure you into spending money to make meaningful progress. Thankfully, Endfield has had relatively little power creep so far and provides a pretty good number of pulls. If I had continued playing since release without taking a break, I'd guess that I'd own most of the characters by now.
That said, the game wasn't without its problems, especially in the earlier patches.

The second region felt unfinished, and its writing was noticeably weaker than that of the first. Another frustrating experience was reaching the point just before a major boss, only to realize that I needed to completely rebuild my factory because I hadn't set it up to produce a required resource. That was enough to make me take a break from the game.
Unfortunately, the story wasn't doing much to keep me invested, either. Throughout patch 1.1 and much of 1.2, the main story felt like it wasn't going anywhere. I was so turned off by the writing and the direction of the story that I struggled to see a reason to keep playing through it. I wasn't particularly interested in the characters being introduced, and I found myself much more interested in the lore and the reasons behind our presence in the region.
These problems weren't really addressed until patch 1.4, but I had no way of knowing that at the time. It wasn't until I watched a few spoiler-free reviews from content creators that I became interested in giving the game another chance.
After returning, fixing my factory, and finally defeating the boss I'd quit right before, I still wasn't entirely sold. However, once I started the 1.3 story, I was pleasantly surprised by the significant improvement in storytelling, writing, and cutscenes. The character side stories I'd missed were well done, too.

One of my favorite pieces of content in the game was a side story for Laevatain, the original banner character. It was great to see that level of storytelling, and I was happy to see future characters receiving similarly high-quality stories.
Then came patch 1.4, and I wasn't prepared for what it had in store.

I started the 1.4 story and was immediately drawn in by its setting, the call to action, and the overall narrative. It also did a great job of reintroducing Arcane, a character we'd encountered in 1.2 but whom I'd previously felt pretty lukewarm about.The story told in this patch genuinely blew me away. I'd go as far as to say it's one of the best stories I've experienced in any game I've played.

Patch 1.5 was great as well, and the newest patch, 1.6, has continued that momentum. The larger stories the developers have been building toward are finally coming into focus, and things seem to be getting better with each update. The new characters are interesting and feel thoughtfully developed.

I've also started reading the original Arknights story to learn more about the lore. It's been interesting seeing how the two games might connect, and I'm excited to see where things go. As far as worldbuilding and setting go, I think Arknights is among the better franchises on the market.

As for endgame content, the developers have added a decent amount, but there's still relatively little to do once you've reached a certain point. Much of the remaining progression revolves around leveling up characters for other teams you might want to play. I'd like to see more activities that give players a reason to keep coming back once they've finished the current content.

I'm also really excited about the quality-of-life features Hypergryph has planned for upcoming updates, along with the new stories they'll be telling. The game has come a long way, and I'm looking forward to seeing how much further it can go.

One final warning about performance: The game has a memory leak, and I experience occasional stuttering on my RTX 4060 with 16 GB of RAM. Changing the graphics settings can reduce the severity of the stuttering, but it doesn't eliminate it entirely. Now it could be my pc or user error but these problems did not exist for me when the game released. 

Despite its flaws, I think Arknights: Endfield is well worth trying, especially if you enjoy factory-building games, action combat, character optimization, and deep worldbuilding. The early story patches nearly made me quit for good, but the later updates convinced me to come back, and I'm glad they did.

Arknights Endfield has many similarities to your average triple-A open world action anime gacha game, but also has factory and automation gameplay that helps it stand out among its competitors. As an added bonus, it has some (fairly direct) thematic and narrative tie-ins to the world of Arknights if you are a fan of the original.

[h3]Main Features[/h3]
= Fast-paced anime-styled combat focused on status effects and team compositions
= Semi-open world exploration for larger zones, linear level design for smaller zones
= Factory automation gameplay

[h3]What I liked[/h3]
+ Gorgeous graphics, animation, and sci-fi aesthetic
+ Great game performance, even on Linux machines
+ Extremely good music
+ Unique EN voicing and engaging character design
+ Fun team composition and easy character building (little to no RNG)
+ Novel factory automation that is both fun and very accessible
+ Automation extending to open world travel and combat (ziplines and turrets, etc.)
+ Fun minigames like goods investing, puzzle fitting, archery
+ Free pulls when new characters drop and free pull vouchers after hitting a pull threshold 
+ Catch up mechanics for periods of absence 
+ Free-to-play-accessible battlepass upgrade

[h3]What I didn't like[/h3]
- Fairly handholdy and dry intro story, even if it improves later on
- Relatively stingy pull currency income outside of quests and events
- Weapon banner is tied to pulling characters for some reason instead of being separate

- Dry periods between patches and events

This game incooperates a different system for exploration, dailies, and growth overall. That's where the factory comes in. This game mode can be overwhelming, but it has very intuitive tutorials, and a strong community that shares blue prints for the most meta factory build per patch!

I like this game, but I'm done with it.

The world is pretty and you're rewarded for going off the beaten path and exploring. The character designs are beautiful and the Japanese VA is great. The game runs really well, performance isn't an issue even on an older GPU like mine. The combat isn't my favorite aspect, but it's fun enough and has a nice flow to it. The factory base building is interesting. Mixing Factorio into a JRPG works surprisingly well and it's quite fulfilling to develop your base and step back to see its growth over time.

The character designs are great, but the enemy designs didn't really sell me for the most part, at least in Chapter I. The Aggeloi, which from the story so far seem to be the primary antagonists of the game, are just rock elementals of various shapes and sizes. They're not engaging to look at, don't instill any sort of dread or fear, and come off as... very safe? They're just not compelling as enemies.

The game itself has no blood or bones. Often times the game goes out of its way to say that people involved, whether allies or enemies like the Landbreaker bandits you fight, were just knocked out. It seems like the game is trying to maintain a balance between dealing with heavy subject matter such as incurable diseases in children while also whitewashing things that might get it in trouble with a ratings board. It just feels like an overly sanitized experience. 

Even with its faults, if this was just a regular JRPG that I could buy for 60 dollars, I would. I like the characters and I want to see where the story goes. I want to see how in-depth the base building and factory mechanics can get.

But this is not a regular JRPG. It's a free to enter, pay with your time (and/or money) always-online gacha game that will eventually hit the end of its lifespan. Servers will go down and all of your time and money invested will be gone forever. To be clear, I don't mind grinding in games! If the grind is fun, then there's no problem. It's just disheartening to know that one day, it'll all be wiped.

There is a good game here to be found. It just sucks to see promising games dangle the characters and content you want to use unlock with RNG pulls rather than story progression. But that's the nature of the beast when you decide to try a gacha game, so really I only have myself to blame for being disappointed.

I'd say give the game a try, maybe you'll be luckier than I was or find that the game is worth sticking around for despite its faults. I'm sure that given enough investment of time and/or money, you will get to a point where you can get the characters you actually want to use.

I'll still recommend it since I do enjoy the game. I'm not going to give it a thumbs down just because it's a gacha game, I knew what I was signing up for when I installed it. It just another game that makes me sad about what could have been if this was just a regular, pay to own game. But I guess that's not where the money is these days.

TLDR; My actual gametime is about 300 hours before the steam release and I can safely say that this is among the best, if not the best, JRPG Gacha game on the market right now. Highly recommended.

A rundown of the most important bits:

Story:
The story starts off slow, like any other game in the genre. However, the Valley IV region is basically just one giant introduction to the game and it's systems. It's therefor easily skipped without missing too much important plot points. The story really starts picking up during the Wuling arc. Conveniently, you can skip the entirety of Valley IV and go immediatly into Wuling using an ingame feature. 

The story itself is fantastic and the future is looking very bright. That's because the original Arknights has a long-running 7 year reputation of phenominal storytelling and this game ties directly into the already established world. 

Combat:
The combat system is incredibly unique and satisfying. This is due to the fact that the player controls a team of four characters all at once. Their kits all play into one another using combo skills, which are skills that automatically trigger when certain conditions are met. This makes team-building very interesting and fun. It also makes it very easy to have a novel experience with your existing characters, since swapping out one teammate for another can completely change the way a team plays. The combat challenges presented in the game play into this perfectly, by letting go of the standard, timed 'DPS-check' model. Instead Arknights: Endfield often opts for a more strategic endgame, where buffs and debuffs, enemy stats, setups and important effects should be taken into account. 

Progression (the factory system):
This game's progression system is different from most gacha games. Usually the player does their daily quests, using some form of energy or 'sanity' and this amounts to 90% of the progression. In Endfield, the game includes (besides the standard 'sanity' model) an entire Factorio-style factory system that directly ties into the player's progression. Mind you, this is not for everyone. Tinkering with the factory system can take a lot of time. Luckily, blueprints for effective factory setups are readily available online and take little to no time to set up. With a good factory running in the background, missing a few dailies is no big deal. This makes Arknights: Endfield a gacha game that respects your time.

Pollish (music and art):
To me, there isn't a single game on the market that looks and sounds as good as Arknights: Endfield. The sound design is crisp and satisfying, from menu elements to combat sounds. The environment art and character designs are downright gorgeous. And then there's the music. I have not heard this level of pollish and quality in games before. I don't remember the last time I've been blown away on such a regular basis simply because of a game's music. 

The gacha system and F2P friendliness:
Sure, it's a gacha game. So, we have to talk about monetization, too. There are a lot of different opinions floating around online, some positive and some negative, and a lot of numbers and spreadsheets and the likes trying to prove some point or another. 

I would implore anyone interested in this game to just try it and see for yourself. There's a lot of the 'feel' of the system that can't be captured in words and descriptions and formulas. All I can say is this: I have been F2P since the start and don't feel like I'm missing out on much. There are tons of characters that are very F2P accesible, and there's a very small difference between some character's signature weapons and F2P alternatives, unlike in other gacha games where characters often need their signature weapons to function at intended levels. For any premium character there's an F2P team to be made that can do fantastic in most lategame content, and the power difference between these teams and fully premium teams isn't all that large. In fact, in some combat challenges an F2P team is actually prefered simply because of the nature of the challenge. Planning out strategies and teams is much more important than having the shiny new character, and that really says a whole lot about Endfield's monetization system.

Be advised before anything else that it's a gacha game with all the usual monetisation pitfalls. Not exactly *greedy* on monetisation as far as gacha games go, but still.

---

That said, it's a fucking gorgeous game with an incredible soundtrack, a story that actually builds upon itself properly rather than entirely abandoning the previous chapter's established story hooks and characters as soon as a new area is accessible. I've been playing it since Day 1 using the standalone launcher with over 600 hours sunk into it there, and I have absolutely no regrets nor do I intend to stop playing any time soon.

Gameplay wise it's a neat blend of your run-of-the-mill action-rpg type of combat that's increasingly popular in gachas nowadays, but allows you to use all four members of your team simultaneously- you control one (and can switch at will) but the others also hang around and continue fighting alongside you as you do. The campaign difficulty is not dramatically high difficulty but does just barely ask you to work, while higher-difficulty versions of fights also become available. The combat is varied such that every character can have a use (some of the hardest combat content available as part of an event that'll periodically return was being outright cheesed with a low-star character), can be challenging enough that creating multiple teams to handle the higher-end combat is a valid use of time rather than a just-for-fun thing, but also has enough skill expression that Agony mode content (which is your lowest-tier "hard" content) was cleared with literally just one of the three starting characters alone on a team despite the time limit.

This is blended with factory gameplay not dissimilar to factorio-but-in-3D, though with limited "plot" areas you're allowed to build in, though you can expand their size a few times each and unlock more of those plots as you continue to progress through the game too- a total of four per region, with the first unlocked in a region being a large "central" area and the other four being "outposts" with a little quest chain associated with each.
I did not expect the factory part of the gameplay to grip me. It did- it's a really good introductory experience even if you've never played a factory game before, and I quickly became obsessed with optimising or reworking parts of my factory to build other parts in. And having 80 thousand throwable bombs on-demand is hard to argue with.
But, if you really don't like factory gameplay or don't find this particular iteration gripping or fun? You can kinda skip it! The game features a blueprints mechanic that allows you to copy/paste parts of your factory and save those designs for later use too, and those blueprints can be imported and exported so naturally there's a section of the community (mostly KyoStinV) who put forward highly-compact-but-high-efficiency designs that require next to no thought to slap down into your factory, and all is well. I've even used KyoStinV's blueprints a few times myself just to save space when a new resource is introduced in a new area. Very little factory gameplay (although not none!) is required for campaign steps, although you will at least want to set up some basic automation for the material-parts because they're used to craft gear for your operators.

Speaking of which: gear. This is not a gacha on which you roll for randomised loot with randomised stats. Everything is fully predetermined, all gear except weapons are crafted, and upgrading that gear only asks for more gear with the same stats to throw into it. The minimum and maximum state of any given equipment is always the same for every person. Weapons are a little more annoying as they're done through a secondary gacha that uses currency obtained from the operator gacha, but you can also earn it slowly but passively through dailies and weeklies (and pull currency too). They, too, do not feature any RNG stats, and the lower-quality gear you can find in chests around the world is generally sufficient for the campaign. If you want to tackle the harder-tier content, weapons obtainable from the paid tier of the pass are also solid picks for that operator's banner and the item that gives you that weapon can also give you the weapon from any previous pass too (but not future, even if you open the box much later). I have found the guaranteed 5-star weapon from doing weapon 10-pulls (you cannot do single-pulls) plus the high frequency in which I also get multiple 5-star weapons in those pulls is sufficient for harder content. 6-star weapons are still annoyingly rare, but they're guarantee-able with enough pull currency too. It's less than ideal, but it's not at a problem level.

If you are a rational enough human being to avoid live service games like the plague, Arknights: Endfield (which I will refer to as just "Endfield" from here on out) is an easy pass just like the rest of them. For all the rest of us who are already on the live service slop treadmill, Endfield is one of the more F2P friendly gachas and actually respects the player's time and need to live their own life.

Gameplay is fun and engaging, having been described as "similar to Xenoblade" by friends of mine who have played those games. Fighting alongside your squad adds a lot to the game and makes it feel far less lonely, something which extends to the exploration side of the game as well. Compared to the Beta, the combat was neutered a bit, particularly in the way skills and targeting are handled, which I see as a shame. Though still, the combat in its current form is far from unengaging. The power creep hit this game quite early with the introduction of Zhuang Fangyi, but thankfully, it seems like most of the new content hasn't crept the power level much higher.

The Factorio-esque automation side of this game will filter a lot of the players, but I see this as a positive. While Endfield respects your time, it also demands that you meaningfully engage with the mechanics. This can be remedied with Blueprints and video guides, but you still need to do the basic legwork to get everything going.

Story and narrative feel weak compared to the offerings in Arknights, and for a while it has really felt like Endfield has been written by the B Team at Hypergryph. Its getting a bit better, especially as we finally approach some big turning points in the narrative, but it is still a sore spot for me as a long term fan who wanted something more engaged with the world rather than the Endmin-centric narrative in the side content that we have in Endfield. The game would be far better off without the trappings of other 3D ARPG gachas and actually allow us to explore interactions and relationships between characters without jamming the Endmin into every scene. Arknights did this far better, where the Doctor (Arknights' player character) rarely shows up in side stories and event content, rather focusing on a distinct group of characters and their endeavors. I hope that in the near future, we see Endfield let the cast explore interactions amongst each other, without every interaction needing to have the Endmin at the center of it  all.

Overall, probably one of the better gachas currently on the market. Its still a live service treadmill, so I cannot really give it a "Must Play" recommendation, but for the unfortunate people like us who are already in this ecosystem, Endfield is one of the most F2P friendly and will actually respect your time.

Arknights: Endfield is a breath of fresh air in the open-world RPG genre. Instead of copying the standard formula, it completely shifts the endgame loop by throwing factory automation mechanics into a tactical action game. If you enjoy games like Factorio or Satisfactory but want fluid, real-time squad combat and an anime aesthetic, this is a must-play.
The Good:
• Addictive Factory Loop: You don't mindlessly grind bosses for random gear drops. Instead, you build mining drills, power grids, and sprawling conveyor belt networks to automate the production of your own high-end weapons and equipment.
• Meaningful Progression: Building infrastructure isn't just a side gimmick. Setting up ziplines, highways, and power relays directly changes how you traverse, explore, and unlock the map.
• Engaging Combat: You manage a four-person squad in real time. It feels incredibly smooth, and the ability to slow down time to precisely aim your characters' skills adds a layer of genuine strategy.
• Great Optimization: The game looks sharp, featuring a unique, gritty cyberpunk art direction, and it runs exceptionally well on PC with excellent frame rate stability.
The Mixed / To Keep in Mind:
• Slow Start: The first few hours are incredibly heavy on tutorials and text-dense lore dialogue. It takes a little while for the game to take off the training wheels and let you build freely.
• Gacha Progression: While the base gameplay is fantastic, it is a gacha game at its core. Premium currency for character pulls is backloaded into the mid-to-late game, meaning you will be relying on your free starter characters for a significant portion of the early campaign.
Final Verdict:
An incredibly unique hybrid of automation and action. The factory building is deep, the combat is satisfying, and watching your perfectly optimized base run itself is pure dopamine. Definitely worth checking out.

**Recommended:** Yes

**Hours Played:** 320+ hours (Played continuously from launch through Version 1.6)

**Completion Status:** 100% Cleared (All main storylines, maps, and current content)

---

### **Overview**

As someone who has played virtually every major gacha game right on release, *Arknights: Endfield* sets a high benchmark for audio-visual quality and player-friendly systems. After sinking over 300 hours into the game and clearing every piece of content through Version 1.6, it’s a title I strongly recommend, even if certain combat elements and endgame loops still need refinement.

---

### **The Good: Audio-Visuals, Optimization, Story & Gacha**

* **Top-Tier Graphics & Cinematic Cutscenes:** Visually, the game is stunning. The environmental design, fidelity, and lighting are top-tier, complemented by breathtaking cinematic cutscenes that rival AAA releases.
* **Absolute Banger Soundtrack & Voice Acting:** The music is an absolute banger from start to finish, perfectly matching the game's atmosphere. The voice acting is top-notch, with distinct regional character accents adding immense depth and personality to the cast.
* **Exceptional PC Optimization:** Despite looking incredible, the game runs buttery smooth. Performance is rock-solid, framerates remain stable, and load times are lightning fast.
* **Best F2P Pull System in the Genre:** Having experienced every major gacha launch, Endfield's gacha economy is easily the most generous on the market. Rates and pity systems are extremely player-friendly, allowing F2P players to effortlessly stack their accounts with 6-star characters and signature weapons.
* **Engaging Story & Epic Bosses:** The main storyline remains consistently strong through Version 1.6. While regular enemy encounters have issues, the major boss fights are dynamic, cinematic, and genuinely fun to play through.

---

### **The Bad: Frustrating Mob Fights & Trash Endgame**

* **Gimmicky Mob & Miniboss Combat:** Regular combat against field mobs and minibosses feels clunky and frustrating. These encounters are bloated with annoying crowd-control gimmicks, invulnerability triggers, and tedious mechanics that turn simple exploration fights into a chore.
* **Dismal Endgame:** The biggest flaw after 300+ hours is the complete lack of a proper endgame. Once you 100% clear the available content, there is no meaningful, challenging, or rewarding repeatable loop to test out your stacked 6-star rosters.

---

### **Final Verdict**

*Arknights: Endfield* is a visual and auditory masterpiece with flawless PC optimization, a captivating main story, epic boss encounters, and the most generous F2P pull system out there. If you can look past annoying mob gimmicks and a currently weak endgame, this is an absolute must-play.

Been playing since the launch in January. 
Great game, really defies the expectations that one would have for a chinese 3d action-adventure gacha game. 

[h2] Art / Graphics / Performance [/h2]
The [b]character animations[/b] are the highlight for me. They mog every other anime-style game, and also realistic AAA games, [b]insanely detailed[/b] and a lot of effort was put into them.
Weapon models and character models are highly detailed, it's a unique style that has the anime-style models with a different-than-usual shading, making it stand out.
The environments could be more varied, but there's only 2 regions (V4 and Wuling) at this time so it's probably going to get better. 

The game looks great once you disable TAA (Temporal Anti-Aliasing). use FSR or DLSS.
FPS has been stable 60 for me for 95% of my experience, 5% being when i stuffed literally every single machine onto the single factory plot and the constant "CLOGGED" blinking on 40 machines started tanking my framerate. This isn't a problem if builds are spaced out between factory plots though.
It is also available on mobile so I don't see why it couldn't run on potato PCs.

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]

The [b]combat[/b] is engaging, I found it a bit easy though, at the time of this review. It's pretty [b]dynamic[/b] and different for different fights, not just spamming the same button or same rotation every single time. 

The puzzles and exploration are fun and simple. there's no climbing or flying, but i don't think it's necessary, the maps aren't bloated with empty space.

The [b]factory[/b] is a bit [b]shallow[/b] compared to what you can find in Factorio or Satisfactory, it's kind of like a minecraft tech mod. 
It's fun to litter the environment with pylons and ziplines though, transforming the map to be [i]yours[/i].

[h2] Story & Music [/h2]

Very aesthetic game, the music is calming when it has to be, and blood pumping when it has to be. All I can say are praises to the OST. [b]Boss tracks especially are really good.[/b] It really shows that the same music company made the music for this as Arknights, which also has an insane OST.

The [b]story starts off slow and cringe[/b], which was a pain point for me at the beginning, it feels like whoever wrote the first bit of the story was some kind of outsource job. It boils down to basically there's an issue and the MC solves it and everyone glazes them. Luckily once you arrive to the [b]second region[/b], (or use the story skip feature) the [b]story finally picks up and becomes enjoyable.[/b]
The exclusion zone story was the highlight for me so far, with an insanely well made boss fight to go with it.

[h2] TL;DR [/h2]
Game good, animations REALLY good, doesn't force you to pull on the gacha to progress, you can complete the story with the starter team if you level them up. You can even complete the combat events with a modicum of skill and sweating, while never rolling the gacha.


[hr][/hr]
[h1] For "Gacha Gamers" [/h1]
[hr][/hr]

If you enjoy a really slow but steady progression of your account, this game is probably not for you.
It [b]respects the player's time way too much[/b], you can skip a lot of grinding, automate gear production. This also means less gameplay once you barrel through the story and events.
If you want this to be a daily 30min-2hour game, then it's perfect, but if you want more depth from it, you will probably drop it down the line.

There are no [i]meta[/i] teams. You can clear [b]everything[/b] with any team that has functional synergy between the operators you choose. This also makes the gacha less predatory, [b]you're not forced to roll for the newest operator[/b] to clear the [i]"""difficult"""[/i] content, you can do it with just free units even.
[b]Powercreep is minimal to none[/b], a release 1.0 character as main dps still clears combats just as fast as the brand new shiny operator. I'd even go as far as beating the new dps operators in specific scenarios.

The [b]character gacha system is good[/b], with just the [b]free[/b] resources you can get [b]every 1 in 3 new operator with worst luck[/b] imaginable. The weapon gacha uses a separate currency from the operator gacha, so you're less restricted on whose weapon to get. That being said, it's not necessarily a great weapon gacha system, because 80% of your weapon gacha income is from rolling the operator gacha. If you get lucky there, you'll be dry on the weapon gacha pulls.
Luckily the freemium battle pass gives you a weapon selector that is basically a cope option for the featured operator you can roll on. The game also gives you a 3-day leeway for progressing the battle pass, so [b]you don't miss out on anything if you don't log in for 1-2 days.[/b]

[b]Gear RNG doesn't exist[/b], which gives the players a way to [i]fully max out[/i] operators, to reach the finish line.
The factory replaces grinding for resources and enemies to drop items, you can just ignore it completely if you enjoy running through the same [i]farming routes[/i] every day.

[h2] TL;DR [/h2]
Are you a gacha savant who loves when number go up? Endfield is not for you. 
Do you want a gacha that doesn't punish you for not logging in and does not enslave you with dark pattern fomo? Endfield is for you.

[h1]THE UGLY REALITY ABOUT GACHA[/h1]

Disclaimer: I will not hold anything back. I will expose the exploitative monetization scaffolding Endfield employs in all its ugliness.

I played Endfield as an F2P back in January, made it to the end of the 1.0 Wuling story, and got Laevatein. I dropped it because of the putrid monetization destroying the game itself. I reinstalled it on Steam to see the state of the game, and nothing has changed.
My profile for any doubter: [url=https://imgur.com/a/aWn05Gz]https://imgur.com/a/aWn05Gz[/url]

These AAA gacha games have two structural layers: the monetization layer and the game layer. The former completely holds the latter hostage, even though the game layer is what gets sold to gamers and holds the artistic merit.

Let's quickly check the game layer:
🟢 Polished presentation
🟢 Great optimization
🟢 Engaging combat and fun exploration
🟢 AIC is fun to build and watch
🟢 Surprisingly great boss fights
🔴 The writing is atrocious
🔴 Quest design is terrible
🔴 Very poor story pacing
🔴 Cluttered menuing
🔴 Limited experimentation (since character gacha is a thing here)

The game is genuinely solid. A great 7/10 game, nothing groundbreaking or GOTY-tier.
So what ruins it?

[h2]The monetization layer[/h2]

Endfield is a gacha, so every psychologically manipulative trick in the book that these "games" use is on full display:
⚪ FOMO: Limited-time banners and characters
⚪ Sunk Cost: I'm halfway through before pity, so I might as well keep spending until I obtain it
⚪ Artificial Scarcity: Economy is unfriendly. Oroberyls and other resources are intentionally scarce; they can't be farmed at the player's own pace. This conditions player behavior
⚪ Endgame with powercreep: The game will always create incentives to pull the latest characters, even at the detriment of the game itself
⚪ Content cadence: Drip-feeding creates the illusion that this much revenue is needed to fund constant content while maintaining player retention. Realistically, all updates combined before a major patch are the size of a $40 expansion pack
⚪ ZERO preservation: The game is supported only as long as the publisher wills it. Once it's done, the game is shut down and gone: FOREVER
⚪ No replayability: Gacha games have no "New Game" option; they're fully account-bound. I don't even need to elaborate on how absurd this is

These are some of the worst ones.

Endfield employs these techniques to maintain player retention and game visibility while targeting compulsive spenders, vulnerable people, and gambling addicts as potential spenders. A single character can cost hundreds of dollars to max out within the limited-time window. It's absolute insanity.

So no, this isn't a "game with gacha". It's a live-service retention platform with a solid game held hostage by it. Its techniques are manipulative, exploitative and designed to push impulsive spending. Questionable at best, unethical at worst, and never something that should be defended or justified. An example of gacha as a complement to a game is Resident Evil 4 (2023), and it's awesome.

So, in short: Endfield is a service where its manipulative monetization and economy dictate every single one of its features. It's not a game designed to played, but to be stayed, as it uses these methods to try to squeeze the player's wallet dry, while the player manages their currencies in search of a short-term dopamine shot.

[h2]The community reaction[/h2]

Fans often try to defuse these criticisms, claiming "what do you expect?", "you don't need everything," or simply "have some self-control." These are mere comforting deflections. It's compartmentalization to adapt to this extremely hostile environment. Once that happens, they resign to this ecosystem and treat these things as features rather than aggressive monetization walls (they normalize it). Fans shift the blame to critics instead of the developer who deliberately chose gacha, deeming these critics ungrateful or spoiled. Again, it's a deflection that doesn't engage with the criticism. Claiming Endfield's gacha is more "generous" ultimately changes nothing. It's still a predatory framework, objectively operating through every mechanism I cited. "Tolerating" these systems is to give the devs a pass for worse precedents (look at HSR).

Gachas are in no way cutting-edge or technologically groundbreaking. They're entertaining, fine-to-good games at best, but are put to shame by some premium games. Crimson Desert, a GOTY quality game, beats Endfield in almost every department without resorting to these aggressive tactics, by simply being a video game. There's NOTHING in Endfield's design or quality that inherently justifies these monetization choices. The game does not require these retention throttles and time-gates, but the monetization does.

Here's the thing: there's no need to be binary. You can love Endfield, call it your comfort game or all-time favorite, and still hold HG and other greedy gacha developers accountable for exploiting the player base and demand better, exposing these systems. Boycotts work when sustained, not as a short-term, two-day thing. HG doesn't need your affection or loyalty in exchange for freebies (or, as I call them, breadcrumbs). THEY'RE the ones that need to be grateful and loyal to you for supporting their game. Unfortunately, we see the opposite, a psychological entrapment.

[h2]Alternatives?[/h2]

The Joker card of deflections is "they need to make money." Every developer needs to make money. Every game has a price. F2P isn't free because the developer gives the product away; it's free because the player is monetized through another mechanism. Because it needs money and is F2P, it does not mean that any approach is justified.

A good alternative is this newer trend of gacha games becoming premium games (DragonSword, Solo Leveling, Mega Man ReDive, the upcoming FF Resonance). My premium example will always be Octopath Traveler 0. It's a conversion of the first major arc of the STILL-active gacha game Champions of the Continent. It brings over the entire story, with many reworks and additions. Not every aspect, event, or collab makes it over, but the core essence is preserved, and that arc can finally be experienced as a video game.

Imagine if HG worked to preserve Endfield's artistic merit by bringing all content before its eventual 2.0 into a game like that. Sell it as a game with its own success criteria. Reworking and porting out its server-side components would be necessary, but if DragonSword's developers pulled it off in such a tight schedule under terrible conditions, you can't convince me a multimillion-dollar company like HG can't. Sell subsequent arcs as DLCs (expansions) and eventual skins at fixed prices. There are many alternatives that could keep the gacha alive while respecting and preserving the work for a different demographic (as Hound13 stated in a Q&A: gacha and premium gamers are two different demographics). Release these archival versions a year or so later so the gacha isn't hurt commercially. That's one alternative, yet players often gravitate toward the F2P comfort zone and accept lowered standards. The lack of perspective and ideas scares me. "It's not financially viable." It's not your job to worry about that; it's the developer's, and they should treat you like the king or queen you are: the customer. They're the ones that should be conducting surveys and publicly addressing these viability concerns. The examples I mentioned will only gradually grow, so I hardly believe this can't be financially viable or profitable. And no, DON'T wait for EOS, it makes the chances of it happening close to zero. Not a perfect world, but a pragmatic approach. A Chinese gacha doing this successfully would create a huge snowball effect. Both sides win. Delusion? Maybe, but the games mentioned point the other way.

I was going to write a big paragraph about this game, its background and what it does best and worst, but I'll just keep it as short and direct as possible.

Endfield is a well made game. It is beautiful, polished and quite unique in its genre. It sports extremely curated locales where Death Stranding sandbox mechanics and pseudo-FromSoft design philosophy are mixed together, which means there's no zooming around with special abilities, vehicles or parkour movement. You'll have to make your way on foot and place ziplines routes to make your way through the maps easier and efficient, which adds to the satisfaction of map exploration while you effectively turn it into your own unique space different from other players'.
Its mix of RPG elements with a factory sandbox works better than you'd expect, but it's by no means perfect nor something that will click within everyone, and the latter is not skippable at all. It is a core part of the game, one the devs will simplify, but do not intend to get rid of. 
The music and presentation are top notch, ESPECIALLY the former... the story not so much. There is absolutely a lot of thought behind it when you dig deeper (documents, foreshadowing, hell even song lyrics from years ago) but in its current state the writing itself leaves a bit to be desired, even though lately it has had some pretty good highs. By the time I'm writing this review, the prologue to the overall plot has just finished (patch 1.6, Sanctuary of Ink) so I'm hoping that what I'm saying will age like milk. The developers have shown interest into expanding the narrative to a wider scope similar to their previous game, and they always collect feedback on the story's writing quality. (Quick parenthesis: while Endfield is officially a spinoff, it is very much connected to 2019's Arknights. You don't need to play the original game as most concepts will be presented to you, but it helps a lot with background context. The writing in that game can hit phenomenal highs, so i still recommend checking it out. There is a PC port and various story readers available online)

Some personal suggestions: 
1) GRIT YOUR TEETH THROUGH THE TUTORIALS: they are kind of too overwhelming, the target audience for gacha games are babies so for a game with so many moving parts like factory, arpg gameplay, stock trading and the like there will be quite a bunch of handholding at first. I'm not sure if they've improved them retroactively, so I'm speaking from 1.0 experience here.
2) DON'T MINMAX: most people in gacha games tend to minmax and burn out immediately, but for this game you genuinely don't need to, and the devs also made it loud and clear. Make your own factory, you own zipline routes, no matter how unoptimized - there is nothing you will be missing out on. This will greatly increase your enjoyment of the game.
3) TAKE YOUR TIME: as of now Endfield's only time-sensitive mode is Echoes of War, and you just need to clear the stages to get the rewards from it which are very little. The developers are putting stronger emphasis on permanent content instead, like Umbral Monument and various other gamemodes, so there is little FOMO to be worried about. Time-limited events vary from fluff quests to experiments for future permanent additions or hardcore combat content like Contingency Contract.
4) SAVE YOUR PULLS: Endfield's gacha system is quite esoteric in the 3D gacha space, my general suggestion is to always have 120 pulls saved up for a character you're interested in. That way you'll either find the character earlier or hit the guarantee, maybe even grab a couple of previous limited characters too. There is no pull pressure or powercreep, so don't feel bad about skipping. The only character that you should prioritize for a rerun would be Arcane, as she's the closest to a meta-defining unit even though the game basically has no meta right now.

There is quite a lot to this game that a single Steam review can't contain. It definitely lives up to its "Potential Game" nickname, but I enjoy many parts of it and frankly it just keeps getting better. The best course of action imo would be to play up to Operation Homecoming (patch 1.4) and see if it sticks with you. It certainly did for me and I look forward to its future, hoping to see its so called "Potential" fully realized.
