Quick thing I want to mention before I get into the meat of my review. Another Steam User has claimed that the game requires you to disable HVCI. Upon starting the game, I did not have such an alert show up, BUT I did notice part of my Core Isolation stuff was disabled due to Easy Anti-Cheat (Which this game doesn't use, from what I can tell). If you have EAC, odds are high that whatever Narakas Anti-Cheat needs disabled is already disabled by EAC.

Okay, so. When I first was considering Naraka, I was on the fence. I didn't really want to get sunk into ANOTHER Battle Royale, as I've kinda checked out of most BRs, these days. That said, Naraka is... weirdly enough, a breath of fresh air. The melee focused approach to it is certainly an interesting idea that I do not hate, but I am also speaking from the perspective of someone who has only played vs AI in the dedicated bot lobby mode. 

Speaking of that, A vs AI/Bot Lobby mode that allows full progression of the game should be the norm nowadays, with how overly competitive games have gotten. Between some players just naturally getting better quicker than others, and the SBMM systems just not working (most of the time), I have enjoyed most of the matches against the AI, and it allows me to just chill and relax, be it on my own, or while in a discord call with friends. I will not speak on the regular BR, as I have no intentions on touching it, seeing as I can play the game the way I want to and still get rewarded as much as others.

Now, onto Showdown, the PvE mode. Its... interesting. On one hand, I wish the missions were longer and had a more cohesive story, but the more I thought about it, the more I didn't mind them being short. It reminds me of mobile games and their incredibly short levels, BUT without the horrendous stamina system that basically prevents you for playing for longer than you want to. I also love how the ranged gameplay was also changed to be just as satisfying as the melee gameplay.

I have not tried the Extraction Shooter gamemode, as I am not a fan of that genre at all (mainly because every single one that has existed is a PvPvE one, and I'm not really into PvP games as a whole, anymore), so I will not be speaking on it. 

As for cosmetics, its a typical Eastern made game, so most high rarity cosmetics are going to show more skin or be very extravagant. If you're into that, I don't judge. My only gripe on the cosmetic part is the fact a lot of cosmetics from Hidden Treasures (The Battle Pass) are seemingly never coming back. But, this is an issue that plagues every live action game nowadays, so I'm not going to hold it against the devs too much. I will say, one thing that I have to praise the devs for is the ability to completely change a characters facial features (For the most part, there is one character that cannot be altered, due to the fact they are a collab character). Being able to use one character as a basis for another character I want to bring into the game is amazing, and I'm glad it is an option.

From my initial perspective, Naraka Bladepoint is a pretty fun game with a fair amount of stuff to do that I'm glad a friend recommended to me. Hopefully it continues to improve as time goes on.

Recipe for Potato Dumplings (Varenyky)
Ingredients:
For the dough:
Wheat flour – 500 g
Water – 200 ml
Egg – 1
Salt – 1 tsp
For the filling:
Potatoes – 1 kg
Onions – 2
Lard or butter – 50 g
Salt – to taste
Ground black pepper – to taste
Preparation steps:
Making the dough:
Sifting the flour: Sift the flour into a large bowl.
Making the dough: Add salt and the egg to the flour. Gradually pour in the water, constantly stirring. Knead the dough until it becomes smooth and elastic.
Resting the dough: Wrap the dough in plastic wrap or cover it with a towel and let it rest for 30 minutes.
Preparing the filling:
Boiling the potatoes: Peel the potatoes, cut them into large pieces, and boil until tender in salted water.
Preparing the onions: While the potatoes are boiling, finely chop the onions. Sauté the onions in lard or butter until golden brown.
Making the potato puree: Drain the potatoes and mash them. Add the sautéed onions, salt, and pepper to taste, and mix well.
Forming the dumplings:
Rolling out the dough: Roll out the dough into a thin sheet about 2-3 mm thick. Use a glass or cutter to cut out circles approximately 7-8 cm in diameter.
Forming the dumplings: Place a spoonful of potato filling on each circle of dough. Fold the dough in half and pinch the edges tightly to seal the dumplings.
Cooking the dumplings:
Boiling water: Bring a large pot of water to a boil, add salt.
Cooking the dumplings: Gently drop the dumplings into the boiling water, stirring carefully to prevent sticking. Cook until done (approximately 5-7 minutes after they float to the surface).
Serving:
Removing the dumplings: Remove the dumplings with a slotted spoon and place them on a plate.
Serving: Serve the dumplings hot, optionally drizzling with melted butter, sour cream, or sautéed onions.
Enjoy your meal!

NARAKA: BLADEPOINT revolutionizes the battle royale genre by emphasizing melee combat and martial arts in ways no other game has attempted. The combat system is incredibly nuanced, featuring a rock-paper-scissors mechanic with attacks, blocks, and counters that creates intense psychological battles. The grappling hook mobility system transforms traversal into an exhilarating experience, allowing players to scale mountains and zip between buildings with spectacular fluidity. Each character brings distinctive abilities and ultimate moves that significantly impact tactical decision-making and team composition strategies. The Far Eastern aesthetic is breathtaking, with gorgeous landscapes inspired by Chinese mythology that create an immersive visual experience. The skill ceiling is remarkably high, rewarding players who invest time mastering combo chains, parry timings, and strategic positioning. The ranged weapons complement rather than dominate the melee focus, adding variety without overshadowing the core swordplay. The regular content updates and seasonal events demonstrate strong developer commitment to maintaining a fresh and engaging experience. While the game requires dedication to overcome the steep learning curve, the satisfaction of outplaying opponents through pure skill makes NARAKA: BLADEPOINT a standout title in the oversaturated battle royale market.

I really enjoy playing Naraka: Bladepoint — it’s one of the most unique battle royale games out there. Unlike most BRs, this one is completely melee-based, which makes the combat feel fast, fluid, and skillful. There are several different modes to choose from like Ranked, Showdown, Casual, and Bloodbath, so there’s always something to dive into.

I love working on leveling up my characters and unlocking their abilities — it adds a nice sense of progression. The Showdown bosses are a blast to fight, and the storyline is surprisingly engaging too. I’m a bit further along on my PS5 account than my PC one, but I enjoy both and have a great time leveling up and experimenting with different heroes.

Overall, Naraka: Bladepoint is an awesome experience for anyone who enjoys action-packed, melee-focused gameplay with tons of style and depth.

My review reflects the NA server. I have around 3-4k Total Hours played including Xbox first 1-2 years of games release in NA.

Player Count: Steam Charts don't reflect NA specifically. NA has little to no players unless you play at certain times.

Performance: No matter how much you train in 1v1 situations, the player with the lower ping will always have the edge. And the server + optimization issues are insane. You can play a custom room at 150 FPS and 60–70 ping against someone running 400–500 FPS with 15 ping. It's hard to take the game seriously on a competitive level outside of Trios in NA with the way it's currently set up. The NA server is terrible, and I've also played on SEA while in Bangkok, Thailand.

Also FPS dramatically improves ping.

Knowledge: There is a lot of information and teaching for this game. It's taken time, but over the years more resources have become available to NA. But the heart of what you really need to know is still in Chinese on Douyin.

Random Person: But it's a fighting game. It requires practice.

Me: Yes, but other fighting games have practical frame data you can train around and understand in a controlled environment where FPS is locked.

Random Person: Yeah, but all the info on the game is out there. You just have to look.

Me: Yes, let me tell someone who's trying out the game to sort through captcha-filled content in a different language and hope they find what they need.

Random Person: NA isn't dead.

Me: Look at the ranks. Look at Steam Charts. If that many people were actually playing, you would see a lot more contenders with over 100 matches played. A healthy server doesn't require you to get on at specific times just to find players or let you reach max rank in 3 days.

Overall: This game is amazing, its concept and everything about it. It just works against itself over time.

"582 hours in, and I'm still theorycrafting in my sleep"

I came for the hype, stayed for the friends I dragged in with me. Two weeks of hard co-op grinding — 130 hours — and not once did the game feel like a chore. Path of Exile 2 is that rare kind of game where you set a small goal for the evening ("just one more map") and surface three hours later with a new build, a dead boss, and a loot filter that needs surgery.

What got me:

Combat with actual weight. Every hit lands like it means it. My Ice Strike Invoker freezes entire screens and it still feels satisfying after hundreds of hours. Skills have momentum, dodge has consequences, fights are honest.
Build depth that borders on pathology. The passive tree, support gems, runes, charms, uniques — the number of ways to break this game is genuinely absurd. Half my hours are probably spent in planning tools, and I regret nothing.
SSF is a real mode, not a punishment. Playing self-found forced me to understand the crafting and the economy of my own inventory. Best decision I made.
Co-op. Running maps with a friend, resurrecting each other, arguing over loot — this is where ARPGs become something more than a slot machine.
Is it perfect? No. Some endgame systems want a manual nobody wrote, trade is its own boss fight, and the difficulty spikes occasionally feel like a wall rather than a curve. But every session gives back more than it takes.

582 hours. Still not bored. Still planning the next build thumbs-up.

This game suffers from the same problems as all games that pride themselves on being "difficult" and "hardcore". Hardcore gamers have a ton of time and focus on their hands, which means they're going to dissect every system you throw at them and find the optimal path through it. The only way to keep them interested is to tune the challenge such that even the optimal path has a difficult time. The core problem is this makes anything that isn't the optimal path completely useless. If you want to play this game and see anything past Act 1, you're not going to be able to play the class you think is fun, or use the skills you think are neat, or try a fun combo you think could be interesting. You will follow a build guide and you will walk one of a handful of paths already carved for you by the unemployed manchildren that found it months ago, or your "playing" will be watching a death screen and wondering how it got there.

tl;dr this game is tuned to entertain someone that's already played it for 2500 hours, memorized the whole thing, and has more or less solved the first 99% of the game. If that ain't you, it's not for you.

Upon the 1.0 release the game will be F2P, even currently there is technically no pay-to-win with you being able to purchase cosmetics and stash tabs. The stash tabs do feel necessary though if you want to play end game or sell your items to other players.

A ridiculous amount of build variety in this game is what makes it so enjoyable and re-playable. You'll notice though that unless you're super knowledgeable about... well everything, that you can't just make any playstyle or skill work in the endgame. This can be frustrating and so I believe the vast majority of new players will just end up following build guides, so I'd start there if you're new.

While there is a lot of endgame content and mechanics, a good amount of it to me feels like clutter. Crafting is way too convoluted, not necessarily with the base currencies but with all the league mechanic currencies. For example, how on earth are you supposed to know how to craft a war-cry helmet without third party resources(the wiki or any crafting site)? The amount of fumbling you'll be doing when you learn how to craft feels too high, it's not intuitive, and the market feels like a knowledge check for buying crafted items. Even so, it's amazing just how you're able to customize your gear, and the in-game market is just brilliant. I love having the option to just buy other players' drops/crated gear.

I note this since a lot of build guides will ask you to get some of these chase items, and odds are you won't have them, and you won't be able to afford them. It can either make for a fun chase item or a very frustrating experience:

Lineage support gems are not explained well enough if at all in terms of how to acquire them. Some of them will just drop organically as you play while as others are only found from a specific mechanic, but you wouldn't know which is which without 3rd party info. 

Jewels are the final convoluted endgame mechanic I will mention. The acquisition of some of these uniques are just not plausible, meaning you will need to buy the exclusive unique jewels if you want or need them for your build. Will you know how to go after these items if you want them? Not without 3rd party info. Will you even know about some of them and what they even really do in game? Not without 3rd party info. I would love GGG to streamline these items, there'll already dropping the 5 affix rares, now I'd recommend a relook at the unique Jewels as well.

A pitch-perfect action RPG with excellent build variety and replayability due to its layers of complexity. The way the already-world-class currency system is intertwined with the economy is engaging, and once the shock wears off about what to do with the passive skill tree, its low-cost respec and slottable skill gems encourage a ton of build exploration that all pays off great in gamefeel.

Aesthetically, the game impresses with a wide variety of settings, skill effects, monsters and gore. The grim lore of Wraeclast somehow brushes against both corniness and edginess, but the story still takes itself seriously and weaves well into the "hack-and-slash until your inventory's full, then take some town time" loop proven by Diablo. The skills look and feel great to use, so you'll be happy to customize them to your delight. Meanwhile, your class and ascendancy offer clever mechanical twists on genre tropes.

It's a game to get lost in. As you approach endgame, you need to start engaging with trade more often (the most valuable ground loot being currency items is ingenious, by the way). It might not jive with everyone, but it does with me; I've gotten two characters to 95+ and been entertained throughout the process each time. The endgame content is meticulously fleshed out at time of writing, and each league introduces more. I'll cherish my EA toons and am surprisingly excited for the 1.0 release!

Nearly 100 hours of my life sacrificed to this game, several weekends mysteriously vanished, and I can confidently say it's been one hell of a ride!

First off, THE SKILL TREE. Actually, calling that monstrosity a tree is an insult to trees everywhere. It's a whole damn UNIVERSE! The sheer amount of customization is absolutely insane. You can build your character in a thousand different directions, assuming you don't spend half your playtime staring at the screen questioning every life decision you've ever made while trying to figure out where to spend your next skill point.

Combat? Fantastic! The spells are flashy, the abilities are satisfying, and watching entire screens of enemies explode into colorful chaos is undeniably entertaining.

BUT... At higher levels, combat starts feeling a bit underwhelming. You're slaughtering wave after wave of enemies, unleashing what can only be described as magical war crimes, and yet somehow the sense of accomplishment just isn't there. Sure, the screen looks like a fireworks factory exploded, but eventually you start wondering, "Am I actually accomplishing anything, or am I just an overqualified exterminator with a light show?"

Despite that, Path of Exile 2 is an incredibly fun and ambitious game with enough build possibilities to keep theorycrafters busy until the heat death of the universe.

Great game. I just hope v1.0 fixes some of the frustrating design choices.

It sometimes feels like Diablo without enough information or on-screen feedback. You get a massive enemy health bar and slowly chip away at it, sometimes repeating the same attacks for so long that your hands start cramping.

What needs fixing:

We need proper death information. Tell us what damaged us and what actually killed us. This becomes especially frustrating in endgame when the screen is filled with effects and it's almost impossible to tell what happened.
Death can feel too punishing at higher levels. When progression becomes extremely slow, losing XP can wipe out a significant amount of grinding.
Crafting is unnecessarily complicated. There are countless currencies and mechanics, with very little guidance for new players.
Core and league mechanics need better explanations. As a new player, I'm constantly left wondering what things mean and how they actually work.
Combat needs better feedback. This is probably my biggest issue. If the game is going to heavily punish death, it should at least give players enough information to understand why they died.

[H1]So what's it about?[/H1]
POE2 takes place 20 years later than the events in POE1. Like the first game, you start with nothing and end up fighting Gods and other divine beings. But to get there you will go through many beautifully crafted levels with many systems. At first it is intimidating and for your first few runs I highly recommend using a guide from for example [url=https://mobalytics.gg/poe/builds]Mobalytics[/url]

Like POE1, POE2 will be F2P upon its release. There is monetisation in different ways: supporter packs (cosmetics that are available for a couple of months), there is a store with QoL improvements like additional stash tabs and more cosmetics and there are loot boxes like in POE1. 

If you want to have the best experience I recommend getting a couple of stash tabs so you're able to manage your inventory better. Everything else is just there to support the devs and of course look super cool. POE2 has the best graphics I've ever seen in an ARPG and the cosmetics do not disappoint. 

There are 8 classes in the game that you can specialise further as you progress; ultimately there are 12 classes planned. I highly recommend picking a class that is less dependent on gear for the first playthrough.

The campaign has currently 4 acts and 1 interlude (spread over 3 areas). When the game releases the interlude will be removed and act 5 and act 6 will be added. All the acts are really just the tutorial to avoid overloading you with the many systems POE2 has. After that the real game begins and it's all about completing maps at an increased difficulty for better rewards. 

[H1]The good[/H1]
Act 4 is amazing - good story, great enemies and a nice pace. It's my favourite act followed by the interludes. I feel this is where POE2 really comes alive as you can get better items from trading, have access to much better skills and there are more interesting bosses. 

It has an extensive customisation system but less complex than POE1. This still allows for a lot of experimentation to find the ideal setup. But unfortunately the boss mechanics will punish you hard if you don't play meta.

I love the voice acting and the enemies and the graphical effects; GGG's actors and artists are some of the best in class. 

There are many different leagues you can play (comparable to seasons in other games), including hard core and you can build even your own if you feel like.

You will have your own hideout that you can decorate as you please. Later this becomes your central hub.

I like the ascendency trials better in POE2 than POE1; it's like a little adventure before you meet the end boss. The rituals are good too: it's fast paced fighting against bosses you have defeated before; if it takes too long a second boss will enter the area making it even more frantic. 

Atlas unlock (the second part of the game after you completed the campaign) applies to your whole account so any new characters that you create can continue where you left with your older ones. Unfortunately this doesn't apply to the main campaign.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
Act 2 and especially act 3 feel too long with too much backtracking. The issue is also that the map is not saved so if you are halfway the act and need to do RL stuff and return a day later you don't really know where to go. You see your objectives and then just try to find the locations - most of the time it's not so clear where you need to go. Not all quests are marked either so sometimes you just need to figure out in what random map an objective is located. 

The Atlas treeis not explained. Many areas are locked and it's cryptic how to unlock these at first. It is also a long winded experience. There are many quests that ask you to travel through the map passing many, many uninteresting maps (bad loot, no experience etc). It feels like a drag and there were quite a few sessions where I got bored and just played something else.

Progression in the Atlas part of the game is locked behind milestones/bosses. It means that even though you have unlocked enough points you can't use them until you beat a certain boss or reached a certain point. This makes the game feel artificially locking your progress; I usually like to explore but I was punished for that as I couldn't progress. 

The worst is that some of the boss will seriously punish you even if you have the best possible gear that you can afford and maxed out your resistance. The Arbiter of Divinity fight for example blocked my progress and insta killed me so many times. It’s just not fun.  

Passing level 9 and higher in the Atlas I noticed a sudden decrease of performance: I found later that it had to do with DLSS - by turning it off the issues disappeared.

I played the druid and the ranger: the ranger has great speed and good control but the druid felt like he was drunk: sluggish with too much momentum. Dodging is even worse; frequently I quit playing a session because I was fed up with how indirect my druid moved. But even with the ranger it feels you're on a grid and can only stop at certain times. 

Some of the bosses rely on one shot mechanics and combined with compulsory multi-stage events it quickly makes you feel it's random whether you lose or win. Skill matters less - if you hit hard and dodge then you may win or maybe the boss decides to use death-to-player attack and it's game over and you can try again. 

For a melee character act 1 and part of act 2 feels unnecessary punishing especially if you can't twink: there is hardly any loot, the enemies kill you with ease and you have only a few skills. In act 2 your resistance take a hit while you are still carry low level gear. It also feels unbalanced in the sense that you are under-levelled even if you do all the quests. You only gain access to trading in act 4 so unless you have already completed a run it's a real struggle where bosses one shot you. It's not fun and makes the campaign much longer than necessary.

GGG should learn from GW2 where when you choose to play the campaign but for subsequent characters it's optional. Giving the player the choice instead of forcing us going through the same story again is not fun. 

I disapprove of the loot box mechanic introduced every season. It's not required, it's not in your face but it can cause serious issues for people that are vulnerable to gambling addiction. The positive maybe is that all the loot from the loot boxes are released later in the MTX store against a much higher price but still it should not be in the game.

[H1]The DLCs[/H1]
There are no DLCs other than supporter packs that only add cosmetics to the game. There is a MTX store to buy cosmetics and QoL items. If you want to get any of those wishlist them and wait for a sale (every couple of weeks). Note that some of the MTX from POE is compatible with POE2 in particular most of the inventory tabs but many are still not; also some cosmetics from POE2 is not compatible with POE1. GGG is busy making more available over time but there is no time given. 

[H1]Bugs[/H1]
I experienced a micro stutter in the later levels in the game. By turning off DLSS it stopped and the game ran a lot smoother.

[H1]Summary[/H1]
As it currently stands POE2 has some of the best graphics, audio, voice acting and effects. In act 4 the game comes alive and gives already a solid experience. It's a bit slower than POE1 but still fast enough to keep you entertained. 

I don’t like how the characters move and it's a pity you have to replay the campaign with every character. Unless you have a perfect build be prepared to die a lot to one shot mechanics. This leaves a lot less space for experimentation as you will just end up frustrating yourself.

The game is good but I hope GGG can work on the negative aspects. If you like ARPGs than POE2 is definitely a game to check out – if you’re unsure wait until December 2026 when it will come out F2P.

It's the true spiritual successor to Diablo 2 and the best modern ARPG. 

The quality of life features added (wasd controls, async trading, in-game price checking, checkpoints, simplified skill gems) make it much more accessible than its predecessor. It has a very fair freemium model allowing players to try out the game and then they can invest in stash tabs if they like it which makes organizing your loot a lot more convenient. I recommend waiting for a stash tab sale which happen pretty often - about every 3 weeks. Whatever you buy also applies to POE 1 so you will have your microtransactions and stash tabs in both games. I recommend buying the [url=https://www.pathofexile.com/purchase#FirstBloodPack]First Blood Pack[/url] to get $20 worth of credits as you get a free stash tab and also a weapon effect for POE 1.

There's about a 20 hour campaign to level up your character and then things get much more interesting in the endgame where you can farm whatever mechanic you'd like and complete season challenges. The economy also opens up and makes it fun to find/craft and sell good loot as well as buy better gear. There's lots to do and you can always create a new character with a different class to try out different playstyles. You can also respec your current character to different passive skills or a different ascendancy to try out different builds for your class.

The devs are very responsive to feedback and are constantly working on updates and patches. There's new seasons every once in a while that reset the economy and add a ton of updates to the game giving you a reason to log back in. Everyone starts fresh with a new character each season. The devs also generously provide free microtransactions (you keep forever and can use on any character) for completing the season challenges which give you something to aim for. There's also occasionally free MTX drops from twitch streams.

The game is not without some flaws. The optimization of the game is not the best and performance can really take a dive. I have an older PC and use low settings to get better FPS but even better rigs can have shaky performance. It does seem to be improving over time and hopefully will be better for the full release. I am also not a fan of the requirement of completing trials with roguelike elements to specialize your character. The Trials of Sekhemas has a different health system than normal play which is really tiresome. Thankfully you can pay in-game currency for someone to carry you through the trials or try the Trials of Chaos which is a different system. Lastly, while you can play with the classic mouse controls, some parts of the game such as bosses feel tuned to wasd play.

[h1]190 hours invested, account permanently banned after account compromise.[/h1]

After 190 hours in Path of Exile 2, I returned from months of inactivity to discover my account had been permanently banned for allegedly using third-party software. I have never used cheats, bots, or automation.

Upon investigating, I found my original character missing, replaced by an unfamiliar high-level character with a randomly generated looking name. I also discovered an unrecognised email address and suspicious login activity, strongly suggesting my account had been compromised.

GGG Support acknowledged that these symptoms were consistent with a compromised account. Despite this, their final response was:

[b]"I have looked into this for you, and I'm afraid this account is to remain closed."[/b]

[b]"You're welcome to create a new account should you wish to continue playing."[/b]

No meaningful explanation of whether the compromise was confirmed or how the evidence influenced their decision.

[b]190 hours of progress, characters, and purchases effectively lost. Just create another account.[/b]

I understand account security is important, but compromises happen. What matters is how companies handle them. The lack of transparency and seemingly dismissive response has completely undermined my trust in GGG.

I genuinely loved PoE2, which makes this especially disappointing.

[b][u]My warning: You can invest hundreds of hours into this game, but if your account is compromised and subsequently banned, don't assume you'll recover your account or progress, even with evidence of unauthorised access.[/u][/b]

I cannot recommend investing significant time or money into a game with an account recovery experience like this (or lack thereof).

Что тут охуенно (по сравнению с первой частью):

ГРАФИКА И АНИМАЦИИ: Первая часть выглядела как игра 2008 года, которую случайно залили в Steam в 2013-м. Вторая — это просто секс. Удары чувствуются, мобы разлетаются, кровь, кишки, расчлененка. БОССЫ: Это не ебля по кругу. Это Dark Souls с видом сверху. Ты учишь паттерны, ты умираешь, ты материшься, ты побеждаешь. Такого удовольствия от файтов в первой части не было. Там были просто мешки с HP, которые надо было переехать.

КАМПАНИЯ: Она не растянута на 10 актов, которые ты проходишь 50 раз за лигу. Она компактная, мрачная, с сюжетом. Первая часть в этом плане — это просто бег по коридорам с криками НАХУЙ, В МАПЫ

А теперь ложка дёгтя. И это не ложка, это черпак.

БИЛДОСТРОЕНИЕ: Вот тут первая часть ебёт вторую. В PoE 1 у тебя 100500 вариантов собрать персонажа. Ты можешь сделать билд на все: на урон, на скорость, на ауры, на то, чтобы мобы сами убивались от твоего взгляда. Во второй части... ну, у тебя есть 6-7 рабочих архетипов. Остальное — это либо мусор, либо «мы это понерфим в следующем патче». Дерево пассивок стало проще, но не в хорошем смысле. Оно стало примитивнее. В первой части ты сидел в POB (Path of Building) часами, чтобы выжать еще 5% урона. Во второй ты сидишь и думаешь: «Блядь, я возьму эти 3 нода, потому что остальные — это +10 к интеллекту, а мне это нахуй не нужно».

КОМПЛЕКСНОСТЬ: Первая часть — это швейцарский нож. Вторая — это хороший, дорогой, но однофункциональный нож. Да, он режет лучше, но открывашку для пива ты им не сделаешь. В PoE 1 ты мог комбинировать камни, линковать их, делать из дерьма конфетку. Во второй части система камней упрощена до безобразия. Это сделано для консолей и для новых игроков, но старики остались с хуем.

ИТОГ:

Path of Exile 2 — это охуенная игра. Это лучше, чем 90% ARPG на рынке. Она красивая, она сложная, она затягивает. Но она не лучше первой части в плане глубины. Она — другая. Она для тех, кто хочет подраться с боссами, а не для тех, кто хочет неделю сидеть в POB и строить билд на 100 миллионов DPS.

И да, новичкам не стоит начинать с первой части. Если вы никогда не играли в PoE, не лезьте в первую. вы утонете в дереве пассивок, вы запутаетесь в камнях, вы сгорите нахуй на первой же лиге. Начните со второй. Она дружелюбнее. Она объясняет. Она прощает ошибки. А потом, когда вы поймете, что такое «резисты под 75%», идите в первую. И вот тогда вы поймете, что такое настоящая боль. И настоящее удовольствие.

Вердикт: 8/10. Минус два балла за то, что вырезали половину билдов. Но плюс один балл за то, что я наконец-то могу смотреть на своего персонажа без слез.

Path of Exile 2 – So much ENDGAME, they forgot about the actual game!

I had such high hopes for Path of Exile 2. I genuinely thought it would become an incredible, story-driven hack-and-slash RPG, filled with interesting adventures, memorable encounters, and a world worth exploring.

And for a while, it actually delivered on that promise.

The acts I got to play in co-op were genuinely a lot of fun. Exploring the world together, fighting bosses, and progressing through the story was exactly the kind of experience I had hoped for.

Unfortunately, the wait for new acts and meaningful story developments dragged on for far too long, and when more content finally arrived, it felt rather underwhelming.

Meanwhile, the game increasingly started feeling like a top-heavy microtransaction platform built around an endless endgame grind.

Don't get me wrong, the character-building systems are incredibly elaborate. There are countless ways to customise your character, experiment with skills, and craft equipment to suit your preferred playstyle.

But eventually, it all starts feeling like an elaborate vehicle for making damage numbers go up. All those intricate systems ultimately serve the same purpose: squeezing another ridiculous amount of damage out of your build so you can grind through more endgame content.

And that's where the game lost me.

I wanted an adventure with a compelling story, where character progression supported the journey. Instead, it feels like the journey is little more than an extended tutorial for the endless grind that follows.

I really wish I'd known beforehand just how heavily the entire experience would revolve around the ENDGAME.

[h2]Endless build freedom[/h2]
The choices in this game are almost endless. Your class is a starting point, not a cage. I play a ranger, but nothing stops me from building a spellcaster, a melee character who throws grenades, or a monk who uses a bow. The game never tells you no.

[h2]Crafting and the economy[/h2]
You can craft endlessly, and if you know what you're doing, you can make a lot of currency and fund your dream build. Around 100 to 200 hours in, the deeper market economy starts to click and the game opens up to a new level. You can predict how markets will move and which items will sell, and trading becomes its own metagame.

[h2]Combat and risk vs. reward[/h2]
Combat is really fun, and mass-clearing maps at a high level feels fantastic. The risk and reward balance is on point: if you don't want much risk, the game won't punish you, but if you take on a ton of risk and succeed, it rewards you heavily.

Most of the bad-feeling bugs have been patched. My one remaining gripe isn't technically a bug: the snakes you can't kill until they finish spinning around. Hopefully that gets changed.

[h2]Visuals and polish[/h2]
It looks great and plays very fluidly. For a game that hasn't officially launched, it's in extremely good shape.

[h2]Looking ahead[/h2]
Sword builds are on the way, which a lot of people are excited about, and I can't wait for 1.0.

[b]Highly recommended, especially if you love build freedom and deep systems.[/b]

It’s definitely not perfect. Melee balancing, endgame progression, Atlas design, passive tree power, build experimentation during league starts, and the variation in skill power, and system optomisation all still need work. Path of Exile 2 — 127 Hours Later, and I'm Still Conflicted

I've played 127 hours of Path of Exile 2 in the past two weeks.

So naturally, I'm having a difficult time deciding how much I actually like it.

I practically grew up playing Diablo 2, and I've always loved ARPGs for their character-building freedom, experimentation, and the satisfaction of creating something ridiculously powerful.

The good stuff:

PoE2 is beautiful. The art direction, detailed environments, world-building, and combat are fantastic. The endgame Atlas is particularly cool, functioning like a giant adventure map where you're constantly discovering new locations and challenges.

Controller gameplay feels surprisingly natural, and the inclusion of local couch co-op is excellent. Playing as a giant werebear smashing everything is pretty damn fun, too.

Now, the frustrating stuff.

I strongly prefer PoE1's character-building philosophy.

PoE1 let you take a skill and pile on mechanics until it became something completely absurd. Projectiles could split, chain, ricochet, leech, and trigger other effects. The passive tree encouraged traveling across enormous sections to unlock abilities that meaningfully changed your build.

PoE2 feels far more restrictive. Many support gems introduce penalties alongside their benefits, and passive tree investments frequently reward you with modest numerical improvements rather than exciting new possibilities.

PoE1 handed me a giant box of parts and said, "See what you can make." PoE2 hands me the same box with a rulebook attached.

And speaking of rulebooks, the item descriptions sometimes make me feel like English isn't my first language.

If this happens, then that happens, unless another condition applies, in which case something increases while something else decreases.

Sometimes I feel like I need three websites, a calculator, and a lawyer just to figure out whether an item is actually an upgrade.

Then there's the Trial of the Sekhemas, or as I call it, the Trial of the Smegma.

I deliberately built a character almost entirely around defense. A tank designed to withstand enormous punishment.

Then the game introduces a trial where taking hits depletes a separate Honour resource, potentially failing the entire run while I'm still at full health.

Yes, there are ways to mitigate Honour loss, but it fundamentally encourages evasive gameplay, even for characters specifically designed to absorb damage.

Why encourage radically different builds if certain challenges effectively punish you for using them?

I'm not opposed to difficulty. I'm opposed to challenges that undermine the character I've spent hours developing.

And while controller combat is excellent, not being able to simply use my mouse to navigate menus while playing with a controller is baffling.

There are also bugs and rough edges, although I'm more forgiving of those during early access. It's the intentional design restrictions that concern me.

So why have I played 127 hours in two weeks?

Because PoE2 is incredibly compelling.

There's always another item, another skill, another combination, or another frustrating obstacle I'm determined to overcome.

Sometimes I feel genuinely rewarded when everything finally clicks. Other times, I'm just relieved to have gotten past the aggravation.

I'm not entirely sure where enjoyment ends and stubborn determination begins.

Would I recommend it? Yes.

At $30 for early access, I'd recommend it primarily to dedicated ARPG fans. More casual players might be better off waiting for the planned free-to-play release.

Despite my criticisms, there's an incredible amount of content here, and clearly I've gotten my money's worth.

I just wish the developers would trust players to experiment more freely.

I'd rather have a game that occasionally lets me break its balance than one that's constantly trying to prevent me from breaking its rules.

A final thought:

Thank you to everyone who's been patient with my multiple review updates as I've continued playing. My opinions have evolved considerably throughout the experience.

I suspect this will be one of those games I play obsessively for a relatively short period, accumulate an absurd number of hours, then suddenly burn out and possibly never touch again.

But that's probably more my ADHD than the game's fault.

One additional recommendation: Play alongside an AI assistant that can actively research game mechanics as you play. With this many complicated systems, conditional effects, and interactions, having something you can ask questions and investigate builds with in real time is incredibly helpful. It's made my experience considerably more enjoyable.

Ultimately, PoE2 is a game I can be thoroughly entertained by and thoroughly irritated with at the exact same time.

After 127 hours, I've definitely gotten my money's worth.

Whether I've gotten my sanity's worth is another question entirely.

Killing white mobs is way too slow, although it did start to pick up some towards the end of Act 1.  You also go from taking almost no damage kiting stuff around to getting 1 shot randomly sometimes.  The skill tree is just broken, it only lets me toggle my next point between one weapon set and the other, I can't have it apply to both.  And I need to advance through that point to continue the build, which I don't know that I can, and I can't be bothered to get another level to find out.

This is a new-ish player's perspective.  I had 200-ish hours in PoE 1 back when it first launched, so I kind of knew how the game goes and is supposed to be played.

What I liked: the art is cool, the music/ambience is cool, 90% of the gameplay in singleplayer is smooth and moderately challenging but not oppressive.

What I don't like:

1) There are bosses (in the early game!) that hardlock you into areas where you can no longer reasonably gain exp if your build isn't correct for the bossfight.  There are no in-game tutorials or warnings about this.  You just run into the boss and lose the fight 30x in a row until you read a walkthrough and realize you were doomed from the start.

2) The game is ostensibly multiplayer, but the multiplayer experience at low levels is essentially: "the 1 guy with the most on-meta minmaxed build (who is actually 3 levels below you) runs through the map screenwiping everything while you struggle to catch up...maybe you get some exp and some scrap drops, maybe you don't."

3) Even the winnable bossfights boil down to "click, dodge, click again," repeat 100 times, and if you miss a single dodge, you get one-hit-killed, try again loser.

4) The "on-meta" builds are not intuitive at all.  If you're a newb and pick a spellcaster, you naturally would think, "oh, I should pick nodes that make my spells do extra damage."  No.  The on-meta builds are dives to nodes that read "When x happens, y triggers, and z does 200% more p while you have q enabled."

If you're a total newbie and haven't read any walkthroughs, you'll probably get hardstuck at the end of Act 1 or the beginning of Act 2, until you get a minmaxer to carry you through the roadblocks.  Not particularly enjoyable.  Also, the community doesn't give a single shit about new players or the early/campaign part of the game--all of the meta discussion revolves around endgame topics and builds that you will never see unless you specifically begin the game with minmaxing in mind and minmaxing as an end-in-itself.

Edited after additional gameplay:  lol, the game actually gets worse as you go on.  There are a couple of later bosses that are strict DPS checks.  I.e. if your build cannot do a certain amount of damage in a certain amount of time, you literally cannot progress without someone to kill the boss for you.  I can understand the endgame being balanced around hardcore minmaxers, but it's unacceptable at low levels.

- Help menu got removed in favor of tooltips that don't explain how stats and items work on a mechanical level.

- Core and League Mechanics are often only explained on a superficial level
- GGG claimed to import all MTX from PoE 1 "with high priority", One year later, none were implemented.

Again, it's a great ARPG. But it has significant flaws and issues that stem from Game design ideas that were getting old in the 90's.

The game is really good, with lots of depth and tons of build variety.  A lot of the more meta builds use similar setups, but you can build just about anything and clear all content with enough investment into your gear.

That being said, the game has issues.  Performance depends heavily on the build you're running - most builds in this game run just fine on my overpowered rig, but some builds simply crash my GPU when things get too crazy.  Disabling my GPU overclock, changing settings in game, doesn't matter - ignited ground plus Delirium plus Archon of Chayula tornadoes will eventually hard-lock my GPU and force me to hard boot my system.  This doesn't happen with any other game, and doesn't do it on most of the builds I've tried in the game (CoC/CoEA Comet and Arc did it a few times as well).  They need to figure out what's happening because the gameplay will literally still be over 90 FPS when it happens, so it's not like my GPU isn't able to perform, it's more like it's causing so much power draw that my GPU shuts down to protect itself.

This game also doesn't support any ultrawide resolution over 21:9.  If you have a 32:9 monitor you'll still be rendering all of the pixels, they just put a black bar over both sides for "fairness" to other players.  It's literally against ToS to install an easy to find mod to be able to see those pixels.  That's honestly total garbage.  If my computer is rendering those pixels, I'm damn well going to see them.  And if it was really about fairness they'd disable all ultrawide modes entirely, but instead they target a small amount of ultrawide monitors to try and appease as many people as possible, leaving those of us who saved up for a really nice monitor out to dry.  They haven't actually banned anyone for using the mod as far as I know, but if you install it that's a risk you're going to have to take.

Overall the game is really good, but has some legitimate downsides.

PoE2 has come a long way since Early Access started.

Early on, it felt unfinished in a lot of ways. But after all the updates, the game is finally starting to feel like the ARPG GGG originally promised.

The combat is probably the biggest improvement. There’s a lot more emphasis on positioning and using your skills properly rather than just deleting everything instantly (although with a good build, you can still absolutely achieve that too)

The game also looks and sounds fantastic. The atmosphere, environments, animations and boss design are a new ARPG industry standart. 

That said, I still think the biggest question is the endgame. PoE1 has years of accumulated content, insane build variety and an enormous amount of things to chase. PoE2 obviously can't compete with that yet, and whether it eventually reaches that level is still something we'll have to see.

[b]But the important thing is that the foundation is really damn good now.[/b]

If you played PoE2 early in Early Access and bounced off it, I'd genuinely recommend giving it another shot. It's a very different game from where it started.

Can't wait to see what the full release looks like.

First, my problems with the game (talking about early game mostly): 

1. No real tank support, especially close mellee like mace (you are presented with builds to become tanky, but you will mostly have to dodge anyway up to the very end game).

2. Horrible hitboxes for big bosses, again, for mellee build it will be very bad. Get used to being moved around the arena with their bodies as if you were palying some 2005 game and at the same time not being able to land a hit.

3. Incredibly slow pace. I like spending time listening to lore, appreciating the scenery. Unfortunately, you just don't have enough mobility to explore at any reasonable pace. If you really unimaginably enjoy the very map you are walking through and you don't have much to do besides this, well, this is a game for you.

4. Tradies vs HCSSF - you either go around in easy mode buying literally anything at any time and so it ges boring fast or you spend hours crawling through campaign without mandatory items (you will die because of dot quasi-oneshot anyway). In the end it doesn't really matter: it gets boring pretty fast or you just find out that you can't sustain the lifestyle this game demands.

4. The story is literally stolen from Diablo 3, it is so obnoxious it is even a bit goofy, one good thing is that not-Leoric's wife this time was not executed by him, she is a strong and relatively independent woman (like Maghda, she is literally Maghda, you'll see in Act 2).

5. I am sure that there are more endgame issues, there are many problems people were discussing in chat, but I didn't experience some of them, so I won't even mention them.

Cool stuff: normal-size enemies feel alive, they react to any impact, that's really fresh, you movements are also very natural. Gem management is cool and simple, much less demanding than POE 1. Well, in general, it's just like POE 1, but with a few tweaks and even slower.

Conclusion: If it was possible, I would make a neutral review, however, choosing between positive and negative, I choose negative now and mostly because I don't think that the problems I was talking about will ever change. This is a wonderful free game, well, just because it is free obviously, but I don't think it will help if I put "thumbs up" at this stage of development, especially because of the fact that I actually bought it and didn't just receive it for free.

Title: A Masterclass in Isometric Malice, Grinding Incompetence, and Betrayed Devotion: The Absolute Extinction Event of Path of Exile 2

I used to believe in this project with every fiber of my being. That unwavering, misplaced faith is now my deepest, most agonizing, and most humiliating wound. I didn’t just follow Path of Exile 2 through its early access trials; I consumed it, breathed it, and sacrificed thousands of waking and sleeping hours to its dark, atmospheric Wraeclast corridors, treating its punishing dodge-roll mechanics and brutal map grinds as a sacred second home. I spent years defending Grinding Gear Games' glacial patch cycles, actively rationalizing their glaring balance oversights, and aggressively dismissing the dark warning signs whispering through the community as the mere whining of disgruntled casuals. I was a foot soldier of a cult-like devotion, utterly convinced that this was a world crafted by visionary creators who understood the fragile, beautiful bond between an ARPG developer and a passionate player base.

How intensely, unforgivably, and pathetically foolish I was.

What the public sees on the store page is a legendary, next-generation action RPG—a modest isometric masterpiece born from years of dedicated work claiming to channel the ultimate hardcore ARPG experience. But beneath that paper-thin, calculatedly deceptive facade lies a predatory, aggressively hostile ecosystem designed to exploit your time, weaponize your passion, harvest your free community wiki labor, and ultimately punish you for the singular crime of actually engaging deeply with their high-tier endgame loop. The harsh reality of Path of Exile 2 isn't a love letter to the genre; it’s an institutionalized insult, a middle finger to anyone foolish enough to invest hundreds of hours into its structurally hollow and fundamentally broken framework.

Let’s pull back the curtain and talk about the unspoken horror that haunts the upper echelons of this game: the arbitrary, indiscriminate, and utterly cowardly ban hammer and trade restrictions that target the most dedicated players the moment they master currency farming or fast mapping. For weeks, the veteran group chats whispered about it in paralyzing dread. Dedicated players—the exact backbone of the economy, the people organizing multi-stash trading syndicates, keeping multiplayer trade websites alive, and filling the community forums with complex build guides—would vanish overnight, or find their accounts locked behind an impenetrable wall of developer silence. Their names were silently scrubbed from ladders, their stash tabs vaporized, and their accounts flagged for abnormal macro usage. I scoffed at the victims. I arrogantly told myself that I played completely legitimately, that hundreds of hours of honest boss killing, meticulous currency management, and raw survival persistence would serve as my shield.

Then my inevitable turn came.

At level 98, deep inside a high-tier heavily-modded map I had rolled a thousand times for an elusive, mathematically insulting rare drop, the screen seized violently. The dreaded, ominous network disconnection warning flashed across the UI, followed instantly by a forced, unceremonious dump to the login screen. My hands shook uncontrollably as I scrambled to re-enter my credentials, hit enter, and was greeted by the most infuriating, gut-wrenching, soul-crushing message any ARPG veteran can possibly receive: “This account has been banned.”

No warning. No specific rule violation cited. No log data provided. No human review whatsoever. Just an abrupt, summary execution carried out by a completely inept, automated detection algorithm that apparently cannot comprehend the basic reality that a human being might actually want to play an ARPG for more than ten hours a day or use third-party trade macros. If you dare to actually play their game, to push past the lazy mid-game wall, and dedicate real, unbroken hours to mastering the convoluted passive skill tree and grinding endgame bosses, their broken, hair-trigger security protocols automatically flag your sheer dedication as anomalous botting behavior. They don't want you reaching the summit because they either haven't built a functional, stable endgame to sustain high-level players, or they are utterly terrified of what veteran players discover when the illusion of depth is finally pulled back.

And when you turn to customer support for even a shred of recourse or human dignity? Prepare to crash headfirst into a brick wall constructed entirely of corporate apathy, cowardice, and condescension. I poured my bleeding, broken heart into a meticulously written support ticket—detailing my exact playtime, my absolute adherence to fair play, and my profound, heartbreaking disappointment. Within minutes, I was hit with the exact same robotic, copy-pasted wall of garbage text that every single banned victim receives: "Your account has been reviewed and the suspension is permanent. This decision is final."

No appeal process. No human being willing to look at your case, check your server logs, or grant you basic respect. Just a cold, algorithmic middle finger from developers who happily take the community promotion, the active player counts, and the free labor of their trade systems while treating us like disposable trash the moment an automated script misfires. The silence from Grinding Gear Games is deafening, pathetic, and entirely telling. They hide behind automated systems because facing the human wreckage of their broken anti-cheat and abysmal balance design requires a spine they simply do not possess.

The technical and design state of the game outside of these tyrannical bans is an absolute disaster anyway, propped up by pure sunk-cost fallacy and endless cosmetic microtransactions ported over from the past. The economy is a chaotic, hyper-inflated mess dictated by market manipulators who sometimes bypass the very detection tools meant for honest players. High-level combat balancing is practically non-existent, featuring lazy one-shot mechanics that demand artificial difficulty rather than tactical engagement. The repetitive grind quickly morphs from an exciting loot hunt into an unrewarding, punishing, soul-crushing chore. Every single system feels half-baked, held together with digital duct tape and the nostalgic goodwill of players who desperately want it to succeed, only to be brutally kicked in the teeth the second they cross the finish line.

My level 98 character—complete with painstakingly optimized passive trees, hard-earned rare equipment, hundreds of hours of irreplaceable memories, and genuine friendships forged in guild chats—was erased in a single, callous click. All of it gone, vaporized into the ether by developers who couldn’t care less if every single veteran player walked away.

If you are a new player currently looking at this store page, reading the glowing expansion promises, or thinking about downloading this action-RPG trap: Stop. Do not install it. Do not give them your metrics. Do not invest your time, your energy, or your passion into a digital world that fundamentally despises its own community. Play literally anything else. Because if you actually stay, if you actually grind, and if you dare to love this game too much, the only reward waiting for you at the top is a permanent ban screen and a developer who refuses to look.

Path of Exile 2 isn't just another failed live-service experiment; it is a meticulously constructed psychological trap for the devoted and an eternal monument to bad-faith development. Save your time, save your sanity, protect your peace, and stay far, far away from this toxic wasteland. It stands as a profound, unforgivable insult to anyone who ever believed that passion, time, and genuine emotional investment in a virtual world would be met with anything other than cold, mechanical betrayal. Every single pixel of this fraudulent project bleeds contempt for its players.

Path of Exile 2 has been a solid time sink. It takes the core ARPG loop and makes them addicting, worth sinking hundreds of hours into. Here's what I love about it so far:

I'm really enjoying the loot loop in this game. Items are actually quick to look through and evaluate, which is a huge relief coming from something like Diablo 4 where every drop feels like a chore to sort through.

The class and ascendancy variety is great too. There's a lot of room to build around different mechanics, and I've personally gravitated toward minion builds. That said, how smoothly you get through the campaign is pretty dependent on your class and build choices, which isn't always obvious going in.

As an example, take the Geonor, the Act 1 boss. He is brutal for how early he shows up and how little power you actually have at that point. He hits hard with chaos and ice damage, and the mist phase with the wolves is especially rough. It's a real wall for a boss you meet that early.

The downside is that these brutal bosses aren't a one-time hurdle. You have to repeat them every league, and there's no way to skip them, so what's a tough fight the first time becomes a recurring slog. Some of the maps aren't much better on that front either. A handful are excessively large and overly complicated to navigate, to the point where I've had to comb through every corner just to find the next map or area.

On the endgame side, the revamp is a big win. I actually feel incentivized to explore the overworld map now to fill out the atlas tree, instead of just beelining to whatever's most efficient.

It's not perfect (the repeat boss grind and maze maps get old) but the addictive loop and endgame changes make it worth sticking with.

Path of Exile 2 proves that GGG knows exactly how to build an ARPG. The gameplay is easy to understand right out of the gate, but the underlying systems are deep as hell. The graphics look crisp, fantastical, and heavy in all the right ways.

Out of This World Customization (With a Bit Too Much RNG)
The character customization here is genuinely out of this world. You can build almost anything you can dream up. The only real sting is that high-end progression relies a bit too heavily on RNG, which can make min-maxing your gear feel like a roll of the dice. Hence a lot of players choose to go on the market, which I will never do because:

SSF Works Beautifully
Playing SSF (Solo Self-Found) works beautifully in this game. Scraping together your own gear and making your own build function without relying on trade is easily one of the most rewarding ways to play.

The $60 Fair Trade
It's a free game, but let's be real: eventually you will need stash tabs if you want to play long-term. I bought stash tabs for 60 dollars in total, which is just the price of a normal AAA game anyway. I would happily throw more money into the pit because I actually trust GGG to support this game for at least 10 years. That level of ongoing commitment is fantastic support for a wonderful game.

We Are Spoiled Players
I saw a YouTube channel mention that we as PoE2 players are spoiled, and because of that, we all want completely different things from the game. They aren't wrong. But I salute GGG for looking at all those wishes and trying to give every player what they want without ruining the core vision.

The Campaign Is Simply Not Good for Multiple Runs
Replaying the campaign over and over is simply not justifiable. It is not good, and the maps are already showing their age—underneath the different settings, you can clearly see they are built up in mostly the same way. The campaign is far too long for repeat playthroughs: 4 acts takes me around 40 hours because I take my time with things. With 2 more acts coming, and potentially up to 10 in the end like PoE1, GGG really needs to shorten it for future runs. The cutscenes are phenomenal as seen in YouTube videos, but you need to be able to skip them eventually.

While leagues are GGG's lifeblood, that model does not cater well to more casual players. I love that the endgame is endless, but I wish GGG would cater more directly to it for casual play. Still, as long as I'm having fun doing SSF—whether taking my time in Standard or jumping into new leagues whenever I feel like it—I see no obvious drawbacks to the system as a whole. The endgame is gigantic, and knowing the game will only expand from here makes it an absolute winner.

I am glad I jumped on the wagon after months of deliberation. ARPGs are one of my favorite genres, and GGG does it very well.

Let's take it back to January of 2025. I found out that Elon Musk was boosting on a game. I decided to look it up and instantly recognized the Diablo influence. I said "okay cool whatever" and decided to move on with my life.

A couple of months later I decided to finally try out Diablo. I hopped on Xbox's Gamepass and downloaded Diablo 4 through Battle.Net. Man what a goddamn disappointment. I made it to endgame and decided to slowly shift my way to penitent. It was just simply boring. Campaign was honestly great, albeit short, but the endgame felt like it was designed to rip the literal wallet out of my pockets. It was incredibly predatory and altogether just not worth the expansions + season pass to me. I quit after 30/40 hours.

Now, in contrast, a couple of months ago, I decided to pick up the EA for POE2. I found out it was planned to be a FTP game and felt slightly scammed. A week later I realized I had received the exact amount of currency in game as I had spent on my EA purchase. I stopped feeling scammed right then.

Let me start by going slightly into depth with monetization. GGG does away with the (what I now consider) primitive practices of scamming your players. One of the best parts about all of this is their 13 year track record and the adaptations that come with it. Almost every cosmetic mtx from POE was ported over to POE2. People have spent thousands on that game, and GGG's willingness to bring those purchases to the next generation, while also backporting new cosmetics, is genuinely exactly what I want to see from FTP games. Hell, I emailed them to refund me on something that said "no refunds" and they were willing to do it no questions asked. One of the only companies in gaming that I do truly think "cares", albeit only as much as capitalism allows it. 

All that being said, the FTP gimmick in this game arises through stash space yet again. Somehow, my least favourite MMO mechanic of locking inventory space behind a paywall finds a way to haunt me in this game as well!!! Truly though, I found it more than bearable in this game. Permanent inventory space that persists over all characters in both games was cool, but giving me the currency to purchase that inventory with my purchase of the game? FUCK IT. I'm about 50usd into my stash tabs already and don't regret a single thing. I could literally not play this game again for another 5 years and I still wouldn't regret it because I know my purchases will be there when I'm back. 

The combat - truth be told - is the best I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing in a true ARPG. When looking at gameplay, I thought it to be almost "souls dodge slop" mixed with the roguelike visual clutter. It's really not. It's an ARPG that actually cares about pacing (at least until endgame lol.) I love that deliberate movements are king over abilities and stat pools, because the game forces you into situations where you would have to dodge attacks during combat or consider positioning prior to attacking. 

Buildcrafting is absolutely king, and without a doubt the best I've ever experienced. The skill tree was honestly what intimidated me more than anything before I picked up the game, but truth be told, as a Destiny 2 fan, I found the buildcrafting in that game exponentially harder because you had to be so precise (To clarify, this perspective is about rigidity and structure.)

While POE2's skill tree may look daunting, it's actually quite simple because 90% of your nodes are about stats rather than abilities. The Skill/Support/Spirit gem system completely alleviates any and all pressure. I even respec'd 1/4 of my tree at endgame for a literal 1/5 fraction of my gold. I can't say the game encourages true creativity in buildcrafting as a full respec is a heavy commitment, but, it does let you fix your mistakes. Despite those economic restrictions on experimentation, it's still - without a doubt - the most brilliant I've ever experienced.

The graphics are absolutely stunning. Diablo 4 looked good, but this is a completely different level (Sorry, I have to compare the 2 biggest ARPGs today.)

 To keep things short, I think POE2's colour grading is some of the best I've ever seen in a video game. This isn't something that most people consider consciously, but it is something EVERYONE considers subconsciously. You don't need the abhorrent 2026  lighting slop package to make a comfortable game that still catches the EYE. This may be the best proof of that concept, like ever. The unique animations, breadth of ecosystems in the maps, and variety of enemies make this game just feel constantly fresh throughout the endgame. Playing on DLAA with a 5070ti gave me some absolutely stunning moments where I would just pause and stare at the scenery.

The netcode is obviously the absolute worst part about this game. I drop from 10-15 ping to 200 at least once a play session. I am playing in my region and I don't think my connection to the server is the issue here. The fact that it is my only complaint though, says a lot.

Overall, I do think this game will one day, not only be a phenomenon, but something the coming generation will love and look back on. This game has the makings of a classic. All things considered, if GGG follows the route they seem to be taking, they have a fan for life.

I played through this game once at launch. The campaign was difficult to get through, but I managed to finish it. After that, I tried playing through it two more times, with my third playthrough being on version 0.5.5.

As much as I like how solid the game runs and how good it looks, GGG unfortunately still insists on this frustrating game design where you have access to a very limited number of skill gems and support gems during the campaign. This becomes a major problem if you make a mistake with your build or choose a skill that isn't particularly strong.

If you aren't following a guide almost 1:1, you can easily end up getting stuck on Count Geonor, the final boss of Act 1, or even the first boss of Act 2.

Yes, if you're a very skilled player who can dodge almost everything perfectly, you can probably get through these fights. But most players are going to get hit, and if your build doesn't have enough DPS, you simply won't be able to kill the boss before you run out of flasks. At that point, there isn't really much you can do other than go back and try to completely change your build.

I think something needs to change with the campaign's early-game design. Either the bosses need to do less damage, have less health, skills need to do more damage early on, or players need access to a larger variety of skill and support gems so they have more options when their original build isn't working.

Until something like that changes, I can't recommend the game.

Yes, you can technically make another character as a "mule" to get access to additional gems, but I think that completely misses the point. It's frustrating to feel like I need to create multiple characters just to get the skills I need to progress. I want to invest my time into the one character and build that I actually want to play, rather than making 10–20 different characters just to get through the campaign.

Outside of the campaign, I think the game is good, although the end game still feels fairly bare-bones at the moment.
That said, my experience with the end game is based on playing through it at launch, before the later updates, so I can't speak for how much it may have improved since then.

Lost Ark is an MMO that hooks you with some of the best action combat in the genre, but traps you in a never-ending cycle of daily chores and brutal RNG. It’s a fantastic game, but it demands a massive time commitment.

Combat/Gameplay: 10/10
Story: 5/10 (Leveling 1-50 is a slog, but the later lore is decent)
Graphics: 8/10
Music: 9/10 (The raid music is absolutely S-tier)
Endgame/Raids: 9/10 (Legion Raids are incredible)
F2P / Honing (Gacha): 4/10 (Prepare for heartbreak)
Bots/Player base: 2/10 (Historically plagued by bots, though improving)

The combat is easily the best part of the game. Smilegate nailed the isometric ARPG feel. Every class feels impactful, and the boss mechanics in Legion Raids (like Valtan or Kakul-Saydon) are incredibly satisfying to learn and conquer. The music and visuals during these fights are top-notch.

However, the game has a massive catch: the "horizontal" and "vertical" progression systems. The leveling process to reach level 50 is incredibly boring and feels like a tutorial. Once you hit endgame, you are introduced to the Honing system—an RNG-heavy gear upgrade system that can be incredibly frustrating. You will likely spend hours doing daily "homework" (Chaos Dungeons, Guardian Raids, daily/weekly una tasks) across multiple alts just to get a single upgrade attempt.

Overall: A great game with phenomenal combat and raid design, but it's a huge time sink. It is very F2P-friendly if you grind, but extremely punishing for casual players. Only dive in if you have the time to dedicate to it.

I've seen braindead takes like "don't cry about being unlucky, that's not the game's fault lol" and "how will the game stay afloat without p2w?", which don't understand the crux of the issue: games are supposed to be entertainment, but Lost Ark [i]feels[/i] terrible to progress through. What good is "good combat" and "shiny new raid" if the game is designed so that "being unlucky" means you cannot play it? How can you justify needing to pay 100x more dollars than the next guy to make the same progression? These problems are fundamental to many live-service MMOs who hold content hostage behind RNG P2W progression, and unfortunately Lost Ark is just one of many such trash.

Funny enough, I have survived over 15k hours of this game across two accounts, precisely [i]because[/i] I have always been the lucky one. I have given this game many years and attempts to fix itself and completed basically every vertical and horizontal content in the process, but after years of hoping for miracles, I'm done. 

I've always known the RNG-P2W was going to be the death of this game in global, and I really hoped SmileGate would come up with an idea that might make the business model viable without making it feel terrible. Instead, it just became another statistic that proves once again that RNG progression and P2W don't mix, not that P2W mixes well with any game to begin with. RNG-P2W might work in Korea where they don't have legal casinos, but the rest of the world does, and the dopamine junkies this game is trying to capture are already wasting away at the slots.

Lost Ark looks gorgeous and plays great. Those are the only two good things I can say about this game. Everything else is, quite frankly, unfathomable.

The design of the game, as is often the case with MMOs, and especially with Korean MMOs, is atrocious. It embodies practically everything I don't want in a game. I played during the initial launch, when things weren't nearly as bad, but it quickly became apparent what direction the game was taking. Before long, it had turned into an elaborate machine designed to extract as much time from the player as possible while giving as little meaningful reward in return.

Lost Ark is a perfect example of why I despise modern gaming, modern MMOs, multiplayer games, live-service games, and free-to-play games. It's almost impressive how many of my least favorite trends in the industry can be packed under a single umbrella. Yet somehow, Lost Ark manages to embody all of them at once. The game treats its players as little more than wallets, and that is perhaps the lowest standard a game can aspire to.

It's genuinely depressing to see people still logging into this game. Not because I have anything against them, but because I can't understand how anyone can willingly subject themselves to this kind of design. There are countless better ways to spend your time. 

So, consider this a warning: don't play Lost Ark. It looks great, as I said. It plays well. But beyond those two qualities, I find very little worth defending. This review isn't so much an expression of my opinion as it is a warning to anyone considering getting into it.

[h2] A surprisingly good free-to-play MMO [/h2]

I honestly didn't expect to like Lost Ark as much as I do.

The game has really good graphics, flashy combat, and a surprisingly beefy storyline for a free game. There is a [i]lot[/i] of content here, and it feels like there's always something else to work toward or explore.

If I had to compare it to other games, I'd say Lost Ark feels like a combination of WoW, Black Desert, ESO, and Diablo. It has the MMO structure of WoW, some of the beautiful visuals and flashy combat of Black Desert, the story and enormous amount of content you get from ESO, and the isometric hack-and-slash feel of Diablo.

That said, starting the game from scratch can definitely feel daunting. there are a TON of systems, currencies, gear mechanics, quests, and menus that get thrown at you. It can feel like you're drinking from a firehose at first. Fortunately, the game does a pretty good job at explaining these things as you encounter them, and the progression boosts are offered frequently enough that newer or returning players aren't necessarily getting stuck grinding through years of old content. 

My advice would actually be to play at least one character through the early game naturally before using any of the boosts. It gives you a much better feel for the story, combat, and all the different systems before the game starts throwing higher level mechanics at you.

I'm still relatively early in my journey, so I haven't experienced everything the game has to offer yet, but I've already been impressed by how much there is to do. For a game that's free, the amount of content and production value here is honestly kind of ridiculous.

If you're an MMO fan and haven't tried it, I'd definitely recommend giving it a shot. Just be prepared to have approximately 47 different menus open and no idea what half of them do for the first few hours. LOL
