Power-creep & lost the plot (lore and gameplay): and now Blackface in a character trailer. I’m done. I’m going to start with the most recent issue: and for context I’ve been playing since 1.0 with no breaks longer than a week over the years. 

HSR has previously faced criticisms of a lack of racial diversity and insensitivity. But Hoyoverse has reached a new low with the new Robin: Summeretto character trailer: “Chasing the Wind” at 0:57-0:58 there’s an explicitly minstrel/blackface caricature. 

I’d love to give the benefit of a doubt and assume “that’s not intentional blackface it’s just an unfortunately similar design choice”

But the why, in the previous scene at 0:56, do none of the light-skinned characters from the same organization, designs meant to mimic each other, not have the red-donut lips. The signature design trait of minstrelsy/blackface.

Hoyoverse needs to fix it and apologize, and better yet, hire some black people for their art and social teams that will stop this kind of insensitive, if not straight up harmful, cultural depictions in their content. 

Moving onto gameplay topics: 
Despite its issues, I’ve enjoyed this game since it was released. But the design of gameplay has steadily decreased for a while. 

New Units are not compatible with old ones, and team building is uninteresting, there very limited choice or variation in what kinds of teams can clear content. 

The powercreep is awful and few characters are lucky to be strong enough to last more than a few patches without vertical investment. 

They no longer have been buffing older characters with NovaFlare, helping them compete, even if only as a worse option, and there hasn’t been a four* character in YEARS. 

And worst of all: there are limited f2p options. You are guaranteed one free 5* weapon/light cone a year, and there are very few 4* options. Even less that are good for characters. 

And on top of ALL of this. There have been very few events as of late, and those events haven’t had a free weapon(light cone) in over a year. 

The female character design especially has gotten strangely bland. I like that old characters have gotten new versions, but so many new characters are the same basic trend of hoyo’s general designs (short frilly dress with no or detached sleeves)

And god forbid any woman gets pants. 

Boss HP inflation (and endgame mechanics that exclude previous teams) gets worse every patch and f2p Artifact farming and reroll tools are so insanely limited. 

Overall, I do not recommend this game until some quality of life priorities start showing. 

While I’d also love the design and story to get better, there’s been some standout quests/characters that would save it otherwise. But considering the slew of other issues I have, it’s just another straw.

Dr. Ratio, my favorite character who debuted in 1.6, has only had one rerun in 3.2.  However, Yao Guang, who debuted only 3 patches ago, already has a rerun?  Make that make sense. Desperate for our money.. As of patch 3.2, the game feels like it’s increasingly desperate for me as a player to spend money. On top of that the game feels as if it’s been dropping in quality every patch since 3.0 started. 

Story telling has taken a noticeable dip in quality from bloated dialogue that’s not engaging to me as a player. On top of that, the amount of black screens with text, which have now been lazily replaced with white screens with black text feel like a lazy and quick way to sum up events instead of creatively showing us happened. 

Drawn out quest lines each patch that take 8 plus hours to complete with no engaging substance to them just feels punishing to play, especially when the game has previously done storytelling much better within a lot less given time.

The game also feels the need to force paywalls down my throat. While I understand the game is free, it doesn’t explain why during the patch where it’s the games second anniversary it’s instead asking me to spend MORE money with events based on paying, enticing me to pull for a new character as soon as I press log in, and making content harder with the best solution being a new shiny character, that’s not even 100% guaranteed. Baring in mind older characters which players like me who have had and enjoyed using for potentially one year or more feel less useable in the current game state with not enough quick response to address/fix it.

For a game that had me hooked all of last year, the last 4 months feel like a slog to play as it feels more prone to unapologetic predatory practices and minimal effort when it comes to game design via balancing and story telling. 

While their are still elements of the game I still enjoy such as team building, and characters themselves being fun to play, especially in certain endgame modes despite power creep getting worse each patch, I still feel my dedication is being punished rather then rewarded. Compared to other games that give us appreciative rewards for dedicated playtime, star rail as of this patch feels desperate to get players to pull and spend money while doing minimal effort to reward us via gameplay. 

I hope positive changes come sooner rather then later because I don’t think I can give the game or devs a years worth of patience to keep playing with a shallow promise of them listening to our feedback to give us minimal returns for our loyalty.

Solved Genshin’s problem(s). As someone who used to play Genshin, for me it had one major flaw and that was grinding. It was incredibly boring to do my daily tasks and use all my resin. However, in HSR, with auto battle and support characters it is so easy to grind materials quickly and efficiently, preventing the burnout that comes with Genshin. 

Not to mention they are much more generous with Stellar jades (primo gems), so I feel like if I stoped playing for a week or even a month I could come back and get enough jades to pull a new character in one update maybe even less.
The content is also a lot less overwhelming. For example the fact that it is not open world. As a perfectionist I always wanted to 100% explore all the areas but it’s near impossible and incredibly frustrating. That’s my issue. Genshin can be soo frustrating, but starrail just works so well around that.

Moving away from Genshin, I love the Sci-Fi aspect and the way that characters wear historical clothing in that context is something I absolutely adore! (Think sparkle, or argenti). The story is entertaining and the characters are sooo well written with consistent personalities. Joke characters like argenti are some of my favourites (hence how I’ve managed to mention him twice) but I really really enjoy the world building too. Super excited to find out what else happens on Penacony, and I’m already looking forward to Pandora! <3

Amazing, perfect after getting bored of Genshin Impact. I started playing Genshin Impact in February 2021 and got to AR 57 but it was honestly a dread to play it sometimes because there was nothing new and the characters didn’t excite me (after scaramouche), I played rarely because I didn’t feel excited anymore. 

Starting out:

BUT I started playing Honkai Star Rail around 20 days ago and got to lv 41 and its AMAZING.
 I felt so nostalgic because of the similar features to Genshin, like it was the same but different which made me experience the whole feel of excitement and novelty again.

Animations: 

HONKAI STAR RAIL ANIMATIONS ARE CREATED BY THE HANDS OF GODS. PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE watch the youtube demos and compare them to genshin ones. Admire the beauty of each ultimate for even 4 stars. 

Lore:

OMG. The story line is so intense and with the addition of the most epic boss fight scenes. (*cough Cocolia boss fight cut scene*)

Wishing / Jades / Characters: 

In HSR, Hoyoverse made it so much easier to get 5 stars even for F2P (e.g Free DR RATIO who is an excellent 5 star Hunt character). Also after certain numbers of pulls on permanent banner, you can get a free 5 star of your choice from the permanent banner (crazy ik). 

I also love how to level up a character it is relatively easy as the domains (calyx and echos ect) are basically always available compared to genshin being a specific day. Also for light cones (eq. to weapons) the materials are the same as for the character leveling up therefore it is SO MUCH EASIER to level up your characters and get really good damage quickly.

Also Hoyoverse is so much more generous with gifting Jades and other things for wishing which is thrilling. 

ALSO, if you want to spend your jades on character banners, no problem, with a bit of time you can grind Simulated Universe and just get free epic 5 star Light cones of your choice. 

There is just so much I can say about this game and I can’t fit onto this review. 

In conclusion, if you are getting bored of Genshin PLEASE TRY HSR because you will feel nostlagia bringing so many great memories.

Story Review. Introduction/Herta Space Station- The start of the game where you learn the mechanics, basic premise, main characters and combat. It’s a basic concept, even if the start is a little underwhelming, they make up with hype moments and funny comedic moments that makes it intriguing.

Jarilo 6/Belobog- An amazing series of stories that all tie together from both the underworld and the over-world side of it. The hype moments are very intense and enticing while also having emotion moments that make you feel things. It does start off slow but makes up for in during the finale

Xianzhou- The first part of it is very interesting but can also leave with a lot of different lore parts that don’t have a conclusion. Having new patches that get added always brings back more hype and a new portion that is interesting to explore. Having intense moments helps keep the less exciting part from being dry. I found it interesting and fun but there are very much mixed opinions about how it’s split up.

Penacony- Made the game 10x more popular because of the beautiful colors and the intense, emotion grabbing story that constantly feels like something bigger will happen. Perfectly wrapped up with complete character development that feels very satisfying.

Amphoreus- The true peak that emotions have during the game. The world building, character development and designs make this whole story feel complete. Grabbing at your heartstrings each patch, it may be long but finally finishing with such a bittersweet ending makes the journey all the more rewarding.

Honest spoiler free review of a day one player. Honkai: Star Rail is technically my first foray into the world of Honkai. You don’t need to have to play the previous reiterations of the title as it is a multi-verse type of game where stories and characters are sometimes nods to the previous games. It is a turn-based game that is more or less story driven. I say that’s because sometimes, it can also be character driven. As of writing this, I am caught up in all the end game content and I’m about two patches behind the main story but everything else is completed. Here are some of the things I want to highlight: 

Gameplay
In terms of game play, as previously mentioned, it is a turned based system. Ultimately the goal is to defeat the enemies within a specific number of turns, for the end game content. I wouldn’t say that there’s a difficulty spike, more like a nice gradual increase if you’re serious about building characters. The game has a character build guide, so if you are the type to not want to think, it’s a pretty solid manual. It literally holds your hand in terms of how to build characters and make teams. I think that’s nice for more casual players but it also gives freeedom for people who like to experiment with their teams and builds. 

Characters 
There is a wide variety of characters. I would say they’re pretty diverse in terms of the tropes they use for characters. The designs are futuristic and unique, they have gorgeous splash art and the in game models are also pretty incredible in terms of details. In terms of merch, if you’re in to that, there is a good verity of characters who get merch so it’s also easy to collect. From a player whose introduction to gacha games back in 2015 is FGO, the ratios of male to female is pretty good, if you care about that sort of thing. You just have to keep in mind that ultimately, the goal of the game is to maintain profit through people paying for their rolls. Do as you want with that statement. 

Overall 
Overall, as a person who plays six gacha games constantly every day, Honkai: Star Rail is a wonderful game. There is an auto function for grinding things, so you really only have to set it and let it run on the side. You really only have to pay attention when doing story, even the end game content could be auto-ed. I don’t really like the direction of the new side game co-op that they’ve introduced. I feel like if you play this game, you’re not really the type to want co-op in your turn based game. 
The story is pretty good, I would say it errs on the typical for gacha in which each big patch is different in quality from the one before. The overarching plot is easy to follow and doesn’t need extra research to understand. 
The experience as a whole is good. Would recommend trying to see for yourself.

Gacha System Feedback. The Gacha System Needs to Be Fixed. The current gacha system is deeply flawed. Having only a 50% chance of getting the character you’ve worked hard and spent time (or money) pulling for is atrocious, especially when the hard pity sits at 80 pulls. That’s an excessive amount of effort for such uncertain results.
This isn’t just a matter of subjective frustration, it’s also objectively unbalanced. The system punishes player dedication instead of rewarding it by a guaranteed that’ll you spend the same amount of your hard-work to get something you should have in the first place. A better approach would be to improve the odds progression after obtaining a guaranteed pull. For example, If a player loses their 50/50, they should still get their guaranteed character next time (as usual). After that guaranteed win, their next banner should have increased odds, say 75/25 up to 100-0 if following streak. Once the player obtains the featured character, the rate resets to 50/50. Additionally, the maximum pity should be reduced from 80 to around 60–70 pulls ( not including the 100-0 ) to make the system objectively more rewarding and respectful of player effort. This isn’t about making the game “too easy” or removing the excitement of chance, it’s about fixing real problems that create player burnout and gambling-like frustration. Games should motivate players, not exploit their patience or emotional investment. Take action before you lose the platform that have made you successful

Veteran player here; ignore older reviews. A lot of the reviews here seem to be coming from people who did not bother to learn Star Rail's combat or those who expect this to be the type of gacha where you are supposed to collect every character.
HSR is a complicated turn-based game, with some of the late-game fights being gruelling to those unprepared. It is also a game that, despite people's complaints, can be beaten using only f2p characters. The game requires you having 8 characters (2 parties of 4) to experience everything it has to offer, including the postgame, and even if you were to never use the gacha a single time or never participate in limited-time events for free characters, the game so far gives you 10 characters, with 1 of those 10 having the ability to change roles in combat over the course of the story.

My biggest advice is take it slow. Only raise the characters you specifically use, make sure your main characters have decent progress with their levels, weapons, relics and traces before increasing Equilibrium (aka the levels your world's enemies are set to). If you see a character you want, make sure to test them out in their trial stage and think about whether or not you actually need them before getting them- the characters do get reruns, so you will always have another chance to get your favourite story characters.

Prioritise getting at least one 'preservation path' (shielding) character besides March 7th. Gepard is the easiest to obtain, but Aventurine is the best. Very few bosses have time limits, so bringing both healers and shielders can help with the most difficult ones.

The gacha is more forgiving than what people claim, with it actually giving better odds even for F2P players than other generally well-liked gachas I've played like Fire Emblem Heroes. As of writing, the devs have just improved the gacha again.

Oh and the story, humor, characters, music, animations and voice acting are all fantastic too. There are quite a few unvoiced parts but for the most part it doesn't take away from the main experience.

Great game I cannot recommend.. I fell in love with Honkai Star Rail(HSR) two years ago, when it was released. I wish that love had remained.

I was initially willing to overlook the monetisation(the Gacha system is essentially a slot machine to unlock DLC characters), due to a compelling story campaign and the promise that anyone, paying or free, could enjoy all the content this game has to offer. Now, as many older characters’ become harder and harder to invest in, and the high level game modes become more and more time consuming — I’m not sure if I want to continue this toxic relationship.

Most players like me still clinging to the game are like bitter ex-es trying to make their former lover improve. HSR demands either your time, or wallet. If you are able to play this game without worrying about the limited events, worrying about logging in daily, or worrying about your roster not having enough damage, then I think HSR is great to play occasionally. Several characters are fun and sweet, and many side quests are genuinely heartbreaking. The combat is also simple enough to understand, but satisfying to optimise.

HSR, currently, suffers from powercreep. Each new character seems stronger than the last — and when each premium character costs either months of saved resources, or $200 worth of premium currency to guarantee, investing into a character, knowing that another playable unit will outrank their damage in three months is harsh.

Aside from premium characters(5 stars), you can also gamble for 4 stars to join your account. There is currently no way to guarantee pulling any 4 star, unless they are gifted through an event. While some of these events are permanent — many are not, and they may not even gift the specific character you wish for. While this might seem minor, the nature of this game’s monetisation as a soft-slot machine makes it entirely possible to spend $250 of currency without pulling a singular copy of a 4 star. While premium characters have a pity system that guarantees a character will eventually be available to you if you spend enough currency — 4 star acquisition relies on hopes and prayers.

These two things mean little if you are able to play this game casually, without spending money/excessive amounts of time — but I would not recommend it for children, students who need to study, or people who might be more inclined to spend money on characters, and people who may become attached to fictional characters easily. Please spend time in nature, with family or with a better game (stardew valley, Elden ring and persona 5 are all games I enjoyed).

Failure to respect the talent this game relies upon continues to be it’s downfall. One of the best things this game has going for it is its high quality voice acting. The cast all bring unparalleled passion to their roles, they are the backbone to the story and emotional experiences that makes this game so fantastic. 

For several months now, many characters in Honkai Star Rail have been muted due to the ongoing voice actors strike. All they are asking for are protections against generative AI, a simple request that will safeguard the future of their industry. The sudden silence from many crucial characters makes cutscenes and intense moments awkward, but that isn’t what’s most disappointing about this situation. 

What is disappointing is that with the simple signing of an interim agreement, every single VA could return to work and provide voices to the characters we adore. But after months, Cognosphere has not done that. Instead, they have left characters silent, and worse, recasted their hard working talent in an act of utter disrespect. 

The decision to sign an interim agreement should be easy, because if Cognosphere chooses to utilise generative AI in their products in any form, they will lose a significant number of customers, including myself. Why would we pay for a product that uses a computer to generate a lacklustre experience, when a human voice actor can do the job 100 times better?

Unless an interim agreement is signed, if Cognosphere continues to disrespect its talent so blatantly, this game is doomed to fail.

Game is good, but lacks in certain aspects.. Honkai: Star Rail is a game I've been playing since it's launch. Prior to it's release, I have been playing Genshin Impact since 1.2 and Honkai Impact 3rd, but lost my account due to problems with the transition to HoyoVerse. 

The turn based combat system is easy to get used to, but ends up being irritating when facing enemies such as Hoolay who have more than 5 turns in one cycle. Characters require an insane amount of grinding to even be usable in the current state of meta and powercreep only gets worse and worse. 

The game has issues with powercreep and hp-inflation. Every enemy nowadays requres too much hp, and even if you have a good character, chances are you'll need their BIS teammates who also happen to be limited characters. In Honkai: Star Rail, if you skip a the banners on just one version, you'll end up falling behind in all endgame content. 

Let's put it like this: Imagine if you got the best character on a lucky pull but you don't have any good teammates for them. You have to wait for their teammates' reruns or for a new character to release that synergise well with them. By the time you have all four teammates (including the first good character you pulled), it's most likely that character has fallen out of meta or become unplayable due to new boss/combat mechanics. 

Free characters are completely unplayable in later stages of the game, forcing players to pull for characters they may not want just for a chance at being able to clear events or certain content. 

The story is amazing and compelling and the worldbuilding is even better. However, transitions from cutscenes into battle are rather choppy and can seem tacky. 

As someone who has been playing since 1.0 and took breaks between patches due to device issues, I couldn't clear any content until I got Firefly on her first banner. Even after getting her, I couldn't make a good team because her best support was locked behind a limited banner and I hadn't progressed far enough to unlock Harmony TB. 

Moving onto 3.0, the game's most recent version, The Herta has definitely made clearing content a lot easier. Creating characters who work well with f2p teammates but even better with limited characters is what I think should be the ideal system of Honkai: Star Rail. Not only does it make things easier for newer or casual players, it also doesn't push an agenda that everyone is a 'must pull', leading to a more enjoyable experience.

In general, the game itself in terms of story, visuals and design is amazing, but the core mechanics of the game and it's content are the issue, such as powercreep and HP inflation.

BEWARE OF GAME - BOTH POSITIVES AND NEGATIVES. Going into this game, I didn’t have a great mindset. I am experienced with HOYO games (genshin, honkai impact) and know that it is very hard to top visually, but the storage consumption, the dialogue and sometimes even hacks and bugs (like deleted weapons etc.) can sometimes be a huge turn off. All my favourite genshin tubers had turned to making Star Rail content and I was determined to try the game and also not like the game.

Going into Honkai Star Rail was a totally different experience for me. The turn based combat and auto battles made it extremely entertaining and unique (for hoyo) and already the events and activities were fun and enjoyable! I soon found myself turning to Honkai Star Rail rather than Genshin.

I’ve been going through some reviews and found people complaining that the game is nothing like genshin, and I need to point out that this is the point! Hoyo should not feel obligated to make copies of genshin all the time, and even though there are similarities, you are able to play Honkai Star Rail in the early phases without feeling the need to play genshin which I think is another great aspect. 

Honkai Star Rail IS a Gacha game, meaning you will either spend lots of money or lots of time grinding for characters that you want, and not playing with event characters will make the game that much more challenging. It is, of course, entirely your take on combat games, and although reading reviews helps, I encourage you to try this game for yourself and take everything into consideration.

That is all. Hope you have a great day.

Extremely good, but know what you’re getting into. It’s a gacha game — getting the best characters requires lots of saving in-game currency, lots of luck, or lots of money. After spending just $15, I’ve gotten enough currency for about 300 warps; already managed to get the current OP destruction character and saving the rest for the next banner; but all I’ve purchased is the slow-drip of 90 gems per day for 30 days, and a battle pass.

The game itself far exceeded my expectations — the graphics, story, voice acting (save for a couple which were completely immersion-breaking — thinking about that guy in the 3rd world which also serves as a random guard in the 2nd world who clearly isn’t cut out to be a VA), and when comparing it to some of the other gacha games I’ve played recently, this one feels the least scummy. They don’t shove in-app purchases in your face, the 5-stars aren’t necessarily required either — they just make the content easier.

Once you’ve finished the campaign it becomes quite grind-y for upgrading your characters and will take several months to get to a full team maxed out, and you’re going to need two teams eventually.

Tip for new players: Use filterblade.xyz loot filters when the screen starts to get too cluttered with drops. And find a good build guide that explains how things work for a starter build, random gear + random skills+guessed passive tree choices can brick your character early. The current gold respec system is much more forgiving than the old system, where you could only use respec points and orbs of regret, but you'd probably want to save the currency and free respec points for later.

The player characters were all sent to a torture hell island by a fascist theocracy (some of them deserved it more than others). They learn to survive and thrive with the hope of getting back at the people who did this to them. If the skill tree scared you off, you can look up builds online (complete with recommendations for how to respec at different level breakpoints), but honestly I prefer to just wing it until I start to feel the game pushing back, and then optimize with tools like Path of Building, which do calculations for stuff like damage output and effective health to more efficiently lay out your skill tree and gem links. Those tools have their own learning curve of course, and they aren't perfect, but they help a lot.

Pros:
* The core gameplay is great. You kill huge hordes of monsters.
* The skill gem system is cool. You can build your own skill.
* Mapping is arguably the best end game system in gaming.
* It's free! If you like it, you will want to spend like $30 on stash tab for quality-of-life.
* Great graphics, controls and production quality.
* Tons of fun content.
* Intricate and cool build options.
* The trade system is arguably the best in gaming.

Cons:
* Too many one-shot mechanics.
* The boss design is often very poor. You must learn the boss mechanics by heart, and the game doesn't teach you those mechanics.
* It is extremely imbalanced. It's not "anything goes". There are only a few "good" builds.
* Off-screening.
* There is grinding.
* Maps have become bloated with content you don't want to interact with.
* Playing standard is miserable because your build often gets nerfed and becomes obsolete. You must play league, which means you must constantly start over. Some people enjoy that. I don't enjoy it because it takes many hours (estimately at least 40) to get a character to the endgame.
* The campaign is not enjoyable. It's boring.
* There is no multiplayer. It is a single player game where you can trade with other players who also play single player.
* Melee builds are much worse than ranged. The clear speed is too low.
* Every monster in the game has stun on hit.
* In spite of much cool content, the addition of the "atlas tree" made it meaningless to interact with most of the content because it became too unrewarding.

I came in as someone who's been only a "casual" ARPG player. I'm a woman in my 40s, and I've been gaming ever since I got the NES I begged for Christmas in 1990. When I was in my 30s, literally 90% of my gaming focused on JRPGs. But in the past few years, I've reduced JRPGs to about 10-15% of my "gaming diet," with a lot more genre variety, including games that aren't RPGs at all.

I probably played OG Diablo and Diablo II a bit as a teenager. Earlier this year, I sunk some hours into Grim Dawn, tried some other ARPGs, and I've now got an original EXE of Diablo II: Lord of Destruction running in Wine outside of Steam, on my Linux desktop. 

I know n00bs are usally scared away from PoE due to the immense skill... not a tree, more like a series of skill forests. I followed some of the advice from PoE YouTubers, I got a loot filter right away and I started following a build guide for a melee attack optimized Scion. But after allocating several points, I realized that the build guide didn't quite align with the skill "forest" I had. I did spend the first several points on upgrading my strength. And now at level 32, I have a few nice attack traits, such as impale anf bleed.

Now that I'm navigating the skill "forest" with a lot more confidence, seeing patterns in how it's laid out while following the general advice to specialize rather than try to make my Scion a "Jill of all trades."

I'm having a lot of fun. I'm glad the Trials of Ascendancy aren't complicated puzzles, The puzzles in CrossCode were bad enough, I don't want them in my more Diablo like ARPGs. 

I'm still not sure how to be more active in my league other than to check the events board (empty for now), and play those sea maps for Valerie. When I know other players can see my character, I will likely buy a few cosmetics.

It took some fiddling to get the game to run well even though this is a mid tier gaming laptop from 2021. It's almost certainly because I'm running a version of Gentoo Linux, something I do because I'm a cybersecurity specialist and anti Gen AI political activist. 

If you have any sort of Linux distro, I strongly recommend going to ProtonDB before you launch the game for the first time and choose the version of Proton, and best launcher settings for your distro. Then, while in the game settings, switch networking (under the game tab) to either auto or predictive, never lockstep. I think I found predictive to be best. Even though my network connectivity is steady and fast, lockstep tends to lock me on the loading screen.

Once I had the right version of Proton and launcher settings (including "no logo"?), and tweaked the in-game settings a bit, with my loot filter from filterblade dot xyz manually added (adding from the filterblade web app didn't work for me, search DuckDuckGo for "Path of Exile Linux loot filter location" if you need to know where to put it in your Linux PC's file system), the game has been running great, with loading screens not lasting more than a couple of seconds and always 60 FPS or more. 

I really appreciate how Chris Wilson and the rest of GGG appear to be very pro-consumer and have no interest in Gen AI or any of that horrifying crap. 

To n00bs, don't be afraid of the skill "forest." Zoom in and out of it, and make note of the patterns of skills in it. Also keep in mind that the kind of attack or magic skills that would consume MP in a JRPG usually come from gems. Make sure to put gems in your equipment ASAP! And keep most  of the same gems through the campaign and end game, because they get more powerful and level up as you use them more.

Path of Exile is an outstanding free-to-play action RPG that delivers an incredibly deep and demanding adventure through a world consumed by darkness, corruption, and supernatural horrors. Developed and published by Grinding Gear Games, it distinguishes itself through extraordinary character customization, challenging combat, and an enormous collection of interconnected progression systems. Set on the hostile continent of Wraeclast, the game places players in the role of an exile fighting to survive against terrifying creatures and powerful adversaries. Its greatest achievement is the freedom it provides to experiment with different playstyles, although that same complexity can make the experience intimidating for newcomers. For players who appreciate intricate mechanics and long-term character development, it offers one of the most substantial experiences available in the genre.

The atmosphere immediately establishes a grim and unforgiving identity. Abandoned settlements, corrupted wildernesses, ancient ruins, and grotesque monsters create a convincing world where danger feels ever-present. The narrative gradually reveals the disturbing history of Wraeclast through quests, dialogue, environmental storytelling, and encounters with memorable characters. Although the lore is extensive and fascinating, its presentation sometimes takes a secondary role to relentless combat and equipment progression. Nevertheless, the dark fantasy setting remains compelling, supported by excellent environmental design, unsettling sound effects, and atmospheric music that reinforces the feeling of exploring a civilization devastated by supernatural forces.

Combat is fast, destructive, and remarkably flexible. Players can specialize in melee attacks, ranged weapons, elemental spells, summoned allies, traps, and numerous unconventional combinations. Defeating large groups of enemies with carefully developed abilities creates an immensely satisfying sense of power, while challenging bosses demand awareness, preparation, and appropriate defensive strategies. The skill gem system is particularly impressive because abilities can be modified through support gems, allowing seemingly ordinary attacks to evolve into devastating combinations. However, encounters can become visually chaotic when numerous projectiles and effects overwhelm the screen. Certain character builds also encourage repetitive ability usage, making extended grinding sessions occasionally monotonous.

Character progression represents the game's most distinctive accomplishment. Its enormous passive skill tree provides an astonishing degree of freedom, allowing players to construct highly specialized characters without being completely restricted by traditional class identities. Ascendancy specializations introduce additional layers of customization, while equipment modifiers and skill interactions create countless opportunities for experimentation. Discovering effective combinations can be incredibly rewarding, especially when a carefully planned build begins overcoming previously impossible challenges. Unfortunately, the learning curve is exceptionally steep. Newcomers may struggle to understand complicated mechanics, and poorly distributed passive points can significantly weaken a character. The game rewards research and patience but offers comparatively little forgiveness for inexperienced decisions.

Equipment acquisition and crafting provide another compelling foundation for progression. Defeated enemies frequently drop weapons, armor, accessories, and valuable crafting materials, encouraging constant experimentation with different combinations of attributes. The unconventional currency system gives numerous resources practical crafting functions, creating a fascinating relationship between item improvement and trading. Finding a rare piece of equipment or successfully crafting a powerful upgrade can feel genuinely exciting. However, randomized outcomes occasionally make progression frustrating, particularly when substantial resources disappear without producing worthwhile improvements. Inventory management also becomes increasingly demanding as players accumulate enormous quantities of equipment and specialized materials.

The endgame offers exceptional longevity through the Atlas of Worlds, challenging maps, formidable bosses, and numerous specialized activities. Completing the main campaign opens the door to increasingly sophisticated progression systems that encourage players to refine their characters and pursue more difficult encounters. Challenge leagues further enhance replayability by introducing fresh mechanics and opportunities to begin new adventures. These features make the game particularly appealing to dedicated players who enjoy optimization and continuous improvement. However, the sheer amount of available content can feel overwhelming, and reaching the highest levels of progression often requires considerable grinding and detailed mechanical knowledge.

Multiplayer adds another dimension through cooperative encounters, trading, and community interaction. Players can collaborate against dangerous enemies or participate in an extensive economy where valuable equipment and crafting resources are exchanged. The game also supports independent progression, although a persistent internet connection remains necessary. Its free-to-play model is commendable because the core adventure and substantial endgame content are accessible without mandatory purchases. Most optional transactions involve cosmetics, while additional stash tabs provide meaningful storage convenience. These purchases are not required to enjoy the campaign, but dedicated players may find them increasingly useful.

From a technical perspective, the game delivers impressive environmental detail, distinctive monster designs, and spectacular combat effects. Its visual presentation successfully captures the brutality of its setting, although performance can fluctuate during encounters involving numerous enemies and elaborate abilities. Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable, meaning the game can be enjoyed on Valve's handheld system but is not fully Verified. Controller support makes combat accessible, although navigating complicated menus, managing inventory, and examining detailed equipment descriptions can feel cumbersome on the smaller display. Graphically demanding encounters may also require reduced settings for smoother performance.

Ultimately, Path of Exile is a remarkable achievement in action RPG design, offering exceptional customization, rewarding combat, and almost overwhelming replayability. Its greatest weaknesses are its intimidating complexity, occasional performance problems, demanding inventory management, and reliance on repetitive grinding. Nevertheless, these shortcomings rarely diminish the satisfaction of mastering its elaborate systems and developing increasingly powerful characters. It is particularly recommended for players who enjoy strategic character building, challenging encounters, and extensive endgame progression. Those seeking a casual adventure may find its demands exhausting, but dedicated enthusiasts will discover an extraordinarily rewarding experience.

[H1]So what's it about?[/H1]
In POE you are a criminal sentenced to death but instead shipped to the cursed continent of Wraeclast. You start with nothing and end up fighting Gods and other divine being. But to get there you will go through many beautifully crafted levels with many systems. At first it is intimidating and for your first run I highly recommend using a guide from for example [url=https://mobalytics.gg/poe/builds] Mobalytics [/url].

POE is an older game but can be measured against new releases as it has received and continues to receive updated. I've been an avid fan of Diablo and Diablo 2 since they were released (I was one of the first in D2 in Europe to hit lvl 99 back in the day). D3 was OK but not what I was looking into an ARPG and I've avoided D4 ever since the "don't you have phones" and all of the monetization; it's clear the Blizzard of old is no longer there.

POE is F2P but it doesn't mean P2W. Every couple of months new supporter packs are released that are time limited. But they are just cosmetics and the game comes with plenty. Only buy those if you want to support the developers. At most you probably spend about £30 to make your life easier with more inventory tabs but only gets those after you've played the game for a while and it's still not required for the first play through but it will help a lot managing all the loot you collect later on. Consider the campaign the trial or demo version to see if the game is for you.

You pick one of the available 7 classes when you start the game. As you progress you can then further specialise the class in the direction you like. There is so much to choose from that it will keep you busy for a long time. 

The campaign has 10 acts and those are really just the tutorial to avoid overloading you with the many systems POE has. After that the real game begins and it's all about completing maps at an increased difficulty for better rewards. Following that you arrive at the real end-game. It's a big game for sure :-).

It's great solo but multiplayer is good too. There is even PVP if you're interested in that. 

[H1]The good[/H1]
It has the most extensive systems I have ever seen in any ARPG. Just the skill tree alone is massive. This allows for a lot of experimentation to find the ideal setup. Your class is just a starting point and you can adjust how you feel fit.

I love the voice acting, the enemies and the graphical effects; GGG voice actors and artists are some of the best in class. 

There are many different leagues you can play (comparable to seasons in other games), including hard core and you can build even your own if you feel like.

The developers play their game and there are frequent updates. Tournaments are organised and if you watch them on Twitch you even get nice stuff from time to time.

The inner loot goblin is always satisfied when doing one of the many side activities in game. There is so much to collect and there is a variation of activities to keep it all fresh. 

You have your own hideout that you can decorate as you please. Later this becomes your central hub.

There is in-game trading with other players and multiplayer is supported. There is also a [url= https://www.pathofexile.com/trade ]trade post [/url] where you can buy and sell items you want or find.
The game plays really fast at times - much higher speed than D2; which is great it’s a constant adrenaline rush. The drawback is if your build has a weakness there is little room for error on the high end levels as it leaves you with little time to counter act.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
There is definitely a deep learning curve hence I advise using a guide for the first play through so you get an understanding of the basics. 

End game (lvl 90 - 100) can be really challenging depending on your build. Some require expensive (as in rare items they are player trade) to be effective and the AI will relentlessly punish you if you have a weak build to the point you want to give up. 

To counter this you probably want to start with a character that is less depended on gear and more on skills which are easier to come by. A second build could be one that is more depending on gear as you can use the first character to farm where necessary. In general: ranged class / skills are easier than melee especially later in the game.

For every new character you create you need to go through all 10 acts of the campaign; thankfully because of the stash, your hideout and all the other different game modes, including the progress in the second part (Atlas) is account wide it's not a major issue but it would be better if you would be given the option to skip the whole campaign after the first time that you've completed it (similar to like GW2 for example).

I disapprove of the lootbox mechanic introduced every season. It's not required, it's not in your face but it can cause serious issues for people that are vulnerable to gambling addiction. The positive maybe is that all the loot from the loot boxes are released later in the MTX store but still it should not be in the game.

[H1]The DLCs[/H1]
There are no DLCs other than supporter packs that only add cosmetics to the game. There is a microtransactions (MTX) store to buy cosmetics and QoL items. If you want to get any of those wishlist them and wait for a sale (every couple of weeks). Note that some of the MTX from POE is compatible with POE2 in particular most of the inventory tabs. 

[H1]Summary[/H1]
The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second best time is now. This is true for POE. I wish I had discovered it earlier but I'm happy I did eventually. If you're into ARPG it's one of the best games to get. Highly recommended.

Title: A Masterclass in Isometric Malice, Grinding Incompetence, and Betrayed Devotion: The Absolute Extinction Event of Path of Exile

I used to believe in this game with every fiber of my being. That unwavering, misplaced faith is now my deepest, most agonizing, and most humiliating wound. I didn’t just play Path of Exile; I consumed it, breathed it, and sacrificed thousands of waking and sleeping hours to its dark, fog-choked atlas corridors, treating its punishing skill trees and brutal map grinds as a sacred second home. I spent years defending Grinding Gear Games' glacial patch cycles, actively rationalizing their glaring resistance penalties, and aggressively dismissing the dark warning signs whispering through the community as the mere whining of disgruntled casuals. I was a foot soldier of a cult-like devotion, utterly convinced that this was a world crafted by visionary indie creators who understood the fragile, beautiful bond between an ARPG developer and a passionate player base.

How intensely, unforgivably, and pathetically foolish I was.

What the public sees on the store page is a legendary, deep-as-an-ocean action RPG—a modest isometric masterpiece born from years of dedicated work claiming to channel the ultimate hardcore ARPG experience. But beneath that paper-thin, calculatedly deceptive facade lies a predatory, aggressively hostile ecosystem designed to exploit your time, weaponize your passion, harvest your free community wiki labor, and ultimately punish you for the singular crime of actually engaging deeply with their high-tier endgame loop. The harsh reality of Path of Exile isn't a love letter to the genre; it’s an institutionalized insult, a middle finger to anyone foolish enough to invest hundreds of hours into its structurally hollow and fundamentally broken framework.

Let’s pull back the curtain and talk about the unspoken horror that haunts the upper echelons of this game: the arbitrary, indiscriminate, and utterly cowardly ban hammer and trade restrictions that target the most dedicated players the moment they master currency farming or fast mapping. For weeks, the veteran group chats whispered about it in paralyzing dread. Dedicated players—the exact backbone of the economy, the people organizing multi-stash trading syndicates, keeping multiplayer trade websites alive, and filling the community forums with complex build guides—would vanish overnight, or find their accounts locked behind an impenetrable wall of developer silence. Their names were silently scrubbed from ladders, their stash tabs vaporized, and their accounts flagged for abnormal macro usage. I scoffed at the victims. I arrogantly told myself that I played completely legitimately, that hundreds of hours of honest boss killing, meticulous currency management, and raw survival persistence would serve as my shield.

Then my inevitable turn came.

At level 98, deep inside a high-tier heavily-modded map I had rolled a thousand times for an elusive, mathematically insulting rare drop, the screen seized violently. The dreaded, ominous network disconnection warning flashed across the UI, followed instantly by a forced, unceremonious dump to the login screen. My hands shook uncontrollably as I scrambled to re-enter my credentials, hit enter, and was greeted by the most infuriating, gut-wrenching, soul-crushing message any ARPG veteran can possibly receive: “This account has been banned.”

No warning. No specific rule violation cited. No log data provided. No human review whatsoever. Just an abrupt, summary execution carried out by a completely inept, automated detection algorithm that apparently cannot comprehend the basic reality that a human being might actually want to play an ARPG for more than ten hours a day or use third-party trade macros. If you dare to actually play their game, to push past the lazy mid-game wall, and dedicate real, unbroken hours to mastering the convoluted passive skill tree and grinding endgame bosses, their broken, hair-trigger security protocols automatically flag your sheer dedication as anomalous botting behavior. They don't want you reaching the summit because they either haven't built a functional, stable endgame to sustain high-level players, or they are utterly terrified of what veteran players discover when the illusion of depth is finally pulled back.

And when you turn to customer support for even a shred of recourse or human dignity? Prepare to crash headfirst into a brick wall constructed entirely of corporate apathy, cowardice, and condescension. I poured my bleeding, broken heart into a meticulously written support ticket—detailing my exact playtime, my absolute adherence to fair play, and my profound, heartbreaking disappointment. Within minutes, I was hit with the exact same robotic, copy-pasted wall of garbage text that every single banned victim receives: "Your account has been reviewed and the suspension is permanent. This decision is final."

No appeal process. No human being willing to look at your case, check your server logs, or grant you basic respect. Just a cold, algorithmic middle finger from developers who happily take the community promotion, the active player counts, and the free labor of their trade systems while treating us like disposable trash the moment an automated script misfires. The silence from Grinding Gear Games is deafening, pathetic, and entirely telling. They hide behind automated systems because facing the human wreckage of their broken anti-cheat and abysmal balance design requires a spine they simply do not possess.

The technical and design state of the game outside of these tyrannical bans is an absolute disaster anyway, propped up by pure sunk-cost fallacy and endless supporter pack monetization. The economy is a chaotic, hyper-inflated mess dictated by market manipulators who somehow bypass the very detection tools meant for honest players. High-level combat balancing is practically non-existent, featuring lazy one-shot mechanics that demand artificial difficulty rather than tactical engagement. The repetitive grind quickly morphs from an exciting loot hunt into an unrewarding, punishing, soul-crushing chore. Every single system feels half-baked, held together with digital duct tape and the nostalgic goodwill of players who desperately want it to succeed, only to be brutally kicked in the teeth the second they cross the finish line.

My level 98 character—complete with painstakingly optimized passive trees, hard-earned mirror-tier equipment, hundreds of hours of irreplaceable memories, and genuine friendships forged in guild chats—was erased in a single, callous click. Path of Exile isn't just another failed live-service experiment; it is a meticulously constructed psychological trap for the devoted and an eternal monument to bad-faith development. Path of Exile has an insane amount of depth.

[b]"That was fun... but I don't think I want to do all of that again."[/b]

And with a new league, a huge part of that progression starts all over again.

For some players, that is exactly why they love Path of Exile.

For me, one serious league was enough.

[h2]GOOD:[/h2]

* Incredible build variety
* Deep character progression
* Huge amount of content
* Very satisfying when your build finally works
* You can play for a very long time without running out of goals
* One of the deepest ARPGs available

[h2]BAD:[/h2]

* Extremely time consuming
* Can be overwhelming for new players
* A lot of systems to learn
* Repeating the progression every league is not for everyone
* It can easily start feeling like a second job if you take it too seriously

[h2]FINAL VERDICT[/h2]

[b]RECOMMENDED.[/b]

I had a good time with Path of Exile and definitely got more than enough entertainment out of it.

But personally?

[b]I finished one league properly, reached my goals and I think that was enough for me.[/b]

**Recommended — 576+ hours**

Path of Exile is a wonderful game about killing monsters, collecting loot, and slowly realizing you've accidentally enrolled in an unpaid university course.

I started playing thinking, "Oh cool, Diablo but free."

576 hours later I'm staring at six different resistance numbers, moving gems around like a crackhead doing electrical work, and getting genuinely excited because a chest has the correct combination of coloured holes in it.

10/10.

I mostly play Necromancer, because why fight my own battles when I can bring an entire unemployment line of skeletons, spectres, golems and other assorted dead people with me?

Sometimes my army deletes half the map.

Sometimes a boss looks vaguely in my direction and I immediately become a historical event.

That's Path of Exile.

The amount of content in this game is fucking absurd. Every time I think I understand it, another mechanic crawls out from underneath a rock carrying seventeen currencies and a crafting system that apparently requires a minor in economics.

And somehow I love it.

The developers and support staff deserve genuine credit too. My experiences with them have been great. I've had reward/drop issues sorted out by actual humans, and I've always gotten the impression that the people behind this ridiculous monster genuinely give a shit about it and its community.

Is it beginner friendly?

Absolutely fucking not.

The passive tree looks like someone dropped a plate of spaghetti onto a motherboard and called it character progression.

But once it gets its claws into you, there really isn't anything else quite like it.

It's complicated. It's occasionally infuriating. It will happily murder you because you forgot that 41% chaos resistance is apparently the defensive equivalent of wearing a promising hat.

Then you'll get one beautiful drop and forgive everything.

Free game, by the way.

I've paid considerably more money for games I've played considerably less.

See you in maps.

As an example, in most other arpgs, a ranged build that reliably shoots something like 10 projectiles with every press, with extra explosions and effects would be considered to be around the endgame point of that build. In PoE i am covering the screen with 100+ arrows per second, and thats not even close to the endgame, that's just a build ive quickly thrown together just to get through the campaign a bit faster. Creating a slam so large it covers the entire screen and more, projectiles and lightning chaining through an entire horde of enemies in a single cast, teleporting and slicing everything across half the map in merely a few seconds with flicker strike, having all the monsters explode by just standing near them. PoE took various old skills and concepts to an extreme that i have not seen before and this is what i love about it.

Technically the gameplay itself is nothing complicated, in fact the goal of most builds is automating and simplifying as many of their skills, buffs and effects as possible, so it often ends up being kind of braindead. The real complexity lies within the process of building up to that point, balancing all the different scaling vectors, all the possible interactions, conversions, etc to maximise damage, clear potential, speed and defenses, and there are a lot of ways to go about it.
To support all that, there is a ludicrous number of skills, supports, item bases, mods and mod types, a giant passive skill tree, customisable passives in the form of jewels and many other things, this game goes all out on quantity over quality, but without completely dropping quality either.

As for the bad parts:

-Crafting 
Technically the crafting system is almost as complex as the builds themselves, there a lot of ways to go about it too. However, realistically, it is an incredibly frustrating system driven almost entirely by RNG.  There are a myriad of generally pointless mods, especially the many uselessly low tier mods that can always appear regardless of item levels and almost every crafting session involves at least one case of spamming whatever currency you need by the hundreds until you finally get the right mod. The chances of getting something good is always low and usually accompanied by a chance to undo some steps or completely brick the item and having to start over, if even possible, and that applies to nearly every single goddamn step in the crafting process.
Even after learning how to optimise it and even crafting for profit, i have to say this is by far the worst crafting system of all rpgs that i have ever played. And i am counting those that don't even have item crafting, it is THAT frustrating and i am neither a masochist nor a gambling addict to enjoy this.

-Visual clarity
Non-existent, with the kind of crazy builds you can get in the endgame. (and they still somehow managed to make this even worse in poe2)

-Player trade / economy
The player market isn't exactly a bad thing by itself, it allows players to trade for various items while focusing on the content they prefer and helps ease out the issues with random loot systems. That's the theory at least, in practice the PoE economy is focused entirely on the market, with the loot being balanced around it instead. Which results in the next part:

-Loot
Extremely random, too scarce, the vast majority of drops are nothing but trash. This is caused both by balancing around the marked and the ludicrous item mod pool that doesn't properly reward or account higher level itemisation. Only in very recent leagues has this been improved and even so, it doesn't feel like it's anywhere near enough still.
This also leads to the worst SSF experience of all games in the genre that i have played.

-Overall balancing
I have mentioned the variety of skills and items already and while most are viable, there are still a lot that do not work outside of extremely specific niche setups, or with prohibitively expensive gear, or some that simply aren't viable at all. All due to bad balancing and power creep

-Lack of QoL in certain aspects 
No inventory sorting, no automatic pick ups, no automatic tranfers, a billion clicks to do anything through your stash even after all the hotkeys they added, always spawn in town when logging in instead of your hideout, not enough inventory filters.

-Others
No way of disabling cosmetics on your end. Lots of players going around with loud, flashy and obnoxious cosmetics so all the town areas end up feeling awful because of it.
Adding poe2 enemies to existing poe1 systems without always properly rebalancing them
Servers aren't always stable and this is an always online game.
No offline game mode.

Regarding the price of the game, on paper it is free but if you do get into it you will eventually need to buy some stash tabs. I have managed to touch the endgame the first time i played without any of the fancy tabs and it was fine, but you will definitely need at least the basic stuff like a currency and trade tab should you go any further than that. Consider the "free to play" aspect to be more of an unlimited trial version.

Thirteen years after its initial launch, the original Path of Exile remains a masterclass in complexity and an absolute powerhouse in the ARPG genre. Despite its sequel heavily dominating headlines in Early Access, the 2026 state of PoE 1—anchored by the recent Patch 3.29: Curse of the Allflame league—proves that the original game isn’t going anywhere. While PoE 2 leans into slower, tactical, "Souls-like" combat, PoE 1 has proudly doubled down on its identity: a chaotic, screen-melting sandbox of infinite depth and speed.

What Makes It Peak in 2026?

Unmatched Zoom & Power Fantasy: Unlike the deliberate pacing of modern ARPGs, PoE 1 lets you break the game. Building a character that fires 50 projectiles a second and clears three screens at the press of a button is still an unmatched rush.

A Sandbox of 13 Years of Content: Nearly every mechanic introduced over a decade of development (Delve, Heist, Expedition, Harvest) is woven into the endgame Atlas. The level of content variety is staggeringly vast compared to any competitor.

The Definitive ARPG Economy: The economy—driven by trading functional currency items like Chaos and Divine Orbs—remains the gold standard for multiplayer ARPGs, creating a thrilling market dynamic every single season.

Thriving Parallel Support: Grinding Gear Games did not abandon the game; it still receives regular, massive four-month seasonal content drops and dedicated balance cycles.

How About The Disadvantages & Outdated Elements?

Cruel Onboarding for New Players: Trying to learn PoE 1 in 2026 without an extensive video guide, a build planner, and a spreadsheet is a recipe for a breakdown. The game severely lacks native onboarding tools.

Outdated Click-to-Move Controls: Going back to click-to-move and strict armor socket-linking after experiencing the fluid WASD movement and separated gem systems of PoE 2 feels like stepping backward in time.

The Infamous "Campaign Tax": Having to trudge through the mandatory 10-act campaign to reach the endgame for every single new character you make remains a tedious chore.

Conclusion. If you can push past the brutal learning curve and the archaic inventory requirements, Path of Exile 1 is a magnificent monolith. It provides a deeper, more customizable experience than almost any other game on the market.

Verdict: 9/10

When Path of Exile launched on Steam in 2013, I played through the campaign's three acts with a friend, took down Dominus and thought, "that was alright", and didn't touch it again for 13 years. After sinking 700+ hours into the sequel and completing everything from 0.5's seasonal content, I was craving more Path of Exile and decided to check it out again. While it's definitely showing its age in some areas, Path of Exile is still an incredibly deep and addictive experience that is somehow free to play.

Playing the original after sinking so much time into the sequel feels like replaying a favorite game in another language with a randomizer mod installed. A lot of the crafting currency is named the same but has different effects, player movement and traversal skills are simultaneously faster and clunkier, crafting is more deterministic but way more complex and fragmented, and old Expedition is still here. Both games are unique enough that POE2 isn't a strict upgrade and both target specific audiences: POE1 is built off of the DNA of Diablo, while POE2 is built off of the DNA of Elden Ring. 

However, the biggest problem with this game is competition from its younger brother, POE2. Last season brought a massive rework and upgrades to that game's endgame, and all of the leagues ported from this game are significantly better in 2 in every way. The only POE1-specific endgame that I really enjoyed was Blight, but that required really specific juicing just to get decent drops from it. Blight also requires a fixed amount of time to complete, so even without optimizing the fun out of the game it feels like your time is better spent just running maps in the long run.

In fact, loot across the board is pretty bad this season, resulting in a "poverty league". Coming from POE2 0.5's buffed endgame loot to this game's un-buffed (from the last league) loot is a huge step down, and the poor player retention shows the playerbase's stance on this. Zizaran, one of the top POE streamers/YouTubers, interviewed the devs about this situation for an hour and a half and their response was basically, "don't worry guys, we'll fix it next season"... two weeks into this season. According to various forums, it seems to be a running theme of unnecessarily nerfing rewards from old content to push people into new content, and it's hard to ignore that when you see clips of streamers getting dozens of Divine Orbs from juicing Voyages (the new league's mechanic) in a very specific manner.

Voyages are fun and all, but they highlight a reoccurring issue with endgame content: single portal instances. Every few years I'd check the reviews for this game and the negatives frequently had the same complaints about connection stability issues. This is still an issue in 2026 and is exacerbated by GGG's obsession with one-shot runs. All endgame content that doesn't take place on the Atlas counts as failed if you leave the instance. It's easy to say, "get gud noob lol just don't die", but this also includes crashes and disconnects, whether its your internet dying or the servers hiccuping and dropping your connection. This season I failed two Voyages near the start due to no fault of my own: one because of a "deadlock detected" crash, and one because the servers lost connection even though my internet was working fine (and on a wired connection too). This is extra frustrating over something like losing a Delve run because you have to first farm Allflame map drops, run the small map to chart the area, chart at least nine maps so you can connect a larger Voyage map together (all hallways have to connect and maps have different shapes), and then run the actual Voyage.

Outside of loot and stability issues though it's an amazing game. If you're looking for a spiritual successor to Diablo 2 that has 14 years of updates and tons of content, this is the game for you. The campaign is a slog, endgame is obtuse, and you'll have to take a college course or two if you want to create your own successful builds, but it's still an incredibly rewarding experience with an unbelievable amount of build diversity. Highly recommended if you're trying to stay sober, since you won't have time for drugs when you could be playing Path of Exile (or Path of Building) instead.

I want to like this game. I want so very, very badly to like this game. But I can't. This is easily the most complex ARPG I've ever played, and I've played a lot, and as a consequence of that and certain design decisions, this game is outrageously hostile to casual blind playthroughs. To clarify what I mean by this, I mean playthroughs where you pick up the game knowing little to nothing about it and do a quick playthrough of the campaign and maybe a little endgame. That's usually what I want out of ARPGs, as I usually find endgame content in ARPGs to be mind-numbingly boring and I'm not super fond of replaying ARPGs to try different classes. So I'm not here to judge POE's endgame, not that I've reached it anyway.

What I am here to judge is the campaign playthrough. The actual campaign, from what I've played, is honestly pretty solid. The issue is the mechanical density of actually playing the game. Everyone knows about the skill tree. The thing is ridiculous, far too large to truly be able to parse and craft a decent build out of without many, many hours of playtime fiddling with it. I would be okay with this, except respeccing without already having a good build to farm currency is sufficiently expensive to be basically impossible. Compare this with, say, Grim Dawn, where unless you're undoing every single skill point, it's viable to respec. Or, Diablo 3 and 4, where respeccing your skills is completely free and can be done at any time outside of combat. This gives a high level of flexibility to try out builds, and if they don't work, you can change them immediately. That just isn't really possible in POE.

Add on to that the relatively high level of difficulty, especially if you don't know about the need to stack resistances, and you can very easily build yourself into a corner where your only viable option to fix things is to start a new character. I hate starting new characters. There's no reason why the game has to make respeccing expensive, or even limited at all. Just let me fix my build without having to play the entire game again.

And this is just the passive skill tree. There are so many mechanics that you straight up are not going to be able to deal with if you don't spend half of your playtime in the wiki. League mechanics that have been added to the main game, item crafting (good luck figuring that out blind), etc etc etc. What it comes down to, again, is that POE is only suited for folks who are willing to play only with build guides or those who are willing to sink dozens upon dozens of hours replaying characters, even if you try to do research to plan out your build beforehand. And frankly, that's just a miserable experience from my perspective. If that sounds like fun to you, then yes, absolutely play POE. If not, avoid it like the plague.

ETA: Okay, so after I posted this, I found out about the change to sockets (gems no longer needing to match socket colors) that had been made, and decided to give the game one more try, with the thought that if GGG is willing to make a big change to make the early game easier, I can at least give them one more chance. What I ended up doing is taking an established build as a baseline, but tweaking it to match my preferred playstyle more.

Over 40-45 hours, I completed the campaign and poked at the atlas a bit. My original review is still valid, the only reason I was able to get through the campaign without exactly following a build guide is because I had about 20 horus of previous experience on failed runs, plus I've watched a ton of playthroughs of the game, and even then, I still had to use a build guide as a base. This game is still completely unapproachable to a casual player who wants to just do a blind playthrough of the campaign. You simply will not succeed.

However, I can at least say now that the campaign is pretty fun. I do think POE is a good game, it just doesn't provide the experience I actually want from a Diablo-style action RPG. That's okay, but I'm still leaving my review as a thumbs down, primarily as a warning for anyone else who also wants the sort of experience I want. I enjoyed my time with the game, but it was largely in spite of the experience it offers, not because of it. Still, I do plan on trying out POE2 when it comes out of early access in December, so we'll see how that goes.

I have over 20,000 hours in Path of Exile. I don't say that to appeal to authority, but to make it clear where I'm coming from. I've played through countless leagues, watched the game evolve, adapted to almost every major system overhaul, and defended GGG through plenty of controversial changes over the years because I believed they were ultimately making the game better.

This is the first time I genuinely feel like Path of Exile has lost sight of what made it special.

I'm not going to speculate about conspiracy theories like the PoE 1 developers intentionally trying to push players toward PoE 2. I have no evidence of that, and I don't think it's a productive discussion.

What I do think is undeniable is that ground loot has been getting worse and worse with all the nerfs and system changes, and Allflame is easily the worst it's been.

The frustrating part is that GGG knows players aren't happy with it.

During the Mirage League Q&A, the developers acknowledged the overwhelming feedback regarding poor ground loot. They specifically said they were increasing loot for Mirage and that they intended to do even more in the following league.

Naturally, many players—including myself—expected Allflame to be the league where those promises would finally materialize.

Instead, the opposite happened.

The primary ground-loot strategy was again nerfed, and nothing meaningful replaced it.

That leaves only a few possibilities:

1. GGG doesn't want Path of Exile to be centered around ground loot.
2. They believe the current state of ground loot is acceptable.
3. They somehow forgot what they had publicly discussed.

The third option seems extremely unlikely, which means we're left with the first two.

And both of those create a much bigger problem than simply "less loot."

---

Right now there are essentially four ways to acquire valuable items:

* Kill monsters and rely on ground drops.
* Do mechanics with predetermined rewards, such as Ritual windows or similar systems.
* Kill bosses for their specific drop tables.
* Gamble through mechanics like Stacked Decks and other RNG-heavy systems.

On paper, that sounds like healthy variety.

In practice, it creates a serious progression problem because only one of those reward types naturally scales with character power: killing increasingly difficult monsters.

Here's where everything falls apart.

The primary way players increase map difficulty is through map modifiers, but those modifiers mostly just scale ground loot quantity and rarity.

This creates a major problem: if ground loot itself isn’t valuable enough, then making maps harder stops being meaningful. You’re simply taking on more dangerous content for rewards that don’t scale in a satisfying way.

That breaks one of the core ARPG loops Path of Exile is built on.

In a healthy system, difficulty and reward should scale together: you improve your character, you take on harder content, and that harder content gives meaningfully better rewards. That loop is what makes progression feel rewarding.

But when the best currency comes from running easier maps quickly rather than engaging with harder, more dangerous content, that loop collapses. At that point, there’s little incentive to push your build further once you can comfortably clear basic endgame maps.

Instead of asking “how strong can I become?”, players are pushed toward “what’s the fastest, easiest content I can spam for profit?”

That shift fundamentally undermines the ARPG experience, where investing into a stronger character should always translate into being able to tackle harder content for better rewards.

---

So here we are 20k hours later, and I'm finally seeing the game I love so much be taken out back for some unknown reason. They were fully bought by Tencent in 2024, so maybe that has something to do with it?

During the Allflame Q&A, Mark emphasized that if player numbers aren't growing, then there's only one direction they can go. This was concerning to me because it felt like the devs' focus was centered around player metrics and business growth rather than what dedicated players found fun and what kept them playing.

It's almost as if they are saying that, at this point, players with 10k+ hours who play 6+ hours a day are becoming less of a priority because they're likely to move on anyway, so the focus shifts toward making the game more accessible for new players.

Historically, GGG built its reputation by making a game for passionate ARPG fans, trusting that if the game was exceptional, the players would come.

Lately, that philosophy feels less visible.

Whether that's actually changed internally or not, it's certainly the impression many veteran players are walking away with.

For the first time since I started playing, I struggle to recommend it to friends.

As much as it pains me to say it, if someone asked me today which game to start, I'd probably recommend Path of Exile 2 instead.
