I've supported Grinding Gear Games for years because I believed in what this company was building. I've spent around €5,000 on supporter packs and MTX because I wanted to support the developers. Looking back, I honestly regret it.

Path of Exile 1 and Path of Exile 2 have become some of the most frustrating games I've ever played, not because they're difficult, but because they're so unstable.

Path of Exile 2 is full of crashes, freezes, random client closures, and bugs that completely ruin entire play sessions. When I got tired of that, I went back to Path of Exile 1, expecting the more established game to be reliable. Instead, I experienced the same problems.

I finally had a great Voyage, found valuable loot, sent it to the surface, and then the client crashed 3 minutes later, just before I completed the Voyage. When I logged back in, the loot was gone. Hours of gameplay wasted because the client couldn't stay open. Losing rewards because the game crashes is unacceptable.

In the most recent Path of Exile 2 league, I dropped an Algur's Legacy only to lose it because an Expedition monster spawned outside the map and couldn't be killed. Then the game crashed, my portal closed, and the item was gone. G-fing-G. 500 DIV gone!

The game is advertised as free-to-play, and technically that's true. You can download it and finish the campaign without spending anything. In my opinion, though, that's where the "free" experience ends. Once you reach the real endgame and start mapping seriously, premium stash tabs become practically essential. Currency tabs, map tabs, fragment tabs, premium tabs for trading, and other specialized tabs aren't luxury purchases anymore. They're quality-of-life features that become requirements if you want to engage with the endgame efficiently. I don't believe the average player can realistically experience the full endgame without spending a significant amount of money. (Around 200 USD)

What frustrates me even more is the communication. Grinding Gear Games constantly talks about transparency, listening to feedback, and improving the game. There are developer videos and statements acknowledging issues, but from my perspective as a long-time supporter, the same problems continue to come back. The messaging is excellent. The execution rarely lives up to it.

The MTX compatibility between Path of Exile 1 and Path of Exile 2 was one of the biggest promises made to the community years ago. That promise still isn't even nearly delivered. It's difficult to keep believing new promises when old ones remain unfulfilled.

I understand that no game is perfect. Bugs happen. Server issues happen. But after years of support, I expected stability, accountability, and for the company to follow through on what it tells its players. Instead, I've experienced crashes that delete my rewards, years of repeated technical issues, and promises that remain unfinished.

After spending roughly €5,000 supporting this company, I can no longer recommend giving them your money. If you're considering buying supporter packs or MTX, I'd wait until the games are stable and the company starts consistently delivering on the commitments it makes to its community. Which by the way won't happen.

- There is no other game that can induce this much rage and bliss in me at the same time. Playing PoE means constantly alternating between praising the developers as geniuses and wondering whether a monkey, homeschooled by a pigeon and armed with a crayon, could design better systems and leagues. GGG can release a genuinely excellent league, then follow it with something as bad as Keepers or Allflame and somehow still appear proud of the result. I have no idea whether their QA team blindly approves everything, whether their playtesters are ignored, or whether everyone occasionally loses the ability to recognize obvious problems. This cannot always be defended with "We take risks, because otherwise every league would be boring". My sweet summer child, veteran players knew within the first 150 hours that your league was terrible. Then you buffed it, and it was still terrible.

- PoE1 no longer feels like a game being developed entirely for the people who actually enjoy PoE1. More PoE2 mechanics, ideas, pacing decisions, visual clutter, friction, and experimental systems keep bleeding into it. Instead of preserving the identity of the game that built their audience, GGG increasingly seems to use PoE1 as a convenient testing ground for PoE2. Stop trying to fix what made the game successful just because it does not match the philosophy of your newer project. If I will want to play PoE2, which I like too, I will play PoE2. Not a reskinned version with worse graphics and rewards in PoE.

- There is also no truly challenging, structured endgame in PoE. If you cannot create your own goals and find enjoyment in optimization for its own sake, you will eventually become bored. The entire endgame is a repetition loop. You juice maps, kill Ubers, farm currency, upgrade your build, and then repeat the same content with larger numbers and often mediocre rewards. 
You need to be a very particular kind of autistic, natural-born tinkerer, theorycrafter, and min-maxer, to keep enjoying it for thousands of hours. Personally, I can spend entire evenings crafting items, planning builds, calculating modifiers, and optimizing systems. The game itself is often boring. Understanding and breaking the game is the fun part.

That leads to another problem. Once your character becomes powerful and you finally understand how to juice maps properly, the game stops looking like an action RPG and starts resembling a graphics-card stress test.

Ten thousand monsters spawn at once. Fifty glowing orbs chase you across the map. A hundred overlapping ground effects cover every surface. Millions of visual and sound effects go off simultaneously, most of them contributing nothing except noise, confusion, and irritation.

Would you like to see your character? Understand what killed you? React to an enemy attack? Play Solitaire.

The two games share a likeness in the name mainly. Defenses and skills are key in the first iteration. In 2, you could get by with overpower and dodge. It's not that way in PoE1. I learned real quick that was not the case in PoE1. Saying all that, I have enjoyed the challenge that 1 has presented. The gameplay is fast and responsive. The many, many, bosses, all have unique mechanics and you have to pay attention or you will die. Repetition and perseverance will be your success. The end game is crazy. Coming from PoE2, decent gear and good movement would get you through most of the end game content. Not so in PoE1. Again, i was humbled quickly. You have to keep up with defenses and gear to progress through PoE1 end game. At least, as a new player, that is what my experience has been. All in all, there is a reason this game gave the king or ARPG a run for it's money.

Starting with context for this review:
These are somewhat first impressions, as I've been playing the game over the weekend, am currently in act 3, and played Path of Exile 2 first. I wanted to try this game out because a new league just started and I was curious how the series got itself going.

The game features a fairly simple to pick up gameplay style in that of Diablo or other Looter Dungeon Crawlers of choice, with a fairly flexible system for building your characters, with characters all sharing the same level up grid but starting at different locations. There are specializations unique to each class though, so that may also determine who you pick to play. Now the fun part are the skills, naturally. In this game you gain skills from gems you find at random around the world, and from quests the game gives out from time to time. There are also gems that don't give skills themselves, but rather add powerful effects to other skills. But the caveat to all this is the way you equip these skills are slots on your weapons and armor. This quickly becomes an issue because it cripples your builds when you don't have sufficient slots on a weapon, or perhaps even the slots not being linked to each other which is required to use those supporting gems. Sure, you can use items to *gamble* for more slots and/or links, but then you have to move all those gems from one piece of armor to another and it gets a bit on the nerves after a while, especially considering how unintuitive the controls are. At least, on controller that is. And no, I will not use KBnM because of a physical disability that cripples my right hand. Digressing aside, this game is rather clunky compared to its successor. There are a lot of Quality of Life features not in this game that are in its sequel that I'm a bit baffled on as to why they're not in this game considering it, being live service, is getting entire content updates still and thus you'd think that little things could be used to spruce up how things go. Maybe they have and I just haven't been around long enough to witness the horror of the earlier builds.

I think what makes this game a "Do Not Recommend" from me, though, has to be the complete and utter lack of enemy variety and the extraordinarily boring bosses. Each of the three acts so far have featured most of the same exact enemies, just recolored and copy/pasted. At least in Act 3 the crabs have been model swapped with beetles. But the most egregious examples are the groups of necromancers with skellymen. And as much as I like a good necromancer and skellyman, it's a bit dull when every dungeon features them, it's just green in act 1, black in act 2, and red in act 3. And it's the same song and dance each time, take out the necromancer so he stops rezzing the skellies and then swat the skellies down. Second most example would be the Golem enemies. They're just the same rockmen, just made of different colored rocks each time. They're not even interesting, they just hobble towards you and bonk you when they're close enough. And as for the bosses, they're rather pathetic. They all follow the same song and dance, you smack them a tiny bit more than a regular mook then they poof and summon a wave of mooks, then they poof back in. Rinse and repeat for as many "phases" the boss has and you're done. Though some lesser bosses at least have the dignity of just going down without summoning ads, but that's just more pathetic. To compare it to the sequel, the bosses don't really ever reach a point where you're just one-shotting until you're at end game when your builds finally kick off and obliterate things, where as I'm not really even optimized and I feel dang near immortal and unstoppable here. 

I dunno, maybe some people are into it, but I am not.

This all said, it's not a bad game. It's got its charms and such, as they say. But I think I'm going to stick with PoE2. Y'all have fun now!

This game gives such a mixed feeling in my mind. I really wish I could recommend this game to new players. Unfortunately, Brawlhalla as it exists (as far as I can tell for the predictable future) has become such a mixed bag that in my opinion the cons outweigh the pros for recommending anyone new to the game. 

For full disclosure, I have earned every character in the game with in-game currency, the only items I have bought for this game is a single taunt (worth around $5). I also bought the all-characters pack for ps4 because I refused to grind the entire roster out a second time. 


I have played this game since the 2010s when the roster was about 10 characters and dashing didn't even exist in the game. I obviously enjoy the gameplay, apparent by my around 800+ hours of time spent since leaving this review. Unfortunately, I have also watched the game's development company completely forget the game it used to be and focus almost exclusively on new characters and weapons that outclass every one of the original characters they have forgotten existed in the roster. They have also altered the primary art direction so drastically that any of the original visual clarity in the game has been painted over with bright neons and cluttery clashing color palettes.

When this game is played casually, it is an absolute blast. Character movement flows smoothly and the basic controls are fairly simple and intuitive to pick up for newcomers after about a couple hours of playing. Brawlhalla excels at creating a welcoming environment for personal games with friends. Where things begin to go astray is once you start attempting to climb the skill ladder in ranked play.  

Brawlhalla's movement tech and more advanced move sets are not explained to the new player until they either search around the main menu and find the tutorials (that I never knew existed until well over 500 hours into gameplay) or you look up tutorials on the internet. Otherwise, you will be completely outmatched by people using movement you never knew was in the game. The developers will also tell you to complete a certain type of move for daily challenges that you have no idea how to complete and that the developers just assume you are aware of. To this day it still happens to me. A player should not have to google a movement tech, that should be explained clearly in-game.

On lower skill levels the game will run mostly fine and your attacks will consistently register and hit their mark. This begins to break down with more experienced players who move significantly faster than a new player. At a certain point the game begins to stutter during particularly important moments in gameplay and you will experience inconsistencies in-game. This has happened to me across multiple computer builds and laptops, but was interestingly absent on the PS4 version of the game. I have always stored this game on my C: drive due to this phenomenon, it seems to lessen the problem slightly. (NVME SSD)

Here is a very short list of Issues I consistently have playing on PC. These tend to be minimal in 1v1 matches but increase in frequency drastically in 2v2 games or larger:

Ghost hits where the character will turn red indicating they were hit but no knockback or damage was registered to the player.
Audio of attacks connecting but the character does not react or take damage.
Certain attack move's visuals covering enemy characters entirely but having no effect despite the enemy having exhausted their dodge and standing on the stage.
The game after about an hour will begin to visually stutter and feel less responsive.
Certain inputs will not register correctly (i.e. flicking the stick upward to perform a recovery but the game registers a down smash instead. Possibly peripheral related due to no snapback capacitors in my controller, but button presses occasionally have similar issues. This has persisted across at least 3 separate wired controllers and a keyboard after testing. Personally, I don't think you should need a $200+ custom controller with snapback capacitors to play a free game without significant input issues.)

Like every competitive game community it can be toxic at times, however I have seen significantly worse communities. This is a game that begs you to grind to be the best but punishes you for wanting to climb. The more seriously you take the game the worse it treats you. I have learned to play ranked with no intention of excelling past low platinum because if I do the game becomes less fun. That is not what you want your players to do when your entire game loop is grinding ELO to be better.

Cosmetics and limited time offers are the lifeblood of any free-to-play game like Brawlhalla. I have very little to complain about with their current monetary strategy. The developers don't seem to intentionally give buffs to players with heavier pockets. Where I do hold issue with is the increasing lack of restraint when it comes to the designs of their skins and especially character crossovers. 

Certain skins will have protrusions or animations that extend significantly further than the character's hitbox making it extremely difficult to time and aim your own attacks. Offering a visual option in the setting to disable skin animations would completely resolve this, but is unlikely to be implemented.

Character crossovers are skins that change almost every visual asset of a standard character. This is a very cool idea in theory since this allows for a character to feel different without changing their stats, special attacks, or hitboxes. Unfortunately, that's where the positives end. These crossover skins become the equivalent to a brand new character unless you already know which crossover skins correspond to each character. The game only gives you 3 seconds where it tells you underneath the enemy's character which moves the crossover skin will use. Unless you know which legend the crossover skin uses for its move set, you just have to guess what moves they can do. This is a direct buff to anyone who can afford a crossover skin. This problem still affects me 800hrs into the game. This can be resolved in the same way as the skin animation issues, just allow players to toggle off crossover skins. 

The art direction in Brawlhalla is unmistakable and quickly recognizable, however the backgrounds have become too flashy and contrasting. Many of the new maps have consistently lost visual clarity for the characters on the screen. The Spongebob map in particular has a notoriously busy background and lacks clarity on the stage. Art design is important, but the gameplay is what we are here for. The moment art detracts from gameplay it supports is the same moment that art ceases to add value to its medium. 

Enemies have blended into the background on many maps due to similar background colors. This isn't something that can be blamed exclusively on the developers, but this can be addressed by disabling certain colors on particular maps (dark red colors on maps with dark red backgrounds for example). They could also offer an option to make the background a neutral color like grey or darken the background to bring the playable characters to the foreground of the scene. It is extremely frustrating to lose to someone because you couldn't see your character or your enemy.

I do love this game. I have had some of my fondest memories playing Brawlhalla with many different friend groups over the years. Unfortunately though, I can't honestly recommend someone new to play this game and try to join a game that I personally feel has left beginner players and the casual players in the dust to chase Esports with an increasingly intolerable core audience. I hope this will change one day so I can amend this review to a positive, but at this point I have resigned myself to these outlined thoughts. Hope you all find this helpful, thanks for reading my manifesto. XD

I have a pure, burning hatred for Brawlhalla—and somehow, I love it more than ever.

This game has a special talent for turning one match into a full emotional journey. One second, I’m landing a perfect combo and feeling unstoppable; the next, I’m flying off the stage because I missed one attack by a pixel. Every loss feels personal, every opponent suddenly looks like a professional, and every time I say, “Okay, last match,” I somehow end up playing five more.

But that’s the magic of it. Brawlhalla is fast, chaotic, and ridiculously satisfying when everything clicks. Pulling off a clean read or making an impossible comeback feels amazing—and just when I’ve decided the game is the worst thing ever made, it gives me one of those moments that reminds me why I keep coming back.

So yes, I hate Brawlhalla. I hate how frustrating it can be, how it makes me blame the game instead of my own decisions, and how it keeps tempting me into “one more match.” But I love the competition, the chaos, and the feeling of finally getting it right.

In short: Brawlhalla is the game I love to hate—and the game I hate to stop loving. 

If you want to jump off a cliff but have a good time doing so then play this game.

I used to play warzone rebirth 24/7, looking up movement tutorials and "meta build" videos every update. in school I cared more about being good at games than getting good grades, and now that I really do care about school and bettering myself, I have dropped all competitive games, except this one. I love that I can spend hours perfecting chains and zoning if I have the time to do so, or I can lose a couple quick matches on ranked and get the same feeling I got from running laps around rebirth island in a short 10-20 minutes. this game has a huge skill roof, but I wouldn't really say the skill gap is any higher than any other technical pvp game (from my experience), and this is why its stuck around for me. I always feel like I'm getting better, regardless of if its through getting my butt handed to me and finding my week spots (and maybe learning a trick or two watching the replay), or showing off my moves that I've been honing against someone that would have wiped the floor with my face a week or two ago. I'm only in plat, but that was such a big goal a year or two ago, and now I have aimed my sight at mid plat or diamond. I know this game isn't for everyone, but that's a given; no game is. with that in mind though, I recommend this game to anyone who likes a challenge (and can handle a lose, yes even if you got cheesed, or spammed to oblivion, or just molly-wopped by a toxic no lifer), anyone who enjoys growing overtime, dedicating conscious effort into getting better at games, someone who doesn't have the time to sink hours of time for a couple matches, or anyone who really liked smash melee. at least play a couple ranked matches if you have a friend who complains about this game so you can understand and sympathize

I didn't just lose matches; I lost pieces of myself. I lost my dignity, my savings, my hair, and any semblance of a future.
Would I rather play another round of Brawlhalla, or sign a binding contract to become an indentured servant for the rest of my natural-born life?
Sign me up for the salt mines immediately.

It only offers a loading screen, a guy named chud_master67  spamming heavy sigs, and the hollow realization that your will to live respawned somewhere deep in the Mariana Trench and isn't coming back.

There are many things in life that test the limits of human patience. Traffic jams, slow internet, and people who chew with their mouths open are all irritating experiences. However, none of these inconveniences come remotely close to the indescribable suffering of fighting a Queen Nai player in Brawlhalla. There is something genuinely fascinating about how an entire playerbase can collectively abandon the concept of intelligence, strategy, and basic human decency in favour of pressing the same two buttons repeatedly. Queen Nai players are not simply opponents. They are walking advertisements for why some people should never have been introduced to video games.
The most unbearable aspect of Queen Nai players is their relentless, shameless, absolutely braindead signature spamming. These individuals seem to believe that the entirety of Brawlhalla's combat system revolves around pressing the heavy attack button until their opponent either disconnects or suffers a psychological breakdown. It does not matter whether they are winning, losing, standing still, or falling off the map. Their solution to every conceivable situation is another signature attack. You could place a Queen Nai player in front of a complicated mathematical equation, and I genuinely believe they would attempt to solve it by using spear down signature.
What makes this phenomenon particularly infuriating is the complete absence of thought behind their gameplay. Most Brawlhalla players occasionally attempt combos, reads, dodges, or positioning. Queen Nai players, however, appear to operate on a fundamentally different intellectual wavelength. Their brains have seemingly been replaced with a single malfunctioning circuit that continuously repeats the words "SIDE SIG, SIDE SIG, SIDE SIG." Watching one of these creatures play is like observing a broken vending machine repeatedly dispensing the same expired packet of crisps. There is no creativity, no adaptation, and certainly no evidence of higher cognitive function.
Even worse is the unbearable confidence these players develop after successfully landing their fifteenth consecutive signature attack. They genuinely seem convinced that they have demonstrated extraordinary mechanical skill. They will spam the same enormous hitbox for three consecutive minutes, accidentally catch someone attempting to approach, and immediately begin emoting as though they have just won the Brawlhalla World Championship. The sheer audacity is almost impressive. Imagine having access to an entire fighting game's worth of mechanics and voluntarily choosing to play like a malfunctioning microwave.
And then there is the Queen Nai playerbase itself. A community seemingly united by one sacred principle: why use your brain when you can use another signature? Every encounter feels identical. The same attacks, the same predictable movements, the same obnoxious celebrations, and the same complete disregard for anything resembling actual skill. They have somehow transformed a fighting game into an endurance test designed to determine how much nonsense the average human being can tolerate before uninstalling.
In conclusion, my hatred towards Queen Nai players transcends ordinary gaming frustration. It is an artistic, philosophical, and deeply personal opposition to everything their playstyle represents. Queen Nai is not merely a character; she is a symbol of repetitive gameplay, undeserved confidence, and the catastrophic consequences of giving someone an oversized hitbox and absolutely no incentive to think. I would rather fight a thousand skilled Mordex players than spend another five minutes watching someone repeatedly slam their spear into the ground.

[h1] Highguard Review [/h1]

[h2]A Game That Doesn't Quite Come Together[/h2]

Highguard has some interesting ideas, but the overall experience feels underdeveloped and fails to come together as well as it should.

The game tries to combine fast-paced combat with large-scale maps, objectives, looting, building and hero abilities, but the different systems don't always work together naturally.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h3]THE GAMEPLAY[/h3]

The combat can be enjoyable, but there isn't enough around it to make the overall gameplay consistently engaging.

Matches can become repetitive, and the amount of time spent moving between objectives can make the action feel more drawn out than it needs to be.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h3]THE MAPS & OBJECTIVES[/h3]

The maps feel unnecessarily large for the number of players involved.

There can be a lot of downtime between fights, which makes the matches feel slower than expected for a game built around PvP.

The objectives are an interesting idea, but the overall match flow doesn't always make them feel particularly exciting.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h3]THE DIFFERENT SYSTEMS[/h3]

Highguard has a lot of different mechanics, but adding more systems doesn't necessarily make the game more enjoyable.

The looting, building, objectives and hero abilities can make the game feel more complicated without providing enough depth to justify all of it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h3]THE REPETITION[/h3]

Once the novelty wears off, the matches can start to feel very repetitive.

The game needs more variety and stronger reasons to keep coming back beyond simply repeating the same match structure.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h2]THE VERDICT[/h2]

Highguard has some interesting ideas and a decent foundation, but too many of its systems fail to come together into a consistently enjoyable experience.

[b]There is potential here, but the game needs more focus and refinement.[/b]

I never cared about Highguard closing the TGA, and honestly, I doubt I ever will. Geoff’s announcement of the game (that he said they were an indie) was, frankly, kinda dumb, but in the grand scheme of things, that’s a minor footnote.

It’s also patently unfair to say people didn’t give the game a chance. They did. It just fell off the map quickly, like countless other live-service titles before it. Still, Highguard is much more of a success story than Concord. And I do respect them for dropping one final content drop before shutting down forever (compared to a more stoic Sony that refused to do anything but to get rid of the game asap).

If I must be clear about the game’s actual merits, plenty of niche multiplayer titles have carved out long-term existences over the years (even if some of them had strong peaks during free weekends etc.): Loadout, Block'N'Load, Natural Selection 2, Guns of Icarus, Defiance. None of those games ever truly reached their full potential or recaptured their initial peaks. In the 2010s, 10k concurrent players was a big deal, and 30-40k was absolutely massive. By that metric, Highguard hit near 100k. Are we ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kidding? It's still massive for a game that people thought it was going to get stoned to death.

It appears that, nowadays, if you can't sustain your launch-day peak indefinitely, you must be sunset. Maybe, from a cold business perspective, that's the right call (I can't be assed to tell if it is). But there's no value in pretending Highguard wasn't capable of more. It was. The core gameplay was competent. It obviously played like a slightly more stripped-back version of Apex, meaning the gunplay and movement were naturally decent right out of the gate. The resource gathering and management system was fine for what it was; maybe not thrilling for quick-play sessions, but I could easily imagine it shining in tense, strategic ranked-mode raids. I am speaking strictly of 3v3 raids though, I was unable to find sessions for 5v5 but I think 3v3 seemed to be a sweetspot anyway.

I genuinely miss games like Natural Selection and Guns of Icarus, titles where gathering resources and maintaining a base felt integral to the experience. That's why it’s so damning to see a game with a similar foundational promise, and the player-count proof of concept, fail to secure a future. It also doesn't help (although it's not a direct comparison) that the Deadlock is and most likely will be around.

But I don't know... the mount combat was actually exciting and seamless, isn't it? The PvP, whether you're on foot or on a mount, was actually quite tight. The raid mode could have used more PvE elements rather than simply going to PoIs to harvest materials, but it's too late to discuss that now. Perhaps in an alternate universe, Highguard is a competitor to Halo's BTB, who knows. I think it's fair to say that PvP on a relatively large map is draining (and uninteresting) to most people when it's not a grand battle.

Regardless of the reasons, the verdict is clear: Highguard would have been far better off releasing in the 2010s. But we don't live in that decade anymore. We live in this one, where you can shut your doors and lay off personnel in just about a month. It's pathetic to go out like this, and the negativity is not aimed at the game itself, but at every little aspect behind its actual making.

Even without considering how Tencent benchmarked the game, the studio behind it should know better — huge drops in player base are the new norm. I'll never understand what they expected from shadow-dropping a new IP. You don’t really get away with axing games too soon unless you're 2K, releasing the same slop every year (and even they postpone server closures by a few months, and giving you well over two years of content).

How could someone not have any B or even C plans to revitalize the game and steadily grow it in a scenario where it takes off big and then falls back hard? This isn’t the first time this has happened, and most certainly won't be the last.

Highguard was not Concord. No matter how similar the circumstances, the short availability, the lackluster player base, the overwhelming hate. Highguard was a free first person shooter that attempted something different and for that I commend it. I spent a fair bit of time with Highguard as I completed the 100% and I can say pretty fairly, it was an alright game. 

At first it was a breath of fresh air even with all its flaws and I enjoyed it, however later on even after all the balance patches the flaws became evident. The balance was not great, certain characters were way better than others, to name an example the ice guy was an insta win if you ulted on any planted bomb as he was impossible to kill, the wolf guy instantly replaced the recon girl as he could perma detect people and his wolf seek could go through anything including the barriers in bases. 

Time to kill became unbearable the longer the game went on with legendary shields sometimes taking multiple magazines and long range overtime fights almost always ended up ending in time. This became especially obvious during raid fights, where it felt like defenders sometimes didnt even get to respawn due to long repawn timers and dying too late. The reviver amulet was way too good and broke advantage instantly, especially if they had the newest legend whom had a shield when reviving and put a shield on enemy souls preventing destruction. This was odd because it felt like if anything the newer characters did more harm than good in terms of balance.

The accessibility and lack of even basic features is something that cannot be ignored. The performance was terrible, from launch to shutdown, my system is fairly good and I struggled to even get 90-100 fps on medium settings or low and that made performance drops during fights noticeable. Motion blur was forced and overall the settings page was lagging major quality of life and necessary options. There were no scoreboards in game and you could not type your sens you had to use a slider.

Overall, I actually think Highguard had a decent premise, the problem was its execution. Highguard was so big it had to fail, the massive budget set it up for failure from the jump, it was never going to make anything close to that much plus enough to keep it alive. In addition to its massive budget of over 200M the game felt underdeveloped for that amount, the lack of basic features I mention before in addition to the poor optimization is something that is unforgiveable for that scale. In addition the criticism that Highguard is just a rip off of a bunch of other games is untrue, it took inspiration for sure but it tackled them in its own way. I actually think that its combination of these mechanics was interesting just poorly executed. 

Im sad that its gone but I will not miss it, RIP Highguard.

There are several things i need to clarify before i get to say anything about this game:
[list]
    [*]I have very little experience in PvP shooters. Sure, i have tried a lot of these games before, but it’s not something i do regularly and my skill level is also below average.
    [*]Funnily enough, if I didn't know this game was about to be delisted, i probably wouldn’t even try it. 
    [*]And the last one - my PC is rather modest by today’s inflated standards: GTX 1060 6GB, 16GB RAM, Intel i7-10700 KF.
[/list]

These things already give you some idea on what kind of game this is - a new shiny online shooter that does its own thing by doing… everyone’s things at once. When [b] [i]Highguard [/i] [/b] just came out people were absolutely lost on what this game is even trying to be. You play 3v3 player matches which start with you picking a character (like in [b] [i]Overwatch[/i] [/b]), reinforcing the walls of your base (a bit like in [b] [i]Rainbow Six: Siege[/i] [/b]), then you go get some loot (in the style of [b] [i]Apex: Legends[/i] [/b]), mine some resources (reminisant to [b] [i]Deep Rock Galactic[/i] [/b]) and only then you get to play a somewhat regular match of [b] [i]CS:GO[/i] [/b] by planting/defusing a bomb. And there are also mounts, just for the flavour.

It all sounds so completely insane and unnecessarily complicated that i can easily image the new players losing their minds over trying to figure out what is even the point of this game. Luckily for me, i only got into [b] [i]Highguard [/i] [/b] during the last couple days of its life, so i’ve had a chance to watch all the videos i wanted and get the general understanding of what am I getting into. And honestly… that was fine!

Yes, the game is quite demanding in terms of hardware and you’ve seen my specs, so, obviously, i was only able to play it on low graphical settings, but it wasn't too bad. Not to mention, some modern projects can’t even hit a bar this low. I also heavily appreciate the fact that [b] [i]Highguard [/i] [/b] only takes 25 GB of your hard drive space. And, of course, the fact that it’s totally free as well. These are the biggest reasons i even gave it a try in the first place. Well, that and a pinch of curiosity. It’s always tempting to be a part of history, after all.

Even though there is too much context around the title to get a full picture, i will drop most of it to discuss some actual features. The shooting itself and the weapon selection turned out quite fine, which is not a big surprise, considering [b] [i]HIghguard [/i] [/b] was created by some of the people who worked in [b] [i]Respawn [/i] [/b] i.e. on aforementioned [b] [i]Apex: Legends[/i] [/b]. The mounts are fun and it feels great to incorporate them in the moment-to-moment gameplay. Another thing I definitely want to praise is spectacle - blazing through ruins on your giant wolf to put the magic sword in the key hole and summon an enormous war machine to start the siege. It could have been better, sure, but the way it’s executed in the game, in a multiplayer one, mind you, is still pretty impressive.

And yet, there is no point in ignoring it - this entire review is pretty much pointless. The project is flawed, its systems violently clash with each other and by the time you read this, the game itself is straight up delisted. It’s dead. Well, unless we live in some parallel universe when it’s somehow being brought back. Which is rather unlikely… but not impossible. 

In the end, i grabbed a couple of my friends, we played several matches and really, we had a lot of fun! And i think that’s what matters the most. Big respect to the devs for updating the game till the very end - my friend went with a nice and useful character and i found the shotgun to be a fun and effective weapon. And both of these were added in the last patch, just a week before the game got delisted. So, when it comes to the Steam review - could i recommend it? Totally!

If you’re up for some PvP fun, it’s pretty much a no brainer. The game is competent, takes only 25 gigs of space and is free! Well, it was… but if it still would be around, i’d say you should give it a try! But for now…

It was a unique game, like the Finals, but was just missing too much to keep people engaged. I completed every achievement and obtained the legendary axe, had 50 hours played. The game needed to be released in beta. changes happened fast, which was amazing, but there shouldn't have been changes in the full release. 
3v3 was bland, and upgrade base time was super slow, especially since saving up upgrades for the first raid was extremely helpful. There were fun tricks in the game, like using the purple hammer in the mines, destroying all the crystals in one swing, and collecting all the vesper. The first round was always kind of bland, though, with a low chance of getting everything you needed out of 2-4 chests. 

There were only 5 needed items, and the blue horse armor gave such a small buff that it wasn't needed. This made new players ask, "Why am I playing this?" as it took so long for the sword to spawn. The game was definitely fun, but the upgrade system wouldn’t have saved the game though. Having to need a key to access the secret rooms now gives players even less to do on the field. Also, being killed by a player with buffs for playing longer wouldn’t be fun. 

Something desperately needed was a scoreboard. Not seeing how many players on the enemy team had dropped out was annoying. In the game, it could feel like it was a dead game, and it was, because two players had left. The tutorial was also boring; it should have been made like the game, ride out to the mines, collect, grab, raid, attack. I think they didn’t do that so they wouldn’t need to create any kind of AI to attack you, but it would have been better.

I think Highguard was a good game; it had some problems but was still unique and fun enough to jump into. Some changes they made were really good, and some weren’t the greatest. Overall, I think this game could have had its own dedicated group of players. But with the online hate & reviews (justified), developers dropping staff, andnot having a good trust value with how the game was looking, it didn't keep the player base alive.

I spent over 100 hours playing this game, exploring every feature so my review could be fair, balanced, and fully informed. After all that time, effort, and questionable life choices… my professional conclusion is: 

This game is garbage, so its removal is completely deserved. Hopefully, in the future, developers will focus on what gamers actually want instead of relying on cheap advertising gimmicks.

It's a game that works. Gunplay is up to modern standards, movement is good and it even has some tight, clutch moments when defending or fighting for the sword that you need to invade the enemy base.

So why, then, did it fail?

First of all, people are sick and tired of live service games, and reasonably so. These games demand too much time from players and lock most of the customization behind microtransactions that are anything but small. And nowadays, there's not even a guarantee that these games will respect your time nor your money as, if they fail (and they often do), they'll shut down the whole operation without a second thought as Highguard has done. Even succesful titles like the original Warzone pull the plug eventuallly, and they take your hard-earned (or handsomely-paid-for) cosmetics and progression down the drain with them.

And yet, gamers are still willing to give new live service games a chance, just look at Marvel Rivals.

So why, then, did this one fail?

I would say that, just like Concord before it, it was the creatively bankrupt concept and art direction that failed to spark any positive interest. Gameplay aside, Highguard's world is not an interesting one. It looks and feels like what a board of out-of-touch executives agreed would be cool for the target audience based on the most generic inspirations imaginable: medieval fantasy! guns! magic! sci-fi! Just take a look at the characters: none of them look particularly interesting, and none of them truly stand out. They're just bland, as bland as they get.

And when it comes to the gameplay itself, there are some good ideas in there, but "good" isn't nearly enough to cut it in the competitive live service market not is it enough to offset the negatives of said model nor the lack of creativity and inspiration of the game's setting. And despite the highs that Highguard's gameplay can achieve at times (and I admit that there indeed are highs), to get those it is inevitable that one needs to endure a lot of tedium: traversing unnecesarily huge maps to get from point A to point B with no action, waiting for a respawn, looting, mining resources, etc.

Highguard feels, and is, an undercooked game. The art direction needed more time in the oven and the gameplay choices needed a lot more refining to fully realize the developer's truly novel FPS concept. It could have been streamlined into a much more exciting experience had they avoided tired genre conventions like looting and classes, and had they done more with the impressive but enormous maps they designed: it feels like they were designed to accomodate for many different game modes and yet the game launched with only one (3v3, with a 5v5 variation added afterwards). It's ironic: the game has too much going on in other areas and yet it decided to bet all its chips on this one, singular game mode that could have been appreciated in a quick-play playlist but that isn't strong enough to carry an entire game on its back.

And that's why Highguard failed. If anything, I hope its demise becomes a learning experience for the gaming industry: people do not want more uninspired, live service games; if you have a solid gameplay idea (like Highguard had), listen to the players, not to the suits.

I never cared about Highguard closing the TGA, and honestly, I doubt I ever will. Geoff’s announcement of the game (that he said they were an indie) was, frankly, kinda dumb, but in the grand scheme of things, that’s a minor footnote. 

It’s also patently unfair to say people didn’t give the game a chance. They did. It just fell off the map quickly, like countless other live-service titles before it. Still, Highguard is much more of a success story than Concord. And I do respect them for dropping one final content drop before shutting down forever (compared to a more stoic Sony that refused to do anything but to get rid of the game asap).  

If I must be clear about the game’s actual merits, plenty of niche multiplayer titles have carved out long-term existences over the years (even if some of them had strong peaks during free weekends etc.): Loadout, Block'N'Load, Natural Selection 2, Guns of Icarus, Defiance. None of those games ever truly reached their full potential or recaptured their initial peaks. In the 2010s, 10k concurrent players was a big deal, and 30-40k was absolutely massive. By that metric, Highguard hit near 100k. Are we fucking kidding? It's still massive for a game that people thought it was going to get stoned to death. 

It appears that, nowadays, if you can't sustain your launch-day peak indefinitely, you must be sunset. Maybe, from a cold business perspective, that's the right call (I can't be assed to tell if it is). But there's no value in pretending Highguard wasn't capable of more. It was. The core gameplay was competent. It obviously played like a slightly more stripped-back version of Apex, meaning the gunplay and movement were naturally decent right out of the gate. The resource gathering and management system was fine for what it was; maybe not thrilling for quick-play sessions, but I could easily imagine it shining in tense, strategic ranked-mode raids. I am speaking strictly of 3v3 raids though, I was unable to find sessions for 5v5 but I think 3v3 seemed to be a sweetspot anyway. 

I genuinely miss games like Natural Selection and Guns of Icarus, titles where gathering resources and maintaining a base felt integral to the experience. That's why it’s so damning to see a game with a similar foundational promise, and the player-count proof of concept, fail to secure a future. It also doesn't help (although it's not a direct comparison) that the Deadlock is and most likely will be around. 

But I don't know... the mount combat was actually exciting and seamless, isn't it? The PvP, whether you're on foot or on a mount, was actually quite tight. The raid mode could have used more PvE elements rather than simply going to PoIs to harvest materials, but it's too late to discuss that now. Perhaps in an alternate universe, Highguard is a competitor to Halo's BTB, who knows. I think it's fair to say that PvP on a relatively large map is draining (and uninteresting) to most people when it's not a grand battle. 

Regardless of the reasons, the verdict is clear: Highguard would have been far better off releasing in the 2010s. But we don't live in that decade anymore. We live in this one, where you can shut your doors and lay off personnel in just about a month. It's pathetic to go out like this, and the negativity is not aimed at the game itself, but at every little aspect behind its actual making.

Even without considering how Tencent benchmarked the game, the studio behind it should know better — huge drops in player base are the new norm. I'll never understand what they expected from shadow-dropping a new IP. You don’t really get away with axing games too soon unless you're 2K, releasing the same slop every year (and even they postpone server closures by a few months, and giving you well over two years of content).

How could someone not have any B or even C plans to revitalize the game and steadily grow it in a scenario where it takes off big and then falls back hard? This isn’t the first time this has happened, and most certainly won't be the last.

The "Isekai" Mashup We Didn’t Know We Needed
If Apex Legends and Rainbow Six Siege got sucked into a portal and spat out in a high-fantasy world, you’d get Highguard. It’s basically an Isekai where the protagonist brought a customized AK-47 to a sword fight. You play as a Warden, an "Arcane Gunslinger" who spends half the match looking for loot like a greedy treasure hunter and the other half summoning a massive siege tower like a final boss.

The Gameplay: "Plus Ultra" or Just Ultra Chaotic?
The core loop is wilder than a tournament arc in a shonen anime:

The Scavenge: You hop on a horse (or a bear, or a panther because why not?) and gallop across maps that are definitely "Small Town Hero" size.

The Shieldbreaker: You fight over a glowing magic sword like it’s the Master Sword or a Dragon Ball. Once you get it, you charge the enemy base.

The Raid: This is the "All Might" moment. You smash through walls, plant bombs on generators, and pray your 3v3 team has better coordination than the A-1 Pictures animation budget.

The Vibes: Aesthetic Identity Crisis
The game's art style is a bit like that one anime that can’t decide if it’s "Steampunk," "Grimdark," or "Saturday Morning Cartoon." It’s got "generic fantasy" vibes mixed with "tactical operator" gear. It’s quirky, it’s muddled, and it’s honestly a vibe that only a true fan could love.

The Final Verdict
Highguard is like that hidden gem anime that gets canceled after one season on a massive cliffhanger. It had the "willpower" (and the Titanfall pedigree), but the "Power of Friendship" (and the player count) just wasn't enough to beat the final boss of "Live Service Sustainability."

The game itself at this point 1 day before it gets shut down is quite good, the version they launched with 5 weeks ago was severely less so. I would pay good money to hear in depth post-mortem on the decisions that led them to determine their launch strategy and design choices. I will discuss both versions of the game in this review:

The primary game mode is quite original and fun at a high level, especially with the post launch changes.

The mode has 3 phases, Looting, Shieldbreaker, and Raid. 2 out of the 3 of these phases received significant improvements within the games 5 week lifespan.

Looting: 
When the game launched the looting was indefensibly terrible and directionless, couple that with the small players count (more on this later) and you end up with a horrific first impression. All of the loot was the same, it was in tiers (blue, purple, orange) so once you opened a chest and got the blue version of the gun you wanted to use, there was nothing to do for the next few minutes until the shieldbreaker formed. Additionally you can harvest crystals to buy weapons from a shop, which again served no purpose because of how plentiful chests were and how likely you were to already get the weapons you wanted.

Shortly after launch they improved this element dramatically, there was still room for significant improvement but they added more variety to the loot, and forced players into contention with each other for the best loot. They added more orange tier weapons (which have unique passives) so the shop also become more useful. Why they felt comfortable launching the game with looting the way it was is a complete mystery to me.

Shieldbreaker: This phase of the game was largely unchanged from launch to death, its a hectic and engaging back and forth reverse capture the flag mode that turns into a tense Search and Destroy style single elimination mode if it goes on too long. Once they upped the player count to 5v5 this became very engaging and fun. Riding your horse in chases, getting epic long range snipes etc... If there was one part of the game that was great out of the gate it was this part.

Raid: 
The raid phase received key improvements that turned it from something alright into something nearly as engaging as the shieldbreaker phase. At launch this part was very simple and unfortunately extremely snowball heavy, teams would often take out both gens in 1 attack, leading to very short matches with no back and forth. Additionally, defensive options were very limited (especially before they buffed the loot) leading to this being more of a raid themed TDM than something that actually engaged with the mechanics.

A key change was making so that the enemy could only destroy 1 objective before the phases reset, putting a good deal of consequence on choosing to destroy the enemy generator (it takes 2 to win) or going for the anchor stone (destroying this instantly wins). These soft "rounds" allowed for a lot more engaging back and forth, and some very epic underdog matches. Another change was the addition of the lockpick, a raid tool that allows you to turn enemy doors/windows to your side, this was another great addition that really spiced up the raid gameplay.

I personally felt that the characters abilities (especially ekon) were very unique and different enough to create engaging team building and diverse enemy encounters. I also think the weapon lineup now is pretty good, compared to the more limited lineup at launch.

The biggest misstep outside of the looting was definitely the team size. These maps are huge, and yet due to hyper competitive balance reasons they launched the game with 3v3, which to me is a massive mistake. Pursuing that type of balance at all was a mistake, but this especially robbed the game of the fernetic action and power interaction that makes the death version of the game very compelling. The looting phase significantly suffered from 3v3, making the game feel egregiously lifeless.

A small feature that I really enjoyed, was the speeches the character who planted the shieldbreaker would make as the battering ram broke down the shield, this element gave the game a lot of personality, which it desperately needed more of.

The game faced a horrendous uphill battle to win people over, it had an actively hostile marketplace and unfortunately it did not put its best foot forwards. Had they launched with the version of the game they ended up with 5 weeks later, it might have been a slightly different story. The inclusion of game changing skill trees and Koldo (the new character) really added to the game.

Overall I would give the launch version of the game a 6 and the death version of the game most probably around an 8. The fact that it improved so fast in just 5 weeks makes its launch and the choices behind it (and so rapidly closing it) so mystifying.

[h1]HIGHGUARD[/h1][h3]A genuinely fun hero shooter that showed up to a graveyard of a genre about three years too late[/h3]

[h2]THE RISE: A GAME AWARDS CLOSER FROM APEX LEGENDS VETERANS[/h2]
Wildlight Entertainment, a studio built around former Apex Legends and Titanfall veterans including game director Chad Grenier, closed out The Game Awards 2025 with Highguard's reveal trailer, a slot usually reserved for the night's biggest announcements. The free-to-play hero shooter launched on January 26, 2026, opened strong with close to 97,000 concurrent Steam players, and for a brief moment it looked like it might actually carve out space in a genre that has eaten almost everything thrown at it lately.

[h2]THE FALL: FORTY FIVE DAYS[/h2]
That moment didn't last. Within a single day of launch, the playerbase collapsed, and the numbers kept sliding from there, down to the hundreds, then down to barely over a hundred concurrent players before the end. Wildlight laid off most of its development team in February, lost backing from Tencent, and confirmed on March 4 that the servers would go dark on March 12. Total lifespan from launch to shutdown: forty five days, for a game that more than two million people had tried at least once.

[h2]MY TAKE: FUN, JUST A FEW YEARS LATE[/h2]
Here's the part nobody wants to admit about this one: it was actually fun. I'd genuinely put it above Apex Legends in terms of how it felt to play, which is more than a little ironic given who built it. The gunplay and movement had real personality, and it never felt like a cheap knockoff riding someone else's coattails.

The problem was never really the game itself, it was the timing. This is a formula that needed to land three or more years ago, before the market got buried in hero-shooter corpses (Concord chief among them) and before "sweaty," competitive shooters without much of a casual on-ramp became a genre nobody wanted to bet on a second time. Wildlight built something with real bones in a market that had already decided it was done giving this genre more chances.

[hr][b]VERDICT[/b][hr]
Recommended, for what little time anyone has left to even play it. It was fun, better than Apex Legends if we're being honest, and it deserved a market that wasn't already exhausted by this genre's repeated failures.

[b]R.I.P. HIGHGUARD[/b]

Now I just want to mention the elephant in the room; apart from the negatives because it's sort of early access, the game could have been way more successful than it did. I'm not gonna elaborate too much because it's besides the review, maybe I'll write about it later...

The reason why the launch was so catastrophic was in 3 parts: #1 trying to stand out in an overcrowded market. Hell, even games inspired by other games or genres (let's say Minecraft) can't compete meaningfully. Really, the only exception to date was Palworld because there was a huge demand for better graphics, thing that Game Freak couldn't deliver, but Pocketpair, using Unreal Engine, did.

I've never seen a Hero shooter ever reach the highs of Overwatch in my entire lifetime, and this game wasn't ever gonna cut it. If it was more derivative and unique it could have attracted a more permanent crowd. We are in a medieval settings and we still get guns, come on now. It should have been bows and swords and then you could have called it a "hero slasher" to stand out, and just to be extra interesting the game could have had pirate characters that are the only class capable of carrying guns, adding another layer to the decision-making when picking a character. This spin could have saved the game. 

#2 There were unrealistic expectations about the game since day one because it was shown off as the magnum opus of The Game Awards' especially given that Divinity was the game that everybody expected to see on the big screen.

Geoff Keighley had no ill will when he reached out to present the game, but this inadvertendly brought too much negative publicity to the game, and the reputational damage that goes with it. Once people had decided their opinion on the game it was never gonna recover.

#3 In tandem with point 1, I think the game would have benefitted with lobbies of at least 20 players (10 vs 10 matches) due to the sheer scale of the maps, and instead of having players leaving or getting disconnected thus causing any games to end prematurely, there could have been a hard cap of 16 players who are required for the game to continue (8v8) which would not throw off the balance too much.

I believe the reason why 3v3 was first opted was due to couch pvp, despite it being an online-only game. It would probably be fun playing with friends - and that would make the game mode make sense. That's an assumption of course, I could be wrong and the game was tested entirely online, but the end result is the same: A lack of strategizing. There are no "shield breaker" players, "defending" players that are at the base permanently to repair and protect it nor "scavenger" players doing their own thing. This would have spiced up the gameplay instead of relying on phases which bloat the time between each matches and contribute into making the game underwhelming.

The first thing that struck the gaming world about Highguard was its announcement.

Aside from the rather questionable nature of Geoff’s taste and enthusiasm, Highguard was revealed to the world through a trailer that was, to put it mildly, chaotic.


What’s so jarring about it? The art direction (AD). It makes no sense, lacks any cohesive theme, and isn’t original.

We could debate that last adjective, but I challenge you to take a screenshot of the environments from [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/2009100/Immortals_of_Aveum/] Immortals of Aveum [/url], [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1845910/Dragon_Age_The_Veilguard/]Dragon Age: Veilguard [/url], and Highuard—and tell me which game each one comes from.

But the worst part is this lack of a unifying theme. Apex Legends has lore; every character has a reason to exist and be there; the settings and art direction come together as a whole; and even if “robots and mercenaries beating each other up” isn’t realistic, we can accept that. On the other hand, people in armor beating each other up with guns while riding horses, all while summoning a medieval battering ram through a time rift using a sword (????). I mean, it could be pretty damn cool, but at the same time, what the heck is this jumble of nonsense?


In terms of gameplay, it’s as basic as it gets. The horse and large map aspects are okay, but there’s absolutely no point in including them in this type of game with so few players. If this were a large-scale 64v64 PvP FPS or something like that, then sure, why not. The two or three mechanics, like breaking walls and so on, are interesting but, once again, don’t serve much purpose. It really feels like the whole game is a missed opportunity.

The latest update (the final one) introduces a skill tree, but there’s really not enough time left to see what it’s worth or what it brings in the long run. The devs threw in the ideas they had—which were more or less finished—before finally calling it quits.

Highuard will ultimately remain just a meme in the gaming landscape, having had neither the time nor the will to be anything impactful or enjoyable.

If there was a middle option, and not just thumbs up or thumbs down, thats what id give this game. Its a very interesting game that NEEDS to be studied long term when it comes to the gaming market, and how not to design a game. There are actually good parts to this game though, contrary to what people say. This game is free, and I seriously think everybody should try a game for at least a three hour session before writing a review. 

Lore: I couldn't give less of a crap about this games lore. It has failed in every regard in my opinion. Ive played for twenty hours so far and I still have no idea why were doing any of this, who the characters are, what their motivations are, or even what a damn warden is. This games world building is truly awful. I dont mean it as an insult at all, theres room for improvement always. We can always learn lessons when games like this flop. Even the technology doesnt make sense. Its fantasy, hyper futuristic, but still uses horses to move around. I couldnt tell you what time period, planet, or city this game takes place in or why. 

Characters: There is a rule about videogame character design, that says if you can recognize a character by their silhouette, you did a good job designing them. I firmly believe this test would fail horribly for each character. I have played at least five games with all of the main classes and I cant for the life of me remember any of their names. The main guy on the cover looks like he could belong to any game in the world. Theyre not interesting. They all have the same personality: serious stoic soldier. This game feels like its insanely serious without having anything to make it so. Overwatch used to be a game that was known for easily recognizable characters, so ill use that as an example. Imagine every character in overwatch one was solider 76 personality wise, and they all had the same color pallets and tone. Thats what this game has done with its characters. If youre going to make an original hero shooter, you NEED compelling heros. Your entire marketing needs to be focused around making us care about them, and pulling us into wanting to know more about them. This game had the nerve to charge $20+ for skins of characters we do not know or care about. I cant even begin to understand this decision. That's like making an action figure of an original character, and trying to sell it before releasing the show or media its from. I don't know these people, so I'm certainly not going to spend an entire indie games price on a skin for them. 

Gameplay: This is where I actually may be in the minority here, but I actually do love the gunplay here. The game creators worked on Titanfall and apex legends and you'll feel right at home if you've played those. Shooting people feels great, and when the core of the game is focused on that, it is actually really fun. Legendary guns have cool perks, and it felt great to find high rarity weapons because they felt insanely better than the starter weapons. However... my complaints arise when a LOT of this game is taken away from gunplay and focuses on random filler. Each match has a reinforcement phase, which should be skipped entirely in my opinion. I don't want to spend a minute each game looking at my walls. I don't care. Next is the looting and farming phase, and I truly couldn't care about this phase either. You spend time looting chests and farming vesper, to buy weapons, items, and ammo. This felt like a boring waste of my time, and each phase of the game made you do this. A raid will start, finish, and you'll still have to loot again. Its just boring. Give each hero specific guns as part of their kit, and start the game sooner. Don't make us loot. Instead of looting after each raid, and farming crystals for some reason, let us pick from a perk system instead. Its way faster, and makes picking a hero more interesting. Most people I played with didn't use hero abilities that often, and I'm worried its because a lot of them weren't impactful enough or engaging to use. 

When the game finally starts, you need to get a shield breaker to the other teams side to start a raid, or prevent them from doing it to you. Its a cool reverse capture the flag idea, and I get it. However, respawn times are WAY too long and maps are WAY too large. Dying even 2-4 times in a match, which is insanely easy, means you're waiting nearly a minute and a half of waiting to play again. That's boring. That's just the respawn timing. Then you have to run on your horse across the map to the fight again. If you get sniped on the way there, that's nearly two minutes of waiting. That's really bad. 

But lets say you're better than me, and you don't die as much. As far as I can tell, there's no way to communicate in game without a mic. I never played competitive so maybe its different there, but this is a bad thing. I never got feedback in chat about where to go or position. Nor could I point out where people should go, or strategies we should implement. 

Lastly, games are WAY too long. I would find myself easily playing games that are 20+ minutes long. In an hour of playing you'll maybe squeeze out three matches. They're too long, and without all the filler they could easily be shortened down to 12 or so minutes. I do think there's good ideas here with the raid system, and the reverse capture the flag dynamic, but there's just so much filler in the middle. I was basically checking my phone while I played this game.

I also want to mention this, but please take out the fall damage. Nobody likes fall damage. Unless there's a balance reason for it, which I couldn't find, all it does is restrict the player. 

Music: Generic and uninspired. I am not a music person, nor do I have the expertise to speak on it, but I played this game for 20 hours so far and cant remember a single song. Probably not a good thing. I did however like some of the sound design on the menus, and think the UI did actually look pretty good. 

I feel for these dev's, and I feel for the company that shut down months into its development cycle, but I really gave this game a fair shot. Ill keep playing it in hopes of getting all the achievements before the servers die off (none of them seem hard, just time consuming), but I cant say ill miss this game. If anything, it makes me want to redownload apex for a bit and enjoy the good parts of this game without all the fat.
EDIT: I did in fact get all the achievements, but I dont think anything changed for me, Gunplay good, everything else not so much

If this game cant last, let it be a lesson in game design and why public feedback is insanely important. I really don't think it deserves the hate it got at all. But I also think if it wasn't shown at the game awards, nobody would have played it at all.

I had doubts on putting this review out. At first is was because of how little hours I had after the first few attempts at playing, then when I reached the 20 hour mark it became obvious that my opinion of the game had not changed since my first match. This game is like the extra mode you would find attached to a single player game made in the early 2000's. 
    For example, the Mercenary mode in Original Resident evil 4, while fun and addicting, would not have created as many wonderful moments of stress induced survival if not for the massive single player story that got me attached to Leon and the other characters that you could play in to try to survive a horde of zombies. Highguard was fun and different, yet that was it. 

    First, the positives: 
I enjoyed being able to "mine" for gems to buy equipment or shops since I am not a very skilled enough player to get a high killing streak to earn them the normal way. I liked the character quotes in their selection screen and even their callouts when the shield breaker is summoned, (my favorites for both being Redmane and Mara's). 
However, my favorite mechanic of this game that separates it from other multiplayer games currently, is the usage of mounts. I absolutely loved being able to escape most of my seemingly inescapable death moments by riding out on my horse. And once I learned you can mount right when attempting to revive someone to actually be able to carry their soul orb with you, I basically made it my mission to save as many allies as I could like this. Even if it would have made much more sense to kill the low health enemies nearby. 
The abilities were a great addition and some were just overpowered, such as Slade's heat walkway and firestorm. Mara's extra shield she can give to her teammates and the extra lives she can give a raiding team with her ult. Even Atticus could be broken if you saved all his tacticals, (or got a tactical recharge amulet), to just surround an anchor stone after deploying a bomb on it to deal huge damage to anyone attempting to disarm it. 
The guns felt great to use, however please keep in mind that shooter multiplayers are not my forte and so I could be completely wrong to say this, but they felt somewhat balanced throughout the weeks playing.
The introduction of the 4 different ability paths completely moved this games re-playability score up for me. Especially as you could reset your point distribution with zero costs. Allowing for on the fly character customization and team building in between matches. 

(Disclaimer: I cannot speak on graphical fidelity as I have a 5070ti and did not need to lower my settings in order to run the game smoothly. I did encounter crashes and other problems which will be discussed in the next paragraph.)

Next, The Negatives: The characters are unbalanced in terms of their abilities. While I am happy that some were overpowered in their own right, I did not like that some characters had a massive weakness in certain moments. Atticus and Mara do not have any drawbacks as their abilities can be used anywhere and at any time, Slade is the only one of the 3 I mentioned earlier whose ablilties might have a drawback and it is that if used in your own base when defending during a raid, you could damage or destroy your own walls in the crossfire. This is not as much as a drawback as other characters though, the most egregious being Redmane, my favorite character. Redmane's tactical can be used to break open iron and regular walls, ensuring that you can get some chests or open a path to an anchor stone without using up a rocket launcher, while also being able to leap tall or long distances when needed. However, His ult is completely unusable if you are defending. It completely damages, if not outright destroys, all nearby walls in a large radius. The drawback is that he destroys "ALL" walls in that radius, meaning if you are using it to knockback the enemy team when they have you surrounded and you want to use the few seconds they are stunned to get away while defending, you are out of luck as your ult has destroyed your own base walls and given them access to Point B or, heaven forbid, anchor stone. Condor's ult allows her to reveal enemies by using large wind bombs, but that's it. Don't get me wrong, it has helped me clinch a win every so often if used perfectly, but when Ekon was introduced and his ult was shown to be superior in everyway since he did not need his enemy to be touching anything to show them to the team, i realized that Condor became obsolete in terms of recon. I think if her ult could not just reveal enemies but also damage them slightly if they remained inside the radius, it would have pushed her usage in teams up more. 
Some times in a match the game would just crash and boot me and my team to the lobby and out of our party. Then, we would need to close and relaunch the game in order to party up again. The game would say that there was an error every time we attempted to party back up right after a crash. In some matches the music and sound would just shut off, this happened twice only thank goodness, as it can be jarring listening for the enemy getting closer, then hearing nothing but absolute silence, not even sound effects. There was even a match where my team and I completely froze mere seconds after the match started, and stayed motionless, with the only input being accepted was the camera angle, for 5-7 seconds. 
The characters needed more to flesh them out. As much as I loved most of their tactical abilities and ults, alongside their beginning match phrases and even their callouts during the matches, I feel that we barely knew them enough to form a connection besides which ones we thought were cooler than others, or who had the best ability. Once again, I feel like this was the added multiplayer to a game that had an established story that I was just not allowed access to.
This last bulletin was fixed with the introduction of 5v5, but still warrants listing in my opinion. 3v3 is too small for the maps. While they ensure that quick matches are available, I believe they should not have been the main focus of the game. I am aware that all the the decisions made by the team were in regards to balance and it led to many of my favorite parts of Highguard being created, but I can't help but feel that 3v3 was for more casual players and 5v5 would have been perfect for ranked mode.

Final Score: For me this game started out as a 5/10 in its first week and slowly climbed up to a 7.3/10 in its final days. I do believe if Wildlight Entertainment was able to work on the game for at least 8 more months before release, then the final product would have survived for longer. I do wish That the "Stop Killing Games" initiative had been successful already so that we could at least play this game on our own servers if we wished.

[h1]🎮 A Beautiful Disaster - Highguard's Short and Painful Life 💔[/h1]

Sometimes a game arrives with so much promise, only to crumble before your eyes. [b]Highguard[/b] is exactly that kind of experience - a shooter that had everything going for it, yet failed spectacularly within weeks of launch. ⚰️

[h2]🌟 What Could Have Been[/h2]

The premise sounded incredible on paper. 📄 A [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/4128260/Highguard/]free-to-play PvP raid shooter[/url] from developers who previously worked on legendary titles like Titanfall and Apex Legends. 🎯 The gunplay has moments of brilliance when it actually works. 💥 Firefights can feel intense and satisfying. 🔫 The art direction shows genuine care and attention to detail. 🎨 For a free game, the production values initially seem impressive. ✨

[h2]⚠️ The Harsh Reality[/h2]

Here is where things fall apart. 📉 Performance issues plague the experience from start to finish. 🐌 Even players with high-end hardware report stuttering and crashes. 💻 The optimization feels like an afterthought rather than a priority. 🔧 Many describe it as a stutter-ridden mess. 😤

The timeline tells its own tragic story. 📅 Launch day brought nearly [url=https://steamdb.info/app/4128260/charts/]98,000 concurrent players[/url]. 🚀 Within days, the Steam reviews turned overwhelmingly negative. ⬇️ Just weeks later, [url=https://variety.com/2026/gaming/news/highguard-developer-wildlight-layoffs-1236660315/]most of the development team was laid off[/url]. 👋 
Now the [url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/highguard-servers-to-go-offline-on-march-12-2026]servers are shutting down on March 12, 2026[/url] - a mere 45 days after release. 🔌

[h2]🌈 The Silver Lining[/h2]

Interestingly, players who stuck with the game for more than a few hours often found enjoyment. 😊 The core gameplay has merit beneath the technical problems. ⚙️ Some console versions received better reception than the PC release. 🎮 This suggests the foundation was solid, but the execution failed. 🏗️

[h2]💭 Final Thoughts[/h2]

[b]Highguard[/b] represents everything that can go wrong with a modern game launch. 🎭 The fact that it is free makes the disappointment sting less financially, but the wasted potential hurts. 💸 [url=https://wccftech.com/highguard-devs-chalk-up-games-failure-to-leadership-hubris-recreate-smash-success-apex-legends/]Leadership decisions and rushed development[/url] created a perfect storm of failure. ⛈️

If you are curious about what could have been, you might find some value here. 🔍 However, with servers closing soon, there is little reason to invest time. ⏰ This is a case study in how not to launch a live service game. 📚
