I finally got around to playing Highguard over the weekend, and honestly, I’ve got mixed feelings. Not about the game itself necessarily, but about the whole bizarre situation surrounding it. We all watched it get the prime-time slot at The Game Awards last December, hyped as this big "one more thing" moment by Geoff Keighley . It was treated like the second coming of arena shooters. And now? It’s shutting down in less than two months . Having played it, I can see why it failed, but also… it’s genuinely not the worst thing I’ve ever played. It’s a textbook case of a game being doomed by its own hype.

Let’s talk about the actual gameplay first, because the bones of something good are definitely there. You can feel the pedigree of the Apex Legends and Titanfall vets who built it . The gunplay is crispy, movement is slick, and summoning a mount Elden Ring-style to gallop across a fantasy battlefield never gets old . The core "Raid" mode is an interesting idea—mixing looting, base-building elements, and a final siege push. When you get a tight 3v3 match where everyone knows their role, it creates these really tense, strategic moments that are hard to find in other shooters .

However, and it's a big however, the game has some rough edges that feel more like a beta than a finished product. The match structure is unnecessarily complicated. It took me a good handful of matches to even figure out what I was supposed to be doing, and I’m a genre veteran—I can’t imagine how it feels for a casual player . Once you do get it, the loop gets repetitive fast. You’re doing the same few things on the same small map pool with a roster of heroes that feel wildly unbalanced . The former devs themselves admitted that leaning so hard into the competitive 3v3 "sweaty" scene alienated the casual audience that any live-service game needs to survive .

But here’s the thing: none of those flaws are unique. Games launch with balance issues and repetitive content all the time and recover.

So why did Highguard die? Because it was sentenced to death by hype. Putting it in the TGA finale slot set an impossible expectation . People were expecting The Elder Scrolls 6 or some earth-shattering new IP, and instead, we got a solid but unpolished hero shooter. When Keighley tweeted about how we'd all be apologizing to him in 48 hours, it just made the eventual backlash so much worse . The game wasn't just disappointing; it became a meme. It was "Concord 2" before anyone even gave it a fair shot .

The hype machine raised the budget through the roof, and the subsequent flop scared off investors like Tencent . The game needed time and grace to grow, but the industry doesn't give that to games that cost that much and are spotlighted that brightly. Highguard had potential. It was a promising contender that just needed a few seasons to cook . Unfortunately, the hype didn't just set expectations high—it burned the whole kitchen down.

The final update added a skill tree and it changes the game a lot. It makes playstyles more different and gives players roles.

-Some paths give more resources from mining and share materials with nearby teammates

-The attack path gives extra rocket launcher ammo

-You can pickaxe the orb of dead players to stop revives or throw your axe at it from far away to cancel revives

-This is really good for 5v5 because it stops revive chains

The core gameplay feels like a mix of Titanfall and Apex Legends.

-The early phase feels a bit like a battle royale

-You choose your loadout, so there is very little luck

-You don’t drop loot when you die

Another big pro is that loot gets better as the game goes on.

-Later you can get full auto snipers, shotguns, and revolvers

The raid phase feels like Rainbow Six Siege.

-Multiple sites to plant and defend

-Lots of destructible walls

-Easy revives and fast respawns at towers

-Feels like a fast Search and Destroy

The old 3v3 mode was too slow and the maps felt too big for it.

5v5 is much better, but right now snipers are too strong early game because people sit far away and revive teammates.

Weak points:

-One floating island map is WAY too big

-The care package weapon is a weak LMG, runs out of ammo fast and has no sight

-Some characters feel underwhelming

-Redmane’s jump is too slow for movement

-Una feels mediocre

The two newest heroes are really good:

-Ekon can turn into a wolf and pounce on people

-Koldo has a shield that protects revives

-The amulet that revives faster with full health is crazy when combined with it

If the game had 5v5 and the skill tree from the start, people probably wouldn’t have hated it as much.

Highguard was a lot of fun. I really enjoyed this game. And I really enjoyed how the devs actually attempted to make something new. I thought the 3v3 was perfect and the 5v5 was enjoyable. I actually enjoyed the looting phase and just the overall pacing of the game. The fights for the Shieldbreaker were extremely fun. And the same can be said for the raids. I thought the Wardens and guns were all fun without being overpowered or broken. And honestly, I was impressed with how well made the game was on release. I personally experienced no server issues even on day one. And even though I am using older hardware (3070 ti), I was able to get 90fps without having to lower all of my settings below high.

Now, i will admit that the game was not perfect. No game ever is. The Wardens and the world were dry. Granted, the Wardens did have some fun and unique interactions with each other. We didn't know much about the world outside of some very small lore passages from the Quests. And while I could list some other issues, the devs addressed all of them within 2 weeks of release. So I don't see the point.

Which brings me to my conclusion. The game was fun. The devs were enthusiastic and passionate. They responded quickly and positively to feedback. They consistently added to and fixed the game. But even from the start, they made a better and more complete game then most AAA studios manage. And they had plenty of room to grow and the strong desire to do so. I will miss Highguard. And I will not forgive the people of the internet who killed the game over stupid things like the Game Awards or the fact that it had the gall to be different instead of another CoD or Battlefield or Battle Royale.

Highguard was a multiplayer hero shooter developed and published by Wildlight Entertainment, a studio formed by veteran developers who had previously worked on well-known shooters such as Apex Legends, Titanfall, and Call of Duty. Released in early 2026, the game represented the studio’s first major project and attempted to carve out a unique space in the highly competitive world of online live-service shooters. Built using Unreal Engine 5 and designed around a blend of fantasy elements and tactical gunplay, Highguard sought to combine the strategic teamwork of hero-based shooters with large-scale objective-driven battles. The project carried considerable expectations due to the pedigree of the developers involved, but it ultimately became an example of how difficult it is for new multiplayer titles to maintain long-term success in a saturated market.

The setting of Highguard revolves around a mythical continent where powerful factions battle for control of strategic territories and ancient artifacts. Players step into the role of Wardens, specialized warriors who combine firearms with arcane abilities. This mixture of magic and technology forms the thematic backbone of the game, distinguishing it from more traditional military shooters. Each Warden functions as a unique hero character with a defined set of abilities, encouraging players to adopt different tactical roles during matches. Some characters focus on aggressive offense, others provide defensive support or battlefield control, and some excel at mobility or scouting. This hero-based structure encourages teamwork and strategic planning, as the combination of abilities within a team can significantly influence how a match unfolds.

The central gameplay structure revolves around an objective known as the Shieldbreaker, a powerful artifact that acts as the key to victory. Rather than simply eliminating opponents, teams compete to locate and secure this object while preventing the opposing squad from doing the same. Once obtained, the Shieldbreaker enables a team to launch an assault on the enemy’s stronghold, shifting the match into a climactic push toward destroying the opposing base. This layered objective system adds a strategic dimension to the combat, requiring players to balance direct engagements with positioning, defense, and coordinated attacks. Teams that focus purely on firefights without considering the larger objective often find themselves at a disadvantage against opponents who coordinate their strategy effectively.

Gunplay itself follows many of the conventions familiar to fans of modern first-person shooters. Weapons feature recoil patterns, limited accuracy while moving, and a strong emphasis on precision aiming. These mechanics ensure that mechanical skill remains important even in a game filled with character abilities. However, the presence of supernatural powers introduces additional layers of strategy during combat. Some Wardens can deploy barriers or traps that control areas of the battlefield, while others possess mobility skills that allow them to reposition quickly or escape dangerous situations. When used in combination with teammates’ abilities, these powers create opportunities for coordinated strategies and dramatic turnarounds during intense engagements.

Another interesting element of Highguard is the scale and design of its battlefields. Maps are larger than those found in many traditional hero shooters, featuring wide environments filled with multiple pathways, fortified structures, and elevated vantage points. Players can traverse these landscapes using mounts, which provide increased mobility and allow for rapid repositioning across the map. This feature encourages flanking maneuvers and quick responses to enemy advances, giving matches a sense of momentum as teams move across the terrain. The environments also include destructible elements that allow players to reshape the battlefield by destroying cover or opening new lines of sight, creating dynamic conditions that evolve throughout a match.

Visually, Highguard embraces a vibrant fantasy style rather than the gritty realism typical of many competitive shooters. The game’s environments depict ancient ruins, magical fortresses, and sweeping landscapes infused with arcane energy. Character designs are elaborate and colorful, with distinctive armor, weapons, and ability effects that make each Warden instantly recognizable during battle. The visual clarity of these designs is particularly important during large firefights, as players must quickly identify enemy abilities and react accordingly. The use of Unreal Engine 5 allows for detailed environments and impressive lighting effects that enhance the atmosphere of the game’s mystical setting.

Highguard was designed as a live-service experience intended to evolve over time through regular updates. The developers planned seasonal content releases that would introduce additional characters, new maps, weapons, and gameplay adjustments. Cross-platform play and cross-progression were included from the beginning, allowing players across different platforms to compete together and maintain their progress regardless of where they played. This approach reflected the modern model for multiplayer shooters, where ongoing updates and community engagement are essential for maintaining a healthy player base.

Despite these ambitions, the game struggled to establish a lasting foothold in the market. Early interest was strong, largely due to the studio’s reputation and the game’s high-profile reveal during major gaming events. However, many players felt that the game did not offer a sufficiently distinctive identity compared to established competitors in the hero shooter genre. Some aspects of the gameplay—such as the original small team sizes relative to the scale of the maps—also drew criticism for feeling mismatched. Although the developers attempted to address some of these concerns through updates and adjustments, player numbers began to decline soon after release.

The decline in active players created a difficult situation for a multiplayer game that relied heavily on a healthy matchmaking population. Within weeks of its launch, the developers announced that Highguard would be shutting down due to insufficient long-term engagement. The servers were ultimately closed in March 2026, bringing an unexpectedly brief end to a project that had been positioned as a major new entry in the live-service shooter landscape. While the game reportedly attracted millions of players during its initial period, retaining those players proved to be the greater challenge.

Even though Highguard’s lifespan was short, the game remains an interesting example of the risks associated with launching new live-service titles. The project showcased polished mechanics, an experienced development team, and a creative attempt to blend fantasy themes with tactical shooter gameplay. Yet the competitive nature of the multiplayer shooter market means that even technically competent games can struggle to survive if they fail to capture sustained attention from players.

In the end, Highguard demonstrated both the potential and the challenges of innovation within the hero shooter genre. Its mixture of magical abilities, large-scale objectives, and dynamic battlefields offered moments of excitement and strategic depth. While the game ultimately failed to establish itself as a long-term success, it still serves as a reminder of how ambitious ideas and talented developers do not always guarantee survival in the fast-moving world of live-service multiplayer gaming.

I am one of the few people who has ever 100%ed Highguard. I am probably one of the few people who ever will 100% Highguard. Having done so, I can say that Highguard is a rotten game that likely would've never been good even if it hadn't died less than two months after launch. It's a pastiche of mindless trend chasing that is all the bad parts of Fortnite and Overwatch combined and thrown in with a bit of Tribes on top. It's a game that dares to make the statement, "Surely, if we make a game out of nothing but bits of financially successful shooters (and Tribes), we too will be financially successful." 

Let me start by addressing the first part of the combination: Fortnite. Like Fortnite, Highguard has a phase where you roam the map opening treasure chests for random pieces of equipment. Unlike Fortnite, this phase effectively determines who wins the game because the guns are that unbalanced and the time to kill is not conducive to being a good FPS. I know this because I farmed 77 kills with "legendary" weapons due to how hard it is to get to the phase where those start appearing.

The game has exactly two viable weapons: the "Vanguard" (a Not-M4A1 that has a big magazine and a high fire rate) and the "Viper" (an SMG that I forget the real-world name of) which is effectively a shorter-range, higher fire rate Vanguard. Going into a 1v1 against anyone with those guns, unless you also have one, is an automatic loss unless they're AFK. Every other gun is a weaker version of one of those two, sometimes laughably so.

Take the "Paladin", the game's automatic shotgun, as an example. I used the Paladin in a match to farm kills, and found that even if your target is unarmored and standing still, the Paladin still takes nearly half of its 30-something round magazine to kill them. This is a situation that would never happen in an actual match, where I have magdumped all 30 rounds into an armored opponent and only barely killed them. Then there's the "Corsair", a three-round burst SMG that is quite possibly the only gun worse than the Paladin - it's so slow that when I was trying for melee kills, I could reliably melee kill people before they could take me down with it even if I had to charge in from a distance. 

Beyond that, even with the better weapons, TTK is RIDICULOUS. Long-range combat is non-viable unless you get a lucky headshot with the sniper rifle because of how much cover there is, and close-range combat largely seems to boil down to how much lag either side has. At the point where most games end, everyone is going to have 200 HP in a game where most guns do 10 to 12 damage a shot. 

Next, there's the Overwatch part. Apart from the character designs being generally trash (there's one guy who looks like the default Fortnite model trying to cosplay Terry Bogard), the unique character skills are generally useless except for one or two that are game-breakers. There's one character, for instance, who has an ultimate that turns him into an invincible melee-only yeti.. except he can still do objectives while he's invincible. Another has an ultimate that summons an invincible sentry gun that they can plant on an objective to stop your team from doing anything for several minutes. On the other side are things like the character whose ultimate is screaming really loud, which does maybe 40 damage and can break certain walls, or the character who gets six throwing knives that have no range and needs to land at least four of them to have a prayer at killing anything.

Then, finally, is the Tribes part. Highguard plays like a more drawn-out version of it, in that there are three gameplay phases and one of them shouldn't exist. The first phase after looting is this kind of pseudo-MOBA where you're trying to teamfight over a magic sword that lets you break the shield around the other team's base. The problem is that in most cases, the teamfight never really materializes: too often, I'd see both teams hiding behind rocks taking potshots at each other and not getting kills because of the stupidly long TTK until overtime occurs, at which point respawns are turned off and the first team to get a kill usually wins. At higher levels, this usually devolves further to a point where no one moves and the game results in an automatic tiebreaker where whoever had the sword closer to their base loses. The sword phase could be removed (and was, for a brief period) without changing a damn thing.

Once the sword phase is over, you have the "raid" phase, where one team gets a limited number of lives to plant a bomb on an objective and babysit it until it explodes, which isn't exactly compelling gameplay. 

Beyond that, there are a lot of orphaned mechanics that don't really make sense. You can upgrade your base's walls to make it harder to enter, but in practice this doesn't matter because most of the bases are set up such that the enemy never needs to destroy more than one or two walls to reach an objective. You can mine crystals to get currency, which in practice no one ever does.

Highguard is a great example of what not to do, and the world is generally better off without it.

Let me start this off by honestly just asking you a simple question: 
Are you hating on Highguard because it’s ass, or because somebody has TOLD you it’s ass?

Because it is lowkey down there, but after playing for a little bit, I can sort of see why the devs of this game had enough copium injected directly into their bloodstream to think this would actually turn out to be a valid product. 

This game is actually much more mid than I expected it to be, and that is honestly a compliment. 

It turned out to be surprisingly enjoyable, and if a majority of its major gameplay issues were fixed, I genuinely could see this product being salvageable. Instead, it died in its second month of release. Worse yet, they laid off most of the dev team just two weeks after launch, even though those developers were the only reason the game held onto any player base to begin with. Honestly, with how fast it crashed and burned despite the obvious effort put into making it run, I wouldn't be surprised if this whole failed project was just being used as some bizarre corporate tax write-off.

Taking elements from games people enjoy and mashing them together doesn't automatically multiply the fun, and Highguard is proof of that. First and foremost, the gameplay suffers from movement that feels far too constrained. At many points, it feels like OG Fortnite movement while desperately pretending it isn't trying to rip off Apex Legends, I swear to god, they literally ripped off the exact same kill sound effect Apex uses when a player is downed. It's a poor imitation of Apex's gunplay slapped together with a mere shadow of Rainbow Six Siege's base defense format. The game feels stiff and slow, and you can tell the devs wanted to allow more movement variety but felt the need to make sliding only occasionally useful to force players onto the mounts.

And the mounts are a disaster. The absolutely most unbearable feeling is when you get thrown off your mount, end up disabled for three seconds, and are forced to bow your head as the emperor of microscopic woodland creatures expands your asshole to be big enough to fit an entire smurf village in there. Riding is slow and jarring, making it a borderline suicide attempt to charge an enemy. In a "Battle Royale Hero Shooter Halo Apex Rip Off," mounts are supposed to be the unique selling point, but you are actively incentivized to get OFF them in a fight. They just feel like a slightly different sprint rather than an actual battle companion.
This mechanical confusion bleeds directly into the worldbuilding, or rather, the complete lack of it. I genuinely have no idea what we are even doing in this game or what the main premise is. It presents itself with a mismatched aesthetic but gives you absolutely nothing to work with to understand the world. You’re in this supposedly magical land, yet all the buildings are either modern industrial or simple stone, and despite the fantasy elements, all the weapons are just normal-looking guns. The whole thing is just a confused mess, slapping together characters from all corners of fiction without any real story explaining why they are fighting together in this environment. It has absolutely no sauce.

This lack of coherence brings me to the character designs, which are absolutely atrocious. I cannot fathom how a studio invests so much time into a project, only to let their characters look this mediocre. Aside from Una, who is genuinely the only character with a visually unique design, good abilities, and a personality that actually feels realized, the rest of the roster is completely bland. None of them scream any kind of personality, and they rely entirely on their inclusivity, backgrounds, and race to carry them. You can't just create bland characters and hope players fall in love with them solely based on their nationality and nothing else. Good design stems from a creative concept before you even see the visual model, like Doomfist in Overwatch, where people loved the idea of the character before his design was even fully revealed. Here, the characters have no describing characteristics beyond their role, race, and gender. I can see how the developers thought making them look like dorks would incentivize buying skins, but it’s an atrocity when the face of your game, Atticus (a moronic name, by the way), is the most boring, self-insert feeling cover character on the planet. They all look like designs cranked out by a high schooler who started their homework a day before the deadline.

Then you have the randomized shop and the tedious fetch-resource loops, which just add to the overall slog. You have to trek across maps that feel like they were scaled for a completely different number of players just to get a mildly better version of the bad weapons you already have. Why is there no system to keep my old gun if I buy a new one and end up hating it? Worse, the randomized gun store gives some players an unfair advantage based purely on store recommendations. The shield building system is just as confusing, I never understood why I constantly had the option to buy duplicate copies of the same level shield during my playtime. This randomized economy just incentivizes players to beg teammates for drops, leading to one guy farming camps all game instead of actually participating in the match.
While the general layout of the maps is actually pretty decent, the base building mechanics are dragged down by monotonous tasks. Making players manually close doors behind themselves is the most moronic system ever, punishing people for something that should just be an automated mechanic when an enemy inevitably sneaks in.

Finally, if the developers want to save Highguard and make an easy hundred bucks: 

Port Highguard onto mobile. 

I cannot begin to explain how much this gameplay formula, the visuals, and the optimization feel exactly like a game meant for a phone. Every time I was walking around my base or dealing with the slow gameplay loop of base camp attacks, I had this nagging feeling I should be playing this in bed on my phone. It literally feels akin to playing a mobile game on a PC emulator. I genuinely see this game thriving, or at least finding moderate success, if it gets ported. As a mobile game, there's actually a future here because the sauce is technically there for that platform, provided they optimize the movement and stop punishing players for using mounts. But as it stands, nobody who plays games on PC is going to be willing to scratch the bottom of the bottle for drops of dried-up sauce when they could be playing the heavy hitters of the platform.

But ultimately, this game felt... lonely in a sense.  3v3 just feels empty, and doesn't embrace any guild value.  How can I build a clan in this?  How can I build a clan larger than like 10 people when the format only allows you to play with 2 of your friends at a time?  5v5?  ok, 4 others?  If I ever play this game, I essentially am a solo player for it.  I just can't see myself constructing a team for this.  Give players something with object permanence to care about.  Something that persists beyond just the match they join and finish.  I'd already been loving The Finals, Battlefield 6, and Planetside 2.  Those scratch an itch for me.  I'm still cycling between em.  This didn't pull me away for more than 2 days.

A world that looks back at you and is rich with world-building is very captivating and sparks curiosity.  I was kind of intrigued by the tutorial's interactions!  Sadly this whimsical place was reserved only for competitive format FPS...?  Feels wasteful, as that's not the kind of thing that hooks a player into competitive FPS.  I can't imagine what the budget must've been here, and it makes me wonder if you guys were meant to make an RPG or something open-world that would finally one-up the Destiny franchise!

What ARE its competing titles?  Apex?  Finals?  Maybe CS2?  Maybe Call of Duty?  Oh man, possibly dozens of others too.  I can see the differences and what makes it unique, but how can a player-base stick with Highguard long term amidst all the currently established games it is competing with for attention?  And without giving players a means to build their own communities on it?  It was never gonna last like this.  Small format games just don't IMO.  Lots of good-quality ones out there - Some died from being mismanaged or imbalanced after the fact to the point of people not enjoying them anymore, but even if they did enjoy them, those games didn't *stick*, did they.  Because you need a reason to call it home, and they didn't establish that.  A bit of a cult following won't make up for that.  Spectre Divide didn't host tournaments or build out a clan system for players to set up shop for.  Unfortunately, it feels like you guys didn't establish that either.  Everyone's just an NPC to me, like nobody communicates, and they all play silly like experimentalists.

Reward us for competing and committing and achieving/discovering things.  The heroes in it were a stale concept to me.  I'm jaded from it.  I sometimes play Quake Champions, that one has unique playable characters in it, but that's not a selling point to me.  I literally just main the Ranger guy (default) and focus more on making the guns work, because as an FPS gamer, I personally enjoy the gunplay, and what makes me stick around is likeminded people and progression while I play. I enjoyed playing this game; however, it released in what I would call a "beta" state.

The core Gameplay Loop is enjoyable and I appreciate the concept they tried to go with. There is not a game that really balances the gameplay in this manner, and I found it to be well paced. I know that a "build up" phase before any actual huge combat can be off-putting to most, so I think the Devs should have hammered that out better. Early ways to sabotage the enemy or even better "high risk, high reward" things to fight over. That way safe players can build up, but sweat players can do more engaging things. 

The reinforce phase needed better work, with perhaps armaments like mounted turrets or other defensive things may have helped. I think giving each hero a specific "reinforce object" that is a trap, buff, etc would def add to the variety and make the characters feel more unique.

Getting to the characters, the designs were on the cusp of unique, but really lacked direction in my opinion. They had their unique traits, but I did not really feel different playing different ones. Fleshing out more voice lines and backstory for the overall world-building could make us feel more attached. While exploring the map it would be cool if the places you loot were of some significance to some of the characters, with even some minor voice lines. 

The last thing I will say about characters is that the roster seemed small. I would have been alright with less different base designs and more hero designs. 

 Account Progression and lack of appealing skins really hurt the game as well. I think having more different skins with lore implications would have made this game more money and perhaps prevented it from being shuttered. Ranked modes came out way too quick, I would have at least given it a couple months. 

Overall it is sad this game is getting shuttered, as it showed promise. I feel the team focused on too many of the wrong things to make it sustainable. 

While I would probably recommend this game if it had a year more to develop, I cannot recommend it in its current state, especially with it closing up shop on the 12th. 

While it would be great to see some independents with heart and passion give it new life like "Predecessor" or "Hytale", I do not foresee that happening. If this game ever comes back in a better form, I would love to see those who I played it with hop in with me!

[h3]Former Apex Legends devs got together and made their dream game: A hodgepodge of looting, bomb defense, and resource gathering... with mounts. It's definitely different than other FPS games out there, but is it any good? It could be, but not in its current state.[/h3]

[i]Note: As of today, the game has officially announced end of service 3/12/26. This is your last chance.[/i]

If I had to summarize my opinion in one sentence, it's that Highguard has an identity crisis. Sure, it's different than the other free to play FPS's out there, but what exactly is it trying to be? After a dozen hours I'm honestly not sure. It wants to be counter strike, but also paladins, but also apex, but also Rainbow Six Siege. Honestly, I think even players will struggle to describe this game to outsiders, and therein lies your core problem: Who is the audience for this, and what does it do better than all of those titles?

That isn't to say you can't blend different genres together to make something exciting (see Deadlock), but Highguard really doesn't do much better in any of these departments than the variety of games it takes inspiration from.

[h3]1. Gunplay[/h3]Apex devs doing Apex things: Fluid control, reliable aim, some bullet drop to acclimate to but nothing as nearly as involved as ARMA etc. There's room for skill expression in movement, with sliding and mount momentum to not only bhop, but also reach unusual heights, arcing overhead and getting the drop on enemies from above.

There were 10 guns since launch, mostly representing all the usual categories. My issue here is that you'll quickly settle in to just 2-3 you're comfortable with and entirely ignore the rest. This makes the looting phase feel like a chore where you're always searching for the same cozy loadout; Virtually everyone runs Vanguard AR and the double barrel or full-auto shotgun. Sniper rifles see little use in raids and are tricky with bullet drop, being cast aside by pro aimers for the magnum revolver that can two-tap headshot all heroes mid and long range. The meta is already stale.

[h3]2. The bases[/h3]Decent variety. From underground paths to tunnel, zipline-worthy roof entry points, maze-like wall paths, or pyramid style layered flooring, there's quite a bit to learn here.

The biggest issue with bases is that there are very few defensive options. Quite literally, the only thing you can do as a defender is to repair walls and reinforce them. That's it. There are no traps, no adding new walls in non-default locations, no mines, no turrets... and even if you reinforce the walls, they're still easily broken by a rocket launcher, a charged axe, bullets, or hero abilities. So why even bother? Let the enemy team breach the walls, the explosions make it easier to locate and dispatch them.

[h3]3. The maps[/h3]Outside of your bases are expansive floating islands, canyons, temples that, admittedly, look impressive. But they are *huge*, and the game launched with 3v3 as its core mode. It was possible to go the entire gear up phase without ever finding an enemy. 5v5 was rapidly made available due to player complaints, and it feels a lot better.

Despite their size and beauty, maps fundamentally don't really add much to the game. Every match devolves into a rush to the shieldbreaker and fight to control it. There isn't any interesting loot outside of its spawn area, aside from an airdrop with one unique LMG that isn't really OP. In most of my games players ignored it, and many died while using it (other guns can out DPS it).

Since we're on the topic...

[h3]4. Loot[/h3]Maps have chests with randomized gear. As the match progresses, gear increases in rarity up to legend. Contrary to expectations, legend copies don't deal more damage, but instead contain mods that hold more rounds, fire faster, or add more pellets. It's possible to outplay a legendary with a starting weapon, so things are balanced.

This is to say, why even loot in the first place? If the rarity is just a suggestion and players will easily acquire whatever guns they're comfortable with by trader purchase or any one of numerous treasure chests, what's the point? Oh, and you almost never run out of ammo, so why do you even need to collect it? Only amulets are arguably important, since their effects can be game changing (faster revive or faster bomb interactions) and have no guaranteed way to find them.

Crystals serve as the in-game currency to purchase gear from the trader, and are tied to a one-button timing minigame to more efficiently collect. It is optional, but strategically essential, to be able to buy what you need when you need it most (shields or tactical tools). It's fun the first couple dozen times, and quickly becomes a chore thereafter. Yawn.

[h3]5. Lore[/h3]What is highguard? Who are these people? More importantly for the devs, why do I want to spend any money on their skins? The game does nothing to connect the players to these characters aside from a Bio and a couple of voice lines (referencing things we never see). Hero shooters live and die on players wanting to dress their favorites up. The game gives me no reason to care. Apathy is fatal.

By the way - why are fantasy characters with magical flair using guns in the first place? Why can't I use cool superpowers instead?

On the topic of the heroes, their abilities are fine. They are diverse enough to warrant use and make their gameplay significantly different. The recon-based wallhacks are possibly a little broken, even with nerfs.

[h3]6. Monetization[/h3]Some of the skins are pretty cool, but expensive. And it makes the cardinal sin of requiring you to buy more currency than the skin pack costs, so you overspend. Games that do this go right to my trash bin. Shame on you for trying to manipulate me.

[h3]7. QOL and optimization[/h3]No text chat, voice only. Absent social features to easily add teammates to friends list and party up. No clans or guilds. No match history aside from last match. No profiles. No rejoin or backfilling so games are effectively over once someone quits. Optimization was bad on launch and players had to manually edit ini files to fix graphical glitches, giving them a competitive advantage.

TL;DR - If you're an FPS player tired of the same FPS games you've been playing, this is new enough to keep your interest. For everyone else, it probably won't last long.

Already, the studio has laid off most of its staff and a skeleton crew is handling content rollout and actually responding to feedback, so kudos to them. That said, if the player counts don't improve in the coming months, it's likely this won't last past the server contracts. Edit: and now shutdown is confirmed.

I know this won’t align with the majority opinion and recognize this is a hot take. But I genuinely believe Highguard had something special going for it.

I think the developers deserve real credit. They’ve been open to feedback and responsive to what the community wants. Whether every change landed or not, you can’t deny they were listening. That level of transparency matters. 
Another thing is the movement is honestly one of the most enjoyable parts of the game. A lot of players never stuck around long enough to understand the mechanics and movement tech built into it. Once you start experimenting and learning how systems interact, it opens up in a satisfying way. example: you could carry all momentum when you B-hop and turn any moving jump into super glide and enjoy being a speed demon. But most people never got there which is crazy bc this game was made by Respwan and they took gunfights as face value like it was a COD clone.

Highguard became the public toilet everyone liked to take a **** on. It feels like a lot of the hate snowballed. People echoed what they heard instead of forming their own opinion. Once the narrative turned negative, it stuck and it stuck hard. Highguard aside I hate that about gaming culture in the past few years. Why is there a such a big audience of haters that want a game to die. I do understand somewhat with these AAA studios. But it hurts the people who actually put there soul and time into making the game just to get laid off. to the point where I feel like its more efficient to make your game non free to play just to lock the comments to people who play the game and not people who downloaded it just to write a review to hate on it.

Now, that doesn’t mean the developers are blameless. There were quality-of-life issues that should have been addressed at launch. When a game relies on players investing time to discover its depth, the early experience cannot be rough. First impressions matter. Most players won’t “let it cook.” If the day one doesn't feel polished, they move on. And the game award situation didnt make it better. I think the game should have launched right after the game awards or not have been in the game awards at all.

I think the community piled on harder than necessary, but I also think the launch needed to be tighter. Both things can be true. At its core, though, Highguard had depth. The movement feels good. The mechanics reward experimentation. And the devs showed a willingness to improve.

It just never got the chance to shake the narrative. RIP HIGHGUARD

I don't hate this game, in fact, I find it fun and enjoyable in a very guilty pleasure way.

I like the concept and ideas of this game. Big Team Battle Assault on Halo was one of my favorite game modes to play, the idea of storming a base and destroying it has always been a gameplay concept I enjoy in any game.

There's quite a bit of information the game expects you to understand right off the bat, despite the mandatory tutorial. The tutorial does not do justice in showing you the gameplay phases, and the pacing of these phases.

A common complaint, and one that I have as well, is the lack of "creep" type enemies and "creep" like camps. It would've been nice during the gear up phase to have small camps with NPC like enemies that reward you for destroying them, maybe even fortified camps that require a bit more resources to break through but are also rewarding. Maybe boss type camps / enemies at the center points of the map, instead of just empty rooms with chests, or empty rooms with vesper. Even useless creep waves that spawn and move from your base to the enemy base, that when wiped out reward you with some vesper or other loot would've been really cool. The gear up phase heavily encourages basically individually resource gathering and no team effort, which is a bit of a shame. Gear up phases eventually get stale, and having camps like this would also allow you to maybe have modifiers to the map to switch up your strategy. Maybe all fortified camps? Maybe an "eclipse" that makes all the creeps stronger? Maybe double loot on camps? Maybe being able to take over these camps and build forward mini bases for your team so you're basically "conquering" the map and pushing forward as the game progresses? So much potential.

There is a lack of base building interaction. You can fortify walls, you can rebuild them, but that's about it. No turrets, mines, traps (expect for the base that has a bunch of explosives everywhere), no friendly creeps.

I don't doubt that some of this stuff was probably suggested during development, and maybe it doesn't work who knows, but all I know from a player point of view right now is that, the general gameplay is fun, gunplay feels fine, but it's average. It's plain, low sugar greek yogurt with some fruit in it.

Overall, I don't want this game to fail because I think it's a cool idea. I'd rather play this than Fortnite, or Apex, or Call of Duty.

Highguard is a competently made game. No major bugs, glitches, oversights or anything major like that. 
The problems that Highguard has are FAR more complicated than "This game is mid fr fr".

Highguard was made by a talented development team for an audience that didn't exist, but Wildlight hoped they could create.

The comparisons to Apex legends are extremely obvious. As much as they don't want you to know this, Highguard was made by many of the same developers that worked on Apex and Titanfall and it's very apparent in their design language. So much so that I want to state that I LOVE the world design. I think the "High fantasy with modern weapons" genre is heavily slept on and deserves more attention than this and Tiny Tina's Wonderlands (Don't play that, it sucks too). So my criticisms of this game don't have anything to do with how it runs or how it looks, but how it's designed.

Highguard is a failed Esports title.

The core gamemode, Raid, has you and 2 other people (originally) defending your base while trying to destroy the enemy base. Both bases have an impenetrable shield around them that can only be broken with the Shieldbreaker, which spawns shortly after the match starts. One team grabs the Shieldbreaker, breaks the enemy's shield and assaults their base. This is done by planting bombs on 1 of 2 generators or the Anchorstone. Once 2 objectives have been destroyed, the game is over. 
On paper, this could sound very fun, but in practice it's a miserable slog. The Shieldbreaker spawns WAY too early in the game. You don't spawn in with a preselected loadout, you have to find loot on the battlefield, which is completely randomized. The maps are WAY too large for the original 3v3 game mode, though they have since added a 5v5 mode. Your abilities' usefulness is all over the place, ranging from gamebreakingly OP to "I can't think of a single instance where I would ever use this". Why does the Anchorstone exist at all as a base objective if all it does is operate exactly like a generator? 

Apex Legends made a name for itself by riding the hype wave of Battle Royales shortly following the success of PUBG and Fortnite. While Apex is far from dead, the competitive scene for it has begun to fade. Sure Apex probably makes a lot of money off of in-game cosmetics and microtransactions, but the real money in is Esports. Multi-million dollar tournaments that bring in hundreds of thousands of viewers. Apex wasn't pulling in nearly as much as it used to, so naturally, the developers decided it was time for a new esports phenomenon. A game so exciting and hyped up that it was sure to take the competitive scene by storm.

Why do you think they bought the biggest slot of the night during the 2025 Game Awards? Why do you think Geoff Keighley was hyping it up as one of the best games ever? Respawn had the money to fund Wildlight so they could fuck up and not put the blame on respawn. Highguard was being astroturfed as the "next big thing" in esports and hype it up like a big deal, but everyone saw through it immediately. Fundamentally, Highguard is a pathetic mashing together of several different esports mechanics with little to no cohesion between them. MOBA-style base attack/defense. FPS style gunplay. CS style bomb planting and defusal mechanics. R6 Siege style reinforcement mechanics. 

Highguard is underbaked, pathetically lacking in basic mechanics, a clear and obvious cashgrab, and is representative of everything wrong in the modern games industry. So much so, that when this game flopped, several developers went online to say that the game failed "because of online content creators who were dogpiling the hate". Not because of anything they did wrong, but because of the gamers. Afterall, All gamers are evil, terrible people. At least I am. 

My favorite example of this is an interview with Josh Sobel, one of the Tech Artists who worked on Highguard who said "If this pattern continues, all that will be left are corporations, at least in the multiplayer space. Innovation is on life support," he added. "Even if Highguard had a rocky launch, our independent, self-published, dev-led studio full of passionate people just trying to make a fun game, with zero AI, and zero corporate oversight…deserved better than this. We deserved the bare minimum of not having our downfall be gleefully manifested."

Maybe trying making a game people actually want to play, dumbass.

Well, I have to admit I’m having a great time with this game and it’s genuinely fun to play.
The first two hours were a bit rough, but personally, I find it really enjoyable.
The game mode is innovative and interesting.

There is a real economy system like in Counter-Strike, but it only lasts for 2-3 minutes, so it doesn't slow down the game's pace. You really have to feel the momentum of the match and adapt your gameplay accordingly: farming, fighting, preparing for a raid, switching to offense or defense, focusing the shieldbreaker, or letting the enemy push...
The mount significantly reduces travel time across the maps, and the gunfights are fast-paced and snappy.

The matches are dynamic because if nothing is happening, the game forces progress:
If no one deploys the shieldbreaker, it switches to team elimination to trigger the assault.
If teams aren't fighting, the assault triggers wherever the shieldbreaker is closest (which favors the attackers).
The assault drains the base's HP, but if the defense wins, the attackers' base also loses health.
Everything is designed to keep the game moving and push for action. Personally, I’ve never felt any downtime during a match.

Now, the game isn't perfect: the art direction, the mix of magic and weapons, optimization, and the fact that it feels like it's still in Beta... but the reviews are overly harsh.

I hope the game can improve at its own pace and bring players back, because it truly brings something new to the table.

I feel so bad for this game. On paper, the idea is pretty sound and awesome. Shooter game with a wide open environment where after I get a REALLY BIG SWORD I get to raid a base, shoot the walls down and blow it sky high? What part of the game's concept screams bad? None of it! The layoffs suck too, I hate to see a studio lose their colleagues that pioneered and worked with them for who knows how long.

Yet when I actually gave the game an honest try? I played the tutorial, I played 2 matches, I gave it an honest try without listening to a single review of the game and found myself, bored. How. So I looked through footage, I recalled my experience talking to it with friends, and everything about the game is just, unsatisfying. Game feel is one of the most important things about a game and I don't recall the feel at all.

Which is so strange to me, because feel is the one thing every shooter aims to impress. I may not be the biggest fans of shooters, but I remember the feel when I do give the shooter a try. When I shoot someone in TF2, I can FEEL the bang for my bullets and rockets. When I enforce a wall in R6, I can recall the THUNKS AND CLUNKS of the reinforcement being applied to the wall. In Valorant, hitting someone with two meat shots of the Judge is the greatest feeling known to me. For the longest time it was a problem with me for Overwatch because it didn't have the feel but that improved, I could sense the difference. Yet here I am, in Highguard, not remembering anything about the feel.

The movement and shooting synergy is a real strength here.

In a lot of games, you either commit to holding angles or you sprint around and hope you catch someone off guard. Here, mobility feels integrated into fights, so repositioning and keeping pressure is part of the skill expression.

That adds variety to engagements and makes matches feel less repetitive, even when you’re playing the same mode.

A lot of team-based games claim to be objective-driven, but in practice they still devolve into endless mid-map fights that don’t really change the state of the match. From the opening moments, the game struggles to establish a strong first impression. Players begin on an isolated island, but instead of intrigue, the introduction highlights noticeable performance issues and an excessively long tutorial. Spending over 20 minutes in a tutorial without meaningful engagement sets a discouraging tone for what follows.

Technically, the game feels poorly optimized. Frame inconsistencies and awkward transitions disrupt immersion early on. One particularly confusing mechanic involves the weapon scope: pressing shift to aim results in a black screen effect that gives the illusion of zooming, but without delivering any functional or visual improvement. It feels less like a feature and more like a placeholder.

The weapon system also suffers from inconsistency. For example, the upgraded revolver holds six bullets in its chamber, yet the user interface displays a total of 20 rounds. The reload animation further breaks immersion  the character visibly loads only a few bullets, but the ammunition count instantly jumps to 20. Such mismatches between animation and gameplay mechanics create a sense of carelessness in design.

Character abilities and environmental interactions are similarly unconvincing. Moments such as a character destroying a large wall with a single roar feel exaggerated without proper narrative or mechanical justification. These elements may have aimed for spectacle, but instead come across as poorly balanced and disconnected from the game’s internal logic.

Creatively, the game struggles to establish its own identity. It draws noticeable inspiration from established multiplayer shooters such as Counter-Strike 2, Valorant, Apex Legends, Paladins, and Overwatch. However, rather than blending these influences into something fresh, the game feels derivative. The lore lacks clarity, teamwork mechanics feel underdeveloped, and the overall experience does not present a distinctive vision.

In conclusion, while the game may have had ambitious ideas, its technical shortcomings, inconsistent mechanics, and lack of originality significantly undermine the experience. With further refinement, optimization, and clearer creative direction, it could evolve into something worthwhile. In its current state, however, it feels unfinished and difficult to recommend.

As someone with tens of thousands of hours playing FPS games, Highguard stands out amongst the sea of CoD and Fortnite clones as an FPS with a unique gameplay loop, satisfying movement and overall solid shooting mechanics.

The game combines elements of a hero shooter, MOBA, battle royale and arena shooter.  The game is divided into phases, with a reinforcement phase, looting phase, shieldbreaker phase and a base attack/defend phase.

The good: The core gameplay loop is interesting and engaging, and allows for some unique application of tactics, particularly during the shieldbreaker phase.  The movement is fluid, and being able to ride a mount while shooting your guns opens up some interesting strategies.  The underlying shooting mechanics are also solid, and feel tight and responsive.  I think the TTK is on the lower side, but I much prefer that to something like Apex Legends or Halo as it allows for individual skill to stand out more.  The hero abilities are impactful, but not overly powerful and its fairly easy to kill roaming ultimate abilities with just basic weapons.  At it's core, the gunplay comes down to who can land their shots better and makes use of better team tactics, not which abilities are used.

The bad: At present Highguard still needs some tweaks and balancing, as some weapons are underwhelming (such as the corsair).  I find the crystal harvesting QTE "mini game" extremely annoying and unnecessary, and some of the phases need to be tweaked (the open looting phase needs to be lengthened imo).

TLDR: The gameplay concept is unique and really engaging, everything else is not where it should be

Pros: 

Highguard is a combination of the apex legends loot and gunplay style, with a counterstrike type bomb planting mode at the end of every round. The gameplay concept is different than every other multiplayer fps I've played before, and is engaging to play.

Cons:

Health system. As someone who is more at home with the battlefield style health system, the gunplay of Highguard does not speak well to me personally. Sneaking up or flanking an enemy does not feel good, since headshots are so important. I've dumped entire mags into the backs of people only for them to spin and headshot me 8 times and kill me instantly. The result of this combat style is that the only metric for success is how many hours players have on aim trainers. Game sense and smart ability use has almost no influence on the outcome of the game. 

Plastic Art Style. The guns in particular have no real depth to them. I can tell somewhere there was a choice to make the guns look cobbled together because there is some element of druid/nature magic in the lore. However, this choice should have affected the look of the game to be ACTUALLY nature themed. Instead, everything is clean and shiny and plastic looking. This makes the guns look like when I spray painted my nerf guns brown and grey.

Game speed. Each stage lasts about 90 seconds. Minus the intro phase (which doesn't give you time to do literally anything other than waste the reinforcement items) you have 90 seconds to get gear, then 90 seconds to fight over the basebreaker sword, then (if no raid has started) 90 seconds to kill the entire enemy team. This is not enough time. Respawns are 30 seconds, meaning you can spend 1 minute getting gear, get in a fight, then have to take another minute respawning and running back to the fight. If this game lived long enough to get a meta, I predict the meta would be to just camp the basebreaker sword until overtime and then kill the entire enemy team, ignoring all the interesting mechanics.

Microtransactions. Despite the low amount of content shipped in the beginning of the game, it was shipped with the entire package of microtransactions. There are 3 different coins. 1 of them is purchase only. You can buy some skins for real money, some for the purchase only coin, and some you have to buy a pack with the purchase only coin in order to buy what's in the pack with the gameplay reward coins.

**★★★★★ "A Truly Unforgettable Experience"**

Highguard is a game that confidently refuses to be distracted by things like exciting gameplay or memorable storytelling. Instead, it delivers a wonderfully consistent experience where every hour feels remarkably similar to the last, making it impossible to forget exactly what you've been doing.

The combat deserves special recognition for encouraging patience. You'll have plenty of time to appreciate every animation as encounters unfold at a deliberate pace, giving you countless opportunities to rethink your life choices between swings.

The world is refreshingly uncluttered. Rather than overwhelming players with meaningful discoveries, Highguard provides vast stretches of scenery that let your imagination do most of the heavy lifting. It's almost meditative.

Character dialogue is another highlight. Conversations are so restrained that you'll never have to worry about becoming too attached to anyone. Every interaction maintains a professional emotional distance, ensuring no one steals the spotlight.

Performance is impressively consistent, too. The game maintains the same level of excitement from beginning to end, so you'll never experience the emotional roller coaster that lesser games provide.

If you've grown tired of games that constantly surprise you, reward exploration, or leave a lasting impression, Highguard is the perfect antidote. It knows exactly what it wants to be, and it never risks being more than that.

9 Years Later, Im Finally Done. I’ve been playing Clash Royale for around nine years, and after sticking with it for nearly a decade, I think I’m finally done.

The biggest problem for me is that the game has simply changed too much. Change isn’t automatically bad, and some updates have definitely improved the game, but over time it’s started to feel like things are constantly being reworked or changed for the sake of it.

The constant balance changes and card reworks are a big part of that frustration. Some cards and mechanics that had been established for years have been changed in ways that just feel unnecessary. It’s not about one card or one deck; it’s the overall direction the game has taken.

What makes it especially disappointing is how long I’ve played. Most games I was playing nearly a decade ago have already shut down or become unplayable. Clash Royale was one of the rare games that lasted, and I genuinely wanted to keep playing it for years to come.

But after nine years, I just don’t feel excited about where the game is going anymore. Too many changes have slowly taken away what once made Clash Royale special to me.

I’ve stuck through update after update, meta after meta, and change after change. At this point, I think I’m finally done.

Nine years was a good run, but after everything that’s changed, I’m done with Clash Royale.

So Many Bugs, Never Fixed. I’ve never played a game with so many game-breaking bugs that remain unfixed for months.

The worst one happens in Merge Tactics. I’ve had multiple games where I sold a 2-star unit, received no Elixir refund whatsoever, and then the unit somehow reverted back into a 1-star unit. This isn’t a rare bug—it happens repeatedly and completely ruins matches. Bugs like this have existed for months, yet they still haven’t been fixed. It’s honestly unbelievable.

And that’s only part of the problem. The balance in Merge Tactics is an absolute mess. There are far too many in-game events that do nothing except frustrate players. Events that fill the board with polluted tiles don’t create interesting gameplay—they just make the game annoying. These mechanics feel like punishment rather than strategy.

Then there’s the ridiculous “All In” event. It’s one of the worst-designed mechanics I’ve ever seen in an auto battler. If you happen to lose the first couple of rounds, the game is basically over. Instead of giving players a chance to recover through smart decisions, it massively snowballs the match and removes any possibility of a comeback.

Merge Tactics has huge potential, but right now it’s being dragged down by constant bugs, terrible balance, and frustrating event design. Instead of adding more content, fix the bugs that have been ruining games for months and start balancing the mode properly. At the moment, this mode feels more frustrating than fun.

Was a good game. A few years ago Clash Royale was a much better game. I’m not going to talk about heroes or level 16, but as a mid ladder player I’m starting to notice people with wayyyy overleveled cards. Most of my deck consists of level 12 cards, but I recently played someone with level 14 and 15 cards. How am I supposed to beat that? Not to mention all the transactions in the game that make the game feel so shamelessly greedy. Besides, I feel like gems need to be more accessible. It’s 990 gems to skip 10 pass Royale tiers for gods sake. Speaking of accessibility, it’s pretty much impossible to get trade tokens. In my opinion, they should just remove trade tokens, because it’s a strange and inaccessible system.

BRING BACK SEASON SHOP. Season shop was the BEST. It awarded playing new game modes and gave you good rewards for it, not just lucky chests. It was the main way to get wild shards and evos and was overall a great mechanic.

I know I said I wouldn’t get into heroes, but I can’t not. They’re so annoying, especially bowler, knight, dark prince, balloon, wizard, not because they suck, but because they give already good cards overpowered abilities for cheap with no cycling. The abilities also have no downside. If you activate the dark prince ability your dp heals and you get another troop, balloon spawns a tanky guy, wizard moves faster, etc. I also find it annoying that the abilities remove some of the cards counters. Barbs around bowler/wizard? Nope. E wizard on balloon? Nope. Skarmy around ice golem? Nuh uh. Heroes need balance asap.

Overall, if you want to start playing, I wouldn’t recommend it. Not because it’s a bad game, but because it has a greedy dev team with balancers that probably don’t play the game. I don’t hate the game because I hate Clash Royale, I hate it because it was a great game that I and many others loved, but the devs greed ruined the experience.

You opened the game, saw your brawler, had a few main buttons, and could jump straight into a match. Everything felt organized and welcoming.

Unfortunately, the game has gradually become the opposite of that.

The current interface is overloaded with buttons, events, quests, currencies, leagues, rewards, notifications, and all kinds of additional systems. There is simply too much going on at once. Instead of feeling like I’m opening a fun mobile game, it sometimes feels like I’m sitting in an airplane cockpit, surrounded by hundreds of controls and trying to figure out what everything does.

This is what I would call visual clutter and cognitive overload. A game should be enjoyable to open, not mentally exhausting before you even start playing.

I understand that new brawlers, skins, and content are important for keeping a game fresh. I’m not against new content or improvements. But why does almost every update have to completely change the interface, rearrange familiar elements, introduce another progression system, or add more unnecessary buttons?

I would much rather see the developers focus on improving the existing game: fixing bugs, improving server stability, addressing connection problems, and making the overall experience smoother. For example, connection issues and sudden lag spikes during matches have been frustrating for a long time, even across different devices and otherwise stable internet connections.

I don’t want Brawl Stars to become a completely different game every few months. I want the game I originally fell in love with, just better, more polished, and more reliable.

Sometimes, less really is more. A clean and intuitive interface, stable gameplay, and a consistent visual identity are worth much more than endless features and unnecessary complexity.

I honestly don’t expect this feedback to change anything. It often feels like player feedback is ignored and that the developers have already decided what direction the game should take, regardless of what long-time players think. But I still wanted to express my opinion because I genuinely remember enjoying this game much more when it was simpler.

Please don’t confuse adding more things with making the game better. We don’t necessarily want a different Brawl Stars. We just want a better Brawl Stars.

Unbalanced. Brawl Stars is genuinely one of the most unbalanced and frustrating games out there, and what makes it even worse is how little actual skill sometimes matters when playing it. The game constantly rewards people for picking overpowered brawlers instead of rewarding players who actually understand positioning, strategy, timing, and mechanics. Half the time, matches feel like they're decided before they even begin because certain brawlers have ridiculous damage, endless abilities, unfair gadgets, and supers that require almost no effort to get value from. Instead of winning because you're the better player, you end up losing because the other team picked a broken character that can practically carry the entire match without needing to think. The matchmaking is another massive problem, constantly putting you against players with completely different skill levels and making ranked feel more like a coin flip than an actual competitive mode. Some brawlers can miss half their shots and still get rewarded, while others require significantly more precision and effort just to be somewhat useful. The balancing changes also seem completely inconsistent, with certain characters being ridiculously strong for months while others become practically unplayable. On top of that, the game becomes repetitive, frustrating, and predictable because everyone just abuses whatever the current strongest brawlers are. There is barely any creativity when the best strategy is simply choosing the most overpowered character and pressing buttons until something works. A competitive game should reward intelligence, consistency, mechanical ability, and decision-making, but Brawl Stars too often rewards luck, cheesy abilities, unfair matchups, and whoever has the more broken team composition. Overall, Brawl Stars has turned into a frustrating experience where losing doesn't necessarily mean someone played better than you, and winning doesn't necessarily mean you demonstrated any real skill. It's less about being genuinely good at the game and more about exploiting whatever ridiculous advantage the developers have accidentally left in the game that season.

Why brawl stars is the best. In mobile gaming, few titles balance quick strategy, thrilling competition, and endless replayability like Brawl Stars. Developed by Supercell, this multiplayer powerhouse has captured millions of players worldwide. Beyond its colorful art style, Brawl Stars excels through accessible mechanics, diverse character design, dynamic game modes, and a rewarding progression system. The immediate brilliance of Brawl Stars lies in its ease of play combined with deep strategic nuance. Anyone can pick up a device, understand the basic controls, and jump into a quick two-to-three-minute match. However, mastering the game requires real skill. Positioning, aim, map awareness, and coordinating team abilities (Supers) differentiate casual players from competitive contenders. Because matches are short, the game delivers intense bursts of adrenaline without demanding hours of continuous commitment, making it perfect for both brief breaks and longer gaming sessions. Another pillar of the game's success is its diverse cast of characters, known as Brawlers. Each Brawler belongs to a distinct class—such as sharpshooters, tanks, assassins, or supports—and brings a unique playstyle to the arena. From Colt’s long-range precision shots to Mortis’s swift dash attacks, the roster offers something for every playstyle. Furthermore, Gadgets, Star Powers, and Hypercharges allow players to customize their favorite Brawlers, adding layers of strategy and personal expression to every match. Diversity extends far beyond the character roster into the game modes themselves. Brawl Stars keeps the experience fresh by offering a rotating selection of event modes. Players can battle for control in Gem Grab, score high-stakes goals in Brawl Ball, survive a battle royale in Solo or Duo Showdown, or outsmart opponents in tactical modes like Knockout and Heist. This variety ensures that gameplay never becomes stale, as each mode requires distinct team compositions and tactical approaches. Social connectivity and live-service updates elevate Brawl Stars from a simple mobile app to a thriving global community. Playing alongside friends in three-player or five-player teams turns standard battles into memorable moments of teamwork and shared victory. Supercell routinely supports the community with frequent updates, introducing new Brawlers, seasonal cosmetics, thematic events, and major balance passes. The game's vibrant aesthetics, memorable sound design, and creative skins give it a charming personality that keeps players invested for the long haul. Ultimately, Brawl Stars stands out as a triumph in mobile game design. By pairing fast-paced action with deep tactical depth, a colorful roster of characters, and a constant stream of fresh content, it provides an endlessly engaging experience. Whether you are a casual gamer looking for quick fun or a competitive player striving to climb the ranked leaderboards, Brawl Stars offers a gaming experience that is nothing short of amazing.

I wish this game was balanced.. I love this game, whatever you throw at me I am loyal to brawl, fun game, no ads, progression, GOOD EVENTS, great brawler design (in general), and playable if you are f2p.
But as you can see, this is a two star review, this is because of two problems: too much RNG & horrid balancing.
It makes me want to give up. When chaos drops first came out, they were exciting. But over time they have become stale. So stop adding gacha and add deterministic rewards like in Brazil. If they can have it, so can we. The problem is that when you implement deterministic rewards, they don’t generate as much buzz so new players take it for granted. But the problem is, not everyone needs 1000 credits, so instead, add a choice, why do you think we love rescource keys? I don’t want 100 bling from a mythic drop! I want coins! The final reason why this is the solution is because a lot of players who should appreciate deterministic rewards don’t. I am talking about experienced players who have fame. Some people like fame (me) and don’t mind credits, but some older players prefer other resources as they believe fame to be a waste. This makes everyone happy but the new players, so add an option for credits, a few gems, and star drops in the resource key selection menu. This allows everyone to enjoy resource keys. So stop giving out a few thousand coins/power points/ bling in community events. Give keys. We don’t need more resources, we need more choice. If you are going to take away any thing from this review supercell, this is important. It will revive your game. Mabye even buff Starr drops? 

The balancing. 
It needs to change, this is what holds back the game, I know you need op brawlers for excitement, but mabye make them a little less op. It kills the game. It kills the players. I am tired. Some people do play the new op brawlers or buffies brawlers etc, but most of us play brawlers we love, who are often not op. The meta is too aggressive and it is toxic. Now credits to you, you did buff throwers and snipers, thank you. But make sure you don’t forget other low dps brawlers, supporters. They often underperform in the current meta. Except Glowy, nerf Glowy, he should not do so much damage it is unholy. I hope you know which brawlers are breaking the game and that you fix them. The amount of times a Damian has jumped me and killed me is insane. These op brawlers have barely any counters, most of the time their counters are: any brawler that can kill them first. There is a big problem there, the op aggressive brawlers are (mainly) countered by other aggro brawlers or the few agro counters. This makes low dps brawlers fall behind and become inherently lacklustre. Another problem is the amount of low skill brawlers, I wish you stopped adding lower skilled brawlers because frankly, there are too many. They are good for the game but there should be a balance. 

Please take into consideration what I have said if you are reading this supercell. Thank you for reading. It was long but that is because I care about this game. I hope you can save it.

Show some respect to players. This used to be a great game, but now it’s completely unrecognizable. 

The matchmaking system is totally unfair, constantly pairing you with toxic or disengaged players. On top of that, many events limit your allowed losses, forcing you to spend gems if you want to keep playing—only to match you with bad teammates all over again. Players are practically forced to burn through gems just to stay in the challenge, yet these pay-to-continue players are the very group providing real value to this game. It’s beyond me how the devs could come up with such absurd mechanics—and once you finally complete an event, the rewards are usually worthless. 

A game shouldn't be designed to inflict frustration on its players. This kind of arrogant attitude is downright off-putting. You need to remember: we loved this game for what it originally was, not the company or the team behind these terrible designs. 

To make matters worse, the Season Pass skins have become repetitive, low-quality, and boring. New heroes are equally uninspired, seeing play only upon release due to temporary, unbalanced stats. As a long-time player, I see no future for this game, and I strongly advise new players to stay away.

Death and harm aimed at the player, no warning. I did not sign up for this. Brawl Stars has always presented itself as a bright, colourful, competitive game, and it is rated 13+ on the App Store, which means young teenagers are part of its intended audience. It is not advertised as a horror game, and nothing about it prepares you for what the #FindGus Brawl-o-ween event contains. The event is optional, but an option means nothing if you don't know what you're agreeing to. There was no content warning or notice of any kind before I started. If I had chosen a psychological horror game, I would have expected disturbing material and could have decided for myself whether to play it. Here, I had no way of knowing until it was already in front of me.
What upset me most is that the event does not just show spooky scenery. It aims death and harm directly at the player. In the first puzzle, I had to spell out the word "YOU" and then dig up a grave with that word on the tombstone. I am very sensitive to the subject of death and harm, and being made to uncover my own grave in a game I play to relax shook me badly. It was not a jump scare or a cartoon ghost. It was a grave meant to represent me.
It did not stop there. A character told me they would keep the coffin for when they no longer needed me. During a puzzle, the game told me it doesn't matter if I lose an arm because I have two. The script also mocked me by saying people jump out the window when they see me. Taken together, these lines tell the player that their death is expected, their injuries do not matter, and their presence drives people to throw themselves out of windows. That is not Halloween fun. It is being singled out and belittled, with self-harm imagery mixed in, and it is directed at you personally.
I stopped playing the event partway through because I did not want to see what else was coming. By then, the damage was done.
Many players, including young teens and people dealing with grief or mental health struggles, could react far worse than I did. A 13+ rating does not tell anyone to expect this. Supercell needs to put a clear content warning at the start of story events like this, so players can make a real choice before they begin, and remove lines that target the player with death, injury and window-jumping jokes. Until then, I can't recommend this game to anyone
