Engineered addiction. ADDICTION WARNING — Great Game, But Know What You Are Getting Into

I played Honor of Kings for years, including the Chinese version. I have also spent thousands of dollars on this game.

First, I will give them credit: this is an extremely well-designed game. The artwork, skins, hero movements, effects and overall gameplay are top of the top.

But that is exactly why I think players—and especially parents—need to understand the other side of it.

This game can become an engineered money and attention trap very quickly.

THE LOSE-AND-PLAY-AGAIN TRAP

If you play long enough, you probably know the feeling.

You win several games, feel like you’re getting better, and then suddenly you enter games that feel almost impossible. Teammates seem completely incompetent while enemies seem to react instantly, move perfectly and punish every mistake.

I cannot prove what Honor of Kings is doing behind the matchmaking algorithm, so I am not going to claim I know exactly how it works.

What I CAN tell you is what it did to me psychologically: losing did not make me stop playing. It made me want to play one more game.

Then another.

“I’ll stop after I win.”

That is the dangerous part.

The emotional cycle of reward → frustration → chasing the next reward is something people should take seriously, especially when children are involved.

This isn’t just me calling gaming “addictive.” The World Health Organization officially recognizes gaming disorder in ICD-11. Its definition includes losing control over gaming, gaming becoming more important than other activities, and continuing despite negative consequences.

And look at what happened with this exact game in China.

Back in 2017, Tencent already limited Honor of Kings players under 12 to 1 hour per day, and ages 12–18 to 2 hours per day, following concerns about children becoming addicted.

China later went much further. Under current national anti-addiction rules, minors generally can access online games only 8–9 PM Friday, Saturday and Sunday, plus that hour on public holidays.

You can argue whether China’s solution is excessive. But you can’t pretend the addiction concern came out of nowhere.

HEALTH — THIS IS THE PART THAT SCARED ME

I didn’t realize what this game was doing to me until I started tracking myself.

I was angry more often. Road rage. Fighting with my partner. Anxiety at work. Trouble sleeping. Constant frustration.

I never connected any of that with the game because I thought I was just “playing a game.”

Then I got an Oura Ring and started paying attention to my body.

During intense sessions, I have personally seen my heart rate approach an average of roughly 150 bpm while playing.

Think about that for a second.

I’m sitting almost completely still. I’m not running. I’m not exercising. My fingers are basically the only thing moving, yet my body is reacting like it is under serious stress.

My reading is obviously personal data and doesn’t prove the game causes heart problems. But gaming-related cardiovascular arousal itself is real.

In one laboratory study of children, average heart rate increased from 86.9 bpm at baseline to 103.2 during gaming, while systolic blood pressure went from 106 to 129.6 mmHg. During the most active three minutes, average heart rate reached 116 bpm.

Research on professional esports players has also found that competitive gaming activates the sympathetic nervous system—the body’s stress/“fight or flight” system.

So when you’re screaming at teammates, heart pounding, staring at the screen for hours and telling yourself “ONE MORE GAME,” understand that your body isn’t necessarily experiencing this as some peaceful little hobby.

And 150 bpm while sitting still for extended periods is not something I’m willing to ignore anymore.

THE MONEY TRAP

This is probably what I regret the most.

I have personally spent thousands of dollars on this game.

And the monetization is extremely clever.

If everything simply said:

SKIN — $129.99

a lot of people would immediately think: “That’s ridiculous.”

Instead, real dollars get separated from what you’re buying through currencies, tokens, draws and limited events.

You don’t always feel like you’re spending $100+.

You feel like you’re doing “one more draw.”

Then one more.

Then you’ve already invested so much trying to get the limited skin/effect that stopping feels worse than spending another $10 or $20.

There is legitimate research behind the concern over this type of randomized monetization.

One study of adolescents found recent loot-box purchasing was associated with 3.7–6.0 times the odds of problem gambling, even after researchers controlled for actual monetary gambling, age and gender. That doesn’t prove loot boxes cause gambling addiction, but the association is strong enough that parents should know about it.

ESPECIALLY THINK TWICE BEFORE GIVING THIS TO A CHILD

Adults at least have a chance to recognize what is happening.

Children have far less experience managing impulse, frustration, money and delayed gratification.

If a grown adult like me can spend thousands of dollars and waste hundreds or thousands of hours before finally stepping back and asking, “What the hell am I doing?”, imagine handing the same system to a 10-year-old.

I’m not saying nobody should ever play Honor of Kings.

I’m saying understand the product you are using.

It is an incredibly polished game built by people who understand human attention, reward and monetization extremely well.

I wish someone had warned me before I gave it this much of my time, money and emotional energy.

So I’m leaving the warning for the next player.

Hok. "Hey everyone, just wanted to drop some honest thoughts on Honor of Kings. It’s a solid MOBA with a lot going for it, but I think there’s still room to make the mobile experience even better.

First off – controls. They’re decent, but giving players more customization would really help. Let us fully remap buttons, resize the joystick, maybe even change the layout based on our playstyle. It’s a small update, but it would make a big difference for comfort and responsiveness on mobile.

Now here’s something I’ve been thinking about – storylines. Right now, the heroes are cool, but we don’t really know them. What if the game introduced a campaign mode or cinematic cutscenes that explored each hero’s backstory? Why they’re in the fight, what their world looks like, their rivalries or alliances. That kind of narrative depth could make players feel way more connected to the characters.

And let’s be real – not everyone wants to play ranked all the time. Adding fun, casual modes would be a game-changer. Maybe some rotating events, creative challenges, or even lighthearted mini-games with crazy power-ups. Something fresh and less competitive to break up the grind.

Speaking of grind – daily missions and rewards need some love. They shouldn’t feel like chores. Give us exciting incentives – limited skins, voice packs, emotes – stuff that feels like a reward, not just another checkbox.

Overall, HoK is doing a lot right, but with some attention to mobile-friendly features, story-driven content, and more ways to just have fun, it could go from good to legendary. That’s my take – curious to hear what you think too!"

I believe the state of Smite 2 is absolutely DREADFUL to play, especially as a support player. These are the complaints I have over about 500 hours of gameplay as a casual player. 
1.	In Smite 1, supports / tanks were actually able to tank things and body block for teammates. In Smite 2, that is not possibly anymore unless you build massive health regen. I was playing Athena late game and peeled a Medusa with 1 pen item and from my 250 physical prots and 4200 health, Medusa did ¾ my health from 1 taunt from just autos. That is not fun to fight against when peeling as a support means I can just die for helping my team. 
2.	Enchanter supports are awful. Most of them on release are bad. The only exceptions are Aphrodite but only in Ranked since you communicate in Ranked and at higher levels of play (best example I have is Brig in OW, where she was very good at Masters GM levels of play but awful everywhere else under that) and Hel. Besides that, Ix Chel was and IS currently still awful, Nox on release was and IS awful, Aphrodite does not feel good since you die very quickly, Ra feels better than Aphrodite, but only because of the protections on his Aspect 3 that stays with someone. Besides that, awful. 
3.	I will never understand why Horus has the best CC in the game. With how much damage and how fast everything can die, one combo from Horus’s 2 and 1 gets people killed instantly. And if you are able to counter that and fight him back, his get out of jail free 3 ability ignores that. Also do not forget his semi global ultimate! But Geb’s 2 knockup is shorter that Horus’ knockup. I would say make the CC the same across characters but maybe I am wrong here. But he also has not been nerfed at all except for his Prot shred on his 2 and his ult speed. Nerf his CC chain! Make his 1 interruptable or slower so people can react out of it. It's also fun how dashes can be cancelled out, but Horus' 1 cannot be cancelled so people still get stunned (which does damage), prot shred attack (more damage), his knockup (damage), his after hit of that (which slows...and does damage). But an Athena taunt (thanks to CC reduction in the game) can go from 2 seconds to 1 if someone was CC'd more than enough times. But Horus' CC does not change. 
4.	The community is awful. I have no examples, it’s just a MOBA, but it feels worse than Smite 1. I will make callouts as a support as in to fight for mid camps and I will be there for support or let us go pick a fight at Gold Fury or something of that nature. People are chasing kills more than they are objectives and it has caused me to lose so many games. Rather, it feels like I cannot control the flow of the game as a support player. 
5.	Backline support is dead, long live aggressive supports only. Only pick Horus, Ares, Cerb, or warrior supports if you want to feel useful. There is no need to pick anything else.
6.	Snowballing feels INSANE! Again, I have no examples, it just feels like you can get snowballed super easy. Not as fun or not encouraging to stick it out in longer games if everyone is dying in under 2 minutes. 
7.	F7 warriors are rampant. Not the “we are even, we will F7 to stay in the game”. I mean we are (hypothetically) 2 kills and 20 deaths as a team, 10-15k gold behind at 30 minutes, have gotten no gold furies or fire giants. 3 people vote yes, 2 people vote no so we are held hostage. But their reasoning? They are 2 friends who want to play, they are “punishing you all for being bad” or some other arbitrary things.


I have currently uninstalled the game and do not plan on playing anymore. After almost 1800 hours on Smite 1 and 2 total, I think this is where my run ends. The game is going in a direction I do not like or enjoy. I wish it felt much more fun as a support player, but I cannot play knowing that I am a decent player (not masters level, just a casual player), making callouts, peeling for my team and feeling completely useless when I die to damage that I build to mitigate and that does not matter or a team does not follow callouts. 

TL;DR: After 1800 hours across Smite 1 and 2, I’m done. Supports can’t tank anymore since everything shreds you no matter what you build, and enchanters are mostly useless. Horus is overtuned, so only aggressive supports are worth picking. Snowballing is insane, people chase kills instead of following callouts, and if you vote to surrender, someone always holds the team hostage. As a support main, this game is awful.

I've been playing both smites for a few years and i enjoy them extensively, and i agree with others about smite 2 bringing lot of changes.

first the items and stats are different,  the developers created a way to allows players to fully customize and play with item builds which i absolutely love. smite 1 you basically got a single extreme direction that sticks to your role and that it.
the god builder allows you to target specific aspects of the gods you understand. i played Xing tian in smite 1 heavy and built my HPS to 100 plus and would steamroll everyone - fun sure but when i tried that in smite 2 i couldn't and that is the correct way to do a sequel. 
Also the fact you can bring any character into any role is awesome, it makes every match challenging and refreshing. smite 1 you basically just saw the same set of super star gods repeatedly but now you get players actually willing to try a new option or test boundaries and fill a role with a god that wouldn't be able to fill that role in smite 1. furthermore in smite 1, some of the gods were so broken you basically knew if the player just knew how to use them functionally, not even good with them, they were gonna be a pain and y'all were probably gonna lose. but now with the new system its much more balanced. Anubis is a great example of this. Zeus is another, both of these gods are a nightmare but not implausible like before.
and they didn't just stop at revamping the stats and item builds, but they also got aspects. now i don't remember if they had aspects in smite 1 but they completely change the character to suite your particular play style. perfect example is Aphrodite. the heal + damage aspect changing her from the original heal + support is a chefs kiss. i used to hate when i played with a Aphrodite because the only realistic way to play her is to leech to a tank and try not getting killed, but with the aspect she has become one of the strongest mages. definitely a absolute nightmare to compete against when a player really knows how to use her but that's part of the challenge of the game. 

another thing is the god choices. dude the potential and outlook for this game is extremely high when you look at the smite 2 original gods. like Hecate, Aladdin, etc.  i mean the options the developers put into these new smite 2 gods tell me that once they satisfy the carryover from smite 1, things are gonna get insane. 
i wish gods came out sooner but i get it, realistically to set everything up for a release takes a lot of time, effort and money. and honestly releasing gods successfully with almost no issues like they have is a serious accomplishment in my opinion.

the skins and customization is a thing i see a lot of complaints on and my opinion on this is people need to be more realistic with expectations. i mean y'all expect them to release all these gods, update them under the new designs and systems, do it with little and no bugs AND do it with little or no money earned? games are a business and they depend on money. the diamonds are earnable enough that you can literally earn any skin you REALLY want with enough time. yes its absolutely a lot slower, yes you spent money on skins from smite 1 , but seriously be realistic. its a new game and these people's livelihood and this games longevity depends on money and to pay for skins is a honest compromise. buy access to all gods, grind for the skins you want and choose to buy the skins if you choose to buy them.

this game is still growing and most of the players are people who are coming from smite 1, so yes the new player acclimation is rough. but they got the VS AI option that i use extensively to test new builds and get used to the god skills and aspects. you can tell how well your build works from a certain K/D ratio against the Bots and you can carry that build to compete against humans. tis not hard.

teamwork sucks for sure but that's against other players, not really about the game itself. i think the heavy mixed reviews is misleading.  the game itself is absolutely a evolution of smite 1 in my opinion. embrace the new challenges, learn the new stats, builds, and aspects and i promise that you will understand the direction this game is meant to take. whether or not you enjoy that direction is personal taste but i truly do and this game is one that i consistently find myself going back to.

I've been playing SMITE since 2011, when I was an alpha tester for SMITE 1. Back then, there were only 10 gods, and I still remember when Sobek and Arachne were released. It feels like yesterday! Those were such good times. ♥

I came to SMITE as an orphan of **Land of Chaos Online (LOCO)**, a game I absolutely loved. SMITE never truly replaced that love, but it brought me comfort and eventually became another game that held a special place in my heart.

After all these years, with over 4,000 hours of gameplay, I'm genuinely happy to see how far SMITE has come. Those thousands of hours represent countless matches, friendships, unforgettable moments, and memories that I'll always cherish.

I invested a tremendous amount of time, effort, and money into SMITE 1. I owned every single skin, representing over a decade of dedication. Naturally, I was extremely disappointed when I learned that my collection wouldn't fully transfer to SMITE 2.

However, I eventually understood that this was a new game, built on a new engine, marking the beginning of a new era.

I resisted SMITE 2 for several months. But after some major updates, I finally decided to give it a chance. I could see how hard the developers were working to create something special, and I'm so glad I gave it that opportunity!

**Today, I can confidently say that SMITE 2 is better than SMITE 1.**

The improved mechanics, smoother gameplay, better graphics, and new aspects that allow gods to fulfill different roles have brought so much more depth to the game. The constant updates, returning gods from SMITE 1, and beautiful new skins make the experience even more exciting.

Of course, competitive gaming communities can be difficult sometimes. But that's not a SMITE problem; it's something we see across virtually every competitive game. With a little maturity and the ability to mute or block toxic players, it's much easier to focus on what truly matters: enjoying the game.

And honestly, **there's nothing quite like SMITE out there.**

The mythology, the different pantheons, the incredible gods, and that unique feeling of exploring the battleground alongside friends or even complete strangers create an experience that no other game has ever managed to replicate for me.

I love this game so much, and I sincerely hope it continues to grow and thrive for many more years. I would love nothing more than to see SMITE live forever. ♥

As for all the negativity surrounding SMITE 2, I feel that many of the harshest comments lack constructive arguments and are driven more by frustration than by a fair assessment of the game. Constructive criticism is always welcome, but we should also recognize the tremendous effort the developers have put into improving SMITE 2.

**From a nostalgic alpha tester to a proud SMITE 2 player, thank you to everyone who has been part of this journey.**

Here's to many more years of gods, mythology, epic battles, and unforgettable memories! ♥

This is a review mainly for people who enjoyed SMITE 1.

Gameplay-wise: this is the SMITE that you like, but improved. Everything feels more smooth, a lot of gods got improvements and are more versatile (you can play Geb as an ADC without trolling), and the graphics are more impressive. The new UI, especially the bland font for damage numbers etc, does take time to get used to but that's alright. SMITE 2 is literally just SMITE 1 but slightly novel and different - usually for the better.

So gameplay-wise we're good and I fully recommend this game, but SMITE 2 really fucked up in several other places.
Most importantly: all your stuff is gone. Your skins, your Masteries; any cosmetic is gone. If you grinded Worshipers in SMITE 1 like I did - all that effort was for nothing. They don't even let you keep your Profile Icons! Come on Hi-Rez they're just JPGs.
You may have heard that you get Legacy Gems based on how much you spent on SMITE 1, but the amount of stuff you can buy with these gems is pitiful and most of it is in chests...

What irks me the most though, is that the game treats you like a literal new player. It KNOWS that you played SMITE 1 but it's still gonna force you to play multiple Bot matches before you can queue for actual games. Oh, also, you have no gods. Zero. Not just that but every 2/3 games, SMITE 2 will throw a pop-up in your face asking if you wanna buy the God Pack (it's on discount!!) and whenever you unlock a new god you need to avoid clicking the "Buy God Pack" button twice. It's the kind of stuff you'd expect from a cheap mobile game and leaves a bad taste in my mouth. At least you unlock new gods quickly, but the fact that you have to unlock them at all does not feel right.

I'm putting this review as a Recommended because this IS a good game and it really improves SMITE 1, but the majority of non-gameplay stuff has been handled very poorly and is just a slap in the face to people who played the original game for so many hours.

This game has the potential to be the best in the Moba genre, but that potential is squandered by a dev team who insists on modeling Smite around the concept of DEI.

Skill gaps between the best & worst players are artificially bridged & normalized by comical gold/exp gain rates, a lack of God kit complexity, & a lack of reward for performance. To delve a little further:

 • There is effectively no skill associated with gold & exp gains. By minute ~35 every person in the match is max level & full build, regardless of how poorly anyone performed. You practically have to full on afk/grief to not be.

 • There's no meaningful way to scale your stats based on performance. The few items which do scale based on minion/God kills are either bad relative to other options competing for a slot, and/or have minimally impactful scaling coefficients. The negative impacts of this compound with the fact that everyone is max level & full build by minute ~35, because of course that means by minute ~35 any gold & exp lead you had gets normalized and the 0/10 troll who fed lane for 35min is now caught up with the 15/0 guy sweating his ass off to win.

 • Because the game does so much work to artificially normalize skill gaps, the quality of your team [b]Completely, Wholly, & Entirely[/b] outshines the skill of any individual player. What this means in practice is that how good you are as an individual means nothing if your team is bad/trolling - it doesn't matter if you consistently drop 30 kills a game, you will consistently lose games if your team doesn't play around your lead while being matched against 5 substantially worse players who do communicate.

 • Party queue becomes borderline mandatory for Ranked play, because the game's fundamental nature makes solo queue an RNG based matchmaking roulette


Hi-Rez has effectively designed the game around pro play involving 10 people in a match who all have comms & work together to win, but in practice the game is virtually nothing like this - & that's doubly true for anyone playing ranked in solo queue. Until you get to high rank, the overwhelming majority of people are in their lanes playing their own game while ignoring objective callouts - & because the game's skill gap is artificially normalized, there's little you can do to carry their weight.

Every other match feels like a competition to see who can be the most egocentric, obnoxious, boosted, or outright toxic player in the lobby. Playing ranked in SMITE 2 feels like sacrificing a little piece of your sanity EVERY SINGLE game. And the worst part? It feels like HiRez doesn't give a shit. There seems to be little meaningful action against the people who repeatedly ruin matches, I call them ranked terrorists, leaving everyone else to waste 30+ minutes of their lives dealing with their bullshit because they're miserable. At some point, you have to ask yourself why you're even bothering to play as this is a consistent theme.

Role identity is practically dead, too. Nobody wants to play traditional roles anymore because apparently everyone can do whatever they want thanks to HiRez's beloved Aspects concept. These gimmicks aren't going to magically outperform the original god archetypes at what they were designed to do. Instead, we get a mess where roles lose their identity and team compositions feel increasingly more meaningless. The balancing is equally atrocious. Why the hell can I build zero damage items, stack tank items, and still kill everyone in the lobby? The meta is so snooze of items such as Lash, Contagion, Cuirass, Nemean the same tank-heavy bullcrap everywhere. Even junglers are becoming the third or fourth tank on their team because apparently doing ridiculous damage while being nearly unkillable is perfectly acceptable. Does anyone actually playtest this shit at HiRez? Dear lord

Then there's HiRez's development and monetization strategy, which increasingly feels like a cash grab. HiRez's other projects got shut down while SMITE 2 slowly rereleases old content with kits that are damn near 1:1 with minor tweaks. At this rate, catching up to the original game's content will be done by like 2028 which would be laughable enough on its own. Guess we'll be in beta for 3 years lol. Meanwhile, diamond/gem prices on skins/travelers/prisms or whatever are becoming egregious, and we're expected to support the game financially through supporter shops. Slow content delivery, terrible balance, miserable ranked matches, but somehow there's always room to monetize more. Jokes... just jokes.

The worst part is that SMITE 2 actually has potential on paper. But potential means nothing when matchmaking is slop, ranked is filled with trolls and questionable behavior, the meta is frustrating, and HiRez seemingly refuses to address the problems that matter. I would also like to say that, I don't mind losing. I simply mind having my time wasted by people ruining matches and systems that make the experience miserable, game after game. A competitive game should reward skill and respect your time. SMITE 2 consistently fails at both. Fun fact the base game across all gamemodes have an above surrender rate of 50%! So potentially 1 in 2 games are surrendered? But yeah, this game reeks of wasted potential and until HiRez gets its shit together with balancing, competitive integrity, role identity, and content delivery, I genuinely cannot recommend it. SMITE 2 takes the recognizable foundation of its predecessor and rebuilds it for a newer generation of competitive multiplayer gaming. Developed by Titan Forge Games and published by Hi-Rez Studios, this free-to-play sequel retains the unusual third-person perspective that separates the series from traditional MOBAs while moving to Unreal Engine 5. Rather than feeling like a straightforward graphical remaster, it is designed as a new foundation that can evolve over many years, with redesigned combat, modernized visuals, expanded strategic possibilities, and systems intended to make the genre easier for newcomers to approach.

The biggest attraction remains the opportunity to control gods and legendary figures drawn from mythology. Characters such as Zeus, Anubis, and Loki are more than visually different fighters because their abilities encourage distinct approaches to combat. Ranged gods can pressure enemies from a distance, assassins can exploit positioning and surprise attacks, and durable frontline characters can create opportunities for teammates. Since everything unfolds from a third-person viewpoint, aiming and spatial awareness feel much more immediate than in an overhead MOBA. Landing an ability, escaping an ambush, or combining powers with teammates provides the responsiveness of an action game without removing the strategic principles expected from the genre.

Conquest remains the centerpiece for players who want the deepest experience. Its 5v5 structure revolves around lanes, jungle areas, objectives, towers, character progression, itemization, and ultimately destroying the opposing Titan. Victory requires much more than mechanical skill. Teams must understand positioning, map control, objective timing, resource management, and when to engage or retreat. The game becomes increasingly rewarding as these systems begin to make sense, although inexperienced players should expect a considerable learning curve once they move beyond casual play.

Fortunately, SMITE 2 makes a serious effort to reduce the initial complexity. Auto-build and auto-level features can handle parts of character progression while a beginner concentrates on movement, aiming, abilities, and surviving team fights. Players who become more comfortable can gradually take direct control over itemization and builds. This approach works well because it does not remove the underlying depth. It simply gives newcomers room to learn one part of the game at a time instead of immediately demanding knowledge of every item and strategic interaction.

There is also more variety than Conquest alone. Arena offers a faster 5v5 environment that emphasizes fighting and makes a good starting point for learning gods. Joust condenses the experience into 3v3 battles on a single lane, while Assault introduces randomized character selection for less predictable matches. Ranked Conquest exists for players seeking serious competition and progression. Having several modes is particularly valuable because not every session needs to become a lengthy tactical commitment. Players can choose between relatively straightforward action and the full strategic demands of a traditional MOBA match.

Aspects add another interesting dimension by allowing certain characters to alter aspects of their established playstyle. Combined with flexible builds and team compositions, they encourage experimentation instead of forcing every god into an entirely rigid role. This can create unexpected strategies and gives experienced players another system to explore. It also provides the developers with considerable room to expand the metagame as additional characters, balance adjustments, and gameplay systems arrive.

The Unreal Engine 5 reconstruction gives combat and presentation a noticeable modernization. Ability effects have greater visual impact, environments appear more contemporary, and character animations contribute to attacks feeling heavier and more physical. More importantly, rebuilding the game on modern technology provides a better foundation for future development. The project remains an evolving live-service title, however, so balance and content can change substantially through updates. That ongoing development is simultaneously exciting and one of its weaknesses, since players looking for a completely settled competitive experience may encounter systems that continue to be adjusted.

Cross-play and cross-progression are major advantages. Friends can play together across supported platforms, while progression can follow the player between them. Returning fans are also acknowledged through Divine Legacy rewards, including eligible cross-gen cosmetics, badges, and Legacy Gems after linking the appropriate account. It does not reproduce everything accumulated in the original game, but it creates some continuity for long-time players making the transition.

Steam Deck support is especially welcome. The game is currently rated Playable rather than fully Verified on Steam Deck. Core functionality works with the default controller configuration and appropriate controller icons are displayed, but some text can be difficult to read on the smaller screen and graphics settings may require manual adjustment for satisfactory performance. External controllers may also require manually changing the active controller. Despite those qualifications, having functional SteamOS support makes portable play a realistic option.

The free-to-play model makes experimentation easy because there is no initial purchase required to discover whether its particular mixture of MOBA strategy and action-oriented combat is appealing. Optional purchases and in-game transactions are naturally part of the package, and Easy Anti-Cheat is also used. The latter may be worth considering for players sensitive to kernel-level anti-cheat implementations. Online competition is fundamental to the experience, so its long-term appeal will inevitably depend on matchmaking quality, balancing, continued development, and maintaining an active community.

Overall, SMITE 2 succeeds because it preserves the series' strongest identity while giving its systems a more modern foundation. The direct third-person combat makes encounters energetic, mythology gives the roster tremendous personality, and the strategic systems offer considerable room for mastery. It still carries some roughness associated with an evolving competitive game, but its combination of accessibility, mechanical depth, varied modes, cross-platform functionality, and long-term potential makes it a compelling alternative to conventional MOBAs.

Okay, so SMITE 2 is and was intended to be a replacement to SMITE 1. Thinking of it like a remaster is somewhat appropriate. Now, I will say, when Hi Rez Studios was on top of the world with SMITE 1, they probably should have spent the money they ultimately wasted on other half baked titles on porting SMITE 1 to Unreal Engine and basically making that game into this game with all the DLC and stuff intact, but that's neither here nor there. I'd going to give my honest opinion from the hands on time I had with SMITE 2.

*** Most of the negative reviews I've seen are complaining about balance issues and having to rebuy things that were owned in SMITE 1. That sucks, and I get that. But due to poor choices that were made long ago, SMITE 2 exists and SMITE 1 is now abandoned. People don't argue that they should have everything for free in Call of Duty just because they bought the last game. Think of SMITE 2 as an actual sequel and that point is less upsetting and more fair from that point of view.

Also, I've seen some reviews saying they were playing with robots that looked like players and didn't realize it. From what I found, yes, you are grouped with AI when you first start playing the game; when you reach account level 5, you can go into classic game modes and start playing with real players. ***

* So, from a gameplay perspective, SMITE 2 starts off like a much more polished and user friendly version of SMITE 1. The store during matches asks you to make decisions to let it auto-buy stuff for you based on your play preferences. Abilities fire as soon as you hit the button. That second thing I absolutely hated, but found that I could turn it off in the settings and play SMITE 2 almost exactly like SMITE 1.

* There's a large roster of gods, but some of my favorites are still missing. There's enough to play with though and there's probably still enough that you'll find some that you enjoy.

* The original SMITE had a crazy amount of skins and most of them haven't been ported over. Most gods that I've seen only have their default skin, a shadow, and mastery skins. There doesn't even seem to be a regular recolor skin for the gods.

* Voice packs... I haven't spent a dime on SMITE 2 yet, and I have the voices for everyone I play. Thank goodness, they seem to have removed the need to buy the voice for the gods. Huge quality of life change there, not hearing default voices because other people didn't spend money.

* Performance/graphics... SMITE 2 is the best SMITE has ever looked. I've been playing SMITE 1 and SMITE 2 and alternating between them. SMITE 2 plays better and smoother. Also, I seem to play with the same handful of people match after match in SMITE 1 now, and I am grouped with unique people each match in SMITE 2.

* Legacy Gems... If you had a SMITE 1 account, they give you credit for all the gems you've ever spent in the form of 50% off coupons. You can spend 50% Legacy gems and the new gems to buy certain skins and stuff. This is less than ideal as a player, but they have to monetize something. I'm pretty sure SMITE 2 is being supported by whales right now, and they have to make it so you spend money on something or else there's no incoming cashflow for the studio. Founders Packs are nice for the studio and all, but that's not recurring income. Problem is, a lot of gods are lacking skins and there's nothing there to buy yet on the ones I enjoy playing.

TLDR: SMITE 2 is here and things within it cost money. The developers need to fund ongoing development now, with a studio that has pretty much discontinued every other game they make. SMITE 2 has good bones, gets regularly updated, and is just as fun as the original SMITE when you give it a chance. But yes, it is jarring to go from having almost everything to having nothing again.

Smite 1 was one of my favorite multiplayer games ever. As I first was a console gamer, Smite was the only MOBA that was available on the PS4, but I was drawn in by the numerous gods across different mythologies. I've spent over a thousand hours on the first game over several years and invested a lot of money (and obviously time) into that game. It was my go-to multiplayer game for years and once I switched to PC, I lost all of that progress because Hi-Rez and Sony apparently couldn't work out cross-platform progression; however, Xbox players and other console players got their cross-platform progression. Anyway, Smite 1 had a huge roster of gods and really fun cosmetics, including a variety of licensed crossovers later in its lifespan. It had a lot of life and personality and the core gameplay mechanics felt like they were improving almost every season and patch. 

In order to fill the void Smite 1 left when I switched over to PC, I linked my accounts and began playing Smite 2 once it became free to play. To compensate and reward players for their time and money spent in Smite 1, they offered the Divine Legacy program, which granted some new skins and legacy gems based on how much you had spent or earned in Smite 1. To be honest, a handful of skins and the legacy gems aren't exactly a great recompense, especially given how much less content is even available in Smite 2, and right now, the lack of content in comparison to Smite 1 is one of the most egregious issues to me. 

Obviously, switching from an older engine means that you need to recreate the new assets and porting everything over takes quite a bit of work, but it's so incredibly disappointing that many of my favorite gods have yet to appear in Smite 2. The main focus of Smite 2's development right now seems to be porting and adding over a lot of these gods, but this process takes a lot of time and considering that there are almost 40 gods that are not yet ported over and available in Smite 2, I don't think we'll even see the full roster ported until late 2027 or early 2028 given that these god ports seem to be bi-weekly. At this rate, Smite 2 will have been out for approximately 4-5 years by the time all of the gods are ported over and it also seems that they're not adding any new gods to Smite 2 until all of the older gods are ported. Instead, we're getting new items, which is okay, but items or reworks end up never being used or completely shift the meta until a nerf is pushed out. Regardless, Smite 2 has a significant loss of content from its predecessor and feels quite empty in comparison. I'm not even sure when some of my favorite gods, like King Arthur, Tyr, or Freya will be coming, but it sucks that many of the things I enjoyed playing or using simply are not available in this game as of yet. 

Smite 2 also feels lifeless and is in definite need of some polish. Even the patch notes themselves are simplified and have a lot less detail in comparison to many of the patch notes of Smite 1, but this extends to how information is presented in-game, too. Many times at God launch and even a while after, text contains typos, incorrect information, or completely missing information that would be useful to know. A passive might tell you that it offers attack speed but neglects to tell you what the increase actually is. Ravana's cooldowns did not reflect the accurate values when checking the ability during matches but instead seemed to show placeholder values. Some ability text or details might not even appear in certain circumstances either, so you'll be wondering what the hell the ability actually does until you play it in-game or in practice mode. Simple quality of life features and details are missing here and it's a huge step down from the first game. They're clearly rushing and pushing things through to get it out fast enough, but there is a sacrifice in quality as a result. I shouldn't have to look up the ability online or go into the practice mode (though that's not a bad idea to learn a God/test a build anyway) when the first game offered all of the information about the ability that I needed and even provided videos demonstrating the abilities. 

And then we have the gameplay, which has a few new additions in the game modes carried over and some updates, such as the Naga bosses and the new jungle camp early-game where the Fire Giant is located, but the biggest change is the God Aspects, which on paper sound great: they offer updates to the existing god's kit to create new ways to play them and in different roles, offering flexibility and diversity to their playstyles. However, quite a handful still lack aspects and some aspects are completely terrible or extremely boring, offering very little change to the god. I like the idea, but the fact that it doesn't seem some of the existing gods are receiving aspects any time soon is very disappointing. Build diversity is a lot larger thanks to the fact that some gods scale both intelligence and strength and there is no restriction on what items you can build, but many gods still don't receive benefit from this, so it feels pointless for many. 

I loved Smite 1 and I do enjoy playing Smite 2 at times -- it's Smite, and playing as a god from a pantheon of mythology is a very fun concept, but it is lacking so much of the content and life that Smite 1 has, and I'd recommend that you play Smite 1 instead of Smite 2; the only reason I play Smite 2 is that I get some sort of my progression from Smite 1 on PC since my data is forever stuck on PlayStation... thanks Sony.

I’ve been playing SMITE for many years. I started all the way back in the alpha days of the first game, and I’ve continued playing it ever since.

Over all those years, SMITE 1 received a huge number of updates, new gods, reworks, gameplay changes, events, and new content. At the same time, I built up a solid account of my own: countless hours played, many gods mastered, skins, and a collection that took years to build.

When SMITE 2 was announced, I was genuinely excited. We were finally going to get a new engine, better graphics, and a more modern technical foundation for the future of the game.

But in reality, SMITE 2 felt more like an almost complete wipe.

Most of the progress I had built in SMITE 1 was basically left behind. In return, I got Legacy Gems, which sound good on paper, but in practice they do very little to compensate for all the years invested in the first game.

In SMITE 2, you have to level your gods again, rebuild your progression again, and, most frustratingly, buy many of the same skins again that you already owned or paid for in SMITE 1.

The graphics are definitely better, and the new engine is noticeable, but the optimization still leaves a lot to be desired.

I’m also not convinced by the new item system.

The fact that gods are no longer as strictly limited between Magical and Physical builds and can build items much more freely may sound interesting in theory, but in many matches it ends up hurting role identity.

You can see gods that would normally be played as supports building almost full damage, or characters abusing strange scaling and unusual builds simply because the system allows it.

Build freedom is a good thing up to the point where almost any god can become almost anything.

For me, that makes matches feel less consistent and reduces the importance of traditional roles.

Another major problem is the reward system.

In SMITE 1, there were constantly events where you could earn currency, chests, or even skins without being forced to pay every single time. Toward the end of SMITE 1, we also had Battle Passes at a reasonable price, around €10, that gave you a lot of rewards and multiple skins, including some very good ones.

In SMITE 2, the whole system feels completely different.

Skins are more expensive, free rewards are much weaker, and one of the few consistent ways to earn Gems is simply by logging into the game every day.

There are also a few chests, but the chance of actually getting something you want from them is very small.

And this is where my biggest problem with SMITE 2 comes in:

At its core, the game is still SMITE.

It has better graphics, a new engine, and a few new mechanics, but I don’t feel like the differences are big enough to justify nearly resetting the progression of veteran players.

After years of playing SMITE 1, I expected SMITE 2 to make me feel like a long-time player moving into a new generation of the game.

Instead, it often makes me feel like a new player being asked to buy back what I already had.

And the current rewards are so limited that the game does not even realistically give you a good chance to earn a decent skin for the god you actually play the most.

SMITE 2 is not a bad game.

The problem is that, for someone who invested years into SMITE 1, it does not feel like an evolution.

It feels more like a restart.

I played A LOT of Smite 1 and now I have some decent hours played in Smite 2. Here's my honest review: 

I recommend this game because, despite all the bugs and issues that come with it, it still feels like something different from Smite 1, it's more fresh, the graphics and abilities feel more smooth. Now, I'm really no expert in technical terminology, but you can feel the difference from Smite 1. What I don't like is that, from my point of view, they ruined Conquest. I cannot really put a finger on why and how they ruined it, I just don't really enjoy playing Conquest in this game. I used to like Conquest in Smite 1 and mastered all the roles. In Smite 2 Conquest feels...more difficult without any reason, if that makes sense? It's not about the builds nor about the skills, I am not talking about the gameplay, I am strictly talking about the mechanics of it. It just feels off. And the map is unnecessarily big. I feel like squishy gods are squishier in Smite 2 and tanky gods are tankier. But hey, maybe it's just me. 

Also, I hate that they didn't make Duel Ranked yet. What's the point of having Duel if it's not competitive? That's basically the whole reason people play Duel, it's 1v1, it IS COMPETITIVE by design. So why not make it Ranked from the first place? I have 0 idea how to make a game and implement a ranking system, but could it be so hard that they postpone it until who knows when?

Finally, in case you're wondering why did I give a positive review to the game, it's because to me the good parts of it exceed the bad ones. I love that they added Strength and Intelligence scaling to the game. It became more diverse in that sense. I also like the gods Aspects, even if sometimes I feel like specific Aspects don't add anything new to the god's gameplay (The Morrigan Aspect for example). The graphics, as I said, feel smoother, the textures of god's skins feel pleasant to the eye, as well as the color palette of the maps. I love that they added the teleport function to Assault and they made Meditation default for everyone. And don't worry about the player base much, if I was to compare, it's not much more toxic than Smite 1 player base was. 

Overall I am looking forward to new updates & god additions and I am being hopeful that the game will improve in the future. Despite all the bugs and issues it has, I recommend you give it a try.

I´ve played a lot of hours in Smite 2, but the transition was a disaster. The devs basically said that Unreal Engine 3 was no longer maintainable, so they remade the entire game in Unreal Engine 5. Problem: The players had to leave behind the very very most of their skin and asset collections. I earned mine over years and greatly enjoyed them. They also found themselves with basically the same game with just three quarters of the content gone. So - bad deal.

Now after roughly 2-3 years, I wondered if that game still exists, saw it gets updates still and installed it. Looks solid so far. Massive graphical improvements, lobbies fill up fast, gameplay is the same and I can say: The cosmetics are very nice! However, here comes the bad stuff: They are still catching up on content. So you will basically still see old content reintroduced for years to come. 

What truly broke the deal for me was the pricing in the shop. Everything is so much worse.
- Old currency was turned into "Legacy Gems" for veterans. You can use them to pay 50% of the price of most of the lower-tier purchases. The good cosmetics (they call them Travelers and Sagas for some reason) you have to pay full price.
- The prices are completely outrageous! For a decent skin you are expected to fork over 10-20€! For a top-tier skin, it is 60€-80€! (In the latter case, you get more stuff, but you have to spend this much on their events to get these.) Effectively, they nickel and dime you as if you were King Midas himself!
- Where you would earn a good stream of free real-money currency in Smite 1 with daily logins, combined with events that allowed you to earn more for playing games, in Smite 2, you just get a measly trickle. You can get a few for grinding Gods up, but that does not really make a difference either. Combine that with the completely out-of-proportion pricing and you can grind and login until the cows come home before you can buy anything worthwhile.

It were these outrageous monetisation changes that basically ruined the game for me. I´m not in it for competition, I do like the casual experience while working on my wardrobe. Endgame is fashion. 

So yeah, not recommended unless you have a trust fund or other massive disposable income and never heard of long-term investing. (Or just care for the gameplay. Guess there´s still hardcore people up there in the non-casual modes to go up against.)

If you’re an old Smite 1 player coming to Smite 2 looking for nostalgia, you probably won’t find it here. The game does a lot of impressive things with its UI, gameplay, and graphics, but at its core, Smite 2 doesn’t hold a candle to its predecessor.

For players who spent countless hours on Smite 1, mastering Gods and collecting skins, the transition to Smite 2 feels like a disservice. We were promised that our Legacy Gems would be duplicated if we purchased the special edition. However, instead of having countless gems to spend on a wide selection of great skins, we were given a handful of Gods with barely any skins available.

That was a year ago. Upon returning to the game, I’m happy to see that the roster has expanded significantly. However, the skins still leave a lot to be desired. Smite 2 seems to prioritize silly, goofy, and colorful skins over designs that feel more godly, powerful, and awe-inspiring. Of course, this may not bother players who enjoy that style, but it’s disappointing for those who wish to feel empowered when playing as a god character.

What bothers me most is what has happened to Legacy Gems. I have over 300,000 of them, yet the few skins I actually want to purchase now require a new currency called Diamonds. The Legacy Gems I was led to believe would carry over and retain meaningful value are now of very limited use, while I’m being asked to spend even more real money to access the content I actually want.

After investing countless hours and supporting the game through its transition, this feels like a betrayal of the loyal player base that helped make Smite what it is today. Smite 2 has clearly made impressive technical and gameplay improvements, but for longtime Smite 1 players, it feels like much of what we valued was left behind.

A lot of people down leaving reviews are mad about skins. Most of them haven't played the game since leaving the review. I wanted to dispel a lot of these negative reviews!

Some people are still waiting for smite 2 to have more gods or their favourite god, or 'be better' or 'be more complete', but the fact of the matter is that the best time to start playing is right now. The meta shifts every 2 weeks, they add a new god AND a new aspect every 2 weeks too. Smite 2 is better than Smite 1 ever was and ever could have been, anyone saying it looks and plays like a mobile game is actually out of their mind. IDK what mobile games YOU guys are playing but they do not have this much combat, fluid action combat, or graphics like these.

Stop waiting. Download the game, try it for yourself. For new comes who have never touched smite I wanna leave you with a few details!

A new, fully developed god is added every 2 weeks. Most mobas you're lucky to get 3 or 4 a year. Ontop of that you get an aspect. Aspects are pretty wide range, some don't change a lot like Khepris aspect which changes his pull to a root in exchange for damage. Some change absolutely everything and are effectively a whole new god, like Kali aspect which takes her from a melee assassin to a hunter, or scyllas aspect which turn her from a crazy burst damage mage to a weird off-tank lategame hypercarry. I'm happy to say that the vast majority completely alter the way a character is played for the better. Want to play Xbalanque with a mage build? His aspects custom built for that, its not just a 'worse, bad' option like it was in smite 1.

Even if you get into smite 2 now and end up taking a break for whatever reason, you know that when you return there'll be a bunch of new items and new characters to play. Plus, anyone saying smite 2 is dead is also silly, smite has always been bigger on consoles and I'm popping ranked queues every 30 seconds even at like 3am. The games BUSY with hundreds of thousands of players every month.

All I or anyone can really ask you is to try the game, especially if you played like a year ago, because the game is genuinely completely different. I played the weekend flash tests, all of them, extensively, games infinitely better. It's a very hard, high skill game, but easy to get into too and I've personally onboarded quite a few newer players.

As for skins, they are adding like 4 every patch--way more if you count recolours of skins which are free on buying the skin. Smite 1 had 1000+ skins. They are adding the classic skins back as fast as humanly possible and you can still get them all for FREE using LEGACY GEMS, literally all you have to do is wait.

As a new player coming into **SMITE 2**, I know there are a lot of longtime players from the original SMITE who are frustrated with the game for numerous reasons, and honestly, I think they have every right to feel that way. I can understand why some of those players may look at SMITE 2 differently, especially after spending years playing the original.

That being said, coming into SMITE 2 as someone who never really played the original, I’ve actually been having a lot of fun with it. I think the game is genuinely enjoyable, and there’s something really satisfying about learning the gods, figuring out builds, improving at the mechanics, and slowly getting better. As a new player, I don’t have the same attachment to the original game, so I’m able to experience SMITE 2 for what it is rather than constantly comparing it to what came before.

Of course, that doesn’t mean I love everything about it. There are definitely moments where I’m having so much fun, followed immediately by a match that makes me want to chuck my controller across the damn room. 😂 Whether it’s getting absolutely destroyed, making a stupid mistake, or having one of those matches where everything seems to go wrong, SMITE 2 can definitely test my patience.

Overall, though, I’m enjoying the game. I think there’s a lot of potential here, and as a new player, I’m excited to keep learning and improving. I can respect the frustrations of longtime SMITE players while also saying that, from a newcomer’s perspective, SMITE 2 has been a pretty damn fun experience so far.

I have about 2000 hours on the original Smite 1 I think and I can say with confidence that this game is a big improvement from its predecessor. The gameplay and mechanics feel smooth (as smooth as they can on Unreal Slop 5) and the game balance generally feels like it's in a good place (for now). If you're looking to scratch that MOBA itch, especially with friends, I would recommend this game above all others in its genre. 
This game's hook being that you get to play as gods and mythological characters and throw hands on the battlefield is awesome, casting abilites and swinging around weapons in this game feels better then ever for Smite standards. The new gods this game has (like Aladdin and Mordred) that SMITE 1 didn't have are also a very welcome addition with very interesting kits that weren't present in SMITE 1. 
The dev team feels like they are trying their best to make a really great game with the manpower and resources they currently have, they have a show they run on their youtube channel called Titan Talk with multiple episodes a week answering questions from the community and showing off new additions to the game, it feels like Hi-Rez is trying it's best to be as honest and transparent with the community as they can and it feels like they genuinely care about this game and its players (Yes this is Hi-Rez I'm talking about here but I don't believe it's run by evil incompetent corporate overlords anymore, just some people keen to make a cool game)
HOWEVER it can feel a teeny bit hostile to newer players, the tutorials kinda suck, the community is unforgiving and downright hateful at times and for the love of god PLEASE GO INTO SETTINGS AND TURN OFF ACTION CAM AND TURN ON CLASSIC CAM. I do not know why this is forced on every new player, this is not Fortnite, your experience with this game will be far worse on action cam.

They are just skins, you don't need them to have fun and enjoy the game they are just differently coloured pixels in a video game at the end of the day. A friend convinced me to give Smite 2 a try, and after spending some time with it, I came away with a pretty clear conclusion: it just isn't for me.

It's important to say that I don't think it's a bad game. I personally prefer League of Legends in basically every area that matters to me, but I can also understand why someone else might feel the exact opposite.

- What I Didn't Like -

Smite 2's third-person perspective, visual style, god designs, movement, combat, and item system all feel less appealing to me than their equivalents in League. The game feels noticeably clunkier, and I never really got comfortable with how movement and combat flow.

The gods also didn't really click with me. Personally, I find League's champions more interesting both visually and mechanically, while Smite's roster simply doesn't appeal to me in the same way.

- The League Comparison -

For me, League of Legends wins in pretty much every category. I prefer its visuals, character designs, movement, camera perspective, gameplay feel, items, and overall polish.

But that's ultimately a matter of preference. Smite 2 isn't trying to be League of Legends with a worse camera. The third-person perspective alone changes how the game plays, how abilities are aimed, how you position yourself, and what kind of experience it offers.

- Final Thoughts -

I don't personally enjoy Smite 2, and playing it mostly made me want to go back to League of Legends. If you're asking me which game I would rather play, it's League without hesitation.

However, after giving Smite 2 a fair try, I don't think it's fair to call it a bad game simply because it doesn't suit my preferences. It has a different perspective, different gameplay, and a style that clearly appeals to people, including friends of mine who genuinely enjoy it.

So while I probably won't be playing much more of Smite 2, I can still recommend it to people who enjoy third-person MOBAs or want something different from the League top-down formula.

Had around 6k hours in Smite across PC and console and played across the entire lifetime of the game. Came to Smite 2 with the promise that a new engine that could expand the possibilities of what Smite could be. Despite losing all the progression and cosmetics I had accumulated playing the game for 10+ years I hoped that Smite 2 could fill the comfortable, familiar gameplay feel that Smite always did. I could not have been more wrong.

  For starters, I could overlook the entire basis of this game's creation being a cash grab if they executed a single aspect of the game's core gameplay in a remotely competent fashion. Between increased engine responsiveness, faster and less readable animations, and larger ability targeters, it feels like most of the player agency gained from good movement has been removed and  most abilities feel nearly impossible to miss. With the removal of the SPL and dwindling player population, the entire competitive aspect of the game is gone and with it, the interest of high-skill players and those just looking to improve. Balance is an absolute nightmare. One week you'll draft triple ADC every game; the next you'll be playing mages in every role; two weeks later, all 10 gods will be building hybrid tank items. Healing is still broken because they arbitrarily decided to cap anti-heal items. The map layout gives the jungler single-player-level agency over the outcome of the game in the first 20mins. New god +1s and aspects are either useless or completely subvert the original design of the god by removing an element of weakness in their kit or simply make their overall gameplay pattern more toxic. Low player populations bring on low quality games the vast majority of the time, especially at the higher ranks, but even in unranked and casual game modes. Bugs are rampant and frustrating. Server quality is horrendous. Desync is ubiquitous. I could continue but I feel I've established why this game is a waste of time and energy from everyone involved and a waste of space on your hard drive.

  As a word of warning to anyone who is considering picking up the game or coming back after a long break and decides to watch some content surrounding Smite 2. The content creators for this game are so occupied with justifying their own dying careers that you will hear things like "Smite 2 is way better than Smite 1" or "We don't need the Smite 1 gods, every new aspect IS a new god". I hope that reading this review will save you the trouble of having to decipher these lies yourself or suffer through the torture that is playing a single match of this poor excuse for a sequel.

Causes of the Reputational Collapse and Prospects for Survival

The story of the transition from Smite 1 to Smite 2 is one of the most striking examples of a management and reputational crisis in the game service industry. The reasons why the studio alienated its most loyal audience are complex and systemic in nature.

The main factors that eroded user trust were:

__ Long-term diversion of resources from the core asset: The systematic redirection of profits from Smite 1 to fund unsuccessful third-party experimental games, rather than the timely and systematic updating of the main game’s technological foundation.

__ A distorted value proposition and inflation: The transformation of the compensation promise into the Legacy Gems discount system, which required mandatory new monetary injections, along with the revocation of the “Ultimate God Pack” lifetime status and the increase in nominal prices for cosmetics.

__ Premature monetization of an unfinished product: Launching the product in an early alpha state with critical flaws in battle readability, a degraded UI, an incomplete roster, and a lack of basic presentation features under the Founder’s Pack paid model.

__ Dismantling of community infrastructure: Cancellation of the SPL esports league, irrational spending on one-off tournaments, and disregard for the interests of content creators, leading to the loss of an organic marketing resource.

At this stage, the survival of Smite 2 and the very existence of Hi-Rez Studios depend on the remaining development team’s ability to radically rethink its monetization policy, accelerate the pace of character transfers, restore the classic “feel of the game,” revamp the user interface, and establish a direct, transparent dialogue with the remaining community. Without correcting these ethical and game design mistakes, the project risks remaining a niche title, unable to recoup its development costs or restore the franchise to its former industry status.

I'm a long time player of smite.  I played on both PC and console for many years, long before smite 2 was a whisper.  I ultimately made the switch to league of legends because at the time, league just had so many more features, even if the graphics were not as good.  With AD and AP scaling items there were more ways to build champions.  Last hitting minions added a level of skill, and more importantly required you to decide between losing life, or losing gold.  The bushes made danger lurk everywhere, or taught me to fire skill shots into them, draining mana to protect myself.  ---  I have since come back to smite 2, and have seen the changes.  I can now say, without a doubt that I consider smite 2 to be the superior game by far.  It has all of the things I just listed that smite 1 was missing, but they now have three really big selling points that league does not have.  1.) The game is just beautiful and alot more interesting to watch.  2.)  Body blocking is only a thing in league with skill shots.  In smite, you can block auto attacks making duo lane interactions way more interesting and skill intensive.  (As well as skirmishes in mid lane)  3.) The ways to win the game are alot more varied at a competitive level.  To elaborate, in league, there's generally 2 styles:  Team fight comps, and split push comps.  It dictates what objectives are more important.  In smite 2, because they have objectives that spawn "lane pushing" minions, you can choose to prioritize those objectives, and win through tempo alone.  Allowing champions that have high early game pressure, but fall off late game, a legitimate path to winning before the late game carries come online.   ----   I am genuinely shocked, and impressed at how far smite 2 has come.  So much so I felt compelled to write this review as a direct comparison.

Smite 1 was a truly great game, which makes the transition to Smite 2 one of the worst decisions and executions in gaming history. Instead of building upon what made the original fantastic, this sequel feels like a massive step backward in almost every single department.
Here is why this game is currently a total disaster:

·	Terrible UI & Missing Features: If a player abandons the match (which happens constantly), their stats completely vanish from the scoreboard. You can’t even see what they did, and the system makes it nearly impossible to actually report these toxic players. How is the basic matchmaking and reporting system worse than a 10-year-old game?

·	The Ultimate Skin Scam: All the skins, cosmetics, and progression you accumulated or paid for over a decade in Smite 1? Gone. You have to start from scratch, which feels like a massive slap in the face to the loyal community.

·	"Next-Gen" Graphics? Think Again: The biggest selling point for Smite 2 was the jump to Unreal Engine 5. But honestly? The game somehow looks worse and less optimized than the original. The art style has lost its charm, and the visual clarity is a absolute mess.

·	A Cash Grab Kept on Life Support: It is a genuine miracle that this game still has the budget to keep its servers running, considering how much the player base dislikes these changes. But then again, I highly suspect Tencent’s deep pockets are the only reason this game hasn't completely collapsed yet.
Save your time, your sanity, and your money. Stick to the memory of Smite 1, because Smite 2 is a soulless downgrade.

Long ass review incoming. This is a new player's perspective, giving the game a shot for about 8+ months with frustrated pauses in between.

It could've been one of the best MOBAs, but it's one of the worst I ever played. I played thousands of hours of MOBAs but somehow SMITE 2 managed to fudge up so many things because this seems so much worse than others.

1. This doesn't affect me directly, but it made me distrust them a lot. All players from Smite (1) lost everything they bought there. Smite (1) is dying slowly, and if you want to migrate to Smite 2, you will lose everything. Skins, emotes, ... and they didn't transfer skins of the heroes available on both Smites. People supported the game, the company, had a community, and they just could not care enough to find a better solution than they did. That's pretty unacceptable, and to me this just leads to never forming some kind of support relationship with a company making these kinds of decisions.

2. Toxicity is SO bad. I've played LoL, HoK, MBLL, WR, and many more, and I've not experienced this amount of toxicity in all of the others combined. I met more hostility and toxicity in Smite 2 than ever before. And what is up with the game quitters? That's something I never experienced like that. Seriously, almost every game has at least one person quitting early game. And I don't mean worst-case-scenario games - normal games. Not every early game is perfect, so how do people quit so often if they die once or twice? And there are just pretty much zero consequences to enforce different behaviour. That's truly just so bad. Same goes for insulting and berating, nothing happens 90%+ of the time. Doesn't matter how often I report people and how bad it gets. People saying the n-word and other insulting things? Feels like they couldn't care less.

Additionally to that, as a console player on Steam Deck, I can't mute people in game. So I have to endure it, which just makes me dislike this game so much more. Because there now is a huge negative bubble around playing it, with no way to escape their toxicity. Playing Smite 2 means being berated. Even if I perform more than decently and we win.

3. How can a game be SO not newbie-friendly? There are soooo many heroes, and as much as I love variety, how the hell am I going to keep up if there are so many of them and they're also adding so many more all the time, as well as changing items? That's just impossible. I played about 150 hours, and I still feel like I don't know 90% of their heroes. People say newbies should play Assault, but playing modes like Assault does not help at all, because there's just no time to get a real feeling for the hero I play, and especially not for all the random heroes other people play. Even though I really tried and practiced, used AI modes, watched guides, made Reddit posts, used OG Discord builds, asked the DC community and support, it barely got better. There are so, so many veterans, and they stomp new players like me. Even if I have a ton of MOBA experience and play in high ranks in other MOBAs, it feels like my experience is worth nothing in Smite. I feel like an ant beneath a horde of giants when I play Smite. Even after I put in so, so much work and practice. And I mean maxing out the skill tree kind of practice, additionally to the other factors (YT guides, Reddit, DC, ...).

4. The matchmaking feels like it gets worse and worse. The matchups feel like they are more imbalanced than before. It already was pretty bad as a new player, but it feels so much worse. The majority feels far away from anything balanced because there are so many hardcore veterans. And as much as I hate bot matches in other MOBAs and absolutely despise EOMM, this is just not working either, whatever they are doing.

5. Small things can go so far - just add fitting community builds to every mode. So many MOBAs have the option while forming a team and picking heroes, even in matches, to pick a full build fitting for this specific hero from multiple options used by the top players in the community. All of them have their win percentage as well as how often they have been used and also basic categories like Poke, so you can just try good builds even though you're new. This would do SO much. The basic builds can be okay. But when a game is as unbalanced as this one, okay is not enough, and this seems like a small thing to change for the better. There are so many great builds on their DC channel, but in game, there are barely any recent community builds and no option to choose recent community ones in game. This makes everything so much worse and inaccessible.

6. Why does it feel like nobody knows about Smite? As mentioned, I hate EOMM so much that I've been looking for alternative MOBAs for years. I asked in multiple huge subreddits, used LLMs, and so on, and none of them ever mentioned Smite. After a pretty desperate day of searching and asking all the LLMs I could, one of them finally mentioned Smite. That's pretty bad. After over a year of actively looking for alternatives in big MOBA communities without a single person mentioning Smite, something must be going really wrong with their advertising.

7. Last but not least, I was really disappointed in their support. At the beginning, I unknowingly played against AI because there was no indicator that Quick Mode was AI. I enjoyed it and bought their most expensive option to unlock all heroes forever. I wanted to support this game and company because diving into the full complexity of companies like Tencent, playing Smite 2, and hearing their podcasts was just really refreshing. It felt more honest, more real. Like the people behind the game really cared about this game and community - and as much as this might be true for at least a couple of them, this feeling changed a lot. When I contacted them and addressed several issues I mentioned here, like players not being able to mute on Steam Deck and the toxicity being so incredibly bad without real consequences, I just got a generic response to post it on their Discord channel. And it might seem small, but combined with everything else, this was the point where I pretty much lost interest in playing and supporting their games immediately. Like, what do you mean you have enough time to read and answer my mail, you don't enforce any real punishments and are solely responsible for the state of the game, but I have to publicly post about those topics on a huge Discord server? So any constructive criticism cannot be processed when I send it by mail, and people have to make a Discord account, join the server, and publicly post it? That just seems like avoiding any responsibility for taking care of these matters, and so wrong. I'm not asking for a favor, I'm trying to give feedback about the things going wrong. Affecting their community and players.

I have played Smite since 2012, and Smite 2 does not feel like the natural evolution of the game I supported for over a decade. It feels like a worse, less focused version of Smite that has lost sight of what made the original game special.

Smite was at its best when it was about gods, strategy, team fights, unique kits, and the feel of mythological characters clashing in a third-person MOBA. Smite 2 currently does not capture that same identity. The gameplay feels less polished, the direction feels unclear, and the game does not feel like a meaningful improvement over the original.

The company behind the game has repeatedly failed to deliver on promises to improve the overall experience. Bugs, balance problems, and unfinished systems continue to be an issue, while the game keeps being filled with lazy cosmetic bloat. The constant fan-service skins, repetitive prism skins, and reworked imported skins make the game feel cheap and unfocused. Instead of building a better game, it feels like the priority is pushing out cosmetics that add nothing meaningful.

The worst part is that Smite 2 does not feel like it respects longtime Smite players. After years of supporting the original game, this sequel feels disconnected from the game many of us actually loved. It is not just “different.” It is worse in the areas that matter most: identity, polish, gameplay feel, and trust in the developer.
