I would like to warn that I am not a moba genre enjoyer or a SMITE 1 player, my only experience in that game was booting the tutorial and enjoying how Medusa was animated back in 2020 so I can't judge on the character roster, the changes made to them after porting or item balacing. I have some fun playing busted or silly builds on bird characters, however, in the 410 hours I've played since last year this game had caused, unfortunately, mostly negative emotions hence my 5th and final uninstallation. So, what are my personal problems aside low enjoyement of moba games as genre? 
1) The powercreep kicked in heavy just after 1 year in open beta. Newer characters are very overtuned so there is little reason to pick from older roster if you have recently added gods with shinier stats. Can't imagine how this will go in the future if the game survives past 2028.
2) I don't know how the gamedev works but I don't see why UE 5 was needed to make this. The game does not have a lot of areas where the golden features of this version of the engine are applied, for example a lot of gods wear clothes that have no dynamic physics simulation, there is no visual interactivity with the environment aside objects like towers or camps. I could not run high lighting settings without drastically losing fps down to 15-ish, so I can not comment on the use of nanite or lumen tech.
3) Bugs, bugs, bugs. Being a Paladins veteran since late 2016, I thought I could adjust to another Hi-Rez early access project, knowing the development for this took priority and lead to the end of active development or support for other games aside SMITE. Writing this as of OB 37, the state is not something I would expect from a priority project, early access or not: the UI for god list occasionally breaks and I can't see 80% of characters, full year after it's first appearance I still get no audio (except VGS and music strings) bug, I get randomly disconnected in the middle of a match and the games sometimes just stop and I see the main menu page, or the newest addition which made me lose some hair on my head and re-assess my attachment to online service games. For some reason, upon loading into the map and after approximately 2 seconds of seeing the blank item shop page, I get thrown into the main menu as if I'd logged out and in, after rejoining the match the same thing happens in an endless loop.
I get that the project is ongoing and every patch there will be new errors to fix but with the studio proritizing this, I think it's reasonable to expect a bit more than this. "Well just restart and the bug will go away" does not fix the time lost, especially considering how the game implemented a "Are you sure you want to exit?" screen some patches ago which requires you to wait at least 10 seconds to quit. In a competitive game this wait time ruins the mood and possibly the win if your teammates don't pause. 
I am glad that there is at least one project that Hi-Rez wants to develop, the creatives working there have stellar ideas that I wish they get to make reality. SMITE 2 has a hard-working team of developers trying to make the game better but, tragically, at the moment I just can't see for what exacty the work on other projects was frozen.

In its current state, I simply cannot recommend spending your time or money on AION 2.

When I first started playing, I genuinely thought the game was fantastic. It was an incredibly enjoyable experience, and starting out with an established group of friends certainly helped. I was fortunate enough to avoid much of the gatekeeping that seems to have become such a significant issue within the community. Unfortunately, that eventually caught up with me, to the point where I felt I had no choice but to create an entirely new character as a Cleric just to be accepted into groups and actually experience the game.

But honestly, that isn't even the biggest problem.

The lack of meaningful communication from the developers, the absence of a clear roadmap, and the overwhelming presence of bots and RMT have created an experience that is becoming increasingly difficult to justify. It has gotten so bad that legitimate players who were interested in giving the game a chance couldn't even create characters because servers were consistently full.

That's an incredibly disappointing state of affairs for a game that initially showed so much promise.

There is a good game buried somewhere underneath all of these problems, but the current state of things makes it very difficult to overlook the issues or recommend that anyone invest their time and money into it.

Until the developers demonstrate that they are willing to address these problems, communicate with their player base, and respect the time and experience of legitimate players, I would strongly encourage people to look elsewhere.

There are plenty of other games out there that deserve your time. Unfortunately, in its current state, AION 2 isn't one of them.

I've been seeing a lot of mixed reviews on this game since launch to the time I am writing this review, positive and negatives,  so I would like to give my opinion on this game and would keep it as short as I can.

for context, before I start, I have 330 Hours total (probably -50 hours for the amount of time afking). Was free to play from launch till 10th of November which I had bought my first sub. not super accurate but am currently GS 2800, 180K CS, No Alts.

In hindsight, this game does have its positives and negatives, which from my experience of playing this game a lot the past month and a half, I would list below:

Pros:
-Fun storyline
-Amazing Graphics
-Its Free to Play
-Alot of content, and more to come from what it seems

Negatives:
-Pay to win is present
-Botting and RMT (Real Money Trading) is present, whilst my server has eradicated alot of them, it is still present
-Gatekeeping on Expeditions is an issue and is annoying
-A lot of content does feel more Solo, then being able to be played with friends, such as Story quests

Now I know I can list much more negatives as what other reviews does, but I would like to say a few things. Firstly when it comes to repetitive gameplay. It is obviously present, however it is a MMORPG, no matter what MMORPG you play, there will always be repetitive gameplay where a lot of grinding is required, and all the complaints on Pay to win is valid.

However I would like to ask you something, are you playing for fun or to speedrun your character to its max in a month? I see many bad reviews complaining on how the endgame is lacking content or lackluster, rolling items is tedious, PvP is a hassle ect. While I do think these are valid points, at the same time I personally feel like so much of these reviewers arent actually trying to enjoy the game, but instead just speedrunning to the furthest part of endgame, min maxing everything and complaining about not being able to get a specific stat for their gear such as "Combat Speed" and then proceeds to say this game is terrible.

Dont get me wrong, I do think many points are valid, there is a lot of RNG to this game. however I do think you aren't actually enjoying the game and instead just racing a pointless and non existent race. 

So for new players who want to try the game and give it a shot. Try it, and dont rush it, enjoy the process, go explore the world, do content ect, and have fun. You have a gazillion things to do in this game, which may be repetitive but in my opinion its fun, and I do not think you would hate this game unless your sole purpose is to be top 1 in PVP as a free to play player, or if you are FOMO and trying to clear every single piece of content as fast as possible.

For current players who is thinking about what to do, whether to stay in this game or not. I hope my words may help. Just relax and enjoy the game, I get the game may feel repetitive, hard and RNG may not be on your side, but we aren't in a race, no one is asking you to be at a certain level at a certain time. Just play at your pace, enjoy and stop overthinking on "if I dont get Combat Speed, I will be the worse player". Min Maxing is a choice, not a requirement.

In the end, its a game, not a marathon. Enjoy the process, have fun, grind, and stop trying to race on who's level is higher. If you cant access a specific dungeon (especially Ludra, which is the latest dungeon as I speak right now), then its okay. This is a game where PvE exists. Whether you are playing with friends or solo, this is not a competitive E-Sports game (unless you are tryharding on being top 1 in every PvP leaderboard, then you do you I guess).

In conclusion, I do really think this is a great game, it has its flaws ofcourse, but for a free to play game, it really has a lot to offer, and if you are a new player, come give it a shot. Its free, you have nothing to lose (maybe some mental health issues when you dont get a specific weapon after 30 expedition runs tho lol), and as long as you arent trying to compete your progression 24/7 with everyone else ESPECIALLY P2W players or Whales. You WILL have fun in this game. You arent required to spend any money on this game. It is a choice. It only becomes a requirement the second you start racing on your progression against the top players and trying to min max everything when this game has only been out for a month.

Just enjoy the ride guys, you will have fun. It stops being fun the second you compare yourself to others and try to reach the top as fast as possible. Not everything is meant to be done fast. Take your time, relax, play and have fun. No one is asking you to beat the hardest contents, min max everything, and be the best player in every single leaderboard. Especially not on a timeframe

For a casual player, AION 2 is a pretty good game.

You may have noticed in the comments that many players feel like the game is heavily focused on solo gameplay and that it's difficult to actually play with friends. This is mostly true, but nothing stops you from running dungeons and doing other activities with your friends. In fact, playing with friends becomes much more beneficial in the later stages of the game.

Most solo-friendly content is usually part of the early endgame. When it comes to more challenging late-game content, such as Hard Mode dungeons, playing with friends can save you a lot of time and make things much easier.

However, if you're a hardcore player who wants to push the hardest content and stay competitive, this game might not be for you. You will eventually run into paywalls.

For casual players, though, it's a decent experience. You can come home from work, run a few dungeons, play some arenas, do whatever you enjoy, and log off. Just don't expect to keep up with players who spend all day grinding.

About bot problems: I personally haven't experienced any of these issues. The reason is that I deliberately chose a low-population server.

Most players tend to stack up on high-population servers because they want access to all three corridors in the Abyss. As a result, bots also seem to favor these highly populated servers.

By choosing a low-population server, you may avoid most of the bot-related problems. However, there is a trade-off: you will usually have zero or just one corridor available in the Abyss. The downside is that the opposing server can have five or even ten times as many players as yours, putting you at a significant disadvantage when competing in the Abyss.

Other than that, low-population servers have some nice advantages. You can comfortably grind for crafting materials and collect hidden cubes without constantly competing with other players. There are plenty of resources around, and nobody seems to be rushing to loot everything. If you don't mind having fewer Abyss corridors available, playing on a low-population server can actually be a much more relaxing experience.

The visuals are also fantastic. However, you might not fully enjoy the cosmetic aspect of the game because shop skins are quite expensive.

There are also some questionable systems, such as RNG-based crafting, that have frustrated players and even made some of them quit. On the positive side, the developers seem to listen to community feedback, often through content creators, and take action when necessary.

At the end of the day, you'll encounter many of the same problems you see in other MMOs, whether it's P2W mechanics or getting completely destroyed by people who have much more time to invest in the game.

I really wanted Aion 2 to be a good game. I gave it my time, patience, and a genuine chance. Yet after 2 months, logging in started to feel like an obligation rather than something I looked forward to. That is probably my biggest disappointment.

Aion 2 is a bottomless pit of both time and money. Paying players can accelerate their progression by months, while free-to-play players are left with endless grinding and little to compensate for that gap. The game has far too many progression systems, most built around repeating the same activities. Every day brings another overwhelming checklist, often requiring hours of work before you can even think about enjoying group content. Eventually, you stop asking what you want to do and start worrying about what you cannot afford to skip.

For a dungeon-focused MMO, Aion 2 does an astonishingly poor job of bringing people together. The UI feels like an unfinished mobile or console interface. Messaging players, finding people, managing parties, and coordinating groups are unnecessarily difficult. Discord and TeamSpeak feel essential because the in-game communication tools are so inadequate. Dungeons are poorly explained, navigation is confusing, and the minimaps are almost useless. The game demands teamwork while making basic cooperation frustrating.

Its energy systems, currencies, and countless reward chests also make progression needlessly complicated. Players who do not immediately understand which resources and activities are worth prioritizing can lose significant progress. RNG makes matters worse: one person gets the equipment they need in a single run, while another needs 60. Crafting suffers from the same problem. Random rewards can be exciting, but here they too often make your time feel wasted.

After reaching max level, progression becomes painfully monotonous. You repeat the same dungeon dozens of times on Easy to unlock Normal, then dozens more on Normal, only for an update to send you back on Hard for another piece of equipment. And that is only part of the routine: 14 Nightmare Dungeon runs per week on every character; 3 Ascension Trials per character weekly; 5 Daily Commissions every day; 4–5 Shugo Festivals; around 20 Commission Scroll quests weekly; 7 Dimensional Invasions per week; and 3 Abyssal Corridor runs per character every four days. Add guild content, PvP, and regular dungeons, and the workload becomes absurd. The issue is not a lack of content. It is that so much of it feels exactly the same. For F2P players, skipping it means falling further behind.

Finding a party can take hours. Combat Power requirements create extreme gatekeeping: you need better gear to enter a dungeon, but need that dungeon to obtain the gear. People can also leave halfway through a run with seemingly no meaningful consequences. Even when a group finally forms, combat often feels more dependent on luck than skill. You can understand a boss perfectly and still get secondary aggro, several overlapping AoEs, and another attack immediately afterward. At that point, the strategy becomes spamming dodge and hoping you survive. The same encounter can be effortless one run and a disaster the next.

Server performance makes this even worse. A game built around perfect dodges and precise reactions should not have ping jumping from 18 ms to several thousand. It is especially frustrating when you already pay for a subscription and may need a VPN just to get a more stable experience.

I do not mind grinding, challenging dungeons, or working for rewards. I just want my time to feel respected. I want progression to be meaningful, combat to reward skill, and group content to encourage cooperation. Instead, Aion 2 seems more interested in keeping players constantly busy than giving them reasons to enjoy playing. I do not want this game to fail. I genuinely want it to improve. But right now, it asks for far too much while giving too little enjoyment in return.

[h2]What I do *like* about Aion 2[/h2]

It's fun! Or it CAN be fun! The game doesn't take itself too seriously. It's not trying to be WoW. It puts its own spin on the familiar DPS/Heal/Tank/Support formula. If you played Aion 1, you will LOVE the nostalgia trip here. Gliding is a perfect replica of how it worked in Aion 1. Aion 2 lets you fly in most places (Aion 1 just allowed gliding mostly). It has Shugo, nyerk! And Shulack, kru! When the title screen first starts and the music hits, the nostalia begins.

It's a pretty game. A lot of the small details are really nice -- props, clutter objects, vegetation. Stop and take a look around you! And the soundtrack is phenominal, adding new music and importing some bangers from Aion 1. The dungeons aren't [i]terrible[/i] and they're difficult enough that you feel like you're improving as you progress. 

As an RPer from ESO, I say the cosmetics system is decent. Leaves things to be desired, but it's aight. It's too expensive though.

Handed to a better steward, this game could grow into something epic and long-lived.

[h2]What I dislike about Aion 2[/h2]

Bigger things:

* The game rewards being fast not being good. DPS > All mechanics. The playerbase is ofc sweaty and gatekeepy about this.
* It's an MMO with no "multiplayer" except abyss PvP and dungeons??? Everything else is either single player or has you compete with other players. There's just nothing to DO with other people.
* Excessive RNG #1: A boss spawns every 12 hours and might drop armor 25% of the time, and it might be a chest piece 10% of the time, and if you decide to disenchant it for the cosmetic skin, it's 10% success. A mere 400 attempts, on average.
* Excessive RNG #2: Most RNG has no pity. Runs of bad luck just suck the life out of fundamental things, like crafting potions for yourself, or filling out your wardrobe with cosmetics.
* Excessive RNG #3: When you craft there's a 25% chance it procs to a better item. Makes it kind of hard to know how many materials you bring. And if you don't want the proc item, too bad.
* Excessive RNG #4: When crafting does proc it's not just a free upgrade, you have to succeed a second time, which can fail, destroying all the ingredients and the item that you already succesfully made. You get nothing for your success. What.
* Sexual Dimorphism: Don't get me wrong, I play a female character for the plot, and male characters in this game can look hot too. But it's a bit... you know? Everyone's super idealised, it's one of those games, which is... eh. But female characters only have high heel shoe/boot options. Like, battle high-heels? C'mon.

Small things:

* There are no Kircas in Aion 2. I am sure this is a mistake the developer will rectify in time.
* There's only one zone per faction, one main mat per craft (ore, wood), one significant questline, only really one enemy NPC faction. Feels like a proof of concept of MMO systems: works, now build the rest of the game?
* The map and worldbuilding suck. It's a series of unrelated locations where a quest takes place then they're just discarded. These are linked by open fields of NPCs that are just standing around, waiting for a player to farm them. It's... weird. No location feels like it could justify why it's there. It's like something an AI would dream up; all of what you asked for but not at all creative.
* Quests #1: So much back and forth. Did you do <thing> at <place>? OK now go back to <same place> and do <next thing>.
* Quests #2: Pointless scene changes. "Let's put the <thing> in the temple." (go in to temple, place thing on altar) "Ok, let's talk about this outside." (go outside) "Great, now we need to go to the village, let's talk there." CAN WE NOT JUST TALK HERE?
* Quests #3: The main questline is the same quest repeated: Head to <place> to do <thing>. But first do <this>. Then do <that>. Repeat for 45 levels.
* Dialog, writing and performance are over performative like children's content? Like "Oh *no* it's the big bad guy, I sure hope he doesn't *do really bad stuff*. LOOK OUT he *is* doing really bad stuff aghast face".
* Cutscenes: Terrible. All recorded at what feels like 10 FPS, with the camera stuck at 100000x zoom and held by someone with instructions to "never hold it still and get as many butt shots as you can."

You rush through the main story to level 45 repeating the same kill a bunch of mobs, click a bunch of items and talk to a bunch of npcs ad absurdum. And once you reach 45 you think finally the real game starts. You couldn't be more wrong. Because before you get on the regular grind treadmill, you are now forced to complete all the side quests and mini dungeons on the map that you've missed while doing the main mission.

Bots in the game are rampant. While I could live with that on the over world, it became extremely frustrating in the dungeons. You are effectively soft locked at around level 38 from progressing in the story because the bots are unable to dodge the boss mechanics, running into the fire wall and dying. Have fun repeating the same dungeons hundreds of times to play with the rng system to raise some arbitrary gearscore number. And remember, you can't even do all the content unless that gearscore number is high enough. I personally like grinding in games, but Aion 2 manages to take all the joy out of it. **1,030+ hours played. Almost €300 spent. Would I recommend AION 2? Unfortunately, no. 💀**

Let me start by saying that AION 2 is genuinely a good game. I love the gameplay, the world, the combat, and the overall experience. I've spent over 1,000 hours playing it since launch, so clearly I enjoy it.

However, the way NCSoft handles paid cosmetics and customer support has completely ruined my experience.

I originally wanted to collect every limited-time wing skin in the game. After an official announcement stated that cosmetics would be shared across character slots, I purchased two limited-time wing skins on my alternate characters, believing they would also be available on my main.

Turns out, they were character-bound.

Here's the confusing part: other cosmetics, including Battle Pass skins and Single Skins, are labeled "(Bound)" and can still be accessed across characters. Paid cosmetic wings use the exact same "(Bound)" terminology, yet they're restricted to individual characters.

These are purely cosmetic wings. They don't provide additional stats like normal obtainable wings.

I contacted NCSoft support, explained everything, and provided screenshots. Several representatives acknowledged that the announcement and item descriptions caused confusion.

Their solution?

**Nothing.**

No transfer. No replacement. No manual reissue.

After nearly two weeks of contacting support and being passed between numerous representatives, I eventually requested refunds for my purchases, including my Founder's Pack.

Rejected because the items were already claimed.

I even contacted Steam Support and provided extensive evidence. Still rejected.

The funniest part is that I never wanted a refund in the first place. I JUST WANTED MY WINGS ON MY MAIN CHARACTER. 😭

Now I've spent almost €300, missed limited-time cosmetics I wanted to collect, and completely lost confidence in purchasing anything else.

**Gameplay: 9/10**

**Monetization: 2/10**

**Customer Support: Final boss with no rewards. 💀**

AION 2 is a great game, but I cannot recommend spending money on it until NCSoft improves how cosmetic restrictions are communicated and how purchase disputes are handled.

**1,030 hours played. €300 spent. 10+ support agents encountered. 0 wings recovered.**

Thanks, NCSoft. 🪽💀

[h1] It's free, so try it; but don't get your hopes up! [/h1]

Like many of the negative reviews already say - yes, it does become a fairly p2w / paywalled game once you start to get into the nitty-gritty of it all, but that doesn't mean you should write it off completely.
It can be played on a fairly low/medium spec PC which helps with a wider reach. 

[h2] The Positives [/h2]
I will begin with the positives because a lot of the negatives are already covered by thousands of other reviews.
Decent artistic style, decent character creation, fairly simple combat system and generally feels..."easy to play".
The mount system is quite interesting; in that you could farm pretty much [b] any wild mob [/b] that you want to ride. They're accessible very early in the game and generally make the game enjoyable.
The "auto-run" feature is very handy, albeit the pathfinding sometimes is very strange.
There's plenty of classes to choose from and the overall feel of the game is quite decent, smooth and polished.
You can unlock [b] most [/b] items and game content without having to pay, albeit you're going to be probably grinding a fair bit more than the others.
Resources are abundant and respawn fairly frequently. You can gather all resources so it removes that alt requirement that specialises on one type of resource, and the game has a way of you practically "transforming" [i] odyle [/i] into other materials which is helpful.

An overall, very decently executed game

[h2] The negatives [/h2]
I won't beat this to death by repeating what all other negative reviews already outline - it is a free MMO, and the p2w aspect is obscenely evident.
What turned me off the game is not even p2w related.
1) Making crafting of [b] basic [/b] materials being locked behind farming mobs, whose drop rates for those materials are about 2% or less is just disgusting. For context: you could kill 100 wolves, and get 2 hides.
2) I can understand making the "Market" (Auction House) locked to sell only for subscribers, but blocking purchases of items even for non-pay players is insane - [b] especially since there is [u] no trading [/u] between players whatsoever [/b]. 
3) The amount of "overall content" is quite limited. You can practically get through the main story and a few side quests in I'd say probably 7h max which will get you to "max" level (lv45) and unlock the rest of the game. Once you get through these, there are about 5/6 different "dungeons" (expeditions), and 3/4 variants of the same, plus some additional other higher level dungeons that you need to grind an insane amount to get the gear to qualify for it.
So once you get up to speed on the basics of having gotten to Lv.45, completed all the single-player "caves" which give you skillpoints, and maybe farmed 1/2 dungeons solo for some gear; you enter a repetitive circular grind.
4) The gear "quality" vs. level vs. stats is just too confusing. Gold "Unique" gear is basically the limit of what you can equip. But different gear has different base stats, different gear levels, there's syncing and morphing and all sorts of various intricate unique mechanics to enhancing your gear that I've lost interest.
+ there's no published / known drop rates for the gear on the world bosses, and the rewards from these otherwise are extremely underwhelming. Unless there's something special about the unique gear from these world bosses - i basically see no reason for them.
5) The price vs. rewards of the monthly subscription is ridiculous; so much so that WoW Forever is cheaper, and gives you access to a fully complete game with about 25x the amount of content this game has. 

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
I think you should try the game regardless - it's free. It owes you nothing. You can decide for yourself whether it's the game for you or not; but the above points are what drove me away from the game.

[h1]Treadmill designed to squeeze fomo[/h1]

[b]Mobile game that you pay a subscription for[/b]

After logging nearly 250 hours on this game, the game doesn't offer enough depth or other systems to keep a player engaged. As someone who looks at a game as a whole and not just its endgame systems, this game was clearly designed to be a mobile game that intends to extract the most amount of fomo and money from the playerbase.

[h2]The good and the bad[/h2]

The good:
[list]
    [*]Amazing world and details
    [*]Great beautiful character creator
    [*]Combat is relatively simple yet reactive and fair in difficulty
    [*]Overworld and seeing an alive population is great
    [*]Many cute and great cosmetics in the shop
[/list]

The Bad:
[list]
    [*]Endgame progression consists of running the same 6 dungeons in all three available difficulties.
    [*]Terrible community if playing and running dungeons with public groups, lots of gatekeeping and rejection
    [*]Non gear scaled PvP modes that directly tie to your account progession, hope you enjoy being fodder and dying.
    [*]Constantly feeling like you're on a timer: Many of the events and systems that provide rewards are on a strict timer. This means missing doing any of your homework essentially 'sets you back' from progression.
    [*]Low drop chances for any gear, many runs feel pointless
    [*]Game is structured like a mobile game, log in and do your countless chores before the reset timers refresh.
    [*]Crafting, gathering and life skills in this game is barebones.
    [*]Content updates are intentionally released fast and early to incite fomo. This is another tactic to get you to feel the need to purchase power (to catch up to the latest release)
    [*]Many bots in the overworld which ruin your ability to farm certain mobs
    [*]RMT and players purchasing power with real money is rampant
    [*]Unable to purchase subscription with ingame currency. This game demands a regular subscription fee with no perks such as unlimited dyes or character creation changes. A very stingy subscription fee so you can 'be more efficient' with dungeon reward claims and using the marketplace
[/list]

[h2]Thoughts from a day 1 player[/h2]

As someone who has been playing consistently since launch day after day, it saddened me that the progression you make will never amount to those who purchase their power directly or people who "just get lucky". What ends up happening if you play with a group of friends is that, eventually you or your friends will no longer need a piece of content. They are heavily incentivized to move onto the next dungeon that they can run at their gear score progression. For context, you only have 10 entries where you don't need to spend energy to run / help with dungeons for your friends, this is problematic for helping your friends and is ANTI MMO.

The crafting and gathering system don't lend itself to anything special, very barebones lifeskills. As someone who appreciates more complex systems when it comes to lifeskills or core gameplay loops that don't involve combat, this game having an open rich world dropped the ball on its potential.

[h2]Fomo and progression[/h2]

Lastly, your progression starts slowing down to a crawl. This game is designed such that, a casual player will have to wait months before they can attempt to do the newly released content, however once they reach that point, it will have been obsolete. Without ridiculous amounts of luck, hours or paying cash for progression, you will always be doing 'old content'.

The good thing is that, if you are unaffected by fomo, take your time with things and find a nice community and enjoy the world, this game is a very easy and light game to play. For the people who want to feel like their time is respected for the money and hours they put in this game, this game does not respect your time. You end up paying a subscription fee for what it feels like a mobile game with predatory monetization systems.

AION 2 – Great Potential, Disappointing Systems

AION 2 has the potential to be a great game. However, several fundamental design decisions are making the overall gaming experience increasingly frustrating.

One of the biggest problems is the crafting system. Progression relies heavily on RNG (random chance), while crafting materials are both expensive and difficult to obtain. Players can invest enormous amounts of time and resources into improving their equipment without making any meaningful progress. A system that constantly punishes players for trying to improve is neither rewarding nor enjoyable.

The marketplace is another serious problem. Prices for essential materials can easily reach unreasonable levels, with insufficient measures to control price fluctuations. Some materials require hours or even days of boss farming. This turns progression into a repetitive and exhausting grind rather than an enjoyable part of the game.

The growing Pay-to-Win concerns are also difficult to ignore. High progression costs, QUNA, and RNG-based systems create the impression that spending real money may be the easier way to progress. Players should be rewarded for their time, effort, and skill instead of feeling pushed toward additional purchases.

The Abyss is another disappointing aspect. PvP-focused players can make farming extremely difficult for others. There needs to be a healthier balance between PvP and PvE. Players should not have to deal with one playstyle constantly interfering with the other.

Finally, I believe the game's current 16+ age rating should be reassessed, considering its monetization mechanics and repeated chance-based systems.

What needs to change?

A fairer crafting system that provides meaningful progression.

More balanced and better-regulated marketplace prices.

Easier access to crafting materials.

Less pressure to purchase QUNA.

A healthier balance between PvP and PvE in the Abyss.

Greater transparency regarding RNG rates and monetization systems.

A game should reward players for their dedication, not turn progression into an endless cycle of grinding, spending, and relying on luck.

AION 2 has a solid foundation. However, its current systems make it increasingly difficult to enjoy the game in the long run. If these issues are not addressed, I believe many players will eventually lose interest.

The game has potential, but potential alone is not enough. The developers need to listen to the community and make genuinely meaningful changes.

AION 2 – Großes Potenzial, enttäuschende Spielsysteme

AION 2 hat das Potenzial, ein großartiges Spiel zu werden. Allerdings sorgen einige grundlegende Designentscheidungen dafür, dass das Spielerlebnis zunehmend frustrierend wird.

Eines der größten Probleme ist das Crafting-System. Der Fortschritt hängt stark vom RNG (Zufall) ab, während die benötigten Materialien teuer und schwer zu beschaffen sind. Spieler können enorme Mengen an Zeit und Ressourcen in die Verbesserung ihrer Ausrüstung investieren, ohne dabei nennenswerte Fortschritte zu erzielen. Ein System, das Spieler für ihre Bemühungen um bessere Ausrüstung ständig bestraft, ist weder motivierend noch unterhaltsam.

Auch das Marktsystem ist ein ernstes Problem. Die Preise wichtiger Materialien können schnell unverhältnismäßig hoch werden, ohne dass es ausreichende Maßnahmen zur Regulierung der Preisschwankungen gibt. Für manche Materialien sind stunden- oder sogar tagelange Boss-Farm-Runs erforderlich. Dadurch wird der Spielfortschritt zu einer eintönigen und ermüdenden Beschäftigung statt zu einem unterhaltsamen Bestandteil des Spiels.

Auch die zunehmenden Pay-to-Win-Bedenken lassen sich kaum ignorieren. Hohe Fortschrittskosten, QUNA und zufallsbasierte Systeme vermitteln den Eindruck, dass man mit echtem Geld leichter vorankommen kann. Spieler sollten für ihre Zeit, ihren Einsatz und ihre Fähigkeiten belohnt werden, anstatt sich zu zusätzlichen Käufen gedrängt zu fühlen.

Der Abyss ist ein weiterer enttäuschender Aspekt. Stark PvP-orientierte Spieler können das Farmen für andere extrem erschweren. Es muss ein gesünderes Gleichgewicht zwischen PvP und PvE geben. Spieler sollten nicht ständig erleben müssen, dass ein Spielstil den anderen behindert.

Schließlich bin ich der Meinung, dass die aktuelle Altersfreigabe von 16+ angesichts der Monetarisierungsmechaniken und der wiederholten zufallsbasierten Systeme neu bewertet werden sollte.

Was sich ändern muss:

Ein faireres Crafting-System mit sinnvollem Fortschritt.

Ausgewogenere und besser regulierte Marktpreise.

Einfacherer Zugang zu Crafting-Materialien.

Weniger Druck, QUNA zu kaufen.

Ein gesünderes Gleichgewicht zwischen PvP und PvE im Abyss.

Mehr Transparenz bei RNG-Wahrscheinlichkeiten und Monetarisierungssystemen.

Ein Spiel sollte den Einsatz seiner Spieler belohnen und den Fortschritt nicht in eine endlose Schleife aus Farmen, Ausgeben und Hoffen auf Glück verwandeln.

AION 2 hat eine solide Grundlage. Allerdings erschweren die aktuellen Systeme den langfristigen Spielspaß erheblich. Wenn diese Probleme nicht behoben werden, werden meiner Meinung nach viele Spieler mit der Zeit das Interesse verlieren.

Das Spiel hat Potenzial, aber Potenzial allein reicht nicht aus. Die Entwickler müssen auf die Community hören und wirklich sinnvolle Änderungen umsetzen.

TL;DR

[h1]An update to my earlier review.[/h1]

[b]The membership. $14.99 a month, per server. It buys:[/b]

- Access to a market the gold sellers have sent into inflationary ascent. The Zimbabwean dollar comes to mind.
- A larger energy bar that fills no faster. A bigger bucket for the same leak.
- The privilege of paying again, Quna for Kinah.
- Double drops at double the energy. The same loot in half the visits.
- Every limit in the game still applies to you. I had understood it to be a fee, not a curfew.
- Someone at NCSoft thought this a good deal. Someone bring them back to reality.

[b]Everything else.[/b]

- Energy returns at 15 every three hours.
- Play past the daily caps and your Kinah is cut to 20%. You are being protected from yourself.
- Crafting is a gacha: it may fail and take everything. The safe recipe guarantees you the worse item.
- Some crafting materials come from capped dungeons and monsters, also low drop rate. Or buy them on the market: see inflationary ascent.
- Stat rolls come after you have the gear. Under 1%, one Unique item per attempt. A gacha inside a gacha, with no pity system.
- Every class wants the same offensive stats, so Clerics and Templars trade support for damage. FFXIV gave each job its own gear.
- Half the game is soulbound and direct trade is switched off. What you earn, you are stuck with.
- PvP: whoever lands the first stun wins. Skill is consulted afterwards.
- Bots everywhere. Some 77,000 accounts restricted in five weeks, and every cure leaves more. They hollowed out the first Aion; at this rate I give this one months. I await the day they clear Ludra.
- Built to make you swipe, and bad at it. $65, more or less, buys ten million Kinah, gone in an evening. $1,000 maxes a Wuthering Waves character; here, players speak of tens of thousands.
- The limits are why a black market exists. It sells Kinah for a fraction of the price. Guess where the whales shop.
- Parties of five, one real tank class, one real healer. Every group waits on a Templar or a Cleric, and they know it.
- Even the party games are ranked. Four prize cards for first, three for you, two for whoever is made the fool. Each pick costs a key.
- There is no honour in the Abyss. The worse you behave, the better it pays. Either they enjoy the power trip, or they sold their conscience for the pay.
- Gathering is as dull as FFXIV's, but there you press buttons to secure the item. Here you gamble, and levels only shave the odds.
- Radiant Odyle sits in the Abyss by design. Land one and an Asmodian, or Elyos, kills you. Working as intended.
- None of these rules is posted. One learns them by breaking them.
- A story that loses its pacing and assumes you attended the first game.

[b]The good.[/b]
-Character creator, that's it

[b]The verdict:[/b] If retention is the goal, well done: you are achieving the opposite. Good luck in the West. You are reminding it why it despises you. And when a gacha game is more generous than you, you make every stereotype about Korean publishers look true. If they expect the West to embrace them as it did FFXIV, they may keep dreaming.

[b]A caution.[/b] They are unpredictable. Knowing NCSoft's history, do not expect them to listen because they care. They might. Business simply ranks higher.

[h2]The story, for those who want it[/h2]

I gave this game one month. One. I arrived willing to be impressed, which I mention only so that no one at NCSoft mistakes what follows for bitterness. Bitterness would mean it mattered. This is merely a record, kept by a man with 482 hours of evidence and a growing fondness for lying down. I'm told the studio reads these. No need to hurry. I didn't.

Those who paid for early admission were treated to an overture of queues and maintenance. So should you come to hate the game for hating you, do try not to act surprised.

They wring every drop of Kinah from the game and then look about, baffled, at the bot farms selling it in the alleys. A child could follow the reason. A reasonably attentive houseplant could follow it. Watching them work it out is the best thing they have staged.

They are working on it, to be fair. As of November they discipline the buyers as well. One does admire a shop that arrests its own queue.

As for the rationing: one does not subscribe to be sent to one's room like a misbehaving child. I did look for the door. It is on a three-hour timer.

When one is at last admitted, the dungeons are lovely. I mean that. To whoever built those rooms: you were let down, and not by me. Not that anyone may admire them, because the party finder demands a Combat Power number at the door. Not to clear the dungeon. To clear it faster. The studio, mind you, takes a dimmer view of haste when it is the one being outrun. They withdrew the Ludra raid at launch because players slew the dragon sooner than planned, and returned it a month later with the entry requirement raised. The audience reached the final act too quickly, so they lengthened the corridor to the theatre.

Then crafting, which I attempted in good faith. I gathered a thousand Odyle Fragments, refined them, sat down to craft a gold bow, and it failed. I looked at the empty window for some time. It looked back. No, no, it's quite alright. It was only a bow. It was only a thousand fragments. It was only my evening. As for those of us who burned our Kinah before the safe recipes arrived, I did look for the refund, or failing that the apology. I'm sure both are on their way. They have been so very busy.

I tried the reroll regardless. It gave me natural HP regeneration. Now when some passing Asmodian lays me out, I may regenerate on the floor. Slowly. With great dignity.

The floor is where I met the PvP. I watched my character hurtle through her entire repertoire without me, and my opponent pressed as few buttons as I did. We were, in effect, two gentlemen who had sent their footmen to duel. Better servers for the great wars were evidently too much to ask, so I shan't ask. I shall simply mention it here, in public, where it can be comfortably overlooked.

The Abyss proper is kept for the heavy spenders, "whales," as you so tenderly call them. Allow me to explain something to whoever balances this, slowly. A whale requires other players: to buy Kinah from, to fill the market, to be better than. Keep driving them off and one day he will stand alone in an empty Abyss, very rich, and surrounded by bots and no players. I should like to see his face.

About that story. A tower broke, God is apparently dead, and I am meant to feel something. And here is the pity of it: I might have. A world broken in two, and its people left to go on living in the halves, is not a small thing to write about. It deserved someone who meant it. Ah, well. One learns to ration one's grief.

Nor am I the first to tire of the place. Kim Hyung-tae gave NCSoft eight years and Blade & Soul, then left more than a decade ago, remarking only that the long timelines weighed on him. He went on to make a gacha game, Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a stamina wall that at least admits to being one, and the women and the story make it worth the waiting.

And so, somewhere in NCSoft's halls, someone surveyed all of this and pronounced it good. Oh, how very tedious. FFXIV still has people paying a subscription, and heavens know it is not for Dawntrail. They stay because that game does not regard them as a problem to be managed.

The character creator is the finest I have ever used. I made someone rather beautiful, which is rare for me. She had excellent posture. One of us ought to. I had hoped to see where she went. Alas, I shall have to imagine it.

Not recommended. But please, do not let me stop you. It is only a month. What is a month to anyone?

And to NCSoft, should this ever reach a desk: no reply is necessary. You have been so busy, and I would hate to add to the list. I have wasted far longer on far less. This is simply the one I should like back.

I'll start with the good:

Combat is fun, and the character creator is gorgeous. You can create pretty, sexy, and handsome characters, an art form I almost considered lost. The game also offers plenty to do while leveling up and exploring the world.

That brings me to the bad:

The shop is predatory, and the developers certainly know how to convince people to spend money. Case in point: the Kitsune outfit, which seemingly every second player, their mum, and their dog have purchased.

Character progression is almost entirely random. Pity mechanics are tied to conditions that cannot be met in certain dungeon tiers, rendering them effectively useless. Loot tables show extremely low drop rates for the gear you actually need. And don't even get me started on crafting, where even successfully crafting the equipment you want is subject to yet another layer of RNG.

PvP is practically forced upon you if you want to make meaningful progress with certain stats and upgrades. PvP itself is largely a numbers game, where stronger players simply overpower weaker ones through numerical superiority.

Some progression resources can be purchased, but at increasingly steep prices.

The game is clearly fishing for whales willing to spend ridiculous amounts of money. Yet even spending real money is NO GUARANTEE of meaningful progression.

I've now played for 124 hours, and I'm thoroughly fed up with running the same dungeon for the 200th time, desperately trying to obtain a specific upgrade, while a friend of mine has had that exact same item drop 20 times already.

So yeah, what could have been a genuinely enjoyable experience has turned into an exercise in frustration, seemingly designed to push you towards spending real money in one of its numerous shops, or perhaps all of them.

The game has a genuinely fun core, but its progression systems and monetization are doing their very best to ruin it.

Aion 2 is Basically High-Graphics Candy Crush (And That’s Okay)

If you are stressed about the monetization in Aion 2, I have found the secret to enjoying the game: stop treating it like an MMO and start treating it like Candy Crush with Unreal Engine 5 graphics.

Once you make that mental shift, everything makes total sense:

• The "Out of Lives" Pop-Up: In Candy Crush, you run out of hearts and the game asks for $1.99 to keep playing. In Aion 2, you hit your dungeon cap or want to use the Auction House, and NCSoft politely slides a $15 Membership across the table.

• Buying Lollipop Hammers: In Candy Crush, your aunt buys boosters to clear Level 4,000. In Aion 2, whales swipe Quna for Kina to skip the gear grind and inflate their Combat Power.

• The Leaderboard Illusion: Nobody actually cares who has the highest score on your Candy Crush friends list. You shouldn't care about the whale dominating the Abyss rankings either.

• The Actual Gameplay: At the end of the day, matching shiny candies for 30 minutes while watching TV is genuinely fun. Flying around, pressing cool buttons, and running casual dungeons with friends is fun too—as long as you don't take it seriously.

The Takeaway:

Play it like a casual mobile puzzle game. Log in, pop some shiny skills, enjoy the free scenery, and close the cash shop without a second thought. You will have a great time.

I recognize AION 2 as a game with potential, but I cannot recommend it yet to most players. It is currently just a mindless nightly slog for me.

The road to the level 45 cap is breezy and can be completed in less then a day if you rush the content. However post-45, the true grind for item and combat power quickly reveals itself and you are forced to grind the same dungeon content over and over again for rare drops. You can do this for hours on end without a single legendary. And with the F2P energy cap and recharge timer, you are hard-capped in the number of dungeon attempts!

The social element of the game is thoroughly underbaked and designed so that players cannot help others succeed. Obtained a weapon that your class can't use? Your alts can't use it either. Want to fill a gap in your gear set with a purchase from the player-run economy? NOPE. As a F2P player, you can't even trade with other players or access the marketplace. 

The story content is designed to be played entirely solo, so you can't even experience the story with a friend. Everyone's story plays out exactly the same. The dungeons are mostly speedruns with virtually no communication(s) needed. It's like playing with the ghosts of players, rather than players themselves. 

PVE Rifts are few and far between. People drop in silently and leave after they've collected the loot they came for. No high-fives, no celebrations. Just the sense that you're alone in the struggle for the next power tier, so you can unlock the next progression path, to get to the next and so on. 

Unlike Guild Wars 2, there are very few reasons to group up with people in a way that's not forced or transactional. The world is pretty for sure, but it lacks variety in biomes and does not react to any of your actions / choices, and exists as just a way to pad out the side quests and make you auto-travel from A to B. If you're near the low end of the gear score requirement for a dungeon, good luck finding a group because you'll experience near instant auto-kicks from people who perceive you as "dead-weight" who will only slow down their gear grind. I don't blame them for this because the game does nothing to incentivize helping others. 

Performance is iffy given this is a UE5 game. You get constant microstutters when mobs spawn, and FPS will tank in the cities. Frame gen and DLSS are almost necessary to get up to 144fps, and I have a pretty powerful rig so I imagine this will be worse for other players.

Great game, but the gatekeeping is ruining the experience for casual players.

It might just be me, but the gatekeeping in AION 2 is honestly getting ridiculous.

I genuinely enjoyed the early game and most of the mid game, but once you start getting closer to the end game, it feels like you hit a brick wall. The biggest problem isn't necessarily the difficulty of the content, it's actually finding people who will let you play it.

So many groups refuse to accept you unless you have a certain power level or DPS. But here's my question: How am I supposed to improve my gear and DPS if nobody will let me join the content I need to progress?

It feels like a lot of players rushed through the game, reached a high power level, and are now gatekeeping everyone trying to catch up. Most groups seem to want the fastest possible clears so they can farm currency and gear, which I understand. But that leaves everyone else stuck.

It also doesn't help that the game has P2W elements. It sometimes feels like people who have spent money to get ahead are now setting the standards for everyone else. If you haven't reached their level, you're either rejected or kicked.

I only get around three hours a day to play, which I personally think is a reasonable amount of time to spend on a game. I'm not expecting to compete with people who play 10 hours a day or spend loads of money. I just want to be able to enjoy the content, improve my character and slowly work towards the end game.

But right now, it feels like the game is becoming increasingly closed off to anyone who hasn't been grinding since day one.

And maybe I'm just bad at the game. I'm happy to admit that could be part of it. But how are people supposed to learn, improve and get better gear if nobody is willing to give them a chance?

The frustrating part is that I actually really like AION 2. The combat is enjoyable, the world is great, and there's plenty of content I want to experience. But the community's obsession with power levels, DPS requirements and rushing through everything is slowly killing my enjoyment.

Would I recommend AION 2?

If you've got a group of friends to play with, absolutely. I think you'll have a great time.

But if you're a solo player hoping to meet people, find groups and gradually work your way towards the end game, I'd honestly struggle to recommend it in its current state.

I don't mind having to grind for better gear. That's part of an MMO. What I do mind is being unable to do the content needed to get that gear because the people running it only want players who already have it.

I want to recommend this game, but right now, the gatekeeping makes it incredibly difficult.

I'm just going to rip the band-aid off, Aion 1 wasn't overly amazing, but it at least lasted 5-10 years worth of actual "MMORPG" gameplay. Aion 2 is not, it is a shallow copy of an MMO at best, it is literally the opposite. All materials are hard to come by with bots, you need to run a dungeon 80+ times to get all the gear you want (40 or so if you pay for the pass to open 2 at once.), and everything gets bound to your current character so you cannot even give it to an alt. This is quite literally a free to single player game with benefits of having friends along the way in instanced dungeons.

I'm not here to make a fancy review, sort it out very well, or use ai to make it "amazing looking". Just here to state facts. I gave this game the "3 days away and see if I have the desire to play" feel, and I had zero feelings of wanting to even touch it. After 200 hours of grinding, and making it to Ludra, This is possibly the worst game to ever exist in recent times. NCsoft is done. They refuse to listen to a lot of complaints and shill out their 30$ skins.

I also got baited into pre buying the game, dealing with server issues, learning the game as it was rolling out, and struggling with the loot refusing to drop for 3 characters. (dont even get me started on gold cards....) 

The energy, or Odyle, is absolutely abysmal of a system the way they laid it out. It's so bad even people that heavy pay to win have no energy to spare. 15 energy every 3 hours, and you need 40(or 80) to open a dungeon box? You only get 120 natural regen a day... So who's the idiot that thought it was a great idea when the drops are horrible in the first place? 

Resurrecting is also just as bad, its gotten around that it is better for the only class in the game (cleric) to not apply revive to their stigmas because they should just run shield or a dps skill. So you have to use res stones. These stones if you do some math are pretty much 1.20$ ish usd per revive. Not doing the math to prove that, but once you run out of all the free ones, you're done, no more reviving in endgame, unless you have a cleric that decides to roll the stigma with a 30 minute CD revive. Sure you can get some revive stones crafted weekly using some of the money currency, but that is only 30 stones a week. (Last i checked before i stopped playing, they added another set of 30 to buy at twice the price as the original 30 stones, and even that might not be permanent.)

I'll also point out the crafting in this game is horrible as well, just like some other people pointed out. That 25% chance is a lie, and it gets worse for each tier of item that you need. 
~ To explain: Crafting gear in this game gets one extra stat line to re-roll verses > dungeon gear gets extra reach for weapons. That system is far too expensive to worry about armor when you are focusing on only weapons with how bad it is. you only have 1 weapon, vs 9 pieces of gear to craft. It is easy to see what would be the best improvement.

Now back to the crafting. It is supposed to be 25% chance to proc a higher level craft after you succeed on crafting a piece of gear. (yes you can fail to craft a gear at max skill before you even get to the chance to see if the 25% procced.) Now do that 7 times for each rank of gear on top of all the other materials you used to get this far. Made it all the way to the end? Nice! Now play this game of watch blue and yellow bars fill up with a chance to fail before you know if you made the last weapon.
>Fail? all materials is gone, poof! and that is not including all of the other failures or non procs. Because in this game there is no upgrades to be had to the next craft if you did not get the 25% and succeed at that. 
(A lot of people say it takes maybe 10 sometimes to get the higher rank of the item so they could use that to the next level. And do that 7 times.....)
>Succeed in crafting? Nice now you just need to use a bit more of the nicer materials to turn it into the best weapon of the first rank. With another nicer quality of a lower level of course. "We don't want to make this too easy now would we?"
You get my point on this. It is not a true 25% when you need to make 10-20 of a weapon multiple times to try and get to the next rank. I once made 80 swords of the lowest rank and only 5 made it to an upgrade. I didn't sit around to watch the craft time as it was going to take a while, but that just means that at least 5 had another tug of war with the bars. Again... first weapon to craft, they do NOT hold back in how bad it is.

-Upgrading is even worse, so I will just point out the bad RNG quickly as that will also be an entire page in itself. I re-rolled a stat with 10 items i had to take forever to farm. (That's how they designed it, use another yellow to re-roll a stat into something you might want or need.) I did that and saw the same stat 4 times. 
-Upgrading is as bas as you can imagine as well, after +10 the chance sits at 80% to succeed, and lowers by 10% each time. So to go from 14 to 15 its 40% chance. Alright, i've seen worse i believe, but not when it costs up to 2 million coins each time to attempt 15 again. It got so bad, min max people found out you could just attempt a 36 piece and then use stones to put those +15 on an endgame piece for 1/4 of the cost.

PVP... tough subject. You can easily get abyss points farming monsters as well. That is if you dont get nuked into oblivion in seconds by someone else that has played longer than you, or swiped away at better gear crafts. Those stigma shards are heavily needed for pve content to max out your skills. So you can't just never pvp, or enter the abyss to farm points. (It is even worse when you need abyss corridors and the enemy holds all 3. This means they get the 22k or so abyss points x3 and your side gets 0.)

PVP battlegrounds is also a joke, matchmaking is nonexistent, and the points that are limited to a set amount of participations and victories is tiny in comparison. I mean, 3k for a 10v10 battle win and the 1k for participating, or kill mobs for about 30 minutes in the abyss., Provided you are not killed of course. 

Shugo festival every hour is a joke as well, you match with other random players and attempt to get first place at a "chance" to get rewarded. Rewards are so-so, but thats not the complaint, its a gamble on the cards you choose, and some times the rewards are crap. The problem being, I have recorded people actually cheating and NC did nothing, how is this a thing? I have seen multiple people in shugo using speed hacks, like how? 

Explanation on that: Enter in a rainbow road ripoff race with maxed out pets for the fastest mount speed. Which by the way is only like 5% faster at best, it is only slightly noticeable. Then this chad just takes off and leaves everyone in his rear view. You see him just zip around the race track and only collect green orbs of pet stamina. The team just had the gall to say he was simply playing better than me and never hit any traps to slow him down. OK, nice, good to know they dgaf.

Don't even get me started on the monetization of this game... They never put a limit on cost for the money boxes, which honestly I am ok with. That means someone has to buy 2 of the most expensive gem packs just to buy 10 million coins. What discusts me is that the skins are 30 bucks, most of them are low effort. One skin was just a tiny bottom underwear, basically panties, and an apron...... There was a mask to go with it as well but thats not the point. 30 usd for a skin that was basically "panty apron" and a serial killer mask.

I could rant about bow bad Aion 2 is as an MMORPG (still don't know how they have this title when the only element of this is possibly a 10 man Ludra fight and open world bosses that die in seconds...) all day but i'll stop. 

I will leave it up to anyone that ever wants to play this slop they swear is an "MMORPG" if they want, but they will not be getting any more of my time or money.

It honestly baffles me how a company managed to convince the playerbase that this game is f2p. In reality, it feels strictly p2p, because without the monthly subscription, progression becomes an excruciatingly slow.

Let's talk about RNG. It's everywhere. The game already operates on an energy system, meaning that once you run out of energy, you're done. No more raids, no more dungeons. You're essentially locked out of meaningful PvE progression until you can replenish it.

Dungeon loot? Practically non-existent (Fairly low drop rates).
Stats on the gear you actually manage to obtain? RNG.
Want to reroll those stats? More RNG.
Crafting gear? RNG again. It can fail, and your materials simply go straight into the trash.

Want to enhance your equipment? Of course, it's RNG! The success rates get progressively worse the further you advance, while the costs can reach millions of Kinah.
"But you can funnel Kinah from your alts to your main!"
Sure, you can. But which other game forces you to play multiple characters just to keep up with progression? Let me give you a hint: two words. One starts with L, the other with A.

[b]And speaking of alts, don't expect them to share much progression. Every character is essentially a fresh start. Achievements, Wings, Stigma, Pantheon, and other progression systems are character bound. So much for making alternative characters without feeling like you're starting the entire game over again.[/b]

After roughly a month, NCSoft released the first raid, Ludra. And what a way to introduce endgame content. The raid is overtuned in our version, forcing an already struggling playerbase to chase combat power and gear score (yes this game has both and one is irrelevant to the other) requirements that players in the Asian version never had to deal with. On top of that, Ludra introduces a rather significant problem: it is the ONLY content that provides you with a bracelet. You might argue that the content isn't going anywhere, and technically, you're right. However, the community's requirements for joining older content or content that has been released for 2 to 3 weeks can be most of the times ridiculous. Eventually, you'll find yourself dealing with requirements that the average player simply cannot meet. This creates unnecessary FOMO around content that should be accessible to a much wider portion of the playerbase.

Now, let's address the elephant in the room: [b]PvP[/b].
Unlike the Asian version, our version doesn't provide an essential progression currency through dungeons. Instead, that currency is tied to the Abyss, a PvP zone that essentially becomes a playground for whales or unbalanced server vs server to obliterate anyone trying to farm it.
So much for optional PvP when an essential part of your character progression is locked behind it.
Let's talk about Mass PvP (Abyss). I initially thought this would be one of the more interesting aspects of the game. Unfortunately, the technical performance is absolutely awful. Character rendering is horrendous, and the constant lag caused by the sheer number of players involved makes the experience frustrating rather than enjoyable.
Playing a melee character? Good luck trying to participate. Ranged DPS will shred you before you can even get close enough to touch them. What about 1v1 encounters? Sure, they're potentially manageable (Extremely rare in Abyss), depending on how much of a whale your opponent is or how much time they've invested into the game.
[b]I still play because I have friends who genuinely enjoy this kind of masochism, and I'll probably continue playing until I eventually hit a quite impossible progression wall. With the sheer amount of RNG involved in practically every aspect of the game, it's only a matter of time.[/b]

[u]However, I cannot recommend AION 2 to anyone who values their time, patience, and sanity. And especially not to anyone who has previously played Lost Ark. AION 2 seems to be following the exact same path, only at a much faster pace.[/u]

TL;DR:
[b]F2P in name only[/b]: The monthly subscription feels practically essential if you want to progress at a reasonable pace.
[b]Alt unfriendly progression[/b]: Characters don't share major progression systems, meaning every alt is essentially another grind from scratch.
[b]PvP disguised as optional content[/b]: Essential progression currencies are locked behind PvP zones, making PvP effectively mandatory.
[b]Terrible Mass PvP performance[/b]: Poor rendering, constant lag, and an unfriendly environment for melee classes make large-scale PvP frustrating.
[b]Toxic community[/b]: Expect trolls and players telling others to uninstall or get out. Ironically, many of these same people will later complain to NCSoft about the declining playerbase.

Ultimately, AION 2 has the potential to be a great game, but its progression systems, monetization, excessive RNG, and questionable design decisions make it incredibly difficult to enjoy. If NCSoft keeps going down this road, don't be surprised when more players eventually walk away.

# AION 2 – A Game With Potential That Is Slowly Destroying Its Own Future

After more than 300 hours of playing AION 2, I genuinely believe this game is heading in the wrong direction. In its current state, I have serious doubts that it will maintain a healthy player base for even the next two months, let alone survive into future seasons.

At first, the game is genuinely enjoyable. There are plenty of quests, dungeons, Daeva tablets to collect and skills to optimise. Exploring the world and gradually becoming stronger makes the early progression satisfying.

The macro system is understandable considering how fast-paced combat is. However, it also removes much of the gameplay. Eventually, you find yourself pressing two buttons and letting the system do most of the work. There is less thinking, less reaction and less skill involved. Combat becomes repetitive rather than engaging.

But the real problems begin when you reach the endgame.

**ENDGAME PROGRESSION – AN EXCESSIVE GRIND**

The dungeons themselves are enjoyable, relatively short and straightforward. The problem is the reward system. You can spend hours repeating the same dungeon only to receive everything except the item you actually need.

The energy-based reward system makes things worse. Once your energy is depleted, you can continue running dungeons, but you no longer receive the rewards that make those runs worthwhile.

The voucher system is not much better. Some items require up to 84 runs, consuming considerable energy and approximately 2 million Kina.

**CRAFTING AND SOUL BINDING – AN ENDLESS LOTTERY**

Crafting the best equipment can cost hundreds of millions of Kina, only for you to discover that the required materials are incredibly difficult to obtain.

In my experience, despite approximately 500 dungeon runs, I have obtained only four of the crafting materials I needed, despite the displayed drop chances ranging from approximately 16% to 66%.

Soul binding is another problem. With chances as low as 1–3% to obtain the stats you actually want, you can spend enormous amounts of resources and still end up with the same terrible stats you were trying to replace.

**RNG – EVERYTHING IN THIS GAME IS A GAMBLE**

This deserves its own criticism because RNG is practically everywhere in AION 2.

Want character skins? Approximately 15% chance when dismantling equipment. Want to combine skins and upgrade them? Another 15% chance. Want to cook? Your attempt can succeed or fail. Gathering resources also comes with its own randomness.

At what point does this stop being an MMORPG and start feeling like a collection of gambling mechanics disguised as progression systems?

RNG has its place in MMORPGs, but when almost every activity depends on random outcomes, players stop feeling rewarded for their time and effort. They simply keep rolling the dice, hoping the game eventually decides to reward them.

**MICROTRANSACTIONS – THE BIGGEST THREAT TO THE GAME**

This is where NCSoft makes its biggest mistake.

Players can purchase Quna with real money, and the currency exchange allows real-money spending to influence the in-game Kina economy. This creates serious pay-to-win concerns because players can effectively bypass enormous portions of the progression system.

On top of that, players are expected to pay for a monthly subscription to access certain marketplace features. There is also a season pass, while premium currency continues to be sold in substantial quantities.

So players are expected to grind endlessly, deal with terrible RNG and pay for a subscription, while others can spend real money to accelerate their progression.

How is that supposed to create a fair playing field?

**BOTS – ANOTHER PROBLEM NCSoft NEEDS TO ADDRESS**

How are legitimate players supposed to compete with automated farming bots that can operate for extremely long periods?

While real players are restricted by energy systems, limited playtime and RNG, automated accounts can continuously gather resources and farm materials.

Combine this with real-money currency exchange and you have an economy where legitimate players are constantly fighting against systems that work against them.

NCSoft needs to take bot activity seriously. An MMORPG should reward the people who actually play it, not punish them for being legitimate players.

**PVP – WHERE ALL THESE PROBLEMS BECOME OBVIOUS**

Certain endgame areas require PVP while farming important progression materials, including Stigma skill shards. You cannot simply avoid these encounters if you want to progress.

Yet the difference in power between players can be overwhelming. You can spend hundreds of hours farming, crafting and optimising your equipment, only to encounter someone who kills you in two or three hits.

I have decent equipment and have invested considerable time into my character, yet I still struggle to keep up with players whose gear progression seems to have advanced at an entirely different pace.

The more players spend real money, the more expensive certain crafting materials become. No amount of energy or repetitive dungeon grinding can reasonably compensate for an economy heavily influenced by real-money spending.

**THE FUTURE OF AION 2**

Players are not against grinding. Players are not against difficult content. Players are not against working towards powerful equipment.

What players are against is having their time disrespected.

A good MMORPG should reward dedication, knowledge, teamwork and skill. Instead, AION 2 surrounds almost every progression system with layers of RNG, artificial limitations, aggressive monetisation and an economy that increasingly favours those willing to spend real money.

If NCSoft wants to make money, sell cosmetics, offer optional services and create worthwhile premium content. Stop selling advantages that undermine the efforts of everyone else.

AION 2 has the foundations of a genuinely enjoyable MMORPG. The combat, dungeons, exploration and progression initially show a lot of potential.

But potential means nothing if the endgame becomes an exhausting cycle of artificial scarcity, terrible RNG and pay-to-win mechanics.

I have invested more than 300 hours into this game. I wanted to enjoy it, progress and see what the endgame had to offer.

Instead, I have reached a point where I question whether continuing to play is even worth my time.

If NCSoft does not make serious changes, I genuinely believe AION 2 risks losing a significant portion of its player base within the next few months.

A game cannot survive on launch excitement forever. Eventually, players realise when their time is no longer being respected.

And when that happens, they leave.

After almost two months and around 500 hours of gameplay, I really didn't want to write a negative review. I genuinely enjoyed AION 2 and wanted it to succeed.

I originally quit Black Desert because I was tired of its P2W mechanics and the growing gap between players, I came to AION 2 hoping for a different experience. Unfortunately, I'm starting to feel like I've walked into something even worse in certain aspects.
1. The Market – Paying $15 Just to Participate in the Economy?

Let's start with the Special Quai Membership.

Why should a game that advertises itself as free-to-play require a $14.99 monthly subscription just to access one of the most fundamental systems of an MMORPG: the player market?
And the frustrating part is that even after paying, the market itself is poorly designed.
For example, if I want to purchase exactly 50 Odyle, I can't simply select that quantity and buy it. I have to work around whatever quantities other players have listed. I might end up buying more than I need or less than I want.
On top of that, prices are ridiculous, materials can be difficult to obtain, and market manipulation makes the situation even worse.

2.Fighting Bots by Punishing the System ?
This is probably my biggest frustration with NCSoft's approach.

I understand that bots, gold farming and market manipulation are serious problems. But why does the solution keep involving restrictions on legitimate players?

Look at the November 11 update:

Kina from Lower Abyss monsters is now bound.

Kina from Krao Cave Conquest is now bound.

Kina from Draupnir Conquest Tier 1 is now bound.

What's next? Will every source of Kina eventually become bound?
I understand that NCSoft needs to control bots, but legitimate players shouldn't have to pay the price for problems they didn't create.

There are much better ways to manage an MMO economy.
Look at Black Desert's Central Market. It uses minimum and maximum price ranges, pre-orders, and purchasing priority rules. It isn't a perfect system, but it provides much better control over prices and gives players a way to buy items even when they aren't currently available.

Why can't AION 2 implement something similar?

A proper market with price controls, buy orders, quantity selection and purchasing priorities would be a much better approach than constantly restricting how legitimate players earn and trade Kina.
3. Kina to Quna – What's the Actual Point?

What's the point of allowing players to exchange the Kina they farm for Quna if the cosmetics people actually want are still being sold directly for real money?
Yes, some smaller accessories are available for Quna, but that's not what most players are asking for.
WE WANT SKINS, NOT ACCESSORIES!

4. Technical Issues 

And finally, the technical problems.
Chat issues, delayed messages and server lag are still affecting the experience. Server freezes during dungeons are particularly frustrating because they can ruin an entire run, regardless of how well you're playing.

Short version: 

This game is a scam and cash grab dont bother getting invested in it
