The only reason I've kept playing is probably “the sunk cost fallacy”

Long version: 

Aion2 has potential but it's all going to waste. For every 1 good thing it has there's always 2 shit things to match.

To start with, the character creator was great, it's honestly one of the best character creators I've seen in any game. I enjoy making my own characters and role playing as them in games. 

In Aion2 for whatever reason I'm not allowed to use my saved character customisations on other character slots on the same server. This is beyond super inconvenient; especially if you spent over an hour in the character creator to get everything perfect. 

If you save a character customisation in the editor then want to play a new character and use your saved customisation it won't be there. A saved customisation won't carry to your character even in the same server.

It's a waste that the game won't allow you to use character customisation saves onto other character slots. You get 8 slots to save character designs on. But its fucking pointless if they cant carry to your other characters.
Why would I pay money to change a character customisation that I've finished and decided to stay with for another one on the same slot. Nobody uses it enough to even need the 8 customization save slots on 1 character. 

The games cash shop is even worse

Aion2 sells outfits, weapon skins, pets and wings that are on sale for a limited time. The problem is that if you buy any of this they wont carry over to other servers you join. If you buy anything on one server, it’s ALWAYS locked to that server.

If you wanna get it again on a new server you gotta buy it again. But
Its impossible if it was a limited time item. 

When all outfits sold in the cash shop are limited time items. What's the point of spending money on them if you don't even get to keep them on other servers and it's not possible to buy them again in the future.

It's worse with wings as they’re always locked to a single character. Which honestly kinda makes it pointless to even buy it in the first place.

It's one thing if they don't want levels, items or character progress to carry over to other servers in this game but stopping paid cosmetics like weapon skins, outfits, pets and etc which don’t give any actual boost in pvp or pve is kind of scummy behaviour from ncsoft.

If I want to join my friend who’s on another server I could not give 2 shits if I restart from level 1 but the fact that I'm not allowed to keep what I've already paid money for is beyond scummy behaviour. 

Another issue with this game is the social element. 

On steam the game calls itself an mmo. But where is the mmo?

I’ve seen so many people online and on the same server on this game. But there's no socializing, no communication between people and rarely does anybody want to say “hi” to each other.

The world chat in my server is full of bots that wanna advertise “cheap kina” on some dodgy website

It's a pain trying to meet and socialize with people in this game. 90% of players in this game that i've seen are just so obsessed with grinding that they won't bother with talking.

When you try to join people in a dungeon, the game puts you in a group. After the dungeon is over everyone just dips to jump onto the next run which is most likely the same dungeon they just did.

If you do ever end up meeting or making a friend in this game, your friends list won't carry over to other servers in this game or even alt characters in the same server. 

Aion2 has guilds that they call “Legions” but right now there’s no guild content. So don't expect any guild vs guild pvp or any guild boss fights, dungeon raids etc.

If you find a guild you like, it's tied to the character you joined it on and wont carry over to other character slots. You have to reach level 16 again then rejoin it on your alt.


Everything else in Aion2 feels like an endless repetitive grind and not the fun kind. If you wanna get strong and powerful in this game you gotta do the same dungeons over and over again for gear, then hunt the same monsters repeatedly all over the map for pet genus and do that again in the abyss for abyss tokens to buy stigma shards to make your character stronger.

Why do you want your character to be stronger in this game?

So you can repeat again at a higher level.

PvP content in Aion isnt worth it imo. If you wanna be good at pvp in this game you gotta be prepared to spend thousands of real life money on this game.

There is a marketplace in game where players sell pretty much everything like armors, weapons, crafting materials, wings, skins and etc for “kina” which is a currency you get from grinding. But you can also buy “kina” with “quna” which is the game's p2w currency.

Most p2w players spend money on quna then buy as much kina as they want to buy all they need from the marketplace. 

If you're free to play you won't be allowed to access the marketplace without buying the subscription. 

Sadly as a free to play player you will have to grind for all the items and materials you need to upgrade your character manually which is extremely time consuming and monotonous while someone who is paying 2 win can dump all their money into buying everything from the marketplace.

In actual pvp anyone who is pay to win, will always have an advantage over free to play.

For this game's combat itself…

The combat in this game is alright but does not feel like anything special. There isn’t any block or parry mechanic. You can press Shift on your keyboard to dodge and that’s pretty much it.

The shift key is also used for dashing unless you alter the keybinds, so sometimes if you wanna sprint and you hold shift, you perform a dodge into the direction you're looking instead of doing a dash. But this won't affect your gameplay too much.

The magic spells, skills and whatnot that you can use in this game isn’t anything new or original, it's the same as every other eastern mmo where you do some super flashy move which is supposed to look powerful with lots of flashing lights and colours but somehow the damage you're doing doesn't match.

What I did find new and original is the in game macro. In AION2 you can put your characters skills into this in game 1 button macro, where you can click a button on your mouse or keyboard to do the full skill combo in order. You won't need to time everything perfectly yourself; you can use the macro to do it for you.

Pretty much everyone ive seen has been using the macro to fight.

Pvp and pve content doesn't feel like you need any skill. It's mostly just who has better stats

As for the main story itself all I can say is some parts were fun and other parts felt like a drag.

I've only played the Elyos faction and at first their plot where the dawn legion wants to cross the bulwark sounded interesting. Later I got so bored that the dialogue just sounded like utter bs I was forced to just spam skip.

You player wont have any say in the story or change the outcome or have any input. All you can do is just stand there and watch every single other NPC talk to each other and watch them while you act like their servant when they tell you to go harvest 5 leather or some other bs. 

The game say’s that you're some sort of “chosen one” with a great destiny and whatnot yet while playing the game…trust me you wont feel like that.

I will hand it to them though, the game does have good cinematics. The visuals in this game are fantastic but the gameplay just doesn't match.

An excessively grindy, bot riddled, RNG heavy, p2w game.  Unbelievably greedy as well.  Player market is not only lvl locked (needing to be max level) but also locked behind the monthly subscription paywall.  The kina <-> quna exchange is also locked by the subscription wall because it is part of the market feature.  What is kina and quna?  Kina is the ingame currency.  Think the typical copper/silver/gold in other games like WoW and Guild Wars.  It comes as either bound or unbound where unbound is the only form that can be used in the market.  Quna is the cash shop currency except only select items can be purchased with quna.  There is plenty, particularly skins, that can only be purchased with real money directly.  That's right, even though quna can be bought directly with real money, because it can be earned (but only if you pay the monthly subscription) it can't be used on skins and some other items.

When you launch the game, you pick a side between two factions (because this is a pvp centric game) and then pick a server.  You will be able to make 4 out of 8 characters, the remaining four character slots can be unlocked by an item purchased with quna.  So you subscribe, pick a side like Elyos and then make a character on a server.  But you want to try out Asmodian.  So you pick a server and make a character.  What's this?  You don't have the benefits of being subscribed.  That's right, subscriptions are server bound.  All the subscription does is allows access to the player driven market, allow you to spend twice the energy at the end of an expedition run to open the cube twice (more on that later) and some minor conveniences like being able to buy certain items and transfer items between character and storage without needing to visit an npc.  You don't even get some quna with that subscription payment.  Best you can do with the subscription is grind unbound kina and use the kina <-> quna exchange.  The exchange isn't even instant when going from kina to quna.  You use the kina to create an unbound kina box and you are selling it on the market for quna so you have to wait for a player to buy it and you can be undercut.

BiS gear.  Two paths, crafting or expedition running (dungeons).  The expeditions have two options.  Exploration and Conquest.  Exploration is soloable and you can even create a private room for yourself so you can run them solo.  The problem is that exploration expeditions are only good for getting armor.  You will need to run the expeditions in conquest mode to get access to weapons and accessories which involves forming a party with other players.  And, well, I've never played an online game which such a level of elitism.  While there is a bot problem, even in expeditions, it's almost better to have bots in your expeditions with the amount of elitism and toxicity.  What's worse is that opening the cube (chest) at the end after beating the final boss is how you obtain your loot.  It cost energy to open and you have a limited supply so it's not like you can just keep running the dungeon (and boy do you have to repeatedly run them) over and over until you get the drop you want.  The drop rates are so bad that they had to introduce a pity system.  Expeditions are gear score locked so you have to obtain, enhance, obtain, enhance, rinse repeat.  With needing to repeatedly run the same expedition multiple times to obtain all the pieces to then move on to the next once you obtained them and enhanced them to reach, not just the gear score, but the dps needed to be accepted into groups which is a higher threshold than what is required for the expedition because heaven forbid it takes a minute or two longer to clear the expedition.

So what about crafting.  Well, to start, you need refinement stones and the best repeatable and reliable way to obtain these is to run the expeditions.  With horrendously low drop rates.  So you will be running the expeditions 1000s of times just to craft a single BiS item.  Bright side is that the you can do the solo runs for them.  There are 16 slots where craftable items can go.  Much of this not only has to do with the low drop chance of higher tier refinement stones that will be needed but also how the crafting system works.  When you craft a particular tier of gear, there is a 25% chance of it offering a chance to craft a splendid version.  Beyond crafting common tier, the splendid version is an ingredient to craft the next tier.  Crafts also have a chance at failing causing you to lose your materials with nothing to show for it.  That 25% chance triggers upon successful completion of crafting the item but you don't automatically get the item.  You then have to craft the splendid version (which replaces the base version you successfully crafted) meaning you can successfully craft an item, trigger the splendid, only to fail crafting the splendid and end up losing the materials with nothing to show for it.  This means, you want to be able to have enough mats to craft 6 times to have a reasonable chance at successfully crafting 1 splendid.  But remember, a splendid of one tier is the ingredient of next tier.  The Tiers are Common (white), Rare (green), Epic (Blue), Unique (Yellow), and Heroic (Orange).  Although heroic does not exist on NA servers.  They do offer a guarantee option for crafting unique tier but you don't get the 25% for the splendid version.  Once you have unique tier crafted, you can then morph craft it up to highest gear score available (making it BiS).  Doing so will require one or two splendids of the previous tier depending on if you are starting with the splendid version of the unique tier or not. 

So lets not leave things to chance and go with the guarantee craft.  That means, when you craft the epic tier, you need 3 splendid to proc.  One to be used to craft the unique and the other two as ingredients in two separate morphs.  If we need to be able to craft 6 times for a decent shot at 1 splendid.  You will need enough mats to craft 18 epics.  Which requires 18 splendids of rare tier.  Which means you will need to craft 108 of the rare tier to have a decent shot (not even a guarantee) at getting those 18 splendid.  Which means you need enough mats to craft 648 common Tier of a single item.  Rince and repeat for the remaining 15 slots.  Now, in obtaining the mats to craft 648 times, you will obtain higher tier mats needed to craft the higher tier item but the drop rate ratio does not match the crafting ratio of 6 to 1.  Meaning, in the process of getting mats to craft 6 of the common tier just to craft a single splendid, you will not have enough of the rare tier mats to utilize that splendid to craft the next tier.  You will have to grind even more.

Not only does crafting have a chance to fail, so does resource gathering with each node allowing for 3 attempts (not shared) before the node is gone and you have to wait for it to respawn.  Worse yet, is what I meant by "not shared".  You go up to a node and begin gathering.  Someone else comes up to the same node and can begin gathering too.  You end up leaving with only one or two out of three extractions.  Players have no concept of courtesy never mind the bots.

Of course, you can always just subscribe, use real money to buy quna and then use the kina/quna exchange to buy unbound kina and use that kina to buy the BiS items.

I think that after more than 200 hours, I can finally write a review about this game (although, to be completely honest, I could've written one after the first 5 hours. But I decided to give it a chance, just like I did with Lost Ark).

So, to save you from the endless grind and wasting your time, this game has absolutely zero respect for your time or effort.
**1. The mandatory subscription**

Don't even dream of playing this game without a monthly subscription. You can try, but the amount of effort required just to enjoy the game and access its content is ridiculously high compared to the rewards you get.

You can't use the in-game market without a subscription, you can't buy the extra energy you desperately need, and you're stuck with a 560 energy limit (840 with a subscription).

And to make things even worse, you can't double-claim rewards without a subscription. So good luck getting that 5% chance of dropping your weapon, which is actually much lower since there's no guarantee it'll even be YOUR weapon. For some reason, you can get a Cleric weapon as a Gladiator, and you can't even sell it or transfer it to an alt character who could actually use it!

**2. The ridiculous grind**

Let's say you're okay with the laughable drop rates and mandatory subscription, so you decide to pay and enjoy the game. Here's the catch: the amount of time and effort required to stay even remotely relevant is HUGE.

Almost every meaningful piece of content is locked behind either Gear Score or Combat Power (mostly the latter). And how do you increase your Combat Power? Either get extremely lucky with gear drops and enhancements, or get lucky enough to have your server win sieges every week.

One of the biggest contributors to your Combat Power is something called Stigma Shards, most of which come from the Abyss, a server-versus-server PvP zone.

You complete quests there, but the most important activity is Corridors: instanced events where you kill monsters for a ton of Abyss Points, which you then use to buy Stigma Shards.

Here's the funny part: twice a week, your server has to fight in sieges to gain access to these Corridors (you can have up to three). And if you're unlucky like me, you'll be matched against a whale server and end up with zero access to Corridors, or even the entire Abyss, because they'll literally spawn-camp you to death.

And to make things worse, the Abyss is where you get the majority of your Stigma Shards. So good luck!

**3. The crafting system**

Oh my god. I don't even want to talk about this because it's realllllly evil. I could write an entire essay about this system alone.

Just know that if you want to craft ONLY your weapon, depending on your server and how lucky you are, you'll need somewhere between 100 and 300 million Kina on average. And that's IF you're lucky. If not, I can't even imagine how much you'll need.

And here's a fun fact: you can actually fail to craft your weapon even with MAX proficiency. So good luck with that!

**4. LUDRA**

This might be one of the biggest fuck-ups of the year.

The first raid this game decided to give us was literally unbeatable. It didn't matter how skilled you were or how many times you tried; it was practically impossible to clear.

The game set the requirement for the raid at 2,800 Gear Score, which isn't particularly difficult to reach if you've managed to survive everything I mentioned above.

But here's the funny part: even at 2,800 GS (roughly 160–180K Combat Power if you've done a lot of horizontal content), you have almost a 0% chance of killing this thing, no matter how many times you try.

The damage checks in this raid are disgusting. My entire guild spent the whole week trying to clear it, with an average of 2,950 GS and 190K Combat Power, and our best attempt got Ludra down to 42%.

The main issue, besides its massive HP pool, is the time limit. You only have ONE hour to defeat all three extremely tanky bosses. And if you run out of time, you don't just get to fight the last boss again. Nope, you have to run the ENTIRE raid all over again.

And what's even funnier is that I'm ONLY talking about NORMAL LUDRA. Hard Ludra is a whole different story. :D

The only group that managed to clear it on our server was a group with a dude literally called "Giga Whale", who had 280K Combat Power, and the entire group was on a similar level.

So yeah, totally achievable, I guess. :D

I could go on for hours explaining why I wouldn't recommend this game, but I think you get the point by now. :D

# AION 2 – Great Potential, Terrible Design Decisions and Monetization

**200+ hours played – NOT RECOMMENDED**

After spending over 200 hours playing AION 2, I can honestly say that the more I play, the more disappointed I become with the direction this game is taking.

At first, AION 2 had a lot of potential. Beautiful graphics, an interesting world, enjoyable combat, flying mechanics and plenty of things to explore. Unfortunately, the longer you play, the more you realize how many unnecessary restrictions, frustrating systems and questionable design decisions are built into the game.

Here are my main issues.

**1. MARKET AND SUBSCRIPTION SYSTEM**

One of the most ridiculous decisions is locking access to the Market behind a monthly subscription (Special Quai Membership), costing approximately €13–15.

This is supposed to be a Free-to-Play MMORPG, yet an essential part of the MMORPG experience, buying and selling items with other players, is locked behind a monthly payment.

And even after paying, you can still encounter additional restrictions that prevent you from selling certain items because of gameplay activity requirements.

Why should an essential MMORPG feature be locked behind a subscription in the first place?

**2. CRAFTING AND GATHERING – TOO MUCH RNG**

Why does crafting have a chance to FAIL? And why can gathering resources fail as well?

You invest hours farming materials, leveling your professions and working towards a specific item, only to potentially lose your hard-earned resources because of RNG.

Even reaching the maximum profession level doesn't necessarily guarantee success.

This isn't meaningful progression. It is frustration disguised as a game mechanic.

For Free-to-Play players, recovering from these failures can be particularly painful because of the amount of time required to farm everything again.

Instead of rewarding dedication and preparation, the game makes you gamble with the time you have already invested.

**3. ODYLE ENERGY SYSTEM**

Another unnecessary limitation is the Odyle Energy system.

Your ability to farm dungeon rewards is restricted, meaning you cannot simply play as much as you want and receive rewards for your effort.

An MMORPG should encourage players to spend time playing, farming and progressing together. Instead, AION 2 puts artificial limits on how much meaningful progression you can make.

It also makes helping friends and lower-level players unnecessarily restrictive.

Why punish players for wanting to play together?

**4. REPETITIVE GRIND AND LACK OF MEANINGFUL PROGRESSION**

A huge part of the game revolves around repeating the same activities over and over again just to collect materials, improve your equipment and increase your Combat Power.

Grinding is a normal part of MMORPGs. I understand that.

But there is a difference between rewarding grinding and forcing players into endless repetitive activities with limited rewards and unnecessary restrictions.

After 200+ hours, I find myself asking whether I am actually progressing or simply repeating the same tasks every day.

**5. MATCHMAKING AND COMBAT POWER GATEKEEPING**

The group recruitment and matchmaking experience is another major disappointment.

You can have 2600 Gear Score, but if you don't have approximately 130K Combat Power, you may struggle to find a group.

Hard Mode is not necessarily difficult because of its mechanics. Sometimes the hardest part is simply finding a team willing to accept you.

Players are being rejected based on arbitrary CP requirements rather than actual experience, equipment, understanding of mechanics or ability to play their class.

This creates unnecessary barriers and makes group content far more frustrating than it should be.

**6. BOTS AND THE ECONOMY**

Bots are another serious problem in an MMORPG.

They compete with legitimate players for gathering nodes and resources, negatively affecting the economy and making an already frustrating gathering system even worse.

When legitimate players have to compete against automated accounts just to collect basic materials, something is clearly wrong.

On top of that, the lack of normal player-to-player trading makes the whole experience feel even less like a proper MMORPG.

**7. LEGION SYSTEM AND THE MISSING MMO EXPERIENCE**

For a game advertised as an MMORPG, there is surprisingly little incentive to build a proper community.

Legions should be an important part of the experience. They should encourage cooperation, group activities, shared progression, events and meaningful interactions between members.

Instead, the social aspect feels underdeveloped.

Where are the meaningful Legion activities? Where are the systems that encourage members to help each other and build a real community?

Even older MMORPGs, including the original AION, understood how important these systems were.

An MMORPG should bring people together, not make so many activities feel like a solo experience.

**8. MONETIZATION EVERYWHERE**

What makes all these problems even worse is the feeling that many of these restrictions are designed around monetization.

Market access requires a subscription. Progression involves layers of RNG. Farming is restricted. Crafting can destroy your accumulated resources.

At some point, it becomes difficult not to question whether these systems are designed to improve gameplay or simply encourage players to spend more money when they become frustrated.

I have absolutely no problem paying for a good game. What I have a problem with is being constantly pushed towards additional payments just to enjoy basic MMORPG features.

**FINAL THOUGHTS**

The most disappointing thing about AION 2 is that the game actually has potential.

The graphics are beautiful, the world is interesting, the combat can be enjoyable and there are plenty of ideas that could have made this a fantastic MMORPG.

But potential means very little when the actual gameplay experience is filled with unnecessary restrictions, repetitive grinding, excessive RNG, monetization barriers and systems that discourage cooperation.

After more than 200 hours, I don't feel that my time as a player is being respected.

I don't want everything handed to me. I don't expect free rewards or effortless progression. I am perfectly fine with grinding, challenging content and working towards difficult goals.

I bought a four-month subscription to unlock trading. I wasn't expecting unlimited power, but I also wasn't expecting to pay for a game that runs out of things for me to do after a couple of hours. The most consistent reward so far is more free time outside the game.

To complete the experience, server transfers have been disabled, leaving me stuck on a Turkish-speaking server where I struggle to communicate or find groups. An MMO where I can barely talk to anyone and quickly run out of meaningful activities is certainly an interesting interpretation of “massively multiplayer.”

What makes this frustrating is that I actually want to play. I want to gather, craft, improve my gear, and join a community. Yet every system seems determined to answer that enthusiasm with “daily limit reached.”

Don't Let the Korean MMO's Bad Reputation Scare You Away!

I was very skeptical before giving the game a try. Usually, Korean MMOs have huge pay-to-win walls, but AION 2 is not like that. Of course, paying to get Kina speeds up the process, but farming a bit and playing the content allows you to progress smoothly, just like everyone else.
The pass is necessary to make things faster, exactly like in every other MMO. It's just 13 euros, and that's literally the only thing I've bought (except for a very pretty fox mount, which is purely aesthetic).
Saying that the pass is a paywall is just stupid. In MANY MMOs, you can't even enter the game without buying a pass. Here, you can play completely for free and do all the content you want FOR FREE, except for the market, which unlocks at level 45 but cannot be used without the pass. It's not a big deal at all, and it's meant to prevent bots, which would obviously ruin the game economy, just like in many, many other games.
The grind is actually very pleasant. It's not designed to be so tedious and painful that you end up thinking, "Oh yeah, I'll just pay to avoid all this." It's really not worth it. I farm my own materials and run dungeons and Transcendence, which give A LOT of money, and the rewards increase with the difficulty.

The game runs super smoothly for such a graphically impressive game, except, of course, during world bosses and PvP events, when you have 200 people flying around and fighting at the same time.
The combat is incredibly smooth and fluid, and the late-game content is insanely challenging, which I absolutely love!

Things I dislike

1. The pass being server-bound -.-

I accidentally unlocked my pass on my Asmodian character, only to find out that it's not account-wide but server-bound. Oh boy, that pissed me off.

2. Cross-faction interaction

We're a premade group of three Elyos players and one Asmodian friend. I can't even send a friend request to our Asmodian friend! For him to join our dungeons, he has to search for the room name every single time. It's such a clunky and unnecessary system. I really hope they change this in the future.

3. Dungeon entry limit

The limit of 10 dungeons without claiming the chest is way too low. It should be at least 20, not 10. I need to keep a couple of attempts in reserve in case I crash, because if the counter reaches zero, you can't enter any more dungeons. I  want to be able to help my friends with their runs without constantly worrying about running out of attempts. That's really frustrating.

Conclusion
Overall, it's a great game with a lot of potential. I'm really enjoying my time in AION 2 and definitely think it's worth giving it a try!

500+ hours and the progression feels amazing

I've played over 500 hours since the game went free-to-play, and I can confidently say it is one of the best MMOs I've ever played. The sense of progression is simply addictive.

What makes Aion special:
- **Constant progression**: You gain combat power from absolutely everything you do. It doesn't matter if it's an event, a raid, a daily task, or PvP—you are always getting stronger. This feeling of continuous growth is incredibly addictive.
- **Fast and fluid combat**: Every skill feels great to use, combos are satisfying, and everything flows perfectly. Nothing feels slow or clunky.
- **Polished experience**: Everything runs smooth, from the interface to the visual effects. You can tell the game is well-optimized.
- **Genuinely Free-to-Play**: You can enjoy the full game without paying a dime. The subscription doesn't affect your competitive standing or progress at all if you aren't into rushing or competitive PvP. Subscribing is purely for convenience and time-saving.

**What the subscription actually does:**
It's basically a convenience pack. The main perks are:
- Accessing your store and storage (Baúl) from anywhere, literally.
- Claiming double rewards at the end of Expeditions (dungeons).
- Access to a special shop to buy more energy (to run more dungeons) and an auto-loot feature for your pets.

If you want an MMO where every minute played makes you stronger and features agile combat, AION 2 is the one. 9/10, highly recommended.

A Familiar Free-to-Play Treadmill That Isn't Worth Your Time

The Bottom Line: TLDR
Aion 2 may be free to download, but your time has value. With better alternative MMORPGs available, this is one title you can safely skip.
[hr][/hr]
Unless you go in fully aware of its heavy structural flaws, I cannot recommend Aion 2. If you are looking for a deep, rewarding MMORPG experience akin to World of Warcraft, Final Fantasy XIV, Guild Wars 2, or even classic titles like EverQuest, you will not find it here. While those established games certainly have their own shortcomings, every one of them offers a vastly superior return on your time investment.

At its core, Aion 2 constantly leaves you asking: Is this supposed to be a mobile game? From the heavy reliance on AI-generated assets to the restrictive "energy gating" systems that throttle content, the design choices feel less like an epic PC MMORPG and more like a mobile title designed to squeeze players.

The leveling process from 1 to 45 is actually reasonably smooth, but that is largely where the enjoyment ends. The narrative fails to grab attention early on—I found myself skipping dialogue around level 10—and once you hit level 45, the game shifts entirely to an endless gear-score chase. This transition immediately kills the experience, collapsing the endgame into a dull, repetitive, and tedious cycle.   

The crafting and enhancement systems only compound the frustration. Progression relies heavily on punitive RNG upgrades where hours of grinding can instantly be wiped out by losing a piece of gear when an upgrade breaks. While failure penalties are a known staple in some Korean MMORPGs, here it simply feels like a artificial sink designed to set players back rather than engaging them with actual, challenging content.

Monetization and UI design also present major red flags:
> Gacha-Style Microtransactions: The game bombards players with a dizzying array of distinct currencies for its various menu stores. Cosmetic items and basic in-game shop prices are wildly inflated.
> Pay-to-Win Concerns: While I avoided open-world PvP and the player market—and thus dodged the worst of the pay-to-win elements reported by other players—the underlying push toward spending is everywhere.
> Aggressive Pricing: As a free-to-play title, it is understandable that the developer needs to generate revenue, and I felt okay buying a low-priced cosmetic wing set early on. However, the pricing structure for almost everything else quickly escalates into territory that is simply not worth the asking price.

This will be a long one. The TL:DR is: A decent game on the surface with its positives and negatives, none of which matter because it's plagued by the East's increasing hyperfixation with pay to win mechanics and actively punishing those that don't.

I have a lot of time. For example, I have 10000 hours in Lost Ark, and I absolutely will not reach that here, because while that game was pay to win, it didn't force me to come to terms with the fact that it was. I would be weaker, I wouldn't always be able to clear new content week 1, but I didn't have to interact with the pay to winners beyond selling them materials and then selling them their gold back for pay to win currency, and for the most part, I'd eventually get the same thing the pay to winners paid for by simply playing the game. I've played this game to death by now and I can safely say that isn't the case in Aion 2.

I won't bore you with the details of the standard. The game looks gorgeous and you'll have plenty of eyecandy akin to most of its predecessors, the levelling is nothing to write home about but doesn't outlast its welcome and the initial post-levelling progression (sidequests, other one-time content) isn't too bad. The only issue here is that it's not optional since they give skill points.

The game runs on an energy system and gives you two things to spend it on for vertical upgrades. You'll be expected to grind the exact same 5-man dungeons (6 for gear, 2 for skill improving cards) on varying difficulties over 50 times a piece. Some more, some fewer, depending on your luck, but even when you're done with all that you still want to spend your energy since it's the primary way to earn currency as well. The dungeons tend to be relatively fun and some have a few cool mechanics that keep you on your toes. This is still not directly where the problem really shows itself yet, though it eventually would without more variance and already does for some since 40+ runs of the same dungeon a week is a lot.

Aside from that, there's a lot of things you can do for horizontal power. You can farm mobs in the open world to learn them as mounts (absolutely incredible design, credit where it's due, to have almost every monster be a viable mount), which give power from more kills. Achievements for doing literally any type of content in the game give titles that give power. Unlocking more wings for flying gives power. Unlocking skins (transmog) gives power. It's a collector's wet dream in that regard, and I'm all for it, though I can see this being a problem in the long term since it's very unwelcome to new players since it adds a mountain of content to catch up on if they want to be equal. But they won't be anyway because of the pay to win.

Then there's some daily/weekly content, generally giving mandatory but limited horizontal power, none of which are too obnoxious since you can ignore most of them after a while if you really don't like them, with the exception of Shugo, a bunch of minigames every hour in which you compete against other players, which ironically gives you some of the most consistent player power. They get boring fast, and will likely burn people out, since you get to do 2-3 of those a day.

But all that pales in comparison to the crafting. The crafting in this game is so bad it would've stained the entire game even if everything else was great. First of, it's literally impossible to do completely free to play. You NEED the subscription (can't get it with the pay to win shop currency for some reason) to be able to use the market and without the market you will never, ever, get enough materials to craft let alone maintain a single piece of equipment. But you don't want a single piece of equipment. You want every single piece of crafted equipment. Because crafted gear is better than any other item you can get in the game by a long shot. It has more stats and it has more item level. Literally being afk in town can get you more power than any amount of time you spend in dungeons ever will. This extends to the recently added raid, because even that gear is worse. This won't ever change. And this is not realistic for even a small payer to keep up with. The material requirement is something that even the whales will struggle with maintaining, not because they can't afford it but because the market is just going to be empty due to dwindling supply as more and more people quit. You have to craft the item which is a (give or take) 20% on top of a 20% on top of a 20% on top of a 20% and if any of those steps fail you're back to square one. And if you do succeed, you'll just have the base item, but at least you're past the resetting part. Then you need to consistently upgrade it which with current prices costs more currency for a single step than you'll get in a week's worth of dungeon runs and these prices are already increasing due to aforementioned dwinding supply, despite bots carrying supply right now.

Now, this is just standard pay to win. Other Asian MMOs have had items you couldn't obtain as free to play player, and those slots can be filled with inferior items all the same. However, the problem is you can't avoid these players. You're literally whale food because of the pseudo-forced PvP. Every single piece of PvP in this game that gives any reward whatsoever is unscaled. So these players can flaunt their crafted gear in your face and you will quite literally not have a chance because the game's stats are designed in a way that being outgeared means you will do 1 damage to them and they will kill you in 1 hit, with varying levels of unfairness depending on how outgeared you are, but that's the crux of it. And while you can ignore most PvP content, it's fairly hard to ignore all of it, especially the Abyss (a PvP zone with 0 redeeming qualities), because a large amount of horizontal power is locked behind Abyss Points, which you can only earn through PvP activities and going into the Abyss, where the whales really get to showcase just how much they spent, and oh my are they willing.

Outskilling isn't an option either regardless of how good you are, because I haven't touched on the combat of the game yet. The combat is fun enough, but to call it anywhere near complex would be a disservice to complex games. You don't have too many buttons, and you are not just incentivized but practically forced to throw most of them into the in-game macro system that will autocast everything put into it for you by holding the macro, since it has automated animation cancelling and the game's attacks become so quick that it's humanly impossible to do manually. It's fine-ish for PvE since the complexity tends to come from executing the boss encounters but in PvP it's literally just a stat check, since the whales just hold their macro and blow you away with a near perfect rotation without any real player input.

The biggest culprit of the Abyss stems from the large scripted server vs server battles. It's just a PvE shitshow of killing some mob in 3 different places, and if it being a PvE objective in a PvP zone wasn't dumb enough, the server that wins is literally just the one that last hits it. So it's pure luck. And due to the scale of it, to avoid your PC from melting on the spot, players from your own server don't even load in, let alone those from the other server. And if you don't win them, you're fucked on Abyss points until the next battle, because these mobs turn into a small 2 minute instance where you just murder a bunch of mobs for a whole lot of Abyss points. But alas, even if your team last hits them, the other server will just camp the entrance until next battle so it's not like you can enter them anyway, since the only other realistic way to earn Abyss points is by farming other players in the Abyss.

I can rant more but I'm running out of space. If the above isn't convincing you to skip, the rest won't bother you either. I'm finishing this season (sunk cost etc.), then I'm out too.

[h1] A enjoyable MMORPG (Don't let the negative reviews Fool You) [/h]

I think a lot of people are forgetting one very important thing: AION 2 is a [b] free-to-play [/b] game. And honestly, we've seen exactly the same situation before with games like Lost Ark, Throne and Liberty, etc. A large part of the negative reviews seem to come from frustrated players who want to play 24/7, become the number one player on the server, and have the best gear available as quickly as possible. When they realize that progression takes time, or that other players have better equipment, they get frustrated and leave a negative review.

Let's get one thing straight from the beginning: yes, the game has paid elements. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. However, most of them are completely optional if you are willing to progress at a normal pace. For example, buying additional OD energy is practically pointless if you don't even have the time to run your dungeons. Paying to speed up progression doesn't automatically mean you are winning, especially when you still need the time and effort to actually play the content. There is a big difference between paying to save time and being forced to pay to enjoy the game.

Putting the Pay-to-Win debate aside, there is genuinely great things:

The graphics are incredible. The dungeon environments are beautiful, the armor textures are extremely detailed, and the overall character design is fantastic. Playing at 4K and 120 FPS makes the visual experience even better. One of my favorite features is being able to dismantle equipment to obtain skins, which adds another layer of customization. Character creation is so enjoyable that I easily spent three hours creating individual characters. There is a surprising amount of satisfaction in building a character that looks exactly the way you want.

The class designs are also very well done. I enjoy the abilities and combat system, although I would personally love to see more visual variety in spells, more vibrant effects, and a greater sense of visual impact during combat. I would also like more flexibility when equipping skills and using macros. Macros make certain classes much easier to play, sometimes reducing the amount of active skill management required. Hopefully, this system will continue to evolve.

Progression and endgame are where things get interesting.

The difficulty gradually increases, equipment becomes harder to obtain, and gathering materials requires more effort as you advance. But isn't that exactly what you expect from an MMORPG? I actually appreciate that dungeons provide guaranteed rewards. Yes, sometimes you have to repeat content several times to obtain what you're looking for, but you're never forced to do so. There are plenty of other activities available.

I love the Abyss system, the Arena, and the team battles. The combination of PvP and PvE, alongside the two different worlds, gives the game a lot of potential. World boss encounters also work surprisingly well. Servers have been running smoothly in my experience, with very little lag, even during large-scale boss encounters.

Another thing I really appreciate is that you can log in for just 15 minutes and still feel like you've made meaningful progress. Side quests provide worthwhile rewards, and there are plenty of activities that make even a short gaming session feel productive. You don't necessarily need to spend your entire day playing to enjoy the game or improve your character.

There are also pets, feathers, Abyss activities, PvP, PvE, the Shugo Festival, and many other activities to explore. I reckon there is something for different types of players here. Not everyone wants to spend their entire gaming experience grinding equipment, and thankfully, the game offers alternatives.

Of course, the game isn't perfect.

The biggest weakness for me is the world itself. It feels quite small and restrictive for an MMORPG. Exploring, collecting feathers, and completing side quests can be enjoyable, but I would love to see a much larger world with more opportunities for exploration.

The story also failed to convince me. I would have loved better cinematics, a much stronger introduction to the world of AION 2, and a deeper explanation of its lore. The graphics engine is beautiful, so I feel the developers could do much more with it from a storytelling perspective. However, I understand that narrative isn't necessarily the main focus of this game.

Professions are another area that could use improvement. They don't feel particularly rewarding or engaging. If you're coming from something like Black Desert, where professions and life skills are a huge part of the experience, you might find them underwhelming. I understand that AION 2 focuses much more on character progression, combat, and endgame content, but I would still love to see more depth in this area.

The cash shop is also very expensive, especially when it comes to skins and convenience items. I won't defend those prices. However, I think it's important to consider the bigger picture: the game is free, and practically all the content currently available can be enjoyed without purchasing expansions or additional content.

Compare that to subscription-based MMORPGs like World of Warcraft or Final Fantasy, where accessing certain content can require subscriptions, expansions, or additional purchases. Here, you can jump in and experience a substantial amount of content without paying anything. Yes, paying can accelerate progression, and free players might need more time to achieve certain goals, but that's a trade-off I'm personally comfortable with.

As for the endgame, I believe we're still seeing the beginning of what this game could become. Current dungeons are relatively simple, and their mechanics aren't particularly demanding. But the content is still developing, and I'm genuinely looking forward to seeing how dungeon complexity, boss mechanics, and endgame challenges evolve as players reach higher levels.

My biggest advice: don't let frustrated players decide whether this game is worth your time.

Some people simply don't enjoy the process of progression anymore. They want to have everything immediately, play endlessly, compete for the number one position on the server, and never feel that another player has an advantage over them. When that doesn't happen, they blame the game.

But MMORPGs have always been about progression, investment, repetition, and gradually building your character. Not every player needs to be the strongest person on the server. Not every piece of equipment needs to drop immediately. And not every gaming session needs to be a race against everyone else.

If you can enjoy the journey instead of constantly comparing your equipment to someone else's, there is a lot to love here.

AION 2 has beautiful graphics, excellent character customization, enjoyable combat, interesting progression systems, smooth server performance, and a variety of activities that make it easy to find something enjoyable regardless of how much time you have available.

It has weaknesses, absolutely. The world needs to be bigger, the story deserves more attention, professions could be much better, and the cash shop is expensive. But none of those things erase what the game already offers.

My recommendation is simple: give it a chance, enjoy the content, take your time, and see where the developers take it.

You didn't pay anything to start playing. If one day you stop enjoying it, you can simply move on. There is no reason to turn a free game into a source of frustration.

I'm genuinely excited to see what the future holds for AION 2. For now, I'm having a great time, and I absolutely recommend giving it a try.

As a brief free-to-play experience, this game can definitely help kill a few dozen hours while being an enjoyable little romp. The graphics are pretty, the character creator is robust (and busty), and the verticality of the world via the Wing system makes travelling fast and easy. Combat is very simple and satisfying when you are first starting out, and there are lots of different sub-activities you can participate in if you get tired of just going to location X to kill Y mobs for the Nth time.

The honeymoon period described above will probably last you through the campaign and the first few tiers of dungeons, until you realize how lackluster and punishingly limited the midgame+ experience of the game is:

- you are limited in the number of times you can interact with the game's primary grinding mechanic, Dungeons, via the Energy system. Save up too much energy? You also have a hard limit of how many dungeons you can run per week before diminishing returns kick in, actively lowering your rewards from the dungeons if you decide to save some energy for a big grinding session for whatever reason

- out of energy and want to just kill mobs to grind money/yellow drops to increase your gear score and power? Sorry, you can only earn a limited amount of money per day, and once you hit that limit (which takes less than an hour if you know what you're doing), mobs will no longer drop money OR items. And to top it off, if you join any Force for a World Boss once this restriction kicks in, your whole Force will be spammed by nonstop drop-related messages, since for some reason your restriction will interfere with other peoples' drops

- out of weekly energy AND at your daily grind limit (something that will happen on Day 1 of a reset if you are an active player and have half a brain)? You can just gather materials in order to interact with the increasingly expensive and RNG-based crafting system, right? Sure, until you hit THAT daily limit as well (which also does not take long, and is account-wide to boot so you can't gather materials on your alts either)

- on top of everything else, if you are unlucky enough to get into an unfair server matchup in the PVP-oriented Abyss system, which is what happened with both matchups that occurred on the server I played on, you will also be effectively locked out of the majority of Abyss points you can earn, which is a significant source of character power

So your only course of action will be to create alts and run the same low-tier dungeons ad nauseam, in order to earn money/crafting mats to pass to your main character to get a single extra roll on an upgrade attempt, or to help cover 1/20th of the cost of crafting a piece of midtier gear. And to top everything else off, because combat is macro-oriented and there are no different builds to explore within each class, there is very little difference between the actual classes, and most combat encounters will play out in extremely similar ways, with 1-2 small variations. So playing your different class alts will not enrich your gameplay in any meaningful way.

TLDR: enjoy the F2P experience for a few dozen hours, maybe throw a single-time Subscription purchase to unlock the Marketplace and vastly improve your QOL and progression speed if you REALLY like the pretty graphics. But don't go into this hoping for a well-defined and rewarding long-term experience, because this game will literally actively prevent you from playing it for more than a few hours a day, while rewarding botters/whales with an unbalanced PVP environment and multiple time-gated systems.

Would you recommend this game? NoI’ve put in 356 hours, and I can’t recommend Aion 2 in its current state. The core problem isn’t just bugs or balance—it’s that the game is built around systems that feel designed to pressure players into spending rather than rewarding time and skill.The technical side is rough. The engine crashes more than it should for a live-service MMO, and server performance is inconsistent. Lag spikes, rubber-banding, and delayed responses show up often enough that it actively hurts both PvE and PvP. When you’re already dealing with timed systems and competitive content, these issues make the game feel unreliable.The bigger issue is the design. Many of the progression and reward systems work like slot machines. Limited energy/resources, gated access, and reward structures that lean heavily on chance create a loop that constantly pushes players toward the cash shop. This is an MMO, not a casino, yet the way power, convenience, and progression are gated encourages whale spending far more than traditional grinding or skill. Soft pressure is everywhere—through inventory limits, energy regeneration, faction/server imbalance, and systems that make non-paying players feel like they’re falling further behind. Over time it conditions people to spend just to keep up or to feel like their time isn’t being wasted.NCSOFT has prioritized monetization density over a healthy long-term MMO experience. When the primary way to meaningfully progress or stay competitive is through repeated spending (or dealing with RMT and imbalance that the systems themselves help create), the game stops feeling like an MMO and starts feeling like a live-service product engineered to extract money. After hundreds of hours, that design philosophy is the main reason I’m quitting.

One of the biggest issues right now is the timer on both the Abyss and rifting.  Two out of the game's three maps are time locked, and if I'm being honest I do understand the rifting time-limit somewhat, but the Abyss one does not make sense.  The only thing I could think of was that since it's such a small map (compared to the Abyss in Aion 1), they have to time-gate it so it doesn't get too crowded.  Frankly, that's a game-design problem and the players should not have to be punished for it.  If the Abyss was so huge in 2009, it can be re-worked now and the time-gate can be eliminated...

Another issue I have is the restriction placed on the amounts of dungeons I do PER WEEK and PER ACCOUNT if I don't collect Od Boxes after a run.  If I want to help a new player out, or if want to continue running dungeons with my friends just for fun despite not needing that dungeon's gear, I don't see why I should be punished and locked out of ALL other dungeons if I don't collect 10 boxes that week.  Let me play your game with my friends.  For context:  Dungeons have a loot box at the end, you need to spend energy to access that loot box.  If you don't collect that loot box, you get a strike.  You can get up to 10 strikes a week, if you get 10, then you're locked out of ALL the dungeons the game offers for that week.

The last issue that bothers me the most is the market being behind a paywall and the new gathering restrictions.  After the gathering restrictions were placed, items in the market began to slowly creep up in price.  Crafting gear is now more expensive than it was at launch. As a fan of the original AION, I was genuinely looking forward to this game. I wanted to experience what made the original so special: open-world PvP, massive faction battles, rifts into enemy territory, a living economy, meaningful guild content, and a real sense of community.

I've been playing since launch, for about a month now, so this isn't a review based on just a few hours of gameplay.

Instead, I got a typical Korean mobile P2W cash grab wrapped in pretty graphics, designed to squeeze as much money out of players as possible.

Here are the biggest problems:

Aggressive Pay-to-Win monetization. Subscriptions, Battle Passes, premium currencies, and the ability to buy your way through progression. Almost every aspect of the game has been monetized.

Premium is practically mandatory. I paid for a premium subscription once, and I can confidently say that playing without it is almost impossible if you have a job, a social life, or literally anything else to do. Unless you're willing to spend an absurd amount of time grinding, you're simply doomed to fall behind. This game doesn't respect your time — it expects either your money or your entire life.

Mobile game mechanics in a PC MMORPG. Od Energy, daily and weekly limits, gazillion of achievements for logging, endless timers, and artificial restrictions everywhere. The game constantly dictates when, how much, and how often you're allowed to play.

The social aspect of an MMORPG is practically nonexistent. No direct player-to-player trading. You can't freely share items with your friends or even transfer gear between your own characters. Meaningful guild content is almost nonexistent. In a supposedly full-fledged MMORPG, this is absolutely ridiculous. They even disable chat every now and then, so you cant communicate at all - in an MMO game.

Disappointing PvP. Instead of the freedom and massive faction battles that made the original AION great, we get time-gated activities, gear imbalance, and a massive advantage for players willing to spend real money.

The servers are infested with bots. After just one month, the situation is already ridiculous. My server is absolutely crawling with bots. In a game where the economy and progression are already deeply flawed, this makes things even worse.

RNG and endless grinding. You can spend hours farming materials only to lose your progress because of a failed upgrade or crafting attempt. Your time and effort mean very little.

Poor optimization. The graphics genuinely look great — probably the only clear positive I can give this game. Unfortunately, the optimization leaves a lot to be desired.

The worst part is that underneath the beautiful graphics, almost nothing remains of what made the original AION special.

This is not a worthy successor to a classic MMORPG. It's a mobile P2W game disguised as a proper PC MMO, built to exploit the nostalgia of longtime fans.

The longer I play, the more obvious it becomes that NCSoft cares far more about monetizing every possible aspect of the experience than actually delivering a good MMORPG.

If you're looking for the original AION experience, don't waste your time.

Aion 2 was genuinely fun in the beginning, but the longer I played, the more repetitive and frustrating it became.

The gameplay eventually turns into an endless dungeon grind. You just keep running the same dungeons over and over, hoping for drops that rarely happen. What started as an enjoyable experience quickly became a repetitive chore.

Crafting is probably my biggest disappointment. I've always loved crafting and gathering in MMORPGs. I usually prefer taking my time, exploring the world, gathering materials along the way, and progressing at my own pace. But Aion 2 completely discourages that playstyle. You can't even properly gather materials until level 45, which essentially forces you to rush through leveling just to participate in a basic MMORPG activity. On top of that, crafting itself is heavily RNG-based, making the entire system more frustrating than rewarding.

The world is beautiful, but the performance is terrible. The environments look amazing, but optimization is a serious issue, especially in the Abyss. Any area with a large number of players becomes virtually unplayable. I'm talking about 10 FPS in crowded areas, which is unacceptable for a game where large-scale PvP is supposed to be a major feature.

Progression is also ridiculously expensive. Drop rates are extremely low, crafting materials are costly, and the resources you earn through normal gameplay barely cover what you need to progress. It feels like you're constantly spending more than you're earning, turning progression into an exhausting grind.

It has a beautiful world and a genuinely enjoyable foundation, but it's held back by repetitive content, terrible crafting and gathering restrictions, poor optimization, and an unrewarding progression system.

I wanted to enjoy the journey, explore the world, gather materials, craft equipment, and progress naturally. Instead, the game pushes you to rush to level 45, repeatedly grind dungeons, and fight against RNG at nearly every step.

There's a good MMORPG underneath all of this, but right now it feels more like a second job than a game.

First up the free to play restrictions are really off putting. You can do the story and lots of side content fine, but when you start running dungeons the half loot rate gets really obnoxious really fast. And the dreams of crafting an actually useful upgrade from the last quest reward weapon vanish when you realise how many dungeons you have to run.

Anyway...

The standard monthly €12.75 PER SERVER subscription (Special Quai Membership) gets you (among other things):

* Access to the marketplace
* The ability to buy (for in-game currency) automatic loot pickup for a month 
* Double loot from each dungeon run, at the cost of double energy

There is no player to player trading. Without the subscription marketplace you will be farming any materials by yourself like it was a single player game with MMO drop rates.

Every kind of content in the game is gated behind some kind of ticket system. If you're a weekend gamer who wants to just sit down and farm the next dungeon for upgrades, beware. The dungeon ticket system lets you save up 840 Energy (less if you don't pay for a subscription), which is enough for 10.5 runs of full loot.

Each run takes about 5 minutes depending on the dungeon once everyone knows mechanics. So that's 1 hour of fun, and then you're waiting for the energy to regen at a rate of 15 per 3 hours, i.e. a new full loot 5 minute run every 16 hours.

If you think that's too slow, don't worry NCSOFT has the solution! You can buy the 35 day premium pass for another €12.75 PER CHARACTER and get another 80 energy every 3 days. Combined with the daily energy regen you can have 30 minutes of dungeon running fun every 3 days!

Subscribers can also buy another 800 energy per week for 2 million in-game currency, and any can craft another 800 weekly.

You're paying a subscription (or two) and they're artificially kneecapping how fast you can go each week.

Other systems are on a fixed timer and most of the systems are required if you want to level up skills. Want the skill shards from Shugo Festival? Better drop what you're doing every hour so you can do 5 minutes of mini games. You get 3 keys per day and you have to wait an hour between using each of them.



The cosmetic system is obnoxious. You have to salvage an item to have a chance to unlock the skin, 10%-25% depending on the rarity of the item. I target farmed a specific dungeon for 70 runs to unlock a dungeon specific set before I gave up and by the end I had 3 out of 7 skins. I also didn't have a full set of the actual useful armour drops from that dungeon.

On top of that it will cost you real life money to dye any of the armour. Besides the few vouchers they've given away as Twitch drops it will cost you €2.5 for every single item you want to dye. And the dye is locked to that item across all your characters.



The Abyss mass PVP system is massively laggy during any of the boss fights and the special bi-weekly Siege event. If your server is outnumbered, you're not winning the siege event or getting a boss kill. If your server is outnumbered you're probably not going to be able to do your weekly solo missions in Abyss unless you bring your guild (Legion) along or play in the middle of the night.  
If you're behind on gear because you started the game later than others, you'll die in 1 second because the gear matters that much. You can go play in the standard gear section of Abyss where you can't do your weeklies, there are no bosses, and the rewards are reduced by 50%-66%.



On a more positive note some of the game mechanics are actually fun. The game systems developers could probably make a very fun game if they worked for a company that wasn't so focused on extracting money from their customers.

The boss fights are well telegraphed and while you can eventually outgear most stuff it's been quite fun doing the solo bosses while still undergeared and trying to solo the 5-man dungeons when I had enough gear to survive and still beat the enrage timers. 

Playing a Gladiator it has been interesting seeing the class progression with each new upgrade. From basic build/spender, to removing cooldowns from a key skill, to being able to dynamically reduce cooldowns on all skills on hit for short durations, and eventually to getting free 100% crit chance for the key skill in the future. 

The fact that you can (and should) currently put 90% of your skills into a priority macro does make the game feel more like I'm playing Path of Exile rather than a traditional MMO.

[h2]Game Experience & PvP Issues[/h2]
Currently, I am a 2603 ilvl and 123.3k power cleric with an alt that is a 1358 ilvl gladiator. This game, basically, is a mobile game in terms of gameplay. PvP is a gear check when running solo, and for server PvP, the side that has more players wins. Because the other server has more players, our server was losing everything in cross-server PvP and everything around that. Basically, the people trying just die every single time trying to get whatever.
[h2]Dungeon Restrictions & Alt Progression[/h2]
Dungeons have limited access by currency. Also, if you run a dungeon and don't use the currency, you only get 10 tries. If you use those 10 times, you cannot enter dungeons anymore, even if you have currency, so you cannot help others either. There are too many restrictions for alt characters, and too much content is restricted by server instead of by character. Furthermore, dungeons in hard mode drop the same gear, even though the difference in requirements goes from 1400 to 2600~2700 ilvl.
[h2]The Bot Epidemic[/h2]
Bots are everywhere, and the updates look more like "devs vs. bots" than actual features. Bots can run dungeons, and this is bad because—even though they do all the mechanics and are better than some players—at the end of the day, they just break the market, farming spots, and materials collection. Even the PvP zones have bots.
[h2]Unfair Reward Mechanics[/h2]
In the latest dungeons, you can get zero rewards because you have no contribution on the last boss. Preventing someone from just leeching is okay, but I am in the final difficulty of the dungeon. Now, I need to verify that others have enough damage to do the dungeon, but I also need to see if they are more powerful than me just so I can get my rewards. Rewards are based on damage, which is a number I cannot even see unless I use a DPS meter or something.
[h2]Pay-to-Win Aspects & Final Thoughts[/h2]
The amount of tries and gear that you can get with the battle pass is significantly more. Claiming twice per run with the pass saves too much time, and being able to buy currency to do dungeons is too much as well. I don't mind gatekeeping normally because I am a healer and I play with randoms, since for me, people who filter by power are just bad. However, my alt can get kicked for no reason, even though I could just play with the bots instead and don't need anything else to run a dungeon properly. Finally, if I just uninstall, they will remove my character in 6 months, so I am probably never going to return.

Aion 1 vs. Aion 2: A Step Backward for True MMORPG Fans

Combat & Gameplay: Streamlined but Boring
Aion 2 comes with improvements regarding the number of skills; the character is much easier to play thanks to the macro system and the significantly smaller number of skills. On the other hand, it becomes boring because, by pressing practically just two buttons, you clear the map of mobs.

Progression: Overcomplicated Mechanics
The character progression system regarding skills is complicated, considering that Daevanion skills, stigmas, wings, pets, plus costumes, manastones, and trade stones, etc., are all mixed together.

Economy & Crafting: The Paywall Problem
Aion 1 on the NA (North American) servers had a free, non-paywalled market, which led Europeans to play there despite the internet latency (ping). This gave you access to the crafting system; plus, making money was a whole progression path in itself. In Aion 2, this is missing for non-paying players.

Monetization: Overpriced Subscription
The subscription fee of 15 euros for 28 days—which means paying 13 times a year—is too high for these features.

Dungeons & Group Content: No More Holy Trinity
In terms of gameplay, another major factor is that dungeons (instances) contain mobs that have no loot at all, leading players to just rush through them. Because of this, players no longer have their required roles in instances, such as tank, healer, or DPS.

Conclusion: A Lonely Experience
Overall, it feels like an MMO that you play solo.

Dear NCSoft developers!

I am addressing you as a player and asking you to pay attention to a number of critical issues that seriously detract from the gaming experience and lead to player attrition.

Observation 1. Lack of balance between beginners and high‑level players in the “Abyss.” At level 45, through quests, I enter the “Abyss,” where the system requires me to kill a условных 10 mobs. However, it’s impossible to complete the task: players from the enemy faction (even those of rank 1, but with strong equipment) kill me with a single button press. A beginner has no chance to fight back. This situation is perceived as unfair and demotivates them from continuing the game.

Note 2. Problems caused by server mergers: terrorizing beginners by “overleveled” players. After the servers are merged, experienced players with high‑level equipment systematically hinder beginners: they seize artifacts, prevent them from completing quests and gathering ether in peace. This creates not a competitive but a depressing environment, where new players have no real opportunities for progress.

Remark 3. The growth of toxicity and aggression between factions. The current imbalance provokes aggression between players, which goes beyond healthy competition and escalates into outright hostility towards members of the other faction. This destroys the atmosphere of the project and drives players away.

Remark 4. Inefficiency of the crafting system. In its current implementation, crafting high‑level items is economically and practically infeasible: enormous resources are spent on creating equipment, while items with better stats can be obtained in dungeons. Because of this, players see no point in mastering crafting mechanics.

Remark 5. Scant energy reserves and lack of content. The amount of energy provided daily for dungeon runs is negligible — it lasts for just a couple of trips. After that, there’s simply nothing to do in the game: no enticing activities, no alternative ways to progress. Players exhaust everything the game offers in a day within 30–40 minutes and leave, because there’s simply no point in continuing. In successful projects, players always have something to do even without combat content — events, individual locations, mini‑games, social activities.

Note 6. The lack of reliance on the experience of successful projects. In the MMO genre, solutions to the problems you stubbornly ignore have long been found. It makes sense to look up to recognized projects:

TERA Online — the player’s actions matter: proper dodging and skills allow even a less‑equipped player to stand up to a strong opponent. This makes PvP fair, rather than a matter of “whoever invested more is right.” In your game, the outcome of a battle is decided solely by the number of GS, which completely devalues skill.
Black Desert Online — instead of harsh faction wars with the suppression of newcomers, optional zones and systems have been introduced, where experienced players don’t “farm” newcomers, and a newcomer can always level up safely. Moreover, BDO doesn’t have a crafting failure: crafted and assembled items are quite competitive with dropped ones.
Lost Ark — daily activities with a clear but generous energy limit: the player doesn’t feel like they’re locked in for half an hour, while the content is scheduled for the whole day.
These projects have been around for years precisely because they respect the player’s time and progress. You, on the other hand, seem to be learning from other developers’ mistakes in reverse: you take their most controversial mechanics, remove the mitigating measures, and exacerbate the consequences.

I have no intention of playing your project again until these mistakes are fixed. Please analyze the identified issues and make the necessary adjustments: ensure protection for newcomers in PvP zones, revise the crafting economy, increase the daily energy reserve, and add content after it is used up; also, refer back to the experience of TERA, BDO, and Lost Ark as reference points.

TL;DR: The foundation is great, but the mobile-game mechanics are awful. The game slowly but steadily burns you out with timed events, progression gates, RNG crafting, and endless chores.

For context, I reached 2,300 Gear Score and 110K Combat Power as a Ranger.

I highly recommend Fubgun's guide. I'm a certified Fubgooner at this point.

The good:

+Character customization is incredibly detailed.
+The world is gorgeous.
+Combat is simple (thanks to macros), yet snappy and satisfying.
+Flying feels amazing. It's a shame you can't fly more often.
+Bosses are great and genuinely fun to master.

The bad:

Subscription: You can technically play the endgame without a subscription, but you'll suffer for it. Realistically, it feels mandatory.

Wasted open world: Remember that beautiful world I mentioned? Throw it in the trash. You'll spend most of your endgame life as a dungeon slave (assuming you have enough energy, of course).

Timed events: Hourly minigames, rifts every three hours, daily tasks, weekly tasks... It never ends.

You can't ignore content: Want to progress efficiently? You'll feel pressured to do practically everything. Shugo minigames are trash. I don't want to play them. Well, guess what? You'd better do them, because you need those shards and board points to get stronger.

Crafting: It's a casino. You've probably already seen the rage-quit posts on Reddit. Yeah, at least I stopped before getting to that point.

No progression at your own pace: Got extra time to play over the weekend? Too bad. You've already run out of energy, tickets

Horizontal progression: Want more board points and shards to make your character stronger? Come back tomorrow. Or next week. Because guess what YOU'RE OUT OF FRICKING TICKETS AND ENERGY.

Vertical progression: Want better gear? Enjoy being pushed into matchmaking with random players who either share a single brain cell or, if you're incredibly lucky, actually know what they're doing.

Gatekeeping: Still want better gear? Oh, you just reached the endgame? Congratulations! Now get kicked from lobby after lobby because your Combat Power isn't high enough. Surely there's something you can do about that, right? Well, kind of. Up to a point. After that, it's misery.

Energy and ticket systems: I don't think I need to explain this one any further. You get the idea.

Community: This community is diabolical. I'm a League of Legends veteran (I don't play anymore), and somehow I've encountered even more toxicity here.

MMO experience: This barely feels like an MMO to me. If anything, it just makes me want to interact with other players even less.

PvP: Don't even get me started. It's trash. Moving on.

Faction balance: Do yourself a favor: think carefully before choosing Elyos. Depending on your server, you might have a miserable time. Becuase guess what? Abyss (the PVP zone) is something you can't ignore. You can ignore most of it and don't engage with enemy players, but you have to do the so called abyss corridors for points and if the enemy factions camps it, well you know the rest

Balance in minigames, dungeons, and PvP: In PvP, you can end up fighting heavily geared players who may have spent hundreds of dollars, while you're standing there with a stick. GLGL.

Making money: There are far too few satisfying ways to earn Kinah through unrestricted solo farming. Running dungeons feels like the default answer to everything.

Open-world loot: You can't realistically farm competitive endgame gear from ordinary open-world mobs.

Final thoughts:

I genuinely wanted to love this game. The world, character creator, combat, and boss encounters gave me plenty of reasons to keep playing.

But the endgame gradually turned something I enjoyed into a checklist of things I felt obligated to do.

I don't mind grinding. In fact, I love grinding. What I hate is being told when, where, how often, and with whom I'm allowed to grind.

The game has an amazing foundation, but its progression systems completely killed my motivation to keep playing.

Thank you for reading through this!
