The Ultimate Review and a Broken Heart.
AION 2 Review (EN / RU) | Обзор AION 2

AION 2 — Disappointment Instead of the Continuation of a Legend
The first thing that stands out is the terrible, mobile-oriented interface. And that's not the only thing that makes the game feel like a mobile title. The combat system itself is extremely simplified: there are very few active skills, many actions are performed automatically. In the original AION, every skill you used could affect the outcome of a fight. Everything depended on your current condition and your opponent's. You had to think and make decisions in the middle of combat. In AION 2, however, this is practically nonexistent. Players use the same pre-made rotations, which can be found online and bound to macros. Instead of dynamic combat, we get players repeating the same sequence of skills.

The Pay-to-Win aspect of this game is massive, and it is made even worse by the game's own mechanics and overall structure, including progression, achievements, and so on. Free-to-play players have practically no chance of catching up with those who spend money. The gap keeps growing, and eventually the game will be divided into two distinct castes: the elite and the rabble. The most disappointing part is that almost everything comes down to gear. It doesn't matter how well you play or how effectively you use your skills. All that matters is having top gear. Even a small gear advantage can determine the outcome of a fight. Individual skill takes a back seat.

The world itself is empty and boring. Everything feels repetitive: endless open fields filled with packs of mobs. Unlike the original AION, where every location had its own unique environment and infrastructure, the world here simply doesn't offer the same level of interest.

Another major problem is the absurd number of restrictions and censorship measures. It feels as though the developers are trying to create an artificially sterile environment where everything has to be extremely polite, politically correct, and tolerant. People in general are already tired of being constantly subjected to forced tolerance and mandatory politeness. The chat has an automatic censorship system, yet you can still get banned for your messages. On top of that, resource gathering is restricted, the auction house is restricted for F2P players, you can get banned for missing a CAPTCHA if you afk, or for cancelling resource gathering several times in a row. Instead of enjoying the game, you constantly have to worry about accidentally breaking yet another rule.

Sieges are disappointing. Required Gear Score and Combat Power thresholds-otherwise you can't enter or nobody will accept you into a party. Players often have unrealistically high expectations: everyone wants to finish dungeons in five minutes. I don't even blame them — that's simply what the game's structure encourages. No wonder social interaction is practically nonexistent.

And all of this is especially disappointing when you remember the original AION.
In the original game, you were encouraged to start your adventure with friends from level one, overcome challenges together, explore the world, and progress as a team. It was genuine teamwork. The arrival of new friends and exciting experiences that will last for years. Sieges turned into massive battles where players imagined themselves as military commanders, developed strategies, and coordinated their efforts to capture fortresses. Every location had its own unique environment and infrastructure. The world truly felt alive. Character progression and obtaining top gear were much more balanced across the player base, the game's mechanics wouldn't allow you to get so far ahead of everyone else so quickly.
The biggest difference between AION 2 and the original is the very philosophy behind the games. The original MMORPG was about adventure, progressing together, teamwork, exploration, and large-scale battles. Now everything revolves around Combat Power, gear, repeating predetermined rotations and endless restrictions.
Instead of a living world and a true MMORPG, we've got a mobile game wrapped in a pretty package, where numbers and the size of your wallet increasingly determine everything.


AION 2 — разочарование вместо продолжения легенды
Первое, что бросается в глаза, — ужасно мобильный интерфейс. И это не единственная проблема, напоминающая о мобильном происхождении игры. Сама боевая система предельно упрощена: очень мало активных навыков, многие действия выполняются автоматически. В оригинальном AION каждый использованный навык мог повлиять на исход сражения. Всё зависело от текущего состояния тебя и противника. Нужно было думать и принимать решения непосредственно во время боя. В AION 2 же этого практически нет: игроки используют одну и ту же заранее заготовленную ротацию, которую можно найти в интернете и забиндить на макросы. Вместо динамичного боя мы получаем повторение одной и той же последовательности навыков.

Pay-to-win в игре колоссальный, и ситуация усугубляется самой структурой прогрессии: прокачкой, достижениями и другими механиками. У free-to-play игроков практически нет шансов догнать тех, кто платит. Разрыв постоянно увеличивается, и в итоге игра рискует разделиться на два кастовых общества: элиту и бомжей.
Самое печальное, что практически всё решает экипировка. Неважно, насколько хорошо вы играете и насколько грамотно используете навыки. В конечном итоге главное — чтобы у вас был топовый шмот. Даже небольшая разница в экипировке может решить исход противостояния. Личное мастерство отходит на второй план.

Сам мир пустой и скучный, всё однообразно: бескрайние поля с пачками мобов. В отличие от оригинального AION, где каждая локация имела свою уникальную природу и инфраструктуру, здесь мир совершенно не вызывает такого интереса.

Отдельная проблема — абсурдное количество ограничений и цензуры. Ограничен сбор ресурсов, ограничен аукцион для F2P. Чат автоматически цензурирует , что вы пишете, но даже это не спасает от банов за сообщения. Можно получить бан за пропущенную CAPTCHA если афк или бан на сбор за многократную отмену сбора ресурсов. Вместо удовольствия от игры постоянно приходится следить за тем, чтобы случайно не нарушить очередное правило.

Осады тоже разочаровывают: дисбаланс и обычная тыкалка по шарику вместо масштабных тактических сражений. Подземелья сводятся к набору необходимого Gear Score и Combat Power- иньше не попадёте в данж или вас не возьмут в группу. При этом у игроков зачастую завышенные требования: все хотят закрыть подземелье за пять минут. Я их даже не виню — сама структура игры приучает оценивать людей исключительно по цифрам. Неудивительно, что социальное взаимодействие здесь практически на нуле.

И особенно обидно всё это видеть, вспоминая оригинальный AION.
В оригинале вам предлагали начинать приключение с друзьями с первого уровня, вместе преодолевать трудности, исследовать мир и развиваться. Это была настоящая командная работа. Появление новых друзей на года и ярких впечатлений .Осады превращались в масштабные сражения, где игроки воображали себя полководцами, разрабатывали тактики и координировали захват крепостей. Каждая локация имела свою уникальную природу и инфраструктуру. Мир действительно жил и дышал. Прогресс персонажа и получение топовой экипировки были гораздо более равными для всех. Нельзя было просто заплатить и получить лучшее снаряжение за неделю. Даже если ты донатил, механики игры не позволяли настолько быстро обогнать остальных.

Главное отличие AION 2 от оригинала — в самой философии игры. Раньше MMORPG была про приключения, совместное развитие, командную работу, исследования и масштабные противостояния. Теперь всё сводится к Combat Power, экипировке, повторению готовых ротаций. Вместо живого мира и настоящей MMORPG мы получили мобильную игру с красивой обёрткой, в которой всё больше решают цифры и размер кошелька.

Aion 2 : L'illusion d'un MMO sacrifiée sur l'autel du mobile et de l'individualisme
Aion 2 n'est pas le MMORPG qu'on nous a promis, mais une boucle de frustration automatisée. Si la direction artistique est au rendez-vous, l'expérience de jeu s'avère particulièrement punitive et profondément solitaire pour les joueurs investis.
Le titre prône un farming intensif et à outrance, pour ensuite paradoxalement le sanctionner en brisant totalement l'immersion par des pop-ups de captchas incessants en plein jeu. La progression et le grind de puissance se retrouvent constamment bridés par le système d'odiles, bloquant toute liberté d'évolution. Pour couronner le tout, l'exploration et les donjons souffrent d'un manque cruel de réel loot : après 82 runs du même donjon, le constat est amer puisqu'on en repart les mains vides, ne pouvant compter que sur le système de pitié (pity) pour obtenir la moindre récompense.
Pire encore, la dimension multijoueur est totalement sacrifiée. L'expérience est réduite à du jeu solo déguisé : la course au gear score pousse les joueurs à l'individualisme le plus total. Les joueurs les plus forts avancent vers le haut sans jamais se soucier de ceux qui sont en dessous, car l'entraide est punie par le jeu. Partager une activité avec un joueur de niveau inférieur prive tout simplement d'odiles ou ruine le score de donjon de la semaine. On se retrouve bloqué par le fameux système du "10/10" : une fois ce quota atteint, le jeu applique une interdiction pure et simple de pénétrer à nouveau dans les donjons et autres activités, tuant définitivement l'esprit de communauté. Une expérience extrêmement frustrante qui piétine les fondements mêmes du genre.

[h2]158 Hours in Aion 2. Did I Enjoy It? Yes. Am I Uninstalling? Also Yes.[/h2]
Apparently, 158 hours was enough for me to fall in love with the game, question my life choices, and finally realize that I already have responsibilities in real life. I don't need another full-time job that doesn't pay me.
[h3]❤️ What I Loved[/h3]
[b]1. Character Customization and Fashion[/b]
The characters look AMAZING. Seriously. The outfits, the glams, the overall aesthetics... absolutely gorgeous.
My Sorcerer looked fabulous while repeatedly questioning her existence. At least she suffered in style.
[b]2. Pets and Mounts[/b]
The pet system is genuinely fantastic. You can collect almost any mob as a pet, and I absolutely love that.
See a cute creature? Adopt it. See a weird creature? Adopt it. See something that tried to murder you five minutes ago? Congratulations, you're a pet owner.
10/10. No complaints.
[b]3. Combat[/b]
Combat is smooth, fun, and flexible. I played Sorcerer and really enjoyed experimenting with different builds.
Throwing spells at things? Fantastic.
Watching things explode? Beautiful.
Actually enjoying the gameplay? Believe it or not, yes.
[h3]💀 What Eventually Made Me Uninstall[/h3]
[b]1. Crafting and Gathering — Welcome to Your Second Job[/b]
Oh, crafting. Where do I even begin?
First, you spend hours collecting materials. Without a subscription, this becomes an exciting exercise in testing your patience.
Then you gather more materials. Then some more.
Finally, you're ready to craft that higher-tier item you've been working toward!
And now... let's roll the dice.
Because apparently, spending half your weekend gathering materials wasn't enough. We also need a success percentage to keep things interesting.
Nothing says "rewarding progression" quite like watching hours of your life disappear because RNG decided you're not worthy today.
[b]2. The Abyss — Welcome, Free AP Is Served[/b]
Ah, the Abyss. Such a wonderful concept.
You enter as a low-ranking player, hoping to earn some points, improve your rank, and maybe collect the materials you need.
Adorable.
Meanwhile, a high-ranking player spots you from approximately three continents away and decides you're today's complimentary snack.
You die. You return. You die again.
At some point, you start wondering whether you're actually participating in PvP or just providing a community service.
And here's the best part: you can't simply ignore the Abyss because you need materials from there to progress.
So the game basically tells you:
[i]"Go to the Abyss to become stronger!"[/i]
The Abyss: [i]"That's cute."[/i]
I'm not blaming the players for killing other players in a PvP zone. That's literally what PvP is.

[h1] QUIT YOUR J*B TO KEEP UP WITH THE LATEST CONTENT AS F2P [/h1]
[h2] My Thoughts [/h2]
Firstly, I do not play this game with the mindset that I will become the best player. Unless you own a multi-million dollar company and can pay your way to the top, do not play this game if you are going to complain that unable to do the things a giga-whale can do. I am strictly F2P and playing this game without paying [b]$15 per month[/b] for its subscription is extremely punishing.

[h2] F2P Experience [/h2]
• No Market Access
Being locked out of the market hinders your progress a lot. You cannot make in-game currency, buy crafting materials, and buy gear that you need to submit for progression currency. Overall this means that you will have less combat score than players that pay for the subscription.

• Less Dungeon Energy
If you have the $15 subscription and/or the $15 battle pass(Which this game has two active at the same time.) you will get [b]DOUBLE or TRIPLE[/b] the amount of energy needed to do dungeons. Being a F2P player in the endgame means that you were really lucky, really smart, or are getting carried through your content by your friends.

• Dungeon Loot claiming
Subscription players get to claim x2 the dungeon loot. At the later stages of the game, you are most likely doing the same dungeon [b]86 times[/b]. Having subscription cuts your farming time in half or more since finding parties also takes time.

• Shugo Festival claiming
"Shugo Festival" is an event that occur once in an hour. Aion 2 gives players three keys a day and expect players to spend them all in a day. As a F2P, you are only allowed to claim one key per event. That means you need to catch the sign-up time three times, once an hour, to spend your daily keys. A casual player will always be capping on their keys.

• Alternative/Sub Characters
Should you want to keep up with the current content's pace, you are required to create multiple characters as a F2P. These characters give you extra dungeon energy and shared loot. You cannot use gear that an alternate character received but, you will get the dungeon crafting materials which can be used.

[h3] F2P TL;DR [/h3]
Your rate of progression is halved, you have access to less QoL, and the you spend double or triple the time to progress.

[h2] Complaints about the Game [/h2]
• Community Content
There is only one considerable community event and it is faction wars/PVP, other than that the next closest thing to a community event you get to do in-game is to clear a world boss.

• Meaningful progression behind game modes
Combat progression should always connect to combat rewards. Why are you forced to play tag and jump-rope to improve your character's damage? The rewards in these events are a nice benefit but they should not be mandatory to your progression.

• Pet farming
The worst grind this game may have. You need to eliminate at least 100 of the same monster, for all monsters, to boost your stats. Although minimal, the game has pretty strict gatekeeping. That minimal boost may be what you need to reach your next benchmark.

• Dungeon Attempt limit
This game punishes the player for completing dungeons without claiming its rewards. Should you hit the limit, you will not be allowed to play any dungeon for the entire week. The limit forces you to only progress what your character needs and does not allow you to help your friends or legion members. Overall hurting community in the game and enforces the strict gatekeep in public matchmaking.

[h1] Overall TL;DR [/h1]
Spend money to play the game as intended. Even when spending money, this game requires a lot of time-investment to keep up with the pace of end-game content. Avoiding the pace of end-game, the gatekeep is too strict to play the game "your way".

[h1]TLDR: 7/10 as a Game — Not Recommended for New Players Mid-Season[/h1]

There's a genuinely enjoyable MMORPG underneath all these systems, but the combination of excessive grinding, pay-to-progress mechanics, technical issues, and an enormous gap between established players and newcomers makes it very difficult to recommend to anyone who hasn't already invested heavily in it.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

Overall, Aion 2 is a decent MMORPG, and the progression itself is generally fine. The world design is enjoyable, with some genuinely beautiful landscapes, although certain environmental textures, particularly rocks and grass, look cheap and outdated compared to the scenery as a whole.

Progression is extremely time-consuming and involves running the same dungeons over and over again, often across multiple characters. Unfortunately, progression is also the main deciding factor in PvP. Since class design is relatively simple, PvP often feels like two calculators competing to see which one has the bigger numbers.

On the positive side, the game offers an impressive number of vertical progression systems, which might appeal to people who enjoy collecting things, optimizing builds, and constantly working towards new upgrades. There's almost always something to improve, even if the process becomes repetitive.

On gameplay alone, I'd give it a [b]7/10[/b].

[h1]The Major Drawbacks[/h1]

[b]1. Server performance and stability[/b]

Lag, desync, and general server instability remain serious problems, especially in large-scale PvP.

[b]2. Absolutely terrible render distance[/b]

Players and mobs practically appear right in front of you, even at maximum render settings. This is particularly frustrating in the Abyss, the game's aerial PvP zone, where you can fly straight into an enemy zerg simply because it wasn't rendered in time.

Combine that with flying gates that provide massive speed boosts, and players can effectively materialize on top of you. From the receiving end, it looks almost identical to someone coming out of stealth.

Think of the rendering issues in BDO, only worse.

[b]3. Progression is bottlenecked by Kinah[/b]

Almost every progression system requires substantial amounts of the in-game currency, and there's never enough to cover everything.

It increasingly feels like the economy is designed to push players towards the solution conveniently provided by the developers: buying Kinah with real money at absurd prices.

The alternative is grinding across multiple characters, which can take days just to set up before they even become profitable.

[b]4. The existence of giga-whales[/b]

If you thought spending $1,000–3,000 a month made someone a whale, you might be surprised.

Some of the supposedly "skilled" players reportedly spent $10,000 or more to obtain full BiS gear shortly after launch.

How? Through what is essentially a backdoor progression system: crafting.

You don't need to clear the hardest content or obtain rare boss drops. You just need Kinah, which can be purchased with real money, to craft gear comparable to or better than equipment obtained from endgame dungeons and raids.

Sure, you can earn that Kinah yourself, but we're talking weeks of grinding for items whose real-money equivalent can approach $1,000 each.

And the funniest part? You're paying all that money to stay ahead for a few months at most.

[b]5. Poorly designed large-scale PvP activities[/b]

The Abyss has enormous potential, but some of its activities feel surprisingly underdeveloped.

Winning a siege essentially rewards you with two minutes of uninterrupted mob grinding. No interesting castle mechanics, no meaningful territorial gameplay, just another opportunity to kill mobs.

It's a rather disappointing use of what could have been one of the game's defining features.

[h1]The Most Antisocial MMO in Existence[/h1]

Since many players run poorly optimized builds, gear score has become the primary measure of someone's usefulness. As progression continues, the minimum requirements for LFG groups keep rising, often far beyond what's actually necessary to complete the content.

People even get kicked from already established groups simply because someone with a higher gear score applies. And since, as I mentioned earlier, the game often comes down to a battle between calculators, individual skill and the human factor seem to matter surprisingly little.

The result is an increasingly antisocial environment where players are treated as numbers rather than teammates, making it even harder for newcomers and returning players to catch up.

[h1]The Biggest Problem: Starting Mid-Season[/h1]

These are all warnings, but they're not even my main reason for recommending against the game.

The biggest issue is that [b]there's very little point in starting Aion 2 midway through a season.[/b]

Progression is so heavily dependent on accumulated resources, repeated dungeon runs, and time-gated systems that catching up to established players can be practically impossible within a reasonable timeframe.

Unless you're playing a support class like Cleric, you may never reach a level where you can meaningfully compete in PvP before the next progression cycle.

And even if you're willing to whale your way through the problem, catching up now can be considerably more expensive than it was at launch, largely because of inflated crafting costs.

[h3]EGG TART RECIPE[/h3]
[b]Ingredients[/b]

[u]For the Tart Shell (Shortcrust Style)[/u]
• All-purpose flour: 200 g (plus a little extra for dusting)
• Cake flour: 25 g
• Unsalted or salted butter (softened at room temperature): 125 g
• Icing sugar (powdered sugar): 55 g
• Egg: 1 large (whisked)
• Vanilla extract: A small dash

[u]For the Egg Custard Filling[/u]
• Hot water: 150 g
• Caster sugar: 70 g (adjust to taste)
• Evaporated milk: 75 g
• Eggs: 2 large (beaten)
• Vanilla extract: ½ tsp

[b]Step-by-Step Instructions[/b]

[u]1. Make the Tart Crust[/u]
1. Cream the butter and sugar: In a large bowl, use a mixer on medium speed to beat the softened butter and icing sugar until light, fluffy, and pale.
2. Add wet ingredients: Slowly add the whisked egg in two batches, beating well after each addition, then stir in the vanilla extract.
3. Incorporate flour: Sift the all-purpose flour and cake flour into the butter mixture in two additions. Gently fold and knead with a spatula or your hands just until it forms a soft dough.
4. Shape the shells: Roll the dough out to about ½ cm thick. Cut out circles slightly larger than your tart molds using a cookie cutter. Press each circle gently into the mold, working from the bottom up to the sides, and trim any excess dough at the top. Chill the shaped shells in the fridge while you make the filling.

[u]2. Prepare the Custard[/u]
1. Dissolve the sugar: Pour the hot water into a bowl, add the caster sugar, and stir until completely dissolved. Let it cool down to lukewarm.
2. Mix custard base: In a separate bowl, whisk together the beaten eggs, evaporated milk, and vanilla extract.
3. Combine and strain: Pour the cooled sugar water into the egg-milk mixture and stir thoroughly. Strain the liquid through a fine-mesh sieve into a jug or measuring cup to remove any bubbles or egg lumps.

[u]3. Assemble and Bake[/u]
1. Fill the shells: Pour the strained custard mixture into the chilled tart shells, filling them about 80% full.
2. Bake: Preheat your oven. Bake the tarts at roughly 200°C to 400°F (approx. 200°C) on the lower-middle rack for 10–15 minutes, then lower the heat (or crack the oven door slightly depending on your oven) until the custard is just set and smooth without puffing up or cracking.
3. Cool and serve: Let them cool for about 10 minutes before removing them from the molds. 
Enjoy them warm.

AION 2: I Loved the Original. This One Is Burning Me Out.

NOT RECOMMENDED

I liked the original Aion, so when Aion 2 came around, I was interested. Then I heard casual friendly and thought, okay, this might work for me. I’m over 250 hours in now, and bro, I don’t know what their idea of casual is.

I actually enjoy playing. The world looks good, the combat feels good, and I like the built-in macro. I’ve spent a lot of time learning my characters and getting my builds working how I want. My sorcerer especially has been fun. But keeping that character progressing is wearing me out.

I’ll spend hours running dungeons, gathering materials and farming Kinah, then finish the day barely better off. I don’t expect the best gear every time I log in. I do expect all that time to get me somewhere.

I went 21 Conquest runs without a gold drop. People will tell you there’s a pity system. Okay, but getting through that many runs is already exhausting, and when gear finally drops, you still have to deal with the stats. Getting the item doesn’t even mean you’re finished spending money on it.

And if I feel like running more dungeons, let me. I’m already there playing your game. Why limit the rewards or make me worry about energy? Give me a reason to keep going. Even clearing the extra mobs could count toward better rewards instead of everyone rushing past them.

Crafting has some things I like. Guaranteed crafting was a good addition. What I don’t understand is why I can’t pass that guaranteed craft to my own alt, but the better Splendent version can go on the market. I gathered the materials and worked on the profession on this account. Let me use what I made on this account.

Alchemy needs plenty of materials too, so gathering becomes another thing I have to spend hours doing. And gathering is so slow. I’m picking grass, man. Why am I standing here watching this bar fill for every plant when I need hundreds of materials?

Make it faster. Or give me something to actually do while gathering, with extra materials if I do it well. I’d take that over standing around waiting.

Then there’s trying to get into a dungeon. The game says my Combat Power qualifies, but the party leader wants more. So I meet the requirement and still can’t play. Private groups can ask for whatever they want, that’s their group. But give the rest of us matchmaking that works with the requirements the game itself sets. I’d even take NPC companions for some of this content.

Stigma Shards have been another headache. I want to improve my PvE build, and I keep ending up in the Abyss farming points for skill upgrades. I don’t enjoy getting ganged up on while I’m trying to kill mobs or finish objectives. Give me a reasonable way to earn those upgrades through the content I actually enjoy.

And if there’s a more balanced PvP option, make the rewards worth doing. I’d rather see people rewarded for competitive fights than have farming someone who barely stands a chance be so worthwhile.

I also like experimenting with builds. I’ve put time into making mine comfortable to play, and that part has been enjoyable. I’d like more combinations to be worth using so I can keep doing that instead of feeling pushed toward whatever build everybody else is running.

Pet Genus has eaten millions of my Kinah and thousands of crystals. I finally get a stat worth keeping, lock it, and now the next attempts cost more. I understand paying extra to protect a good roll, but the amount of money you can burn without getting another useful one is ridiculous. Then Soul Binding wants its share too.

At some point there needs to be a limit to how unlucky you can get. Let enough failed attempts count toward something. I’m not asking to pick perfect stats for free.

Kinah is involved in so much of this that I spend a lot of my playtime trying to afford the next attempt. I’ve even made alts partly to help with resources. I’d rather make another character because I want to play it, not because my main needs financial support.

That’s also where spending real money bothers me. When so much character strength can be bought through the economy, someone with enough money can skip a lot of what I’m spending hours working through. Add bots and real money sellers to that, and it makes the grind feel worse.

I want the market to stay useful. Sell materials, sell ordinary crafted gear, let people trade. But I’d like the strongest upgrades to depend more on what you’ve actually done with your character.

Even crafting could have more to it. Let me make the basic item, then give me an optional challenge to improve it. If I earn that better version through playing, bind it to me. Give skilled crafters something to work toward beyond paying for more attempts.

I’m fine with rare gear being rare. I’m fine with difficult bosses, and I don’t mind putting hours into a game I enjoy. But between dungeons, gathering, crafting, Abyss, Stigmas, Genus, Soul Binding and keeping enough Kinah to pay for everything, I don’t see how someone playing an hour or two is supposed to keep up.

Lately I’ve been thinking about logging in, remembering what I need to farm, and deciding I can’t be bothered. That’s disappointing because I was enjoying my sorcerer enough to switch over from the character I’d already invested so much into.

I still want to play Aion 2. I just need the time I spend playing it to feel worthwhile. Right now, I can’t recommend it.

[h1] Aion 2 Review – Great Potential, but Progression Needs Work [/h1]

I genuinely enjoy Aion 2. The combat, character progression, gearing system, classes, and overall MMORPG experience have kept me coming back. There is a lot to like about this game, and I want to see it succeed.

However, there are two major areas where I think the developers need to make improvements.

1. Shugo Modes Need to Be Rethought

I absolutely hate Shugo modes. I don't find them enjoyable, engaging, or rewarding from a gameplay perspective. They feel disconnected from the actual MMORPG experience.

I play Aion 2 because I want to develop my character, fight enemies, run dungeons, participate in PvP, craft, and improve my equipment. I don't want to be forced into minigames that feel like a completely different game.

I understand the desire to provide different activities, but these modes should be optional. Players should have alternative ways to obtain meaningful rewards through traditional MMORPG content.

2. New Player Progression Needs to Be Faster

This is probably my biggest concern for the long-term health of the game.

The current gear progression feels increasingly difficult as you get further into the game. I'm currently around 2,100 GS, and even with consistent play, progression can feel painfully slow because so much depends on RNG and equipment drops.

Meanwhile, players are racing toward 3,000 GS to access the latest content. For newer players, catching up can feel like an enormous undertaking, particularly when some of the progression systems encourage spending significant amounts of real money.

I understand that endgame progression should require effort. I don't expect to reach the highest gear score overnight. However, there needs to be a better progression path for players who are joining later or who don't want to spend heavily.

As the game receives more content, I would like to see:

Increased catch-up progression for newer players.

Better equipment drop rates or more reliable ways to obtain specific upgrades.

More meaningful guaranteed rewards for time invested.

Reduced reliance on RNG for essential character progression.

Older content remain relevant while providing better rewards for players catching up.

3. Think About the Long-Term Player Base

A healthy MMORPG needs new players to feel like they can catch up and participate.

If the gap between established players and newcomers continues growing, it risks making the game increasingly intimidating for anyone who wasn't there from the beginning.

Not everyone wants to race to the top of the gear score leaderboard. Some of us just want to enjoy the game, steadily improve our characters, and experience the content without feeling like we're constantly falling further behind.

Final Thoughts

I like Aion 2. That's why I'm providing this feedback.

The game has tremendous potential, but I believe the developers need to reconsider Shugo modes and make character progression more accessible, especially for newer players.

I want to keep playing for years, not feel like I'm constantly fighting the progression system just to enjoy the content.

Please focus on rewarding players for playing the MMORPG itself, making catch-up progression more accessible, and giving players more freedom in how they earn their rewards.

[b]Could Have Been Better.[/b]


That's the first thought that comes to mind after several dozen hours of gameplay.

This isn't the sequel I expected from the legendary MMO of my childhood and teenage years. That said, I can't exactly call it reheated dogshit either. It's just... okay by modern MMO standards. Nothing spectacular. Nothing that comes even close to the impact AION 1 had on me 15 years ago.

[b]Graphics & World Design[/b]

The graphics are great, and UE5 does its job pretty well — you get the usual UE5 assets, shaders reused by dozens of other games, and absolutely dogshit optimization.

The locations and hubs, however, feel completely soulless. They're there just because an MMO is apparently supposed to have them. There's no sense of history, no vibe, no atmosphere. They don't feel like the locations from AION 1 at all.

And no, I'm not asking for a carbon copy of the original or some lazy remake. I'm talking about legacy. About creating that feeling of "Oh yeah, I've been here before. I remember this place. It's cool to see how much the world has changed over the years." That sense of continuity is completely missing.

[b]Music & Sound Design[/b]

The music and sound design are competent. The nostalgia-baiting tracks reuse familiar arrangements and melodies, and honestly, they're still fucking gorgeous. The new music is great too. I'm particularly fond of the sci-fi + ambient stuff in the Abyss. This is one area where the game genuinely delivers.

[b]Combat & Automation[/b]

Combat is pretty much typical AION, with one very important asterisk: it's almost an auto-combat system.

The game has built-in macros that let your character endlessly cycle through whatever abilities you've assigned while holding a button. 

Given today's lifestyle and the pace at which people play MMOs, some degree of automation is probably expected. So I guess this is their pseudo-compromise.

And NCSoft clearly fucking loves botters and has basically given them free rein.

[b]UI & Activities[/b]

The UI design is a fucking piece of mobile-game shit. I genuinely hoped they'd do something about it since the Taiwan version, but nope. Absolutely talentless and tasteless design.

There's no shortage of activities, though. You'll always find something to waste your time on. That said, Throne and Liberty handled the presentation of its activities much better. Having to use a fucking mobile-style interface to queue up for boss runs is just cringe.

[b]Balance, Economy & PvP[/b]

I don't see much point in discussing balance, the economy, or pay-to-win here. This review is strictly about the aesthetic and gameplay experience.

And if you're tired of getting your ass handed to you by whales, you can always switch from PvP to PvE and keep sucking their dicks from a safe distance. Hell, keep whining long enough and maybe they'll turn the Abyss into PvE as well. 

NCSoft has effectively killed the whole point of ganking enemy territory — something that was an actual core gameplay element in AION 1. What a fucking shame.

[b]Wings & Character Customization[/b]

Finally, after all these years, wings actually have a purpose: you can fly in pretty much every location. This is exactly what I wanted from AION 1, and the developers absolutely nailed it.

Character customization, appearance editing, and cosmetic skins are top-tier, just like they were in AION 1. Creating your dream waifu or husbando and dressing them up in some gorgeous outfits is incredibly easy. Though you'll definitely have a good laugh once you see the prices of those skins.

[b]Final Thoughts[/b]

I have no desire to dissect every single aspect of the game, and I won't. You can figure out for yourself that this is just another typical MMO.

But I [b]DON'T RECOMMEND[/b] this game.

I'll obviously keep playing from time to time because I'm a fucking degenerate but if you have any brains, stay the fuck away from this game until NCSoft actually finishes developing it. (in a couple of years)

Lots of criticism around Aion 2 stems from people claiming the game is too grindy or that it's pay2win or that it's time gated or that it's a mobile game. None of these are really true, except the grindiness, but come on, it's a vertical MMO - YOU SHOULD WANT TO GRIND, or at least expect it. You play MMOs for months, years. 

For context, so far I've played the game completely Free2play. I haven't had a guild or some OP friends to carry me. I've been playing an ok amount and have mainly been casually enjoying it and learning it on my own. Character is 2.7k ILVL Templar, and climbing further (which I'd say is a very decent point to be at in the end-game).

[h2] Pros: [/h2]

+ If you're into grinding lots and lots of content and vertical progression then you're at the right place. I've played many Old-school/ eastern MMOs that tend to be grindier and for said the grind to be enjoyable enough, along with the milestones you're grinding for - to feel rewarding. Aion 2, is very good at this. It reminds even of Path of Exile or Warframe. You can just jump in and engage in some pretty decent grinding while you talk with friends or watch something on your second screen. There's very high ceilings, so you can keep coming back for more.

+ The Free to play experience : many people complain that it's malicious for the game to hide an important system such as the Marketplace behind a pay wall (monthly subscription), but this is confusing to me. Any MMO game with a subscription always hides the marketplace/auction house behind it, to prevent bots and so on from destroying it easily. Same with games like Path of Exile. So to me, this is really nothing damning. The issue here is that the game's free 'trial' is so GOOD, that people have naturally began to see this game as a FREE GAME that just happens to have a subscription, but how I see this game is more like a subscription-based game that has an extremely good Free Trial. Think of World of Warcraft. Its free trial allows you to level only to level 20 and of course you can't use the auction house, along with many other bits of content. In Aion 2 on the other hand, not only can you reach max level (currently 45) but you can also continue doing any and all content. There's not a single piece of content that tells you "Hey you have to pay to do this". Again, I've played for free so far and I am not falling behind at all, nor am I short on any integral resources.

+ Character customisation is pretty extensive, though limited in terms of races and so on, you are still able to create neat characters.

+ The game is very visually appealing. I, and many others, am on the opinion that when I see a new game release with this graphics engine and visual style, to just think "Ah, it's one of those...", and it's usually the devs telling you "Hey! look at this very detailed rock! And this very detailed dude!!" But then it's just a mish mash of random assets in random places and it looks unappealing. Aion 2 on the other hand, feels like for the most part, people sat down who had a good idea of map design and thought "Hey, how can we make this both high quality but also immersive". I can't count how many times I've just stopped to appreciate some amazing vistas or areas where the lighting hits in a spectacular way. It reminds me of the Elden Ring world in a sense, and how you can look over to the horizon and spot many different points of interest or locations that make you go "Wow that's cool/ Oh, what's that about?".

+ Mounts in this game are great. Most are simple to obtain and have lots of charm and character, as shown through their animations and sound effects. Many of which are delightfully unusual.

+ Combat feels pretty decent. Not the greatest ever, fairly streamlined but feels decent yes. People claim that it's simple 1 button mobile game combat - not the case. 

+ Community is pretty active. I hear complaints that the game is very non-community focused but I don't quite agree with that. People chat often and lots are pretty supportive or willing to help out. Big groups organise for objectives, and the game's PvP scene gets a lot of people strongly invested and eager to coordinate with their faction or server. Yes, it's not the most social community ever and there are toxic people (common in these games) but it's far from the soulless and lonely experience some make it out to be.

+ Lots to do every week. People claim that so many things are time-gated and they can't do what they want. Now, although I'll agree that yes, the game has a lots of time-gating, it really isn't that bad. There're many different pieces of content for you to do and grind each week that it's honestly hard to get to the bottom of everything and shake your fist in anger because the game stops you from doing something. Again, I'd say I've played a decent amount and haven't felt like that at all. If you no-life it 10 hours a day you might get locked out of stuff to do yes, but i'd say most people can't afford to play that much. You can also swap on an alt. Does this deserve some criticism? Sure, time-gating is generally an eye-rolly addition that is by default unfun but not as dire as it sounds.

+ Devs so far listen and react quickly.

+ (Most) Bosses are really cool. Think FFXIV fights, just way faster. Fun to learn.

[h2] Cons: [/h2]

- By far my personal biggest gripe with this game - The use of generative AI. I am utterly dumbfounded. The game clearly has a lot of effort put into it by talented people and then when you turn to some systems, like Arcana Cards or the Genus Insight which are both important systems you progress - the art for said pages and items is just clearly bland AI. I am so confused, it just stains the whole thing. I have to tell my friends who I recommend the game to "Hey guys I found this great game! But uh--.. it has AI." Why? Literally pay anyone 10$ to draw you something decent you can put there instead. It's also just bad AI, that you can spot from a mile away. Pretty sure some stylised cinematics are also AI. So disappointing.
 
- Playing with friends is very difficult in this game. This problem stems from a combination of Odyle Energy (The resource you expend each time you complete an instance to receive loot) and the various pieces of content you can do being locked behind an Item level requirement (For example you can do a certain dungeon if you have 700 ILVL, and a bit harder one at 1400, a harder than that - 2100). So if you want to help your friend let's say, who's iLVL 700 and you are 2500 then it means you have to do the lowest difficulty dungeon with them. But hey, you're awesome, of course you'd help out a friend! But wait! You don't really need anything from that instance since you're so far ahead, so you decide to NOT expend your Odyle Energy at the end of the run so you can save it for your own endgame progression, since it's so valuable. BUT  O-OH - the game has a weekly cap of 10 runs you can do where you can SKIP ON OPENNING THE CHEST AT THE END (so you can save your odyle energy), meaning you can only help 10 times a week before you're locked out from doing Any instances. In an ideal world, they continue to tinker with Odyle Energy as a whole until it feels better.

- Subscription price is a bit steep at 12,75 euro a month.

- No interesting playable races. Mostly caters to people that want characters that look like super-models, but you can be a bit creative still.

- Pay for convenience. People can pay to excel faster than you, but you can at least eventually catch up through playing.

- MSQ is bland. English voice acting is very bad or just AI. Shame cause some bosses have actually decent voices.

My first impression of the game:
- The Elyos story is nice, while the Asmodian story is boring.
- The combat is combo-specific, which is fine.
- The Abyss (PvP zone between the two factions) actually sucks due to how it works- as well as how people abuse it.
- Currently you can only get to Level 45 at maximum, where all the other boring content is available. By that time, you are finished with the current chapter of the story, which took me around 8 in-game hours / 2 real days.
- The voice lines are fine, both English and Japanese.
- The gameplay is pretty repetitive: Do missions ->  Go to dungeons / places with minor objective to them -> Get loot -> Spend loot -> Repeat.
- There are other stuff that you can do, like collecting, harvesting and other uninteresting things... those are not exciting in the slightest- because by the time you collected, harvested and done other uninteresting things to get a better equipment, you already get a way better equipment by just doing the Story missions / dungeons. So in hindsight: Doing anything other than clearing dungeons are useless Early game.
- There is a "Daeva pass" which is just your typical Battle pass designed quota that you can reach. And believe it or not, the premium version gives you more stuff which lets you clear more dungeons.
- Speaking of dungeons, it's not infinite. You'll need "Odyle Energy", which is the consumable to attempt a dungeon run. This means you can run out of it- which means in order to attempt to clear dungeons; you'll have to re-fill them somehow. And that somehow is mostly presented behind paid content. This, in my eyes is predatory.
- You can upgrade your equipment, but... eh Metin2 style? Your equipment upgrade can cause the equipment to break if you fail the upgrade at a certain percentage (For example, 65% chance to be successful, from a Level 10 equipment). There are also ways to ensure the upgrade is successful, under way more grindy efforts in which a beginner immediately flinches and quits the game because of it.
- Most of the systems that upgrade your skills are fine at best. Not great, not terrible.
- Classes are fun tho, there are some interesting classes that have unique purposes to be useful in a team.
- The rewards you get in the beginning of the game are super forgiving, letting you finish the Story missions without massive travelling hurdle.

Some problems that I encountered which could be fixed:
- There isn't enough guidance on having the player manually upgrade their storage (both player storage & stash)
- There is not enough motivation to play some events, like the Shugo Festival, Daily dungeons & such.
- The Abyss' entrances can be camped, leading to a sad reality of that game mode being highly exploitative and unreachable in terms of content.
- Dungeons are designed for a full Squad of players, and not really viable doing it Solo. There are no alternative ways to grind for the required items, if you are dependent on player count and dungeon interest. With less player count, this will be one of the major problems to tackle.
- There are currently no news from NC (creators of the game) about how the story is going, as in no transparency over their future content via some sort of public milestone post. Without getting excited for new content, player count will drop- as in no further interest towards the game will stay.
- There is no motivation, nor a forced guidance on playing Ranked PvP game modes. No motivation- as in no clear rewards that would give people more interest towards those game modes, and no forced guidance- as in letting players know that these game modes exist and worth investing your time into them.
Either give more & better rewards to those PvP game modes, or make it a priority to progress.
- Skins are, at best; uninteresting. Some weird people may be into flashy skins, but there could be skins similar to Path of Exile- with extra effects for your skills, more warrior-like skins and more visual interactions with those skins.
In short: expand on different skins which also target other sides of the MMORPG communities.

Some things that are just unfixable:
- The game performs badly on Low-end devices, and barely functions at 60 FPS from Medium-end devices. It is mostly because of Unreal Engine 5's rendering and plugins (some plugins cause insane performance drops).
- The game is getting updated almost daily, for security reasons. The problem starts with those updates being over 200MBs (sometimes even more, reaching to gigabytes), which quickly gets frustrating. Not all people have fiber speeds, nor even have a decent connection at all.
- The bot situation. The game is free, all the content is available after finishing the Story mode (An hour of two speedrunning it) and grinding for resources without early game restrictions result in mass-botting potential. If the early game is not nerfed, then the bots will keep coming on no-end. If the early game is nerfed however, then the player base would dip further. It is a downfall cycle with no way of going up, unless the efforts on improving the game goes towards the Story a LOT more.
- Pay to win situation. Some people say that the game is pay to win due to how dungeons (main way of improving your character) is gatekeeped with Odyle energy, but I tend to look at it as "Pay to skip grinding". Eventually- a Free to play player could get to the same exact position as those who paid for it, but takes way longer. So the only advantage a player could get in this game, is skip waiting- which is the purpose of the Odyle energy in the first place: making sure you either wait for the energy to come back, or grind for it to be re-filled.
Both ways suck by the way, so those who have spare money could just skip the time hassle and get to the grinding part immediately.
Waiting -> Grinding -> Upgrading -> Winning
(Currently players who pay for the Daeva pass will go straight to the "Grinding" part.)

I do not recommend the game, because the game felt more of a waste of time to me, than actual content thrown at me with whatever I do. This isn't the same as hating the game, where I actually don't hate it. But I actually hate how the game wants me to waste my time and how the game would eventually force me to pay up in order to stop waiting.

The rest of the review notwithstanding, my feedback is a strong "not recommended". 

Aion 2 is a pay-as-you-go game where the things you pay for can get taken away anytime for no particular reason, and the only way to prevent that from happening is spending more money... maybe. 

The game has an economy that players rely on for income and progression, yet the market is locked behind the game's cash-only subscription. It is viable to stay F2P if you don't care about progressing pace at all, but joining up with any friends who have this access on their main characters in the highest difficulty or in endgame content is outright a no-go. The hardcore playerbase does not even consider a sub to be "P2W", because it is so essential that it might as well be a subscription MMO at base.

What is truly egregious is that the sub doesn't guarantee you market access in practice. NCSoft randomly restricts players from listing in-demand items and imposes varying daily limits on their sale profits. It doesn't matter how long you've played for, the game's bot-detection system casts a wide net and it will decide a random number of players can't use the feature they paid for - just because. Support will not unlock market access on request and will tell players they're SoL. I have seen the playerbase speculate what prevents restrictions, and the only constant seems to be spending more money be more likely to gain enough "trust" to not get flagged.

"Predatory" doesn't begin to describe this game's monetization, before even talking about the game itself. 

The rest of the review is as below.


Positive:

+++Character creation and customization are very detailed and varied, from goonmaxing to making dwarves. Skins and dyes are expensive but there are also lots of free skin options.

++You can farm and ride monsters that you kill in your journey, which is real cool.

+Game looks good in UE5 but it is not particularly coherent in its aesthetic or presentation. Players spend most of the time zoomed out, the game loses its graphical luster at distance and a lot of assets are were made to be looked at in small screens. Good game for screenshots and sightseeing, but it can be a visual mess in motion due to mobile-minded design. It does consider the fact you can fly around the map, which looks good at it.

Mixed:

=Dungeons and raids can be decent fun, but gets boring quick due to janky combat that's little more than macro spam arcade and travelling/mob aggro between bosses. Solo challenges aren't any better and get repetitive quickly. Has potential to get better with time but as it is it's very uninteresting outside of fulfilling MMO roles in a group.

=Servers can handle huge populations at once so there are massive World Boss fights and Abyss PvP battles, which can look like a beautiful clusterf*ck. But participating is mostly bad - servers eat World Bosses like locusts, PvP participation is forced for timely progression, the server PvP itself is highly unbalanced both in-game and in numbers, there are many ways for one server to grief another out of non-PvP rewards, etc. 

=Main story is fine and side quests are underrated. Decent amount of lore to dig through during solo content without being overly pretentious or ambitious, with context from first  game existing. Lots of exploration but experience is dumbed down into map markers and checklists, not as much fun moving around the map outside of questing. Many NPCs are AI voiced and in-game assets are also gen AI, which unfortunately shows in how generic yet non-hollistic the art and voice directions are.

Negative:

-A lot of the questing is "spend 5-7 minutes farming X mobs then report back to NPC" that gets dull very quickly, dialogue skippers will mostly experience the story that way.

-Few social mechanics for a MMO. Barebones friend/legion systems, no home or friend hangout place/system on release, outside of dungeons/raids interactions are mostly solo or inherently toxic (shared lifeskill nodes, PvP, etc.). Everyone uses Discord for any proper socialization.

--Lots of boring daily chores like Shugo, Daily Dungeon, Nightmare runs, Duty quests, etc. on top of weekly dungeons. Some are skippable but others like Shugo aren't, even if you aren't progressing to endgame, and they mostly give pathetic amounts of rewards for the time spent.

--Energy system coupled with low drop rates and lengthy pity counters means having to rerun dungeon/raids many times over in a week for a *chance* to progress that specific dungeon's content. The chore is literally doubled without a paid subscription. And this is very early in the game's lifecycle, so it will only get worse with time.

---Insane amount of vertical progression systems that require heavy investment, grind and RNG. Many link poorly with the concept of gearing at all and aren't intuitive in the ways they're supposed to make characters stronger. Some like crafting and clash runes will even have a chance to destroy all prior progression with an unlucky roll, while others like pets require so much pointless grind even active players bot to farm them.

---Game is overrun with bots, even EA servers. Lifeskilling is a lot harder because of it, doing everything from pets to doing quests suck because bots keep taking away mobs, low-level dungeons are often hijacked by bots, the economy is diluted, etc. The matter of NCSoft very literally profiting off their activity while restricting legitimate player activity is described at the beginning of the review.

---Notwithstanding the first part of this review, the monetization is extremely aggressive and hinders the playing experience at every step of the way. Nearly all other reviews talk about it in length; I have nothing new to add.

This game was the first MMO to make me want to play it non-stop since Black Desert Online. The graphics are also stunning. Even though i am not much of a graphics enjoyer, i could not help but be amazed by some of the sights i saw while doing the quests and exploring. I spent over 400 hours in less than a month playing this game as a sub-only player, and i enjoyed it, because i'm not opposed to repetitive, maybe even stale grinding.
But eventually it gets to a point of no return.
You spend 100 hours to go from Point A to Point B, then from Point B to Point C there are 3 stops on your way there, and 2 of those 3 stops either require you treat this game with more respect and invest more time into it than an actual job, or you just pay the price tenfold in cash. 
The way they decided to do monetization is very scummy, very KoreanMMO-like. If you do not know yet what i am talking about, i am talking about a monthly subscription exclusively paid with real money, no way to earn it in-game that LIMITS your energy (what you need in order to run 80% of the content in this game) from 840 automatically regenerating to 540. Second of all, which in my opinion is the most egregious one is that you are not allowed to interact with a big portion of the market (one of the if not the most important feature of a game that thrives on player interaction) UNLESS you pay that subscription fee. The sub also offers a lot of QOL features that are ALREADY implemented in the game, you can see them from the moment you open the shop, yet when you dare click on them you get very kindly reminded that you are not someone that paid for the system, so you are not worthy of even looking in that direction. 
I did not cover even half of what the monetization of this game is, but i will move on to what generally made me and all of my friends quit this game, and that is THE COMMUNITY. I have played League of Legends for about 5-6 years, and i will say, right now, that the LoL community is healthier than the AION2 community(at least from my perspective and the perspective of my friends). At least when you get flamed in League, people sometimes tell you what you did wrong. In this game, you don't even get to that point. There are 2 big scenarios in this game(of course there are other small scenarios, but 75% of the time you will be hitting one of these 2 scenarios) : 
1. GATEKEEPING - This game requires you to hit certain threshholds of ItemLevel/GearScore in order to join specific dungeons/content forms. Let's take the Tier 3 dungeons for example here(Fire Temple + Ferocious Horn Den), that require you to have 2100 gear score to access them. You'd think once you reach that, you will slowly but surely make progress with that dungeon and get your gear, right? WRONG. Because, there is a SECOND threshhold you need to hit, but this time not imposed by the game on you, but by the players. There is a second metric in this game (that makes no sense in how it's calculated, but that's beyond the point) called CombatPower. This metric scales with EVERYTHING you do, but the impact gear/item level has on it is minimal. So, if you just reached Tier 3 dungeons, chances are very high that you will spend time looking for a room master WILLING to accept you in their party the same amount of time it would take you to clear that exact dungeon 4-5 times, even longer if you're unlucky.
2. TOXIC/ENTITLED MENTALITY - Let's say you get into a dungeon and you start clearing it with your party. And since it's your first time, or somebody else's first time running that dungeon, you all die to a wipe mechanic of a boss. It's fine, it happens, we can try again, team, right? WRONG AGAIN. Why wrong? Because (again, from my experience) in that 5 man lobby you just joined there usually is a person that feels entitled to having a perfect team, with perfect coordination, and the second any of you mess up a mechanic, skip, take longer to do ANYTHING than the "optimal way", guess what he does? Exactly, he QUITS THE DUNGEON. Now you and the 3 other people left have 3 options. You either try to beat it as a 4 man, which is usually never going to work, you wait for a 5th to join randomly, which again, rarely happens or you quit as well and go back to Square 1, looking for a dungeon.
I could write thousands of words about the community in this game, about the gaslighting, the gatekeeping, the toxicity and more.
I will not sit here and say i did not enjoy my time here, i clearly did, hence this many hours in just under a month since the game came out. I will not sit here and say i can reccomend this game to anybody, either. This game is not for casuals, this game does not take lightly to you not willing to spend either thousands and thousands of dollars on it or hundreds and hundreds of hours grinding. As a final conclusion, i would say that this game was a very pleasent activity for a very boring and empty month for me, but that's it, nothing more than that. Now that my friends quit as well, i find that i have less and less reasons to come back to this game. PvP is very one dimensional because of how combat is designed around a 1 button held macro, PvE could be fun or could be miserable depending on how your luck with interacting with the community is, gathering and crafting is a typical RNG-based system meant to drain you of your time, energy, patience, and eventually money. Everything in this game is designed for you to keep playing, but never for you to actually enjoy your time doing so. If you actually enjoy taking your time, exploring different ways to do things, taking a different approach or any sort of creative thinking, this game is not for you. This game has 2 paths, first one you do what every guide tells you to do and nothing else, then you quit, and the second one is you just quit from the start.

[h1] Bottom Line Up Front: Aion 2 delivers strong character customization and visual appeal but offers little novelty over existing MMORPGs, while its multi-layered subscription model and persistent bot problems make it difficult to recommend for long-term play[/h1]

[h1]I wanted to love this game, however it reminds me of the disappointment I felt with the  release of the Batman Movie all the pieces but somehow not delivering the impact it should and unfortunately not what I would ever classify as a must play.[/h1]  

[h2]Beautiful and Customizable, but familiar to a Fault [/h2]

Aion 2 is a polished, free-to-play MMORPG sequel that looks excellent and gives players one of the deeper character creators in the genre. It does not, however, meaningfully distinguish itself from the long line of similar games that have come before it. For someone who has been playing these type of games since Meridian 59 and earlier text-based MUDs/MOOs before that, that lack of novelty is hard to ignore.

[h3]What Works[/h3]
The character customization stands out. With more than 200 options across face, hair, body, style, and other details, you can create characters that feel personal rather than preset. Combined with the overall aesthetic—visuals, strong lighting, and a fantasy world that emphasizes verticality and flight—the game is frequently pleasant to look at. Flight itself remains one of the more appealing parts of the package, letting you move through a large world in a way that still feels like a signature of the series.

Combat and exploration are competent. The world is large, the presentation is attractive, and there is enough activity (dungeons, faction conflict, gathering, etc.) to keep you occupied for a while if you enjoy this style of game. It is free to play, if you can live without some perks and cosmetic elements, which lowers the barrier.
[h3]What Doesn’t[/h3]
The bigger issue is that Aion 2 does not introduce much that feels new. It refines the classic formula—faction war, progression systems, skills, dungeons, and open-world activities—with modern production values, but it does not rework the underlying loops or systems in a way that sets it apart from the many other MMORPGs available. If you have spent years (or decades) in this space, the sense of familiarity can quickly turn into fatigue. if you find yourself feeling this way this way, the self-awareness that you might simply be jaded is fair, but the game does little to challenge that feeling or offer a fresh hook.

The monetization and live-service realities amplify the problem. The game is free-to-play with an optional membership (around $15 for 30 days) that unlocks meaningful economic features such as full market/trading access and related convenience tools, plus the usual cosmetics and battle-pass layers. Multiple overlapping paid elements make the experience feel heavier than a simple free game or a clean subscription model. Constant bots and related gold-farming/RMT activity have also been a visible issue since launch. The presence of bots undercuts the sense that you are playing in a living player world. 

[h3]Bottom Line[/h3] Aion 2 is a good-looking MMORPG with strong character customization and a competent execution of familiar ideas. It is worth sampling if you want a free, visually appealing game with flight and solid production values. For players who have already lived through multiple generations of these systems, however, it does not deliver enough novelty to stand out, and the combination of subscription-style gating plus ongoing bot activity makes the overall package harder to recommend as a long-term home.

If the aesthetic and character creation pull you in, try it. Just go in with clear eyes about how much it actually moves the genre forward (or fails to).

With about  170 hours invested in this game, I feel like I’ve put in enough time to offer a fair and balanced review.

One of the biggest criticisms I’ve seen is that the game is pay-to-win. Personally, I would describe it more as pay-to-progress. I played entirely for free until approximately 150 hours in, when I had reached a gear score of 1750. At that point, I decided to purchase a membership to see whether it would make a noticeable difference, particularly when it came to dungeon drops and overall progression.

I did notice that I was receiving drops more frequently. The ability to open two chests at once is also a really nice quality-of-life feature. Another convenience I appreciated was being able to access the shop and purchase potions directly rather than having to travel to a physical shop. That said, I don’t think a membership is necessary to enjoy the game or make meaningful progress. In fact, I don’t plan on renewing mine. You can absolutely play and progress without spending money.

Another common complaint is that progression is too slow and grindy. To that, I would argue: I would hope it is! What’s the appeal of a game you can complete in just a few hours? This is designed to be a long-term game, and I think progression is a big part of what makes it enjoyable. You can play at your own pace, work toward your own goals, and always have something to look forward to.

I also don’t think progression is nearly as slow as some reviews make it out to be. Although I’ve accumulated around 170 hours, a significant portion of that time was spent creating multiple characters and leveling them up. I currently have five characters at level 45, one sitting at 1500 gear score, and my main character at 2145. Considering that, I’d estimate that getting a single character to 2100 gear score takes somewhere around 80–100 hours, depending on how you spend your time. Personally, I don’t find that unreasonable at all for a game designed to keep players engaged over the long term.

Overall, I think the game has a fantastic progression loop that keeps you coming back for more. The world is beautiful, the character customization is incredibly detailed while still being easy to understand, and there is always something to work toward. There’s a satisfying sense of accomplishment as you improve your gear, explore new content, and develop your characters.

I’ve also recently started creating characters on the opposing faction because I want to experience its storyline and explore the world from a different perspective. It’s been a blast! There’s genuinely so much to do, and I still feel like I’ve only scratched the surface.

At the end of the day, I understand that the game isn’t going to appeal to everyone, and it certainly isn’t without its flaws. However, I think some of the negative reviews overlook what makes this type of game enjoyable in the first place: the journey, the progression, and having a world you can continue coming back to.

I absolutely recommend giving this game a chance. I have no intention of stopping anytime soon, and am genuinely excited to see what future updates and expansions bring. Here’s to many more hours of grinding!

100+ Hours in Aion 2: My Honest Take

The first 45 levels of Aion 2 are genuinely excellent. The world looks great, exploration is fun, and the main story kept me engaged the entire way through.

Then the endgame starts.

The biggest problem isn't the grind itself. MMOs are supposed to be grindy. The problem is that almost every progression system in Aion 2 seems designed to slow players down rather than move them forward.

Want PvP gear? Head into the Abyss and collect feathers from fixed locations. Sounds fine until you realize geared players know exactly where you'll be and simply camp those spots. Reaching Abyss level 12 cost me around 40-50 deaths. That's not PvP. That's a feeding system for veterans.

Want dungeon gear? My weapon alone requires 42 dungeon clears through the token system. When you apply the same logic to the rest of the gear set, you're looking at roughly 200 runs just to catch up to content like Ludra. Not for BiS. Not for min-maxing. Just to participate.

"Just craft your gear."

Sure. Except even at max Blacksmith, I've failed Grey-tier crafts. Out of roughly 50 Grey weapon crafts, five failed outright and only four progressed. Then you repeat that process through Green, Blue, and Yellow tiers while praying to RNG at every step.

And the RNG never stops.

Gear upgrades become RNG.

Runes become RNG.

Crafting becomes RNG.

Skin collection becomes RNG.

You can finally get the item that completes your appearance collection and still fail the extraction.

Even paying doesn't solve the problem.

Buy the pass? Great.

Now enjoy the weekly time gates.

I've never seen a game monetize progression while simultaneously restricting progression quite this aggressively.

The frustrating part is that there's actually a good MMO underneath all of this. The world is beautiful. The leveling experience is great. The classes are fun enough. The open world and the Abyss have huge potential.

But every time the game lets itself be fun, another layer of RNG, time-gating, or repetition gets in the way.

Would I recommend Aion 2 to MMO veterans?

Maybe.

Would I recommend it to someone who has never played an MMO before?

Absolutely not.

There's a very good chance they'd never touch the genre again.

Aion 2 is a good experience on the surface, but as you get into it you begin to see some very deep flaws.

As with any MMO, the endgame involves the pursuit of gear upgrades.  You have the choice of cycling through various dungeons, or pursuing crafting.  Crafted gear is Best in Slot, but requires a comical amount of RNG to get there.  

For one, gathered materials have four quality tiers by color.  White, Green, Blue, Gold.  While gathering the default is as one would expect, white, and gathering for a higher tier requires a proc.  Then you get to wait while the Pass/Fail passive game is played.  You can spec into chances for additional materials or a second upgrade proc, but these are still typically low.  You also have a daily gathering limit of 1000, a system added to deter RMT bots.  You're also no longer able to gather until you reach level cap.

So you've gathered enough materials and are now ready to try to craft an item.  You need to rely on the same Pass/Fail flow, and there is a 25% chance for your craft to proc to the next tier.  If you get this proc, then you can use the item to try for the next highest tier.  If not, well, stinks to be you, doesn't it?  So in order to work toward the highest level of gear you need to rely on multiple layered procs.  It's not fun, and it's not engaging.

Next we have dungeons.  At the end of a dungeon you have a chance to open a chest at the cost of 40 Odyle Energy.  Odyle Energy charges at a rate of 15 per 3 hours, and you can store a maximum of 560, 840 if you pay for a subscription.  Subscription also allows you to open the chest twice at twice the cost, so it could be a time savings, but you still have the same base recharge rate.  To be fair, there are items that you can purchase and craft with a weekly cap that can add to Odyle Energy.  If you want to run dungeons to help friends without opening the cube, you have a weekly limit of 10 of these runs before you are locked out of dungeons.  Both of these systems are stated to deter RMT. 

There's an extensive skin (transmog) system that is tied to power.  When you receive gear you can extract it and you have a 10% chance to receive the skin.  Much of this gear is low drop rate from dungeons and other sources.  I've run dungeons multiple dozens of times and still not received all of the skins from that dungeon even though I received the armor as multiple drops.  There is a convoluted system to try upgrading skins, but it also has a very low rate of success and is not worth talking about.  

The game has an integrated macro functionality.  You stack your attack chain in the macro and hold down the button.  Many classes are able to essentially hold down their left mouse button, and macro button while occasionally using direct inputs for 2-3 other skills as needed.  Some people use a variation of the right mouse button as well, but the concept is fundamentally the same.  It's boring, and there's no skill expression.

The PvP is a joke.  Gear wins.  Due to the above described macro system, there's no skill expression.  You're generally not going to outplay another person and it's going to come down to a factor of gear and latency because most people will be using some variation of the same build and macro.  There's also a PvP centric area called The Abyss where the two factions are able to fight for objectives.  The area is quite small, and the faction populations aren't anything resembling balanced.  I don't believe that any of the major objectives have been consistently won by the underpop faction.

The monetization model isn't  The subscription adds very little value, and there are season passes that can be purchased and again generally add very little value.  With a subscription you can use the market (Auction House) and are able to trade Quna (premium currency for real cash) from other players in exchange for Kina (ingame currency).  As you play in the end game you begin to get a sense that the underlying game systems were designed as such in order to frustrate people into finally swiping for Quna to advance their character.

There are some high points.  The character creator is excellent, as are the animations, models, world, skins etc.. Those only carry a game so far.

As much as I wanted to really recommend this game, and I truly did, it's really not worth playing unless they make an effort to address the systemic issues.

The game is enjoyable enough while there are quests to complete. But once you run out of quests, it turns into just another typical MMORPG: farming materials to craft items, joining guilds and alliances, and fighting against players from your own faction or opposing factions, depending on whatever events the server has scheduled.

If you want to trade on the marketplace, you need a level 45 character and a monthly subscription, which costs around $19. Honestly, that's not unreasonable. This is a commercial product, not a charity project. There are maintenance costs, salaries for staff across various departments, and plenty of other expenses to cover. It's actually quite similar to the early days of MMORPGs, when games operated on an airtime subscription model.

However, when free-to-play games started appearing and making money through in-game purchases instead, players gradually moved over to them. Subscription-based MMORPGs eventually had to adapt by becoming free-to-play and selling cosmetic items instead. Nexon should consider doing the same, rather than relying almost entirely on selling cosmetic gacha items.

Now, here's something I personally absolutely hate: kill stealing. Players jump in and attack monsters without caring whether someone else is currently trying to complete a quest or doing something else. The loot then goes to whoever deals the most damage. In most cases, that's usually magic or ranged classes. It's quite rare to see melee players stealing kills. Of course, this is a common issue in open-world games where multiple players can hunt the same monsters simultaneously. I understand that, but I still hate it.

Another issue is how high-geared players behave in dungeons. They often seem to have no interest in helping ordinary players. Their only goal is to rush straight to the dungeon boss, kill it, and leave. If you can't make it to the boss room in time, you're basically left behind and locked out. Once the boss dies, the dungeon ends. Anyone who got stuck outside and missed the fight receives no loot for that run, meaning their dungeon entry points were completely wasted.

Overall, the game is playable, sure. But I quit and uninstalled it after just one or two days. There's nothing particularly new or innovative about it, and the online community is still the same old toxic mess. It's extremely rare to come across genuinely decent people to party up with.

In the end, Vindictus still reigns supreme!!
