[b][i]Caution![/i][/b] [b][i]It will be a LOOOOOONG review[/i][/b][i].[/i] 
[b]Keep in mind that this review comes from a non-membership player's perspective but[/b] even though I'm reviewing the game from an F2P perspective, I think most of these issues affect members as well. The game is [b]technically free-to-play[/b] but it doesn't feel like it's designed to be enjoyed as a free-to-play game in the long run.
As a F2P player, I don't mind spending more time grinding or progressing at a slower pace compared to paying players and that's perfectly understandable. However AION 2 takes this to another level where several basic systems and progression opportunities are locked behind a monthly subscription and for me that's where the problem starts.
[h3][b][u]Membership & Monetization[/u][/b][/h3]
Without a membership, you don't even have access to the in-game marketplace. On top of that you can only claim dungeon rewards once instead of twice. Considering how heavily the game relies on RNG for gear progression this is a pretty significant disadvantage.
Another major restriction is the Quna-Kinah exchange. For short Kinah is the game's regular currency while Quna being the premium one which can also be used to purchase things like cosmetics, passes etc. Without a membership you cannot exchange between these two currencies. This also means F2P players have no way of accessing the other two battlepasses through this system. And let's not forget that membership itself costs around [b]$15 per month[/b]. I wouldn't have much of a problem with optional cosmetics or convenience features but locking marketplace access and additional rewards behind a monthly subscription is a different story. It feels like the game is deliberately making the F2P experience more restrictive to push players towards spending money.
[h3][b][u]Progression & RNG[/u][/b][/h3]
Gear progression is another major issue especially for F2P players. Yellow gear already has a pretty low drop rate and even when you finally get a drop there's no guarantee it will be something you actually need. You can get the same item multiple times while still missing several other pieces. This makes progression extremely frustrating and can leave you stuck at the same item level for a very long time.
For example, I've done around at least minimum [b]70 dungeon runs[/b] so far and gotten the [b]exact same gloves three times[/b]. I've been stuck around 1400-1500 item level for quite a while now while the next dungeon requires somewhere around 1600-1800. For math lovers like me, for Vakron yellow item drop chance per boss is 1st 3.5%, 2nd 3.5%, 3rd 7.5% which means every run you have 13.86% chance getting a yellow item and lets say you need the helmet which has iirc %5 chance it means you have 0.693% chance to get it lol. Of course there is a pity system to prevent this but you need to run the same dungeon 21 times to get a ticket that allows you to craft a specific item. Sounds good on paper but even that doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Since you're still missing other gear pieces, you might not even be able to make meaningful use of that ticket when you get it. 
[i]Crafting your weapon is another alternative but without access to the marketplace, it becomes extremely expensive and requires a ridiculous amount of farming. And guess what? It's RNG-based as well. So even the alternative progression paths are heavily dependent on luck and endless grinding.[/i]
[h3][b][u]Gameplay & Combat & Long-Term Progression[/u][/b][/h3]
There's also a lot of FOMO involved. Shugo events, raids, Abyss and Rifts all have specific time windows or limited entries and most of the time they overlap. So missing them means potentially missing out on rewards and progression. Combat also feels rather shallow. Most of the time you're just pressing macros with very little need for reactive healing or well-timed buffs. Build diversity doesn't help much either. 
PvP is another issue, as faction balance heavily depends on server population. Some servers are dominated by one faction, making Abyss farming and progression frustrating for the other side.
Finally, the game heavily encourages playing multiple characters to funnel materials and upgrade your main. However the story is extremely long and you have to repeat a lot of the horizontal progression on every alt, no way to skip story. Without membership's additional dungeon rewards, keeping multiple characters geared as an F2P player becomes even harder.
[h3][b][u]Performance & Optimization[/u][/b][/h3]
Performance is another weak point. Even on high-end hardware, FPS drops are quite noticeable, especially during crowded Field Boss fights. The game could definitely use more optimization.
[h3][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/h3]
AION 2 has a beautiful world and a lot of potential but unfortunately its monetization and progression systems overshadow most of its positive aspects. It's hard to recommend a game that feels like it's constantly pushing you towards a monthly subscription just to enjoy basic gameplay features.

I've been playing Rainbow Six Siege since 2017, originally on console before making the switch to PC around 2024. It's easily one of my favourite competitive games, offering an experience that most other FPS games simply don't. The tactical gameplay, destructible environments, operator abilities and endless strategies make every match feel different.

However, Siege is far from perfect. It can be incredibly rewarding but equally frustrating. Common complaints within the community include inconsistent matchmaking, cheaters, balancing issues and some questionable decisions from Ubisoft regarding updates. There's also nothing quite as frustrating as dealing with spawn peeking or teammates who make questionable decisions.

One of the biggest things worth mentioning is the learning curve. If you're thinking about getting into Siege now, I'd absolutely recommend giving it a go. It's still a fantastic game, especially when playing with friends. However, if your goal is to actually become good at Siege, you're going to have a much longer journey ahead of you. With the growing operator roster, gadgets, map knowledge and constant changes, there's a lot for new players to understand before they can consistently compete against experienced players.

Overall, Siege is a fantastic game that has kept me coming back since 2017, despite all its frustrations. I'd recommend it to anyone interested in tactical shooters, but don't expect to master it overnight. It has an incredibly high skill ceiling, and that's both one of its greatest strengths and biggest weaknesses.

Hello, this is Caydly. There are many video games that people enjoy playing, but few games have captured my attention and kept me entertained as much as Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Siege. Ever since I started playing it, I have developed a strong appreciation for everything the game has to offer. From its competitive gameplay and unique operators to its intense matches and teamwork, Rainbow Six Siege is more than just a regular first-person shooter. It is a game that challenges players to think strategically, communicate with teammates, and constantly improve their skills. What makes Rainbow Six Siege so special to me is that no two matches ever feel exactly the same. Every round brings a new challenge, and every victory feels rewarding because of the effort it takes to achieve it. I love Rainbow Six Siege because of its exciting gameplay, unique characters, competitive environment, and the memories I have made while playing it.

One of the biggest reasons I love Rainbow Six Siege is its unique gameplay. Unlike many other first-person shooter games, Siege requires players to think carefully before making decisions. Players cannot simply run around shooting everything they see and expect to win. Instead, they have to use strategy, patience, and awareness to outsmart the opposing team. The destructible environments make the game especially interesting because walls, floors, and ceilings can be destroyed to create new opportunities. A defender might think they are safe behind a wall, only for an attacker to create an opening and surprise them. This feature makes every round exciting because players must constantly pay attention to their surroundings. I enjoy how the game rewards creativity and smart decisions instead of relying only on who has the fastest reaction time. Every successful play feels satisfying because it usually takes planning and skill.

Another reason Rainbow Six Siege is one of my favorite games is its wide selection of operators. Each operator has a different ability, weapon selection, and purpose on the battlefield. Attackers and defenders have different responsibilities, which creates many ways to approach a match. Some operators are designed to gather information, while others specialize in breaking through reinforced walls, protecting teammates, or stopping enemy advances. This variety allows players to find characters that match their individual playstyles. For example, someone who enjoys playing aggressively might choose an operator that can enter rooms quickly, while someone who prefers helping the team might choose an operator focused on gathering information or supporting teammates. I love experimenting with different operators because it keeps the game interesting and gives me something new to learn. Even after playing for a long time, there are still strategies and combinations that I can discover.

Teamwork is another major reason why I enjoy Rainbow Six Siege so much. Unlike games where one player can easily carry an entire team, Siege often requires everyone to work together. Communication can make the difference between winning and losing a round. Players need to share enemy locations, provide information about traps, and coordinate their attacks or defenses. A teammate might spot an enemy camera, another might reinforce a wall, and someone else might create an opening for the team. When everyone works together, the game becomes much more enjoyable. Some of my favorite moments happen when my teammates and I successfully coordinate a plan and win a difficult round. Even when a match does not go as planned, playing with friends can make it entertaining. The funny conversations, unexpected moments, and close victories create memories that make me want to keep coming back.

The competitive nature of Rainbow Six Siege also makes me love the game. Winning is exciting, but losing can make me want to improve even more. There are always new things to learn, whether it is improving my aim, learning maps, understanding operator abilities, or developing better strategies. The ranking system gives players goals to work toward and encourages them to become better. Sometimes a match can be extremely frustrating, especially when the other team is playing well or when I make a mistake that costs my team a round. However, those moments can also teach me what I need to work on. I enjoy the feeling of finally improving at something that I struggled with before. Getting a difficult elimination, successfully defending an objective, or winning a close match makes all the practice feel worthwhile. The constant challenge is one of the biggest reasons the game never gets boring for me.

Another thing that makes Rainbow Six Siege special is how unpredictable it can be. Even if I play the same map several times, each match can turn out differently depending on the operators, strategies, and decisions made by both teams. Sometimes a round goes perfectly according to plan, while other times something completely unexpected happens. A player might accidentally make a mistake that turns into a hilarious moment, or someone might pull off an incredible play when the team needs it most. These unexpected situations make the game memorable. I also enjoy how the game continues to change through updates, new operators, balance adjustments, and other improvements. These changes give players new things to experience and different strategies to explore. It is exciting knowing that there is always something else to discover.

Beyond the gameplay itself, Rainbow Six Siege has become a way for me to spend time with friends and enjoy myself. Playing together gives us something to talk about, compete over, and laugh about. Some of the funniest memories come from matches that were supposed to be serious but ended up being chaotic. Even when we lose, we can still have a good time joking around and remembering what happened. Video games are not only about winning or losing; they can also bring people together and create friendships. Rainbow Six Siege has given me countless entertaining moments that I probably would not have experienced otherwise. That is another reason why I have such a strong connection to the game.

In conclusion, Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Siege is much more than just a video game to me. It is a game that combines strategy, teamwork, competition, creativity, and entertainment in a way that keeps me interested. Its unique operators, destructible environments, challenging matches, and unpredictable moments make every experience different. Although the game can sometimes be frustrating, the excitement of improving, winning difficult rounds, and playing with friends makes it worth it. I love how Siege constantly challenges me to become a better player while also giving me opportunities to make great memories. There are plenty of other games available, but Rainbow Six Siege will always be one of my favorites because of the experiences it has given me. No matter how many matches I play, there is always another strategy to learn, another victory to chase, and another reason to keep playing.

Tactical Perfection: Why Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Siege Remains Unmatched
In the crowded landscape of modern first-person shooters, few titles demand as much patience, intellect, and teamwork as Ubisoft’s Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Siege. Originally released in December 2015, the game rejects the fast-paced, run-and-gun formula of traditional arcade shooters in favor of methodical, high-stakes tactical combat. What makes Rainbow Six Siege so endlessly compelling is not merely its realistic weaponry or tense atmosphere, but the way it transforms every match into a dynamic chess game of destruction, information, and strategy. Over a decade after its debut, its unique mechanics and deep strategic complexity continue to make it an extraordinary gaming experience.
The defining feature of Rainbow Six Siege is its intricate system of environmental destruction. Unlike standard shooters where walls and floors serve as permanent, indestructible barriers, Siege treats the map itself as a malleable tool. Attackers can breach through ceilings, blast open reinforced walls, or punch tiny sightlines into drywall to catch defenders off guard. Conversely, defenders must carefully decide which walls to reinforce, where to create rotation holes, and how to reshape the battlefield to funnel enemies into crossfires. This level of interactivity ensures that no two rounds ever play out the exact same way, rewarding creativity and map knowledge over simple reflex speed.
Equally brilliant is the game’s diverse roster of playable operators, each equipped with specialized gadgets that dramatically alter the flow of a round. Every match is a tense battle of counter-picks and adaptation between five attackers and five defenders. An attacker might deploy drones to gather intelligence or use hard-breaching charges to open a fortified objective, while a defender might rely on electronic jammers, cameras, or traps to stall the assault. Because players do not respawn until the next round and lethal gunplay can end a firefight in a single headshot, every decision carries immense weight. Success requires constant communication and synergy, turning a well-coordinated five-person squad into an unstoppable unit.
Furthermore, the longevity of Rainbow Six Siege is a testament to its evolving design and dedicated support. Through continuous seasonal updates, reworked maps, and the ongoing addition of new operators and tactical mechanics, the game consistently challenges veterans to relearn strategies and adapt to shifting metas. The sheer adrenaline rush of winning a one-versus-three clutch situation as the round timer ticks down to zero is a thrill that few other competitive games can replicate.
Ultimately, Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Siege stands as a masterpiece of competitive game design. By seamlessly blending destructible environments, specialized operator abilities, and unforgiving tactical gunplay, it rewards players who think critically and communicate effectively. While its steep learning curve demands persistence, the payoff is an unmatched sense of mastery and excitement that makes Rainbow Six Siege truly unforgettable.

Ubisoft Account Verification emails sent to my original email in 2024
Past support cases under my original username
My Rainbow Six Siege profile folder and in-game screenshots from 2020 showing my account logged in on my PC
Twitch Drops received on this account, and stream clips of me playing on it with my webcam on
Steam purchase receipts and my linked Steam ID

Rainbow Six Siege is one of those games that's incredibly fun with friends, but can also test your patience more than a little.

I absolutely love the variety of operators and their unique abilities. The teamwork, strategy, and different ways you can approach each round are what make Siege stand out from other FPS games. Casual matches with friends are easily some of the most enjoyable experiences, and there's always something new to learn or improve on.

Unfortunately, the game isn't without its problems. The toxic community can make matches frustrating, and dealing with cheaters, sweaty try-hard players, and questionable matchmaking definitely takes away from the experience. Bugs and glitches are another ongoing annoyance, and some of Ubisoft's decisions regarding the game and its monetization leave a lot to be desired.

A frustrating game? Absolutely. A fun game? Also absolutely.

Overall, I'd recommend it, especially if you have friends to play with. Just don't expect every match to be a peaceful experience!

Rainbow Six is a strategy, tactical team shooter game as you know. [h1]Rainbow Six Siege – 4/10. Over 100 Hours Played, Still Not Having Fun.[/h1]
Rainbow Six Siege is probably one of the strangest games in my Steam library. I've spent over 100 hours playing it, yet I can't honestly say I ever particularly enjoyed it.

I understand why people love Siege. Its tactical depth, environmental destruction, and emphasis on teamwork are impressive. But personally, I found the experience increasingly exhausting rather than entertaining.

[h2]I Miss the Original Siege[/h2]
I started playing back when the game was much simpler, when Tachanka still had his legendary mounted machine gun and the original Spetsnaz operators actually felt like a proper counterterrorism unit.

Tachanka, Fuze, Kapkan, and Glaz were my favourites.
The early game had a certain charm. It was tactical, occasionally ridiculous, and still gave you room to experiment without feeling like you needed to study an entire textbook before every match.

I especially enjoyed the more grounded atmosphere and distinctive operator identities.

Unfortunately, that feeling gradually disappeared.

[h2]Too Much Information, Too Little Fun[/h2]
My biggest problem with Siege is how much attention it demands at every moment.
Cameras, drones, gadgets, enemy positions, destructible walls, operator abilities, teammates, and an increasingly complicated meta.

You're constantly checking something, listening for something, or worrying about something.
And while you're concentrating on one problem, three more appear somewhere else.
Sometimes your teammates help. Sometimes they're the reason everything goes to shit.

I enjoy tactical shooters, but Siege often felt less like an exciting counterterrorism operation and more like an extremely stressful job where everyone expects you to know everything.

The constant information gathering and cautious movement simply weren't my idea of fun.

[h2]The Operator Problem[/h2]
I understand that introducing new operators keeps the game alive.
But over time, the growing roster made Siege feel increasingly disconnected from what originally attracted me.

There are so many abilities, interactions, counters, and strategies that keeping up with everything becomes a commitment of its own.
I preferred the original operators, their relatively straightforward equipment, and the freedom to experiment with different approaches.

Nowadays, it feels like there's always an established meta you're expected to follow.
And when a multiplayer game starts making experimentation feel like a mistake, something important has been lost.

[h2]The Community Didn't Help[/h2]
The community was another major reason I struggled to enjoy the game.
Toxic behaviour, excessive competitiveness, and frustrating moderation or penalties made an already demanding experience even less appealing.

I understand the need to deal with cheating and genuinely disruptive players, but the overall environment often felt unnecessarily hostile.

Not every match needs to be treated like an international esports championship.

Sometimes people just want to play a f*cking video game.

[h2]Why Did I Play Over 100 Hours, Then?[/h2]
Simple. My friends and colleagues.
Playing together was the main reason I kept returning.

The conversations, occasional funny situations, and shared experiences made those hours worthwhile.
But there's an important difference between enjoying a game and enjoying the people you're playing it with.

For me, Siege was mostly the latter.
Without that group, I doubt I would have spent nearly as much time playing.

[h2]Final Verdict – 4/10[/h2]
Rainbow Six Siege isn't a terrible game. It has excellent destruction mechanics, substantial tactical depth, and a dedicated audience that clearly enjoys its competitive nature.

I respect that.
But it simply isn't for me.

I preferred the earlier, more grounded version, when the operator roster was smaller, the gameplay felt less overwhelming, and there was more room to experiment.

The constant drone and camera management, complicated meta, toxic community, and excessive pressure gradually removed most of the enjoyment.

I don't need every tactical shooter to be easy. I just want the difficulty to feel rewarding rather than exhausting.

[b]4/10 – Over 100 hours played, mostly because of my friends.

I miss the original Spetsnaz, Tachanka's mounted machine gun, and the days when experimenting with a ridiculous strategy didn't feel like a criminal offence.

I understand why people love Siege. I just wish I had enjoyed it half as much as they did.[/b]

Multiple Gameplay, Visual & Quest Issues Feedback
I encountered several gameplay and visual comfort issues while playing The First Descendant, and I would like to share my feedback here.
The Shift hotkey for bulk marking items as junk is nearly non-functional during missions. It has only worked once in my gameplay experience. I am forced to manually mark every loot item one by one. While sorting inventory, my character stands still, which may cause other players to falsely report me for AFK. Although my previous restriction has expired, this flaw remains in the game and continues to create risks of false AFK penalties for other players. This bulk marking function and AFK judgment logic require optimization.
The matchmaking system has persistent problems. When I log in for the first time each day, the public matchmaking queue often freezes and fails to find teammates for a long time. I frequently need to complete a solo mission to restore the matchmaking function. Matchmaking remains unstable, and teammates often leave without warning. False penalties and unreliable matchmaking create unnecessary frustration for players.
The penalty judgment mechanism needs improvement. Hidden matchmaking isolation rules and multi-player report priority punishment create risks of false judgments for players who are simply farming normally. The complicated appeal process disrupts normal team gameplay.
The Excessive glare and sudden screen transitions cause eye strain and dizziness during extended gameplay. Bunny’s bright flashing bloom effects are just one example. Many other skill effects from different characters create overexposed bright lighting along the screen edges, resulting in continuous visual discomfort. When the character dies or falls into pits, the screen instantly turns black without a smooth fade transition, and this abrupt screen change is harsh on the eyes. I have played Destiny 2 and Dead by Daylight for a long time and have not experienced this level of visual discomfort from special effects. The game lacks independent options to adjust bloom, glow and flash effects, and simply lowering overall post-processing cannot solve the root problem. The dev team should add more visual adjustment options and prioritize player visual comfort, as poor visual experience contributes to player burnout.
The Base Quality system feels unbalanced. My Base Quality has reached the cap of 400, yet the guaranteed high-quality drop bonus only applies to limited content such as Onslaught, Sanctum of Restriction, and Hold the Line. AT Research missions appear to have a hidden quality lock, with the minimum drop quality capped at 325. The large amount of resources invested to max Base Quality does not match the corresponding rewards.
There is a bug with Yujin’s exclusive quest. After finishing the main story and obtaining a Level 40 Yujin, I switched to Yujin in the Albion medical area. Most Medic Corps NPCs including Valby, Dia, and Serena disappeared, leaving only Kate. I could not interact with the missing NPCs, and Yujin’s exclusive descendant story quest never appeared in the Records menu. I tried restarting the game, verifying Steam files, waiting in Albion, and completing Void Intercept missions, but the quest flag still could not be triggered.
Random network error NE4003 often occurs during team missions, disconnecting players in the middle of battles and interrupting mission progress, AT level farming and gear development.
The Dessaline shop refresh mechanism is inefficient. The refresh cycle is too long, and the variety of refreshed items is limited, slowing down material and equipment collection.
These are repeated bugs and unreasonable mechanic flaws I encountered in the game, rather than operational errors. I hope the development team can review these issues and implement corresponding optimizations.:LIS_butterfly:

After over 600 hours in this game, I’ve come to believe that the developers have a serious problem with listening to player feedback.

Even putting the P2W issues aside, this game still suffers from repetitive content and rewards that simply aren’t worth the time invested. And if you’re unlucky, the game will even limit your character progression by locking certain things behind weekly caps. I honestly consider this one of the worst ways to retain players I’ve ever encountered.

The developers keep making insignificant things into major selling points and presenting them as updates, while seemingly ignoring the issues that actually matter to players.

I think the only reason many veteran players are still here is that they’re clinging to the illusion of what this game seemed capable of becoming in its early days. After investing so much time and money, it’s hard to walk away and admit that it hasn’t lived up to those expectations.

At this point, what keeps many of us playing isn’t enjoyment anymore. It’s sunk cost.

We’re not staying because the game is still fun. We’re staying because we don’t want all the time and money we’ve already invested to feel like a waste.

Before getting into my criticisms, I want to make one thing clear: I genuinely enjoyed playing The First Descendant. Experimenting with Descendants, crafting builds, and tackling challenging content kept me coming back. I've wanted this game to succeed and improve, which is why its current direction has been so disappointing.

I started playing at launch, but most of my playtime has come since Season 4. I've played almost every day, going from Mastery Rank 21 through casual play to Rank 35 by leveling nearly every Descendant and weapon I could obtain. Rank 37 is the highest currently available. I mention this to show how invested I've been in the game's systems, not because my rank is why I'm leaving a negative review.

One of my biggest frustrations began with Raven's release in Season 4. In my experience, she's so obscenely overpowered that playing another Descendant often feels like deliberately putting yourself at a disadvantage. The only time I've seen a Raven player struggle to survive was in Karel's Mothership on Conquest difficulty, which was removed in Update 1.4.5 for reasons I still don't understand.

This isn't just about damage numbers; it affects cooperative play. In Trials, Onslaught, Karel's Mothership, and Cradle, I've struggled to contribute alongside Raven players. Her Nightfall module can cover huge areas with up to ten AoE zones, wiping out groups before others can participate. What's the point of carefully crafting a build if you barely get to use it? I don't blame players for choosing a powerful character. I blame the imbalance that makes everyone else's contribution feel unnecessary.

Freyna makes this even more frustrating. She was my first main at launch, and I loved spreading Toxic damage and watching it chain through groups of enemies. But as power scaling increased, especially since Season 3 in early 2025, she struggled to keep up with newer endgame content. She still excels in older activities, but those aren't where I want to push her limits.

Update 1.4.5 was supposed to rework Freyna. I won't bury this review in skill coefficients, but after testing her updated abilities, it's one of the most disappointing character updates I've experienced. Her Toxic rotations demand far more setup and effort than other Descendants' abilities, often for worse results. Raven can accomplish more with a few button presses, while Serena, Ines, Blair, Luna, and others clear difficult content faster. What was this rework supposed to improve?

What finally pushed me to my breaking point was Trials: Protocol 002. I enjoy difficult content, but this feels less like a test of skill than a test of how often I can tolerate losing control of my character. Vanguards, Miscreants, and other enemies constantly knock you backward or to the ground. Recovery takes several seconds, only for another knockdown to happen almost immediately. Combat zone timers continue while you're unable to act. Boss fights add pulls, knockbacks, damaging ground effects, and endlessly spawning enemies that interrupt you. The issue isn't that enemies hit hard. It's that I can barely perform the actions my build was designed around.

I tried Protocol 002 with Freyna, Hailey, Blair, Lepic, Viessa, and Dia before bringing out Ultimate Ajax, a tank built around defense and protecting his team. With Variable Code buffs earned in Trials, my Ajax reached 1,108,472 DEF, 33,961 HP, and a -37.5% Incoming Damage Modifier, alongside Mobile Fortress and protective barriers. I completed Round 4, Zone 7 in 48 minutes and 15 seconds, dealing over 408 billion total damage. Yet I was STILL being knocked around constantly. That durability kept me alive but didn't make the interruptions enjoyable. I don't expect a tank to ignore every mechanic. I do expect meaningful responses to crowd control beyond watching my character repeatedly recover from the floor, especially when some skills require getting close to enemies to proc certain buffs/debuffs.

Public matchmaking wasn't much better. Solo meant nonstop interruptions; with Raven or Luna teammates, enemies often died too quickly for me to contribute. I briefly returned to Protocol 001 and genuinely enjoyed it, only for it to be temporarily removed over a bug, leaving Protocol 002 as the sole option. Even normally, Protocols 001 and 002 rotate  daily rather than being available together. I shouldn't have to skip Trials for days just to avoid an encounter designed around constant knockbacks, or choose between losing control solo and feeling unnecessary in a team.

I also question where we're meant to properly test builds. The Laboratory caps enemies at Level 260 while current endgame content reaches Level 400. You also can't meaningfully configure enemies as Elites or apply the modifiers needed to replicate actual endgame encounters. That makes it a poor substitute for testing the builds we've worked on. Meanwhile, Karel's Mothership on Conquest difficulty was one of the few activities that truly pushed my builds, and it's been removed.

Update 1.4.5 also introduced a Halloween Pass costing 700 Caliber, with 30 reward levels and some free rewards. Yet as of October 16, Albion has no noticeable Halloween decorations or atmosphere; the main hub looks the same as ever. Previous Halloween skins aren't scheduled to return until October 29, TWO DAYS BEFORE HALLOWEEN. For a seasonal update, that feels incredibly underwhelming.

All of this makes me question how thoroughly these changes are playtested. Raven has remained dominant through multiple updates and hotfixes. I suspect backlash to Ines's earlier adjustment, which stopped her killing enemies through walls without directly reducing her damage, may have made the developers reluctant to tone down popular Descendants. I can't know their reasoning, but the result feels like relentless power creep without meaningful balance changes to keep other characters competitive.

With Destiny 2 no longer receiving regular content at the time, I hoped The First Descendant could be my next game for years. For a while, it felt like it could. Even in Destiny 2's worst periods, I can't recall being as consistently frustrated with its gameplay as I've been with TFD lately. That's especially disappointing because I wanted this game to succeed.

And I haven't even touched on the frustrating RNG surrounding Transcendent Weapons and Ancestors Modules, the leaderboards, or other FOMO-driven design choices. There are more problems I could discuss, but the issues above are what finally pushed me away.

Ultimately, poor character balance, the removal of challenging content I enjoyed, questionable gameplay decisions, and Protocol 002 have killed my enthusiasm. I no longer enjoy The First Descendant the way I used to, and I never wanted to say that. I want this game to be better. I want to feel excited about testing builds and playing different Descendants again. But in its current state, I can't recommend it.

If mediocrity was a contest, this game would no doubt get first prize. It's neither excitingly good nor terribly bad. Just... ehh~
It starts out okay, as with all games, it has a decent hook. But everything just kind of immediately falls off once you get past the starting quest. But even then, you might get bored early because there's no one doing early missions, so you'll be playing solo for the first 10 hours or so.

The issue ultimately comes with the mission, maps and game designs.

[h2] Mission design [/h2] 
Pretty much every mission boils down to go to place, kill 200-300 enemies, kill 1-5 elite enemies, go to next area. Rince and repeat. It's so mind-numbingly dull. It was somewhat  cathartic at the beginning when everything was weak and you could mow people down by the dozens easily, but the difficulty just randomly jumps once you reach a certain point. Enemies go from having 400k hp to 70 million HP. Not only is their HP inflated to fuck, but they also gain a ton of damage resist, making them even bigger damage sponges.


[h2] Maps [/h2] 
They started out decent. Each biome has an unique theme and look, but once you get through the start of the game, and get into the late game, they ditch those interesting and different looking biomes immediately, replaced with borderline UE5 asset flip maps.
Big, massive featureless room with maybe a few boxes, platforms and nothing else. There's nothing worth exploring and nothing worth seeing. One "open world" map is literally just a grey wasteland with nothing to explore or find except resources crate scattered around as haphazardly as breadcrumbs on your kitchen counter.
Worse though is how boring the map actually plays. They seem massive in scale, but they are so barren you'll find more things of interest in 1.0 No Man Sky.
And don't worry, the maps aren't randomized, they will be the exact same every time. You'll get sick of them very quickly.

[h2] Game Design [/h2]
The balance is all screwed because the devs apparently can't playtest their game at all. Guns, in this "third person shooter" basically become pea shooters in the late game because enemies get so bullet spongy. Even fully modded, my biggest baddest chunky sniper rifle deal 50k damage, maybe 100k on a good day. Sounds like a lot?  Remember earlier I said enemies have 70 million HP? Only 700 more bullets to go.

This happened because the devs released a character that buffed her guns and she became extremely broken as a character. So the devs, not wanting to nerf her, decided to nerf all guns. So this makes all the weapons you've grinded and built nothing more than stat-sticks for the majority of the characters who don't have gun-centric abilities.


Will I still play it? Probably. I'm a bit deep in the grind atm so it's a bit hard to leave. But I assure you, you will find absolutely nothing of interest in this stagnant swamp that they call a game..

[h1]A GAME I SHOULD LOVE - BUT SOMEHOW I GET BORED EVERY TIME[/h1]

The First Descendant has almost everything that should make me addicted to a looter shooter.

Great looking characters.
Satisfying gunplay.
Abilities.
Build crafting.
Weapons to farm.
Rare drops.
Bosses.
Constant progression.

On paper?

[b]This should absolutely be my kind of game.[/b]

And yet every time I play it, I eventually get bored surprisingly fast.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h2]>>> THE PROBLEM ISN'T THE GRIND <<<[/h2]

I don't mind grinding.

I actually LIKE grinding when the goal feels meaningful.

The problem is doing different grinds that all feel like the same activity.

Enter room.
Kill wave.
Run forward.
Kill another wave.
Kill elite.
Kill boss.
Collect loot.
Repeat.

Again.
And again.
And again.

Sure, my character becomes stronger. My weapons improve. My numbers get bigger.

But the actual gameplay often feels almost identical.

At some point I am not thinking:

[b]"I can't wait to become stronger."[/b]

I am thinking:

[b]"Why am I becoming stronger?"[/b]

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h2]>>> PROGRESSION NEEDS A PURPOSE <<<[/h2]

I can farm a better Descendant.
I can farm better weapons.
I can improve modules.
I can optimize my builds.

And I genuinely enjoy that part.

But once I finally have that amazing build...

[b]What am I supposed to do with it?[/b]

Farm the same activities even faster?

Defeat enemies that already weren't particularly challenging?

Start another grind just to repeat the process?

I want my progression to unlock meaningful challenges, new experiences and interesting gameplay.

[b]A great progression system should make me excited about what comes AFTER the grind.[/b]

Not just make me better at grinding.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

[h2]>>> THE SAD PART <<<[/h2]

The First Descendant isn't a bad game.

Far from it.

I really want to love The First Descendant. At a high level, it is exactly what I want. It's a randomized looter game with lots of gooner elements. Unfortunately, the execution is not very good, and it hasn't been good for many years. I have a pattern where every few months, I will install this game, play it for an hour, not have fun, and then uninstall it. I write this review in hopes of giving some insight for people considering this game and the developers, and also to remind myself in a few months the disappointment I am about to have.

In my opinion, there are two main issues with this game. First, the gameplay loop, including the loot, is not very good. Second, the goonery isn't very good, either. Sadly, this leads me to believe that the developers do not know what they are doing. They have been making the same mistakes over and over, and while they always apologize, the result never changes. This is what the player count reflects.

The gameplay itself has 3 issues, each of which has either not improved, or has gotten worse. First, there isn't a sense of variety, in terms of what you do in a mission, or what the enemy does. Because of the RNG, you end up running the same dungeon over and over. Unlike say Path of Exile, where the same map could have different layouts or mods or enemies or encounters, The First Descendant dungeons feels like the same thing, over and over. You go from one identical mob to another, using the same skill over and over a thousand times, and it's soul crushingly boring. Secondly, the loot itself is not very fun. The mods are pretty generic, and it's hard to tell if they're useful in the end or not. Worse, you target farm specific powerful items on RNG, that take a long time, and then after that, stuff you find in missions become worthless. So, the loot is not exciting. Lastly, The First Descendant has a TON of content, and it's unapproachable for new players. Should you do void vessels? Axiom Plains? Bosses? Onslaught? Why? It's not clear, and many of these give outdated rewards, but you wouldn't be able to tell which ones as a new player. Instead of being fun content, this ends up being deep bloat.

As for the goonery, while the outfit designs are pretty good, they're not very deep, and they're not accessible. The immediate problem is that if you don't spend money, then there's basically no way to get almost all of the cosmestics. So, if you are the type of player who likes to farm different outfits, this game is not for you. Some people say they hope this game doesn't turn into a gacha, but honestly, I think gacha games are a lot more generous. Yes, gacha games have psychological tricks to make you want to pay, but even if you don't pay, at least you have a hope of farming diamonds over time, and pulling for random outfits or whatever. It's possible. In The First Descendant, it's faltly impossible. Then the next problem is that the outfits in The First Descendant are very static. You either put on the whole dress as it is, or you don't use it. You can dye parts of it, which is nice, but you can't change the gloves or use the bikini top of one outfit with the shorts of another outfit. In many other games, you can do that, but not here. Moreover, the fashion language is all over the place. Some have sci-fi designs, while others are modern pop-stars, while others still are giant walking teddy bears.

Both the bloated gameplay and the erradic outfit designs tell me that the developers do not know what they are doing. They are throwing everything at the wall, hoping that something sticks, but really, they're making the mess bigger.

Right now, the only way I can have faith in this game again is if the developers do two very drastic things:
1) Remove 80% of the gameplay, because it's mostly bloat, and remake it with a lot more thought and consistency.
2) Hire new designers for gameplay and visuals, because currently, they have no cohesive gameplay loop nor identity.

[h1]Not Recommended — for now.[/h1]

I have put a lot of time into The First Descendant, been playing since day 1, and I want to start by saying that I genuinely like this game. The combat is fun, the Descendants are well designed, buildcrafting can be extremely satisfying, and over the last two years I have spent countless hours farming weapons, Descendants, modules, reactors, cores, and everything else that comes with progressing in a looter shooter.

[b]That is exactly why I cannot recommend the game in its current state.[/b]

My biggest concern with Season 4 is the direction monetization is taking.

TFD has always been a grindy game with aggressive monetization. I was willing to accept that when spending money primarily meant cosmetics, convenience, or getting something faster. You could spend money, or you could put in the time and eventually achieve essentially the same result through gameplay.


[h2]Transcendent Weapons feel like that line has moved.[/h2]

These weapons represent a new level of power and, in many cases, make weapons we spent months or even years perfecting feel obsolete. Power creep is inevitable in a live-service game, so I don't object to stronger weapons being introduced.

[b]What I object to is how their acquisition and optimization have been designed.[/b]

The normal gameplay path is extraordinarily stingy and heavily dependent on RNG. Then, alongside that system, we have paid Battle Pass benefits that directly increase Transcendent Weapon acquisition and the resources obtained from dismantling them. There are also extremely limited resources for modifying these weapons, including weekly limits, while additional opportunities are available through monetized systems.

[b]That is no longer just selling convenience to me.[/b]

When you create an intentionally scarce RNG-based progression system and then sell players better odds or substantially more opportunities to participate in that system, you are selling an advantage.

And that concerns me far more than the price of any individual item.


[h2]I WANT TO FARM.[/h2]

I don't expect everything to be handed to me. This is a looter shooter. [b]I want to farm.[/b]

Give me difficult content. Give me a 2% drop. Make me run something 50 times. Give me a long-term progression system that rewards actually playing the game.

What I don't want is for the best way to overcome intentionally restrictive progression to increasingly become opening the cash shop.

[b]The grind is supposed to be the game. Selling the solution to the grind is something very different.[/b]


[h2]Previous investment is being devalued.[/h2]

There is also a growing feeling that previous progression is being devalued too quickly.

Players invested enormous amounts of time and resources into Ultimate Weapons, perfect cores, reactors, modules, and carefully optimized builds. Transcendent Weapons aren't simply another interesting sidegrade; they risk becoming the new mandatory tier while much of that previous investment becomes irrelevant.

That creates a progression model that looks increasingly like this:

[b]Farm for hundreds of hours → perfect your gear → introduce a significantly stronger tier → make that tier extremely RNG-dependent → sell ways to improve the RNG/progression.[/b]

That is not a progression model I want to support.


[h2]There are broader problems as well.[/h2]

Ancestor Modules introduced yet another layer of RNG into build progression. Farming has become increasingly repetitive, and some recent balance decisions have made it feel like player investment can be invalidated very quickly.

The recent handling of farming methods and enforcement has also damaged trust within the community and deserves a much clearer and more consistent approach from Nexon.

None of this means TFD is suddenly a terrible game.

There is still a lot here that I enjoy. The gunplay is good. The Descendants are fun. Buildcrafting is one of the reasons I have played for as long as I have. Season 4 contains genuinely good content and ideas, and I want this game to succeed.

[b]But that is also why I think players need to push back when monetization starts affecting gameplay progression this directly.[/b]

I don't mind paying for cosmetics.
I don't mind supporting a free-to-play game.
I don't even mind paying to save some time.

[b]I DO mind when the game makes progression deliberately scarce and then sells the solution.[/b]

Right now, the balance between [b]play to progress[/b] and [b]pay to progress[/b] has moved too far toward the latter, and Transcendent Weapons make me concerned that the eventual destination is outright [b]pay for power.[/b]

So after supporting and playing TFD for a long time, I am changing my recommendation to:


[h1]NOT RECOMMENDED.[/h1]

Not because I hate the game.

[b]Because I still like it, and I don't like where it is going.[/b]

If Nexon makes Transcendent Weapons and their modification resources reasonably farmable through gameplay, removes paid advantages to weapon drop rates, respects previous player investment, and demonstrates that spending money will not become the preferred route to character power, I will gladly change this review.

Until then, I can't recommend investing your time or money into The First Descendant.

### From Free-to-Play to Pay-to-Win — and Now Selective Bans?

I genuinely enjoyed *The First Descendant*, but the direction this game is taking is becoming extremely disappointing.

The **Ancestor Module system** and the new **Transcendent Weapon system** feel like another major step toward pay-to-win progression. On top of that, limiting certain purchases/progression to once per week while allowing players to purchase unlimited amounts directly from the shop gives the impression that the game is intentionally creating progression bottlenecks to push players toward spending money.

But the situation with content creators makes this even worse.

A content creator was banned for using and **teaching an exit-based farming method for Transcendent Weapons**. Even if the method was considered an exploit and deserved some form of punishment, the underlying farming process is still extremely lengthy and grind-heavy.

What makes the ban particularly questionable is that other content creators have apparently **openly admitted to using the same exploit**, yet they have not received the same punishment. If multiple people used the same method, why are some being banned while others appear to be getting away with it?

That creates a serious perception of **selective enforcement**.

If the exploit violates the rules, then enforce the rules consistently against everyone. If it doesn't, then explain why one creator was banned for using and teaching it.

The combination of increasingly aggressive monetization, artificial progression limits, and seemingly inconsistent enforcement is seriously hurting my trust in the game and its developers.

I don't want *The First Descendant* to become a game where the solution to a progression problem is simply **"buy it from the shop"**, while legitimate players are punished for finding ways to reduce an unnecessarily long grind.

The game has fantastic combat and a lot of potential. That's exactly why this direction is so frustrating. **Please prioritize the players and the gameplay instead of pushing the game further toward pay-to-win.**

First of all, I really liked the design aesthetic of the game. So far that and the relatively f2p aspect of it(aside from paid cosmetics which is fine), had kept me from returning to a daunting content catch up experience in Warframe. The game has been struggling for seasons to retain players because of content design choices and player unfriendly rng practices that swung into the frustrating far too often for the casual player.

S4 was a giant step in the right direction. Right up until the novelty of transcendent weapon farming wore off and people realized how predatory and frustrating it is to have a system that is NOT ONLY time gated but also time consuming and expensive to get the most value out of for the casual player. I do not want to play a game as a job, i already have a job. The problem only got worse when the store allows people who pay for caliber to completely bypass the weekly time gates, but also massively jump ahead in terms of the layers of rng required to farm the weapons you want. There was also battlepass and boosts sold in store to boost your chances of this dropping. More on this later.

Then enters the loot cave fiasco. This was an infinite spawning section of the mission where the boss was coded to stay in one area near the objective and didnt follow the player at all, allowing people to infinitely spawnkill enemies forever. This was an oversight by the devs that never got corrected until S4 came around with the introduction of the transcendent weapons. Now that players could kill thousands of enemies to drop the weapons, suddenly the developers move at light speed to remove access to the content, push for a fix, and PUNISH the players for farming an oversight that had been known, reported, and never fixed. Other game breaking bugs with newly released characters that were the highlight of the season and existing bugs have still not been fixed this quickly. What does that tell us?

That isn't the only time a farm like this had been used, either. Previously a character could essentially do the same thing with infinitely spawning enemies and a damage immune boss to farm resources and materials. When it was fixed by the devs, they deemed it creative and boosted the resource gains in other areas to compensate. This was a good response. This time, however, due to the incentive to sell boosts and materials through the shop to accelerate peoples' progression, they deemed a similar oversight as abusive. Abusive to whom? Their bottom line of course.

Now, it took on average of 50k kills to get 1 weapon to drop. The drop rate on that mathematically is abysmal. Now also see that the boosts they sell in the store advertise up to 30% increased chances of dropping. Do the math on that average drop rate chance and you'll see how predatory that system really is. When comparing the disparity of response when the players farming practices impact their bottom line directly, you start to see how and why this game is struggling to keep a playerbase.

And then came the bans. They are not only rolling back the materials and weapons farmed, but also dishing out bans for an oversight the developers themselves never addressed. Even a simple fix like the boss following a player would have invalidated the entire method. But no, the developers would rather excessively punish the players for their own mistakes rather than own up to it. This combined with the poorly implemented design choices they seem to routinely make has convinced me to uninstall this game until i see meaningful improvement that isnt catered to pay2win mechanics and anti player practices. Do not install this game if you don't like having your time and effort wasted.

As a side note, this game really needs to have chat moderating. The amount of racist and hateful shit i see regularly in world chat is incredibly offputting and any game worth their salt would have moderation to remove egregious offenders quickly. There is also a chat bypass that players have discovered that also hasnt been fixed nearly as quickly as the loot cave, but money above all, right?

[b]The Part Where I Ramble About My Story/Experience:[/b] 
I’ve been with the game since day 1 (worldwide release) because looter-shooters are my thing. This game came out at the perfect time, I had just stopped playing Destiny 2, and I was too intimidated by Warframe to give it a shot. But a brand-new game that was basically a gooner version of Warframe, without all the confusion and dread of having to go thorough almost a decade of content with VERY attractive characters, I was all for it. Cue the usual daily grind for the sake of the grind, making builds, and chasing the 'watching number go up' dopamine hits, which I genuinely enjoyed through the highs and lows of the seasons.

I actually thought about quitting about six months into the game’s lifecycle because Season 2 was pretty dull and I was falling into the “I’m only logging on to do dailies” fatigue. Then the devs refunded Caliber, the premium currency, that players had spent on duplicate skins and duplicate paints. In all my time playing games on console and PC, I had never seen a game retroactively refund purchases just because they were duplicates. So I figured the devs actually had our best interests at heart, or at the very least listening to criticism, so I stuck with it.

I kept playing and buying skins for the weapons and Descendants I used, spending thousands of hours, and, to my dismay, even more actual money (I checked), on a game I thoroughly enjoyed. And I’ll give credit where it’s due, the vast majority of the skins are extremely good, even if they are a bit overpriced. Everyone knows fashion is the true endgame of any looter-shooter.

Then Season 4 hit. A new character, Raven, joined the roster, and the story the game had been telling for two years ended on a pretty satisfying note with a sprinkle of hints for the story's continuation. As usual, things were broken at launch, but I’d gotten used to the jank getting fixed a week later, and I’m not expecting devs to work weekends and being sympathetic to them making things easier by just updating at the weekly reset.

But Season 4 also introduced Transcendent Weapons, the new endgame gear. The RNG required to (1) get them to drop, (2) get the one you want for your build, and (3) roll the stats you want is brutal. I know this will improve with later updates, as it often does, but right now it's very rough, rougher than usual. Even the monetization around the materials used to reroll Transcendent weapons, which I consider egregious, felt like something they might eventually walk back by adding those materials to more activities.

Context: dismantling Transcendent weapons gives you a currency you can use to buy reroll materials. For F2P players, there’s a weekly cap, and the drop rates are so low that even playing constantly might not get you enough materials. Even if you do get lucky, the materials are expensive and the weekly limit is low, so you might be able to reroll one or two perks on a SINGLE transcendent weapon per week. Meanwhile, someone who pays can effectively get far more materials with far less time investment, then sell the weapons on the in-game market/trade system next month to recoup costs. I played TFD's season 4 for minimum 4 hours a day, 8 or more on weekends, and I didn't get enough weapon materials for meeting the weekly limit for the re-roll materials. I am employed, just single, so good luck if you can only play for 30min to an hour a day due to spouse, kids, friends, or just life in general.

Then the Onslaught loot “cave” was popularized/publicized by TFD YouTuber/streamer Sen Evades, where you can farm constantly respawning enemies and get dozens of Transcendent weapons, like loot caves in other looter-shooters. Loot caves have existed in various parts of the game since release, they aren’t new, and players have used them to power-level battle passes for months, since the devs don't fix them for months, like this most recent loot cave. But now that regular players started using the cave and can get Transcendent weapons more easily, the drop rate is still terrible, my experience was about one Transcendent weapon per 40,000 kills, the devs clamped down immediately to protect their bottom line.

Let me be clear to anyone defending the devs, I get it. I 100% agree that fixing an exploit to protect the market system, loot rarity, and the TOS matters, and I applaud a quick fix. My issue is the vilifying language used to describe normal players taking advantage of the devs’ own mistake. Destiny had loot caves too, and the usual approach was basically: “Oops, we messed up, have fun with it until [time], then we’ll patch it on [day].” Nobody got banned, and nobody had their loot confiscated. But TFD’s devs are calling loot-cave users “users who severely abused the system,” issuing game bans, and planning to reclaim items acquired during the exploit. That’s absurd, and it’s not how you keep players, especially when:

1) the bans appear random (someone who spent 30 minutes in the exploit gets banned while someone like me doesn’t after ~5 hours), which makes it look more like a scare tactic than an integrity measure. Even their bans are RNG based, go figure;
and
2) actual cheaters still keep slipping past detection, taking top leaderboard spots, and claiming rewards over legitimate players.

This is unacceptable. Punishing normal people for an exploit that’s been in the game for months, by the devs' own mistakes and negligence, only patching it once it made the Transcendent grind meaningfully easier (and less monetizable), is, frankly, stupid. 

It's even crazier that during the Valby farm phase of the game, the devs did exactly what I mentioned above!!! The "Oops, we messed up, but you guys put work into building Valby so we'll let you have fun for now until we patch it on [day]." So they fact they they gave a ban response on this most recent issue, CLEARLY shows that it's because of the potential lost monetization revenue from Transcendent weapon trading, it's absurd. So I’m out. Even if the bans are temporary, it's the principle that matters to me here.
 
It’s a real kick in the teeth for me, because I originally stuck with this game due to the opposite kind of behavior back in Season 2 (as mentioned above). I guess the real sucker was me all along. Let me be clear I don't care about spending absurd amounts money on my primary hobby: gaming, it's more the fact that I kept giving money to devs who gave us a bone which I latched onto, and I was burned for it later. Something, something Stockholm syndrome something, something.

If you’re looking for a looter-shooter to play with friends or solo, with attractive male and female characters, varied skills and personalities, a fairly decent story, and a large amount of content to play, I’d still recommend it for that audience. But don’t be an idiot (like me) and spend money on this game, the devs clearly care more about their bottom line than their players.

I genuinely hope that this review is proven wrong in the coming months, that the devs actually fix the issues for the sake of all players new, current, and returning and reverse the bans. Because I still like the game for the gameplay and the grind, but these loot cave bans and criminalizing normal players was the last straw for me and I won't be coming back.

Devs take one step forward, only to realize they're standing on an escalator going downwards.

I've played The First Descendant long enough to see the cycle repeat itself: something is broken, players report it, the issue sits around for weeks or months, and eventually the community finds a way to work around it. Then, suddenly, that workaround becomes the highest priority because players are actually benefiting from it.

That's where my biggest problem with Nexon lies.

I'm not against fixing exploits. If something is clearly unintended and completely breaks progression or the economy, obviously fix it. But you can't leave bugs, broken missions, busted interactions, and dysfunctional mechanics sitting around indefinitely, then turn around and treat players like they're the problem for taking advantage of something you've allowed to exist for an absurd amount of time.

The priorities feel completely backwards.

We've had missions that fail to progress, rewards that don't properly register, abilities that don't function as described, modules behaving incorrectly, UI issues, and various other problems that have required repeated hotfixes and patches. Nexon's own patch notes and Known Issues posts show just how many of these problems continually make it into the game.

And yet when players discover an unintended interaction that actually makes the grind less miserable? Suddenly the response is immediate.

That's the part that leaves a bad taste.

The First Descendant has the foundation of a genuinely good looter shooter. The gunplay is solid, the Descendants are fun to build, the visuals are great, and when the systems actually work together, the game can be incredibly satisfying. But the constant grind, questionable design decisions, bugs, and inconsistent approach to fixing problems slowly chip away at that enjoyment.

It often feels like the game is designed around making everything take as long as possible, rather than making the grind enjoyable enough that players actually want to keep doing it.

And that's especially frustrating because the developers clearly can move quickly when they want to. Hotfixes can be pushed out to address progression and reward issues, and patches routinely contain long lists of bug fixes.

So the question becomes: why does it sometimes feel like player-friendly problems get treated as emergencies while player-hostile problems are allowed to linger?

Nexon doesn't need to eliminate the grind. They need to make the grind feel worthwhile.

Stop treating the community like we're constantly trying to break the game. A large portion of the playerbase is simply trying to make the best of systems that already feel unnecessarily restrictive. If an exploit exists for weeks or months and thousands of players are using it, maybe the first question shouldn't be "How do we punish the players?" but rather "Why did this remain possible for so long?"

The game doesn't need more reasons for players to leave.

It needs the developers to start listening to the reasons players are leaving in the first place.

TLDR: The First Descendant is a great game, however it has several issues. The main one is that its published by greedy nexon.

What do I mean by this?
The game has really good mechanics and really good feel. I really enjoy playing it; the combat and skills feel both smooth and fluid and if you like warframe you will enjoy the combat of The First Descendant. The issue that forced me to give this game a negative review is that the game is designed to DRASTICALLY slow your progression. The way you acquire new weapons, playable characters and upgrade materials is through research. This mechanic is good in itself, literally a copy-paste from warframe. But it does something horrendous: it allows you to only research 7 things at a time. It may sound like much, but it is extremely limiting.
The research system is designed to frustrate you and either make you turn off the game for couple of days or to PAY to accelerate it.
Now one may argure that the need to make money somehow, but it is not lacking in those areas. The game is life-service (battlepass) and is saturated with gooner skins - lyngerie and jiggle physics. It has no shortage of money- making apparatus. However designing one of the main game mechanics around predatory micro-transactions is something where one should draw a line.
There are also issues where late game quests give you literally nothing, not even EXP points for killing enemies, so you are trapped in a cutscene purgatory waiting to see what kind of big reward you are getting at the end, but it never comes at the end. To unlock one endgame mission you are required to spend 2 hours or so grinding story quests where you run around the entire map like a jackass for nothing.
As it stands I cannot reccomend this game for any commited long playthrough.

[b]THE FIRST DESCENDANT[/b] is a really amazing Warframe/Destiny 2 style MMORPG looter shooter, and yes, it is absolutely without it's faults, but the negative reviews are in no way reflective of whether you should try the game if you like that genre. The game has a huge variety of playable characters with their own beautiful style, skills and voice-acting. The game is filled with exactly what makes a looter shooter that, large amounts of mobs to grind for drops, crafting materials, world events, raid bosses, and partying up with random players. Additionally, the game follows an engaging story, with stunning environments, fairly interesting characters and an ever expansive lore. The game is quite predatory with it's micro-transactions but that should not be held against the game, it is no less predatory then many other free-to-play MMORPGs. You can absolutely get everything free, or pay your way through the game. However, that clearly is completely against the spirit of these types of games. The grind, the loot drops, the eventual reward is exactly what makes it satisfying. Character skills are impactful, are interesting, and unique. Weapons are unique, the way to augment them, and yourself is unique, but again, very grindy. If you have played NEXON games, especially their original international games, you know exactly the type of micro-transactions will be. For a game being released two years ago, updates continue to happen regularly, they are transparent in how they are handling cheaters, and are fairly responsive to player criticisms. Gunplay is really snappy, and damage feels impactful. The raid bosses are cool as hell, the world is beautiful, and the models are stunning. Running dungeons, and world events are grindy but never felt TOO bad, it was just what I signed up for, and had fun gambling for loot drops. My biggest complaint is so much has been released for the game, but zero new Steam achievements? That really sucks for that community.

[b]PROS[/b]:
          - Really engaging lore
          - Beautiful visuals
          - Lots of characters, weapons, and modules
          - Epic raid bosses
          - Consistent updates and newsletters

[b]CONS[/b]:
          - Very predatory micro-transactions
          - No Steam achievement updates
          - Lots of sexual bait

Every once in a while I like to download another game that requires little brain power and grind for some gear.

As of the writing of this review The First Descendant has the following content released completely for free: there is the prequel "Pre-Season" content and 3 other "Seasons" that are divided into regions, raids, and bosses. The Pre-Season content took me about 40 hours to complete, and afterwards is when the mid game content becomes available alongside some end game activities. I spent another 10 hours with the mid game content in Season 1, and some of Season 3 then got bored. These "Seasons" are able to be experienced out of order once the main story is complete, but I would recommend playing sequentially for the over arching story to make sense.

For spending zero dollars, max leveling 10 characters once, and experiencing the main story with 50+ hours of gameplay, it wasn't awful. You can easily have fun and grind solo or with friends until you get bored and put it away. 

The game doesn't require much thought, there are numbers (Damages, Shields, Cooldowns, Buffs, Ect.) and builds that people in the late game will focus on for faster and wider output, but for most of the content enemies are killed with just a few bullets or a single button push.

The First Descendant isn't a well written game... but it's free, and I've played MUCH worse F2P shooters. Graphics are great, guns feel fun, abilities are alright, mobility is slick, and you can easily get 100+ hours of story, grind, bosses and trading without a single dollar spent.

3rd person sci-fi run-n-gun looter shooter.

It's addicting. Craft a crapton of guns and characters (descendants), and use them to kill a crapton of enemies. The descendants are all great, individual personalities, stories and combat styles. The scenery is gorgeous, the music is top-tier (every descendant has their own combat theme that plays while you're fighting during most missions), and the combat in general is super satisfying. And the storyline has been getting better and better every patch.

Cosmetics might be a mixed bag for most people. Store outfits are very expensive, but it's how the game keeps the lights on. Crossover events are only shop updates, But there is some amount of cosmetic rewards from all the events constantly going on, as well as the battlepasses, which are a bit better than the usual industry standard, so you will have outfits and skins to play with even as a free player.

The endgame is improving, bit by bit. Various missions types, and more being introduced every patch. You'll be happier if you enjoy collecting new weapons and descendants, and building them in various ways depending on the mission and enemy type. There is a playstyle for everyone, and the systems used to gather the blueprints and materials to make everything has been dramatically streamlined in recent patches, so nowadays it is more fun and less frustrating. And getting a new weapon or character is always exciting.

Speedrunning, farming, colossus fights, emoting in Albion, grinding achievements, changing your outfits and using the (admittedly slightly clunky and costly) dye systems, co-op, solo runs, testing builds in the laboratory, racing, training your doggo, decorating your private lounge and visiting others, and lots of other things to do in the game. There is actually a pretty huge amount of content for a new player.

Veteran players will bemoan the endgame, but these players have done everything in the game a hundred times over and are just waiting for something new. It should say a lot that they have milked the game dry and are still here waiting for new content because they themselves love the game so much. Don't let them discourage you from trying this free game, you will have PLENTY to keep you busy having fun for a good long time. At over 800 hours myself, I always have something to work on, something to build, gear to optimize, leaderboards to push, etc. Hell, sometimes I just go out and look at the scenery, because it's damn beautiful.

Play this game if you are looking for something that will trigger massive amounts of dopamine, if you like buildcrafting and theorycrafting, and if you like fanservice.

I think I'm starting to finally understand the trend of these free to play games that I don't like. They are incredibly steeped in Microtransactions where you can pay for in-game things like the descendants, weapons, material etc or you can spend hundreds of hours grinding/farming the same repetitive, tediously boring, bland overland content for material and XP in order to not only have best in slot gear, but also get access to content that should not be blocked by any kind of grind, more specifically, Story content.

I gave The First Descendant a solid try, even coming back years after it's initial launch to see how far it's come but it wasn't enough, even after 36 hours, to keep me interested. As a Story-driven gamer, the story of First Descendant from what I have played (up to Season 2's story quest requiring you to be Master Rank 20, I was MR 12 to fight a Colossi) is very mediocre and super trope heavy and not all that entertaining especially not to grind for hundreds of hours to see if it gets any better. Weather it's seen as a clone of Destiny or just that Destiny and Warframe were heavy influncers, The First Descendant doesn't really feel like it does much to be unique or a stand out.

Pros:
-Visually it's pretty solid especially considering it's made in Unreal Engine 5
-Gunplay, while simple and easy to pick up it feels good.
-Voice acting for the characters that I came across were decent enough

Cons:
-Super grindy and repetitive gameplay loop with little to no diversity in activities and structure.
-Story is pretty forgettable and generic and leaves a lot to be desired espceially since exposition is through conversation briefings that feel very one side between missions and there are very few cutscenes throughout.
-Over Sexualization of Women all over the place and in your face. Skimpy and/or tight fitting outfits and incredibly unnecessary over the top "Jiggle physics" that thankfully can be turned down or off in the settings...if you go digging.

Overall: It's an okay game if you have nothing better to play and would be very enjoyable to those who are big into grinding/farming through a very repetitive gameplay loop for gear, materials and XP with little to no intertest for story but for me, This was not it.
