Reaching 100 hours now so it felt like a good time to spit out some pros and cons, to whoever is interested in a honest review:

1- I guess it's not rocket science to figure this point by yourself: Dont play this game if you dont like games with very, and i mean VERY sexualized characters. Not in a background/story sense, but more with the 1 million possibilities to costumize them being 999,999,999 cute & sexy options. Accept it.. Even youre not into it, most people around you will be wearing VERY revealing outfits. Is not something that will influentiate your gameplay at all, but your descendants will be ALL very attractive and beautiful and the means of costumize them with outfits and such, will always push more into the "Lets show as much skin possible" in a somehow reasonable and fun/cool looking way.

2- Grinding maybe will feel hard and frustrating sometimes, but trust me and others when we say: It was wayyyyyy harder back on start. Devs are doing a fairly good job imho, buffing this and that, increasing the chances of obtaining X or Y, and probably the most welcoming factor for newcomers being regular events where you can get a wide variety of vital things for free. And that leads me to the next and extremely important point in my eyes.

3- Micro transactions are 100% optional. Sure you can make a big list of games that work the same way, but this game does a pretty awesome job balancing the "Attracting players by offering free stuff vs Draining the wallets of the ones who stay and willingly want to buy things" - Dont get me wrong, i say this in a good sense. For exemple, if you enjoy the game, is fun progressing, unlocking new descendants etc. You grind hard and while at it, you think that would be cool to have another outfit/look on your descendant? Well, you can fairly easy get a free and tbf nice looking outfit. 

3.1- Between the multiple methods, i need to compliment the attendance events that been going non-stop, and the insertion of the attendace coins that you earn along the process and can spend in case you missed some days to claim rewards. With a simple login offering outfits, descendants, consumables and so much more. I found that pretty newcomer friendly and overal rewardingly positive towoards the player base.

3.3- The devs make a pretty good job constantly adding new and fun cosmetics to the in-game shop regularly. Which means, if you are into buying with real money cool stuff for your descendants you have a pretty wide variety for what i would call 'Average & affordable prices' - No different from the majority of games you can get a cool looking outfit or pass for around 10-20 bucks. Means to support the game, as also satisfy your visual look in-game are completly optional, which i feel once more, it needs to be complimented.

4- As briefly mentioned before, the devs been doing (At least in my eyes) a fairly good job adding new content and diversifying the game with time. Yes, you can as i at somepoint find yourself thinking "Hey this is getting boring and repetitive, i made this mission 400 times already" But, and thats a big BUT.. Updates are very regular, you been getting a new descendants if im not in mistake every 3-4 months. Between that time as it happened in past SUPER nice adds came along like companions and rides. So yeah, imho if they had been doing a great work keeping the new content pace steady and fast, i can see the future being promising. And not (at least that soon) driving players towards the path where your time ingame keeps getting repeatitve and pointless.

4.2- A mixed opinion, but i honestly love this game, yet is not a game i would play daily specially for multiple hours. The First Descendant Review

The First Descendant is a free-to-play looter-shooter developed by Nexon that combines fast-paced gunplay, impressive visuals, and cooperative gameplay. Built using Unreal Engine 5, the game immediately stands out with its detailed environments, flashy abilities, and smooth character animations.

One of the game's biggest strengths is its combat. Players can choose from a variety of Descendants, each with unique skills and playstyles. Whether you prefer dealing massive damage, supporting teammates, or controlling crowds of enemies, there is a character that fits your preferred approach. The boss battles are particularly exciting, requiring teamwork, strategy, and quick reactions.

The game's graphics are another highlight. The environments look modern and polished, and the special effects during combat make battles feel intense and rewarding. Character customization also allows players to personalize their appearance and equipment.

However, The First Descendant is not without flaws. Like many looter-shooters, the gameplay loop can become repetitive after long play sessions. Grinding for materials, weapons, and upgrades may feel tedious for some players. Additionally, the game's monetization system has received criticism from players who feel certain progression elements can be slow without spending money.

Despite these issues, The First Descendant offers an enjoyable experience for fans of games like Destiny 2 and Warframe. Its engaging combat, strong visuals, and cooperative gameplay make it a solid addition to the looter-shooter genre. While it may need further updates and balancing to reach its full potential, it provides plenty of action and fun for players willing to invest the time.

Rating: 8/10

A visually impressive and entertaining looter-shooter with satisfying combat, though repetitive grinding and monetization concerns prevent it from reaching greatness.

The First Descendant might not be the perfect game everyone wants it to be, but there's just something about it that keeps pulling me back. It has a charm that no other game has really managed to capture for me. The gameplay is pretty straightforward, and most of the mechanics are easy to understand, so it's the kind of game where you can just switch your brain off, watch huge damage numbers fly across the screen, and feel ridiculously overpowered.

That said, the game definitely has its issues. The balancing can be all over the place, with some Descendants getting buffed into the stratosphere while others are left feeling weak or forgotten. The monetization is also pretty aggressive, especially when it comes to cosmetics, since a lot of the outfits are pretty expensive. The good news is that you don't really need to spend money to enjoy the game. Pretty much everything important can be earned through gameplay, so you're not missing out on much if you stay Free to Play.

Whenever I don't have another game I'm interested in, don't have much time to play, or just don't feel like sweating in something more demanding, I always end up coming back to The First Descendant. It scratches a specific itch that no other game seems to hit. If you're bored, looking for something to grind, or just want a game to help pass the time, I'd say it's worth giving a shot. It does a good job of always giving you something to work toward.

Missions/Content
This game has a ton of content from what I have experienced. Various types of Main missions, and side missions. Even Dungeons (Infiltration operations)
There are boss battles that you unlock and can just choose to play against a specific one.
A new onslaught mode that I have not looked into.
And more not listed.

Crafting, and upgrading.
Can progress in free to play. I didn't use it much until much later. But in late game i'm crafting quite a bit.
Upgrade system for weapons and descendants. As well as some more complex options.
Options to add modules to both, which take up slots up to a max. And these can also be upgraded.

Free Items
The game has given out alot of free stuff, through login rewards and special events. Not sure what they'll give out in the future. (They've given out descendants (new characters) for free multiple times, even allowing you to choose one from a selection) Ultimate weapons, resources and boosts, and cosmetics.

Weapons and Abilities
I like the gunplay for a third person game, many weapons to choose from as you unlock them.
the descendants abilities are unique between each of them. 4 abilities each and a passive ability.
They have attributes like fire, lightning, ice, and a few others. As well as neutral types.
 
Transactions and progression
You only start off with one descendant but can obtain others through crafting (Free to play) or just straight up buying them.  Materials for upgrades can be farmed. With crafting, can pretty much unlock everything essential through farming if you want to take that route. You can obtain almost every weapon without spending any money.
Crafting takes time (minutes, hours, or less than a day as i've noticed) gold, and materials.

Many battle passes have been released, with free rewards scattered along the levels, that are claimable. Can either buy the premium version or just level them through free to play, with less rewards.

As a final note, many items can be held in the inventory, and more as you increase rank. Consumables and materials dont take up space and seem to be unlimited to hold. The game has a lost and found system which finds some items. And a storage system which can hold another 100 pieces of gear.

I generally love grinding in games. To mention the pros of this game: the gameplay mechanics are nice, it looks visually great, and the boss fights are also good. The cons? They couldn't optimize it properly on the UE5 engine, and constantly running from place to place exhausts you (with endless loading screens, even though I have an M.2 SSD).

What I complain about the most is that I’m constantly farming, but I never feel like I’m getting any stronger. I keep checking the leaderboard, and it's always the same people whose weapons and mods are way, way superior to yours. Okay, I have nothing to say to that—those guys traded and got ahead of you, I have no problem with that. But that means the foundation is "pay-to-win." Now, you're going to say, "Bro, why don't you drop stuff and sell it too, then go buy mods and weapons and get strong yourself?" Bro, do you think I didn't try? Is the story nonsensical? Yes.

Does the game try to nickel and dime you early on with power ups, components, and outfits, etc? Yes

BUT

Is it one of the most entertaining and mechanically satisfying third person shooters I've played in the past couple years? A resounding yes. 

You've got an arsenal of weapons and cool superpowers to use with whoever you end up picking as your character and the gameplay shifts from shorter missions that take a few minutes to complete, to longer 15-20 min missions that closely resemble an old school "level" from a single player game. There's a decent enough variety where you don't feel like you're doing the same thing over and over again. You can also play on a private server too if you don't want randos dropping in to your game either. 

If you can get past its free to play structure by picking your main and sticking with her, the loot drops are more than enough to keep you progressing in the game without any need for further microtransactions. There is no "pay to win" feeling that you hit during missions. 

I've played it for 7 hours on Steam, but played it even more on my PS4. And in case you'd like to reactivate your PS4 account (since the game is no longer playable on that console), you can link it to the dev's servers and upload it to Steam like I did.

This is quite simply the best game I have played post Destiny 2: The Final Shape and it is the only game that filled the void that game left behind. It has more than satisfied the power fantasy Bungie's sandbox was too technically limited to embrace and it has admittedly satisfied the itch to have more overtly attractive characters in a looter shooter.

I have sunk many hours and more than $200 dollars into TFD and do not regret it, the game has many strengths I will outline below but many have had unintended consequences for the long term health of the game. Make no mistake however, it is an amazing game with a massive amount of content that is worth investing into

[b]POSITIVES[b] 
[list]
[*]Power Fantasy and Build Progression
[*]Many Descendant builds are mechanically pleasing to play and are distinct from one another in play style
[*]The game is 99% soloable (There is 1 boss fight that is matchmade only)
[*]Old Descendants & Weapons are reworked often
[*]New Descendants are powerful and worth unlocking
[*]Descendant designs are fantastic
[*]Descendant cosmetics are also fantastic
[*]Recent seasonal storyline and payoff to past seasons was amazing
[*]Base campaign is lengthy and the areas traversed are definite visual highlights
[*]The music and sound design is very solid
[*]Several long term pursuits exist for veteran players to pursue
[*]Web events and Twtich events are common, fun, and rewarding
[*]Daily and weekly events encourage you to run all kinds of mission types
[*]Trading desirable items for the game's premium cosmetic currency (Caliber) is possible with other players
[*]Dev team is passionate and they put in a lot of work to continuously improve the game
[/list]

[b]NEGATIVES[b] 
[list]
[*]The scantily clad elephant in the room, the more recent Descendant cosmetics have slapped this game with a Sexual Content tag. It has a reputation that is unfortunately earned as a "gooner" game which is another nail in the coffin for the community expanding past niche status. I enjoy the character designs as stated in the opening and have accepted there is no putting the genie back in the bottle on this as it was only going to get worse over time. It is not a game you can play with many people outside of those who already play it which is a massive shame as the game itself is great.
[*]Universal cosmetics (apply to all Descendants of that gender) are fairly priced but bundles of separate skins even with the bundle discount is seen as too pricy for many.
[*]Because the game is overwhelmingly soloable and many areas can be set to private the game can feel empty, there's very little forced interaction which has made it hard for this game to build anything larger than a niche community. It is hard to meet people organically in game outside of the main player hub Albion.
[*]The open Campaign zones become largely irrelevant in the endgame and many endgame activities are missions that are started from a menu or a positional marker which is far less immersive. Many endgame missions are just clearing rooms of enemies with an occasional mini boss. Many of the missions break the formula enough to be fun even after many, many runs. I'd argue it's fun for those seeking to break personal best time records for certain missions but I suspect many people will find unappealing. 
[*]Lack of exploration, secrets, or hidden events in any open zone (as a Destiny fan this is a hard one to overlook)
[*]Male Descendants do receive less cosmetics overall, since the devs and players recognize what really sells, what is available is very good though and some of the best designs for cosmetics are for the male Descendants
[*]Devs listen to the players a bit too much and many hard activities have been power crept or made less difficult over time. 
[*]The campaign and some endgame builds for specific Descendants are the only places where the balance of gunplay and abilities feels right, and outside of that the game becomes really just a looter and not really a looter shooter. It's ability spam or rocket spam in the endgame and that's a shame, because weapons were fun and meaningful in the campaign. I am being hypocritical here though because I absolutely love Viessa's Glacial Cloud build and going back to gunplay after experiencing that level of fun and power is not something I'd do unless the game made sweeping changes overnight.
[/list]

So in summary, the game has a huge amount of content, Descendants, & builds to unlock and try. It is a godsend for solo players but does not foster the kind of organic interaction with it's mission structure to have a larger community. It has really amazing cosmetics just be prepared for the sights you will see in the player hub Albion. It's a game that is consistently supported by the devs and it is far better than the rating it currently has. It is worth every single hour I have sunk into it and I hope it runs for as a long as possible.

Warframe vet, 5k hrs., so I will obviously have to compare this game, as it they are so similar, yet differ in some significant ways. I like them both, but TFD appeals way more to me at this point. 
- Biggest win for TFD: No loss of ressources on mission failure. Always been a gripe for me, and this game thankfully lets you keep ressources even if mission fails.
- Much more engaging combat in terms of difficulty. Even when things start to melt in the end game with a stacked out build (the void bosses can die in seconds), there are still some of the missions where you have to pay attention and play to your descendent's strengths. Especially if you play a glass cannon type. As with Warframe, as soon as you max out your character, the challenge is heavily diminished, but at least you don't have literally immortal characters like you will find in Warframe. 
- not as smooth feeling as warframe, especially since there is no bullet jump (although vehicles are much better)
- typical UE5 issues: Occasional crashes (very rare though), decent performance with great graphics. Although, AA is poor (blurry) and you should run it with FSR4 native-AA or equivalent, because it looks much clearer and detailed. Stay away from Cinematic setting and raytracing, not worth the massive performance hit in any way shape or form.
- Story is meh - especially as new or returning player, because you don't really go through the "campaign missions" (although most of the cutscenes, especially in Dia's story line are well done).
- horrible character sync in english, but the characters are much more unique and fitting in english imo.
- repetitive mission formats (like Warframe), but the fast repeat/return options make it much more convenient than warframe imo.
- you are supposed to be a lead descendant or something, but you always control one of the descendents on the roster. Makes in-game universe ẃierd, especially when that characters speak to you.
- biggest up on competitors (mainly warframe):
- For a new/returning player, the systems, the order of unlocking new areas and missions, and the many mechanics that makes you actually strong, are difficult and confusing to get a hold on. Look into weapon and external component cores.
- I love that you can polarize the mod slots several times to lower the cost of the mod for several types. Makes it so much more convenient and easy to have multiple different builds, in contrast  
- easy to grind the upgrade components like catalysts and mod expansion, as opposed to warframe where it is limited how many you get. Much more convenient and approachable. 
- MUCH better grinds than Warframe (and I say that with 5k hours in that game). Word of advice: USE TARGET REWARD, as there is a pity system percentage buildup.
- hard to get into because of the many systems (again, nothing 
- The women are insanely hot and the game knows its audience. 
- I hate the FOMO of the game skins and pray that it is changed. I missed out on some of the previous seasons, and some of the skins I really want, even some of the less "premium" skins like helmet-less, regular skin variations, are tied to that particular season. It's fine to have some timed stuff, but at least BRING THEM BACK, either through a rotational shop, or by making previous battle passes available to purchase and progress! Massive L on their part.
- World Chat is full of weirdos and massive freaks (to be expected) or trolls, but there are the occasional funny moments. You get some strange moments when different parts of the world gets to interact directly - both good and bad. 
- cosmetics are fairly expensive imo, but if you don't do much customization, it's easy not to spend money, as you usually get cosmetics and colors with gameplay or in-game currencies from challenges.  
- End game is pretty lacking. It doesn't have a solid gameplay loop, and even if you have plenty of stuff to grind, you will end up not having much content other than the occasional events or farming to do. But I'd argue that any game - especially Warframe is the same way. Their grinds are just way more expansive and stretched out over many years of updates with many world and factions. TFD devs have stated that they are looking to producing better end game content to make the game more sustainable, and progress is already starting to show, with additions like the Onslaught beta.

Overall, I really like it. It doesn't have the rich story of Warframe (scattered as that shit might be), the voice acting is not superb, and the gameplay doesn't offer much outside of the core loop. To watch a goldmine of a player base evaporate because of greed and incompetence is almost poetic. When it comes to respecting the player's time, this development style truly knows no bounds. The First Descendant is a game that arrived wearing every cosmetic feature a live service looter shooter could possibly have and somehow managed to make all of it feel hollow simultaneously.

Nexon developed this one and if that name makes you instinctively check your privacy settings that instinct is not entirely without basis. Nexon has a long history of aggressive monetization practices that makes the tinfoil hat reaction less paranoid and more historically informed. The data concerns are real enough that it trended as a conversation topic at launch and the monetization structure is aggressive enough that it colors the entire experience even if you never spend a dollar.

The gameplay itself is Warframe adjacent in ways that are hard to ignore and impossible to unsee once you notice them. Which is fine except Warframe exists, is free, has over a decade of content, and has a developer relationship with its playerbase that Nexon has never historically demonstrated any interest in replicating.

The early hours not selling you is a pattern with this type of game but also a legitimate red flag specific to this one. Games that front load cosmetics and monetization while back loading meaningful content are making a specific bet about player psychology and it doesn't always pay off. If the hook isn't there in the first few hours with a live service game the grind required to reach the content that allegedly justifies everything before it is a significant ask.

With all that said, the first playthrough of the game forces you on normal mode and over the years the power creep has gotten so bad you can one shot all the bosses if you're building yourself normally as you play. You only unlock hard mode after beating the games short story and then it just puts all the enemies at level 100, more of bullet sponges than actual difficulty increase. The new game mode has fixed these issues but it takes awhile to get to as its end game. I found the best way to enjoy the game is to just not upgrade anything until you absolutely have to. Overall, The First Descendant is a game that completely refined the gooner game genre and innovated on gooner technology. I can't help but to recommend it for it's replayability and it's regoonabilty.

After playing for 5 hours, here are my first impressions.

First of all, the graphics are absolutely top-notch. This is one of the first multiplayer games that actually made me stop moving just to enjoy the scenery. The visual style is excellent, and honestly, the character design – especially the female characters – is clearly one of the game's main selling points. They look beautiful and very well crafted.

The gameplay itself is good. I would rate it 8/10. The shooting feels satisfying, and the battle controls are smooth and responsive. In my opinion, the combat quality is on par with Warframe, which is a very positive point.

However, what I feel is lacking is the story. In a time where free-to-play games like Genshin Impact, Zenless Zone Zero (ZZZ), and Wuthering Waves offer strong narratives, this game feels quite weak in terms of storytelling.

Another downside is the gameplay cycle. The game heavily emphasizes grinding materials in order to unlock new characters. Unfortunately, the material drop rates feel very low, especially for free-to-play players, which can make progression feel slow and sometimes frustrating.

Overall, I still recommend this game if you want to try it and enjoy its character designs and visuals. Just make sure you are prepared to do a lot of grinding, because it is definitely required to progress.

The First Descendant resembles a mix of Destiny and Warframe's game mechanics, with local influence from  Korean and other Asian countries' shooter games. The gameplay is generally repetitive and grindy, but still gives a good sense of reward after working for an item without feeling like time was truly wasted while searching for it. Systems have been put in place time and time again simply due to player request, the development team makes a point to address players wants when it comes to gameplay and style choices.

This being said, the repetitive gameplay, coupled with mechanics that actively discourage group play, and encourage solo play within an MMO. This leaves the game feeling shockingly lonely during a lot of the experience, even the new 'open world' zone is just large and still only supports 4 concurrent players. In addition to this, you're forced to look at half-naked women every time you want to go upgrade your modules or craft a new item. Magnum unfortunately listened to the wrong portion of their playerbase, and created a goon-bait game with hollow mechanics and performance problems they're still trying to clean up two years later. If you're wondering how a game could have 250k players and go down to 10k, this would be why.

Ultimately, the game has plenty of good features, but falls short in critical aspects. This is fine, but based on the amount of effort put into sexualized designs and physics, if this effort had instead been focused towards creating an engaging gameplay experience, maybe the game would look very different today.

The first 60 hours of this game are a blast delivering engaging gameplay, a decent story, fun & hot characters, and plenty to do. Whether you still play the game after that is decided by whether you like the gameplay loop enough in endgame to farm out all the content.

Not every game needs to be an always online "Games as a Service" product. The mechanics are fine, the level design is fine, but the micro-transactions and "Free To Play" gimmicks are not. 

The First Descendant should have been a $35(US) locally hosted title with $10(US) expansion packs every 6 months bringing new zones and story modes; maybe with additional costume options. The First Descendant should not have been always online title balanced around "Pick up Group" matchmaking. 

The fact that seems to take every "G.A.A.S." publisher by surprise is that they don't control the player population. The Publisher does not control when players have time to "Log In" and play a game. The Publisher does not control player stratification, the inevitable event where player population is weighted towards a particular set of levels and or powers leaving gaps in the leveling experience.  

Much like "Competitors" in the shooter genre, like Destiny, for most players "The First Descendant" is a primarily a single player title. Forcing online/multiplayer aspects into what is fundamentally going to be a single player experience just doesn't work.

"New" players, or returning players, are heavily discouraged from playing the game as much of the player base is already at a higher level on different content; while simultaneously "Older" players are running out of a reason to play as they complete the storylines. The stratification of the player base is further complicated by "PvP" elements. More so a problem with Destiny than one I encountered with First Descendant as my play time clearly indicates, but PvP is simply not a selling point for a game. It just isn't. 

What irks me the most about The First Descendent is that none of the lessons to have been learned by Nexxn are new. These are the same kinds of problems that "Online" games have been facing since Meridian 59. Nexon chose the wrong kind of model to build a game around, and what could have been an enjoyable shooter is now one that Nexon has no idea what to do with. Even the CEO of Nexon is filing "The First Desscendant" under the slide "What Did Not Work."

Well, how about not trying to make every game as an always online experience. Instead focusing on making a great game that can be run locally on a LAN disconnected from the Internet and getting the basics down first.

[h1] The First Descendant: A Looter Shooter Worth Every Hour [/h1]
[hr][/hr]
[h2] Overview [/h2]
I have put [b]803 hours[/b] into The First Descendant and I am still coming back for more. This is one of the better free-to-play games on Steam right now. The [b]Unreal Engine 5 visuals[/b] look great and the world feels well built, with solid character designs and detailed environments throughout.
[hr][/hr]
[h2] Gameplay and Combat [/h2]
The [b]gunplay[/b] feels good. Weapons have real weight to them and combining them with your [b]Descendant abilities[/b] makes for some fun moments. Each Descendant plays differently so there is always something new to try. I have spent a good chunk of my hours experimenting with builds and loadouts, which has kept things feeling fresh over time.
[hr][/hr]
[h2] Solo Experience [/h2]
I play almost entirely [b]solo[/b] and the game holds up well on your own. The progression gives you plenty to chase and working out a solid build for your favourite Descendant is genuinely enjoyable. There is always something to work towards, whether that is farming a specific module, unlocking a new character, or pushing harder content.
[hr][/hr]
[h2] Criticisms [/h2]
It is not perfect. The [b]grinding[/b] can get repetitive, especially when farming the same mission repeatedly for a specific drop. It is part of the genre but it can wear on you after a while. The [b]microtransaction shop[/b] is also worth mentioning. Cosmetics are priced on the higher end and some content feels pushed toward paid options. Nothing is pay-to-win, but it is good to know going in.
[hr][/hr]
[h2] Pros and Cons [/h2]
[b]Pros:[/b]
[u]Good looking visuals with nice environmental detail[/u]
[u]Satisfying gunplay and combat[/u]
[u]Good variety of unique Descendants to try[/u]
[u]Lots of content available completely free[/u]
[u]Rewarding build crafting and progression[/u]
[b]Cons:[/b]
[u]Farming loop gets repetitive over time[/u]
[u]Microtransaction shop is on the expensive side[/u]
[hr][/hr]
[h2] Final Verdict [/h2]
[i]803 hours in and I still load it up regularly. The visuals, the characters, and the combat all come together to make something worth playing. If you enjoy looter shooters and want something to sink real time into for free, it is an easy recommendation. Just go in knowing the grind is real.[/i]
[b]Score: 8/10 - Recommended[/b]

Needs improvement in server matchmaking. I’m genuinely frustrated with how PUBG Mobile is handling server selection and high-ping/cross-server gameplay.

PUBG has rules against glitches, exploits, and abusing unintended game mechanics because they can give players an unfair advantage. I completely understand and support that principle. But then I have a serious question: why is intentionally playing on a server from another region to take advantage of high or unstable ping treated as completely acceptable?

I’m talking specifically about players who are clearly based in regions such as the Middle East, Europe, or the UK, but repeatedly and intentionally play on the North American server. This isn’t simply someone occasionally connecting to another region because they are traveling or because matchmaking happened to place them there. There are players who consistently choose NA servers despite being physically located thousands of miles away.

As an actual North American player, it is extremely frustrating to fight against this.

High or fluctuating ping can create situations where the experience between two players is completely different. Hit registration, peeking, movement, damage registration, and the timing of shots can all feel inconsistent. Whether PUBG considers this an “exploit” or not, intentionally choosing a distant server specifically because the resulting latency can benefit certain interactions deserves to be addressed.

And this raises an obvious question:

What is the purpose of having a North American server if a large portion of the lobby is made up of players who aren’t actually playing from North America?

There are matches where it feels like only a small fraction of the lobby is actually North American. If the NA server is routinely being used by players from Europe, the Middle East, and other regions, then the concept of regional matchmaking becomes meaningless.

I understand that PUBG needs enough players to fill lobbies. I also understand that restricting regions could increase matchmaking times. But I would rather wait another minute or two for a fairer lobby than have a fast matchmaking experience where the competitive environment is compromised.

There are several ways PUBG could investigate this without simply banning people based on their location:

• Monitor a player’s average in-game ping over multiple matches rather than judging them from one match.

• Detect players who consistently play hundreds or thousands of miles away from their normal region.

• If someone repeatedly maintains extremely high latency while playing a specific server, temporarily restrict them from that server or place them into an appropriate regional matchmaking pool.

• Introduce a soft regional lock with exceptions for legitimate travel.

• Use repeated ping history rather than a single connection measurement to identify intentional cross-region play.

• Allow players to select their preferred region, but automatically recommend or require their local region when their connection quality consistently indicates they are elsewhere.

• Create a warning system first. If a player repeatedly plays outside their expected region with unusually high ping, warn them that continued cross-region matchmaking may result in temporary restrictions.

• Most importantly, publish a clear policy explaining whether intentional cross-region matchmaking for the purpose of obtaining a latency advantage is allowed or prohibited.

I am NOT asking PUBG to punish someone simply because they are traveling, studying abroad, temporarily living in another country, or have an unusual internet connection. I’m asking PUBG to address players who repeatedly and intentionally use a distant server as their normal matchmaking region, particularly when the resulting latency creates an inconsistent competitive experience.

If PUBG is willing to ban players for abusing glitches because those players gain an unfair advantage through unintended mechanics, then there should at least be a serious discussion about other forms of intentional competitive exploitation as well.

Right now, it feels like North American players are being asked to accept the consequences of a system that is being used by players from other regions without meaningful restrictions.

Please explain what the purpose of regional servers is if players can freely ignore regional matchmaking whenever it benefits them.

I’m not asking for shorter matchmaking times at any cost. I’m asking for fair matchmaking, consistent competition, and meaningful regional server integrity.

Please take this issue seriously and consider implementing a system that distinguishes legitimate cross-region players from players who repeatedly and intentionally use another region’s server for a competitive latency advantage.

A Letter for the Devs. Yo devs, where do I start… with this 20GB game? Hmm… well first off, the compatibility and ease of use that the game offers could be worse. It’s not the most compatible with older models and DO NOT play without WiFi unless it’s 5G full bars. The game gets progressively better as it gets progressively harder the higher ranked you are as a player. I must say, I spent a few months playing this game before removing it. I removed it because it was time for a new game. Not because I didn’t like PUBG. 

Anyway, menus… there are too many of them. I would like the devs to condense the menus in the game. Make the UI easier to navigate and understand. It’s not very intuitive. So many buttons. You can easily spend an hour going through settings and menus. It takes away from the game. 

As for the other cons, there aren’t many. Devs nailed the graphics, updates and hell of an active community engaged in the game. Moderation and security are actually monitored although I would expect it from a game of this top notch quality. 

It doesn’t lag for me on an iPhone 12 base model (5 or so years old). There are always players online, now earlier I said it gets better as you climb the ranks- well at the start it is understandably easy because the majority of servers are bot lobbies. This is intentional so I have heard… 

When you reach let’s say Gold or just below (I reached Crown I) the bots are mostly gone and you get actual sweaty players. Millions of them. 

The content and the pricing add up, it’s a worthwhile investment if you buy something in the shop that is cosmetics or aesthetics… you could go down a spending rabbit hole if you spent too much time in the enticing shop.

The best game ever. PUBG MOBILE is honestly the best game I have ever played, and after playing for around 8 months, I can confidently give it a 10,000,000,000,000/10. I have played many games before, but none of them have kept me entertained like PUBG MOBILE. Every match feels different, and there is always something exciting that can happen. Whether I am playing seriously, trying to win, improving my skills, or just having fun, I always enjoy coming back to the game.

The gameplay is absolutely amazing because every match requires you to think quickly and make smart decisions. You have to choose where to land, find weapons, collect supplies, watch the zone and figure out where enemies might be. Sometimes you can have a peaceful start, and suddenly you hear footsteps and have to prepare for a fight. I love how unpredictable the game is because you never know what is going to happen next.

The gunfights are probably one of my favourite parts of PUBG MOBILE. Winning a difficult fight feels incredible, especially when you are under pressure and manage to stay calm and defeat your opponent. There are also those moments where you completely destroy someone and feel like the best player ever, only to get eliminated a few minutes later because of the most random mistake. 😂 Those moments make the game even more fun and memorable.

The final circle is another thing that makes PUBG MOBILE so exciting. After surviving through most of the match, having only a few players left makes everything much more intense. You have to listen for footsteps, watch your surroundings and think carefully about every move. When you finally win the last fight and see Winner Winner Chicken Dinner, it is one of the best feelings in gaming.

Playing with friends makes PUBG MOBILE even better. Having a squad means you can communicate, make plans, revive each other and help each other during fights. Sometimes everything goes perfectly and you get an amazing win, while other times your entire squad is running around doing completely different things. 😂 Even when you lose, there are usually funny moments that you remember afterwards.

I also love how much I have improved during my 8 months of playing. When I first started, I was still learning the maps, weapons, movement and strategies. Now I understand the game much better and can make quicker decisions during fights. There is still always something new to learn, which keeps me interested and gives me a reason to keep playing and improving.

The maps, weapons, vehicles, sounds and different game modes also make PUBG MOBILE feel fresh. Every match can give you a completely different experience, and there are so many ways to play. Sometimes I want to play aggressively and look for fights, while other times I prefer to play carefully and focus on surviving. That variety is one of the biggest reasons I never get bored of the game.

Overall, PUBG MOBILE is an incredible game that has given me so many fun, exciting and unforgettable moments over the last 8 months. It has made me laugh, challenged me to improve and given me some amazing victories. Even after losing a frustrating match, I still want to play another one. That is why I give PUBG MOBILE a 10,000,000,000,000/10. It is easily the best game ever, and I honestly cannot give it a high enough rating. 🔥🍗

Lag and High Latency Making the Game Harder to Play. PUBG Mobile has long been one of the most engaging and popular battle royale games on mobile devices. With its intense firefights, strategic gameplay, and great visuals, it continues to attract millions of players worldwide. However, recently my experience has been significantly affected by high latency and lag issues — and it’s making the game far less enjoyable.

Gameplay Experience:
PUBG Mobile still offers the same core excitement it always has: dropping into a large map with up to 100 players, scavenging weapons, and fighting to be the last one standing. The graphics and audio design remain top-notch for a mobile title.

Countries like Australia has impacted highly recently. The Problem — High Latency:
Lately, I’ve been experiencing consistently high latency during matches. This “ping” delay causes several problems:
	•	Delayed responses: Actions like aiming, shooting, and moving don’t register instantly. Often, enemies seem to teleport or jerk around, making accurate shooting almost impossible.
	•	Hit registration issues: Shots that should land sometimes don’t register, or enemies take damage with a significant delay.
	•	Unfair deaths: Getting killed behind cover or just after ducking behind a wall has become common because the game state doesn’t sync correctly with my device.
	•	Freezes and frame drops: Combined with latency, moments of frozen frames or sudden drops in frame rate make maneuvering and reacting properly very difficult.

Impact on Playability:
Whether in casual matches or ranked games, the latency problem has disrupted the competitive balance and overall fun. PUBG Mobile’s gameplay relies heavily on timing and precision — lag undermines both.

Possible Causes:
High latency can stem from:
	•	Local network instability (Wi-Fi or mobile data)
	•	Server overload or regional server issues
	•	Recent updates that might not be fully optimized

Final Thoughts:
PUBG Mobile still has massive potential and remains fun when the connection is stable. But right now, the high latency issues make it frustrating and sometimes unplayable. Until the developers address these performance problems — either through server optimization or improved netcode — many players might find the experience more stressful than enjoyable.

“Building Bonds and Beating Stress: The PUBG Experience”. Playing PUBG can be both a fun way to make friends. The game’s team-based setup often requires players to communicate and strategize, fostering connections with teammates. Whether playing with existing friends or meeting new ones online, the shared experiences of intense battles, funny moments, and close victories can build strong bonds. Also PUBG is a great stress reliever after a long day. The immersive environment, combined with the adrenaline rush of survival, can help shift focus from daily worries. Exploring the vast maps, looting, and battling other players offers a mental escape, giving players a sense of accomplishment when they outlast opponents.
However, it’s important to recognize that PUBG can be a time-consuming game. Matches can last up to 30 minutes or more, and it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement, leading to hours of playtime. While it’s enjoyable, managing time wisely is crucial to ensure it doesn’t interfere with other responsibilities.

The Game Just Keeps Getting Better. I’ve played this game nearly every day since it’s launch and so far I’m very pleased with the dev team. This has probably been my favorite game over the past few years and I’m happy to say it’s only getting better. As far as TCGs go, I grew up mainly playing Yu-Gi-Oh and Magic and I’m very familiar with those systems as well as a few others. One of the best parts about Pokémon TCGP is how carefully the meta evolves over time, and how balanced it usually is across a handful of deck types. The gameplay is simple but easy to get the hang of, and it doesn’t involve any crazy long combos or complicated strategies. All you need is your favorite Pokémon and a little bit of luck on your side to get some wins. The dev team is doing great with the features they’ve added over time like wishlists and community decks, and the next features they’ve announced sound awesome. One thing I’d like to see a little more love put into is card customization. I have a ton of stardust and I’d like to be able to use it on great looking animations, skins, and text colors/border colors. I’d also like for the customizations to remain visible on the card after the card is played, and perhaps a corresponding switch in the settings menu to turn it off for slow/older devices.

PvP is ruined. Pokémon TCG Pocket used to be genuinely fun for me, especially the PvP. It was never the deepest card game in the world, but matches felt casual enough that I could experiment with different decks and still have a good time.

Nowadays, PvP is honestly unbearable.

The power creep has gotten ridiculous, and it feels like every new expansion introduces cards that make older decks less and less viable. Instead of experimenting, you’re basically encouraged to run whatever the current meta decks are or accept that you’re putting yourself at a huge disadvantage. A lot of matches also feel like they’re decided by who gets their key cards first rather than who actually plays better.

The RNG doesn’t help either. Bad opening hands, coin flips, and draw luck can completely decide games, and because matches are already so short, there usually isn’t enough time to recover. Sometimes you know you’re probably going to lose within the first couple turns. Combine that with constantly running into optimized meta decks and PvP starts feeling less like a casual Pokémon card game and more like a sweat fest.

I’ve seen other players describe the same problem: less room for creative decks, increasingly powerful cards, repetitive matches, and games where strategy feels secondary to drawing the right cards at the right time.

Thankfully, the collecting side of the game is still great. I genuinely love opening packs, getting rare cards, seeing the artwork, and building my collection, so I still come back for that.

It’s just a huge bummer that the actual battling side has gotten so sweaty and, at times, genuinely unfair. Pokémon TCG Pocket is still a great card-collecting game, but PvP has gone from one of the reasons I played to something I mostly avoid.

Painfully Unforgiving. As with any gatcha game, RNG plays a significant role but this is typically offset by pity systems. In TCGP the only version of this are pack points, requiring 250 packs to be opened to get one card of 2 star rarity and those pack points are exclusive to each pack. 

Those who end up on the unlucky end of the bellcurve will find themselves with a dreadful slog and no growing benefits or support such as increasing pack points or eventual guaranteed hits. Combined with the general lack of resources given for anything but money it can quickly become the furthest thing from fun when trying to collect your favourite Pokémon.

Additionally, for a game with “Trading” in its title the system is severely limited with immense in-game currency costs tied to any trade of value. Once again, the only solution is to spend more money.

Overall, I cannot recommend Pokémon TCGP in its current state, especially when the solutions to its many problems have long since existed in other games. Without the goodwill of Pokémon fans and the IP this app would not have survived.

Newest update breaks a new low for TCGPocket. Paldean Wonders has released to… zero fanfare from me.
Fantastical Parade already cut back severely on the permanent free pack hourglasses, alongside stuffing as many cards as it can into one pack. This lead to a massive increase in duplicate pulls in an attempt to chase specific cards.
That was already rough, but Paldean Wonders has made me, not even want to chase those cards. While TCGPocket has always dug from the franchises past and reissued old cards from the real life card game, in the over one year of the apps life it has never dipped its toes into make rare cards reprisals. Ex cards, along with illustration cards, full art cards, and even the games rainbow rarity (akin to the real sets special illustration rates) have all been brand new artworks across the games previous 14 sets. 
But Paldean Wonders? Every ex is a real card. Every full art is a real card. 4/5 full art supporters are real cards. 5/6 illustration rares are real cards. 2/5 rainbow rares are real cards.

This is a brand new low following already disappointing changes made the previous set.

Hour played: circa 650
Two reasons you should play this P2W game as a free-to-play player
Tl;dr: The game is fun, and the rich players who sponsor this game sponsor you as well! You can be a top-geared player in a top guild and get access to “premium content” like skins and battle passes without spending a dollar! You don’t have to say goodbye to your real life but this game is definitely a substantial time commitment.
Warning: This is a review by a returning player. I was inactive for over a year and a half. The reason for this review is that I see a lot of misleading reviews debating whether this game is pay-to-win (P2W) and to what extent. As far as I can tell, the game hasn't changed much in terms of P2W.
First, I want to answer the question of whether this game is P2W:
Yes, it can be, but there is a good chance this doesn't matter for your experience. In fact, you might even benefit from it as a free-to-play player. You absolutely can be a top-geared player in a top guild without spending a dime and with a reasonable time investment (not more than 3.5 hours per day on average, which is still a lot but manageable). I will explain in more detail and share my experience later.
What you need to know:
You can buy a premium in-game currency called LUCENT with real money. It can be used to buy cosmetics, battle passes, AND items from the in-game shop that contribute to your character progression. Furthermore, you can spend Lucent to buy gear and materials from the auction house.
My opinion:
If you've read this far, you might think that this is TERRIBLE and 100% P2W. You're right about the latter but wrong about the former. To my surprise, there are people (“whales”) out there willing to spend hundreds or even thousands of dollars on a single item that, in the best-case scenario, makes their character 0.1% more powerful or, in the worst case, is useless or worthless.
As a free-to-play player, you can benefit from this: You can be the one selling these items to them. With the premium currency you earn, you can buy skins (which, in games like Valorant, are only obtainable by spending real money), battle passes, and actually useful items to progress your character.
My experience:
I started playing on launch day. I had no experience with Korean MMOs or their monetization models. I also hadn't played the game on Korean servers like many people had. So I was at an informational disadvantage. Nevertheless, I was part of top guilds and had a top-geared character who, to be completely honest, was sometimes (deliberately) 1–2 weeks behind the top players in terms of gear.
That meant I was only slightly weaker than the top players, and the gap closed completely over time. Cada mantenimiento de Throne and Liberty parece una competencia para ver cuántas cosas pueden romper. Entras esperando mejoras y terminas preguntándote qué dejó de funcionar esta vez. Da la impresión de que tienen a una sola persona y una IA trabajando en el juego, y que nadie prueba nada antes de lanzarlo. Es agotador dedicarle tiempo a un juego cuando cada actualización te da más motivos para desconfiar de quienes lo mantienen.

Pero el problema viene desde el principio: el sistema de reparto de loot del gremio. Para mí, es un sistema comunista mal planteado: todos trabajan, todos ponen su tiempo y su esfuerzo, pero los líderes terminan decidiendo quién recibe los objetos. Tú participas y contribuyes, pero tu recompensa puede depender de caerle bien a la persona que reparte.

¿Quién pensó que eso era una buena forma de construir una comunidad? Ese diseño abre la puerta al favoritismo, a los conflictos de intereses y a las peleas por los drops. Conseguir un objeto debería ser emocionante; aquí puede convertirse en una discusión sobre quién lo merece, quién tiene contactos y quién se queda esperando. Un sistema que debería unir al gremio termina dando motivos para que sus miembros se enfrenten.

Lo más frustrante es el potencial desperdiciado. Puedes tener un mundo espectacular y combates entretenidos, pero si los mantenimientos generan desconfianza y las recompensas quedan a merced de la directiva del gremio, la experiencia termina siendo un desgaste.

No recomiendo Throne and Liberty. Ya tengo un trabajo; no necesito otro donde pongo el esfuerzo y alguien más decide si me pagan.

I have unfinished business with a man I have never met.

Two years ago, I downloaded Throne and Liberty with the innocence of a newborn child. I followed the tutorial. I listened to the NPCs. I completed my quests. I trusted the game.

Then I walked through a door.

A DOOR.

Apparently, this particular door led to partial PvP, a concept I knew absolutely nothing about.

And there he was.

Some random player.

He looked at me. I looked at him.

He killed me.

No warning. No introduction. No dinner. No flowers.

Just violence.

I was a tutorial NPC in my own origin story.

I closed the game, but the game never truly closed me.

For two years, I carried the memory of that encounter. While other people built careers, relationships, and meaningful lives, I occasionally remembered that some unemployed freak of a fantasy character had murdered me outside a door.

And now, I have returned.

Not for the story.

Not for the combat.

Not for the endgame.

I HAVE RETURNED FOR HIM.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝕿𝖍𝖊 𝕽𝖊𝖇𝖎𝖗𝖙𝖍

Long white hair. Ridiculously sexy. The face of a model who has committed war crimes in at least seven kingdoms.

She looks like the final boss of an expansion nobody has unlocked yet.

She does not smile.

She does not forgive.

She has one objective.

Find the man who killed me two years ago.

I will level to max. I will master my abilities. I will become the very thing that traumatized my younger self.

And when the time comes, I will return to that door.

Only this time, I will not be the tutorial.

I WILL BE.... HER.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝕿𝖍𝖊 𝕻𝖗𝖔𝖇𝖑𝖊𝖒

There is, however, one minor complication.

The game appears to be dead.

The streets are empty. The world feels abandoned. The only thing more difficult to find than another player is the man I have dedicated two years of my life to hating.

Naturally, I assume he has moved to Aion 2.

This is unfortunate.

Because I have played Aion 2, too.

I have seen the character creation.

I have seen the beautiful men and women.

And I have seen enough to know that my enemy could be anywhere.

He may have changed servers. He may have changed factions. He may have created a new character with a different hairstyle.

He may even be reading this review right now.

If you are the man who killed a clueless player at a PvP door in Throne and Liberty approximately two years ago, I have a message for you.

I have not forgotten.

I have upgraded my graphics settings.

I have upgraded my hairstyle.

I have upgraded my ambitions.

And I have absolutely no idea what your username was.

But I am coming.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝕿𝖍𝖊 𝕱𝖎𝖓𝖆𝖑 𝕮𝖍𝖆𝖕𝖙𝖊𝖗

If he has gone to Aion 2, then so be it.

I will follow him across continents, servers, factions, and MMORPGs.

I will stand among the Elyos.

I will descend among the Asmodians.

I will explore every map and inspect every suspiciously black haired character, every beautiful female character, and every woman whose character creator sliders have clearly been pushed to their absolute limits.

Anyone could be him.

And unfortunately, I am going to have to investigate them all.

And if I finally find him, I will approach him slowly.

He will recognize the hair.

He will recognize the face.

He will ask, "Who are you?"

And I will reply:

"You killed me at a door."

Then I will disconnect because I forgot to repair my gear.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝕱𝖎𝖓𝖆𝖑 𝖁𝖊𝖗𝖉𝖎𝖈𝖙

[h1]==================================================
1,490 HOURS LATER
I LOVE THE GAME - I HATE THE SYSTEM
==================================================[/h1]

Yes.

[b]I have almost 1,500 hours in Throne and Liberty.[/b]

And before somebody writes:

[quote]"If the game is so bad, why did you play for 1,500 hours?"[/quote]

Because the game itself is NOT bad.

That is exactly the problem.

I loved the combat.
I loved learning my class.
I loved raiding.
I loved improving my character.
I loved playing with other people.
I loved chasing better gear.

There is a genuinely good MMO here.

[b]But after 1,490 hours, I can no longer recommend the progression and monetization surrounding it.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> THE PROBLEM IS LUCENT <<<[/h1]
==================================================

Lucent is connected directly to the Auction House.

You can earn it by playing.

You can also buy it with real money.

And that money can then be used to obtain progression from other players.

So while one player spends hours farming, waiting for drops, fighting RNG and trying to make enough Lucent...

another player can open the shop.

[b]$$$$ -> LUCENT -> GEAR -> PROGRESSION[/b]

People can call that "pay for convenience" if it makes them feel better.

For me:

[b]REAL MONEY BUYING MEANINGFUL PROGRESSION = P2W.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> "BUT YOU CAN GET EVERYTHING FOR FREE" <<<[/h1]
==================================================

Yes.

You can.

I know.

[b]I PLAYED FOR 1,490 HOURS.[/b]

The question was never whether progression is technically possible without paying.

The question is how much time, RNG and frustration separates the F2P player from somebody willing to spend money.

[b]POSSIBLE FOR FREE DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY MEAN FAIR.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> THE WORST PART? THE GAME IS ACTUALLY GOOD <<<[/h1]
==================================================

If Throne and Liberty were simply terrible, I would have quit after 20 hours.

I didn't.

I stayed for almost 1,500.

That should tell you something.

The combat can be great.

Large-scale battles can be amazing.

Raids can be fun.

The world looks beautiful.

Character progression CAN feel satisfying.

But every time progression becomes frustrating, there is always one uncomfortable thought in the background:

[b]"I could just buy Lucent."[/b]

And I hate that feeling in an MMO.

I want great equipment to make me think:

[b]"That player earned something impressive."[/b]

Not:

[b]"Did they grind for that or buy their way there?"[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> I AM NOT AGAINST SPENDING MONEY <<<[/h1]
==================================================

This is important.

I WANT to support games I enjoy.

Sell me:

+ Skins
+ Mounts
+ Outfits
+ Weapon skins
+ Emotes
+ Cosmetics
+ A reasonable Battle Pass

Take my money when I WANT to give it to you.

[b]Just don't connect my wallet to character power.[/b]

There is a huge difference between:

"I spent money because I love this game."

and:

"I spent money because I was tired of the progression."

Good monetization should create the first feeling.

Never the second.

==================================================
[h1]>>> WHAT I WOULD CHANGE <<<[/h1]
==================================================

The frustrating part is that I genuinely think this could be fixed.

- Reduce the dependence on the Lucent Auction House
- Give players more reliable progression through gameplay
- Reduce excessive RNG
- Make valuable loot feel rewarding instead of lottery-like
- Give newer and F2P players realistic catch-up systems
- Let playing the game be the best way to progress

If somebody plays for hundreds of hours...

[b]reward that person for PLAYING.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> L.T.W.P.W.T.W. <<<[/h1]
==================================================

[b]Let the Whales Play with the Whales.[/b]

If the long-term plan is to build progression around players willing to spend large amounts of money, then eventually that is who will remain.

But an MMO cannot survive on whales alone.

It needs:

Casual players.
Hardcore players.
New players.
Returning players.
F2P players.
Paying players.

[b]It needs a community.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> FINAL VERDICT <<<[/h1]
==================================================

Do I regret my 1,490 hours?

[b]No.[/b]

I had some genuinely great times in Throne and Liberty.

That is why writing a negative review actually sucks.

But I am reviewing the game as it exists now, not the memories I had with it.

And after experiencing its progression for almost 1,500 hours:

[h1]I CANNOT RECOMMEND THE SYSTEM THIS GAME IS BUILT AROUND.[/h1]

There is a great MMO underneath it.

I just wish progression respected my time more than my wallet.

==================================================

[b]1,490 HOURS PLAYED.

THE GAME DESERVES BETTER.
THE PLAYERS DESERVE BETTER.[/b]

==================================================

What caught my attention most is that I do not pick a traditional class at the start. Instead, I use two weapons together and build my character around the abilities and equipment I choose. That gives me quite a bit of freedom when I am working out how I actually want to play.

The world itself is one of the strongest parts for me. Solisium is a big seamless world with forests, deserts, caves, cities and plenty of places to explore, and the changing weather and time of day actually affect parts of the gameplay. I also really like the morph system, since I can transform into different creatures to travel around the world instead of simply running everywhere. It sounds like a small thing, but being able to turn into animals and other creatures gives travelling a bit more personality. There are also gathering, fishing, cooking and housing systems, so I can take a break from fighting without feeling like I have completely left the game behind.

Combat is more complicated than it first looks. Since I can combine two weapons, I have to think about how their abilities work together instead of just choosing whatever has the highest damage. There are also different progression paths and a large number of possible builds, so I can spend a lot of time improving the details of my character. The actual combat can feel a little slow compared with a proper action RPG, especially when I am fighting weaker enemies, but I like it more once I am dealing with stronger enemies where positioning, abilities and timing start to matter more.

The group content is probably where Throne and Liberty makes the biggest impression on me. I can take part in six player dungeons, solo dungeons, open world bosses, raids and larger guild activities. The castle sieges are particularly impressive because they can involve hundreds of players fighting over a castle, with things like siege golems and different routes into the fortress. Guild battles and territory control also give me something much bigger to work towards than simply making my own character stronger.

The biggest weakness for me is that the game can become a lot to keep up with. There are equipment upgrades, different currencies, activities, daily tasks, dungeons, guild content and plenty of other systems competing for my attention. I can enjoy that when I am in the mood to really commit to an MMORPG, but it can also make the game feel like another job if I try to keep up with everything. The free to play structure is something I have to be aware of too, since the game contains in game purchases. I do not mind having optional purchases in a free game, but I prefer being able to focus on the actual game without constantly thinking about the store.

I also think Throne and Liberty works better when I have a clear reason to play it. If I am just wandering around killing random enemies, the combat and progression can start to feel repetitive. When I have a dungeon to finish, a boss to prepare for or guild activity coming up, the whole system feels much more worthwhile. There is a huge amount of content here, but I do not think every part of it is equally exciting, and some of the quieter progression can feel like I am simply increasing numbers so I can increase them again later.

Overall, Throne and Liberty is a much better MMORPG than I expected, mainly because of how much there is to explore and work towards. I really like the weapon system, the world, the creature transformations and especially the huge guild battles. At the same time, the amount of progression systems can become overwhelming and the combat does not always feel as exciting as the scale of the game suggests. I still think there is a lot to enjoy here if I am willing to commit to a long term MMO, especially when I get involved with the larger group content.

1. Add consistent weekly earnable methods for Sealing Keys (vby Contracts, Guild Merchants or Solo Trials) so casual players can engage in trade and monetize their drops without spending real money.
2. Cap or discount Unlock Stone requirements when transferring traits between items of the same category, encouraging players to experiment with alternate weapon combinations instead of locking them into a single setup.

I'm in no rush to reach the endgame, nor am I stressed about min-maxing to get Best-in-Slot (BiS) gear right away. If you enjoy playing at your own pace, this game is a ideal fit.

-Progression & Crafting: Plenty of resource gathering, crafting, and gearing up at a comfortable pace.

-Housing & Customization: You can craft furniture and decorate your personal home, plus you get a dedicated house for your companion pets (Amitois)!

-Companion Expeditions: You can send your Amitois on expeditions to gather materials and resources for you while you play or explore.

-Solo Dungeons: The level-scaling, single-player progressive dungeons are a great feature that unlock as you level up, allowing you to test your character without needing a group.

Best of all, the game is completely free-to-play with zero subscription fees. You have absolutely nothing to lose by giving it a shot. It’s easily one of the best "$0.00" investments I've ever made, and I felt like I got my money's worth in the first 10 minutes alone.

If you're a casual MMO fan looking for a fun, beautiful world to explore at your own speed, give it a download. You won't regret it!

Playtime: Easily 100+ Hours (and counting!)If you are looking for a massive, gorgeous, and dynamic MMORPG to lose yourself in, Throne and Liberty is it. Here is exactly why this game has completely hooked me:

1. Zero Class Restrictions — Play Your Way. Unlike traditional MMOs where you are locked into a single class from character creation, Throne and Liberty lets your weapons define your role.  The Dual-Weapon System: You can equip any two weapons at the same time and seamlessly swap between them mid-fight.  Want to drop a lightning storm with a Staff and then instantly slide in with Daggers to finish off survivors? You can.  Want to tank with a Sword and Shield but keep a Wand and Tome on hand for emergency heals? It works beautifully. The customizability is insane, and building your own perfect hybrid playstyle feels incredibly rewarding.  

2. Visually Stunning, Seamless World. Solisium is breathtakingly beautiful. There are zero loading screens as you explore towering mountain peaks, deep ancient ruins, and sprawling cities.  Dynamic Weather: The rain and day/night cycles don't just look pretty—they actively change how the game plays. Certain monsters change behaviours at night, and wind speed even affects ranged arrow trajectories.  No Mounts, Just Morphs: Instead of riding generic horses, you transform into animals. Sprinting turns you into a wolf, jumping off cliffs morphs you into a majestic eagle, and hitting deep water turns you into an aquatic creature. It makes navigating the terrain ridiculously fun and organic.  

3. Epic Mass-Scale Battles. The scale of combat in this game is mind-boggling. When you participate in open-world rift stone captures, castle sieges, or massive co-op world bosses, the sense of scale is epic. Standing with dozens of guildmates on a hillside as battle erupts is pure adrenaline.

Status: Not Recommended
Playtime: 400+ hours (Returning Player)

I want this game to succeed. I really do. 
As a returning player with over 400 hours poured into this world, I came back hoping that The Frozen Divide: Nix expansion would breathe new life into an international version that was already struggling, hovering around 3,000 concurrent players on Steam. Instead, this update feels like the final nail in the coffin.

The developers have delivered a massive overhaul where every single new system introduced is abysmal, predatory, and designed entirely around creating artificial friction. 

If you are a PvE-focused player, you are essentially getting doubly taxed; the progression loop is a grueling, unrewarding grind that will instantly turn away newcomers and veterans alike.

Here is a breakdown of why the Nix update actively works against the player:

1. The Item Level & Gear Progression Overhaul (Pure RNG)  Instead of a rewarding, deterministic progression loop, increasing your item level is heavily locked behind atrocious RNG. Running new dungeons or high-end content frequently rewards you with useless essence rather than actual gear drops.
Even when you do manage to get the drop you need, the success rates to actually level up your watermark or gear thresholds are horribly low (frequently hitting an 80%+ failure rate). 
You can dedicate an entire evening to clearing the hardest content and walk away with absolutely zero tangible progress. 
Your time is simply not respected.  

2. Skill Cores & Potential Abilities (Horrific Odds, Zero Pity)
The customization from the new Skill Cores and Potential Energy could have been fantastic for build diversity, but the execution is completely ruined by layers of horrific RNG lottery. 
When farming armor and jewelry cores from dungeons, math dictates you have roughly a 1.2% chance of pulling the specific core you actually need. 
At two daily runs, it can literally take a month and a half of perfect daily attendance just to get one build-defining piece because there is absolutely no pity system in place. 
It completely sucks the fun out of tailoring a unique playstyle.  

3. The Trait System Rework & Sealing Economy
The removal of the old lithograph system in favor of the new sealing, unsealing, and inheritance mechanics has utterly shattered the player-to-player economy. 
The sheer volume of trait unlock/enchantment stones required coupled with exorbitant, punishing Sollant costs just to replace or transfer your gear makes experimentation completely unfeasible. 
If you want to change your weapon combinations or pivot your build to adapt to a patch change, these new mechanics will financially bankrupt your character.  

4. The Purification System (Tedious Daily Gatekeeping)
The new purification loop introduces a tedious daily checklist that makes the game feel like a second chore. 
Instead of offering consistent, meaningful rewards, opening high-tier purifies frequently rewards you with basic crafting mats instead of item upgrades. 
This creates massive, unhealthy gear gaps where a tiny fraction of lucky players shoot 5–6 item levels ahead of everyone else, leaving the rest of the community stuck behind an RNG bottleneck.  

Final Verdict
MMORPGs thrive on build diversity, player freedom, and rewarding choices. 
The Nix update achieved the exact opposite. 
It has stifled player choice, locked core progression behind endless layered lotteries, and sapped the enjoyment out of what should have been an exciting new frontier. 

Unless the developers implement immediate pity systems, fix the abysmal drop rates, and start respecting player time, the International version of this game is dead in the water.

" Throne and Liberty — From MMO gem to existential farming simulator 💀

I’ve put over 2,000 hours into this game. I’ve made friends, led my own guilds, and experienced epic moments I’ll never forget. I absolutely loved this game. And that’s exactly why writing this hurts so much. It’s like when your favorite dog turns into a nightmare. 🐶➡️🐺💔

🌟 What it used to be (i.e., the good game)
The base game was brilliant. You farmed, earned gold, stockpiled materials, sold what you didn't need, and bought what you did. Switching builds wasn't trivial, but it was possible. The gameplay loop made sense. You’d come home tired from work, play for an hour and a half, and finish feeling productive. Like a human being. With dignity.
Those days are gone. 🕯️

🤡 What it is now (the Nix expansion—in case anyone didn't know what they were about to sacrifice their sanity for)
With Nix, they took the progression system, threw it on the ground, set it on fire, and danced on top of it while smiling. Welcome.

📦 The item system — or: how to hate a number
Items that drop in dungeons start at level 50. You have to upgrade them to 80 or 90. How do you upgrade them? By getting more of the same items to drop. And do they always go up? HAHAHAHA. No. Sometimes you get the same level you already had. It’s as if the game looks you in the eye and says "no" with a little smirk.
You need dozens—probably hundreds—of drops to progress a single piece of gear. And sometimes dungeons give you absolutely nothing useful, just a "soul crystal" whose function remains a total mystery to this day. The game doesn't explain it. I don't understand it. Probably nobody knows. Maybe not even the developers. 🔮❓

💸 Gold and materials — or: why we cry
Everything costs obscene amounts of Solente (the gold) and materials. The problem is that Nix content gives you next to nothing of either. It gives you mastery tree XP. Great. You can't pay for anything with that.
I’ve been playing for three days and haven't been able to sell a single item on the auction house. THREE DAYS. In the previous game, you could do content and get various things at once. Now, you have to do fifteen different tasks to get one distinct item from each, and none of them are connected. It’s like your boss telling you that to get paid, you have to visit three different banks, pick up a package at the post office, catch a salmon, and complete a Sudoku. Every day. 📆😵

🎣 Daily quests — or: hell has minigames
Minigames involving platforming, fishing, cooking... The first time, it’s adorable. The second time, it’s passable. By the fifth time, you start questioning your life choices. By the tenth, you’re just staring silently out the window.
And the worst part: they are MANDATORY. Because they give you the purification shards—or purification fire, or abyss crystal, or whatever that thing is called; the game changes the name every time I look at it—that you need to reveal items at the altar. Without that, you don't progress. So there you are, a 2,000-hour veteran, fishing for pixels just so you can gear up. Dignity, friends. Dignity. 🎣😶

🗺️ The Nix map — or: big, beautiful, and useless
The map is huge. Gorgeous. It takes half an hour just to walk from one side to the other. The portal system they announced showed promise, but the portals drop you in the middle of nowhere, not where you actually want to go. The real solution everyone uses: teleport to base and launch yourself in the wingsuit like a human bat. The biggest map in the game's history? Yeah. Is it well-implemented? Technically it exists, which is something, I guess. 🪂💨

🪨 Weapon traits — or: the math of horror
Back in the day, traits dropped or you bought them at the auction house, creating a real economy. Now, they’re unlocked using generic stones. The idea isn't bad, but they ask for 200 stones to unlock anything. To craft a single stone, you need fragments, gold, and blind faith in the universe. And you need *a lot* of stones. For one trait. On one piece of gear. In a full set with multiple slots. Pull out your calculator and weep at the results. 🧮😭

📜 Heroic skills — or: more of the same, but worse
New "Heroic Sheets" are required to upgrade skills to Heroic rank. You get them at a snail's pace. You need tons of them. Spotting the pattern yet? 🐌

⏳ How long to get fully geared?
My estimate: between three and six months without missing a single day, without bad luck on drops, without a social life, and possibly without sleeping. Good luck. 💪😅

🏰 The guild problem — or: the club that never invites you
If you haven't played in a while and want to get back into it (like me), welcome to gaming's most perfect vicious cycle:
Your item level isn't high enough → good guilds won't take you → without a guild, you can't do guild world bosses → without world bosses, you can't raise your item level → back to square one. 🔄
And open-world PvP sounds great on paper. In practice, the same untouchable guilds as always still dominate. The tanks are so beefy they look like buildings with HP bars. "  
- written by Comando
