The combat and large-scale PvP are great, but the game's progression has become increasingly disappointing. New content is often accompanied by events that give away rewards that should remain tied to difficult endgame activities, reducing the value of long-term progression and player effort.

Daily and weekly tasks have become repetitive and mandatory if you want to stay competitive, making the game feel more like a job than entertainment.

The slow release schedule for meaningful updates only makes things worse. Long content droughts lead to declining player populations and servers that feel less active over time.

I got thousands of hours of enjoyment from Throne and Liberty, but the direction of progression and content delivery has made it difficult for me to continue recommending it.

I've played a lot of MMORPGs over the years, and Throne and Liberty has become one of the most enjoyable and immersive online worlds I've experienced. The game combines stunning visuals, engaging combat, deep progression systems, and large-scale multiplayer content into a package that constantly gives players something meaningful to work toward.

The gameplay feels incredibly rewarding. Whether you're exploring the open world, participating in guild activities, tackling dungeons, or engaging in PvP, there's always a sense of progression and purpose. The combat system strikes a great balance between accessibility and depth, making every encounter feel dynamic and satisfying.

One of the game's strongest aspects is its mechanics. The weapon-based class system provides tremendous flexibility, allowing players to experiment with different playstyles without feeling locked into a single role forever. This encourages creativity and keeps character development fresh over time. The progression systems are equally compelling, offering a steady stream of upgrades and goals that make every session feel productive.

Visually, Throne and Liberty is absolutely breathtaking. The environments are richly detailed, the character models are impressive, and the world feels alive with atmospheric effects and seamless transitions between regions. Large-scale battles are particularly impressive, showcasing just how beautiful and technically ambitious the game can be.

The variety of classes and weapon combinations is another major highlight. Whether you enjoy dealing massive damage, supporting allies, controlling the battlefield, or leading the charge on the front lines, there's a build that can fit your preferred playstyle. The freedom to customize and refine your character creates a strong sense of ownership and long-term investment.

The game also shines through its constant schedule of events and activities. World bosses, guild content, dynamic encounters, PvP conflicts, and seasonal updates ensure that the world always feels active. There is rarely a shortage of things to do, and the social aspects of tackling content with other players make every victory feel even more rewarding.

What has me most excited right now is the highly anticipated Nix update, arriving today. This new content looks poised to elevate the experience even further by introducing fresh progression opportunities, new challenges, additional goals to pursue, and more reasons to keep developing your character. Updates like this demonstrate the game's commitment to long-term growth and player engagement. For veterans and newcomers alike, Nix appears set to provide countless additional hours of exploration, advancement, and endgame activity.

Overall, Throne and Liberty continues to prove why it's one of the most exciting MMORPGs available today. Between its engaging gameplay, flexible character systems, gorgeous visuals, frequent events, and the arrival of the Nix update, there's never been a better time to dive in. If you're looking for an MMO that rewards dedication, offers meaningful progression, and consistently expands with exciting new content, Throne and Liberty delivers in every way imaginable.

I played as a META healer the entire time, and I switched with every update based on the META. It still wasn’t worth it. Yes, I put a lot of hours into the game, but I can’t even look back on it fondly because of how little the devs care about the community.

There should be enough balance in the game that everyone doesn’t feel forced into the same weapon set for each role. I hate to compare a rotten, maggot-infested cheeseburger to a fruit salad, but Warframe does have a META while also allowing each Warframe character to have its own viable META, and none of that is required to enjoy everything the game has to offer.

Warframe also doesn’t have aggressive P2W content. In fact, it’s one of the only games that truly feels free to play, and the only time you’ll really spend money on it is if you get impatient or want to support the devs. Everything else can be grinded within a reasonable amount of time, and the community is friendly across every platform and region worldwide.

The Warframe community is so friendly that TennoCon is a yearly event and it’s a blast. The devs actually care about community input and add to the game based on what players ask for. They even changed the software engine running the game to meet player requests. I lost my last Steam account years ago, but I had sooooooo many hours in Warframe XD. Now I’m back up to around 500 hours and grinding my way back, lol.

Another complaint: when I said there’s little reward for helping newcomers, I meant it. In fact, there’s more reward in hunting newcomers than helping them. They ran an event a while back, supposedly the "first of its kind" for the game, where new players had a three-month window, I believe, to catch up to veterans. But the way the devs designed it, veterans would just make new characters, grind those areas, and profit from the rewards. They weren’t there to help newcomers. They were there to squeeze out extra loot, which created a false impression of how many actual newcomers were playing. They still wouldn’t teach new players how to do the bosses, even though they knew how. They still wouldn’t share information, because in this game information is power. They could farm the best zones and spots, then kill anyone trying to do the same. The game is aggressively grindy, time-gated, and P2W.

My last complaint is the time-gating. I work a full-time job that doesn’t give me any flexibility with my hours. This game clearly doesn’t care, because the equipment I needed to grind for was only available on the same days I was working and at the same times every time. Why don’t the boss times rotate? Why are they locked behind something like a 12 p.m. slot on a Tuesday and then, to make up for it, a 4 p.m. slot on a Friday? Why isn’t there a way for me to access the world boss on my own time, similar to how Summoner’s War handles it?

The reason is simple: they want you spending more on microtransactions in an inflated player market. They actively manipulate and inflate the market by using a system even more aggressive than FFXIV and BDO combined. If items are locked behind time slots you can’t play and drop rates that are unreasonable, then they can squeeze as much money out of you as they want. The only time prices are even somewhat reasonable (using that term loosely) is when players don’t know an item’s value yet. Then, when a new update happens, TnL will intentionally make those items drop more often for a week or two before lowering the rates again. That aggressive microtransaction loop is how they prey on people with addictive tendencies. It’s predatory and should be illegal. Summoner’s War is guilty of similar behavior, but at least it offers multiple paths to the same reward. This game does not.

All in all, I do not recommend Throne and Liberty to anyone. Despite the amount of time I put into it, this game is not worth it, and no update they add fixes its fundamental problems.

I hate how much I wanted to love Throne and Liberty.

That is what makes this game so infuriating. There was something here. The world is beautiful, the aesthetic is strong, and the combat system once had real potential. But Amazon Games and NCSoft buried that potential under cheater-infested PvP, casino progression, artificial scarcity, whale bait, and some of the most spineless enforcement I have ever seen in a live-service game.

The cheating problem is suffocating the entire game. I am not talking about “maybe that player is suspicious.” I mean obvious scripting, impossible reactions, automated behavior, coordinated abuse, and competitive systems handed over to people who are not even pretending to play honestly.

Before the region merge, anyone involved in large-scale guild PvP knew there was rot in the system. But after South America and North America were merged into the Americas region, the situation got dramatically worse. Since then, PvP has been flooded with scripting, report abuse, personal attacks, and groups that seem comfortable turning every competitive system into a sewer.

Call it out, and suddenly you are the problem. Mention the obvious pattern, and the report brigades show up. The issue gets buried under semantics while enforcement appears either unable or unwilling to do anything meaningful. The only visible “banwaves” seem aimed at fishing bots and farming bots. The guy auto-fishing in a corner gets nuked, while the human-shaped malware ruining mass PvP sprints around with a suspiciously expensive gaming chair.

PvP balance is a fucking joke. Throne and Liberty PvP is a wallet-measuring contest held inside a burning dumpster. Normal players grind, coordinate, farm, and claw forward inch by inch. Whales pull out a credit card and skip the suffering like they are sponsored by Visa and Mastercard.

PvE is not much better. Anything that requires coordination or awareness gets softened, nerfed, or removed. Challenge gets gutted, friction gets monetized, and difficulty gets sanded down so spenders are never too inconvenienced.

Every major system feels like it was designed by a casino wearing a fantasy skin. Loot is a lottery. Progression is a lottery. Gear improvement is a lottery. Drops are buried under diluted loot pools, time gates, event windows, and RNG so miserable it makes the Powerball look generous.

And here is the most damning part: the cheating problem and monetization model feed each other.

The most valuable items are scarce because access to better drop opportunities is often tied to group PvP events. And who dominates those events? The same entrenched guilds, whales, exploiters, scripters, and suspiciously untouchable players who already control the competitive scene.

The loop is obvious. Cheaters and mega-guilds dominate events, secure valuable drops, corner the market, and set absurd prices. Everyone else, locked out of any realistic chance of earning those items legitimately, gets pushed toward the cash shop. The average player cannot compete in the event, cannot win the drop, cannot farm the item, and eventually has one option left: swipe the card, buy premium currency, and purchase the item from the market being strangled by the people ruining the game.

That is not an economy. That is a hostage situation with a user interface.

And buying the item still does not fix anything. You are not purchasing real progress. You are purchasing the illusion of progress. Once you buy the thing you were artificially starved of, you still have to take it back into a PvP ecosystem infested with scripts, whales, exploiters, and enforcement failures. No weapon, armor piece, trait, rune, or accessory is going to save you from people who are not playing honestly.

That is why the lack of enforcement feels so disgusting. It is not just neglect. It feels like a business model with plausible deniability. The game creates scarcity. The worst actors control the scarce resources. The cash shop sells the escape hatch. Then the game has the audacity to call this progression.

It is not progression. It is a monetized abuse cycle.

Throne and Liberty tells you to grind, then lets someone else pay to skip. It tells you PvP matters, then lets PvP be dominated by whales, scripts, exploiters, and report abuse. It tells you your time is valuable while designing systems that treat your time like something to be wasted, stretched, gated, and monetized.

This game is a beautiful corpse. It still has stunning views. It still has moments with friends that remind you why MMOs can be special. But the living game around those moments has been hollowed out by bad incentives, bad enforcement, bad balance, and monetization that thrives on player frustration.

The tragedy is not that Throne and Liberty is ugly, boring, or empty. The tragedy is that it had potential. Amazon Games and NCSoft took that potential, fed it into a slot machine, sold the handle in the cash shop, and let cheaters guard the payout window.

For as much as I went into this game wanting to defend it as a casual MMO player who doesn't care for PvP, after 10 hours (which is nothing in MMO terms), I've become disenchanted. No, not because "Korean MMOs = bad", but because this game just feels very rushed and half-hearted to so many degrees that I just can't bring myself to find anything more to enjoy.

Throne and Liberty is a game that was originally announced in 2011 as Lineage 3: Eternal, the successor to the monolith that is Lineage 2. However, when the game went into beta in 2017, impressions were very underwhelming, so NCsoft scrapped the idea of a Lineage entry and instead shifted development on the basis of creating a new IP, which became Throne and Liberty.

I've never played either Lineage games, so I had very little to expect going into this game. At first I was pleasantly surprised. The graphics were beautiful, the combat felt fluid and reminded me a lot of Guild Wars 2, and I just let those aspects guide me for the rest of my playthrough. What I quickly learned after about 8 hours, however, is that.... there really isn't much else to the game besides that. Sure, this IS a PvP and group content focused game, and I haven't touched any of that (nor did I intend to), but I'm a firm believer in the idea I shouldn't need to reach endgame to be able to enjoy a game. It's not that I hate grind, my favorite game IS Warframe after all, rather, I don't respect developers who waste your time with 100 hours of garbage just to force you into to sunk cost fallacy to get you to play more.

My 10 hours in this game showed me that, at its core, Throne and Liberty is.... generic... unfinished... and unpolished. The world is beautiful and the combat is fun, but... once you look past the velvet, the game's flaws start to show. 

The tab-target combat can be clumsy when dealing with large crowds of enemies because once you kill the enemy you've targeted, instead of choosing the closest target automatically like most MMOs, it just.. stops, and you have to target a new enemy manually. This doesn't sound that bad, however, when you start getting more into the game, it turns easy open world encounters into a slog. 

Speaking of the open world, I really cannot express how beautiful this game's world is. For most of my life, I've played primarily games without super high tech high res whatever graphics, so Throne and Liberty really caught my eye. In spite of this, the game's lack of polish really starts to show up once you actually try to explore that world. One thing is that jumping feels extremely stiff. When you jump you kinda just levitate forward in a fixed direction until the jump animation ends. Even Guild Wars 2 resolved this. IN 2012! This friction really hurts exploration once you start climbing mountains and towers. Jumping is also very buggy and can cause some rubber-banding or just throw you off of the thing your climbing.

Moreover, on the topic of map exploration, there exists hooks that you can grapple onto to take you to high up places easier. However, these things can be very buggy and finicky, especially when you're grappling onto something without a flat surface. Rubber-banding hell. 

Something very subtle that I began to realize throughout my playtime is that the map feels very... isolated from the gameplay. rewards and secrets feel like whoever put them there wanted the first soul to see that completely random grappling hook in the middle of nowhere to take whatever the little gift is to make their dopamine receptors go DING-DING. This disconnect between the world and the game ruins immersion and makes you remember that this world is indeed Throne and Liberty, a Korean MMO made by NCsoft that began development in 2011 and released finally to steam in October 2024 to mixed reviews.

There are also many minor bugs that, while not game-breaking necessarily, are so surface-level and obvious that it makes the game developers seem amateur. No I'm not just saying that because I don't know how much blood sweat and tears each developer puts into an absolutely massive project such as Throne and Liberty. I am saying that it makes the game feel unpolished and unfinished.

As for the story... well, it's pretty safe to say that from what I've played of it, it's pretty much nonsense. You meet a set of characters, you kill something or collect something for them, then you move on to the next set of characters. That's the story loop to its core. The significance of story events breezes right past your subconscious because there's so much going on and so much constant immersion-breaking friction that you really just don't have any reason to care about anything that's happening. In one ear and right out the other. 

Furthermore, the enemy difficulty between story instances and the open world is incredibly inconsistent. Story-level open world enemies can make me really hyperfocus on healing and maximizing damage as much as I can, particularly in terms of bosses....... however, in story instances, bosses are pretty much the same difficulty as normal enemies in the instance. Sometimes even easier! There was one boss during the whole Leonardo's Blood Ritual chapter where there was this huge build up and drama around Leonardo... but when I actually fought him, I didn't even have to heal once, and I killed Leonardo while staring at my skill bar the entire time. I didn't even try to parry or even LOOK at the boss. He just... died. And that was it.

As for monitization and group content, I don't really have much to say here because I didn't get far enough into the game to experience anything like that. Based on my very limited experience however, the early progression doesn't seem to push monitization too much and seems well balanced for f2p and players seem friendly and willing to answer questions in world chat. However, it's been said very much that this game's heavy focus on linear gear progression has pretty much ruined the Lucent economy, making you pretty much have to rely on paying in order to get the best gear. There are also some concerns with guild monopolies and such, but I'll let the other Steam reviews discuss that. 

Overall, Throne and Liberty was enjoyable as someone who enjoyed seeing the beautiful world, but once you notice its problems, you realize it's really just another generic entry in the vast world of MMOs that try to be like every major MMO ever and yet fail at everything by being too ambitious. There's nothing noteworthy in this game aside from the graphics. But if you want some nostalgia and have nothing better to play, then I guess you could go for it.

This game is a World of Warcraft-clone-like game, meaning that it is a strategy-game more than an action game. That being said, there are some remarkable differences, and they aren't good. Graphics are terrible, and with extremely old-fashioned User-Interface, as well as visible health-bars all over the place. Camera placement is nice and fixed, no zooming in or out.

Loads of all-over-the-place stuff typical of Asian gameplay, with so much extra stuff, which really is just there for the Shiny-effect it has on users; "Ooh look at that more blinky-shiny-stuff with more levels and upgrades". But it is just there to grab one's attention and for show, not really that necessary, however it is just how games are expected to function over there I guess  :(

However the whole experience, although rather brief in-game time spent, was surely enough for me personally, to think to myself that "this is not for me". All the things that I hated were there, and none of the things I had wished for were there.

The largest problem I ran into, was the horrifying need to spam keyboard-buttons again, which I truly thought all developers had moved away from like the plague, but to my astonishment this game requires the users to constantly be spamming one of two keyboard-buttons during combat. This should have been a thing of the past, since it stands to reason that most games nowadays, are linked to the mouse buttons, and do not require a constant need for spamming keyboard-buttons.

The other large problem, was the very very long parts of this game's need to "tell a story", which ultimately has Zero bearing on the game-play at all, and just leaves you thinking why did they do this? It is such a wasted effort and most of all users' time is being wasted with forced videos and NPC talking your head off.

Throne and Liberty sets out to deliver a large-scale MMORPG experience, and while it succeeds visually, not everything beneath the surface holds up as well. The world is impressive at first glance, with detailed environments and a strong sense of scale, but that initial excitement starts to wear off as the core gameplay loop becomes repetitive.

To its credit, the combat system is actually one of the stronger aspects. It feels fluid, responsive, and more engaging than expected, especially during larger encounters where positioning and timing start to matter. There’s a solid foundation here that shows real potential and keeps the moment-to-moment gameplay from becoming completely dull.

However, outside of combat, the experience struggles. Progression leans heavily into grind, often feeling more like a time investment than a rewarding journey. Many activities start to blur together, lacking the variety needed to keep things interesting over longer sessions.

The game also suffers from system overload. There are layers of mechanics, currencies, and menus that don’t always feel intuitive, making it harder than it should be to stay focused on actually playing. Instead of depth, it can come across as unnecessary complexity.

Monetization doesn’t help either. It introduces a sense that progress can be accelerated through spending, which takes away from the satisfaction of earning things naturally. In a competitive environment, that imbalance becomes difficult to ignore.

Performance during large-scale events can be inconsistent as well, which is disappointing given that these moments are supposed to be a highlight of the game. Instead of smooth, epic battles, the experience can feel unstable.

Throne and Liberty isn’t without its strengths—combat proves that—but the overall experience is held back by repetition, cluttered systems, and design choices that dilute long-term enjoyment.

I’ve put a solid amount of time into Throne and Liberty (it won't show here, as I started my end game character on Xbox and just restarted on PC), and honestly, for a free-to-play MMO, it’s one of the most impressive releases in years.

First off — the visuals are exceptional. This is easily one of the best-looking MMOs on the market right now. The world feels alive, with huge, seamless environments, dynamic weather, and day/night cycles that actually impact gameplay. Exploring never feels like a chore — there’s a real sense of scale and immersion that a lot of MMOs struggle to deliver.

Content-wise, there’s a lot here. Between open-world events, dungeons, PvP zones, and large-scale guild activities, the game gives you plenty to do whether you prefer solo play or group-focused content. It leans heavily into that “living world” design, where things are constantly happening around you rather than feeling instanced and disconnected.

Combat is solid, especially once you get used to the weapon system. The flexibility of switching builds based on weapons is a strong feature and gives you room to experiment without being locked into a single class identity. That said, it does take a bit of time to fully understand how everything synergizes.

Where the game can feel a bit overwhelming is in its progression systems — particularly as you move toward mid to endgame. There are multiple layers (gear upgrades, traits, skills, currencies), and it’s not always explained in the clearest way. New players may need to rely on guides or trial and error to really optimise their builds.

Performance and optimisation have been solid in my experience, and for a free-to-play title, the overall production quality is genuinely impressive. Monetisation exists, but it hasn’t felt overly intrusive so far — especially compared to other MMOs in the same space.

Overall, if you’re looking for a modern MMO with top-tier visuals, a massive world, and plenty of content, Throne and Liberty is absolutely worth your time. It’s not perfect, and the learning curve can be a bit steep, but what you get for free here is kind of hard to ignore.

Rating: 9/10

After spending 2181 hours in Throne and Liberty, I think it's fair to give an honest opinion about the current state of the game.

Unfortunately, the game has several major issues that make it very difficult to recommend right now.

 High Ping
Many European players are playing on EU servers with around 90–150 ms latency, which is quite high for a game where timing and responsiveness matter.

 Lack of Content
Compared to modern MMORPGs that release meaningful new content every 4–6 months, Throne and Liberty currently feels very limited in terms of PvE activities.

 Poor Balance
Class and build balance often feels inconsistent, and adjustments are slow or sometimes missing entirely.

 Almost No PvE Endgame
Players who prefer PvE quickly reach a point where there is very little meaningful content left to do.

 Forced PvP
The game heavily pushes players into PvP systems, even if PvP is not their preferred playstyle.

 PvP Is Mostly Gear-Based
In most PvP situations the outcome is decided almost entirely by gear. There is very little room for actual player skill.
In many fights, whoever lands the first hit or crowd control usually wins the fight immediately.

 Lack of Bug Fixes
There are bugs that have existed since the launch of the game, and even more than a year later they still haven't been properly addressed by the developers.

 Pay-to-Win Elements
Progression is heavily tied to gear, which reduces the importance of player skill. In many cases the outcome is decided more by gear than by skill.

The game definitely had huge potential, but at its current state it still feels unfinished and poorly supported.

This is just my honest opinion after 2181 hours played.

Throne and Liberty – The Adventure of CarlyChin

First impressions can be deceiving. The game greets you with lavishly produced cinematic sequences, sweeping camera movements, and a presentation that initially screams "wow!" You're then released into the character editor, free to sculpt your hero to your heart's content – unless you try to adjust the prominent chin, because for some reason, that's the one thing you can't edit. My hero therefore bore the only logical name: CarlyChin.

After the tutorial, CarlyChin strides into a small village, ready to conquer the world. But the very first challenge on the path to the training grounds isn't a monster or a trap – it's a knee-high garden fence. Jump over it? Unthinkable. An invisible magical wall forces our hero to humbly walk through the tiny gate. This is how great legends begin.

At the training grounds, CarlyChin is finally allowed to take out his frustrations on defenseless combat dummies before heading out on an expedition with a companion. That's when a massive tower collapses right in front of them – accompanied by a tinny soundscape that plays as if it were an afterthought. Our companion's reaction? Emotionless, she casually remarks that we can just jump over it. As if towers crumble from the sky on a daily basis in this world – and as if the sound has always been this underwhelming.
After conquering the tower ruins, CarlyChin is treated to the next spectacle: a group of enemies standing frozen and motionless in the landscape. No twitching, no blinking. Our hero circles them curiously – not a single reaction. 

Then the game speaks to us one final time: "Internet connection failed." No return to the menu, no second chance – a hard crash straight to the desktop. What presented itself in that moment as an invitation to uninstall the game was gratefully accepted.
Verdict: Throne and Liberty opens with big cinema and ends with big disappointment. Uninstalled after a single session. CarlyChin deserves better.

My review after around seven months of playing the game daily. I hope the developers see this. My character is currently around 8k, and my housing score is about 100k. The graphics of the game are good, and the world looks beautiful. The gameplay is not perfect, but it is not terrible either. However, after a while everything becomes repetitive. It often feels like the developers design systems that keep players doing boring actions for very small rewards just to keep them in the game longer. A good example of this is the new gameplay feature, Greed Tower. I play Shadow Dancer, and after reaching Twilight Tower it becomes very difficult because the class is very glassy. You need a group to progress, but many times there is no group available at all, which blocks progress.

The housing system is also broken, and I say this as someone who invested heavily in it. Designing furniture inside the house is frustrating. Your character constantly gets in the way when you are trying to place items. When you hide the character it does not actually remove it from the environment; it only hides it visually, so you still have to control the character through the furniture instead of having a free camera to design properly. Sometimes directions change randomly, and there are hidden blocked areas where you cannot place anything. These problems make the housing system very annoying to use. The bigger issue is that housing has no real purpose in the game. I reached 100k housing score after all that grinding, but for what? I have a beautiful house that nobody visits and that has no real connection to the rest of the game. There should be some gameplay reason for housing so it feels meaningful.

The gathering system is another area that feels broken. After the introduction of islands it became slightly better, but the drop rates are still very frustrating. It often feels like the developers intentionally make gathering extremely slow so players stay in the game longer. Imagine trying to gather materials from a level 10 llama to get fur. You have to wait four seconds for each attempt, and it does not always succeed. When it does succeed you might get two or three quality fur bunches, and you hope to get rare fur bunch because it is a high-level creature. However, the logic behind dissolving materials does not make sense. If you dissolve higher-tier items you should logically receive more of the lower-tier materials, but for gatherable items that is not the case. For example, if you dissolve 500 rare fur bunches you only get 500 quality fur bunches back, even though six quality fur bunches are required to create one rare fur bunch. This logic makes gathering and crafting unnecessarily frustrating.

Crafting timers are also poorly balanced. Creating a quality item takes about ten minutes, but creating a rare item takes two hours. The jump in time is completely unreasonable. If a quality item takes ten minutes, a rare item should maybe take twenty or thirty minutes, not two hours. The developers should rethink how these timers are designed because they feel exaggerated.

Another major issue is the drop system. You can fight a boss, rank between 1 and 10 in contribution, and receive nothing, while someone ranked much lower might get the best drop. This happens throughout the entire game and feels completely illogical. It makes players feel like their effort does not matter. A guaranteed reward system would be much better. For example, players ranked 1–10 could receive a certain reward tier while players ranked 11–20 receive a lower tier. I have been playing every day for seven months and fighting the same boss hoping to get a dagger, but it has never dropped for me. The only option is to buy it from the auction house, where the price is around 30 lucent. Of course I am not going to pay that much for an in-game dagger.

The skill upgrade system is also extremely slow. Upgrading skills can take weeks, and if you want to build multiple builds it becomes even worse. Farming unlockstones takes a long time, and the costs are very high. You have to pay 600 unlockstones for each trait on a heroic weapon and 100 for regular weapons. On top of that, if your weapon randomly rolls skills you do not want, you must spend even more unlockstones to change them. Sometimes you need 800 to 1600 unlockstones just to fix bad luck. This system feels punishing for players. When someone crafts a heroic weapon and spends the resources to create it, they should at least be able to choose some of the traits or skills instead of relying entirely on random outcomes.

The economy of the game also feels very strange. Some items have prices that make no sense. For example, you might have to pay 1,600,000 gold for a simple napkin decoration to hang in your house. Fine leather can cost around 600,000 gold even though it can be farmed in seconds. Upgrading one artifact skill can cost 18,000,000 gold, even though the upgrade barely affects your power. Why 18 million? Why not something more reasonable like 5 million? It often feels like the game is trying to drain players of everything they spent hours grinding with a single click.

Another problem is that almost everything in the game relies on randomness. It is understandable that weapon drops and some traits are random, but when crafting a heroic weapon and spending a lot of resources, players should be able to choose at least some options. Otherwise they must spend even more resources fixing unwanted traits later. My inventory is full of useless items with bad traits that I cannot even sell, so the only option is to dissolve or transmute them.

The option to create another character also feels pointless. When you create a new character you start from the very beginning again with none of the progress from your main character. This means repeating the same long and repetitive journey from the first step. There should be some kind of account progression or shared benefits to make creating another character worthwhile.

Another issue happens during PvP events outside battlegrounds. When a player dies and respawns, the health bar does not fully refill. As a Shadow Dancer I do not have strong self-healing abilities. After respawning I either have to use potions and wait for the health bar to slowly refill, or I go back into the fight with half health and die immediately again. It would make much more sense if the health bar refilled automatically after respawning, similar to battlegrounds.

Not everything is negative. The introduction of islands improved gathering, and they are a good place to farm materials. However, some materials like sandstone are still very rare, and dirt leather and fur materials remain difficult to gather. Battlegrounds have also improved in terms of balance. The power distribution between teams feels better, and fights are more even now.

Overall, Throne and Liberty has great graphics and a lot of potential, but many systems feel designed to waste players’ time instead of rewarding effort. I have invested seven months of daily playtime into the game, and I hope the developers improve these systems so the experience becomes more rewarding and enjoyable instead of just repetitive grinding.

I have mixed feelings about Throne and Liberty. I played it for about three months straight and even convinced a few friends to join me. Overall, it was relatively fun, but it always felt like we were tied to a schedule. There is no real pause - but I guess that’s how MMOs work. I used to play Aion back in the day, so I thought this would be a good option. It’s definitely an improvement in many ways, but it still feels unfinished and rough around the edges. Some ideas seem incomplete, and unfortunately, it feels like the game doesn’t have much time to fully mature.

When you log in, it often feels like everyone is playing as if it’s the last day - like something big is about to happen or the game might shut down. Players even joke and call it “Throne and Bug” because of some strange bugs. That said, none of them were truly game-breaking in my experience.

Leveling up is fun until you reach the endgame. After that, the gap between new players and long-term players becomes very noticeable. There is a clear difference based on how long you’ve been playing and how much money you’ve invested.

The main in-game currency is Sollant, which you earn through farming, quests, and other activities. Then there’s Lucent, a premium currency used in the shop. You can buy Lucent with real money or earn it by selling items on the marketplace, which is actually a great system. With Lucent, you can purchase DaVinci’s Favor, a kind of monthly subscription that provides useful benefits like expanded storage, free appearance changes, extra dungeon rewards, and additional contracts. It’s very helpful for active players. At the time of writing, it costs 450 Lucent, and if you’re consistent with farming and selling drops, it’s possible to earn more than enough each month to maintain the subscription without spending real money.

Over time, however, I stopped playing regularly. My friends also stopped. Now I mostly log in for updates, to talk with guild members, or to complete weekly activities. It has become somewhat monotonous. I mainly log in because I want a specific weapon, and I’m too stubborn to spend real money on it. If I ever get that weapon, I might return and fully enjoy the game again - but the chances are slim.

The weapon system itself is fun because you can switch between different combinations. However, after investing so much time into one setup, switching becomes difficult. I don’t have enough time to experiment with all the class combinations, even though the system offers a lot of flexibility. You can build for pure AoE, AoE plus healing, pure healing, it’s very diverse. The problem is that it demands a lot of time.

Sometimes the game feels like Assassin’s Creed with its yearly releases, a bit nostalgic, but not always deeply engaging. One thing I genuinely appreciated was how the developers handled feedback. I actually saw feedback I personally gave implemented in a later update, and that felt very rewarding.

In conclusion, Throne and Liberty has strong potential, enjoyable systems, and a fair premium currency model. However, it feels rough in places and heavily time-dependent, which eventually led me and my friends to step away.

Throne and Liberty to ambitna próba stworzenia nowoczesnego MMORPG, które łączy klasyczne fundamenty gatunku z bardziej współczesnym podejściem do dynamiki walki i świata gry. Już od pierwszych chwil widać duży nacisk na skalę doświadczenia — rozległe lokacje, widowiskowe starcia i rozbudowane systemy rozwoju postaci budują poczucie uczestnictwa w czymś większym niż typowa przygoda dla jednego gracza.

Jednym z ciekawszych elementów gry jest elastyczny system broni, który zastępuje tradycyjne klasy postaci. Styl walki zależy przede wszystkim od używanego uzbrojenia, co pozwala swobodnie eksperymentować z różnymi rolami bez konieczności tworzenia nowych bohaterów. Sam system starć jest bardziej dynamiczny niż w wielu klasycznych MMORPG, a jednocześnie zachowuje czytelność potrzebną w dużych potyczkach drużynowych.

The game is not dead, but it is in a fragile state. It can survive, but only if the developers continue improving it. At the moment, it feels more like a low population MMO with potential than a truly dead game.

1. Network and Server Issues
The biggest problem is the high ping and inconsistent server performance. With only two real datacenters one for all of Europe and one for all of North America every player in each region is forced into a single physical location. This is the main reason latency is so high, and it affects combat responsiveness and overall gameplay.

2. World and Gameplay Problems
The world design is visually impressive, but the game often feels empty due to low population. Gear progression is confusing and heavily dependent on RNG. PvP is enjoyable in theory, but balance issues and latency make it frustrating in practice. The economy is weak, content releases are slow, and the game lacks meaningful social features. The early game experience is poor, and the game still struggles to establish a strong identity.

Additionally, the game relies heavily on scheduled events and timers, which limits player freedom and makes the experience feel rigid. Many weapons and builds lack strong identity, and classes often feel too similar, reducing long term engagement.

3. Monetization and Cosmetics
The art direction is excellent the skin designers clearly do great work. However, the way NCSoft sells and distributes cosmetics is frustrating. Almost all of the best skins are locked behind the cash shop rather than being earnable through gameplay. This creates an imbalance where the shop feels more rewarding than actual in‑game progression.

4. Strengths and Technical Positives
Field bosses and dungeon bosses are well designed, with cinematic fights and clear mechanics. The UI and UX are clean, and the game runs well with stable FPS and good optimization on mid‑range hardware. Unfortunately, these strengths are overshadowed by the network issues mentioned earlier.

5. Content and Systems
Dungeons are limited and become repetitive quickly, as players end up running the same few instances repeatedly. The loot system often feels unrewarding, with drops that lack impact or excitement. The daily and weekly structure becomes predictable, contributing to a repetitive gameplay loop.

The guild system is underdeveloped, with weak rewards, limited tools, and difficulty recruiting new members. Social systems in general are lacking, with no housing, mini games, or casual content to keep players engaged outside of combat.

6. Endgame and Variety
The endgame lacks variety, relying heavily on repeating the same dungeons, waiting for world bosses, and grinding materials. There is not enough diverse content to keep players engaged long term, and the game needs more meaningful activities beyond the core loop.

Final Thoughts

Throne and Liberty — Great MMO foundation, but the endgame comes with baggage
Rating: ★★★☆☆ (3/5) | Verdict: Recommended (with caveats)

This is a good modern MMO with amazing presentation and a ton of content. I had a blast for the first 2–3 months, but the endgame leans hard into a daily/weekly checklist and eventually started feeling like a chore. PvP (especially siege/open world) is fun, but pay-to-win and guild dependence are real factors.

Pros
- Graphics are stunning
- Sound design is solid
- Strong setting with lots of distinct areas to explore and fight in
- Customization is awesome (weapons/armor combos + tons of skins)
- Tons of content (siege/open world PvP, arena PvP, PvE, dailies/weeklies, quests)
- Large community, easier to find a group if you look

Cons
- Endgame becomes a chore list (daily/weekly pressure) and that’s what made me quit/lose interest
- Not solo-friendly, you’ll have a much better time with a guild, and I wouldn’t start alone unless you plan to join one ASAP
- Pay-to-win gives a major advantage (enough that lighter-play P2W can beat heavy-play F2P, which isn’t ok)
- Toxicity exists (MMO reality)
- Story is very meh (standard MMO situation)

Best for: Guild/group players who want siege + open world PvP and don’t mind theme-park endgame structure.
Skip if: You want fair PvP, a relaxed endgame, or a solo-friendly MMO.

Bottom line: Worth trying (arena PvP is worth checking out now), but if you hate chore lists, you’ll probably burn out.

Even with guild play and PvP engagement, something about the overall experience just didn’t hook me long-term. That’s very much a matter of personal taste rather than a flaw in the game’s design.

If you enjoy large-scale MMOs, PvP-focused systems, and beautiful open-world exploration, this is worth trying. It just wasn’t the right fit for me, despite doing many things very well.
The art style is impressive; however, the characters’ behavior aligns more closely with East Asian social culture, which contrasts with the game’s Western setting.

However if you get a boss drop or gear in the world or if you want to wear it because it looks cooler; you cannot do so because it will be worse then what is given to you by developers. To use this gear you have to wait and invest in that gear until it is better then what you are wearing which takes time and resources. If you mistakenly got ride of tutorial gear or invested early and wore this newer cooler gear you set yourself behind and lock yourself out of Raid content and PVP matchmaking. 
If you want to take a weekend off and play a game this is not the game for you. If you want to play in a beautiful game with friends and do all the content together this is not for you; you have to wait for your friend because if you play and burn your resources and your friend didn't well no point in playing together now. I have been playing video games for over 40 years, going back all the way to the ColecoVision console. I have been playing MMORPGS's since 2004, World of Warcraft off course. With all that experience I can honestly tell you that Throne and Liberty is by far the most entertaining and addictive video game I have ever played. From the very beginning the game sucks you in and keeps you wanting more. The theory crafting system's in place are all design to keep you busy no matter how many times you log on. Every single day there is something new to learn as mixing different gear pieces and different character abilities and equipment all change the way you play. This in turn provides and endless amount of combinations on the power your character truly possess. 

A lot of folks will say that the game is P2W but believe me it is not. Yes, you can purchase armor and abilities with real. money via the auction house, however, this is only a benefit if you do not like grinding. Like every Korean mmorpg, Throne and Liberty requires a lot of grinding to strengthen your character. If you do not have the time to invest into the game and its multiple resources necessary to grow your characters power, you can, via the auction house, purchase many of these abilities and even some gear as well. Keep in mind, that everything in the AH was farmed by another player. NCSOFT and AGS DO NOT sell weapons and gear. You're simply paying other players for their time since you may not have enough of it to grind. 

In the end, after almost 200 hours invested, I have managed to get my character to Character Power 6700 without spending a single dollar. Obviously I play an average of 5-8 hours a day due to the fact that I have Cancer and this game provides the highest level of relaxation while I undergo rigorous treatments. I have sold that grind to the tune of 9,000 Lucent, the Auction House Currency, to other players who may not have that much time to invest. In the end, the game balances time with growth by allowing players to sell their time invested. 

I do not know anything about PvP in this game as I really don't enjoy PvP in any game. I hear mix things about it, but overall from what I have seen, it's pretty fun. 

Here is a short list of pros and Con based on my 200 hours of gameplay:

Pro:
1. Absolutely amazing graphics (Unreal Engine 5)
2. Incredibly moving soundtrack
3. One of the best Action Combat mmo's in the market
4. Endless combinations of abilities providing multiple ways to play
5. Highest level of immersion of any mmorpg in the market
6. Realistic weather, day/night cycle, and territory influence on both characters and enemy.

Cons:
1. Long grind for higher power
2. Endgame can be very punishing if not powerful enough
3. Learning curve can take some time
4. Only two characters per account allowed
5. Auction House can be very tempting when trying to avoid grinding
6. PvP is another game completely separated from PvE in both gear and abilities.
7. Very demanding graphics. Video Card will sound like a Jet Engine.  

Overall, in the 4 weeks I have been playing I have not been able to put the game down for longer then it takes to do treatments, sleep, and eat. The game is extremely addicting, at least for me. Since it is free, you will not regret trying it out. It looks next gen, so make sure you got the horsepower to run it if you want to truly see what it looks like.

Visually, it’s your typical Eastern MMO style—sometimes even reminiscent of Final Fantasy XIV. I only tried it after seeing a YouTube clip where you morph into an animal. Yes, you can, and if you’ve ever played a druid in World of Warcraft, the only difference is a smoother transition. Graphically, though, it’s far from the “Unreal Engine” wow factor.

Combat? Think ESO. Ranged weapons cut off if you’re a few steps too far, and button‑mashing feels like a newbie Death Knight in WoW. Add a layer of mobile gacha mechanics—daily rewards, random upgrade boxes, endless UI screens—and you’ve got the full package. Character options? Humans only (with optional cat eyes and spiky ears). Lip‑sync is off, voice files sometimes missing, and the “storyteller” randomly rehashes dialogue you just read.

The real problem: the writing. ESO’s story kept me hooked despite its flaws; here, the narrative nosedives from a passable tutorial into bland fetch‑and‑kill quests. If AI only handled translation, I almost wish it had written the story too.

Would I recommend it? Since it costs nothing, sure—if you’ve got no alternatives. Otherwise, play something better. Oh, and about thirty minutes in, you’re saddled with a permanent plushie companion whose face expressions are like a light-switch.

Throne & Liberty feels like a confused mix of MMO ideas that never fully come together. The game systems are unnecessarily fragmented, with progression split across weapon levels, traits, litography, codex entries, enchantments, and multiple currencies. None of it is explained well, making the early game feel like a chore instead of a learning curve.
Combat is functional but lacks depth, and the game heavily pushes you into group play. If you prefer playing solo, you will quickly fall behind. Even basic progression feels slow unless you join a guild or spend money on boosts. The game clearly leans toward a pay-to-progress model, even if not outright pay-to-win.
UI and menus are overcrowded, unintuitive, and often feel like they were designed without considering new players. Important features are buried under layers of tabs and submenus.
Overall, the game looks good and has potential, but the experience is frustrating, overwhelming, and unfriendly to anyone who is not already familiar with modern Korean MMO design. If you’re coming from classic RPGs or older MMOs, expect a steep and unpleasant adjustment.

A Player’s Opinion for Players – Thrones and Liberty

Thrones and Liberty is a fascinating game full of promise, carried by breathtaking environments, a polished artistic direction, and an absolutely incredible soundtrack that elevates every zone and greatly enhances immersion. The gameplay mechanics are enjoyable to handle, and while the story isn’t groundbreaking, it remains coherent overall. On paper, it’s an MMORPG that truly makes you want to dive deep into its world.

From the very first hours, you’re struck by the vastness of the map and the variety of dungeons, crypts, and zones shifting between PvE and PvP. The experience is dynamic and engaging at first, though the gameplay loop unfortunately becomes repetitive over time. Thankfully, the presence of numerous diverse guilds helps keep things fresh: you can choose to play casually with friends or commit to hardcore groups where “IRL first” quickly gets pushed aside.

However, despite its undeniable strengths, Thrones and Liberty suffers from several major issues. Castle captures completed without fighting through exploit abuse, an unusually high level of toxicity, hundreds of bots and cheaters pulling off “legendary parries” in PvP, and questionable class balance all weigh heavily on the overall experience.

To make matters worse, the business model leans dangerously toward pay-to-win, creating unfair progression gaps and discouraging players who simply want to advance at their own pace without reaching for their wallet. The situation has degraded to the point where, a year after launch, players practically have to queue as tanks if they want to access group content—because no one plays the role anymore. Meanwhile, healers like myself now wait over an hour just to enter a dungeon instance.

It’s particularly disappointing because I’ve spent nearly 1,000 hours in the game with friends and genuinely had great moments—though far fewer than some veterans. Thrones and Liberty had everything it needed to aim for a solid 10/10, but today, it struggles to reach more than a 3.5/10. 

L’avis d’un joueur pour des joueurs – Thrones and Liberty

Thrones and Liberty est un jeu fascinant, plein de promesses, porté par des environnements à couper le souffle, une direction artistique soignée, et une bande-son absolument incroyable qui sublime chaque zone et renforce l’immersion. Les mécaniques de gameplay sont agréables à prendre en main et, même si l’histoire n’a rien de révolutionnaire, elle reste globalement cohérente. Sur le papier, c’est un MMORPG qui donne vraiment envie d’être exploré en profondeur.

Dès les premières heures, on est frappé par l’immensité de la carte et la variété des donjons, cryptes et zones, alternant entre PvE et PvP. L’expérience est dynamique et engageante au début, même si la boucle de jeu finit malheureusement par devenir répétitive avec le temps. Heureusement, la présence de nombreuses guildes, très diversifiées, permet de varier les plaisirs : on peut jouer tranquillement entre amis, ou s’investir dans des groupes hardcore où le “IRL first” finit très vite relégué au second plan.

Cependant, malgré ses qualités indéniables, Thrones and Liberty souffre de problèmes majeurs. Les prises de château réalisées sans combattre en exploitant des failles, une toxicité omniprésente, des bots et des cheaters par centaines capables de sortir des “parades légendaires” en PvP, ainsi qu’un équilibrage des classes souvent discutable, viennent plomber l’expérience.

À cela s’ajoute un modèle économique qui glisse dangereusement vers le pay-to-win, créant des écarts de progression frustrants et décourageant les joueurs qui souhaitent simplement avancer à leur rythme sans passer par la caisse. La situation en arrive même à un point où, un an après la sortie, les joueurs sont pratiquement obligés de se taguer “tank” pour accéder au contenu de groupe — faute de joueurs dans ce rôle. Pendant ce temps, les healers comme moi attendent désormais plus d’une heure pour entrer en instance.

C’est d’autant plus regrettable que j’ai passé près de 1 000 heures sur le jeu avec des amis, et vécu de vrais bons moments — même si ce n’est rien comparé à certains passionnés. Thrones and Liberty avait toutes les cartes en main pour viser un solide 10/10, mais aujourd’hui, difficile de lui accorder plus qu’un 3,5/10.

Pro's and Cons

Pros: It's fun to play, pretty, and the open world dungeons are really neat. The enemy variety in game is great. Bosses and PVE content seem well designed. Loads of stuff to waste time on PVE wise. 

EVERYTHING is voiced over. The stories are... largely forgettable - but fun to follow along with nonetheless. World bosses, hidden areas, and a good amount of content, it has a lot going for it. 

Recently, they added a "Path of Ascension", which get's players pretty yoked (6000GS) by the end of it. This takes a lot of the grind out of the game, which is nice. Makes it fun. 

Castle Sieges are fun as hell if you're geared, It's like the entire server vs 1 guild, vs eachother and things get hectic. There really is no other pvp like it. 

Okay, so now that I've made the game sound like Emma Watson with D cups, let's get into the fact she doesn't shower, sleeps with people for money, and has a raging case of the clap. 

Cons: *deep breath* It can feel very buggy at times, Especially some of the jumping/morph/grappling hook things. When you get a few dozen players together, shit just performs poorly. 

This in and of itself would be forgivable - buuuuuut the auction house is a paid feature and this is where the cracks really show up. 

The player trading/Auction house is entirely handled in Lucent - the games premium in game currency. Throne and Liberty: A Promising MMO Undermined by Lockouts and Pay-to-Win Tactics

Throne and Liberty begins with a captivating premise, boasting an immersive world, compelling lore, and thrilling combat. However, this promising foundation is severely hampered by irritating mechanics, particularly lockouts and pay-to-win (P2W) elements, which detract from the authentic MMO experience players crave.

The game initially lures players with a world brimming with adventure. The combat is dynamic, and the expansive world offers ample opportunities for exploration, quests, and group activities. The game's potential is undoubtedly enticing.

However, beneath the surface, it becomes clear that the game is engineered to encourage spending over genuine gameplay. Lockouts, which restrict content access on a daily or weekly basis, are a significant issue. It's frustrating to encounter a barrier after a few hours of play, realizing that further progress or access to certain features requires waiting for reset timers or, worse, paying to bypass the wait. This artificially extends playtime and constrains the enjoyment within a session.

The pay-to-win (P2W) mechanics further exacerbate this issue. While MMOs typically offer microtransactions for cosmetic items, Throne and Liberty goes a step further by providing powerful in-game advantages for a price. From paying to skip timers to purchasing top-tier gear, it's evident that the game prioritizes player spending over their time. This imbalance favors paying players, leaving those who opt not to spend at a severe disadvantage, unable to compete with those who invest money for advantages.

Perhaps most disappointing is that Throne and Liberty feels more like a monetization scheme than a game. Instead of creating engaging content that rewards skill, strategy, and player investment, the game forces players into a cycle of either paying to skip tedious tasks or being locked out of progress.

In summary, Throne and Liberty has the potential to be a great MMO, but its focus on lockouts and pay-to-win mechanics ultimately undermines this potential. For players who value fair play, skill-based progression, and a sense of achievement, this game will be a source of frustration. Unfortunately, it appears that the developers prioritize monetization over delivering a quality, player-first MMORPG experience.

This game had potential, but there are far too many negatives to give this a positive review.
Firstly, it's buggy & laggy (at times, but those times are often). The updates are not well tested and often break parts of the game, usually not fixed for several days and resulting in additional downtime (I am writing this during another one of those times - the 3rd time this week).
The play limitations are very annoying (and are made to maintain value of their premium currency); there are a few specific ways to move forward with your character progression, all of which are limited by several in game tokens/currencies which refresh slowly over the course of a week. To give an example of how this works: Do you want to get new gear (or traits for your gear)? Do a dungeon, but you can only get rewards once per day (with the refresh cycle of tokens). Do you want to level up your gear or mastery? Do open world dungeons, which require tokens primarily granted from dungeons, and have a limited time you actually get rewards from it. It prevents people from playing too much and deprives them of the choice of how spend their time in game, all to mitigate impact to their monetization strategy.
Now their premium currency (lucent).. that's interesting. Everything you want to buy or sell is done using their premium currency (which means you can pay to win) - however, you're limited to how much you can earn. I'll explain with another example: want to make lucent? Sell items/traits. Want to sell items/traits? Use trait unlock stones. Want trait unlockstones? You can only buy a certain amount by week with another currency gained by doing quests. Also, you can only completed limited quests per day (5).
Essentially, the game is an interconnected web of grinding that is purposely made slow by the developers with small incremental impacts to your characters power. 
Pay for Convenience is a little annoying. Spend about a week grinding lucent to buy Davinci Blessing, and for the next 4 weeks you can spend your activity tokens (e.g. dungeons, open world dungeons, quests) twice as fast.
Same idea with Battle Passes, it's about 1 week worth of lucent grind to get a 30 day battle pass that grants you rewards that are so useful you can't "not" buy it. Then you need to do several side-quests daily & weekly, forcing you to engage in content that you may not enjoy, like Fishing/Cooking.
Oh yeah, there are weekly rewards that require you to engage with different kinds of content. For this weekly reward and battle pass, if you go to the Lawless Isle (Nebula Island) and step off the portal platform, you'll find a dozen players afking to get their obligatory 2-4 hours spent in that zone to complete the weekly/battle pass quest.

Now some positive elements (I mean, there must be some if I played for several hundred hours.. right?).
The combat, abilities, creating builds - it's fun. They have built in systems like Item Sync to allow you to play around with different equipment builds. You can move your class/skill & ability progression to another by using vouchers earned from Battle Passes (albeit not often).
I'm not a fan of PvP in this game, it's very "rock/paper/scissors" with very little balance. Example: the "meta" is critical damage, so the counter is stacking Endurance & % critical damage reduction. Or one ranged class is dominating in PvP, so people counter by stacking Ranged Evasion to mitigate the hits the land. It's not skill, it's luck & "strategic engagement" (if that were really possible).
Dungeons are decent, however there is a lot of unecessary "puzzle" mechanics during the boss fights. Example: arena gets divided into purple/yellow colors, players can't move across the border or they get damaged constantly. The boss throws a ball at one side, a player has to "catch" the ball while facing the opposite colors side and "throw" the ball for a player on the opposite side to "catch". Then they get a magic tether which they have keep lined up on the boss to break their shield, otherwise the mechanic might insta-kill the group. It's adding complexity for it's own sake, rather than difficulty or making engaging content.

I digress... if you've read this and feel like you'll enjoy the game, check it out. There is some fun to be had, it is a bit addictive - but it is also frustrating.. often.
I guess I'll check if they've fixed the issues causing downtime on a Friday evening, but I doubt it.

I really have enjoyed the game.

Throne and Liberty lays down a strong foundation, especially for large-scale PvP. Its Guild vs. Guild and siege systems are well-implemented, offering organized and satisfying conflict on a grand scale. The story is enjoyable and does a good job introducing the player to the world, its mechanics, and various systems without feeling overwhelming. Group Finders also work surprisingly well, making the early social experience smoother than in many MMOs.

Mechanically, the game feels solid. Core systems—from combat flow to progression and encounter design—are well thought out, even if some elements could run smoother or feel better tuned. Boss and dungeon fights show variety and creativity, though not all mechanics are well telegraphed, which can lead to a few frustrating moments. Overall, it’s clear that Throne and Liberty has been built on a sturdy mechanical base.

Unfortunately, there simply isn’t enough content yet to keep players engaged for long. The endgame world feels small, and with only three dungeons and a single raid, repetition sets in quickly. The daily grind doesn’t help, and the content loop wears thin faster than expected. Personally, I found myself running out of motivation after about a week—the framework is there, but there’s not enough to sustain long-term commitment.

Combat is fast—Black Desert Online–fast—and while that intensity has its appeal, it may not suit everyone. The game also heavily rewards winners: the best-geared players get the best rewards, which widens the gap between top and average players and encourages spending to stay competitive.

Adding to this, Throne and Liberty’s somewhat less successful launch has unfortunately branded it as “bad” in the eyes of many MMO veterans. That stigma lingers despite clear signs of improvement—the developers have fixed, refined, and rebalanced many systems since release. Still, the game needs continued investment, content expansion, and community rebuilding to reach its full potential.

In the end, Throne and Liberty is a title with great mechanical depth, strong PvP foundations, and a fair early-game experience. With more content and long-term developer commitment, it could evolve into something genuinely special—but for now, it feels like a solid framework waiting for its defining moment.

Pros
+ Well-implemented core mechanics and solid technical framework
+ Strong Guild vs. Guild and siege warfare systems
+ Engaging story that introduces systems effectively
+ Functional Group Finder helps early social play
+ Player- and guild-focused progression that rewards teamwork
+ Fair weekly caps balance casual and hardcore pacing

Cons:
- Too little content to support long-term engagement
- Endgame feels small and repetitive, with limited PvE options
- Some mechanics aren’t clearly telegraphed, leading to frustration
- Fast time-to-kill may turn off some players
- Winner-takes-all rewards widen the gap and push pay-to-progress
- Lingering negative perception from launch still affects community growth

Final Thought
Throne and Liberty has the framework of a good MMO, but not yet the substance of one worth committing to. Its solid mechanics and PvP systems show potential, yet the lack of meaningful content and dated design make it hard to recommend at this stage. Unless you’re deeply curious or just passing through, it’s best to wait and see if future updates can turn potential into staying power.

My favorite feature of all time from this game is the morphing feature, you have dash, swim, and glide. The map is quite large, and if you have a beefy PC you’ll be able to take in how beautiful it is as well, it’s hard finding MMO’s out there that have equally a good story line but also equally appealing to the eye. As a pro cut scene skipper, I will say the storyline of this game sucks you in pretty quick and I was surprised of how many times I’ve caught myself actually sitting through the cut scenes through and through. 

The combat mechanics aren’t half bad though could use improvement, I feel as though the blocking mechanics are essentially useless unless you have your keys mapped out specifically but even then it’s pretty tricky, you go through skills like water if your not strategic and depending on what you use your skill points on it can take a fat minute for each of them to recharge. I don’t like the cooldown for the potions, it’s too long and sometimes when used prematurely it can be fatal to your gameplay experience with certain bosses. 

Now on the other hand is the player base.. not bad when I got this game it was mostly negative because of how toxic the players were, they’ve gotten better but it’s pretty easy to find yourself alone throughout the game and the chances of finding reliable help in a party matchmaking are pretty low. Sometimes I’ve found myself better off alone as most just get in the way. 

I urge everyone who looks at this game and sees this review to atleast give it a try, I’ve put this game down at first thinking it was dog sh**, but I was very pleased to stand corrected, this game has the potential to become something other MMO’s haven’t achieved yet, I just hope the dev’s see that and use that potential correctly, I think we’ve all seen quite a few games go down the drain due to crappy dev’s.

Essa é minha análise sobre o jogo. Basicamente, tenho tentado achar um novo jogo para mim, e o TL não será esse jogo por enquanto. Afinal, a otimização do game não é das melhores, e meu PC também não ajuda.

Curto mais jogos de action, mas o combate do jogo é bem gostoso. Achei meio lento e cadenciado. Falta a liberdade que um Black Desert me daria e é um pouco injusto comparar, já que são propostas diferentes, mas é só para exemplificar.

I have played most of the lineage games since their original release, with a group of close friends so it's been like 20+ years. I got tired of the franchise eventually and have been playing other games but my friends were so excited when TL came out. Anyway, I joined to play with them but objectively speaking, I don't think TL is a game I would recommend.

The main gripe I have with it is two-fold:

1 - Game development and vision:
The intentional choice and design to constantly make strong people stronger to create a gap between players to incentivize money spending is the questionable side of the game for me. Key features like field / world boss, content release of legendary / new tiers and the "release new content, add 10 packs to the in-game shop" mentality makes it clear that the only thing devs care about is money. You may or may not enjoy the content of the game, regardless, I am doubtful that things will change given how they have been handled this year. I understand this is free to play, and people don't be working for free, but there are better ways to monetize your game without creating a toxic community.

2 - Game maintenance and overall health.
Weekly maintenance and new content patches often break game functionality. Some things are addressed after days, some after weeks, and some are still broken months later. One good example is the matchmaking system: sometimes it works, sometimes you can't join other people; sometimes people don't see you after joining so you have to disband and make a new party. Sometimes dungeon matchmaker works but raid mm is broken. Sometimes the mm just doesn't work at all and you have to join through party board and look for a party manually. Most of the time it is just broken until the following week things are not addressed at all. There are also game breaking exploits which aren't fixed until weeks later; to mention a few from the past year: dimensional trials boss exploits, world boss item duplicates, hyperboost inter-server world boss loot hijacking, etc.

Overall, the game can be fun if you play with friends, but the repetitive gameplay and monetization model are something you need to be aware of. I played Lineage 2 for a long time; the grind was much worse back then and we also had boss loot which sold for real $$$ but the high risk / high reward open pvp servers brought something different to the game. TL right now is barely different from a mobile cash grab android MMO; if you haven't started yet, I just wouldn't.

Throne and Liberty – Looks Great, Plays Meh

Throne and Liberty is a gorgeous game with epic music and stunning visuals. But once you get past the surface, things start to fall apart.

Gameplay
• 	Combat and mechanics are just okay—not bad, but nothing special.
• 	Crafting is boring and doesn’t feel rewarding.
• 	The class system is weak. Roles are kind of blurry—not as messy as Blade & Soul or Lost Ark, but nowhere near as solid as Lineage 2 or Final Fantasy XIV.

Monetization
• 	You can technically access everything, but good luck getting the cosmetics you want without spending real money.
• 	The trading system? Easily one of the worst in any MMO. It’s clunky and frustrating.
Polish
• 	Lots of dialogue isn’t even voiced, which kills immersion.
• 	For a company that made Guild Wars 2, Lineage 2, and Aion, this feels like a major step down.

Final Verdict
Beautiful world, great music—but the systems underneath are half-baked. If you’re looking for deep gameplay or fair progression, this one might disappoint.

The most disappointing aspect, however, is that Throne and Liberty feels less like a game and more like a service designed to extract money from players. Instead of designing engaging content that rewards skill, strategy, and time invested, the game constantly pushes players into a cycle of either paying to skip tedious elements or being locked out of progress.

In conclusion, Throne and Liberty has the potential to be a great MMO, but it is ultimately ruined by its focus on lockouts and pay-to-win mechanics. If you’re a player who values fair play, progression based on effort, and a sense of achievement, this game will leave you frustrated. Sadly, it seems like the developers are more focused on monetizing the experience than delivering a quality, player-first MMORPG.

Lastly, I would say the game has a strong emphasis on Guilds. They are a group of people that will protect you in the conflict zones, and also feature a lot of objectives to tackle together as a group. Guild Contracts are your standard "quests" that you do with them, and doing them levels the guild up to unlock perks and benefits. Then there is the Guild Raids, which are instanced fights of the world bosses.

In summary, I think Throne and Liberty is a game that improves upon the design of old school MMOs, but it might not resonate well with a modern audience. People expecting a coherent story are probably better off playing FFXIV or ESO, and people just looking to run dungeons and raids are better off playing WoW. That being said, I think the game has enough potential to carve its own niche with the Guild vs Guild and gear farming community. If you enjoy killing monsters for the chance of a rare drop that you can later sell for cash shop currency or use yourself, then this might be the game for you.

At over 100 hours so far, its fair to say its time for a review. 

Where Winds Meet is a game about menus. Jokes aside, it feels amazing to play. Take the vast open world with multiple POIs popularized by The Witcher, add optional multiplayer modes, add multiple slice of life wuxia activities, stealth resembling modern Assassins Creed titles, boss design reminiscent of a souls-like, guilds, crafting, martial arts, and so much more, and you have Where Winds Converge. There are tons of menus tracking literally everything you can do: most of these menus are not actually needed. The game gives you every single possible option to track your progress and find things to do, but you dont actually need to interact with most of them. Where Breezes Intersect honestly has very little flaws. Now, you might say, "Oh, there's a cash shop AND a gacha system", but here's the kicker: the shop and gacha system is purely for cosmetics. Yes, the cosmetics are visually stunning, but also lean heavily into the fantasy aspect of wuxia, and less so the accurate parts: think massive fire effects, glowing armors, etc. The last big hurdle is the size. Now, rumor has it it will be shrunk, but as it stands, its a massive 200GB of storage. 

Gaming has been tough the past couple of years: there's just too many great games being released. This is one of them. Look, for the low price of FREE (and 200GB of storage), you get a game that EASILY meets AAA standards for a... kitchen-sink style adventure action solo-but-with-optional-co-op-and-multiplayer RPG/Slice-of-Life/Exploration Wuxia/Cultivation/Ancient-China game.

Look, this game is like All the Mods for Minecraft: massive in both storage and content, with far too much to do.

I'm someone who almost never writes reviews, but I just had to make an exception for this special game.

I'm a returning player who originally started playing when the game launched, but ended up quitting after about a month. Back then, the game felt clunky, lacked variety, and just wasn't very engaging to me.

Now, almost a year later, I decided to give it another chance before the anniversary, and I have to say, I'm genuinely impressed by how much it has improved.

Yes, the core mechanics are still the same. It's an open-world game that you can enjoy in both single-player and multiplayer, but the gameplay has improved significantly. They've added new weapons, martial arts, bosses, and just so much more to do in general.

But what impressed me the most are the new maps. At launch, I found the first two maps a little boring and basic, but the newer ones are absolutely amazing. They're beautiful, distinct, and genuinely fun to explore. The difference in quality is honestly incredible.

Another thing that has improved significantly is the voice acting and translations. Both feel much more polished than they did at launch, and the story itself has also gotten a lot better, making the overall experience much more engaging and enjoyable.

A lot has also been added to multiplayer, although I haven't had the chance to dive too deeply into that side of the game yet.

Overall, it's a really good game, and the fact that it's completely free makes it even better. There's no pay-to-win system, with monetization focused on cosmetics instead.

I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a massive, constantly evolving fantasy adventure. Whether you're a new player or someone who gave up on it early like I did, it's absolutely worth giving it a chance.
