The ultimate wuxia fantasy sandbox MMO with Soulslike combat, an enormous open world, and plenty of freedom to explore. If you can look past the ridiculously exploitative cash shop, you're going to have a fantastic time.

Fortunately, the game isn't pay-to-win, and combat is largely skill-based, meaning your ability to fight actually matters more than how much money you're willing to throw at the game.

However, the monetization is where things start getting absolutely ridiculous. The developers use the **"we're a free-to-play game"** excuse as a scapegoat to justify charging ridiculous amounts of money for cosmetics, including outfits, hairstyles, and even hair colors.

While the cash shop primarily focuses on cosmetics, the way it's implemented is incredibly exploitative. Imagine Black Desert Online's monetization, except cranked up to 100.

There are around **12 different in-game currencies**, including premium currencies tied to cosmetics and gacha mechanics with ridiculously low drop rates.

That's right... **Drop rates.**

You're lucky to get even a single Harmonic Core after 100 pulls on what is essentially a gambling mechanic. Some outfits and mounts have drop rates as low as **0.0415%**, meaning you could potentially spend hundreds or even thousands of dollars trying to obtain something you actually want.

Not even Genshin Impact feels this bad!

And what's worse is that even when you finally get a rare drop, the developers fill the reward pool with a bunch of useless items that can share the same rarity as desirable outfits or hairstyles. It's absolutely ridiculous.

I mean, seriously, the fact that a fictional boat can potentially cost **$40,000 or more through gacha mechanics** is absolutely disgusting, especially when a game like BDO allows you to obtain a boat completely for free through normal gameplay.

It just makes me sick because underneath all that unnecessary monetization is a genuinely fantastic game with an incredible amount of content. The combat is satisfying, the world is beautiful, and there's an impressive amount of freedom in how you approach the game.

Despite my complaints, I still highly recommend it. I've already sunk nearly **460 hours** into the game, which should tell you just how much I've enjoyed it.

See, the game ties switching between weapons (something very important for certain quests, to the point where you can get soft-locked without the ability to do so) to the scroll wheel on a mouse. For most players, I'm sure this is fine. Completely inconsequential even. But as a player who doesn't have a mouse, and thus doesn't have a scroll wheel, and thus doesn't have access to the very important feature of *switching from one weapon to another*, it made the game mostly unplayable. As far as I am aware, there was no way to change the keybindings for the switching of weapons, so I was ultimately forced to drop the game. A shame, really, since it meant I played Where Winds Meet for less time than I waited for it to download, but what can you do? (And that's without mentioning the egregious file size lol)

That being said, the game wasn't all bad. The graphics were brilliant! And the little part of the story that I got to see was also very intriguing. So if you're interested in playing the game and aren't going to be impacted by the keybinding issue, or the file size, then I don't see why you shouldn't play it. Just a shame that I won't be able to enjoy it too.

not gonna lie... I downloaded this as soon as I heard there was a good character creation system. I'm a doll artist, so naturally I had to test it. I was not disappointed. Wow. genuinely WOW. Not sure why this isn't mentioned much in other reviews, but I was absolutely blown away by the customizability. While there seems to only be a single hair color (which I don't really mind), the amount of eye types is insane (I went for a more modest pupil, but you can have heart or cat eyes if you'd like). Yeah, the amount of sliders might be a bit overwhelming... but having so many offers a ton of fine-tuning. I could spend hours upon hours perfecting my character (as I have in many other games) but amazingly, I created a character I genuinely like in under an hour. And the best part? SHE LOOKS THE SAME IN-GAME! This is literally the first time I've experienced this, so it is definitely worth noting.

Unfortunately I crashed before spending too long experiencing the open world (my own fault. I decided to test the limits of my computer and it obviously couldn't handle everything on ultra, lol).

However, I think I saw enough for a review - to those who haven't played and are pixel/poly snobs like me:
On low graphics, this game is still gorgeous. It runs incredibly smooth even during combat. I don't know how I feel about the UI or interactions yet... kinda don't like them tbh. But I'm an oldschool MMORPG player so that's probably just the old-timer in me.

200gb is a lot... but honestly...? these days, many games are close to this size. It's unfortunate but kinda to be expected.
I can see myself coming back to this one - when I'm not playing events in my favorite games. However, I doubt Id ever spend money on it. Though I saw a ton of quality content that looked freaking AMAZING.. it's simply not my style or aesthetic. I would honestly love to see more furs and genuine armor type cosmetics (nothing too pretty, especially for female players), and I do love that none of the cosmetics are super revealing (please keep it that way).

The story seems genuinely good, but hasn't hooked me quite yet. I love the little girl and that the main character and her are clearly close. I cannot wait to build (at level 25, apparently)! Hoping that aspect of the game is not a disappointment. I LOVE to build in games (or even sketchup)! If the building aspects of this game are decent, I might just make "Where Winds Meet" my new favorite.

I also laughed [way too loudly; woke my kid up] at the goose, kite, and "fleet foot" mounts. Clearly the devs have a sense of humor, which I love.

If you've got the space for it, I definitely think you should give "Where Winds Meet" a try. I can see this game going far.

If you'd like to use 200 GB of space on your drive to spend hours walking 6-7 steps (not a joke, I counted) to go from one cutscene (written and directed by ChatGPT) to another, and occasionally pressing G to follow someone while they talk to you between cutscenes, then this uninteractive movie might be for you. 

Sometimes the game forces you to click a box during a cutscene, and generally there is literally just one box to click. Sometimes there are multiple boxes, but they will always lead to the same outcome. For example, the closest the game got to allowing me to make a choice was picking an option to fight instead of taking a pill, at which point 3 invulnerable guards attacked and 1shot me. This immediately triggering a cutscene in which I swallowed the pill while complaining about it.

To be fair, there are some instances of combat with enemies that can take damage, which consist of you spamming leftclick and Q (as well as tapping E or F when the game tells you to). However, you generally have to sit through at least 10 cutscenes between each such instance (and sometimes up to 30, again I counted).

You can also choose to explore "freely" if you get tired of watching cutscenes, I did this for a while and had some fun cutting bamboo and fighting some random enemies that spawn on the map. You can't travel too far though, however, since the game will literally teleport you backwards while telling you that you have to finish a quest.

This also one of those gacha games with a billion menus (with sub-menus) that you'll be drawn to through red notification dots to claim insignificant rewards. The point of this is literally just to show (and then remind) you of the gacha-cosmetics that you can unlock by paying money.

Finally, the multiplayer might as well not exist while leveling, since only the host progresses their story and unlocks things if you choose to play co-op. This is on top of the fact that the other player will also occasionally be booted out of the game, since some content is solo-only. 

Overall, I think I had more fun during the hours I spent downloading the game when compared to the ones I spent actually "playing" it, since I didn't have to spend that time sitting through the AI-generated dialogues that the game mostly consists of.

I would very much recommend this game. 

[b]Story:[/b]
I think the story elements of this game are generally beautiful, though sometimes the narrative can feel a little one-dimensional due to its recurring themes. It may also feel a bit foreign to audiences who aren't used to Asian cultural norms, but overall it presents an immersive, high-quality narrative experience.  

[b]Combat & Gameplay:[/b]
The combat is really good. It pushes the player on higher difficulties enough that defeating bosses feels like a meaningful achievement, while still giving room for casual players to grow or enjoy the boss battles as a cinematic experience. 

However, where I feel this game falls short is that it tries to be an MMO and a single-player experience at the same time. The problem is that the scope of MMO-style content—such as raids or group activities—is nowhere near as engaging or incentivized as industry titans like FFXIV or WoW. The tight combat you experience in single-player becomes a somewhat cluttery mess of visual spectacles and awkward encounters in group content that will test your patience. Furthermore, the social aspects can feel slightly intrusive, as the game tries to push players toward certain activities in a way that may not appeal to everyone. 

[b]Interface:[/b]
While the UI design is decent, the sheer volume of elements can feel jarring. At times, finding specific info about certain objectives is difficult to navigate. The biggest shortcoming in design is its social interface—the chat system isn't fluid, and navigating through social chats to find specific sections on the go can feel like a real challenge.

[b]Monetization:[/b]
The monetization will feel very generous if you aren't heavily into cosmetics, but very expensive otherwise. Yes, it is strictly a free-to-play experience with progression that isn't gated behind pay-to-win mechanics at all, but compared to other live-service games in this genre, the pricing of cosmetic items is quite stiff.

[b]Visuals:[/b]
The graphics quality is fairly good; areas and maps are often spectacular enough to rival any AAA experience available on the market.

[b]Final Verdict:[/b]
* As a Single-Player Game: 8.5/10
* As a Multiplayer Game: 7/10

I've really been enjoying Where Winds Meet so far! The graphics are absolutely stunning, and the world is beautifully designed, making exploration and questing an incredibly immersive experience. The attention to detail, atmosphere, and overall aesthetics are fantastic!

One of the first things that amazed me was the Character Creation. The customisation options are superb and offer an immense amount of freedom to create a character exactly how you envision them. The gear designs and appearances are equally impressive, with so many beautiful options to choose from. In general, the game's visual presentation is outstanding!

The Combat System is another highlight! The animations, skill effects, and fighting styles are visually spectacular, making battles exciting and satisfying. Combat feels dynamic, and the variety of abilities adds another layer of depth to the experience.

The UI, menus, and Game Settings are generally clear and well organised, and the tutorials do a good job of introducing players to the game's mechanics. However, I do think the sheer number of systems, features, and options can feel a little overwhelming at first. There's quite a lot to learn, understand, and remember, especially when you're just getting started. Fortunately, once you become familiar with everything, the different systems are relatively easy to navigate and follow.

I particularly enjoy the amount and balance of Main Quests, Side Quests, Exploration, and Collection Activities. There's always something interesting to discover or work towards, and the game offers a wonderful sense of freedom. Whether you enjoy following the story, exploring the world at your own pace, collecting items, or taking on more challenging activities, there's plenty to keep you entertained.

With dungeons, PvE, PvP, and a wide variety of other activities, the game caters to different playstyles. I especially love that it offers so much content for solo players while also providing opportunities to team up and enjoy the experience with others.

Another aspect worth mentioning is the Community! My interactions with other players have been genuinely enjoyable, and the overall atmosphere feels friendly, lively, and fun. It definitely adds to the experience!

The Storyline, Storytelling, and Cinematic Presentation are also fantastic. The cutscenes are beautifully executed and really help bring the characters, events, and world to life. The combination of storytelling, visuals, and atmosphere makes it easy to become invested in the adventure.

Overall, Where Winds Meet has been a fantastic experience so far! It combines stunning visuals, engaging combat, extensive character customisation, immersive storytelling, and an impressive variety of activities. While the number of systems can initially feel overwhelming, the experience becomes much more intuitive once you've familiarised yourself with them.

I particularly appreciate the freedom to explore and enjoy the game at my own pace, without feeling restricted to one specific way of playing.

Definitely recommended! Especially for players who love beautiful open worlds, immersive storytelling, martial arts combat, character customisation, and having plenty of different activities to explore, whether alone or with friends!

Where Winds Meet is genuinely an amazing game. The in-game shop mainly offers cosmetics, mounts, and similar items, without selling anything that makes you stronger than other players. It's refreshing to see a game like this. And that should honestly be the norm... But one can dream!

One thing worth mentioning is that it's not fully multiplayer. You have an open-world map where you can see other players, but there isn't a huge amount to do together in the open world itself, aside from a few activities. Most PvP and PvE content takes place in instances, so you'll either need to group up with friends (guildmates, anyone?!) or use the matchmaking tools provided by the game.

The story can be a little difficult to follow at times, especially as a European unfamiliar with some of the cultural references. But you get used to it. Like any game, it has its highs and lows, but Where Winds Meet has genuinely broken my heart and made me laugh. It's one of those games where you eventually realize that you need to be ready for the emotional roller coaster.

Gameplay-wise, there's honestly not much to complain about. There's a ton of exploration, loads of side content, and the developers keep adding more and more to the game. We recently got a new martial art, and I'm still waiting for hidden weapons. The Tang Clan dream is still alive!

Anyway, highly recommended. Whether you're here for exploration, combat, the story, or PvP, there's plenty to keep you busy. And for a free-to-play game, that's pretty incredible.

[h3]tl;dr[/h3]
A gorgeous, challenging action RPG blending Sekiro and Elden Ring within a rich Chinese historical and mythological setting. It functions primarily as a solo/co-op adventure rather than a traditional MMO. Incredibly, it is completely free with zero pay-to-win mechanics and cosmetics-only monetization. It respects your time by avoiding heavy grinds, offering high technical depth, and delivering top-tier value.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]Review:[/h3]
Where Winds Meet accomplishes what few modern AAA releases manage, let alone free-to-play titles. The monetization model is entirely non-predatory, strictly limited to cosmetics without locking player power, convenience, or progression behind paywalls. The sheer volume and standard of content rival full-price major studio releases, making the value proposition difficult to overstate.

The core gameplay loop centers on highly responsive, kinetic movement and a parry-driven combat system. Rather than the heavier, deliberate input-buffering framework found in traditional Souls-likes, Where Winds Meet opts for a fluid, momentum-based choreography reminiscent of Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. Boss encounters on higher difficulties demand rigorous pattern recognition and precise deflection timing, delivering a high-reward sense of mastery without feeling mechanically sluggish or unrefined.

For players balancing a demanding work schedule, the game’s pacing is a standout feature. Unlike live-service titles or traditional MMORPGs that often pad playtime with mandatory time-gating, repetitive daily quests, or artificial material grinds, Where Winds Meet keeps progression tied purely to player skill and technical execution. Patch cycles deliver concise, substantial story beats and new content drops that allow players to stay engaged without turning the hobby into a second job.

Between the responsive combat, thoughtful world design, and developer transparency evidenced by frequent quality-of-life updates and hidden mini-games, Where Winds Meet sets a high benchmark for the genre. It is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for deep, skill-based action without the usual predatory monetization or exhausting time sinks.

I had a conversation with a friend on Discord recently about Where Winds Meet and they asked my thoughts on it, so instead of a standard review I'm just going to post that reply here:

Saebin — 22:26
I think "Online RPG" describes Where Winds Meet accurately. Kinda like the original Guild Wars. Online, but you actually can ignore that element almost entirely and choose not to interact with it. It's not unheard of, just kind of rare in more well-known games or games that have/had a budget behind them.

Overall to me it's built like a mobile game in terms of it's sub-menus and sub-systems (Maybe even worse). The gameplay and story are solid up until endgame, delivering exactly on what the game sells itself as and shows in trailers. You can do just about anything in this game, even pretty much fly and ontop of that even build. However, the wild and over the top eastern mythology here at play and the story is what will keep most invested and wanting to continue playing in the end.

There is a currency limitations in Where Winds Meet (WWM) and I believe the currency limitation actively holds back WWM since players cannot do things at their own pace - this is probably done to create a returning playerbase more than anything, but that strategy is likely to also see players leave like I did in the end. It's a fun game at least worth checking out since it's free, but, if you do reach endgame you'll find very little reason to stay when you ask yourself "What am I actually doing this for?" because the answer to that is "Just to see larger numbers in a mostly singleplayer experience." or "Just to unlock a hard to obtain skill that'll just increase my numbers slightly and change part of my rotation and style in combat for a bit." and those novelties wear off pretty quickly in a mostly singleplayer adventure when you're done with the storylines and the mystery of exploration and learning new mechanics.

While I do recommend the game, I don't think it's worth keeping installed once you're "Done" due to the significant amount of real estate it demands from a hard drive (Nearly 200gb), especially when you are limited in currency gains which you don't truly feel until endgame. So to me... It's a one and done game.

[Overview]

I'm not gonna act like it's a flawless game. A lot of the cons others are listing are accurate, even if some may feel disingenuous. That said, I feel like the Pros still outweigh the cons. I'll start listing them both and let you make your own choice based on these. 

[Pros] 

1. Free to play game with no pay-to-win.
2. The only Microtransactions are purely aesthetic - clothing, fashion, etc
3. 10/10 Beautiful Graphics and Background scenery. Too beautiful to not be immersed in.
4. You can change the time - and in some areas the season - of the setting you're in. Speaking of which...
5. The game gives you your own world similar to games like Genshin Impact and Wuthering Waves, but with way better features compared to when those games started out.
6. Best/Most Detailed facial character creation settings in gaming history to date.
7. Gives you at least a dozen different fun ways to traverse the world you're in; from riding different kinds of mounts to literally flying and gliding.
8. Also gives you countless ways to make resource gathering/management fun.
9. GOATed Wuxia-style story for your main character.
10. Souls-like Combat Mechanics - stamina (endurance) bar, rewarding deflects, dodges, perfect dodges, stagger meters (Qi bar), powerful 'magic' abilities (Mystic Skills), Executes, etc.
11. Despite this, it allows you to choose the difficulty of content in your own world. Not something souls-like games allow. If you personally want hardcore content, the game has that available too.
12. Recently introduced a system to help newer players get caught up faster to veteran players. 
13. Low-stress grind systems with limits and weekly limits rather than the seamingly endless grinds from games like Warframe or FF14. 
14. Playerbase is a mixed bag of hostile and friendly, but from my experience, it's been 70% more friendly... when you ignore the wild world chat at least. 
15. The game allows you to join fun Sects/Factions that usually help other players determine what kind of player you are. Highly advised you look into these before choosing. 
16. Like most Chinese games, it does have gacha elements, but the paid gacha system is strictly for fashion. 
17. The game highly supports PvP and PVE modes. PvE is super fun for people that like team-based fights against bosses like me.
18. PvP, while full of issues, is still almost addicting to do anyway even when you know you may lose a fight.
19. The game has a lot of different PvP modes. Even allowing for 30v30 combat. 
20.  The various systems (gear, inner ways, mystic skills, etc.) while they 'seem' complex, are actually very easy and simple to understand. 
21.  The game allows you to bounty hunt and be bounty hunted (the latter usually done if you choose to commit crimes in your world like murder or theft).
22.  The game lets you form marital partnerships. For those that care, same sex marriages are also a thing. 
23.  If you join the Velvet Shade Sect, you can have a whole harem of up to 5 partners (with some strings attached of course if they choose to divorce you).

[Cons]
1. The Gacha and Fashion, when purchased normally, are somewhat expensive. Especially so for gacha. An outfit with glowing effects or special VIP victory animations could cost you several hundreds if it's gacha. And that's with guaranteed rolls/pity. There are some methods involved to make it cheaper though.
2. Multiplayer content, especially PvP, is extremely ping reliant. If your ping or upload speed is poor, even with the game's official ping booster (GearUp), you may find yourself struggling horribly in PvP scenarios. 
3. PvP is very unbalanced with builds revolving around tenacity being the absolute meta. 
4. There are a lot of menus. Easy to navigate, but still A LOT of menus. 
5. The game has two versions; a CN-only version and a Global Release (this one). Sometimes, with the lingering issues we have had since season 0, it feels like the devs care more about their CN counterpart than the Global. Some of which I'm about to describe.
6. The game, especially in very congested multiplayer modes, have a lot of lag when simply trying to roam about. This I suspect is more of an Unreal Engine issue than a WWM one, but it's still noticeable enough to ruin immersion at times. 
7. Controller gameplay in the game is fun, but there are fixes and input lag issues with it that the game needs to fix. 
8. Sometimes, in congested PvP modes with 12+ players, players won't properly load on your screen. When they perform certain ranged attacks, for example, they might not be immediately visible on your screen. 
9. Some Sects, particularly Velvet Shade, actually require you to look as fashionable as possible if you want to excel in them. This is due to player voting-related systems passively created by the game. 
10. The game needs more PvE group fight Modes. Modes that don't have an energy system or only exist as temporary events. 
11. If you avoid joining a guild, or avoid multiplayer content entirely, build optimization will become much slower. Optimally getting the best gear requires team-based battles that cost energy. 
12. If playing solo and grinding as a newer player, it can be a bit more challenging for players that prefer solo mode. 
13. A lot of issues are [allegedly] not being fully fixed until the game catches up with the CN version. But that version is still leaps and bounds ahead of us in content so real fixes could take at most a year. At minimum 6-8 months. Alas this is purely speculation. It could take longer or shorter. 

Overall though, I still feel the game is absolutely worth playing, but only if you're willing to be patient and spend at least 1-3 months catching up with other players.

Where Winds Meet is the wuxia game I have been waiting my whole life to play. It does not borrow the look of old China and paste martial arts on top. It builds a Jianghu you can walk through, and then lets a story of family, honor, and a breaking empire grow inside it.

You begin as an orphan raised in Qinghe by Aunt Han and Uncle Jiang, a wine-maker’s household that is also a school of the sword. The opening already tells you the stakes: a flight through bamboo, a child carried out of danger, a life that was never as ordinary as it looked. When that home comes apart, the road opens. You go looking for the people who raised you, and the search carries you out of villages and reed beds into Kaifeng, a city of lanterns, markets, and imperial intrigue sitting on poverty and conspiracy. The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era is the right century for this. The Tang has fallen, the Song has not yet settled the map, and power is a thing clans and courts tear at in the open and in the dark. History is not a lecture. It is the weather the story moves through.

What I loved most is that the tale keeps offering you a self to become. Chivalry is not a menu perk. You can be the wanderer who rights a wrong, or the one who takes what the road offers and lives with the stain. Side stories branch in ways that sting. A keepsake returned to a waiting wife does not guarantee mercy. A ghost that needs guiding home asks you to sit with someone else’s grief before the sword comes out. The main campaign has the sweep of a serial — palaces, haunted ground, mechanical wonders, masters who treat the air like a road — and the endings of its quieter tales are where it becomes personal. I finished chapters feeling I had chosen a kind of person, not just cleared a quest log.

The world earns that feeling. Qinghe is water, mist, and working villages. Kaifeng is density: shopfronts, alleys, theaters, people who sleep when the light goes and argue when it returns. Hundreds of them have trades, stations, and gossip. Patients need healing. Puppet shows play. Martial masters wait on ridgelines for a duel that is also a conversation. The Jianghu here is the old idea, not just a combat zone: a place outside the suffocation of court, where reputation answers to no emperor. Society is visible in who bows, who won’t, who is hungry under the grandeur.

And the color. This is the most painterly landscape I have moved through. Ink-wash mountains go violet at dusk. Bamboo is a hard, living green. Kaifeng golds and crimsons pool under lantern light. Rivers take the sky. Nothing is the desaturated “ancient” filter so many games use as shorthand. It looks like a scroll that remembered it was also a place: wet stone, dyed silk, kiln smoke, festival red against grey water. The accuracy of the land and the people sits under that beauty. Architecture, dress, faith, craft, and the political fracture of the tenth century are treated as craft problems, not costume. You do not need a dynasty chart to feel it. You feel it in who holds a street and who is hiding under it.

The fights are the sieges of this world. Movement is the fantasy: walls, rooftops, bamboo, the brief lie that a body can fly. Duels are operatic without turning into noise, and the larger clashes — cities under strain, set pieces that collapse around you — land because the quiet hours taught you what a reputation costs. Side quests kept me longer than the critical path. Some are short. The good ones are full stories, better written than plenty of main campaigns, and they are how the map becomes a society instead of a backdrop.

I have played a lot of open worlds that gesture at history. Where Winds Meet is the one that made the Jianghu feel inhabited. The story stayed with me. The colors stopped me on ridgelines. The side roads were the point. It belongs with the games I will go back to for years.

Breathtaking introduction, but slowly but surely it fades into annoyances.

Visually, it's fantastic. Great artstyle and a beautiful world. Not a single complaint here.

BUT, the issues, which there are TONS of... Slowly but surely the're revealed, and not everything is obvious either, far from it.

The menues... You've probaly already heard it, but this is not just bad, it's INSANELY TERRIBLE. Most progress is buried deep into menues that sometimes is EXTREMELY hard to find. There are constantly some milesones you reach which gives you some rewards. The thing is, you must find WHERE these milestones are hidden in the menues and claim rewards from there. There ARE small red dots on most menues hinting about something there, but then you have to go through submenu after submenu to find it.

For character progression, it's not better, far from it. Also here, there are soooo many systems it's retarded. Gear isn't a problem until at least lvl 65-70. Every time you reach certain leveling "tiers" (lvl 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, etc) you need to do certain fights in a seperate solo arena to unlock the next tier, else you won't level anymore. When capped, exp from anything you do is pooled, and you'll get it after unlocking next tier. At first, the fights are quick and easy to do, but after a while, you'll need to go through 2 sets of fight, typically 3 waves of mobs + a boss per set. It's annoying as hell, since this is absolutely NOT optional at all. The only positive here, is that you're given gear that will be enough till you reach next tier (not at the highest levels).

And about character progression... There are several systems to upgrade gear and slots you have gear in, but that's not all, far from it. There are the typical skill points, but you MUST also do sh!tloads of "optional" stuff in the world, since that increases stats like agility, intelligence, and more. Which again unlocks increases in attacks, defence, etc. Skipping this is NOT optional because you won't be able to even wear certain gear unless you increase these stats. Also, you'll become quite weak at higher levels.

I'm not gonna go into details, but at lvl 41, a new system unlocks (tuning, basically merging weapons to improve them), and a little later, there's the arsenal, a "storage" you put gear you don't use, and their combined item levels now increases damage and hp.

And believe me, it does NOT end there. For example, for some upgrades you need stuff  you have do buy, and there are limits to how many you can buy per week... Ridiculous.

Minigames... To me, these are annoying as hell. Example: you have this one game where you have to keep your mouse pointer within a moving circle, then at the same time use the keyboard to keep an icon within another. Skip these, and you won't increase that stat enough. Then there are these RETARDED multiplayer mini-games. For some, just enter a circle, press F to participate, and a counter starts. You can now just leave the PC, go make a snack or something, and it's done when you come back. The positive is that these ARE optional, but since they're a great source for jade fish (a useful currency), it's not a good idea to ignore them.

There are several more issues I have with this game, but I think it's enough for now.

Bottom line, this could have been a MASTERPIECE, but they over-complexed it and added bullsh!t the game would be FAR better without. I'll keep on playing a little more to see if I change my mind as I progress more (I'm lvl 74, I think), but I fear this will disapper from my PC completely in the near future.

[h1]Not Recommended.[/h1]

[h1]They are wasting an incredible game.[/h1]

Where Winds Meet has an incredible foundation. The combat is great, the world is beautiful, the wuxia setting is fantastic, and there is a ridiculous amount of variety.

[b]And that my friends, Is exactly why it's so frustrating.[/b]

The problem isn't a lack of content. It's that too much of the content feels restricted, unrewarding, repetitive, or disconnected from the actual gameplay loop.

[h2]1: The multiplayer is almost pointless[/h2]

For a game with such a strong MMO identity, an absurd amount of content is [b]solo-only[/b]. Story content, quests, encounters, and even some new boss first encounters can force you to play alone.

I'm not asking for mandatory co-op. [b]Just give players the choice man![/b]

If someone wants to experience difficult content with friends, let them!

[h2]2: The game has content, but very little feels meaningful[/h2]

World bosses, campaign bosses, events and many other activities often don't provide rewards that feel worth the effort.

You defeat a difficult boss and think:

[i]"Okay... what did I actually get for doing that? Just 50k gold and 400 insight points? (useless)"[/i]

[h2]3: The endgame is "spend your energy and leave"[/h2]

Progression is heavily time-gated.

Eventually the gameplay loop becomes:

[b]Log in → spend energy → collect rewards → log out.[/b]

If you actually want to keep playing, the game gives you surprisingly few meaningful ways to do so.

This also creates a terrible experience for new players. Veterans are already at the progression ceiling while new players have to slowly crawl through old progression gates.

Then they reach multiplayer activities and discover that [b]everyone else is already at the current max level.[/b]

Sword Trial, Hero's Realm and similar activities become extremely difficult to find players for if you're behind the current progression.

[h2]4: The gacha and gear RNG are brutal[/h2]

The gear system already has layers of RNG.

Then you add the gacha.

The result is an extremely [b]unforgiving[/b] progression system where RNG can stack on top of RNG.

You can spend huge amounts of resources trying to build around a specific setup and still be nowhere near the build you actually want.

[b]Grinding should eventually guarantee progress. It shouldn't just give you more chances to get lucky.[/b]

[h2]5: PvP has a serious ping problem[/h2]

This game is extremely sensitive to latency.

Small differences in ping can have a huge effect on reactions, parries and combat consistency.

It's gotten to the point where players are paying for [b]cloud gaming services specifically to get better routing and lower latency[/b] for competitive play.

You shouldn't need to pay another company every month just to remove a regional disadvantage.

Ping also affects PvE combat and general responsiveness.

[h2]6: Dead regions + fragmented matchmaking[/h2]

Some regions simply feel dead.

You can enter multiplayer activities or events and barely find anyone.

[b]You can't heavily restrict multiplayer, fragment the playerbase, and expect the MMO side of the game to thrive.[/b]

The game needs better matchmaking, better cross-region solutions where latency allows it, and ways to keep new and veteran players connected.

[h2]7: World Chat is basically dead too[/h2]

The social side of the game is getting worse.

World Chat has become almost completely [b]soulless[/b]. Instead of actual conversations, it's constantly flooded with [b]image spam and other low-effort guild invite spam[/b].

Reporting doesn't solve the problem when spammers can simply create an alt account and do the exact same thing again.

This needs to be handled at the chat-system level.

[b]Give images and other spam their own dedicated channel, or heavily restrict what can be posted in World Chat.[/b]

World Chat should be a place where players actually talk, find groups and build a community. Not something you intentionally avoid.

[h2]8: New content isn't fixing the problem[/h2]

I appreciate that the developers keep releasing updates.

But another event, another few quests, another boss and another currency don't automatically make the game more engaging.

The game needs [b]repeatable, meaningful content[/b] that gives players a reason to keep playing after they've consumed the latest update.

Right now, too much content feels like something to consume rather than something to engage with.

[h2]9: And the technical side...[/h2]

Performance can suffer, especially with newer regions and content.

And the game's storage requirements are getting ridiculous.

Steam lists [b]130 GB minimum and 200 GB recommended[/b].

For a game that is supposed to keep expanding, better asset management, compression and optional content packages are desperately needed.

[h1]And you know what hurts? I actually like this game.[/h1]

If it were simply bad, I wouldn't care enough to write this.

The combat is good.

The world is good.

The setting is good.

[b]The foundation is there.[/b]

But the progression is too restricted, multiplayer is too limited, rewards are too meaningless, RNG is too punishing, the gacha is too unforgiving, latency matters too much, new players struggle to catch up, the social side is deteriorating, and the endgame becomes repetitive extremely quickly.

[b]The game doesn't need more systems.
It needs the systems it already has to actually matter.[/b]

Give us meaningful rewards.
Give us meaningful multiplayer.
Give us proper catch-up mechanics.
Give us more deterministic progression.
Fix the regional and latency problems.
Clean up World Chat.
Stop forcing so much content into solo play.

And most importantly:

[b]Give players a reason to keep playing because they WANT to play, not because they still have 600 energy to spend.[/b]

Where Winds Meet has an incredible foundation.

[b]They're just wasting it.[/b]

You can fight directly, use techniques, disguise yourself, listen for movement, or decide that the valuable item is not worth staying for. I lost time to screenshots and failed jumps, and none of it felt wasted.

tldr: this game is designed to tickle your joy receptors at every opportunity and to get you hooked. the graphics are beautiful, the combat can be entertaining, enemies might pose a challenge, which feels rewarding to overcome. some npc are memorable and fit well into the alright story.

so, on the surface, at first glance, it should be a good game, no?

at its core the game relies on three key selling points: the sensory experience with its graphics and sound design, its fast paced and captivating content unlocked through its action based combat systems, and the social satisfaction via prestige, leaderboards and events.

as context for the following, i do think that in a RPG, you want to immerse yourself in a different world, you want your character to grow - in capability or style - and to grow with them; to git gud, to understand the lore of the world. in a MMO, you want to be part of a cherished group.

starting with the story, i think it is coherent and plausible, somewhat engaging but it felt slightly rushed from the beginning. i have no strong feelings about it; some characters are memorable, mysteries are intriguing and the world is interesting. your character is the faceless canvas to project yourself into the world; a no-name brat that is destined to be the hero. the character lacks any real peronsality, as not to conflict with the intentions of the player, and you as a player have no agency over what is happening at all.

the central part of the gameplay loop - combat - got surprisingly boring, surprisingly quick; you only need to be fast enough to press your buttons and, after some trial and error, know the timing of individual enemies. beyond that, its the same over and over: the enemy attacks, you defend and counterattack once the opportunity arises.
every trash mob has two types of attacks - bland ones, and ones that can be punished harder with a counter. boss enemies get a third variant that can not be parried but only evaded. every trash mob can be parried/countered, every boss has moves that must be dodged. thus, if you focus on one or the other way of defense, you can do your thing with every opponent. the timings differ, the animations are different, but at its base, its without fault always the same layout that does not favor any build, weapon or adaptation at all.

as for your tools? you get to equip two weapons that have five moves in total, that should be complementing each other if it were a better game. to get into more detail: there's one spammable basic attack, there's an equally spammable 'heavy' attack that is effectively as hard hitting and fast as the basic attack and there is one move to switch your weapons while performing a pretty basic attack. the remaining two moves have cooldowns and are usually quite flashy and - in comparison to the three other moves - more potent. sadly, they usually do two flavors of the same thing; the fan, for example adds a heal over time paired with a healing over time zone. dual blades come with an ability for movement paired with damage, and a move for damage only. the single sword provides an additional ability for damage, paired with a move that deals damages and moves the character. with so few abilities, they should be much more focused on filling different needs, really.
there is no way to individually swap these abilities, there's only a handful of weapons that have either one or two styles of moves. additional, passive choices can add a chance for bleed or poison effects, or give the opportunity for a generic hit after certain attacks, or various other small boosts or generic effects. there is fundamentally no way to customize or expand your fighting style and unlocking these individual tools can be done easily in half an hour or less for each of them, once you decide on what to get and have access to the general zone.
movement around the world is, while appearing varied at first, also disappointing; walking and running works well and as intended, swimming always drains your stamina until you drown - or stay still for long periods to replenish your energy. once flying is unlocked, you are spending more time in the wind-up animation than with the traveling itself and riding the horse is janky, not much faster than on foot and much slower than flying. as many variants of traversal as would fit in the setting and genre, but riding, swimming and flying is done quite poorly, while basic walking and running would have been really hard to mess up.

what about the customization in terms of style, cosmetics? some pretty, but comparatively simple unlocks are gifted to you early on, with all the many other things. some other hairstyles or clothings can be unlocked in the course of the game. but most is locked behind the cash shop and/or loot boxes.
an example for all the weapon designs: there's exactly one default design that is applied to every weapon of that type (spear, sword, etc) and one other design that can be gained by playing: with loot boxes, contained in certain boss loot, that may individually be aquired every 160 minutes or more. then there's one or two weapon skins that can be bought directly with money at prizes that will get you entire other games. but the vast majority of the skins is locked behind layers of lootboxes, various chained in-game currencies to fuel the lootboxes and rng-pity-mechanics if your 200th roll went bad again. i can only guess at how many hundreds of moneys one has to throw at the game to get one desired skin.

there's tons and tons of game systems, spread around many, many more menus; there's more different game systems than i have ever seen in a single other game, and every one that i have engaged with has pretty graphics, but is mechanicly shallow. while there might be quite a lot more, i have already tested: homesteading/basebuilding with farming and industry options, the gathering of collectables or crafting materials, crafting, fishing, pet companions, mounts and puzzles, healing with a card game as well as debating with a card game, maybe more. none of them were engaging or revolutinary in any way and some were clearly designed to form player habits with timers, daily rewards and similar ways of repeated engagement.

in summary: at the beginning of the game, there's quite a number of ways to chose your style and to pick some minor specializations, while you are being showered with rewards, free stuff and satisfying sounds and animations. the game does have a very, very satisfying starting experience, if dopamine fueled highs are your goal. but once i saw the progression that followed, i was quite disenchanted: no new mechanics and only incremental, grinding stat changes for each and every single equipment slot and abilty in a system that sells this as ' character progression'. and as soon as your rewards from the gift boxes run out, you realize that spending 10k of a currency for a +1 for a single equipment slot is a steep prize, when an enemy drops like 30 coins of that type. from my experience, the grind i experienced in the early game is factors of magnitude less time consuming than the typical end game grind; because if you still play at that point, you are very much invested enough in the game, that paying a hundred moneys for that booster might just seem a wise investment, compared to hundreds of hours of your life...

i don't mind playing a game that hits me with satisfying sounds and flashy animations with the intention of releasing happy-chemicals in my body. but i do mind if the game that delivers that to me is a cluster of shallow systems designed to form addictions, a piece of software that has gambling at its core with a dizzying amount of lootboxes and menu layers to distort any orientation or feeling for monetary value spent. this is a game that aims to reward whales with social validation by awarding boons to those players that show up and admire the whales.

a sad product, all in all. the social messaging could not be clearer.

The map marker said the objective was close. The missing information was that it was two levels above me and separated by a broken rail. I found the route after entering a tunnel that looked completely unrelated. This city enjoys technicalities.

The first full view of the broken city stopped me cold. Half the buildings are hanging over open air, the lower streets disappear into cloud, and every moving platform makes the whole place feel slightly unsafe. I went there to continue the story and spent twenty minutes trying to reach a balcony that probably had nothing important on it. The route involved one wall run, a moving slab, and a jump I absolutely did not measure correctly. I missed twice. On the third attempt I landed, turned around, and finally understood how high the city actually was.

Hidden Mountain already taught me to look above and below the marker, but Skyward City takes that habit much further. A route that looks close on the map can be two collapsed levels away, while a distant bridge may connect through a lift hidden under your feet. I spent an evening building a mental map around one waterfall, a damaged rail, and a tower with a missing wall. By the end I could lead a friend through it without opening the map. I still took one wrong turn and dropped us into a workshop full of enemies. I called it the scenic route and kept moving.

The best sign that the final chapter landed is that our group did not leave voice chat after the credits. We stayed there going through earlier scenes, comparing what each of us thought one character wanted, and trying to decide whether the last answer was actually an answer. The boss fights gave the chapter a strong finish, but the conversation afterward is what stuck with me. I still disagree with my friend's interpretation of Elder Peng. He also thinks my build is terrible, so his judgment is already questionable.

I played most of Skyward City alone, and the quieter pace helped the space make sense. I could stop at every broken intersection, listen for machinery, and test a route without someone waiting at the next objective. The parkour is dramatic, but the best moment for me was finding a small workshop below the main path and realizing its lift connected to a tower I had visited an hour earlier. One chase through the collapsing upper city made me grip the controller harder than any boss in the update. The route keeps moving forward while platforms shift, fire cuts off the comfortable landing, and the next ledge appears slightly later than my nerves would prefer. I failed near the end twice because I rushed the same jump. On the successful run, I waited half a second longer, caught the platform at the edge, and finished the sequence with almost no health left. Parkour should not have a clutch moment. Apparently it does now.

The floating swords in the Elder Peng fight are rude in a very specific way. They do not just add more damage to avoid; they quietly remove the spot where you planned to recover. I kept retreating to the same side, and the magnetic mechanism punished that habit three attempts in a row. Once I started reading the whole arena instead of only the boss, the fight clicked. I still got clipped by a sword during the clear because I celebrated a deflect too early. The replay looks heroic until that exact second, so naturally that is the clip my friends saved.

Poor optimization, translation, and an increasingly confusing UI alongside AI chatbot NPCs and camera/screenshot "tools" makes for a frustrating experience. The graphics are pretty, the combat is fine, and the story seems interesting, but I will not be continuing my playthrough.

Golden Colossus Taicu looked like part of the landscape until it moved. Then the camera tilted up, kept tilting, and I realized the thing in front of me was the boss. Fighting at its feet changes the whole sense of scale. A normal dodge is no longer about slipping past a weapon; it is about getting out from under a step that covers half the screen. Our group spent the first run calling out mechanics and the second run arguing about whether anyone had managed to see its face. I had not. I have excellent screenshots of one enormous ankle.

A moving platform carried me past the safe ledge because I jumped early. I blamed the camera, tried again, and made the exact same mistake. Third attempt was clean. The landing felt better than the chest waiting there.

There is a lot happening in the new boss fights, but the important attacks still have tells. Elder Peng's wings shift before the arena changes, Halcyon's mechanical arm carries a different weight from her sword, and the giant announces a step with the shadow before impact. I lost plenty, but I rarely felt that the answer was hidden behind effects. Most failures were mine: staring at the wrong threat, moving too early, or squeezing in one greedy attack. That is exactly why I kept retrying. The game gave me enough information to know what I had done wrong.

Photo mode is a serious threat to progress in this city. The broken bridges create ridiculous silhouettes, the clouds move through the lower structures, and every burst of fire makes the metal surfaces look different. I climbed one tower because I thought it would give me a clean view of the main route. It did, but the better discovery was a tiny ledge on the opposite side where the whole city lined up behind my character. Reaching it took four failed jumps and one accidental fall into a lower district. I got the picture. The quest can wait.

I tried to create space against Halcyon and learned that the chain exists specifically to reject that idea. She pulls you back into range, follows with the mechanical arm, then changes pace for the sword sequence. The fight is aggressive without becoming visual noise because the important motions are readable once you stop panicking. My first attempt ended with me rolling in three different directions and choosing the only unsafe one. By the sixth, I could hear the rhythm of the combo before it finished. Where Winds Meet has genuinely surprised me with how much there is to do and how easy it is to get lost in the world. The open-world setting is beautiful, with some fantastic scenery, detailed environments, and moments where I’ve found myself stopping just to look around instead of rushing to the next objective.

One of my favorite parts is the freedom to switch between solo open-world play and co-op/online play. I can explore at my own pace when I want a more immersive RPG experience, then jump online when I feel like playing with other people. That flexibility makes the game feel much less restrictive than a lot of other online RPGs.

There’s also an impressive amount of variety. You’re not just running from fight to fight. There are side stories, exploration, puzzles, martial arts, different weapons and builds, NPC relationships, professions, healing, collecting, housing, mini-games, hidden areas, and all kinds of strange little encounters scattered around the world. I’m still discovering systems I didn’t even realize were there.

Combat has been fun too, especially once you start experimenting with different Martial Arts and Mystic Skills. The ability to switch styles and build a character around the way you actually enjoy playing gives the game a lot of room to grow.

It can definitely throw a lot of systems at you early on, and some mechanics aren’t explained as clearly as they could be, so there are moments where you may find yourself wondering what you’re supposed to do. But once things start clicking, the sheer amount of freedom becomes one of the game’s biggest strengths.

Overall, Where Winds Meet feels like a world meant to be explored rather than simply completed. I can spend one session progressing the story, another wandering around finding secrets, and another doing side activities or playing online. Between the gorgeous world, martial-arts atmosphere, open-ended exploration, and the ability to move between solo and co-op play, I’ve been having a great time with it.

Definitely recommended if you enjoy open-world RPGs where wandering off the main road is half the fun.

This is the hardest review I’ve ever had to write. The game is absolutely gorgeous, the graphics are spectacular, and the only things you can pay for are cosmetics—some of which you can even earn for free through the game’s own mechanics. Now comes the complicated part. In this Wuxia world you can do almost everything, to the point where I think the player base ends up spreading out into whatever interests them, and after a while they lose appreciation for the game itself.

My biggest recommendation: create only one character. Making two or more will drain an immense amount of time and attention. It will consume all your patience, and you’ll end up exhausted and eventually abandoning the game. You have many martial arts to explore, so try to find the one you enjoy the most and stick with it. Otherwise, you’ll spend a lot of time farming resources just to experiment with other techniques.

The core of the game—the story—is extremely good. The bosses are souls‑like, and you can raise or lower the difficulty whenever you want depending on how you prefer to play. As for the story, it’s very much in “GOT mode,” meaning: don’t get too attached to the secondary characters. A lot happens in this game. Recently, you can also do housing, farming, or jump into multiplayer events.

The big problem with the game is this: as beautiful as it is, and as strong as its narrative arc can be, some parts of the story can last an hour or more of just watching cinematics or choosing dialogue options. This can be very boring. It becomes a graphic novel—some parts are excellent, and others might make you want to uninstall the game.

There are many reasons to love this game and very few to hate it. It’s FREE. Find your own way to play, invite friends, create your guild, explore, hunt bosses, go to PvP, or simply have patience and appreciate the masterpiece that is the main story and some of the side stories in this world.

This game is sooooo weird. 

TL;DR: It could have been great if they fixed a few things and fleshed out the NPCs. Instead they chose to slap on Gen AI like it's flex tape.

Graphically there's not much to say, the gameplay videos are pretty much wysiwyg. The game is pretty, but you'll need a beastly machine to have all that run smoothly.

Combat is being lauded as unique with all those martial arts but if you look past the animations and fluff it's your run of the mill ARPG. Granted, it's definitely on the side of more complex with a huge number of options to choose from almost from the start. Movement is somewhat in the vein of Assassin's Creed, with less acrobatics and more flying, pretty fun stuff but can get annoying in tight spaces.

The UI is serviceable, though the myriad of menus is a complete chaos and for a beginner finding specific options is a time-consuming, frustrating chore.

Now, in terms of multiplayer aspect there are two modes - one alone with ability to invite friends and the other is a rando-palooza. Needless to say, I played SP only, but there are still some odd interactions with other players coming through. Firstly, you can leave twitter-esque messages pinned to the ground wherever you want in the form of "signposts", these can be absolutely anything, from straight up asking for likes (yeah, there are thumbs up buttons on them, ikr, smh), to sort of "memories" of players with a ghost-like remnant doing an emote, to actual useful hints about nearby chests, secrets, dangers or even what to expect from an NPC. I'm a bit torn on that one because, although often helpful, they definitely break immersion and they also take away from the fun of exploration. Sure, you can technically ignore them but it's really hard to resist the temptation of saving yourself a lot of time combing through the area for loot and stuff.

Finally, my biggest gripe is with the LLM chat (aka GenAI) that is added everywhere, and I do mean added, because it feels like feature that's been clumsily tacked on, instead being woven into the mechanics (which I would hate anyway but for different reasons), while being completely unnecessary. It's as if the devs were forced to put it in, who knows, maybe they couldn't finish the game in time and figured this will patch the holes somehow. It does not. For example, there is a huge number of NPCs in the game, most with spoken dialogue and at least a little bit of backstory and some are genuinely interesting characters. The problem is that, aside of the ones involved in the main quest, almost all the others will have only one topic to talk about, usually with no branching and the option to switch to talking to AI which is supposed to take the role of the NPC. And it sucks at it, you're clearly just talking to the same AI engine that just had like a one line prompt as a seed while having no other information about the character nor the background and the world around them. You sometimes have to tell them about events mentioned in their own scripted dialogue! All they had to do is add a few more dialogue options for the quest givers, the AI chat is text only anyway so they needn't have had to even record any additional voices. This just feels sloppy and makes some side-quests hard or even impossible to complete.

If you enjoy playing against hacks, nonstop lag in Arena, and constant stagger-locks where you can barely control your character, then this is the game for you.

Where Winds Meet has a lot of potential, but its PvP is being ruined by some major issues. The stagger system is probably the worst offender. Certain weapon combinations can keep you in almost continuous stagger, leaving you pressing buttons while your character just stands there getting beaten. The developers are aware of the complaints about stagger, yet there has been little meaningful improvement.

Arena also suffers from frequent lag, which makes an already frustrating PvP system even worse. GvG has become Nameless Sword R-spam central—stack enough Nameless Sword players and suddenly you have a top GvG strategy. It gets repetitive very quickly.

Outside of PvP, I personally don't find enough content compelling enough to make up for these problems, and unfortunately PvP—the part that could keep me playing—is in a bad state.

I've submitted my concerns to the developers, but I haven't seen meaningful acknowledgment or changes. From what I've observed, more and more players are becoming frustrated with the lag, stagger mechanics, and overall PvP balance.

This game genuinely has huge potential, which is what makes this so disappointing. Instead of addressing issues affecting the broader PvP experience, it feels like balance decisions are being made around a small portion of the player base.

Fix the lag. Fix the stagger/combo-lock system. Bring actual variety and counterplay back to PvP. There is a great game underneath these problems, but right now that potential feels wasted.

Still, some progression especially with the gear will become highly competitive since the game soft locks you. Better to just do 10 of them every week for the guild, win or lose, it would still count towards the progress. Relaying gears is always available, but the stats you gain are 5-10% less than the maximum stats of the gear you relay them to, its good enough but also not the best, depends on how you look at it.

[u][h2] In a nutshell / tl;dr [/h2][/u]
I wouldn't be mad if this game was 60$ or more, but it's free. No significant issues so far, and I keep getting positively surprised constantly by all aspects of the game. It can be overwhelming at first, but following the story and taking things one step at a time eases you in nicely. The installation size is big, yes, but so is the game, and I'm sure people can manage if a very big (free) game takes 10% of their SSD's space. The only obvious negative thing so far seems to be the ridiculous maze of menus, but that is something you can mostly ignore at first, and personally it took me 3-5 days until I got really comfortable with the navigation; not 1000 hours, like some demented people here say.
[h3] Graphics, art style and world fidelity [/h3]
The game is absolutely beautiful to the point where I sometimes just spend time looking at the scenery and forget what I was doing. This is one of the few games EVER where I keep taking screenshots. 
The art style is consistent and well done. All the places that I've been feel well thought out and carefully crafted. One minus is that the game has a low distance for some LOD's, but so far that has bothered me in only one specific area, and even then it's bearable. 
[h3] Monetization [/h3]
It's hard to believe that a game of this quality and size is free and without pay to win, but I was very pleased to find out this is the case here. There's nothing you need to buy with real money and you don't even feel like you're missing out on anything if you don't pay. None of that feeling. There really isn't even any pressure to buy anything. It's cosmetics only. It feels like a gaming utopia, where you get a wonderful, beautiful game FOR FREE, and then you support it if you want, as you go, as much as you want. Perfect! Or... almost perfect, because there is of course the gambling element that seems to be the norm these days. Like I said, it's not needed, it's not pushed too much imo, but it is there and those who have 0 tolerance of it... well actually you can still enjoy the game, just don't support it financially.
[h3] AI [/h3]
I think the AI NPC's in the game are really well done. This is what I was thinking about many years ago, when I thought it would be cool to have a game where some NPC's would be AI's. Of course it's not perfect, but in my opinion it brings more to the game than it takes from it. It's also not a major part of the game in any way. And the in-game helper AI is very limited in ability, but can sometimes be useful and I'm glad it's there.
[h3] Privacy [/h3]
I went through their privacy policy and ToS (used AI to help summarize and point out key spots) and nothing seemed alarming. Game seems quite transparent and honest (more so than most "western" games) about their usage of data, though who knows. Leave a comment if you've found anything suspicious. 
[h3] Combat [/h3]
It's satisfying to the point where I've had fun playing over 100 hours with just one weapon combo. The mechanics are easy to grasp at first, but difficult to master, and that's just the way it should be. There's a fitting challenge for all levels of players, solo or coop. I haven't had much experience with PvP yet, but some say it's too laggy to be enjoyable, some say it's fine. Can't comment on that yet.
[h3] Story [/h3]
The story isn't anything revolutionary, but it's very good and enough to keep you constantly wanting to know more. The characters are nice and there's a lovely balance of humor and seriousness. Also, there's huge amounts of side missions, encounters, background stories, etc. The world truly feels alive and real.
[h3] Exploration and the world [/h3]
It's great. Sometimes feels like a bit too much stuff to do at the same time, but that's also because I sometimes run around like a crazy person and stumble into a dozen encounters without doing any of them :)
Every area, nook and cranny of the world seems interesting and full of surprises. Is there a treasure behind the waterfall? You bet! Also, the world is freaking huge AND detailed. NPC's feel more alive than in most other games.
[h3] Coop/multiplayer [/h3]
Haven't had a lot of experience with multiplayer elements, but all the things I've tried so far have been great, and all the things I've seen but haven't tried yet, seem exciting. The most impressive part to me and what I like personally is that you never feel alone. There's constantly things to do with other players, from just chatting, to healing others, to bounties, events, guild stuff, a million minigames, etc., but it doesn't distract you from the singleplayer part at all, it complements it.
[h3] Menu's/UI [/h3]
UI is great and you have options to have it full on, more minimal or completely off. Love it. However, the amount of menu's is absolutely ridiculous and so is some of the ways you navigate between some of them. I was searching for one specific menu for over an hour, until I got the answer from another player. BUT... after two days I got over the neurotic need to constantly click every menu and gather every reward. I realised that it wasn't necessary at all, and that I could just enjoy the game. After 3 to 5 days I was totally comfortable with the menu's and actually started to like all the different aspects of it. Not saying that it's ok for the menu's to be that challenging, but I am saying, that the most negative part is only in the beginning, and it then gets easier to the point where it isn't a problem anymore. At least that's my experience. 
[h3] End Game content [/h3]
Haven't had enough experience with end game content yet, so can't say. Maybe I'll update the review later.

I now have almost 1,500 hours of playtime, and this is probably one of the first truly negative Steam reviews I have ever written.

If you want to pick flowers, explore the world, and casually follow an AI-generated story, then go ahead and play the game.

However, if you want to do boss runs or take on genuinely difficult challenges, stay away from it.

Almost every boss is bugged, and it feels as though every animation or cutscene has the potential to interfere with the fight. The game features a challenge mode with hitless runs, which was originally the part that interested me the most.

However, you are not simply fighting the boss and learning its attack patterns. You are fighting against developers who apparently do not play or properly test their own game.

You are given unfinished bosses whose actual attacks sometimes do not match the animations being shown. Some attacks are so inconsistent and off-rhythm that it can take ten hours or more to memorize them. Not because the mechanics are particularly challenging, but because the timing, animations, and actual hit detection do not reliably match.

Once you have finally memorized every pattern, every delayed rhythm, and even every misleading animation, you still have to deal with input registration issues. The game sometimes fails to recognize that you dodged or parried an attack. During phase transitions, the fight can also freeze and prevent you from entering the second phase altogether.

The worst part is that some of these bosses have already been in the game for more than a year. Despite that, their existing issues are rarely—if ever—fixed retroactively.

The gear system is also a complete disaster. Yes, the game is not directly pay-to-win. Instead, your progress is artificially restricted by an energy system. You are only allowed to improve your equipment at the pace dictated by the game. Once you have spent your energy, it feels as though you are being starved of resources, because you may only make around two percent progress on your gear in an entire day.

At the moment, completing a single gear set takes approximately two to three weeks. I have now reached the point where I am gearing my third class. This means it takes around six to nine weeks just to build three complete sets.

And what happens after six to eight weeks? The level cap increases, and you need an entirely new gear set. Your previous set may not even be finished before you are forced to start all over again. Proper min-maxing is nearly impossible because the game constantly starves you of materials.

Class balancing also only happens roughly once every two months—if it happens at all. At the same time, there is a class called “Nameless,” which is clearly the developers’ favorite child. This class attacks safely from range, mainly uses charged attacks, and still consistently achieves the highest damage. Almost no risk, very little mechanical skill required, yet always the highest DPS.

As I said before: if you simply want to play casually, collect flowers, and explore the world, you may have a good time.

However, if you expect a fair challenge, technically polished boss fights, and reliable mechanics, stay away from this game. You are better off investing your time in a more polished game made by developers with enough experience to properly test their own content.

I will not say much about the gacha system. If someone wants to spend €300–€500 on a legendary skin with generic animations that ultimately does little more than glow slightly brighter, they are free to do so.

That is for everyone to decide for themselves.

Aside from the awkwardness of quickly navigating menus with a controller, I have nothing to complain about regarding the gameplay.
However, if you’re a free-to-play player who likes gacha, I wouldn’t recommend this game because its gacha system sucks. In 2020, Chinese developers invented the so-called “losing the 50/50,” and in this game it has evolved into “losing 50/50 at 90% five times” before you are guaranteed to get the banner item.
(Don’t get me wrong—you can still get it after losing twice by exchanging two Legendary items you receive from losing. The game doesn’t want to drive you away; it just wants to find a different way to humiliate you. A loser is still a loser.)
There’s a Chinese saying, 不過三, meaning that bad luck doesn’t happen more than three times. Clearly, this game has failed to promote Chinese culture because of the publisher’s greed. Why not just get rid of the safety shorts altogether? The game would attract more players that way—after all, profit comes first.
That said, the wuxia style is beautiful and the game is free. Outfits don’t give stats, but without them you look like an NPC in someone else’s game. Even with free outfits, you still look like a homeless guy.
Even if you fully clear the map, the currency you earn cannot buy pulls: 3 pulls per week and 2–4 per event. You need 150 pulls for one failed 50/50 (maybe sooner but they won't add the 20% bad luck point if you get it before 131)—that’s about $340 if you have money to spare.
In short, after all those hours, I only had enough resources to lose three times, and there will not be a fourth (I’m a battle pass player). Somehow, this game makes me feel like a clueless tourist getting ripped off by the locals.

i massively underestimated this game. its great. as if Nio, dark souls, an actual MMORPG and a story-focused RPG had a child. 

pro: 
- its not pay to win and F2P. only real money things you can buy are cosmetics and the ones that are in the game are already pretty decent. you can also get all of them in theory as a F2P just much worse odds obviously. 
- it is incredibly gorgeous. visually its an artform. the wind-effects, the weather effects, the general quality for something you can play as an actual MMORPG, the biomes, the lighting, etc. ; some of the clothes you can get are also reallllly good. 
- the biomes/areas/general map. very good use of verticality. you have some grass-planes which are flat and also beautiful but generally this game has beautiful landmarks to orient by, dungeons and other things have layers upon layers of verticality, and very often things loop back or are visually hinted at the same way you would expect it from good old dark souls. everyting is detailed and filled with life, quests, things to do, things to collect, things to kill. i often scale games by a pseudo-score of how many times they satisfied me when looking behind a waterfall and expecting loot. this game KILLS that score lol. love it. everything feels handcrafted, no generic giant empty world. 
- the dialogues are actually good and quite funny, quests very original and bringing a "fresh wind" pun not intended. i was ready to spam skip and just go collect and kill lik in moost games of this type, but quickly found out they have incredible charm and it would be an insult to skip them. i could tease so many things that would convince you to play it, but they would all spoil the first-time experience. 
- combat is actually very good and satisfying. general game loop is also great. you explore, kill, farm, craft, build, enjoy the scenery, nothing feels wasted, everything gets rewarded with smth you need for smth else. its great. i recommend to enjoy the game in solo mode till you finished campaign, its worth it to go at your own pace and slowly discover/learn everything yourself. also will make you a more skilled fighter later on. 
- so much random stuff you would have never expected from a game like this. i had to laugh out loud multiple times and was flabbergasted even when smth unexpected happened. last time (spoiler) i red a message (people can leave them, they help you a bit) that i missed smth under the elevator. everyone commented how crazy it was and how many chests they missed (rediculous amounts) and that they struggled to get through that incredible content etc. - i thought "fool me once..." like it was one of those "try jump" messages from darksouls xd. was curious though as that part of the dungeon really was kinda bland (still good enough) and went back to check the chest under the elevator. it was there. and i fell through the ground. under there was fucking anor londo from dark souls ahahaha im not kidding. i was underleveled too, im not even in that zone yet, just wanted to explore a bit. god it was HARD. and took so LONG. but it was awesome. had many restrictions too, one i never had before that made it so much harder. dont wanna spoil it more than that. the satisfaction when i came back out and commented on that  note lol. it was like a 2h content adventure that you would EASILY miss if you dont check under the elevator. incredible. other games could never. 
- events give good rewards, it doesent feel dead or unsuported. 
- skills, weapon sets, monsters and bosses, etc. all feel varied and diverse. some are very original. 
- you can let your mastery score be translated into "goose". "0,812 goose" for example. let that be a warning lol. 
- they implemented AI as NPCs you have to convince and befriend lol. gets a bit tedious but its smth new. 

con:
it is not perfect. i have two main cons with the game. 
1. the god damn menues (UI) xd. menues in menues in menues, its menuesception. finding stuff is hard and you better get used to it over time and dont think to much of it when you start out. just chase the red dots lol. wish they would simplify/overwork these and give us a meta-collect-all-button. 
2. while the synchronization is really good, its a bit odd what is and what isnt synchronized. sometimes it just gives you text, sometimes really great professional voices, sometimes an AI-voice lol. 

conclusion: overall it is an incredible and immensely underrated game/ hidden gem IMO (should be much more popular(hyped). the couple flaws and imperfections it has are easily overshadowed by the massive wins this game has over and over and over. the mine gripe really are the UI/Menues. try it, it is F2P and i would even call it a worthwhile purchase if it was a AAA full price titel.

EDIT: 120 hours in. game is incredible! here some tipps to maximize fun/experience.

1. play solo mode (besides events etc.) in your own pace and enjoy it all, take it in, no one talking over, no one rushing, immerse yourself into the jianghu. 

2. swap between progressing main quest and exploration/outposts/side-quests. main quests are incredible IMO but they are very emotional/dialogue intensive, so some "Mindless" slaughter or collectable run inbetween is a very nice "taste-bud-clenser"-

3. ignore the fact the menues have menues which have menues xd. slowly get used to it. if you leftclick a resource the game tells you where to get it. VERY useful. it also has inbuild "guides" to advance your favourite martial arts/weapons (Which quests to undergo to get your stuff). 

4. pick up and kill everything you can find. it is ALL very useful. exploration also progresses the areas "mobility" for your character. aka how fast you can run, if you can fly through the sky, walk over water, etc. 

5. auto-upgrade is pretty convenient. prob not "optimal" but as a beginner i recommend using it. no need to break your head in the submenues of all the shops to buy the needed resources when you can one-button it.
